items.stem: For the standard optical setup, what is the magnification of the fluorescent band image?
items.explanation: Magnification for a thin lens is m = -di/do. With di = 24 cm and do = 12 cm, m = -24/12 = -2.0. The negative sign indicates inversion, and the magnitude indicates the image is twice the object size. Common miss: Using do/di instead of -di/do for magnification. This correctly calculates magnification from image and object distances. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.A: This has the wrong magnitude and sign.
distractorRationales.B: This has the correct sign for inversion but the wrong magnitude.
distractorRationales.D: This has the correct magnitude but misses the negative sign for a real inverted image.

passage.title: Electrophoretic Separation with Optical Readout
passage.body:
A fictional capillary electrophoresis device separates carboxylate-labeled peptides. The capillary contains buffer at pH 7.4. The fluorescent carboxylate label has pKa 4.5, so labeled peptides are predominantly negatively charged. The electric field magnitude is E = V/L, where V is the applied voltage and L is electrode spacing. A higher electric field generally increases migration distance over a fixed time, but excessive current can cause Joule heating and band broadening. The fluorescent band is imaged onto a camera using a thin converging lens. For the standard optical setup, the object distance is 12 cm and the image distance is 24 cm.

Electrophoresis conditions and separation results after 3.0 min.
Run | Applied voltage (V) | Electrode spacing (cm) | Current (mA) | Relative buffer strength | Migration distance of analyte X (cm) | Band width (mm)
A | 300 | 6.0 | 1.5 | 1x | 2.4 | 0.50
B | 600 | 6.0 | 3.0 | 1x | 4.8 | 0.80
C | 600 | 6.0 | 6.0 | 2x | 4.9 | 1.40
D | 300 | 3.0 | 3.0 | 1x | 4.7 | 0.85

Optical imaging of the fluorescent band. — A real image of the fluorescent band is formed on a camera sensor. The image is inverted relative to the object in the capillary and appears larger than the object under the standard setup.

passage.title: Regulation of a bacterial nucleotide-reduction operon
passage.body:
A fictional bacterial operon, nrdPQ, encodes proteins required for deoxyribonucleotide synthesis during low-oxygen growth. The operon contains a sigma-factor promoter, a 5' untranslated region with a metabolite M-sensitive attenuator, and a Shine-Dalgarno sequence upstream of the nrdP start codon. When metabolite M binds the nascent 5' untranslated region, a terminator hairpin forms before the coding sequence, reducing production of full-length mRNA. Researchers constructed mutations and measured full-length nrdP mRNA, NrdP protein, and NrdP enzyme activity.

Expression and activity of nrdP constructs.
Construct and condition | Full-length mRNA (%) | NrdP protein (%) | NrdP activity (%)
Wild type, no M | 100 | 100 | 100
Wild type, +M | 30 | 28 | 30
-10 promoter mutant, no M | 12 | 10 | 11
Terminator hairpin disrupted, +M | 95 | 92 | 90
Shine-Dalgarno mutant, no M | 105 | 15 | 14
Active-site Cys to Ser mutant, no M | 100 | 98 | 8

Model of metabolite M-dependent attenuation. — In the presence of metabolite M, the 5' untranslated region folds into a terminator hairpin that causes RNA polymerase to stop before transcribing the nrdP coding sequence. When M is absent or the hairpin is disrupted, RNA polymerase usually produces full-length mRNA.

items.stem: A peptide hormone binds a Gq-coupled receptor on a target cell. The most direct next membrane-associated event is:

choices.text: activation of adenylyl cyclase and a rise in cAMP
diffusion of the hormone through the bilayer into the nucleus without any receptor
opening of a nuclear pore so the intact hormone can bind chromatin as a free ligand
activation of phospholipase C, producing IP3 and DAG from PIP2

items.explanation: Gq activates phospholipase C-beta, which cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and DAG. IP3 releases ER Ca2+ stores and DAG activates protein kinase C. Adenylyl cyclase/cAMP is the Gs (or Gi) module, not Gq. Peptide hormones do not freely diffuse to chromatin; they remain extracellular ligands of membrane receptors. Nuclear pores do not import the peptide hormone as a transcription factor substitute.

distractorRationales.A: Adenylyl cyclase is downstream of Gs (stimulatory) or Gi (inhibitory), not the defining Gq enzyme.
distractorRationales.B: Peptides are hydrophilic and do not cross the bilayer to the nucleus as the receptor-bypass mechanism.
distractorRationales.C: The hormone does not need a nuclear pore; its receptor is at the plasma membrane and the second messengers are intracellular.

items.stem: A person can tell two closely spaced points apart on a fingertip but feels only one point when the same two are applied to the back. This difference in spatial acuity is because the fingertip has:

choices.text: A lower absolute threshold for pain
A higher density of receptors with smaller receptive fields

items.explanation: Spatial acuity (the two-point threshold) depends on receptor density and receptive-field size: fingertips have dense receptors with small fields → fine discrimination; the back has the opposite. Takeaway: Two-point discrimination is finest where receptors are dense with small receptive fields (fingertips, lips), poorest where sparse (back). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fingertips pack many receptors with small receptive fields (fine discrimination); the back has sparse receptors with large fields. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.A: Adaptation speed governs timing, not spatial resolution.
distractorRationales.B: Pain threshold is unrelated to two-point spatial acuity.
distractorRationales.C: Receptor adaptation class doesn't set spatial resolution.

items.stem: A radioiodine scan labels thyroid follicles intensely but does not label parafollicular C cells. The iodinated hormones stored on thyroglobulin in the follicular colloid are:

choices.text: T3 and T4, whose aromatic rings are iodinated on thyroglobulin in the follicle
Calcitonin, which is an iodinated peptide made by C cells
PTH, which incorporates iodine in the parathyroid chief cells that the scan also lights up
Cortisol, iodinated in the adrenal cortex after iodide trapping by follicular cells

items.explanation: Follicular thyrocytes trap iodide via NIS, oxidize it with thyroid peroxidase, and organify it onto tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin, later coupling them to form T3 and T4. That is why radioiodine concentrates in follicles. C cells secrete calcitonin, a peptide that is not iodinated on thyroglobulin, so they are cold on an iodine scan. PTH is made in the parathyroids without iodine organification, and cortisol is a cholesterol-derived steroid from the adrenal cortex. Distinguishing follicular versus C-cell products is a standard endocrine-anatomy point.

distractorRationales.B: Calcitonin is uniodinated and comes from C cells, which the scan does not label.
distractorRationales.C: PTH is not an iodinated follicular hormone, and parathyroids do not trap radioiodine like thyroid follicles.
distractorRationales.D: Cortisol is not iodinated in the thyroid; adrenal steroidogenesis does not explain the follicular iodine signal.

items.stem: A spherical zygote has diameter 200 µm. Cleavage conserves total cytoplasmic volume through the 8-cell stage (each blastomere a sphere). Volume of a sphere is (4/3)πr³, so diameter scales as the cube root of volume. At the 8-cell stage, what is each blastomere’s diameter, and which later distinction is correct?

choices.text: 100 µm; all 8 cells are already extra-embryonic trophectoderm
100 µm; the blastocyst then allocates an inner cell mass (embryo) versus trophoblast (placenta)
200 µm; cleavage increases total volume eightfold

items.explanation: Eight equal blastomeres share the original volume, so each has volume /8. Diameter scales as ∛(volume), and ∛(1/8) = 1/2, so diameter = 100 µm. Diameter does not fall eightfold (that would be 25 µm), which would be confusing linear with volume. Total volume is conserved, not multiplied, so cells cannot stay 200 µm. After compaction the blastocyst inner cell mass forms the embryo proper while trophoblast forms extra-embryonic chorion; the 8-cell stage is not yet all trophectoderm.

distractorRationales.A: The 100 µm figure is right, but inner cells of the later blastocyst are embryonic, not all trophoblast.
distractorRationales.C: Halving diameter at every cleavage would be correct only if volume halved while remaining one cell; here volume per cell is /8, so diameter /2 once at the 8-cell stage.
distractorRationales.D: The stem states volume is conserved; diameter therefore must fall.

passage.title: Neutral Style (1979)
passage.body: Priya Raman published “Neutral Style” in 1979 after a season in community radio. The argument is that the archive is a construction site, not a warehouse. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: Fidelity of a threonyl-tRNA synthetase
passage.body:
A fictional threonyl-tRNA synthetase, ThrRS-F, attaches threonine to tRNAThr during translation. The first active site activates threonine by forming threonyl-AMP from threonine and ATP; the amino acid is then transferred to the 3' end of tRNAThr. Because valine is structurally similar to threonine, ThrRS-F also contains an editing domain that hydrolyzes mischarged Val-tRNAThr. A reporter protein loses activity when valine is inserted at positions normally encoded by threonine codons.

Aminoacylation and editing properties of ThrRS-F.
Condition | Thr-tRNAThr charging rate (%) | Val-tRNAThr accumulation (%) | ATP-to-AMP conversion rate (%) | Active reporter protein (%)
Wild-type ThrRS-F + wild-type tRNAThr | 100 | 1 | 100 | 98
Editing-site D201A + wild-type tRNAThr | 95 | 28 | 125 | 62
Activation-site K55A + wild-type tRNAThr | 8 | 1 | 10 | 12
Wild-type ThrRS-F + acceptor-stem mutant tRNAThr | 18 | 1 | 22 | 20
Editing-site D201A + excess free valine | 90 | 45 | 140 | 45
Wild-type ThrRS-F + noncognate tRNAAla | 3 | 0.5 | 5 | 8

Two-site model of ThrRS-F specificity. — The activation site forms aminoacyl-AMP intermediates using ATP. Correct threonylated tRNA is released for translation. Incorrect Val-tRNAThr can enter an editing domain, where the aminoacyl ester bond is hydrolyzed before the tRNA reaches the ribosome.

items.stem: Young’s double slit uses λ = 5.0 × 10−7 m, slit separation d = 5.0 × 10−4 m, and a screen at D = 2.0 m. Fringe spacing (adjacent bright fringes) is β = λ D / d. The third bright fringe from the centre (m = 3) is at y = 3β. What are β and that y?
items.explanation: β = (5.0 × 10−7 × 2.0) / (5.0 × 10−4) = (1.0 × 10−6) / (5.0 × 10−4) = 2.0 × 10−3 m = 2.0 mm. The m = 3 bright fringe sits at 3 × 2.0 mm = 6.0 mm. Leaving out the factor 3 reports only one fringe spacing. Inverting D and d or dropping a power of ten can produce 0.50 mm or 5.0 mm. Constructive interference at mλ path difference maps linearly to y = m λ D / d on a distant screen, so the arithmetic is a direct substitution.

distractorRationales.A: 0.50 mm would be d D / λ or a swapped 10−3/10−something; the formula is λD/d.
distractorRationales.B: 5.0 mm is λD/d with d taken as 2.0 × 10−4 m, not 5.0 × 10−4 m.
distractorRationales.D: β = 2.0 mm is right, but m = 3 places the fringe at 6.0 mm, not at the first fringe.

items.stem: Relative fitnesses at an autosomal locus are w(AA) = 1.00, w(Aa) = 1.00, w(aa) = 0.50. In a large population, p(A) = 0.90 and q(a) = 0.10 before selection. Mean fitness is w̄ = p²wAA + 2pq wAa + q² waa. After one round of selection the new q is q′ = q (p wAa + q waa) / w̄. What happens to q, and what is w̄?

choices.text: w̄ = 0.995 and q falls to about 0.095, as expected for a recessive deleterious allele
w̄ = 0.50 and q doubles, because the aa class has fitness 0.50
w̄ = 1.00 and q is unchanged, because A is dominant
w̄ = 0.995 and q rises, because rare alleles always increase

items.explanation: w̄ = (0.81)(1) + (0.18)(1) + (0.01)(0.50) = 0.81 + 0.18 + 0.005 = 0.995. Then q′ = 0.10 × (0.90 × 1 + 0.10 × 0.50) / 0.995 = 0.10 × 0.95 / 0.995 ≈ 0.0955. Selection against aa therefore trims q slightly. Dominance of A means heterozygotes are spared, so a rare recessive is only slowly purged, not instantly eliminated and not increased. Mean fitness is near 1 because aa is only 1% of the population.

distractorRationales.B: Mean fitness is not equal to the lowest genotype fitness; aa individuals are rare, so w̄ stays near 1 and q does not double.
distractorRationales.C: Dominance keeps heterozygote fitness at 1 but aa still dies back, so q is not strictly unchanged and w̄ is 0.995 not 1.000.
distractorRationales.D: A deleterious recessive decreases when rare; there is no general rule that rare alleles increase.

items.stem:
Measured enthalpies:
N2 + O2 → 2 NO    ΔH = +180 kJ
2 NO + O2 → 2 NO2    ΔH = −114 kJ
Adding these equations gives N2 + 2 O2 → 2 NO2. What is ΔH for that sum?

choices.text: +180 kJ, keeping only the first equation
−114 kJ, keeping only the second equation
+294 kJ, adding 180 + 114 without the sign on the second ΔH

items.explanation: Hess’s law adds ΔH when equations add. The two NO intermediates cancel, leaving N2 + 2 O2 → 2 NO2, and ΔH = +180 + (−114) = +66 kJ. The overall formation of NO2 from the elements is slightly endothermic in this data set because the costly NO-forming step is only partly repaid by the exothermic NO → NO2 oxidation. Dropping either equation, or flipping the −114 to +114, does not match the algebraic sum.

distractorRationales.A: The second step still occurs in the sum and contributes −114 kJ.
distractorRationales.B: The first step is required to produce the NO that the second step consumes.
distractorRationales.D: The second ΔH is −114, not +114; 180 − 114 = 66, not 294.

items.stem: Yeast hexokinase phosphorylates glucose with ATP. In the absence of sugar the enzyme’s rate of ATP hydrolysis to ADP and inorganic phosphate is very low. Glucose binding closes a domain cleft around the active site and then ATP hydrolysis (now as phosphoryl transfer to glucose) accelerates. Which model best explains the idle ATPase suppression?

choices.text: A rigid lock-and-key site that is preorganized equally for water and for glucose
Ping-pong substitution in which ATP phosphorylates the enzyme before glucose is possible
Competitive inhibition of hexokinase by glucose with respect to ATP
Induced fit that excludes water and aligns catalytic groups only after glucose binds

items.explanation: Hexokinase is a classic induced-fit enzyme: glucose binding drives closure of two lobes, dehydrating the active site so that ATP’s γ-phosphoryl is transferred to glucose rather than to water. That conformational requirement explains why abortive ATPase activity is low without sugar. A rigid lock-and-key site already open to solvent would hydrolyze ATP continually. Glucose is the phosphoryl acceptor, not a competitive inhibitor versus ATP, and yeast hexokinase uses a sequential ternary-complex mechanism rather than a substituted-enzyme ping-pong path as the explanation of the water-exclusion observation.

distractorRationales.A: A permanently open, rigid site would allow water to attack ATP; the data show that sugar-triggered closure is required.
distractorRationales.B: The observation is about excluding water by domain closure, not about a covalent phosphoryl-enzyme intermediate.
distractorRationales.C: Glucose is a substrate. Competitive inhibition would decrease, not enable, phosphoryl transfer.

passage.title: Pigment inheritance and enzyme oligomerization in a model yeast
passage.body:
A fictional yeast synthesizes a purple pigment in two steps. Enzyme A converts a colorless precursor to a blue intermediate, and enzyme B converts the blue intermediate to the purple product. Loss of enzyme A prevents blue intermediate formation and produces white colonies regardless of enzyme B genotype. Loss of enzyme B in a strain with functional enzyme A produces blue colonies. The genes A and B are autosomal and are hypothesized to assort independently. Researchers crossed AABB yeast to aabb yeast, then selfed the AaBb F1 progeny.

Observed F2 colony phenotypes from AaBb selfing.
Phenotype | Observed colonies
Purple | 178
Blue | 59
White | 83

Biochemical characterization of enzyme B variants.
Enzyme B protein | Dimeric protein (%) | Km for blue intermediate (mM) | Relative Vmax (%)
B wild type | 95 | 0.10 | 100
b Gly45Asp variant | 25 | 0.12 | 20
b Gly45Asp + stabilizing osmolyte | 70 | 0.11 | 65

Native gel analysis of enzyme B. — Wild-type enzyme B migrates mainly as a dimer. The Gly45Asp variant shows a stronger monomer band and weaker dimer band. Adding a stabilizing osmolyte partially restores the dimer band.

items.stem: An RC circuit has R = 2.0 MΩ and C = 2.0 μF, so τ = RC = 4.0 s. The capacitor starts uncharged and is connected to a 12 V battery at t = 0. Qualitatively, Vc(t) = V(1 − e−t/τ) and Ic(t) decays from V/R. Which snapshot is consistent?

choices.text: τ = 4.0 s means the capacitor is fully charged at t = 4.0 s exactly (Vc = 12 V, Ic = 0)
At t = 0, Ic = 6.0 μA and Vc = 0; at t = 4.0 s, Vc ≈ 7.6 V (about 63% of 12 V) and Ic has fallen to ~37% of 6.0 μA
At t = 0, Vc = 12 V already, because the battery is connected
Ic is constant at 6.0 μA for all t, as in a resistor-only circuit

items.explanation: Initially the uncharged capacitor behaves as a short, so Vc = 0 and Ic = 12 V / 2.0×10^6 Ω = 6.0 μA. After one time constant the exponential (1 − 1/e) ≈ 0.63, so Vc ≈ 0.63 × 12 ≈ 7.6 V and current is 1/e ≈ 0.37 of its initial value. The capacitor voltage cannot jump to 12 V at t = 0; charge takes time to arrive. Current cannot stay at 6.0 μA once Vc has risen. One τ is not complete charging; that is approached only as t → ∞ (about 5τ for practical purposes).

distractorRationales.A: At t = τ, 1 − e−1 ≈ 0.63, not 1.00; fully charged is the t → ∞ limit.
distractorRationales.C: Voltage on C is zero until charge has flowed; t = 0 is the uncharged state.
distractorRationales.D: As C charges, the remaining voltage on R falls, so Ic decays.

items.stem: A child reaches for a cookie, narrates “I want it,” then pauses: “they’ll say I’m greedy if I take it,” and puts it back. In Mead’s terms, which analysis is best?

choices.text: Self-efficacy has dropped to zero, so no future cookie-seeking is possible
The “I” is the spontaneous actor and the “me” is the internalized attitudes of others; role-taking is regulating the act
The child has an external locus of control for all food, which forbids wanting a cookie
Deindividuation in a kitchen erased personal standards

items.explanation: Mead’s self is a social process: the “I” is the unorganized, impulsive subject of action, and the “me” is the organized set of others’ attitudes one takes toward oneself. Role-taking is seeing one’s act from the other’s standpoint. Wanting the cookie then inhibiting it after imagining “they’ll say I’m greedy” is that dialogue, and it is how self-concept and identity are practiced in social interaction. A single inhibited reach is not zero efficacy, not a global external locus, and not crowd anonymity.

distractorRationales.A: Putting one cookie back is self-regulation, not a prediction that the child can never act.
distractorRationales.C: The child still wants the cookie; the issue is an internalized social standard, not luck as the cause of outcomes.
distractorRationales.D: Deindividuation reduces self-awareness in anonymous groups; the child is applying, not losing, a personal standard.

items.stem: Hepatocytes are given either [1-14C]glucose or [6-14C]glucose, and early 14CO2 release is measured before extensive recycling. If the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway is active, which labeling result is expected?

choices.text: 14CO2 appears faster from C-1-labeled glucose than from C-6-labeled glucose, because 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase releases C-1
C-1 and C-6 are chemically equivalent in the first turn of the oxidative PPP, so early 14CO2 rates are equal
Only C-6 is decarboxylated by 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase, so C-6 glucose labels CO2 first
GAPDH decarboxylates C-1 of glucose directly, independent of the pentose phosphate pathway

items.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase oxidize G6P and then decarboxylate 6-phosphogluconate to ribulose-5-phosphate. The carbon lost as CO2 is C-1 of the original glucose. C-6 remains in the pentose and is not released in that first oxidative pass. Therefore a C-1/C-6 14CO2 ratio greater than one is a classic assay of oxidative PPP activity when measured at early times, before pentoses are recycled into hexoses that scramble labels. GAPDH is an oxidation of an aldehyde to an acyl phosphate; it does not release CO2. C-1 and C-6 are equivalent in the later symmetric fructose-1,6-bisphosphate of glycolysis, not in the first PPP decarboxylation.

distractorRationales.B: The oxidative decarboxylation is specific for C-1; early CO2 from C-1 and C-6 is not equivalent.

distractorRationales.D: GAPDH does not decarboxylate; CO2 from glucose C-1 in this assay is a PPP signature.

passage.title: Electron transport, proton coupling, and cytochrome c release
passage.body:
A fictional study examined isolated mitochondria from cultured liver-derived cells. Investigators supplied either pyruvate plus malate, which generate NADH for Complex I, or succinate, which donates electrons through Complex II. They then added inhibitors or a pore-forming BAX-derived peptide. Oxygen consumption, ATP synthesis, inner mitochondrial membrane potential, and cytochrome c detected outside mitochondria were measured. Values are normalized to untreated mitochondria supplied with pyruvate plus malate unless otherwise noted.

Effects of mitochondrial perturbations.
Condition | O2 consumption with pyruvate/malate (%) | O2 consumption with succinate (%) | ATP synthesis (%) | Membrane potential (%) | Cytochrome c outside mitochondria (%)
Control | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 5
Rotenone | 25 | 90 | 35 | 45 | 5
Antimycin A | 10 | 12 | 10 | 20 | 5
Oligomycin | 35 | 38 | 8 | 130 | 5
CCCP | 160 | 155 | 15 | 15 | 5
BAX-derived peptide | 70 | 72 | 60 | 70 | 65

Simplified map of oxidative phosphorylation. — Electrons from NADH enter at Complex I, electrons from succinate enter at Complex II, both pathways pass through ubiquinone to Complex III, cytochrome c, and Complex IV. Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons to create the proton-motive force used by ATP synthase.

passage.title: Gas Collection During Electrolysis of a Buffer
passage.body:
A fictional laboratory exercise uses water electrolysis to calibrate a gas-volume sensor. At the cathode, hydrogen gas forms according to: 2H2O + 2e- -> H2 + 2OH-. The gas collection tube is adjusted so that the total pressure of the collected gas equals 1.031 atm. The Faraday constant is 96500 C/mol e-. A 6.0 V source supplies the cell through external circuit elements.

Electrolysis trials and collected cathode gas.
Trial | Current (A) | Time (s) | Total gas pressure (atm) | Temperature (K) | Collected cathode gas volume (mL)
1 | 0.100 | 1930 | 1.031 | 298 | 24.0
2 | 0.100 | 3860 | 1.031 | 298 | 48.0
3 | 0.200 | 1930 | 1.031 | 298 | 46.5
4 | 0.100 | 1930 | 1.031 | 310 | 25.0

Cathode gas collection apparatus. — Hydrogen produced at the cathode bubbles into an inverted graduated tube filled with water. The gas volume is read after equalizing the water levels inside and outside the tube.

passage.title: psg-cp-4
passage.body:
Diagnostic imaging often relies on how waves interact with tissue. In an ultrasound scanner, a transducer emits pulses of high-frequency sound into the body and listens for echoes returning from boundaries between tissues. A common obstetric probe operates at 2.0 MHz, and sound travels through soft tissue at about 1540 m/s. The scanner forms an image from the time delay and strength of each returning echo, and clinicians choose the probe frequency to trade off image detail against how deep the sound can penetrate.
A Doppler mode measures blood flow. When a pulse reflects from red blood cells moving relative to the transducer, the returning sound is shifted in frequency; the scanner converts this shift into a flow velocity and direction, coloring flow toward and away from the probe differently.
A second instrument, a fiber-optic endoscope, guides visible light instead of sound. Light travels along a thin glass fiber whose core has a higher refractive index (about 1.5) than its surrounding cladding (about 1.2). Rays that strike the core-cladding boundary at a large enough angle are trapped inside the core and travel the fiber's length with little loss, so the endoscope can illuminate and image tissue deep inside the body and around bends. The physicians rely on the same refraction principles when a laser beam crosses from one tissue layer into another and changes direction. Throughout, the team treats soft tissue as a uniform medium for sound and the fiber as an ideal light guide.

items.stem: Cholesterol is incorporated into a phospholipid bilayer held at 37 C, well above the phospholipids' gel-to-liquid transition temperature Tm. The most accurate description is that cholesterol:

choices.text: restricts phospholipid tail mobility and decreases fluidity of the already liquid bilayer
converts the bilayer into a detergent micelle
opens nonspecific aqueous pores so Na+ and K+ equilibrate freely
abolishes the hydrophobic interior so integral proteins can no longer embed

items.explanation: Above Tm the bilayer is already in a liquid-crystalline state. Cholesterol's rigid steroid ring intercalates among fatty-acyl tails, reducing their conformational freedom and thereby decreasing fluidity and permeability of that liquid phase (while also broadening the transition). It does not turn a bilayer into a micelle, punch ion pores, or destroy the hydrophobic core that anchors transmembrane proteins. The opposite, fluidizing role of cholesterol is mainly in preventing tight packing below Tm, which is not this experiment's temperature regime.

distractorRationales.B: Micelles form from single-tailed detergents in water. Cholesterol modulates a bilayer; it does not convert it into a micellar detergent phase at physiologic loading.
distractorRationales.C: Cholesterol generally decreases small-molecule permeability of a fluid bilayer; it is not an ion channel.
distractorRationales.D: The hydrophobic core remains. Cholesterol is itself hydrophobic and sits within that core.

items.stem: A purified enzyme loses activity in 8 M urea but regains most activity after slow dialysis into physiological buffer. Which statement best explains this observation?

choices.text: Urea hydrolyzed peptide bonds, and dialysis allowed the original primary structure to reform.
The enzyme's amino acid sequence retained enough information to refold when denaturant was removed.
Urea irreversibly reduced all peptide bonds, but dialysis restored the active-site pH.
The enzyme must be a ribozyme because proteins cannot regain activity after denaturation.

items.explanation: Urea disrupts noncovalent interactions that stabilize secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure, but it does not normally cleave peptide bonds. If primary structure remains intact, some proteins can refold after denaturant removal. Common miss: Assuming any loss of activity means covalent cleavage of the protein. This reflects the principle that primary structure can encode folding information when covalent structure is preserved. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.A: Urea does not normally hydrolyze peptide bonds under these conditions, and peptide-bond reformation would require biosynthesis or chemical ligation.
distractorRationales.C: Peptide bonds are not reduced by urea, and pH alone would not restore an irreversibly damaged primary structure.
distractorRationales.D: Proteins can sometimes refold after denaturation; the observation does not imply an RNA catalyst.

items.stem: A hospital chart records chromosomes and anatomy under “sex.” A separate intake asks how the patient lives and is treated as a man, a woman, or another gender, and which jobs the patient considers appropriate for each. For some patients the social answers diverge from the biological record. Which statement is most accurate?

choices.text: Sex and gender are interchangeable names for chromosomes, so divergence is a charting error
Gender is assigned only by immigration status and cannot diverge from anatomy
Social roles always match gametes in every society, so the split sample is impossible
Sex indexes biological characteristics; gender indexes social roles, identity, and expectations, which can be measured separately

items.explanation: In MCAT sociology, sex refers to biological categories (chromosomes, gonads, anatomy), whereas gender refers to the social meanings, roles, and identities organized around those categories. Because gender is socially structured, self-identification and role expectations can diverge from a chromosomal record. That is why surveys treat the variables separately. Treating them as synonyms, tying gender solely to immigration documents, or claiming a universal match between gametes and roles, contradicts the distinction the intake form is built on.

distractorRationales.A: If the terms were interchangeable, a split instrument would be pointless; the divergence is the sociological phenomenon of interest.
distractorRationales.B: Immigration status is a different demographic axis; it does not define gender.
distractorRationales.C: Cross-cultural and within-society variation in gender roles is a standard finding, not an impossibility.

items.stem: A campus health campaign tests vaccine ads. Undergraduates who expect to be eligible this month and who score high on need for cognition change intention only when the ad cites strong randomized-trial evidence, regardless of whether a celebrity appears. Students who will not be eligible for years change more when a celebrity appears, even if the evidence is weak. This pattern matches:

choices.text: Cognitive dissonance created by watching a celebrity while sitting still
Social loafing, because viewers process less when seated in a lecture hall
The elaboration-likelihood model: high motivation and ability favor the central route (argument quality); low involvement favors peripheral cues (celebrity)
Demographic transition stage 2, the only population in which celebrity ads can work

items.explanation: The elaboration-likelihood model splits persuasion into a central route, in which people scrutinize message arguments, and a peripheral route, in which they rely on cues such as source attractiveness or fame. Motivation (personal relevance, need for cognition) and ability push processing toward the central route, so argument strength should dominate. When involvement is low, the same people should be more moved by a celebrity than by evidence quality. Dissonance and loafing are different mechanisms, and demographic-transition stages do not gate advertising psychology.

distractorRationales.A: Sitting through an ad is not the inconsistent-cognition setup that dissonance theory uses to predict attitude change.
distractorRationales.B: Social loafing is reduced effort on a collective task, not a dual-route persuasion pattern.
distractorRationales.D: ELM is not restricted to stage-2 societies; the stem varies involvement, not fertility and mortality.

passage.title: The museum as a verb
passage.body:
Conservation used to mean stopping time. A painting was a patient; varnish was a bandage; the ideal was to return the object to a single authentic hour and then prevent further hours from occurring. That ideal had a hidden historiography. It assumed the authentic hour was already known, usually as the artist’s last brushstroke, and that later repairs, soot, liturgy, and even damage were noise.

A newer conservation talk prefers verbs. To museum an object is to keep choosing which traces will remain legible. Cleaning is not the removal of history; it is the promotion of one history over another. The nineteenth-century restorer who “completed” a medieval panel was not more ideological than the twenty-first-century restorer who leaves the lacuna as a paler mute. Both are editors. They differ in which audience they imagine and in how proudly they sign the edit.

Critics of reversible methods sometimes complain that visible fills and honest seams break the spell. They want the old miracle: an untouched past that happens to hang at eye level under LEDs. The complaint is aesthetically sincere and philosophically confused. The spell was always produced with scaffolding, attributions, and lighting. Reversibility is not a refusal of beauty. It is a refusal to trap the next generation inside today’s certainty about what the object “really” was.

There is a colonial edge. Objects that arrived by seizure were often cleaned into a style that made them readable as art in the receiving capital, which is to say, cleaned of the uses that had made them un-museumlike. To restore the pigment without restoring the right of refusal is to complete the seizure in a gentler font. Some institutions now consult source communities about smoke, wear, and whether an object should be seen at all. Consultation is slow and can be theater. It is still a different verb from rescue.

If this sounds like relativism, notice what it does not say. It does not say that all edits are equal, or that pigment chemistry is a matter of taste. It says that technical competence cannot supply the missing decision about which past is being kept available. The decision will be made. Calling it science does not make it less a decision. Calling it care does not either. The more honest museum is the one that can show its verbs.

passage.title: psg-cars-9
passage.body:
Classical economic theory rests on a conception of the agent as fundamentally rational: possessed of stable, consistent preferences, capable of processing available information, and motivated to maximize personal utility. This model has extraordinary analytical power. It generates precise, testable predictions and underlies the welfare theorems that have guided economic policy for generations. Yet beginning in the latter decades of the twentieth century, a body of research in behavioral economics accumulated evidence that humans deviate from this ideal in systematic, predictable, and consequential ways.
Among the most robust findings is loss aversion: people respond more strongly to losses than to equivalent gains. The discomfort of losing one hundred dollars is experienced as more intense than the pleasure of gaining the same amount. This asymmetry has significant implications. It helps explain why people hold losing financial assets far longer than rational profit-maximization would recommend — they prefer the pain of waiting to the certain loss of selling. It also explains why contract and policy framings that emphasize avoiding losses are more motivationally effective than those that emphasize equivalent gains.
A second set of findings concerns heuristic judgment under uncertainty. When people lack the time or information to calculate expected values precisely, they rely on cognitive shortcuts that usually suffice but sometimes produce systematic errors. The availability heuristic leads people to estimate the probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind: dramatic events, such as airplane crashes, are overestimated in frequency because they are memorable, while mundane but statistically commoner risks, such as car accidents, are underestimated. The representativeness heuristic leads people to assess probability by how closely an instance resembles a prototypical category member, often ignoring base-rate information entirely. A familiar illustration involves base rates. Told that a quiet, orderly person who loves books was drawn from a group made up mostly of salespeople and only a few librarians, many respondents confidently judge the person a librarian, swayed by resemblance to a stereotype while all but ignoring how rare librarians are in the sample. The mistake is not stupidity but the misfiring of an ordinarily useful strategy: resemblance is frequently a serviceable guide to category membership, and only in cases engineered to pit it against base-rate information does it lead reliably astray. The shortcuts that behavioral research exposes are, in most everyday settings, both fast and surprisingly accurate; they betray us mainly in the artificial problems constructed to reveal their inner workings.
These findings have generated debate about the appropriate policy response. Some argue that behavioral insights justify 'nudging': designing choice environments so that the default option is the one that most people would choose on reflection. Automatic enrollment in retirement savings plans, for instance, exploits the tendency to accept defaults, boosting participation without eliminating freedom of choice. Critics of nudging worry that it is paternalistic, that it manipulates rather than informs, and that it presupposes policymakers know better than individuals what those individuals' reflective preferences actually are.
The behavioral economics literature does not establish that markets always fail or that regulation is always beneficial. It establishes only that the idealized rational actor is an incomplete description of real human psychology, and that understanding how people actually decide is essential to designing institutions that work well in the world as it is.

passage.title: Philosophy — can we learn from fiction?
passage.body:
Can a novel teach us anything true about the world? The doubt is old and not unserious. A novel, after all, is by definition a made-up story; its characters never lived, its events never happened. Whatever a novelist asserts through the tale is unsupported by evidence — the author simply stipulates that things are so within the fiction. If I want to know how grief works, or how power corrupts, it seems I should consult a psychologist or a historian, not a storyteller who has invented her data.

This objection has force against one kind of knowledge but not another. It is true that fiction cannot establish general facts: no number of novels about ambitious men could prove that ambition corrupts, since the novelist controls the outcome. But not all knowledge is knowledge of general facts. There is also knowing what something is like — what it would be to face a certain choice, to bear a certain loss. And here fiction has resources the treatise lacks: it can place us, in imagination, inside a situation and let us try it on.

Consider the difference between being told that jealousy distorts perception and following, page by page, a character's jealous misreadings of an innocent scene. The first hands us a proposition to file away; the second rehearses the experience, and may leave us better able to recognize the distortion in ourselves. The novelist need not prove that jealousy works this way. It is enough that she renders it so vividly that we recognize it — the recognition, not the proof, is the point.

A skeptic may reply that this "knowledge" is merely emotional, not cognitive — that we have been moved, not taught. But the line is not so clean. To grasp what a situation is like is often a precondition for judging it well; the person who cannot imagine another's suffering will reason poorly about how to treat them. If fiction cultivates that imaginative grasp, it is doing cognitive work, even if it proves no theorems.

The modest conclusion is that fiction and science divide the labor of understanding rather than compete for it. Science tells us that things are so and why; fiction shows us what their being so is like from the inside. To ask a novel to furnish general laws is to misunderstand the kind of knowledge it offers — and to conclude, from its failure to do so, that it offers none, is to make the same mistake twice.

passage.title: psg-ps-1
passage.body:
Researchers investigated how listeners detect faint tones and how expectations shape perception. In Experiment 1, 40 young adults sat in a soundproof booth and reported whether a brief 1000-Hz tone was present on each of 400 trials. The tone was actually presented on only half of the trials; on the rest, participants heard only background noise. Investigators varied the tone's intensity to estimate each listener's absolute threshold, defined as the intensity detected on 50% of trials. They also recorded four response categories - hits, misses, false alarms, and correct rejections - and computed a sensitivity index (d') separately from each listener's response criterion.
In Experiment 2, the same listeners were told before each block whether tones would be 'rare' or 'common.' When told tones were common, listeners reported hearing a tone more often, producing more hits but also more false alarms, even though the physical stimuli were identical across blocks. Sensitivity (d') did not change between the 'rare' and 'common' blocks; only the criterion shifted.
In Experiment 3, listeners judged whether two successive weights differed. The smallest detectable difference grew in proportion to the starting weight: distinguishing 102 g from 100 g was as hard as distinguishing 204 g from 200 g. Finally, when a steady tone played continuously, listeners' reported loudness declined over several minutes, though an abrupt change in intensity was noticed at once. The authors concluded that detection reflects both sensory capacity and decision processes, and that the sensory system is tuned to change rather than to constant stimulation.

passage.title: psg-bb-9
passage.body:
Neurophysiologists used a squid giant axon and fine electrodes to record the membrane potential during a nerve impulse. At rest, the inside of the axon measured about -70 mV relative to the outside. A brief electrical stimulus that depolarized the membrane to a threshold near -55 mV triggered an all-or-none action potential: the potential shot upward to about +30 mV (the rising phase) and then rapidly returned toward rest (the falling phase), briefly overshooting to a value more negative than -70 mV before stabilizing.
The team dissected the ionic basis using two toxins. Applying tetrodotoxin (TTX), which blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, abolished the action potential entirely: stimulation no longer produced the rapid upstroke. Applying tetraethylammonium (TEA), which blocks voltage-gated potassium channels, left the upstroke intact but markedly slowed the return to rest, prolonging the action potential. Blocking the Na+/K+ ATPase with a separate agent did not abolish individual action potentials over the short term but, over many impulses, degraded the ion gradients on which they depend.
In a final experiment the researchers compared conduction along a myelinated axon with an unmyelinated one of similar diameter. The myelinated axon conducted impulses far faster, because the action potential regenerated only at the gaps in the myelin (nodes of Ranvier), jumping from node to node. The results tied each phase of the action potential to specific ion channels and showed how myelination speeds signaling without changing the underlying ionic mechanism.

items.stem: E. coli aspartate transcarbamoylase (ATCase) is inhibited by CTP. A mutation in a regulatory chain prevents CTP binding but leaves the catalytic chains kinetically intact in isolation. In the holoenzyme this mutation is expected to:

items.explanation: ATCase is the textbook allosteric enzyme of pyrimidine biosynthesis: catalytic subunits bind aspartate and carbamoyl phosphate, while regulatory subunits bind CTP (and ATP) at a distinct site. passage.title: psg-ps-5
passage.body:
Researchers ran three studies of behavior in groups. In Study 1, a participant judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line, answering aloud after several confederates. On critical trials the confederates unanimously gave an obviously wrong answer. Participants conformed to the wrong answer on about 35% of critical trials, and three-quarters conformed at least once; conformity fell sharply when a single confederate broke from the majority. Most conformers later said they knew the group was wrong but did not want to stand out.
In Study 2, participants completed either a simple, well-practiced task or a complex, unfamiliar task, alone or in front of an audience. An audience improved performance on the simple task but worsened it on the complex task.
In Study 3, participants heard what sounded like a fellow participant having a medical emergency in another room. When participants believed they were the only witness, 85% sought help within a minute; when they believed four others were also present, only 31% did, and those who helped took longer. Interviews suggested that the presence of others reduced each individual's felt responsibility.
The authors distinguished going along with a group to fit in from the effect of an audience on task performance, and linked Study 3 to a well-documented reduction in helping as the number of bystanders rises. They emphasized that these effects reflect the social situation rather than stable personality differences among the participants.

passage.title: The Roster (1976)
passage.body: Clara Voss published “The Roster” in 1976 after a season in broadcast newsrooms. The argument is that local knowledge is treated as anecdote until a model needs it. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: An inhibitor I is added to a Michaelis–Menten enzyme. Apparent Km falls from 2.0 mM to 1.0 mM and apparent Vmax falls from 80 to 40 μM s−1 (the Lineweaver–Burk slope Km/Vmax is unchanged). Which inhibition mode is indicated, and why can extra substrate not restore Vmax?

choices.text: Competitive: I and S bind the same site, so high [S] must restore Vmax; the data are misread
Uncompetitive: I binds only the ES complex, lowering both Km and Vmax by the same factor; extra S creates more ES–I rather than free E
Pure noncompetitive: I binds E and ES equally, so Km is unchanged; the reported Km drop must be experimental error
Irreversible active-site alkylation, which always leaves Km unchanged and cannot produce parallel Lineweaver–Burk lines

items.explanation: Uncompetitive inhibitors bind ES exclusively. Sequestration of ES pulls E + S ⇌ ES to the right, so the apparent substrate affinity increases (Km app decreases) while the amount of productive ES that can proceed to product falls (Vmax app decreases). When both parameters are scaled by the same factor, Km/Vmax is constant and Lineweaver–Burk lines are parallel. Adding more substrate makes more ES and therefore more ES–I; it cannot outcompete an inhibitor that does not bind free E. Competitive inhibition raises Km at constant Vmax. Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax at constant Km.

distractorRationales.A: Competitive inhibition increases Km and leaves Vmax unchanged. These data show both parameters falling, the opposite pattern.
distractorRationales.C: Pure noncompetitive inhibition (equal affinity for E and ES) does not change Km. A halved Km with halved Vmax is uncompetitive, not noncompetitive.
distractorRationales.D: Covalent inactivation typically decreases the amount of active enzyme (Vmax down) without systematically halving Km in a parallel-line pattern diagnostic of uncompetitive inhibition.

items.stem: For the equilibrium N2 + 3H2 2NH3 (exothermic forward reaction), what happens if the temperature is increased?

choices.text: The equilibrium shifts toward the products (more NH3) to absorb the extra heat.
Nothing changes; equilibrium is unaffected by temperature.
The equilibrium shifts toward the reactants (less NH3), since the reverse (endothermic) reaction is favoured to absorb the added heat.

items.explanation: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium shifts to counteract an applied change. Adding heat is treated like adding a "product" of the endothermic (reverse) direction, so the equilibrium shifts toward the reactants, favouring the reverse (heat-absorbing) reaction. When you stress an equilibrium (change in concentration, pressure/volume, or temperature), the reaction shifts in the direction that partially opposes that stress. For temperature specifically, treat heat like a reactant/product: increasing heat favours whichever direction absorbs heat (the endothermic direction). Memory tip: "The system pushes back": treat added heat like an extra ingredient on whichever side absorbs it (the endothermic direction), and picture the equilibrium physically leaning away from the stress you applied. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: psg-cp-2
passage.body:
Atherosclerotic plaque narrows an artery and changes how blood moves through it. In a benchtop model of a coronary artery, a pump drives an incompressible fluid with the density of blood (1050 kg/m^3) through a rigid tube at a steady volume flow rate. Midway along the tube a molded plaque reduces the internal radius to half its normal value over a short segment before the tube widens again. Pressure sensors record the fluid's lateral (static) pressure against the wall upstream of, within, and downstream of the narrowing, while a Doppler probe measures flow speed at the same locations.
Away from the narrowing the fluid moves at 0.20 m/s. Because the fluid is incompressible and the flow is steady, the same volume per second must cross every section, so the fluid accelerates as it enters the constricted segment. The investigators also compare the pump pressure needed to maintain the flow rate before and after the plaque forms, and they note that the vessel's resistance is extremely sensitive to its radius.
A second module models gas exchange. Air in an alveolus is held at an oxygen partial pressure of about 100 mmHg, while blood entering the surrounding pulmonary capillary has an oxygen partial pressure of about 40 mmHg. A thin, moist membrane separates the two compartments, and the team measures how quickly oxygen crosses as they vary the partial-pressure difference, the membrane thickness, and its area. Height differences in the standing circulation are represented by raising or lowering the capillary bed relative to the pump. Take g = 10 m/s^2.

items.explanation: Coping is the effort to manage a stressor after it has been appraised. Problem-focused coping aims at the situation itself (information, treatment choices). items.explanation: T2 phage injects its genome into E. coli while the protein coat remains outside. distractorRationales.D: 32P did enter, and T2 heredity is not a medium polysaccharide; the phage genome is DNA.

items.stem: The sentence “To mistake a folder for a microphone is to forget that someone built the studio, invited some guests, and switched the machine off when the conversation became inconvenient” primarily functions to

choices.text: concede that audio recordings stored in archives are more reliable than paper because they capture tone as well as wording.
introduce a practical proposal that historians install recording equipment so that future selection can be avoided.

items.explanation: The first paragraph has already framed historians as interviewers of documents that supposedly speak if handled gently. The microphone sentence keeps that metaphor in play but turns it: a folder is not a pickup pointed at a willing past; it is the output of a studio someone designed, staffed, and could silence. The function is therefore integrative: it binds the “reluctant witness” picture to the claim that archives decide eligibility for recovery. distractorRationales.B: No policy of installing microphones is advanced; the studio is a figure for prior institutional control, not a facilities request.

passage.title: The archive and the street
passage.body:
Historians often speak as if the past were a reluctant witness who can be coaxed into testimony if only the right box is opened. The letter, the minute-book, the trial transcript, and the parish register are treated not as remnants but as the event itself, patiently waiting to be interviewed. The metaphor is professionally convenient. It locates virtue in attentiveness and implies that an archive, handled without aggression, will speak of its own accord. Archives do not speak. They are offices that decide, usually long before a scholar arrives, which traces of life will be kept, numbered, and thereby made eligible for later recovery. To mistake a folder for a microphone is to forget that someone built the studio, invited some guests, and switched the machine off when the conversation became inconvenient.

This is not a case for abandoning documents. It is a case against a piety now common in public history: the belief that proximity to a primary source is itself a moral credential. Museum captions announce that an object was found in an attic or rescued from a demolition site, as if its later career in a glass case were a continuation of its first life rather than a conversion into evidence. Conversion is what historians do. Trouble begins when conversion is narrated as rescue, because that narration conceals the historian's power and, more consequentially, conceals the people who never generated a paper trail to be rescued.

Oral historians have pressed this objection for decades, sometimes with more hope than caution. They have offered the recorded interview as a democratic patch, a way of admitting those whom the file forgot. The patch is real; it is not automatic. An interview is also a document, made under conditions of prompting, recording, transcription, and later cutting. It can be managed as tightly as a colonial gazette. What distinguishes a responsible oral history is not orality as such, but the historian remaining visible in the manufacture of the record—visible enough that a later reader can see where a question steered, where a narrator pushed back, and where a silence was not a hole but a refusal.

The sharper problem is civic rather than technical. If the only past that can be cited is the past that was filed, public memory will go on over-representing those who employed clerks. Cities make the point more bluntly than seminars do. A demolished neighborhood deposits fewer cartons than a merchant's townhouse; a street seller deposits fewer than a chartered company. When a preservation trust then campaigns to save the townhouse because it is richly documented, the trust is not merely selecting architecture. It is ratifying a distribution of paperwork as a distribution of historical weight. The house is asked to stand for an age, and the undocumented street is invited, if at all, to supply atmosphere.

Honesty does not require the fantasy that every life can be reconstructed with equal density. Some absences are final. The decent procedure is to treat those absences as facts about power rather than as temporary vacancies that a more heroic search will fill. A history that admits what cannot be known is more public-minded than a history that performs completeness by adding still more pages to an already thick dossier. The archive will remain necessary. It need not remain innocent.

items.stem: A molecule of palmitoyl-CoA (C16, saturated) is fully β-oxidized to acetyl-CoA in a hepatocyte mitochondrion. How many rounds of β-oxidation occur, and how many acetyl-CoA, NADH, and FADH2 are produced by those rounds before the citric acid cycle?
items.explanation: Each round of mitochondrial β-oxidation shortens an acyl-CoA by two carbons, releasing one acetyl-CoA and producing one NADH and one FADH2. Palmitate has 16 carbons, so it yields eight acetyl-CoA units. Generating eight two-carbon units from a single chain requires seven cleavage rounds: the last round splits a four-carbon acetoacetyl-CoA into two acetyl-CoA. Therefore the reduced-cofactor count is 7 NADH and 7 FADH2, not 8. Counting one round per carbon, one acetyl per round, or 16 acetyl-CoA all mis-map the two-carbon arithmetic of β-oxidation.

distractorRationales.B: Eight acetyl-CoA are correct, but that requires only seven thiolytic cleavages. An eighth round would require a two-carbon acyl-CoA that is not a substrate of another full cycle.
distractorRationales.C: Palmitate has 16 carbons but yields two-carbon acetyl units, so 8 acetyl-CoA, not 16, and not 16 rounds.
distractorRationales.D: Seven rounds is correct, but those rounds produce eight acetyl-CoA (the last round yields two) and seven NADH, not seven acetyl-CoA and eight NADH.

passage.title: The Caption (1975)
passage.body: In “The Caption” (1975), Mei-Ling Vargas writes from inside court translation. The argument is that the archive is a construction site, not a warehouse. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

An animal has 2n = 8 chromosomes. DNA is scored relative to a diploid G1 nucleus (= 1.0, which is 2C). Four cells are examined:
Cell W: 8 chromosome bodies, 2 chromatids each, DNA 2.0.
Cell X: 4 chromosome bodies, 2 chromatids each, DNA 1.0.
Cell Y: 4 chromosome bodies, 1 chromatid each, DNA 0.5.
Cell Z: 8 chromosome bodies, 1 chromatid each, DNA 1.0.
Which cell is a haploid product of meiosis I that has not yet completed meiosis II?
items.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologues, so each daughter is haploid in chromosome number (4 bodies when 2n = 8) but each chromosome is still duplicated (two chromatids) and DNA is 2C relative to a haploid genome, which is 1.0 on the diploid-G1 scale. That is cell X. Cell W still has 8 replicated chromosomes and 4C DNA, so it is pre-division diploid. Cell Y has 1C DNA and single chromatids, so meiosis II has finished. Cell Z is an ordinary diploid G1 cell.

distractorRationales.A: Eight replicated chromosomes and DNA 2.0 (4C) describe mitosis or G2, not a meiosis-I product.
distractorRationales.C: DNA 0.5 with single chromatids is a gamete after meiosis II, not a secondary gametocyte.
distractorRationales.D: Eight unreplicated chromosomes and DNA 1.0 is diploid G1, not haploid.

items.stem: A hydrolyzed sample contains two related species derived from the same DNA sequence: a short oligonucleotide with a 5′-monophosphate and a free 3′-OH, and the corresponding nucleoside of the 3′-terminal residue. Which chemical distinction is correct at physiologic pH?

choices.text: Both molecules contain internucleotide 3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds; they differ only in whether the bases are methylated.
The nucleoside contains a 5′-triphosphate that the oligonucleotide lacks, so only the nucleoside is strongly anionic.

The oligonucleotide contains 3′–5′ phosphodiester linkages and a terminal phosphate, so it is polyanionic; the nucleoside is a base plus sugar with no phosphate and is not negatively charged from phosphate.
Nucleosides are negatively charged because of phosphate groups, whereas oligonucleotides are uncharged polymers of bases.

items.explanation: A nucleoside is a nitrogenous base linked to ribose or deoxyribose by an N-glycosidic bond and contains no phosphate. A nucleotide (or an oligonucleotide) includes one or more phosphates. Internucleotide bonds in DNA are 3′–5′ phosphodiesters, and a 5′-monophosphate end adds additional negative charge, so the oligo is polyanionic at physiologic pH. The nucleoside has no phosphate to ionize, so it is not an anion for that reason. Confusing the two names, assigning the triphosphate to the nucleoside, or claiming oligonucleotides are uncharged all reverse the structural definitions used to discuss DNA/RNA chemistry and hybridization.

distractorRationales.A: A nucleoside has no internucleotide phosphodiester bonds. Phosphodiesters exist between residues of the oligonucleotide, not in the free nucleoside.
distractorRationales.B: A nucleoside has no phosphate at all, so it cannot carry a 5′-triphosphate. Triphosphates are nucleotides (NTPs/dNTPs), and the oligo, not the nucleoside, is the anionic species here.
distractorRationales.D: This reverses the charge pattern: phosphates make oligonucleotides (and nucleotides) anionic; nucleosides lack those phosphates.

passage.title: psg-cars-3
passage.body:
Few debates in literary theory have proved more durable than the question of authorial intent: does the meaning of a text reside primarily in what its author meant to communicate, or does meaning emerge through the activity of reading itself? At one extreme, the intentionalist holds that misreading is always possible — that interpretations diverging from the author's design are simply mistaken, however ingenious or culturally resonant they may be. At the other extreme, the anti-intentionalist insists that once a text is released into the world, the author's psychological states become strictly irrelevant: what the words mean is fixed not by biography but by the conventions of the language and genre in which they are embedded.
The anti-intentionalist position gained influential expression in mid-twentieth-century criticism, when theorists argued that treating the author's intention as the criterion of correct interpretation commits a category error. Evidence about what a poet hoped to achieve, they maintained, cannot settle what a poem achieves, because a poem is a verbal artifact that may realize meanings its creator did not foresee — meanings that become available only through the community of readers over time. The celebrated example of an ironic text serves as illustration: a writer may compose a scathing satire of nationalistic rhetoric while sincerely believing the rhetoric they are parodying; the satiric meaning is there in the text whether the author intended it or not.
Intentionalists counter that language is an intentional practice: utterances mean what speakers mean by them, and written language does not somehow escape this fundamental feature of linguistic communication. To read a text in complete disregard of what its author was trying to do, they argue, is to treat it as a natural object rather than a human creation — to decode it the way one might decode an accidental inkblot rather than a deliberate message. Moreover, intentionalists point out that appeals to 'the language and genre' still presuppose communicative conventions that are themselves constituted by the intentions of the linguistic community.
A mediating view distinguishes between actual authorial intention (the historical individual's specific psychological states) and what might be called the implied author: the authorial persona that a competent reader constructs from the textual evidence alone. On this account, interpretation aims neither at private biography nor at free-floating textual play but at the coherent communicative project that the text itself invites. The implied author is, in effect, the best hypothesis about what an ideally communicative author of this text would have intended — a construct that disciplines interpretation without requiring access to historical documents.
What unites all parties to this dispute is the recognition that texts are not transparent windows onto authors' minds or onto a language-independent reality. They are artifacts whose significance is never simply given but must always be construed — a fact that makes hermeneutics, the theory of interpretation, as much a practical as a philosophical discipline.

Using only one recombinant class halves the value to 0.10. Using 200 as the denominator doubles it to 0.40. The parental fraction 0.80 is 1 − RF, not RF itself. items.explanation: For the ideal relation T² = (4π²/g) L the gradient of T² versus L is 4π²/g, so g = 39.48 / gradient. The Table 1 endpoints give gradient = (3.220 − 1.610)/0.400 = 4.025 s² m^{-1}, hence g = 39.48/4.025 ≈ 9.81 m s^{-2}, closest to 9.8 m s^{-2}. Reporting the gradient itself as g leaves 4.0 m s^{-2} with impossible units for a gravitational field. The numerical estimate is locked to the tabulated T² pair and to the 39.48 factor given in the passage.

distractorRationales.C: 2.5 m s^{-2} is on the order of 4π² divided by a Δ(T²) that was never converted into a per-metre slope, or of other inverted constants, and is far below terrestrial g.

passage.title: Period of a simple pendulum and the value of g
passage.body:
A student determines the gravitational field strength g from the small-angle period of a simple pendulum. Length L is measured from the support to the centre of a spherical bob of diameter 3.0 cm. For each length the student times 20 oscillations and divides by 20 to obtain the period T; the procedure is repeated three times and the mean is recorded. The timing uncertainty on each 20-oscillation interval is estimated as ±0.20 s from reaction time, so the uncertainty in a single mean T is about ±0.010 s. All runs in Table 1 used a maximum angular displacement of about 5°. Take 4π² = 39.48. For an ideal simple pendulum, T² = (4π²/g) L, so a graph of T² against L should be a straight line through the origin with gradient 4π²/g.

Table 1. Mean period versus length (θ ≈ 5°)

| L (m) | Mean T (s) | T² (s²) |
|-------|------------|---------|
| 0.400 | 1.269 | 1.610 |
| 0.500 | 1.419 | 2.012 |
| 0.600 | 1.554 | 2.415 |
| 0.700 | 1.678 | 2.817 |
| 0.800 | 1.794 | 3.220 |

The student then holds L fixed at 0.600 m and varies the release angle (Table 2).

Table 2. Period versus amplitude at L = 0.600 m

| Maximum angular displacement θ (°) | Mean T (s) |
|------------------------------------|------------|
| 5 | 1.554 |
| 10 | 1.557 |
| 20 | 1.571 |
| 30 | 1.595 |

passage.title: psg-cars-11
passage.body:
Among the foundational distinctions in the sociology of religion is the division of the world into two mutually exclusive domains: the sacred and the profane. The sacred encompasses all things set apart and forbidden, surrounded by special prohibitions and observed with reverence; the profane designates everything else the ordinary, the utilitarian, the everyday. This distinction is not primarily about supernatural belief. A society without gods can still organize its collective life around sacred objects and practices; conversely, explicitly theistic language can be deployed in contexts so routine that nothing sacred attaches to it at all. The sacred is a structural feature of collective life, not a property of any particular theological tradition.
What makes something sacred is not its intrinsic properties but its relationship to the collective. The sacred object or practice has been designated by the community as set apart, invested with a significance that transcends individual preference and commands a distinctive emotional response. Violations of the sacred provoke not merely practical objection but moral indignation and often the collective sanction of the group. The sacred functions, in this analysis, as a boundary marker: it demarcates what the collective treats as inviolable from what can be freely negotiated, exchanged, or modified. The power of the sacred is thus inseparable from the collective from which it derives and to which it refers. A corollary is that the sacred is hedged about with rules of separation. Precisely because sacred things are set apart, they must be kept from casual contact with the profane: they are approached through prescribed gestures, handled by designated persons, and encountered on appointed occasions rather than at will. Transgression is felt less as a mistake than as a kind of pollution, calling forth rites of purification or punishment rather than simple correction. This logic of separation explains why the sacred can inspire dread as readily as devotion: what is marked off as supremely valuable is also, for that very reason, treated as perilous to handle carelessly. The boundary, in short, is enforced as much by feeling as by rule.
This framework has been applied far beyond explicitly religious contexts. National flags, war memorials, and constitutional documents can function as sacred objects in secular societies: they command a special reverence, their desecration provokes communal outrage, and they focus the collective sense of identity and shared purpose. Academic ceremonies, such as the conferral of degrees and the inauguration of presidents, likewise exhibit a ritualized formality that marks them off from ordinary transactions. The secular and the sacred are not opposites; rather, the sacred is a structural feature of collective life that may attach to entirely secular objects and occasions.
Critics of this framework have worried that extending the concept of the sacred to secular contexts dilutes it beyond usefulness. If anything sufficiently cherished by a community counts as sacred, the concept loses its explanatory precision. Moreover, the framework has been criticized for underplaying internal dissent: in any actual society, which objects are sacred and which are merely important is itself politically contested, and the boundary between the sacred and the profane is drawn by those with the social power to draw it. Sacred designations can thus serve ideological functions, naturalizing existing arrangements by placing them beyond ordinary critical scrutiny.
These tensions notwithstanding, the sacred/profane distinction continues to illuminate the emotional architecture of collective life in ways that strictly rational accounts of social organization cannot easily replicate. Communities that lack shared sacred commitments often struggle to motivate the sacrifices that sustaining collective institutions requires.

passage.title: psg-cars-10
passage.body:
The relationship between mind and body has occupied Western philosophy since antiquity, but the specific problem of consciousness has acquired a new urgency in an era when neuroscience can map the brain in unprecedented detail. Even if we knew the complete physical state of every neuron in a human brain at a given moment, would that knowledge exhaust our understanding of what it is like for the person whose brain it is to be having the experiences they are having? Many philosophers believe the answer is no — and they argue that this gap between complete physical description and subjective experience reveals something fundamental about the nature of mind.
This 'hard problem' — why any physical process should be accompanied by subjective experience at all — is distinguished from the 'easy problems' of consciousness, such as how the brain integrates information, controls attention, or generates verbal reports about mental states. The easy problems are not trivial; they may require decades of research to solve. But they are, in principle, amenable to explanation in functional and computational terms. The hard problem seems to resist this treatment: even a complete functional account of how a system processes information leaves unexplained why processing should feel like anything at all. To feel the force of the puzzle, imagine two systems that process a stimulus in functionally identical ways — the same inputs, the same discriminations, the same outputs — and ask whether it follows that there is something it is like to be each of them, and, if so, whether it must be the same something. Nothing in the functional story, defenders of the hard problem insist, settles the matter: one could in principle specify every computational step by which an auditory system registers a rising tone without thereby explaining why those steps are accompanied by any felt quality at all. It is this apparent slack between function and feeling — not mere complexity — that makes the problem look hard rather than merely unsolved.
Physicalists respond in several ways. Some deny that there is a genuine explanatory gap: what seems like an inexplicable residue is, they argue, an artifact of our limited cognitive access to neural processes rather than evidence of a non-physical dimension of reality. Once neuroscience matures sufficiently, the sense that something has been left out will dissolve, just as vitalism — the doctrine that life requires a special non-physical force — dissolved when biochemistry revealed the mechanisms of metabolism. Others accept that qualia — the intrinsic qualitative character of experience — are real but argue that they are identical with, or constituted by, physical brain states in ways we do not yet fully understand.
Dualists, by contrast, maintain that the hard problem reflects a genuine ontological gap: minds and physical processes belong to categorically different orders of being. This position preserves the intuition that experience is irreducibly subjective but faces the difficulty of explaining how non-physical minds causally interact with physical brains — a puzzle that has shadowed substance dualism since its classical formulation. To say that minds and brains interact is plausible as ordinary description; to explain the mechanism of that interaction without smuggling physical causation back in is a philosophical challenge that has resisted resolution for centuries.
The hard problem of consciousness thus sits at the intersection of metaphysics, philosophy of mind, and neuroscience. Whether it admits of a naturalistic solution remains one of the deepest unresolved questions in intellectual life.

passage.title: Who Is a Speaker (1983)
passage.body: Hanae Morioka's 1983 essay “Who Is a Speaker,” on vaccine campaigns, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

The Henderson–Hasselbalch relation for plasma is pH = 6.10 + log10([HCO3−] / (0.030 × PCO2)), with [HCO3−] in mM and PCO2 in mmHg. Three arterial samples:

Sample | PCO2 | [HCO3−]
N | 40 | 24
R | 80 | 24
M | 40 | 12

log10(20) = 1.30; log10(10) = 1.00. What are the three pH values?

choices.text: N 7.40; R 7.70; M 7.70, adding rather than taking the log of the ratio
N 6.10; R 6.10; M 6.10, ignoring the bicarbonate/CO2 term
N 7.40; R 7.40; M 7.40, because 6.1 is constant

items.explanation: Sample N: 0.030 × 40 = 1.20, and 24/1.20 = 20, so pH = 6.10 + 1.30 = 7.40. Sample R doubles PCO2 at fixed bicarbonate: 24 / 2.40 = 10, pH = 6.10 + 1.00 = 7.10, a respiratory acidosis. Sample M halves bicarbonate at fixed PCO2: 12 / 1.20 = 10, pH = 7.10, a metabolic acidosis. The same pH of 7.10 is reached by two different ratio changes. Adding 20 instead of taking log10(20) would not yield 7.40. The pKa 6.10 is not the blood pH.

distractorRationales.B: The logarithm of the ratio is required; 6.10 + 20 is meaningless as a pH, and raising PCO2 cannot alkalinise.
distractorRationales.C: Dropping the log term leaves only pKa, which is not arterial pH.
distractorRationales.D: pKa is constant, but pH still changes when the [HCO3−]/(K × PCO2) ratio changes, as R and M show.

passage.title: psg-cp-1
passage.body:
A biomechanics laboratory studies vertical jumping with a force platform, a rigid plate that records the force a person exerts on it as a function of time. A 60 kg athlete stands motionless on the platform and then performs a maximal jump: she dips down, drives upward, and leaves the plate. High-speed video tracks a marker on her hip to follow the vertical motion of her center of mass.
While the athlete stands still, the platform reads a steady value equal to her weight. During the propulsion phase the reading rises well above this baseline, climbs to a peak, and then drops abruptly to zero at the instant her feet leave the plate. The interval from the start of propulsion to takeoff lasts about 0.20 s. After takeoff the center of mass rises to a measured peak height of 0.45 m above its takeoff position before falling back. Treating the body as a point mass at the center of mass and neglecting air resistance, the researchers reconstruct the takeoff velocity, the mechanical energy of the jump, and the forces during landing.
On landing, the athlete returns to the plate moving downward, and the platform again registers a large force as she decelerates to rest over about 0.15 s. The researchers note that athletes who land with stiff legs stop in a shorter time and record much larger peak forces than athletes who flex their knees and ankles to cushion the impact. Throughout, the platform measures the contact force between athlete and plate; gravitational acceleration is taken as g = 10 m/s^2.
