items.stem: 1,3-Butadiene treated with 1 equivalent of HBr at −80 °C yields mostly 3-bromobut-1-ene. After the same mixture is warmed to 40 °C and allowed to equilibrate, 1-bromobut-2-ene predominates. Which analysis is correct?

choices.text: Low temperature selects the 1,2-adduct because it forms faster (kinetic control); heat allows equilibration to the more substituted 1,4-alkene (thermodynamic control)
The 1,4-adduct is always the kinetic product because allylic cations always react at the far end first
Temperature cannot change product ratios for a reaction with a single mechanism
HBr cannot add to conjugated dienes; both products must arise from radical substitution on butane

items.explanation: Protonation of 1,3-butadiene gives an allylic cation that can be captured at C2 (1,2-addition) or C4 (1,4-addition). The 1,2-path has the lower activation energy and wins when the first-formed alkyl bromide cannot revert, i.e., at low temperature under kinetic control. The 1,4-product is a more substituted (internal) alkene and is thermodynamically more stable. At higher temperature the addition is reversible, the system reaches equilibrium, and the thermodynamic product accumulates. This is the textbook illustration that the fastest product and the most stable product need not be the same species.

distractorRationales.B: The kinetic product in this system is the 1,2-adduct, isolated at −80 °C. The 1,4-alkene is the thermodynamic product.
distractorRationales.C: When two products form from a common intermediate and one path is reversible only at higher T, the ratio is strongly temperature-dependent.
distractorRationales.D: Electrophilic addition of HBr to conjugated dienes is a standard polar reaction of alkenes, not a free-radical substitution on an alkane.

passage.title: psg-cars-4
passage.body:
History is not the past itself but a selective reconstruction of the past, assembled from fragmentary evidence by scholars whose questions, categories, and assumptions are inevitably shaped by their own time and place. This observation, often associated with the philosophy of history that emerged in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, does not reduce historical writing to fiction. Yet it does demand that historians acknowledge their craft as an interpretive one rather than a neutral transcription of what happened.
The most influential historians have always made choices: choices about which events to emphasize, which actors to foreground, and which causal chains to trace. A military historian who concentrates on battles and generals produces a different account of the same period than a social historian who foregrounds the lives of ordinary laborers, or an economic historian who treats fluctuations in grain prices as the deeper explanatory variable. None of these accounts is simply wrong; each illuminates a dimension of a complex past while necessarily leaving other dimensions in shadow.
Critics of this pluralism worry that it licenses an anything-goes relativism in which no historical account is better than any other. Defenders respond that recognizing the constructed character of historical narratives is compatible with rigorous standards of evidence, logical consistency, and fidelity to the archival record. An interpretation can be shown to be false if it contradicts well-authenticated documents, or shown to be weak if it ignores a large body of relevant evidence. The standards are not arbitrary, even if the questions that animate historical inquiry are themselves products of particular intellectual climates.
A further complication arises from the role of the historical archive itself. Archives are not neutral repositories of the past; they are collections shaped by decisions about what to preserve, who had the resources to produce written records, and which categories of information administrative systems deemed worth tracking. Consequently, the voices most abundantly represented in archives tend to be those of literate elites, state bureaucracies, and dominant institutions, while the experiences of the illiterate, the dispossessed, and the colonized are filtered through the records of those who observed or administered them from a position of power.
Contemporary historians have developed a range of techniques to recover marginalized perspectives: reading documents 'against the grain' of their intended purpose, triangulating between different types of sources, and drawing on oral traditions and material culture as complementary evidence. These methods have expanded the scope of historical knowledge considerably, even as they have deepened awareness that the gap between the past and the historian's account of it can never be fully closed.
None of this counsels despair about historical knowledge. The recognition that every history is written from somewhere, on the basis of imperfect and unevenly preserved traces, is better understood as a discipline than as a defeat. It obliges the historian to state her guiding questions openly, to weigh the silences of the record as carefully as its assertions, and to hold her conclusions as revisable in the light of new evidence or sharper questions. Readers, for their part, are invited to judge a historical account not by whether it achieves an impossible neutrality but by the range of evidence it engages, the rival explanations it takes seriously, and the candor with which it marks the limits of what it cannot know.

passage.title: psg-ps-9
passage.body:
Sociologists analyzed how a chronic illness is understood and managed in a mid-sized city. Using surveys and interviews, they documented three patterns. First, physicians and hospitals coordinated with schools and workplaces so that ill members could be temporarily excused from normal duties while being expected to seek treatment and cooperate with doctors. Second, patients with more education and income obtained diagnoses and specialist care far faster than poorer patients, who often relied on crowded clinics; the researchers traced this to differences in insurance, flexible work hours, and familiarity with medical institutions. Third, behaviors once seen as ordinary or as moral failings - such as persistent sadness or restlessness - were increasingly defined and treated as medical conditions.
The team framed each pattern with a different theoretical lens. The coordinated excusing of the sick was described as an institution maintaining social stability by managing how illness disrupts roles. The unequal access was described in terms of groups with different amounts of resources and power competing for a scarce good. The redefinition of ordinary behaviors as illnesses was described as a process by which the meaning of 'sickness' is negotiated and expanded within a society. In interviews, patients described how a formal diagnosis changed how others treated them, sometimes granting sympathy and sometimes attaching stigma. The authors noted that the fastest-growing diagnoses clustered among specific age groups, and that the city's aging population was projected to raise overall demand for chronic-disease care over the coming decades.

passage.title: psg-cp-6
passage.body:
Water's ability to dissolve ions and to resist changes in acidity underlies much of physiology. Blood plasma is held near pH 7.4 largely by the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer: dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which dissociates into a hydrogen ion and bicarbonate, H2CO3 H+ + HCO3-. The effective pKa for this equilibrium in plasma is about 6.1. Normally the concentration of bicarbonate is roughly twenty times that of dissolved carbonic acid, and the lungs and kidneys adjust the two components to hold that ratio steady. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation links the pH to the ratio of conjugate base to weak acid.
To study buffering directly, students titrate a weak acid at 25 C. They place 0.10 M acetic acid (pKa 4.74) in a flask and add sodium hydroxide from a burette while a pH meter records the curve. Early on the pH rises slowly through a buffering plateau; near the end it climbs steeply through the equivalence point, where exactly enough base has been added to neutralize all the acid. A separate reference solution at 25 C is measured to have a pH of 3.0.
The students note that at 25 C the ion product of water fixes pH + pOH = 14, and that a solution's acidity reflects the balance between hydrogen and hydroxide ions produced when water and solutes interact. They also test the buffer's resilience by adding a few drops of strong acid to the bicarbonate system and to plain water, comparing how far the pH of each moves.

Forward blood-typing mixes unknown cells with known reagents. Agglutination is scored + or − after 60 s on a slide. Three unknown samples are tested.

Reagent | Person W | Person X | Person Y
Anti-A | + | − | −
Anti-B | − | + | −
Anti-D (Rh) | + | + | −

ABO antibodies in plasma are the reciprocal of the antigens on the person’s red cells (Landsteiner). Which plasma antibodies and Rh status follow?

choices.text: All three have anti-A and anti-B because agglutination reagents are antibodies
W: anti-B, Rh+; X: anti-A, Rh+; Y: anti-A and anti-B, Rh−
W: anti-A, Rh+; X: anti-B, Rh+; Y: none, Rh−
W: anti-A and anti-B, Rh−; X: none, Rh+; Y: anti-D only

items.explanation: W cells agglutinate with anti-A only, so W is group A and therefore circulates anti-B, not anti-A. X is group B and circulates anti-A. Y cells react with neither anti-A nor anti-B, so Y is group O and has both anti-A and anti-B. Anti-D agglutination marks Rh+ for W and X; Y is Rh−. Reversing A/B antigens relative to plasma antibodies is the standard Landsteiner trap. Group O plasma is the universal antibody-containing plasma, not an empty plasma. The typing reagents’ identities do not put those same antibodies into every person’s plasma.

distractorRationales.A: Only the reagent wells contain those antibodies; a person’s plasma antibodies are complementary to the antigens they lack.
distractorRationales.C: That option assigns each person the antibody against their own antigen, which would agglutinate their own cells in vivo.
distractorRationales.D: W is A-positive, not AB-negative; X is B, not AB; Y is O Rh−, whose plasma has anti-A and anti-B, not anti-D as the defining feature here.

items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's argument?

choices.text: Newton also worked on alchemy in his private notebooks.

items.explanation: B directly contradicts the passage's central claim by supplying genuine counter-examples of isolated discovery with no collective scaffolding. A, C and D are either irrelevant details or compatible with the author's thesis rather than undermining it. To weaken an argument, a new fact has to attack the link between the evidence and the conclusion — not just add an unrelated detail. Ask: does this fact make the author's conclusion less likely to be true, or does it just sit beside the argument without touching it? Memory tip: Picture the argument as a table standing on legs (its supporting claims). A weakening fact kicks out a leg; an irrelevant fact just puts something unrelated on the tabletop. Ask which one you're looking at. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: Critical Reasoning · Philosophy of Science
passage.body: For centuries we have told the story of the solitary genius: Newton alone under his apple tree, Curie alone in her laboratory, the writer alone at her desk producing a masterpiece from nothing but personal brilliance. This narrative is comforting because it is simple, and it sells a great many biographies. It is also, historians of science increasingly argue, badly incomplete. Newton corresponded for decades with a network of mathematicians whose incremental work he built on and later minimised in his own accounts. Curie's laboratory depended on instruments, techniques and a body of prior findings assembled by dozens of researchers across Europe. Even the writer's "original" idea usually turns out, on close inspection, to be a recombination of things read, overheard, or absorbed from a wider culture. None of this makes any of these individuals less remarkable. But it does suggest that crediting a single mind for a breakthrough often erases the scaffolding — the teachers, rivals, funders and quiet collaborators — without which that mind would have had nothing to work with.

items.stem: Along a typical systemic pathway, the largest drop in blood pressure occurs across the arterioles. This is because arterioles:

choices.text: are the principal resistance vessels: they present the greatest frictional drop for a given cardiac output
are the highest-pressure vessels in the circuit, so more of the pressure head is spent there by definition
have the smallest total cross-sectional area, producing the highest linear speed and therefore the largest Bernoulli pressure drop
contain one-way valves, so pressure must fall to zero on the downstream side of each valve

items.explanation: In a series circuit the pressure drop across a segment is ΔP = Q R. Cardiac output Q is the same through aorta, arteries, arterioles, capillaries, and veins; the segment with the largest resistance therefore takes the largest ΔP. Arterioles combine modest radii with muscular walls that set tone, making them the main resistance vessels and the site of the steepest pressure fall. The aorta, not the arteriole, is the highest-pressure vessel. Total area is smallest and speed greatest in the aorta, so a Bernoulli argument aimed at arterioles is pointed at the wrong segment. Venous valves do not explain the arteriolar pressure drop.

distractorRationales.B: The aorta and large arteries are the high-pressure reservoir. Pressure is already lower as blood enters the arterioles; what is distinctive is the drop across them, not a peak value inside them.
distractorRationales.C: Total cross-sectional area is smallest in the aorta, where speed is greatest. Arterioles are not the Bernoulli-fast segment, and the physiologic pressure drop is resistive (Poiseuille), not a reversible Bernoulli trade.
distractorRationales.D: One-way valves are in veins (and lymphatics), not arterioles. They prevent backflow; they are not the reason arterial pressure falls.

passage.title: The Archive Test (1975)

items.stem: A CNS axon loses myelin internodes in a demyelinating plaque. Conduction through the affected stretch:

choices.text: slows or fails because local-circuit current leaks across internodal membrane
speeds up because more axonal membrane is now exposed to ions
reverses its physiologic direction and travels only toward the soma
converts the axon into a chemical synapse in white matter as the default repair

items.explanation: Myelin increases effective membrane resistance and decreases capacitance, so depolarizing current is funneled to the next node (saltatory conduction). When internodes are stripped, current leaks across the internodal axolemma, the length constant falls, and the next node may not reach threshold—slowing or block. Simply exposing membrane does not speed conduction; it removes the specialization that made conduction fast. Direction reverse and wholesale conversion to a synapse are not the primary physiologic results of demyelination.

distractorRationales.B: Exposed internodal membrane is a current sink, not a speed advantage. That is why demyelinating disease slows conduction.
distractorRationales.C: Demyelination does not invert the orthodromic rule. Block or slowing can occur in the original direction.
distractorRationales.D: A denuded internodal axon is not automatically a chemical synapse; synapses require active zones, vesicles, and postsynaptic receptors.

items.stem: A population of beetles has varying shell colour. After a change in habitat that increases visibility to predators, darker beetles start being eaten more often. Over many generations, which outcome does natural selection predict?

items.explanation: Natural selection acts on existing variation: individuals whose traits improve survival and reproduction (here, lighter colour, better camouflage) leave more offspring, so that trait becomes more frequent in the population over generations — not within one individual's lifetime. No individual organism "evolves" during its own life. Selection changes the frequency of traits across a population over generations, because individuals with advantageous variations survive/reproduce more. Variation must already exist for selection to act on it. Memory tip: "Survival of the fittest population, not the fittest individual's lifetime": no single beetle chooses to lighten up. items.stem: A rat in a cooled chamber presses a bar that turns on a heat lamp; pressing falls once core temperature is restored. A second, sated rat in a warm cage still works for highly palatable sucrose. Which pairing of theory to finding is most accurate?

passage.title: psg-bb-6
passage.body:
A cell-biology group compared how three different solutes cross the plasma membrane of cultured cells. For each solute they measured the initial rate of uptake into the cell as a function of the solute's external concentration, under conditions where metabolic ATP could be depleted with an inhibitor when desired.
Solute X, a small hydrophobic steroid, entered at a rate that increased linearly with external concentration and did not plateau even at very high concentrations; depleting ATP had no effect on its uptake. Solute Y, a polar sugar, entered at a rate that rose with concentration and then leveled off at a maximum, tracing a curve resembling enzyme saturation; adding a structurally similar sugar reduced Y's uptake, but ATP depletion did not. Solute Z, an ion, was accumulated inside the cell to a concentration far higher than outside, against its concentration gradient; this uptake collapsed when ATP was depleted.
The researchers interpreted the linear, nonsaturable, ATP-independent uptake of X as simple diffusion directly through the lipid bilayer. The saturable, competable, but ATP-independent uptake of Y indicated a finite number of specific membrane transport proteins moving the sugar down its gradient. The accumulation of Z against its gradient, abolished by ATP depletion, indicated a pump doing work at the expense of cellular energy. The experiment thus separated three transport modes using two simple criteria: whether the rate saturates, and whether it requires cellular energy.

passage.title: Gluconeogenic flux in hepatocyte-like cells
passage.body:
Researchers used fictional hepatocyte-like HGL cells to study glucose production from lactate and alanine. Pyruvate generated in the cytosol must enter mitochondria through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC). In the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate carboxylase (PC) uses ATP, bicarbonate, and a biotin cofactor to convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate. Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) then uses GTP to convert oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate. The pathway requires substantial energy input and is sensitive to cellular ATP availability.

Metabolic effects of perturbing gluconeogenesis from lactate and alanine.
Condition | Glucose output (%) | Cytosolic pyruvate (%) | Mitochondrial OAA/malate pool (%) | O2 consumption (%) | ATP/ADP ratio
Control | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 5.0
MPC inhibitor B | 20 | 190 | 35 | 90 | 4.8
PC inhibitor C | 12 | 220 | 28 | 82 | 3.9
PEPCK knockdown | 18 | 120 | 210 | 85 | 4.2
Low-dose ETC inhibitor | 44 | 115 | 82 | 34 | 1.5
Acetyl-CoA analog | 135 | 70 | 155 | 112 | 4.6

Simplified route from lactate and alanine to glucose. — Lactate and alanine are converted to cytosolic pyruvate. Pyruvate enters mitochondria through MPC and is carboxylated by PC to oxaloacetate. Oxaloacetate-derived carbon returns to the cytosol and proceeds through gluconeogenic reactions to form glucose.

items.stem: A three-point testcross of a trihybrid in coupling (ABC/abc × abc/abc) yields eight progeny classes. The two rarest classes are AbC and aBc. Which gene is in the middle of the map?

items.explanation: Parental (nonrecombinant) chromosomes are ABC and abc. A double crossover changes the allele of only the middle locus relative to those parentals. The rarest classes are the double crossovers: AbC and aBc differ from ABC/abc solely at B, so the order is A–B–C with B in the middle. passage.title: psg-bb-11
passage.body:
To characterize kidney function, a renal-physiology team infused test substances into volunteers and measured how the kidneys handled each, using the concept of clearance: the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute. They relied on three markers.
Inulin, a plant polysaccharide, is freely filtered at the glomerulus but neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the tubules. Its clearance therefore equals the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which averaged 125 mL/min in the study. Para-aminohippurate (PAH) is both filtered and actively secreted into the tubule, so nearly all PAH is removed in a single pass; its clearance (about 600 mL/min) approximated the renal plasma flow, a value much larger than GFR. Glucose, by contrast, is freely filtered but then almost completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by carrier proteins; at normal plasma glucose levels its clearance was essentially zero, and none appeared in the urine.
The team then raised plasma glucose experimentally. Below a threshold, urine remained glucose-free. Above the threshold, the reabsorptive carriers became saturated (their transport maximum, or Tm, was exceeded), and glucose spilled into the urine. Because the unreabsorbed glucose held water osmotically within the tubule, urine volume also rose.
The investigators noted that comparing a substance's clearance with the inulin clearance reveals its tubular handling: a clearance below GFR implies net reabsorption, a clearance above GFR implies net secretion, and a clearance equal to GFR implies filtration only.

Bilayer P (di-C16:0): a sharp endotherm peaking at 41 °C.
Bilayer Q (equimolar C16:0 / C16:1): a broader endotherm centred at 18 °C.
Bilayer R (di-C16:0 plus 30 mol% cholesterol): no sharp peak; heat capacity is a low, broad hump from 20–50 °C, and a fluorescence anisotropy probe at 25 °C reports fluidity between the gel-like P and the liquid-like Q.

choices.text: The 41 °C peak of P is protein denaturation; lipids do not show cooperative melting.
Cis unsaturation lowers the gel-to-liquid transition temperature, and cholesterol smears that transition rather than acting as a simple melting-point depressant like the alkene.

Cholesterol in R abolishes the cooperative spike and yields intermediate order at 25 °C, the classic buffering of membrane fluidity rather than a shift of a still-sharp Tm. The traces therefore separate the effects of unsaturation (lower Tm) from cholesterol (damped transition).

passage.title: psg-bb-5
passage.body:
To probe how mitochondria couple fuel oxidation to ATP synthesis, researchers suspended isolated mitochondria in a buffered chamber fitted with an oxygen electrode, so that the rate of oxygen consumption could be followed continuously. Because the electron transport chain uses O2 as its final electron acceptor, oxygen consumption serves as a readout of electron flow.
The team added an oxidizable substrate (to feed electrons into the chain) plus ADP and inorganic phosphate (the raw materials for ATP synthesis). Oxygen consumption rose to a brisk, steady rate, and ATP accumulated in the chamber. They then added oligomycin, a compound that blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase. Oxygen consumption fell almost to zero, and ATP synthesis stopped. Finally, they added 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), a small molecule that ferries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Oxygen consumption surged back to a high rate, yet no ATP was produced; the released energy instead appeared as heat.
The investigators explained the pattern in terms of the proton-motive force. Electron transport pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building an electrochemical gradient; ATP synthase normally lets those protons flow back into the matrix, harnessing the gradient to make ATP. Blocking ATP synthase lets the gradient build until it opposes further pumping, so electron flow (and O2 use) slows. A protonophore like DNP short-circuits the gradient, so electron transport races ahead while its energy is dissipated as heat rather than captured as ATP.

items.explanation: Heating increases the average kinetic energy (speed) of gas particles. At constant volume, faster particles hit the container walls harder and more often, increasing pressure — consistent with Gay-Lussac's Law (P proportional to T at constant V). Think of gas laws through particle motion, not just formulas: temperature reflects average particle speed; pressure comes from particles colliding with walls. Raise temperature at fixed volume -> more forceful/frequent collisions -> higher pressure. This intuition covers Boyle's, Charles's and Gay-Lussac's laws. Memory tip: Picture gas particles as tiny tennis balls bouncing off the container walls: heat them up and they slam the walls faster and more often — "faster particles hit harder," which is why pressure rises. passage.title: psg-ps-7
passage.body:
Researchers studied how people view themselves and explain behavior. In Study 1, community volunteers completed a scale measuring their belief that they could organize and execute the actions needed to reach specific goals. Independently, they rated how much they felt their life outcomes were controlled by their own actions versus by luck or powerful others. Volunteers high on the first measure attempted harder tasks, persisted longer after setbacks, and reported less anxiety. Those who attributed outcomes mostly to outside forces set fewer goals and gave up sooner.
In Study 2, participants read vignettes about a student who failed an exam. When explaining the student's failure, observers most often cited the student's laziness or low ability, rarely mentioning the situation (an unfair test, a family emergency). Yet when participants recalled a time they themselves had failed, they overwhelmingly cited situational causes. In a variation, participants watched a peer perform poorly under obvious time pressure; even so, most still rated the peer as low in ability.
The authors linked Study 1 to two related constructs: a person's belief in their capability to succeed at specific tasks, and a general expectancy about whether outcomes are internally or externally controlled. They interpreted Study 2 as showing a systematic bias in how observers explain others' behavior, together with a divergence between how people explain their own versus others' outcomes. They stressed that these attribution tendencies operate even when situational information is clearly available.

items.stem: Puromycin, a structural analog of the 3′ end of aminoacyl-tRNA, is added to actively elongating ribosomes. Nascent chains are released as peptidyl-puromycin. Which mechanistic description is most accurate?

choices.text: Puromycin binds the E site and hydrolyzes the P-site ester by mimicking release factor RF3 GTPase.
Puromycin occupies the A site; the peptidyl transferase center forms a peptide bond to its amino group, but puromycin is not tethered by codon–anticodon pairing, so the chain dissociates.
Puromycin covalently cross-links 16S rRNA to the Shine–Dalgarno sequence, aborting initiation without affecting elongating ribosomes.
Puromycin inhibits aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, so ribosomes stall with empty A sites and RF1 then cleaves the P-site chain.

items.explanation: Puromycin’s amino-nucleoside mimics the 3′ aminoacyl end of tRNA and binds in the ribosomal A site without mRNA decoding. The peptidyl transferase ribozyme (23S or 28S rRNA) transfers the nascent chain to puromycin’s free amino group, forming a genuine peptide bond. Because puromycin is not held by codon–anticodon pairing or a full tRNA body, peptidyl-puromycin drops off, terminating elongation. It does not act in the E site as an RF3 mimic, does not specifically freeze initiation via 16S–Shine–Dalgarno crosslinking in this assay, and does not primarily empty the A site by blocking synthetases.

distractorRationales.A: Release factors promote hydrolysis in the peptidyl transferase center; puromycin is an A-site acceptor substrate, not an E-site GTPase mimic.
distractorRationales.C: The classic puromycin reaction releases nascent chains from elongating ribosomes; it is not an initiation-only 16S cross-link.
distractorRationales.D: Peptidyl-puromycin formation shows that the chain is transferred to the drug, not hydrolyzed by RF1 after a charging blockade.

passage.title: Tone as Rule (1982)
passage.body: Leo Nyathi published “Tone as Rule” in 1982 after a season in vaccine campaigns. The argument is that the archive is a construction site, not a warehouse. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: A biochemist wants a buffer at pH 7.2. Which weak acid is the most appropriate starting point (effective buffering is typically pKa ± 1)?

choices.text: HCl, which has no pKa in water because it is strong

items.explanation: A buffer resists pH change best when pH is within about one unit of pKa, because both HA and A− are then present in useful amounts. Imidazole’s pKa near 7.0 matches the target pH 7.2, so the ratio [A−]/[HA] is close to 1.6 and both species are abundant. Acetic acid’s pKa 4.76 is 2.4 units away, so the acid would be almost fully deprotonated and the buffer capacity at 7.2 would be poor. Phenol’s pKa 10 is similarly too far. A strong acid such as HCl is fully dissociated and does not establish a conjugate pair with a useful pKa in water.

distractorRationales.B: Acetic acid buffers near pH 4–6. At pH 7.2 it is almost entirely acetate, so added acid or base changes pH sharply.
distractorRationales.C: Phenol buffers near pH 9–11, not 7.2; at pH 7.2 it is almost fully protonated.
distractorRationales.D: Strong acids do not form buffers; there is no undissociated HA reservoir in water to absorb added base.

Memory tip: "Transcription in, Translation out": DNA is transcribed into mRNA inside the nucleus, then mRNA is translated into protein at the ribosome. items.stem: Which candidate thesis for a Task A set on public expertise is still a thesis but is too brittle to control under time, and which is stronger?

choices.text: Brittle: “Anyone who questions a specialist is an enemy of democracy.” Stronger: “Democratic equality of standing is not the same as equality of expertise; a public that cannot tell the difference will harm the people in waiting rooms first.”
Brittle: any sentence with a semicolon. Stronger: a sentence that never takes a side.
Brittle: the stronger thesis in A, because Task A requires absolute slogans. Stronger: “Experts are always right.”
Brittle: all theses; Task A should only narrate a childhood memory of a teacher.

items.explanation: A thesis can be clear without being a bludgeon. The first sentence in A collapses questioning into enmity and will force the essay into cartoon villains. The second keeps a hard distinction—standing versus expertise—and names a harmed public (waiting rooms) without claiming specialists are sacred. That is still evaluative. B treats punctuation as vice and praises sidelessness. C inverts the standard: slogans are what make essays brittle. D misassigns the personal-memory task to A. Under time, a precise distinction is easier to illustrate than an absolute war on questions.

distractorRationales.B: Semicolons are irrelevant; refusing a side is the survey problem, not a virtue of Task A.
distractorRationales.C: Absolute slogans are harder to defend and invite strawmen; “experts are always right” is the brittle form.
distractorRationales.D: Childhood memory of a teacher is Task B territory if it stays personal; it is not the required form of Task A.

items.stem: Trypsin is stored in the pancreas as trypsinogen, which has very low activity until a peptide bond is cleaved and the new N-terminus forms a salt bridge that orders the oxyanion hole. A mutation allows trypsinogen to autoactivate inside acinar cells. Which clinical-level consequence is most directly expected from this loss of zymogen control?

choices.text: Complete inability to digest dietary protein because trypsin can never become active
Conversion of trypsin into an aminotransferase that no longer hydrolyzes peptides
Irreversible competitive inhibition of amylase by the uncleaved activation peptide

items.explanation: Zymogen storage is a physiological control that keeps a dangerous protease silent until it reaches the intestinal lumen, where enterokinase and trypsin itself generate active enzyme. Premature autoactivation inside the pancreas produces active trypsin among abundant protein substrates, including other zymogens, launching a cascade of autodigestion and inflammation. The mutation described increases, not decreases, activity in the wrong compartment, so dietary protein digestion is not the primary failure. The enzyme remains a hydrolase, not an aminotransferase, and the vignette does not implicate amylase inhibition.

distractorRationales.B: Autoactivation creates active trypsin; the problem is location and timing, not absence of activity.
distractorRationales.C: A zymogen-processing defect does not reclassify trypsin as a PLP-dependent aminotransferase.
distractorRationales.D: There is no mechanistic link from trypsinogen autoactivation to competitive inhibition of amylase.

items.stem:
A 10.00 g sample of boron contains 19.9 atom % 10B (10.013 u) and 80.1 atom % 11B (11.009 u). The average atomic mass is 0.199(10.013) + 0.801(11.009) = 10.811 u. Mass of an isotope in the sample = (atom fraction × isotope mass / average mass) × 10.00 g.
What mass of the sample is 10B?

choices.text: 1.99 g, taking 19.9 atom % as 19.9% by mass
8.01 g, taking 80.1 atom % as the 10B mass fraction
5.00 g, an unweighted half of the sample

items.explanation: Mass fraction of 10B = (0.199 × 10.013) / 10.811 = 1.993 / 10.811 = 0.1844, so the mass is 0.1844 × 10.00 g = 1.84 g. Atom percent is not mass percent because 10B atoms are lighter than 11B atoms; using 19.9% of 10.00 g (1.99 g) slightly overestimates the 10B mass. The 80.1% figure belongs to 11B atoms, not to 10B. An arbitrary 5.00 g split ignores both the abundances and the two isotopic masses given in the stem.

distractorRationales.A: Atom % equals mass % only if the isotopes have identical mass; here 10B is lighter, so its mass fraction is 18.4%, not 19.9%.
distractorRationales.B: 80.1% is the atom fraction of 11B, not of 10B.
distractorRationales.D: The isotopes are not present in equal mass; the weighted mass of 10B is 1.84 g.

passage.title: psg-cars-8
passage.body:
Ritual occupies a paradoxical place in modern social thought. On one hand, it has been systematically studied as a fundamental mechanism of social solidarity: shared symbolic performances bind participants together, express and reinforce collective values, and mark the transitions — birth, initiation, marriage, death — that punctuate the human life course. On the other hand, modern societies tend to regard ritual with a degree of unease, as if elaborate ceremony were a relic of pre-rational ages unsuited to a world governed by science and voluntary choice.
Early sociological and anthropological accounts emphasized the integrative functions of ritual. Ceremonies, on this view, do not merely reflect an already-existing social order; they actively produce and sustain it. When a community gathers to mark a harvest, a coronation, or a national founding, participants do not simply observe an event — they enact membership in a collectivity that transcends any individual. The shared emotional experience generated by such occasions — what early theorists called collective effervescence — temporarily dissolves the boundaries between self and group, creating a felt sense of unity that persists in social memory long after the ceremony has concluded.
Later anthropologists complicated this functionalist picture by attending to the internal diversity and contestation that characterize real rituals. Ceremonies are rarely performed identically across time or across the different status groups within a community. The ruling class and the subjugated, men and women, elders and youth — each may experience the same ceremony quite differently, and the ritual may serve to reinforce not solidarity across the board but specific hierarchies of power. From this perspective, treating ritual purely as a mechanism of integration ignores its role in legitimating and reproducing asymmetric social arrangements.
A third approach draws attention to ritual's cognitive and communicative dimensions. Rituals encode information in a form — embodied action, sensory symbol, repeated performance — that is particularly durable and memorable. Unlike propositional statements that can be contested or forgotten, knowledge embedded in ritual is resistant to revision precisely because it is experienced rather than merely asserted. This explains why ritual tends to be invoked when other communicative resources fail: in the face of death, catastrophic loss, or radical uncertainty, shared performance provides a structure of meaning that discursive language alone cannot furnish. Grief rituals in particular demonstrate how embodied collective action can sustain communities through episodes of radical disruption that would otherwise threaten social fabric. The contrast with ordinary instruction is telling. A fact conveyed in a lecture can be doubted the moment the lecture ends; a truth rehearsed year after year in fasting, procession, or song is renewed in the body and rarely submitted to cross-examination at all. This is why communities so often entrust their most load-bearing commitments — who belongs, what is owed to the dead, which obligations the future imposes — not to argument but to observance. The very features that make ritual knowledge conservative, and sometimes an obstacle to reform, are also what allow it to hold a group together when argument alone would divide it, carrying shared meaning across generations that never meet.
Each of these accounts captures something genuine. Ritual is simultaneously a mechanism of solidarity, an arena of power and contestation, and a form of embodied knowledge. Understanding any particular ceremony requires attending to all three dimensions and to the historical context that shapes their relative salience.

items.stem: The Ksp of AgCl is 1.8 × 10^−10. Compared with pure water, the molar solubility of AgCl in 0.10 M NaCl is:

choices.text: higher, because extra chloride complexes all of the silver and pulls more AgCl into solution.
unchanged, because Ksp depends only on temperature.
lower, because the common chloride ion appears in Ksp = [Ag+][Cl−], so [Ag+] must fall when [Cl−] is already 0.10 M.
lower because Na+ precipitates NaCl and removes chloride.

items.explanation: AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag+ + Cl− has Ksp = [Ag+][Cl−]. In 0.10 M NaCl, [Cl−] is fixed near 0.10 M, so [Ag+] = Ksp/[Cl−] ≈ 1.8 × 10^−9 M, which is also the molar solubility. In pure water the solubility is √Ksp ≈ 1.3 × 10^−5 M, about 10^4-fold higher. The common-ion effect therefore decreases solubility. Ksp is unchanged with added NaCl at constant temperature; what changes is how that product is partitioned between [Ag+] and [Cl−]. Dilute chloride does not create enough [AgCl2]− here to reverse the effect, and NaCl is already dissolved, not precipitating.

distractorRationales.A: High [Cl−] can form [AgCl2]− at much larger chloride concentrations, but the standard common-ion result at 0.10 M is suppressed solubility, not enhancement.
distractorRationales.B: Ksp is constant at a given T, but solubility is not; added Cl− changes the equilibrium position.
distractorRationales.D: NaCl is highly soluble; Na+ does not precipitate and remove the common ion under these conditions.

passage.title: Pentose phosphate pathway flux during oxidative stress
passage.body:
A fictional erythroid cell line lacks mitochondria after differentiation and relies on glycolysis for ATP. It also uses the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) to generate NADPH for reduction of glutathione. Researchers compared wild-type cells with cells expressing a mutant glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD-M). They exposed cells to an oxidant and measured redox status, lactate release, and radiolabeled carbon dioxide production from glucose labeled at carbon 1 or carbon 6. In the oxidative PPP, carbon 1 of glucose 6-phosphate is released as CO2 while NADPH is produced.

Metabolic responses to oxidant exposure.
Cells and condition | NADPH/NADP+ | GSH/GSSG | Lactate release (%) | 14CO2 from [1-14C]glucose (%) | 14CO2 from [6-14C]glucose (%) | Viable cells (%)
Wild type, basal | 4.0 | 8.0 | 100 | 100 | 5 | 98
Wild type, +oxidant | 2.0 | 4.5 | 120 | 180 | 8 | 92
G6PD-M, basal | 1.5 | 3.0 | 110 | 35 | 5 | 95
G6PD-M, +oxidant | 0.4 | 0.8 | 145 | 40 | 7 | 55

Purified G6PD kinetic parameters.
Enzyme | Km for glucose 6-phosphate (mM) | Relative Vmax (%)
Wild-type G6PD | 0.08 | 100
G6PD-M | 0.09 | 30

Relationship between glycolysis and the oxidative PPP. — Glucose 6-phosphate can enter glycolysis or the oxidative PPP. The oxidative PPP produces NADPH and ribulose 5-phosphate, releasing carbon 1 as CO2. Glycolysis in these differentiated erythroid cells ends mainly in lactate formation.

items.stem: In a Hubel and Wiesel-style recording from cat striate cortex, a cell fires briskly to a thin bar of light at 30° in a small receptive field and is silent to the orthogonal bar in the same place. Diffuse illumination of the whole field also fails to drive it. The cell is most likely which kind of unit?

choices.text: A retinal ganglion cell with an on-center, off-surround receptive field
A lateral geniculate relay cell summing concentric spots from one eye
A V1 simple cell whose elongated on-region is orientation-selective
A photoreceptor whose photopigment absorbs only 30° polarized light

items.explanation: Hubel and Wiesel showed that many V1 simple cells have elongated, antagonistic subregions and fire to bars of a preferred orientation. Concentric center–surround fields dominate retina and LGN and would respond to a small spot or to a bar of any orientation that covers the center. Photoreceptors are not orientation-tuned in this way and do not require a cortical bar. Feature detection in primary visual cortex is the named mechanism that matches the recording.

distractorRationales.A: Ganglion cells have concentric fields and would not show this sharp orientation tuning.
distractorRationales.B: LGN cells remain largely concentric and spot-like, not bar-and-orientation selective.
distractorRationales.D: Photoreceptors encode wavelength and intensity, not bar orientation in visual space.

items.stem: A tetrahedral carbon has Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priorities 1 = Br, 2 = CH2OH, 3 = CH3, and 4 = H. With H pointing away from the observer, moving from Br to CH2OH to CH3 traces a counterclockwise path. What is the configuration?

items.explanation: When the lowest-priority substituent (H) points away, a counterclockwise 1→2→3 sequence is the definition of the S configuration. Clockwise would be R. E/Z nomenclature describes relative positions of higher-priority groups on a double bond, not a tetrahedral stereocenter. The carbon here has four different substituents (Br, CH2OH, CH3, H), so it is a stereocenter and is chiral. Reversing the assignment because H is already away is the usual error; no extra reversal is needed in this viewing geometry.

items.stem: Using Table 1, which description best matches the effect of Compound P on the dehydrogenase?

choices.text: Competitive inhibition: apparent K_m rises while V_max is unchanged, so saturating S fully restores uninhibited velocity.
Uncompetitive inhibition: apparent K_m and V_max fall by the same factor, leaving V_max/K_m unchanged.
Noncompetitive inhibition: apparent K_m is unchanged while V_max is halved, so inhibition persists at saturating S.
Irreversible active-site alkylation: dialysis cannot restore activity because a covalent adduct has destroyed catalytic sites.

items.explanation: Table 1 shows that 2.0 μM Compound P leaves apparent K_m at 0.50 mM, identical to the uninhibited enzyme, while apparent V_max falls from 80 to 40 nmol s^{-1} mg^{-1}. That pattern is the diagnostic of pure noncompetitive inhibition: the inhibitor does not alter substrate affinity in the Michaelis sense but lowers the concentration of productive enzyme, so the remaining activity saturates at a reduced ceiling. Competitive inhibition would have raised K_m at constant V_max, and uncompetitive inhibition would have lowered both parameters together. The dialysis result in the passage rules out irreversible covalent inactivation, which would not wash out.

distractorRationales.A: Raised K_m at constant V_max is Compound Q’s pattern in Table 1, not P’s; P does not shift K_m.
distractorRationales.B: A matched decrease in K_m and V_max is Compound R’s pattern; P’s K_m does not fall.
distractorRationales.D: The passage states that dialysis restored full activity after exposure to P, so the inhibition is reversible, not a covalent kill of active sites.

passage.title: Reversible inhibitors of a cytosolic dehydrogenase
passage.body:
Investigators purified a cytosolic NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase that oxidizes a small-molecule metabolite S. Initial velocities were measured at 25 °C by following NADH formation in 1.00 mL assays. Nonlinear fits of v versus [S] produced the apparent Michaelis constants and maximal velocities in Table 1. When an inhibitor was present, its concentration was 2.0 μM in the assay mix. Dialysis that removed unbound compound restored full catalytic activity after incubation with P, Q, or R, indicating reversible binding rather than covalent inactivation. Active-site titration with a tight-binding stoichiometric inactivator found 4.0 nmol of catalytic sites per milligram of protein.

Table 1. Apparent kinetic parameters from initial-rate fits

| Condition | Apparent K_m (mM) | Apparent V_max (nmol s^{-1} mg^{-1}) |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------------------------|
| No inhibitor | 0.50 | 80 |
| Compound P (2.0 μM) | 0.50 | 40 |
| Compound Q (2.0 μM) | 1.50 | 80 |
| Compound R (2.0 μM) | 0.25 | 40 |

In a separate progress-curve experiment, 25 μg of the same enzyme protein was mixed with 0.50 mM S and no inhibitor in a 1.00 mL reaction. Product concentration was recorded as a function of time (Table 2).

Table 2. Product appearance at [S]_0 = 0.50 mM without inhibitor

| Time (s) | [Product] (μM) |
|----------|----------------|
| 0 | 0.0 |
| 10 | 9.9 |
| 20 | 19.6 |
| 30 | 29.1 |
| 60 | 56.2 |
| 120 | 102.4 |

items.stem: A quantitative trait (beak depth) is measured before and after a drought. Surviving birds are those with either very shallow or very deep beaks; intermediates die. After several generations the phenotypic variance increases and the distribution becomes bimodal. Which mode of selection occurred?

choices.text: Stabilizing selection, which removes extremes and shrinks variance about an intermediate optimum.
Directional selection, which shifts the mean toward one extreme without favoring both tails.
Disruptive (diversifying) selection, which favors both extremes over the mean and can increase variance and bimodality.
Sexual selection based on heterozygosity at MHC loci, which does not act on beak depth during a drought.

items.explanation: Stabilizing selection culls both tails and reduces variance about an intermediate optimum. Directional selection favors one tail and shifts the mean. Disruptive selection favors both extremes over the intermediate, which is what the drought did for beak depth. After several generations, increased variance and a bimodal distribution are the expected phenotypic signatures and can contribute to divergence if mating becomes assortative. MHC-based mate choice is not indicated by survival as a function of beak depth during a resource crash.

distractorRationales.A: Stabilizing selection would have favored intermediate beaks and decreased variance, the opposite of the survival pattern and the later bimodality.
distractorRationales.B: Directional selection would enrich only one tail (deeper or shallower), not both, and would move the mean rather than split the distribution.
distractorRationales.D: The fitness function is explicitly beak depth under drought; MHC sexual selection is an unrelated mechanism.

passage.title: Conditioning and Sound Sensitivity in a Virtual Environment
passage.body:
A behavioral science lab used a virtual environment to study how neutral sounds can acquire emotional significance. During acquisition, participants repeatedly heard Tone A immediately before an unpleasant but safe burst of white noise. Tone B was presented equally often but was never followed by the white noise. Skin conductance response was recorded as an index of autonomic arousal. In an extinction phase, both tones were presented without the white noise. In a final test, participants heard Tone C, which was acoustically similar to Tone A but slightly lower in pitch.

Mean skin conductance response in arbitrary units
Phase and stimulus | Mean response
Late acquisition: Tone A | 0.78
Late acquisition: Tone B | 0.22
Late extinction: Tone A | 0.31
Late extinction: Tone B | 0.20
Final test: Tone C | 0.49

Stimulus arrangement — Tone A and Tone C were similar in pitch, whereas Tone B was clearly distinct from both.

passage.title: psg-cars-13
passage.body:
The global spread of American popular culture -- film, music, fast food, digital platforms -- has prompted a long-running debate about whether this constitutes cultural imperialism: the imposition of one civilization's values and forms of life on peoples who have not chosen them. Critics of globalization in this register argue that the sheer economic asymmetry between media corporations based in wealthy nations and the domestic cultural industries of smaller, poorer societies creates a structural disadvantage. When production costs and distribution networks favor global products over local ones, communities find their own cultural expressions marginalized not by legal prohibition but by market logic. The displacement is quiet, cumulative, and often more thoroughgoing than any direct act of censorship could achieve.
The cultural imperialism thesis has been challenged on several grounds. The most telling challenge is empirical: audiences in different societies do not passively absorb global content but actively interpret it through their own cultural frameworks, adapting, subverting, and hybridizing imported forms in ways that produce genuinely new cultural expressions. The global spread of hip-hop, for instance, has generated distinctive local variants -- from Algerian rai-inflected rap to Japanese-language hip-hop -- that bear the unmistakable imprint of their cultural contexts. Reception is not passive consumption, and the audience is not an empty vessel waiting to be filled.
A second challenge concerns the directionality of cultural flows. While American products dominate certain global markets, cultural influence runs in multiple directions: South Korean popular music has captured youth audiences worldwide, Indian cinema occupies an outsized position in African and diaspora markets, and African musical rhythms have profoundly shaped what is recognized as American popular music in the first place. To speak of unidirectional cultural imperialism flattens a more complex and multi-directional reality in which no single center fully controls the terms of global cultural exchange. Nor is the traffic confined to entertainment. Telenovelas produced in Latin America command devoted audiences from Eastern Europe to the Philippines; Nigeria's prolific film industry circulates across the African continent and its diasporas; culinary forms, religious movements, and styles of dress migrate along routes that begin far from the wealthy media capitals. None of this shows that the largest studios and platforms have ceased to enjoy real advantages of scale and reach. It shows, rather, that 'flow' is the wrong picture if it implies a single faucet and a passive drain: global culture is better imagined as a dense weave of currents, some far stronger than others, but none issuing from a lone source.
Yet critics of the critique resist premature optimism. They argue that hybrid cultural forms, however creative, may still be produced and distributed through infrastructure owned by global corporations, whose financial interests shape which hybrids achieve wide distribution and which remain marginal. The creative agency of local audiences does not by itself dismantle the structural power asymmetries that determine which voices are amplified and which are muffled in global cultural markets.
This debate resists tidy resolution because it operates at two levels that its participants often conflate: the empirical level of how people actually engage with global cultural content, and the structural level of which actors control the conditions under which such engagement occurs. Progress requires holding both levels in view simultaneously.

items.explanation: Sodium (a metal) transfers an electron to chlorine (a non-metal), forming oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction (ionic bond). In water, two hydrogen atoms share electrons with oxygen (covalent bonds) since both are non-metals. As a rule of thumb: ionic bonds form when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal, creating charged ions that attract. Covalent bonds form when two non-metals share electron pairs. This single rule predicts bond type for most GAMSAT-level compounds. Memory tip: "Metals give, non-metals share": a metal + non-metal pairing means one atom GIVES away an electron (ionic bond); two non-metals SHARE electrons because neither wants to give theirs up (covalent bond). Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: The Metric (1982)
passage.body: Ingrid Nilsen published “The Metric” in 1982 after a season in municipal archives. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Rotenone blocks electron transfer within Complex I. In isolated mitochondria, oxidation of malate/glutamate (NADH-linked) stops, but addition of succinate restores oxygen consumption and some ATP synthesis, with a lower P/O ratio. Why does succinate bypass the block?

choices.text: Succinate dehydrogenase reduces ubiquinone via Complex II, entering the chain after Complex I.
Succinate is oxidized by cytochrome c oxidase directly to fumarate and water.
Rotenone is competitive with succinate, so succinate displaces the inhibitor from Complex I.
Succinate donates electrons to NAD+, reversing Complex I despite rotenone.

items.explanation: Rotenone prevents NADH dehydrogenase from reducing ubiquinone, so NADH-linked substrates cannot feed the chain. Complex II oxidizes succinate and reduces the same ubiquinone pool downstream of the rotenone block. Electrons then continue through Complexes III and IV to oxygen, restoring respiration. Because Complex I is still out of the circuit, those electrons miss Complex I proton pumping and support a lower P/O ratio, matching the stem. Succinate is not a substrate of Complex IV, rotenone is not a succinate-competitive ligand on Complex I, and succinate does not reverse Complex I by reducing NAD+ in this bypass experiment.

distractorRationales.B: Cytochrome c oxidase reduces O2, not succinate. Succinate’s dehydrogenase is Complex II, which feeds Q rather than donating electrons directly to Complex IV.
distractorRationales.C: Rotenone binds Complex I, not the succinate site of Complex II. Excess succinate does not competitively strip rotenone off Complex I as the bypass mechanism.
distractorRationales.D: The educational bypass is forward electron flow from Complex II to Q, not reverse electron transfer through blocked Complex I to NAD+.

passage.title: Local Knowledge (1975)
passage.body: In “Local Knowledge” (1975), Marta Górska writes from inside urban cycling. The argument is that a metric can become the mission that it was supposed to measure. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Mean arterial pressure is modeled as MAP = CO x TPR (central venous pressure neglected). A drug halves TPR while cardiac output is experimentally held constant. MAP is expected to:

choices.text: Halve, because the product CO x TPR scales linearly with TPR at fixed CO
Double, because resistance and pressure are inversely related at fixed flow in this model
Remain unchanged, because MAP is set only by heart rate
Fall to zero, because any vasodilation abolishes arterial pressure

items.explanation: Ohm's-law analog for the circulation is (MAP - CVP) = CO x TPR. With CVP ~ 0 and CO clamped, MAP is directly proportional to TPR, so a 50% TPR cut halves MAP. Flow Q = DeltaP / R rearranged is DeltaP = Q R; there is no inversion that would double pressure when R falls. Heart rate influences CO but is not an independent setter of MAP once CO is fixed. Vasodilation lowers MAP; it does not require MAP to reach zero unless TPR itself is zero. Reflex tachycardia would normally raise CO, but that pathway is excluded by the clamp.

distractorRationales.B: At fixed flow, pressure drop falls when resistance falls; it does not double.
distractorRationales.C: HR can change CO, but CO is held constant here, so MAP tracks TPR.
distractorRationales.D: Halving TPR halves MAP in the model; it does not imply zero pressure.

items.stem: A ray traveling in aqueous humor (n = 1.33) strikes the anterior surface of the lens (n = 1.40) at 30 degrees to the normal. The transmitted ray:

Transparency does not forbid refraction; it only means some light is transmitted rather than absorbed.

items.stem: A PCR is designed to amplify a 400 bp genomic target using two oligonucleotide primers. In one tube the reverse primer is omitted. After 30 thermal cycles, that tube is compared with a complete reaction by agarose electrophoresis. Which result is most likely?

choices.text: Exponential amplification still occurs because Taq polymerase synthesizes both strands from a single primer by looping the template.
The yield of the 400 bp band is identical because primers are needed only to set melting temperature, not to prime DNA synthesis.
A bright smear of random genomic fragments appears because Taq initiates de novo at every nick independently of primers.
Exponential amplification of the defined 400 bp amplicon fails; at best, linear copying from the remaining primer produces heterogeneous products that do not accumulate as a discrete band.

items.explanation: Exponential PCR requires two primers that anneal to opposite strands so that each newly made strand becomes a template for the other primer in the next cycle. With only the forward primer, Taq can copy the original template in a linear fashion, generating single-stranded products of heterogeneous length that do not define a uniformly accumulating 400 bp duplex. Taq cannot loop to copy both strands from one primer, primers are 3′-OH substrates rather than mere Tm sensors, and primer-independent de novo initiation at nicks does not produce a specific, exponentially amplified target band.

distractorRationales.A: Taq extends a primer 5′→3′ on a linear template; it does not convert one primer into a two-strand exponential engine by looping.
distractorRationales.B: Without both primers there is no geometric amplification of a defined amplicon; Tm is a property of duplexes, not a substitute for priming.
distractorRationales.C: Taq is primer-dependent under PCR conditions; random nick initiation would not specifically explain loss of the 400 bp product relative to the complete reaction.

passage.title: Critical Reasoning · Literary Tone & Inference
passage.body: The chair called the meeting to order at exactly nine, though half the room was still finding chairs. She thanked everyone for their punctuality with a smile that did not reach her eyes, then spent the next forty minutes explaining, in exhaustive detail, why the decision that mattered had already been made without them. When someone finally asked a question, she paused just long enough to make the silence uncomfortable before answering it with another question. By the time the meeting closed, three action items had been assigned, none of them to her, and everyone filed out thanking her for her time.

passage.title: Who may be loud
passage.body:
Noise ordinances are written as if they were thermometers. A number of decibels is named; a clock hour is named; a fine is attached. The language of public health does real work here: sleep is not a luxury, and a child whose window faces a compressor is not being precious. But the thermometer conceals a second instrument, which is a social sorting device. Cities do not merely suppress loudness. They decide which kinds of loudness will be classified as vitality and which as nuisance, and the decision tracks, with embarrassing regularity, the prestige of the people making the sound.

Walk a mixed street after dark and the taxonomy is audible. A licensed terrace with heaters and a playlist is "activation of the night-time economy." A storefront church whose singing lasts past the same hour is a complaint waiting to be logged. A terrace is a business; a congregation is a disturbance that happens to own a building. Street vendors packing ice and calling prices are "chaos"; a restaurant's Friday overflow onto the pavement is "vibrancy," provided the overflow has paid for a permit. The ear that writes the ordinance has already been trained to hear money as atmosphere and unpaid sound as aggression.

Defenders of the ordinances will say that the issue is volume, not culture. Sometimes it is. A speaker stack aimed at a bedroom is a harm whether the music is sacred or commercial. The author's claim is narrower and more awkward: when two sounds of similar intensity are sorted differently, the sorting is not acoustics. It is a theory of who belongs in the air. "Quiet" is then sold as a natural baseline, like clean water, when it is often an aesthetic associated with certain housing and certain hours of salaried rest. Night-shift workers returning at dawn, whose rest is real, rarely get to define the city's sonic morals. People who sleep when the ordinance writers sleep do.

None of this is a brief for unlimited noise, or for the romance of the unregulated street. A city that cannot protect sleep will punish the poorest first, because they cannot buy distance from compressors. The decent aim is not a louder city but a less hypocritical one: a city that admits that permission to be loud is a scarce good, distributed by licensing, policing, and taste, and that "quality of life" is never only a medical phrase. It is also a claim about whose life is the measure.

The rhetorical trick is hygiene. Once noise is framed as dirt, opposition to a particular sound can wear the costume of sanitation rather than of preference. Dirt, unlike preference, does not have to justify itself at a public meeting. It only has to be pointed at. That is why a campaign against a night market can speak the idiom of rats and refuse even when the photographs show swept stones, and why a campaign for a waterfront festival can speak the idiom of civic joy even when the sound spill is identical. The same wave-form, two moral uniforms.

If the argument holds, then reform is not a new app for logging complaints. It is a requirement that like sounds be given like reasons, and that exemptions be named as political choices rather than as nature. A hospital generator may deserve its exemption. So, perhaps, does a funeral that spills into a street. What cannot be defended is the pretense that the ordinance is only a meter reading. Meters do not know the difference between a hymn and a brand. Officials do, and they should have to say so.

passage.title: The museum as a verb
passage.body:
Conservation used to mean stopping time. A painting was a patient; varnish was a bandage; the ideal was to return the object to a single authentic hour and then prevent further hours from occurring. That ideal had a hidden historiography. It assumed the authentic hour was already known, usually as the artist’s last brushstroke, and that later repairs, soot, liturgy, and even damage were noise.

A newer conservation talk prefers verbs. To museum an object is to keep choosing which traces will remain legible. Cleaning is not the removal of history; it is the promotion of one history over another. The nineteenth-century restorer who “completed” a medieval panel was not more ideological than the twenty-first-century restorer who leaves the lacuna as a paler mute. Both are editors. They differ in which audience they imagine and in how proudly they sign the edit.

Critics of reversible methods sometimes complain that visible fills and honest seams break the spell. They want the old miracle: an untouched past that happens to hang at eye level under LEDs. The complaint is aesthetically sincere and philosophically confused. The spell was always produced with scaffolding, attributions, and lighting. Reversibility is not a refusal of beauty. It is a refusal to trap the next generation inside today’s certainty about what the object “really” was.

There is a colonial edge. Objects that arrived by seizure were often cleaned into a style that made them readable as art in the receiving capital, which is to say, cleaned of the uses that had made them un-museumlike. To restore the pigment without restoring the right of refusal is to complete the seizure in a gentler font. Some institutions now consult source communities about smoke, wear, and whether an object should be seen at all. Consultation is slow and can be theater. It is still a different verb from rescue.

If this sounds like relativism, notice what it does not say. It does not say that all edits are equal, or that pigment chemistry is a matter of taste. It says that technical competence cannot supply the missing decision about which past is being kept available. The decision will be made. Calling it science does not make it less a decision. Calling it care does not either. The more honest museum is the one that can show its verbs.

items.stem: A student plans to write Task B as a film script with camera directions and no interior thought. Which judgment is most accurate?

choices.text: Excellent, because markers award extra marks for genre variety regardless of thinking.
Risky: unless the script form is the only way to show how a family performed itself, the directions will eat minutes and hide the reflective work Task B scores.
Required, because personal writing is invalid in prose.
Excellent if the script copies the plot of a well-known film so the marker will recognise it.

items.explanation: Optional form is a tool, not a bonus genre. A script can show performance—who gets the close-up in a family—but camera directions are expensive under time and often replace the very interiority Task B needs. Unless that showing is the thought, prose will think more per minute. There is no extra-marks-for-genre rule, no ban on prose, and copying a famous film’s plot would be both generic and a copyright problem this bank refuses. The accurate judgment is risk plus a narrow justification. B is that judgment. Choose form last, after the thought is clear.

distractorRationales.A: Markers score thought and control of language, not novelty of format as such.
distractorRationales.C: Prose is the default that still works; it is not invalid.
distractorRationales.D: Borrowing a famous film’s plot is the opposite of particular lived grain, and this trainer does not want reconstructed copyrighted stories.

items.stem: A health campaign tells people that 'nine out of ten people in your neighborhood have received their flu vaccine' rather than describing the vaccine's medical benefits. This strategy most directly exploits which behavioral finding?

choices.text: The tendency to accept defaults, since vaccination appears to be the expected norm
Loss aversion, by implying that unvaccinated people are losing something the majority has gained
The availability heuristic, by making vaccine uptake easy to imagine through social examples
The representativeness heuristic, by making the unvaccinated person feel unlike a typical neighbor

items.explanation: (C) is best: the passage describes nudging as designing choice environments around 'the default option [that] is the one that most people would choose,' and telling people that nine of ten neighbors are vaccinated presents vaccination as exactly that expected, majority choice. (A) fails because nothing in the message is framed as a loss relative to a reference point. (B) misapplies the availability heuristic, which concerns judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind, not conforming to what most people do. (D) misapplies the representativeness heuristic, which concerns judging probability by resemblance to a prototype, not social conformity. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passage.title: psg-cars-9
passage.body:
Classical economic theory rests on a conception of the agent as fundamentally rational: possessed of stable, consistent preferences, capable of processing available information, and motivated to maximize personal utility. This model has extraordinary analytical power. It generates precise, testable predictions and underlies the welfare theorems that have guided economic policy for generations. Yet beginning in the latter decades of the twentieth century, a body of research in behavioral economics accumulated evidence that humans deviate from this ideal in systematic, predictable, and consequential ways.
Among the most robust findings is loss aversion: people respond more strongly to losses than to equivalent gains. The discomfort of losing one hundred dollars is experienced as more intense than the pleasure of gaining the same amount. This asymmetry has significant implications. It helps explain why people hold losing financial assets far longer than rational profit-maximization would recommend — they prefer the pain of waiting to the certain loss of selling. It also explains why contract and policy framings that emphasize avoiding losses are more motivationally effective than those that emphasize equivalent gains.
A second set of findings concerns heuristic judgment under uncertainty. When people lack the time or information to calculate expected values precisely, they rely on cognitive shortcuts that usually suffice but sometimes produce systematic errors. The availability heuristic leads people to estimate the probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind: dramatic events, such as airplane crashes, are overestimated in frequency because they are memorable, while mundane but statistically commoner risks, such as car accidents, are underestimated. The representativeness heuristic leads people to assess probability by how closely an instance resembles a prototypical category member, often ignoring base-rate information entirely. A familiar illustration involves base rates. Told that a quiet, orderly person who loves books was drawn from a group made up mostly of salespeople and only a few librarians, many respondents confidently judge the person a librarian, swayed by resemblance to a stereotype while all but ignoring how rare librarians are in the sample. The mistake is not stupidity but the misfiring of an ordinarily useful strategy: resemblance is frequently a serviceable guide to category membership, and only in cases engineered to pit it against base-rate information does it lead reliably astray. The shortcuts that behavioral research exposes are, in most everyday settings, both fast and surprisingly accurate; they betray us mainly in the artificial problems constructed to reveal their inner workings.
These findings have generated debate about the appropriate policy response. Some argue that behavioral insights justify 'nudging': designing choice environments so that the default option is the one that most people would choose on reflection. Automatic enrollment in retirement savings plans, for instance, exploits the tendency to accept defaults, boosting participation without eliminating freedom of choice. Critics of nudging worry that it is paternalistic, that it manipulates rather than informs, and that it presupposes policymakers know better than individuals what those individuals' reflective preferences actually are.
The behavioral economics literature does not establish that markets always fail or that regulation is always beneficial. It establishes only that the idealized rational actor is an incomplete description of real human psychology, and that understanding how people actually decide is essential to designing institutions that work well in the world as it is.

passage.title: The Caption (1981)
passage.body: In “The Caption” (1981), Naomi Kline writes from inside municipal archives. The argument is that the archive is a construction site, not a warehouse. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Which of the following was deliberately kept constant across all five trials, allowing temperature’s effect to be isolated?

choices.text: The time taken for the reaction to complete.
The identity of the enzyme used across different trials.
The concentration of amylase and starch used in each trial.

items.explanation: The passage states that amylase and starch concentrations were kept constant in every trial. This is what makes it possible to attribute any change in reaction rate specifically to the one variable that was deliberately changed — temperature — rather than to some other difference between trials. A fair test changes only one variable at a time while holding everything else constant. If concentration also varied between trials, you would not be able to tell whether temperature or concentration caused any observed change in rate. Memory tip: "One dial at a time": if you only turn the temperature dial and leave every other dial fixed, any change in outcome can only be blamed on the dial you turned. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: Chemistry · Enzyme Kinetics
passage.body: A student investigates how temperature affects the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction, using an enzyme called amylase to break down starch into sugar. They measure the time taken for a fixed amount of starch to be fully broken down at five different temperatures: 10°C, 20°C, 30°C, 40°C and 50°C, keeping the amylase concentration and starch concentration constant in every trial. The reaction is fastest at 40°C. At 50°C, the reaction is slower than at 40°C, and even slower than at 30°C, despite the higher temperature. At 10°C, the reaction is very slow but still eventually completes.
