Stereology of a hepatocyte with total volume 5000 µm³ gives these volume fractions and counts:
Cytosol 54%; mitochondria 22% (1400 organelles); rough ER 9%; nucleus 8% (1 nucleus); lysosomes 1% (250 organelles); other 6%.
Which numerical comparison is correct?

choices.text: The nucleus occupies 54% of the cell (2700 µm³).
A typical mitochondrion (0.79 µm³) is larger than the nucleus (400 µm³).
Lysosomes occupy more volume than all mitochondria combined (50 µm³ versus 1100 µm³).
Mitochondria together occupy 1100 µm³, which exceeds the 400 µm³ nucleus.

items.explanation: Nuclear volume is 0.08 × 5000 = 400 µm³. Combined mitochondrial volume is 0.22 × 5000 = 1100 µm³, so the mitochondrial population is larger than the nucleus even though each mitochondrion is small (1100/1400 ≈ 0.79 µm³). Cytosol, not the nucleus, is 54%. Lysosomes are only 0.01 × 5000 = 50 µm³, far below 1100 µm³. The arithmetic from the given fractions therefore shows mitochondria as a major volumetric compartment relative to the nucleus.

distractorRationales.A: 54% is the cytosol fraction; the nucleus is 8%, or 400 µm³.
distractorRationales.B: 0.79 µm³ per mitochondrion is much smaller than the 400 µm³ nucleus.
distractorRationales.C: Lysosomes are 50 µm³ versus 1100 µm³ of mitochondria; the inequality is reversed.

Ksp(AgCl) = 1.0 × 10−10 at 25 °C. Two experiments:
(1) AgCl(s) in pure water: Ksp = s2, s = [Ag+] = [Cl−].
(2) AgCl(s) in 0.10 M NaCl: Ksp = [Ag+](0.10).

passage.title: Cartoon: Clinic time
passage.body:
A single-panel cartoon, unsigned, published on a letters page.

Foreground: a waiting-room bench. Four people sit. Above each head a small clock; the hands are at 1:10, 2:40, 4:15, and 9:50. None of the clocks match the large wall clock, which has no hands.

On the wall, a framed motto: WE VALUE YOUR TIME. The frame is gold. The glass is cracked.

To the right, a receptionist window. The receptionist smiles with many teeth and holds a clipboard titled TRIAGE (PRIVATE). On the clipboard the only visible line is: “Can they still sit up?” A potted plant on the sill is fake; its price tag remains.

Under the bench, a fifth clock, face-down.

Caption, in small type: “The system is coping.”

A letter printed beneath, from “Concerned, Upper Shore”: “Cartoons like this undermine dedicated staff. If people arrived on time and did not bring relatives, clocks would match.”

passage.title: psg-bb-4
passage.body:
In a classic-style linkage experiment, geneticists studied two genes in a fruit fly stock: one affecting body color (B = gray, dominant; b = black) and one affecting wing shape (V = normal, dominant; v = vestigial). The two genes reside on the same chromosome. Females heterozygous for both genes, with both dominant alleles on one homolog and both recessive alleles on the other (arrangement B V / b v), were testcrossed to males that were homozygous recessive (b v / b v). Because the testcross father contributes only b and v alleles, each offspring's phenotype directly reveals which allele combination it received from the mother.
Among 1,000 offspring, the researchers counted four phenotypic classes: 425 gray, normal-winged; 415 black, vestigial-winged; 82 gray, vestigial-winged; and 78 black, normal-winged. The first two classes matched the parental (non-recombinant) allele combinations, whereas the last two classes represented new combinations that could only arise if the maternal homologs exchanged segments.
The team used the frequency of these new-combination offspring to estimate how far apart the two genes lie, applying the rule that one map unit (centimorgan) corresponds to a 1 percent recombination frequency. They noted that if the two genes had been on different chromosomes, or extremely far apart on the same one, the four classes would instead have appeared in roughly equal numbers.

passage.title: psg-cars-12
passage.body:
One of the most consequential shifts in twentieth-century philosophy of language was the move away from the view that words get their meaning by standing for objects in the world. On the referentialist picture, to know the meaning of a term like 'gold' is to know which substance the term picks out; to know the meaning of 'Julius Caesar' is to know which historical individual the name refers to. The attractions of this view are obvious: it grounds meaning in something outside language itself, connecting our words to the world they describe and offering a clear criterion for distinguishing correct from incorrect usage.
Yet referentialism encounters serious difficulties when applied to expressions whose meaning does not seem to consist in any reference at all. Words like 'and,' 'perhaps,' 'nevertheless,' and 'of' do not pick out objects, properties, or relations in any obvious sense. Equally problematic are terms whose reference appears to shift depending on context: 'here' refers to wherever the speaker happens to be, 'now' to whenever the utterance is made, and 'I' to whoever is speaking. The meaning of these expressions cannot be their reference, since their reference changes while their meaning remains constant across every ordinary use of the word.
An alternative tradition proposed that meaning is constituted by use. On this view, to know the meaning of a word is not to know what it refers to but to know how to use it -- in what contexts it is appropriately deployed, what inferences it licenses, how it interacts with the meanings of other expressions. This account handles the problematic cases naturally: logical connectives like 'and' are explained by the inferential rules governing their use (the conjunction of P and Q implies both P and Q separately); indexical expressions like 'here' are explained by specifying the rule that they refer to the context of utterance. Knowing the meaning of 'here' means knowing that it picks out the speaker's location, not knowing any particular location.
Critics of the use theory worry that it leaves too little stable content in meaning. If meaning is just use, and use can vary between individual speakers or across historical periods, then there seems to be no fact of the matter about whether two speakers mean the same thing by a word, or whether we mean the same thing by 'democracy' as people in ancient Athens did. Some philosophers have sought to address this by distinguishing between the linguistic meaning of an expression (shared by competent speakers of a language) and speaker meaning (what a particular individual intends to convey in a specific utterance). Semantic theory can then concern itself with the former -- a stable, shared content -- while acknowledging the latter's irreducibly contextual character and the inevitable gap between what a speaker means and what a sentence means.
None of this need force an exclusive choice between the two pictures. A mature semantics may well be pluralistic, allowing that proper names and natural-kind terms lean heavily on reference while connectives, indexicals, and evaluative vocabulary are better explained by the rules governing their use. What the twentieth-century debate established is less the triumph of one theory than the inadequacy of assuming that a single mechanism must underwrite meaning across the whole of a language. The more durable lesson is methodological: before asking what a word means, one does well to ask what kind of word it is, since expressions of different types may secure their significance in quite different ways.

items.stem: Glutamine synthetase catalyzes glutamate + NH4+ + ATP → glutamine + ADP + Pi. The uncoupled condensation glutamate + NH4+ → glutamine + H2O has ΔG°′ ≈ +14 kJ/mol, whereas ATP hydrolysis has ΔG°′ ≈ −30.5 kJ/mol. Which statement is most accurate in the cell?

choices.text: The unfavorable glutamine-forming step cannot occur even when coupled, because ΔG°′ is a state function that forbids any positive partial reaction.
Coupling phosphoryl transfer from ATP makes the net standard free-energy change negative (≈ −16 kJ/mol), and a high [ATP]/[ADP][Pi] ratio further drives ΔG negative, allowing net glutamine synthesis.
Enzymes rewrite ΔG°′ of the uncoupled condensation to a negative value without chemical coupling to ATP.
Because ΔG°′ of ATP hydrolysis is negative, every ATP-dependent reaction runs to completion regardless of mass-action ratios.

items.explanation: Standard free energy is path-independent for a defined chemical change, but cells couple an unfavorable process to a favorable one so that the net reaction has negative ΔG°′. Adding +14 kJ/mol to −30.5 kJ/mol yields about −16 kJ/mol for glutamate + ATP + NH4+ → glutamine + ADP + Pi. Actual ΔG also depends on mass action; a high [ATP]/[ADP][Pi] ratio makes ΔG even more negative. Enzymes accelerate approach to equilibrium; they do not change ΔG°′ without changing the reaction stoichiometry, and they do not force every ATP-dependent reaction to completion independent of Q.

distractorRationales.A: A positive ΔG°′ for an isolated step is allowed if it is coupled into a net reaction with negative ΔG°′; metabolism routinely uses such coupling.
distractorRationales.C: Catalysts do not alter standard free-energy differences of a given reaction; coupling changes the reaction that is actually catalyzed.
distractorRationales.D: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q; mass action can reverse or stall ATP-dependent reactions when products accumulate or ATP is low.

passage.title: On keeping a promise to a stranger
passage.body:
When the magistrate asked why he had returned the purse, the clerk did not say honesty. He said habit. He had been taught, in a household that measured virtue by small repetitions, that a found object remains someone else's until the world has been given a fair chance to reclaim it. The purse contained little money and a letter, unsealed, beginning: I will not be there when you arrive. He did not finish it. To finish it, he thought, would convert a duty into a story, and stories have a way of making the finder important.

Philosophers like to treat this as a puzzle about property and knowledge. If he does not know the owner, is the duty weaker? If the letter would have saved a marriage, does withholding it become a harm? The clerk would have found the questions indecent. He was not refusing knowledge so much as refusing a role. The city had clerks for lost property; it did not have clerks for other people's farewells.

A later commentator, writing after the clerk was dead, praised him as a Kantian saint: he acted from a maxim he could will as universal. The praise is too clean. The clerk's maxim was local and slightly ashamed. He did not want to be the man who had read the letter. Shame, not universality, kept his eyes off the page. That is not a lesser ethics. It is an ethics that knows how quickly curiosity dresses itself as concern.

The owner collected the purse the next morning and did not thank him. In the commentary this becomes a test of whether virtue needs recognition. The clerk, if asked, would have said only that the counter was busy.

passage.title: The Metric (1977)
passage.body: Hanae Morioka's 1977 essay “The Metric,” on vaccine campaigns, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that speed of publication is being mistaken for care. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: Multisensory Influences on Beverage Perception
passage.body:
A behavioral neuroscience lab examined whether ambient odors influence taste judgments. Seventy-two adults sampled the same unsweetened citrus beverage in three counterbalanced conditions: no ambient scent, a congruent lemon scent, and an incongruent coffee scent. Participants were not told that the scent condition changed across trials. After each sample, they rated perceived sweetness, perceived sourness, and purchase intention on 1 to 7 scales. In a separate adaptation task, participants detected faint lemon odors before and after continuous exposure to a moderate lemon scent for 3 minutes.

passage.title: Who Counts (1979)
passage.body: Fatima Al-Hassan published “Who Counts” in 1979 after a season in municipal archives. The argument is that neutrality is a style, not an absence of interest. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: The borrowed coat
passage.body:
He wore other people's sentences the way some men wear coats: against weather, and with the labels left in. At the seminar he began, "One might argue," and then produced, almost unaltered, a paragraph his supervisor had emailed at midnight to save him. The room nodded. He felt the coat settle on his shoulders, warm and slightly too large in the sleeves.

Afterward a friend said, "That was the first time you sounded like yourself." He laughed too quickly. In the bathroom mirror the coat was still on. He tried to take it off by telling the truth to the glass: I do not know whether I think this. The glass, being a glass, offered his mouth moving.

Ethics talks as if authenticity were a mineral you either contain or fake. The evening suggested something cheaper and more ordinary. A borrowed argument can keep you from freezing. It can also teach your arms the wrong length. The crime, if there is one, is not the borrowing. It is the nod you collect as if the sleeves had always been yours.

He sent the supervisor a note: Thank you. I sounded like myself. He deleted it. He sent: Thank you. I used your paragraph. He left that one in the outbox until morning, which is a kind of cowardice that still knows the difference.

passage.title: psg-cars-2
passage.body:
Among the most contested claims in moral philosophy is the assertion that ethical judgments are irreducibly relative to the cultural frameworks that produce them. Cultural relativism, in its strongest form, holds not merely that different societies happen to endorse different moral codes, but that no standpoint outside all cultures exists from which those codes can be objectively ranked. If morality is constituted by social practice rather than discovered through reason or intuition, then condemning another culture's practices amounts to little more than projecting one's own conventions onto alien terrain.
Defenders of this position often draw strength from the anthropological record, which reveals a startling diversity of moral norms across societies separated by time and geography. Practices that one tradition regards as obligatory — ancestor veneration, dowry exchange, arranged marriage — strike others as superstitious, exploitative, or coercive. From this diversity, relativists infer that no norm enjoys a privileged status independent of its cultural home. To insist otherwise, they argue, is to mistake familiarity for objectivity.
Yet the relativist position encounters formidable internal difficulties. If moral judgments are valid only within the culture that generates them, then the reformer who criticizes her own society's practices — the abolitionist in a slave-holding nation, the suffragette in a society that bars women from public life — is simply wrong by definition. Her protest cannot be morally correct because the dominant convention of her society says otherwise. This consequence strikes many philosophers as a reductio ad absurdum: a moral theory that silences the reformer and vindicates the oppressor cannot be adequate.
Universalists reply that moral diversity, while real, does not demonstrate moral relativism any more than disagreement among scientists demonstrates that there are no scientific facts. People may disagree about the boiling point of water and still be wrong; analogously, cultures may disagree about the permissibility of torture yet one of them may be mistaken. The universalist identifies certain core norms — prohibitions on gratuitous cruelty, requirements of basic reciprocity — that appear in some form across virtually every known society, suggesting not conventional agreement but convergent recognition of genuine moral truths.
The exchange rarely ends there. Relativists counter that the universalist's alleged core norms are either too thin to settle any real dispute or are honored more in word than in deed. Nearly every society condemns killing, they concede — yet societies differ profoundly over which killings count as murder, whom the prohibition protects, and when violence becomes duty. A principle so abstract that rival cultures can all recite it while behaving in opposite ways, the relativist argues, marks no genuine agreement at all. Universalists answer that shared abstract commitments are precisely what one would expect if morality tracked real but imperfectly grasped values, and that quarrels over application no more dissolve an underlying norm than disputed measurements dissolve the quantity being measured.
A nuanced middle position distinguishes between first-order moral claims (what is right or wrong) and metaethical claims (what makes moral judgments true or false). One may acknowledge deep cultural variation in first-order norms while still holding that some metaethical framework — natural law, contractualism, or sentimentalism — provides a transcultural criterion of moral evaluation. On this view, the diversity of moral codes is evidence of human fallibility and limited information, not of the absence of any moral standard. Whether such a criterion is ultimately defensible remains among the central unresolved questions of moral philosophy.

passage.title: A Slow Era (1981)
passage.body: In “A Slow Era” (1981), Owen Blake writes from inside broadcast newsrooms. The argument is that fairness talk often arrives after the decision has already been made. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: psg-cp-10
passage.body:
A research team studies both how fast a reaction goes and whether it goes at all - kinetics and thermodynamics, two independent questions. They first examine the decomposition of a reactant, X, measuring its initial rate as they vary the starting concentration at fixed temperature. In three trials the initial concentration of X is 0.10, 0.20, and 0.30 M, and the corresponding initial rates are 2.0x10^-3, 8.0x10^-3, and 1.8x10^-2 M/s. From these data they extract the reaction order in X and the rate constant.
They then vary temperature and find, as expected, that the rate rises steeply as the sample is warmed. They interpret this with the Arrhenius picture: only molecules with at least the activation energy can react, and warming increases that fraction. Adding a catalyst speeds the reaction further, and the team is careful to note what a catalyst does and does not change.
Separately, they assess the reaction's thermodynamics. Calorimetry gives a standard enthalpy change delta_H = +50 kJ/mol, and the standard entropy change is delta_S = +100 J/(mol.K). Using the Gibbs relation delta_G = delta_H - T*delta_S, they compute the free-energy change at 298 K to judge spontaneity, and they determine the temperature above which the reaction becomes spontaneous. They stress that kinetics (how fast) and thermodynamics (how favorable) are separate: a reaction can be thermodynamically favorable yet immeasurably slow, or fast yet unfavorable. They treat delta_H and delta_S as approximately constant over the range considered.

items.stem: Crushing a solid reactant into a fine powder before reacting it with an acid speeds up the reaction. Why?

choices.text: Powdering changes the chemical identity of the solid.
Powdering increases the total surface area exposed to the acid, allowing more frequent collisions between reacting particles.
Powdering lowers the activation energy of the reaction.
Powdering increases the temperature of the mixture.

items.explanation: Reaction rate depends on collision frequency between reactant particles. A powder has far more surface area exposed than a single lump of the same mass, so more particles are available to collide with acid particles per second. Reaction rate increases whenever particles collide more often or with more energy: higher concentration/pressure (more particles per volume), higher temperature (faster, more energetic particles), greater surface area (more exposed particles), or a catalyst (lowers activation energy, without being consumed). Memory tip: "Crushed ice melts faster than an ice cube": more surface area means more particles exposed and able to collide, which is exactly why powdering speeds up a reaction. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: Stress Appraisal and Working Memory During Social Evaluation
passage.body:

In the evaluative-challenge group, participants gave the same speech while being observed but were told that increased arousal could help them perform effectively. Participants completed a working-memory task afterward and provided saliva samples before and after the task.

Condition | Perceived control, 1 to 7 | Heart rate increase, beats/min | Salivary cortisol increase, nmol/L | Working-memory accuracy (%)
Private reading | 5.8 | 4 | 0.7 | 86
Evaluative threat | 2.7 | 18 | 4.6 | 71

The solution is clearly basic (pH > 7), which already eliminates any answer near 2. The weak-base square-root step is the same algebra as for a weak acid, but the logarithm is of [OH−], not of [H+].

distractorRationales.A: pH 2.00 would describe a 0.010 M strong acid, not a weak base. The species B produces OH−, so the solution cannot be this acidic.

distractorRationales.D: pH 13.00 is the strong-base result for 0.10 M OH−. Only a fraction of B is protonated, so [OH−] is 10^−3 M, not 0.10 M.

items.stem:
Two purified organelle enzymes are assayed versus pH (activity in the same arbitrary units):
pH 5.0: hydrolase L = 92, catalase P = 8.
pH 7.0: hydrolase L = 14, catalase P = 88.
pH 8.0: hydrolase L = 6, catalase P = 71.
Compartment L has a measured luminal pH of 5.0; compartment P has a luminal pH of 7.2.
Which assignment fits both the pH data and standard organelle chemistry?

choices.text: L is the mitochondrial matrix (pH near 8), because hydrolase L still has 6 units at pH 8.
L is lysosomal (acid-optimum hydrolase) and P is consistent with peroxisomal catalase.
Both enzymes are cytosolic, because cytosol is pH 7 and hydrolase L still has 14 units there.
P is lysosomal, because catalase destroys H2O2 most rapidly at pH 5 (activity 8).

items.explanation: Lysosomes maintain an acidic lumen so that acid hydrolases work at their pH optimum; hydrolase L is almost fully active at pH 5 (92 units) and nearly inactive at pH 7–8, matching that compartment. Peroxisomal catalase operates near neutrality; catalase P peaks at pH 7 (88 units) and is weak at pH 5 (8 units), matching lumen pH 7.2. Residual activity of L at pH 8 is only 6 units, far below its acid peak, so L is not a matrix enzyme. Catalase’s low activity at pH 5 rules out a lysosomal assignment for P.

distractorRationales.A: Activity 6 at pH 8 is a trough, not an optimum; the mitochondrial matrix would not house an acid hydrolase of this profile.
distractorRationales.C: Fourteen units at pH 7 is a small fraction of L’s pH-5 peak, so the enzyme is not tuned to the cytosol.
distractorRationales.D: Catalase P has only 8 units at pH 5 and 88 at pH 7, the opposite of a lysosomal acid optimum.

items.stem: Freshly dissolved α-D-glucopyranose mutarotates in water until [α]D reaches the equilibrium value of the anomeric mixture. Methyl α-D-glucopyranoside, dissolved in the same neutral water, shows a constant specific rotation for hours. Why?

choices.text: The methyl glycoside is an acetal at C1; the ring cannot open to the aldehyde without acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, so anomers cannot interconvert
Methyl glycosides are aldehydes that racemize instantly, so rotation is already zero
The methyl group inverts configuration at C5, destroying the D series and freezing rotation
Glycosides have no stereocenters, so they cannot be optically active in the first place

items.explanation: Mutarotation of glucose proceeds by reversible ring opening of the hemiacetal to the open-chain aldehyde, which can reclose to either the α or the β anomer. A methyl glycoside is a full acetal: the anomeric carbon bears two C–O bonds (the ring oxygen and OMe). Acetals are stable in neutral or basic water and open only when acid catalyzes hydrolysis. Without access to the aldehyde, the anomeric configuration is locked and [α] does not drift. The glycoside remains chiral (multiple stereocenters) and optically active; methylation does not invert C5 or erase stereochemistry.

distractorRationales.B: A glycoside is an acetal, not an aldehyde. Instant racemization to zero rotation is not observed; the rotation is simply constant.
distractorRationales.C: The methyl is attached to the anomeric oxygen at C1. C5, which defines the D/L series, is untouched.
distractorRationales.D: Methyl glucopyranoside has five stereocenters and a large specific rotation; it is optically active but configurationally locked at C1.

passage.title: Recycling Behavior and Reinforcement Schedules in Dormitory Kitchens
passage.body:
A campus sustainability team tested behavioral strategies for improving recycling accuracy in dormitory kitchens. Twenty dormitory floors were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: informational signs only, a fixed-ratio points program in which floors earned a reward after every fifth correctly sorted item, a variable-ratio points program in which floors earned rewards unpredictably after an average of five correctly sorted items, or an observational-modeling condition in which residents watched a peer demonstrate correct sorting before signs were posted. In the reward conditions, a green light on the sorting station indicated that the sensor was active and points could be earned; a red light indicated that the sensor was off. After four weeks, point rewards were removed for one week while signs remained.

Mean percentage of items correctly sorted
Condition | Baseline week | Week 4 | Reward-removal week
Informational signs only | 43 | 55 | 52
Fixed-ratio points | 42 | 68 | 50
Variable-ratio points | 44 | 75 | 63
Observational modeling plus signs | 41 | 70 | 66

Assignment unit — The dormitory floor, rather than the individual resident, was the unit of assignment because rewards and signs were shared within floor kitchens.

passage.title: Note on a cancelled tram
passage.body:
In the third week of the lockout the company ran a single tram, brightly lit, along the route at dusk, with no passengers permitted. Officials called it a demonstration of service. Strikers called it a lantern on a coffin. Children ran beside it anyway, as they had when the cars were working, and were photographed. The photograph was printed in the morning paper under the heading NORMALITY RETURNS, and in an overseas paper under the heading CHILDREN MOCK THE DEAD LINE.

A clerk in the tram office, years later, wrote that he had been told to leave the lights on even if the generator complained, because darkness would look like surrender. He added, without apparent bitterness, that surrender had already occurred in the timetable. What remained was a moving argument about who owned the look of a street at evening.

Historians still disagree whether the empty tram lengthened the dispute by humiliating the men or shortened it by frightening the board with the cost of theatre. The clerk’s sentence is more useful than either camp: the fight had become, for a night, a question of illumination.

passage.title: psg-cp-6
passage.body:
Water's ability to dissolve ions and to resist changes in acidity underlies much of physiology. Blood plasma is held near pH 7.4 largely by the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer: dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which dissociates into a hydrogen ion and bicarbonate, H2CO3 H+ + HCO3-. The effective pKa for this equilibrium in plasma is about 6.1. Normally the concentration of bicarbonate is roughly twenty times that of dissolved carbonic acid, and the lungs and kidneys adjust the two components to hold that ratio steady. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation links the pH to the ratio of conjugate base to weak acid.
To study buffering directly, students titrate a weak acid at 25 C. They place 0.10 M acetic acid (pKa 4.74) in a flask and add sodium hydroxide from a burette while a pH meter records the curve. Early on the pH rises slowly through a buffering plateau; near the end it climbs steeply through the equivalence point, where exactly enough base has been added to neutralize all the acid. A separate reference solution at 25 C is measured to have a pH of 3.0.
The students note that at 25 C the ion product of water fixes pH + pOH = 14, and that a solution's acidity reflects the balance between hydrogen and hydroxide ions produced when water and solutes interact. They also test the buffer's resilience by adding a few drops of strong acid to the bicarbonate system and to plain water, comparing how far the pH of each moves.

items.stem: Which of the following best states the author's central claim about translation?

choices.text: Fluent, natural-sounding translations are the only honest ones, because delay is proof that a translator has failed.

Translation is a set of decisions about which foreign silences remain audible; selling fluency as fidelity recruits the text into local habits rather than receiving it, so a trace of difficulty can be a form of hospitality.
Wooden calques and untranslated exhibits are the only ethically acceptable methods, because any English rendering is a betrayal.
Publishers should be abolished, since markets can never influence which books readers finish.

items.explanation: The passage rejects the pipe metaphor and treats translation as decisions about audible silences. Fluency sold as fidelity enrolls a text in local etiquette and hides hospitality; delay can honestly report a conceptual mismatch. The author equally refuses the opposite piety of difficulty-as-exhibit. Choice B keeps both refusals and the hospitality thesis. The other options inflate a rejected tactic, invert the smoothness critique, or turn a market remark into an abolition program the text never offers.

distractorRationales.A: The author treats the belief that a text which does not delay us has been understood as the more serious failure, not as a standard of honesty.
distractorRationales.C: The third paragraph explicitly denies a case for wooden calques and the museum of untranslated words, calling those tactics their own piety.
distractorRationales.D: Publishers are said to be right about the market and wrong about meaning; the passage does not propose abolishing publishing.

passage.title: The courtesy of untranslatability
passage.body:
Historians of language like to treat translation as a pipe: meaning enters one end, equivalent wording exits the other, and any turbulence is a defect in the plumber. The figure is flattering to publishers, who can then sell fluency as fidelity, and it is flattering to readers, who can then consume a foreign argument as if it had always been written in their kitchen. The figure is also false. A translation is not a transfer of a stable cargo. It is a series of decisions about which silences will remain audible and which will be paved over so that a page turns without snagging.

Consider the ordinary boast that a novel has been rendered into "perfectly natural" English. Natural for whom? The boast treats the target language as a climate rather than as a historically specific set of habits, class markers, and tolerated opacities. When a rural insult is recast as a metropolitan joke, or a liturgical cadence is recast as a magazine paragraph, the text has not been rescued from awkwardness. It has been enrolled in a local etiquette. The reader who thanks the translator for making the book "not feel translated" is thanking the translator for hiding the fact that hospitality occurred. Hospitality, if it is more than a smile, leaves a trace of the guest.

This is not an argument for wooden calques or for the museum of untranslated words left standing like exhibits. Those tactics can become their own piety, a performance of difficulty that congratulates the reader for enduring it. The more serious failure is the opposite one: the belief that a text which does not delay us has therefore been understood. Delay is sometimes the only honest report of a conceptual mismatch. A legal term that organizes a whole civic world cannot be swapped for a near-synonym without smuggling in the civic world of the synonym. To refuse the delay is to pretend that the two worlds already agreed.

Publishers will object that readers abandon books that snag. They are not wrong about the market. They are wrong to treat the market as a theory of meaning. A culture that will only receive what has already been made to sound like itself is not receiving; it is recruiting. The translated page then becomes a mirror with a foreign name on the title page, and the prestige of the foreign name is used to ratify what the reader already believed. That is why "accessible" can function as a political adjective. It names not a reading level but a refusal of conceptual immigration.

None of this requires contempt for the reader. It requires a different courtesy: the courtesy of letting a sentence remain slightly foreign so that the reader can notice the foreignness as information rather than as a stain. The translator's invisibility, long praised as professionalism, is in this light a kind of disappearance of evidence. We might instead want translators to be visibly responsible for their choices, not as celebrities, but as people who can be asked why a silence was kept or filled.

The practical consequence is modest and severe. Reviewers should stop treating smoothness as a synonym for accuracy. Teachers should stop treating a bilingual dictionary as a moral instrument. And readers who want to be hosts rather than consumers should learn to tolerate, even to prize, the small resistances that prove a text has not been entirely naturalized. What cannot be made to sound like us is often the part that most needed to travel.

choices.text: −29.3 kJ mol−1 (reporting the heat per gram as if it were per mole)

items.explanation: The calorimeter absorbs q = 2000 g × 4.18 J g−1 °C−1 × 3.50 °C = 2.926 × 10^4 J = 29.26 kJ for 1.00 g. One mole is 180 g, so 29.26 kJ g−1 × 180 g mol−1 = 5.27 × 10^3 kJ mol−1. Combustion heats the calorimeter, so the chemical system released that energy and ΔU is negative: −5.27 × 10^3 kJ mol−1. Treating 29.26 kJ as already molar, or dropping the factor of 1000 between J and kJ incorrectly, produces the smaller distractors; a positive sign ignores that the water warmed.

items.explanation: Equivalence for this 1:1 titration occurs at 25.0 mL of NaOH, when essentially all CH3CO2H has been converted to CH3CO2−. The flask then contains a solution of the conjugate base of a weak acid. Acetate reacts with water (CH3CO2− + H2O ⇌ CH3CO2H + OH−), so the equivalence-point pH is basic (typically ~8.7 for these concentrations), not 7. pH 7 is the equivalence pH only for a strong acid–strong base titration. pH = pKa occurs at the half-equivalence point, not at equivalence. No significant free acetic acid remains at equivalence.

passage.title: psg-ps-6
passage.body:
A study examined how persuasive messages change attitudes. Undergraduates read an editorial advocating a new campus exam policy. The message was either strong (well-reasoned arguments) or weak (superficial slogans), and was attributed either to a distinguished professor or to a first-year student. Crucially, half the participants were told the policy would take effect next year (high personal relevance) and half were told it would begin in a decade (low relevance).
Among high-relevance readers, attitude change depended almost entirely on argument strength and hardly at all on the source; among low-relevance readers, the reverse held - the prestigious source mattered, but argument quality did not. A follow-up a week later showed that attitudes formed by high-relevance readers persisted and better predicted sign-up behavior than those of low-relevance readers.
In a second study, participants who volunteered to argue publicly for a position they privately opposed later shifted their private attitudes toward that position - but only when they felt they had freely chosen to do so and were paid little. Those paid a large sum, or who felt coerced, showed no attitude change.
The authors mapped the first study onto a dual-route model of persuasion: one route processes the substance of a message when motivation is high, while the other relies on surface cues when motivation is low. They explained the second study as the reduction of an uncomfortable inconsistency between behavior and belief, resolved by changing the belief when the behavior could not be justified by an external incentive.

items.stem: Stokes’ drag is F = 6π η r v. Force has dimensions M L T−2, r is L, v is L T−1. What are the dimensions of viscosity η, and which of the following is dimensionless? (Reynolds number Re = ρ v L / η, with ρ = M L−3.)

choices.text: η is dimensionless; Re has dimensions of η
η has dimensions M L−1 T−1; Re has dimensions of density
η has dimensions M L−1 T−1; Re is dimensionless
η has dimensions M L T−1; Re has dimensions of velocity

items.explanation: From F = η r v, ignoring the 6π, η = F / (r v) so [η] = (M L T−2) / (L · L T−1) = M L−1 T−1. Then Re = ρ v L / η has [ρ v L] = (M L−3)(L T−1)(L) = M L−1 T−1, which cancels [η], leaving a pure number. That is why Re can be used to compare flows of different size and speed. η is not dimensionless (oil and air have different SI values with units Pa s). Re is not a velocity or a density; those dimensions already cancelled. The 6π factor is a pure number and does not affect dimensions.

distractorRationales.A: η has SI unit Pa s = kg m−1 s−1, so it is dimensional; Re is the dimensionless combination.
distractorRationales.B: The η dimensions are right, but Re is constructed precisely so density cancels.
distractorRationales.D: The extra L in the numerator of that option would be [F]/[v] without dividing by r.

Ignoring friction or adding the friction force both produce a wrong net force.

passage.title: psg-cars-6
passage.body:
Social capital — broadly understood as the networks of relationships, norms of reciprocity, and trust that enable collective action — has become one of the most debated concepts in contemporary sociology. Proponents argue that it explains why some communities flourish economically and politically while others, equally well endowed in financial and physical resources, remain mired in dysfunction. Where citizens trust one another and are embedded in overlapping civic associations, cooperative ventures are easier to organize, contracts are more reliably honored, and public goods are more effectively maintained.
The concept distinguishes between two broad types. Bonding social capital refers to the dense ties within homogeneous groups — extended families, ethnic neighborhoods, religious congregations — that provide strong mutual support and a sense of belonging. Bridging social capital refers to the weaker but more diverse ties that link members of different social groups, enabling information and resources to flow across community boundaries. Theorists have argued that bridging capital is especially important for economic mobility and democratic stability, because it prevents the insularity and exclusivity that can calcify into tribal antagonism. The interplay between the two forms often matters more than either in isolation. Newcomers to a city, for example, tend to rely first on bonding ties — kin and compatriots who supply lodging, informal credit, and job referrals — and only later cultivate the bridging ties to employers, officials, and institutions beyond their original circle that permit genuine advancement. A community rich in bonding capital but starved of bridging capital may be tightly knit yet economically trapped, whereas one with abundant bridging ties but thin internal solidarity may struggle to sustain the everyday obligations on which cooperation depends. On this view the vitality of a community turns less on how much social capital it can claim than on how its bonding and bridging forms are balanced against each other.
Critics have raised several concerns. First, they argue that the concept is so capacious as to be analytically vacuous: if social capital includes trust, networks, and norms all at once, it risks becoming a label that explains everything and therefore explains nothing. Second, the emphasis on voluntary civic associations may obscure the role of institutional design and state capacity in producing the outcomes attributed to social capital. A society with strong courts, reliable public services, and enforceable property rights may achieve cooperation through formal mechanisms, regardless of the density of its associational life.
A third critique focuses on the dark side of social capital. The same dense ties that produce cohesion within a group can generate exclusion and hostility toward outsiders. Historically, tightly bonded criminal networks, nativist movements, and exclusionary professional guilds have all exhibited strong social capital while causing harm to those outside the charmed circle. If social capital is a neutral resource that amplifies whatever goals a group pursues, then celebrating it uncritically is a mistake. A community of mutual trust can be a community of mutual hostility toward all who fall outside its boundaries, and the literature on ethnic cleansing, organized crime, and racially restrictive covenants demonstrates this possibility in grim historical detail.
These debates have produced a more nuanced research agenda. Scholars now investigate not just the presence or absence of social capital but its distribution across social groups, its articulation with formal institutions, and the conditions under which it promotes rather than undermines democratic participation and social equity.

passage.title: Regulation of a bacterial nucleotide-reduction operon
passage.body:
A fictional bacterial operon, nrdPQ, encodes proteins required for deoxyribonucleotide synthesis during low-oxygen growth. The operon contains a sigma-factor promoter, a 5' untranslated region with a metabolite M-sensitive attenuator, and a Shine-Dalgarno sequence upstream of the nrdP start codon. When metabolite M binds the nascent 5' untranslated region, a terminator hairpin forms before the coding sequence, reducing production of full-length mRNA. Researchers constructed mutations and measured full-length nrdP mRNA, NrdP protein, and NrdP enzyme activity.

Expression and activity of nrdP constructs.
Construct and condition | Full-length mRNA (%) | NrdP protein (%) | NrdP activity (%)
Wild type, no M | 100 | 100 | 100
Wild type, +M | 30 | 28 | 30
-10 promoter mutant, no M | 12 | 10 | 11
Terminator hairpin disrupted, +M | 95 | 92 | 90
Shine-Dalgarno mutant, no M | 105 | 15 | 14
Active-site Cys to Ser mutant, no M | 100 | 98 | 8

Model of metabolite M-dependent attenuation. — In the presence of metabolite M, the 5' untranslated region folds into a terminator hairpin that causes RNA polymerase to stop before transcribing the nrdP coding sequence. When M is absent or the hairpin is disrupted, RNA polymerase usually produces full-length mRNA.

items.stem: A state funeral draws together citizens from rival political factions, who report afterwards feeling temporarily united despite their differences. This phenomenon would best be explained by which account described in the passage?

choices.text: The integrative account, because the shared ceremony produced collective effervescence
The power-hierarchy account, because the funeral reinforces the legitimacy of the political elite
The cognitive account, because the funeral encodes propositional knowledge about succession
None of the accounts, because state funerals are modern inventions outside the passage's scope

items.explanation: (A) is correct: rival factions feeling 'temporarily united' despite their differences is precisely what the integrative account explains through collective effervescence, which 'temporarily dissolves the boundaries between self and group.' (B) is unsupported by the scenario: the described phenomenon is unity across factions, not the reinforcement of any elite's legitimacy that the power-hierarchy account would require. (C) does not fit, since the scenario turns on felt unity rather than the transmission of propositional knowledge. (D) is false; the passage treats ceremonies like 'a coronation' as within its scope. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passage.title: psg-cars-8
passage.body:
Ritual occupies a paradoxical place in modern social thought. On one hand, it has been systematically studied as a fundamental mechanism of social solidarity: shared symbolic performances bind participants together, express and reinforce collective values, and mark the transitions — birth, initiation, marriage, death — that punctuate the human life course. On the other hand, modern societies tend to regard ritual with a degree of unease, as if elaborate ceremony were a relic of pre-rational ages unsuited to a world governed by science and voluntary choice.
Early sociological and anthropological accounts emphasized the integrative functions of ritual. Ceremonies, on this view, do not merely reflect an already-existing social order; they actively produce and sustain it. When a community gathers to mark a harvest, a coronation, or a national founding, participants do not simply observe an event — they enact membership in a collectivity that transcends any individual. The shared emotional experience generated by such occasions — what early theorists called collective effervescence — temporarily dissolves the boundaries between self and group, creating a felt sense of unity that persists in social memory long after the ceremony has concluded.
Later anthropologists complicated this functionalist picture by attending to the internal diversity and contestation that characterize real rituals. Ceremonies are rarely performed identically across time or across the different status groups within a community. The ruling class and the subjugated, men and women, elders and youth — each may experience the same ceremony quite differently, and the ritual may serve to reinforce not solidarity across the board but specific hierarchies of power. From this perspective, treating ritual purely as a mechanism of integration ignores its role in legitimating and reproducing asymmetric social arrangements.
A third approach draws attention to ritual's cognitive and communicative dimensions. Rituals encode information in a form — embodied action, sensory symbol, repeated performance — that is particularly durable and memorable. Unlike propositional statements that can be contested or forgotten, knowledge embedded in ritual is resistant to revision precisely because it is experienced rather than merely asserted. This explains why ritual tends to be invoked when other communicative resources fail: in the face of death, catastrophic loss, or radical uncertainty, shared performance provides a structure of meaning that discursive language alone cannot furnish. Grief rituals in particular demonstrate how embodied collective action can sustain communities through episodes of radical disruption that would otherwise threaten social fabric. The contrast with ordinary instruction is telling. A fact conveyed in a lecture can be doubted the moment the lecture ends; a truth rehearsed year after year in fasting, procession, or song is renewed in the body and rarely submitted to cross-examination at all. This is why communities so often entrust their most load-bearing commitments — who belongs, what is owed to the dead, which obligations the future imposes — not to argument but to observance. The very features that make ritual knowledge conservative, and sometimes an obstacle to reform, are also what allow it to hold a group together when argument alone would divide it, carrying shared meaning across generations that never meet.
Each of these accounts captures something genuine. Ritual is simultaneously a mechanism of solidarity, an arena of power and contestation, and a form of embodied knowledge. Understanding any particular ceremony requires attending to all three dimensions and to the historical context that shapes their relative salience.

items.stem:
Optical density (OD600) of a bacterial batch culture:

Time (h) | OD600
0.0 | 0.10
1.0 | 0.20
2.0 | 0.40
3.0 | 0.80
4.0 | 1.50
5.0 | 1.60
6.0 | 1.55

Which description of growth phases is justified?

choices.text: Death phase begins at 1 h because the first doubling has already occurred
Exponential growth continues through 6 h because OD remains above 0.10
Exponential doubling time is 1.0 h from 0–3 h; the culture is entering stationary phase by 4–6 h
The culture is in lag phase for the entire 6 h because OD never exceeds 2

items.explanation: From 0.10 to 0.80 in 3 h the OD doubles every hour (0.10→0.20→0.40→0.80), the definition of exponential growth with a 1 h doubling time. Between 3 and 4 h the increase is less than a doubling (0.80→1.50), and by 5–6 h OD plateaus near 1.6, i.e. stationary phase. Lag would be a delay before doubling starts, but doubling is immediate here. Death phase would be a sustained OD fall, not a 1.60 to 1.55 wobble after a plateau. Remaining above the inoculum OD does not mean exponential growth continues.

distractorRationales.A: Completing a doubling is exponential growth, not death.
distractorRationales.B: After 3 h the successive ratios are 1.50/0.80 and 1.60/1.50, not a constant factor of 2, so exponential growth has ended.
distractorRationales.D: Lag is a period without net increase; this culture doubles immediately, so it is not in lag.

passage.title: psg-bb-4
passage.body:
In a classic-style linkage experiment, geneticists studied two genes in a fruit fly stock: one affecting body color (B = gray, dominant; b = black) and one affecting wing shape (V = normal, dominant; v = vestigial). The two genes reside on the same chromosome. Females heterozygous for both genes, with both dominant alleles on one homolog and both recessive alleles on the other (arrangement B V / b v), were testcrossed to males that were homozygous recessive (b v / b v). Because the testcross father contributes only b and v alleles, each offspring's phenotype directly reveals which allele combination it received from the mother.
Among 1,000 offspring, the researchers counted four phenotypic classes: 425 gray, normal-winged; 415 black, vestigial-winged; 82 gray, vestigial-winged; and 78 black, normal-winged. The first two classes matched the parental (non-recombinant) allele combinations, whereas the last two classes represented new combinations that could only arise if the maternal homologs exchanged segments.
The team used the frequency of these new-combination offspring to estimate how far apart the two genes lie, applying the rule that one map unit (centimorgan) corresponds to a 1 percent recombination frequency. They noted that if the two genes had been on different chromosomes, or extremely far apart on the same one, the four classes would instead have appeared in roughly equal numbers.

items.stem: What is the most reasonable conclusion from the finding that changing the bob's mass produced no measurable change in the period?

choices.text: Within the range tested, the pendulum's period does not depend on the mass of the bob.
The experiment was flawed and should be discarded.
Heavier bobs always swing faster than lighter ones.
Mass cannot be measured accurately using standard laboratory equipment.

items.explanation: A "no effect" result is itself informative: it supports the conclusion that, across the masses actually tested, period does not depend on mass. There is no basis in the passage for concluding the experiment was flawed or that mass cannot be measured. Finding that a variable has no measurable effect is a legitimate scientific finding, not evidence of a failed experiment. Don't assume something went wrong just because the result was "nothing happened" — sometimes nothing happening is the answer. Memory tip: "No effect is still an answer": a flat line on a graph is data too, not a broken experiment — don't throw out a null result just because it isn't exciting. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: Physics · Pendulum Motion & Energy
passage.body: A student sets up a pendulum using a string and a small metal bob, and investigates what affects the time for one complete swing (the period). They test three string lengths (25 cm, 50 cm, 100 cm) while keeping the bob's mass and the release angle constant, and separately test three different bob masses (10 g, 50 g, 100 g) while keeping the string length and release angle constant. Increasing the string length increases the period. Changing the bob's mass, however, produces no measurable change in the period. In a separate trial, the student releases the pendulum from a fixed height and measures its speed at the lowest point of the swing using a sensor, finding that the speed is slightly lower on each successive swing as the pendulum gradually loses height.

items.stem:
Physical data for three chlorides:

Compound | melting point (°C) | electrical conductivity of liquid | ΔEN (Pauling)
NaCl | 801 | high | 2.1
MgCl2 | 714 | high | 1.8
SiCl4 | −70 | none | 1.2

Which bonding assignment matches the table?

choices.text: NaCl and MgCl2 are ionic lattices that melt to mobile ions; SiCl4 is a covalent molecular liquid with no free ions
SiCl4 is ionic because chlorine is present, which is why it melts at −70 °C
NaCl is molecular, because 801 °C is too low for a lattice
All three are giant covalent networks, so all should conduct when molten

items.explanation: High melting points plus molten conductivity are the ionic-lattice signature: Na+Cl− and Mg2+Cl− melt into mobile ions. SiCl4 melts at −70 °C and does not conduct, so it is a discrete SiCl4 molecule held by weak intermolecular forces, consistent with a smaller electronegativity gap. Chlorine content does not make a compound ionic. 801 °C is a typical ionic melting point, not a molecular one. A giant covalent chloride would not melt at −70 °C, and molten NaCl/MgCl2 conductivity would then be unexplained if there were no ions.

distractorRationales.B: An ionic lattice does not melt at −70 °C, and molten SiCl4 does not conduct.
distractorRationales.C: 801 °C and high molten conductivity are ionic, not molecular, markers.
distractorRationales.D: SiCl4’s −70 °C melting point and zero conductivity rule out a giant network, and networks do not produce ionic conductivity on melting.

items.stem: A hoist lifts a 50 kg crate at constant speed through 4.0 m in 8.0 s. g = 10 m s−2. Work against gravity is mgh. Average power is W/t. What are W and P? If the motor is only 50% efficient, what electrical power input is required?

choices.text: W = 16 000 J; P = 2000 W (using mgh t)
W = 2000 J; P = 250 W; input 500 W
W = 2000 J; P = 250 W; input 250 W, ignoring efficiency
W = 400 J; P = 50 W (using 50 kg as if it were newtons)

items.explanation: Weight = 500 N, so W = 500 × 4.0 = 2000 J. Average output power = 2000/8.0 = 250 W. At 50% efficiency the electrical input must be 250 / 0.50 = 500 W. Efficiency less than one always means a larger input than the useful mechanical output. Treating 50 kg as 50 N undercounts work by g. Multiplying by t instead of dividing inflates power. Constant speed means the motor force equals weight, so W = mgh is the useful work.

distractorRationales.A: Power is work/time, not work × time; 2000 J in 8 s is 250 W.
distractorRationales.C: 50% efficiency doubles the required input relative to the 250 W mechanical output.
distractorRationales.D: Force is 50 × 10 = 500 N, not 50 N; work is 2000 J.

items.stem: Expert typists and novices type a standard paragraph either alone or with three classmates watching. Experts become faster and more accurate with the audience; novices become slower and make more errors. Which account best fits both results?

choices.text: Social loafing: an audience always reduces effort, so both groups should slow
Deindividuation: the audience makes experts anonymous and therefore more skilled
Social facilitation (Zajonc): presence of others raises arousal and the dominant response—correct for experts, errors for novices
Bystander effect: each spectator assumes another spectator will type

items.explanation: Social facilitation is the effect of an audience or co-actors on individual performance. Zajonc’s drive account says mere presence increases arousal, which potentiates the dominant response. For a well-learned skill the dominant response is the correct one, so experts improve; for a poorly learned skill the dominant response is error, so novices worsen. Loafing predicts less effort when output is pooled, which is not this design. Deindividuation is reduced self-awareness in anonymous crowds, not a skill-enhancing audience. Bystander logic applies to helping in emergencies, not to typing.

distractorRationales.A: Experts improved, which loafing cannot explain, and typing was an individual task with identifiable output.
distractorRationales.B: Named classmates watching is the opposite of anonymity, and deindividuation does not turn novices’ errors into expertise.
distractorRationales.D: Spectators were not potential helpers in an emergency; they were an audience for a performance task.

items.stem: After a steelman of “speed is care,” which closing move actually answers it rather than merely mentioning it?

choices.text: “Of course some delays harm, but that fact supports targeted speed for clinical windows, not a general rule that whoever can buy a shorter clock is therefore caring.”
“As mentioned, there is another view. In conclusion, waiting is deep.”
“I respect all opinions equally, so both speed and waiting are correct.”

items.explanation: Answering a counterargument means altering or delimiting your thesis in light of it, or showing why the strongest objection still fails. A grants medical windows and then blocks the slide from those windows to a market in shorter clocks. That is a reply. B names the other view and then vapours. C collapses into a draw that the task did not ask for. A bare “see comment 2” is a pointer, not a thought. The craft is steelman-and-answer, not a polite wave. Under time, one precise delimitation is enough. A is the delimitation.

distractorRationales.B: Mention plus a vague profundity about waiting does not meet the harm-from-delay objection.
distractorRationales.C: Equal respect for all opinions abandons evaluation, which is the Task A job.
distractorRationales.D: Pointing at a comment is not an answer; the essay still has to do the distinguishing work.

passage.title: Gluconeogenic flux in hepatocyte-like cells
passage.body:
Researchers used fictional hepatocyte-like HGL cells to study glucose production from lactate and alanine. Pyruvate generated in the cytosol must enter mitochondria through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC). In the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate carboxylase (PC) uses ATP, bicarbonate, and a biotin cofactor to convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate. Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) then uses GTP to convert oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate. The pathway requires substantial energy input and is sensitive to cellular ATP availability.

Metabolic effects of perturbing gluconeogenesis from lactate and alanine.
Condition | Glucose output (%) | Cytosolic pyruvate (%) | Mitochondrial OAA/malate pool (%) | O2 consumption (%) | ATP/ADP ratio
Control | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 5.0
MPC inhibitor B | 20 | 190 | 35 | 90 | 4.8
PC inhibitor C | 12 | 220 | 28 | 82 | 3.9
PEPCK knockdown | 18 | 120 | 210 | 85 | 4.2
Low-dose ETC inhibitor | 44 | 115 | 82 | 34 | 1.5
Acetyl-CoA analog | 135 | 70 | 155 | 112 | 4.6

Simplified route from lactate and alanine to glucose. — Lactate and alanine are converted to cytosolic pyruvate. Pyruvate enters mitochondria through MPC and is carboxylated by PC to oxaloacetate. Oxaloacetate-derived carbon returns to the cytosol and proceeds through gluconeogenic reactions to form glucose.

passage.title: psg-bb-5
passage.body:
To probe how mitochondria couple fuel oxidation to ATP synthesis, researchers suspended isolated mitochondria in a buffered chamber fitted with an oxygen electrode, so that the rate of oxygen consumption could be followed continuously. Because the electron transport chain uses O2 as its final electron acceptor, oxygen consumption serves as a readout of electron flow.
The team added an oxidizable substrate (to feed electrons into the chain) plus ADP and inorganic phosphate (the raw materials for ATP synthesis). Oxygen consumption rose to a brisk, steady rate, and ATP accumulated in the chamber. They then added oligomycin, a compound that blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase. Oxygen consumption fell almost to zero, and ATP synthesis stopped. Finally, they added 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), a small molecule that ferries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Oxygen consumption surged back to a high rate, yet no ATP was produced; the released energy instead appeared as heat.
The investigators explained the pattern in terms of the proton-motive force. Electron transport pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building an electrochemical gradient; ATP synthase normally lets those protons flow back into the matrix, harnessing the gradient to make ATP. Blocking ATP synthase lets the gradient build until it opposes further pumping, so electron flow (and O2 use) slows. A protonophore like DNP short-circuits the gradient, so electron transport races ahead while its energy is dissipated as heat rather than captured as ATP.

items.stem: An autosomal recessive disease occurs in 1/10,000 newborns in a large, randomly mating population that meets Hardy–Weinberg assumptions. What is the expected frequency of heterozygous carriers?

choices.text: 1/10,000, equal to the incidence of affected homozygotes.
Approximately 1/50, because q^2 = 10^−4 so q = 0.01 and 2pq ≈ 2(1)(0.01) = 0.02.
1/100, equal to the allele frequency q rather than the heterozygote frequency 2pq.
1/200, because Hardy–Weinberg counting includes only half of the heterozygotes.

items.explanation: Under Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium the frequency of affected homozygotes is q^2. If q^2 = 1/10,000, then q = 0.01. For a rare allele p ≈ 1, so the heterozygote (carrier) frequency 2pq ≈ 2 × 0.01 = 0.02, or 1 in 50. The incidence of affected births is q^2, not the carrier rate. The allele frequency q is 0.01 (1/100), which is not 2pq. There is no Hardy–Weinberg convention of counting only half of heterozygotes; 2pq already is the full heterozygote frequency.

distractorRationales.A: 1/10,000 is q^2, the affected homozygote frequency, not the much larger pool of heterozygous carriers.
distractorRationales.C: q = 0.01 is the recessive allele frequency; carriers are 2pq ≈ 0.02.
distractorRationales.D: 2pq already counts all heterozygotes; there is no extra factor of 1/2 in the standard carrier calculation.

passage.title: Speed and Care (1975)
passage.body: In “Speed and Care” (1975), Hanae Morioka writes from inside heritage listing. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: A radiology group installs a new computer-aided detection overlay. The same attendings read the same chest films. Hit rate for subtle nodules rises, but so does the false-alarm rate; a signal-detection analysis finds d′ unchanged. Which change in the decision process best accounts for the pattern?

choices.text: Sensory discriminability improved, because more true nodules are now named
Readers adopted a more liberal criterion, accepting more yes responses at a fixed d′
The payoff matrix became more conservative, raising the criterion and cutting false alarms
Weber fractions for luminance shrank, so smaller density differences became detectable

items.explanation: Signal-detection theory separates sensitivity (d′, distance between noise and signal-plus-noise distributions) from criterion (β or C). A liberal shift increases both hits and false alarms while leaving d′ unchanged, which is the overlay pattern. Improved discriminability would raise d′ and typically improve hits without a matched false-alarm rise. A conservative criterion does the opposite of what was observed. Weber’s law is a ratio of intensity increments, not a yes/no decision policy on films.

distractorRationales.A: More hits with matching false alarms and flat d′ is a criterion shift, not a true sensitivity gain.
distractorRationales.C: A conservative criterion would lower, not raise, both hits and false alarms.
distractorRationales.D: Weber’s law does not describe yes/no nodule calls or ROC parameters on radiographs.

passage.title: Kinetic analysis of a cytosolic lactate dehydrogenase variant
passage.body:
Researchers studied LDH-R, a fictional homotetrameric cytosolic lactate dehydrogenase that catalyzes the reversible reaction pyruvate + NADH + H+ -> lactate + NAD+. LDH-R helps maintain cytosolic redox balance when oxidative metabolism is limited. The investigators purified wild-type LDH-R, two point variants, and one truncation variant. Initial velocity was measured at saturating NADH unless NADH affinity was being assessed. PYA is a pyruvate analog that does not undergo reduction.

Properties of LDH-R proteins under selected assay conditions.
Protein or condition | Km for pyruvate (mM) | Relative Vmax (%) | Tetrameric protein (%) | Km for NADH (micromolar)
Wild type, pH 7.4 | 0.10 | 100 | 94 | 25
Wild type + PYA, pH 7.4 | 0.55 | 96 | 93 | 25
H177Q, pH 7.4 | 0.11 | 6 | 92 | 27
L246D, pH 7.4 | 0.12 | 38 | 35 | 26
Wild type, pH 6.6 | 0.08 | 125 | 94 | 22
C-terminal tail deletion, pH 7.4 | 0.28 | 70 | 90 | 80

Initial velocity curves for LDH-R. — At saturating NADH, wild-type LDH-R shows a hyperbolic increase in velocity with increasing pyruvate. PYA shifts the wild-type curve to the right without lowering the plateau. H177Q has a very low plateau. L246D has a lower plateau than wild type. At pH 6.6, the wild-type curve shifts slightly left and reaches a higher plateau.

items.stem: A thin converging lens has focal length 10 cm. A real object stands 30 cm from the lens. Using the real-is-positive convention, 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Linear magnification m = −v/u. Where is the image, and what is m?

choices.text: Real image 7.5 cm from the lens, m = −0.25
Real image 15 cm from the lens, inverted, half size (m = −0.50)
Virtual image 15 cm behind the object, m = +2.0
Real image 30 cm from the lens, m = −1.0

items.explanation: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30 = 3/30 − 1/30 = 2/30 = 1/15, so v = 15 cm, real, on the far side. m = −15/30 = −0.50: inverted and half as tall. A virtual image would require a negative v, which occurs for u < f, not for u = 3f. Equal object and image distances would need u = 2f = 20 cm, the 2f–2f case, not 30 cm. 7.5 cm would be f/something other than the lens equation. The object is outside f, so the image of a converging lens is real and inverted.

distractorRationales.A: 7.5 cm is not 1/(1/10 − 1/30); that difference of reciprocals is 1/15.
distractorRationales.C: u = 30 cm > f, so the image is real and inverted, not virtual and upright.
distractorRationales.D: u = v = 30 cm would require f = 15 cm (1/30+1/30=1/15), not f = 10 cm.

A stock solution is 2.00 M HCl. Dilution uses C1V1 = C2V2.
Step 1: 10.0 mL stock is made up to 100.0 mL (flask A).
Step 2: 10.0 mL of A is made up to 100.0 mL (flask B).
Step 3: 10.0 mL of B is made up to 100.0 mL (flask C).

items.explanation: Each step multiplies concentration by 10.0/100.0 = 0.100, a tenfold dilution. Three successive tenfold dilutions multiply by 10−3, so 2.00 × 10−3 = 0.00200 M. After one step the solution would be 0.200 M and after two steps 0.0200 M; stopping the count early produces those distractors. Four tenfold steps would give 0.000200 M. The volumes are consistent with C1V1 = C2V2 at each stage: 2.00 × 10.0 = C × 100, and repeating.

distractorRationales.B: 0.0200 M is the concentration after two dilutions, flask B, not flask C.
distractorRationales.C: 0.200 M is flask A, after a single 10 → 100 mL dilution.

items.stem: A uniform 4.0 m beam weighs 80 N. It rests on supports at both ends (A left, B right). A 40 N crate sits 1.0 m from A. Vertical equilibrium: RA + RB = 120 N. Torque about A: clockwise 80 N at 2.0 m plus 40 N at 1.0 m equals RB × 4.0 m. What are RA and RB?

RA = 60 N; RB = 60 N, splitting the 120 N equally

items.explanation: Moments about A: 80 × 2.0 + 40 × 1.0 = 160 + 40 = 200 N m = RB × 4.0, so RB = 50 N. Then RA = 120 − 50 = 70 N. The left support carries more because the crate is closer to A. Equal 60 N reactions would be correct only if the extra 40 N sat at the midpoint.

distractorRationales.B: Equal reactions would require the 40 N load at mid-span, not 1.0 m from A.
distractorRationales.D: The crate is nearer A, so A must carry the larger share; moments about A already fix RB = 50 N.

items.stem: Which paraphrase best captures the author's view of notation without turning it into a call to abolish scores?

choices.text: Notation is a historically specific technology that captures some relations and leaks others; scores remain tools, not the work's ontology.

The metronome proved that village dances were secretly in three all along.
Recordings have finally made the score unnecessary because microphones are neutral.

items.explanation: The passage attacks score-as-work while saying the upshot is not to burn scores: maps are superb, the crime is calling the map the territory. Notation captures and leaks. That is A. B inflates critique into abolition the last paragraph denies. C inverts the village-dance remark. D ignores the politics of which night and which microphone. A good paraphrase keeps the tool/ontology split rather than picking a pole the author refused.

distractorRationales.B: The author explicitly says the practical upshot is not to burn scores.
distractorRationales.C: “In three” is a notational decision a dance may never have made; the metronome is a later fantasy of a ruler.
distractorRationales.D: Recordings are a new paper with their own aiming and hierarchy, not a neutral replacement.

passage.title: What the metronome cannot hear
passage.body:
Musicology has a long habit of treating the score as the work and the performance as a more or less obedient copy. The habit is understandable. Paper sits still. It can be compared, edited, and taught in rooms where no instrument is present. A performance disappears as it occurs, leaving only memory, a recording, or an argument.

Yet the stillness of paper is not neutrality. Notation is a technology with a history: it captures some relations (pitch against a staff, duration against a beat) and lets others leak away (the weight of a bow, the delay before a singer accepts a consonant, the social fact of who is allowed to ornament). When a textbook says a movement is “in three,” it is reporting a notational decision that a village dance may never have made in those terms. The metronome, arriving later still, offers a fantasy that time is a ruler laid beside sound. Dancers know otherwise. So do jazz rhythm sections, whose time is a negotiation, not a grid that failed.

Scholars who defend the score-as-work often point to the composer’s authority and to the need for a shared object of study. Without a text, they say, we are left with impressions. The worry is real in a university. It is less real in a tradition that already treats the night’s playing as the work, and the paper, if paper exists, as a prompt. To call that tradition incomplete because it will not sit still is to confuse the archive’s convenience with the art’s ontology.

Recordings seemed to solve the disappearance problem. They created a new paper: a fixed take that can be looped, transcribed, and worshipped. The solution smuggles in its own politics. Which night was recorded, from which seat, with which microphone aiming at which social center of the band? A “definitive” recording can freeze a hierarchy that a living scene would have kept in motion. The fan who owns every take may know more facts than a player and still know less about what the music is for.

The practical upshot is not to burn scores. Scores are superb tools, as maps are superb tools. The upshot is to stop calling the map the territory in order to make seminars easier to grade. A pedagogy that can only hear what the metronome can hear will keep producing excellent accountants of pitch and a thin audience for everything else. If musicology wants to study music rather than the paperwork of music, it will have to tolerate objects that do not hold still, and to admit that some of the most precise information arrives as a glance between players that no staff line was built to hold.

distractorRationales.C: Opponent-process theory is about color vision.

items.stem: Equal amounts of NADH and of succinate (feeding electrons via Complex II) are oxidized by intact mitochondria. Why does NADH oxidation support more ATP synthesis per pair of electrons?

choices.text: NADH dehydrogenase (Complex I) pumps protons, whereas Complex II does not, so NADH-derived electrons drive a larger proton-motive force per 2e−.
Electrons from succinate enter at Complex IV, skipping Complex III and cytochrome c, so fewer protons are pumped.
NADH reduces oxygen directly in the matrix, producing an extra substrate-level GTP.
Succinate dehydrogenase consumes ATP to transfer electrons to ubiquinone.

items.explanation: Electrons from NADH enter at Complex I, which translocates protons, then proceed through ubiquinone, Complex III, cytochrome c, and Complex IV, which also pump protons. Electrons from succinate/FADH2 enter at Complex II, which does not pump protons, and join the chain at ubiquinone; they therefore miss the Complex I contribution to Δp. The smaller proton yield per 2e− means a lower P/O ratio for succinate than for NADH. Succinate does not skip Complex III, NADH does not reduce O2 directly, and Complex II does not hydrolyze ATP to reduce Q. Those facts explain why NADH oxidation supports more ATP per electron pair.

distractorRationales.B: Succinate electrons enter at Complex II/ubiquinone, not at Complex IV, and they still pass through Complex III and cytochrome c. Skipping pumps is not how succinate feeds the chain.
distractorRationales.C: NADH is oxidized by Complex I, not by a direct matrix reaction with O2, and that path does not make substrate-level GTP.
distractorRationales.D: Complex II transfers electrons from succinate to Q without ATP hydrolysis; it is not an ATP-consuming pump.

items.stem: An inhibitor binds the FAD-dependent enzyme that oxidizes a four-carbon citric-acid-cycle intermediate to a trans-unsaturated four-carbon product. The same polypeptide is an integral component of the inner mitochondrial membrane electron-transport chain. Which enzyme is it, and which reduced cofactor does it produce?

choices.text: Succinate dehydrogenase; enzyme-bound FADH2 that reduces ubiquinone

items.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase oxidizes succinate to fumarate (trans-butenedioate) and is the only citric-acid-cycle enzyme that is also Complex II of the electron-transport chain, an inner membrane protein. Its bound FAD is reduced to FADH2, and electrons pass to iron–sulfur centers and then to ubiquinone, forming ubiquinol. Malate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are soluble-matrix NAD+-dependent enzymes (α-KGDH uses NAD+, not NADP+ as the primary acceptor). Fumarase hydrates fumarate to malate and is not a dehydrogenase and not an ETC complex. The dual TCA/ETC identity uniquely identifies SDH.

distractorRationales.A: Malate dehydrogenase is a matrix enzyme that reduces NAD+ to NADH and is not an inner-membrane ETC complex. It also oxidizes a four-carbon hydroxy acid to oxaloacetate, not to a trans-alkene.
distractorRationales.C: α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase oxidizes a five-carbon α-keto acid to succinyl-CoA using NAD+, not NADPH, and it is not Complex II.
distractorRationales.D: Fumarase adds water across fumarate’s double bond; it does not reduce NAD+ and is not an electron-transport complex.
