items.stem: Which opening uses a reflective first-person without collapsing into solipsism?

choices.text: I am unique and no one else has ever had to choose between speaking and staying.
I kept my mouth closed at that table so the rent would still be paid, and I am still not sure whether that silence was love, cowardice, or both—a question many people inherit with a house.
I hate everyone in my family and this essay will list them.
One must not use “I,” because reflection is only valid in the third person.

items.explanation: Reflective voice is first-person that thinks, not a claim of cosmic uniqueness and not a prosecution file. B names a particular table and rent, admits mixed motives, and then opens the question outward—many people inherit that silence—without pretending the writer is a universal spokesman. A is solipsism. C is a vent. D invents a ban on “I” that would make Task B impossible. The craft is to let the self be a specimen, not a monument. Under time, one honest uncertainty does more than a manifesto of uniqueness.

distractorRationales.A: “No one else has ever” seals the essay against the reader; that is solipsism, not reflection.
distractorRationales.C: A hate-list is expressive, but it does not turn toward a question the reader can share.
distractorRationales.D: Task B expects a personal voice; a third-person-only rule is not ACER’s.

items.stem:
Normal boiling points of four hydrides:

Compound | Mr | bp (°C)
CH4 | 16 | −162
NH3 | 17 | −33
HF | 20 | 20
H2O | 18 | 100

Dispersion forces increase with Mr in the absence of hydrogen bonding. Which explanation of the table is best?

choices.text: CH4, with no N/O/F–H bonding, boils far lower than the three hydrogen-bonded hydrides of similar mass; H2O boils highest because each molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds in a network
Boiling point simply tracks Mr, so HF must boil below CH4
NH3 has the highest bp because nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen
All four compounds are hydrogen-bonded equally, so the 262 °C spread is random

items.explanation: Mr values lie in a narrow 16–20 window, so dispersion alone cannot explain a 262 °C spread. CH4 cannot hydrogen-bond and boils at −162 °C. NH3, HF and H2O all hydrogen-bond and boil much higher. Water’s tetrahedral two-donor plus two-acceptor capacity builds a three-dimensional network, placing its bp well above HF (which has a donor/acceptor mismatch) and NH3. Tracking Mr would rank HF highest and CH4 lowest by only a few degrees, not 182 °C. NH3 is not the highest, and the four species are not equivalent in hydrogen-bond inventory.

distractorRationales.B: HF (Mr 20) boils 182 °C above CH4 (Mr 16); mass does not dominate.
distractorRationales.C: NH3 boils at −33 °C, below both HF and H2O.
distractorRationales.D: CH4 cannot form conventional hydrogen bonds; the spread is systematic, not random.

passage.title: psg-cp-3
passage.body:
Students build and analyze a galvanic (voltaic) cell and then use batteries to study simple circuits. In the cell, a strip of zinc metal sits in zinc sulfate solution and a strip of copper metal sits in copper sulfate solution; a salt bridge connects the two half-cells, and a wire with a voltmeter links the metal strips. Under standard conditions the tabulated reduction potentials are Zn^2+ + 2 e- -> Zn, E = -0.76 V, and Cu^2+ + 2 e- -> Cu, E = +0.34 V. When the wire is connected, one electrode gains mass while the other slowly dissolves, and the voltmeter registers a steady potential difference. The students confirm which metal is oxidized by weighing the electrodes before and after.
They then replace the standard 1 M solutions with more dilute ones and record how the measured cell voltage shifts away from its standard value, relating the change to the reaction quotient Q for Zn + Cu^2+ -> Zn^2+ + Cu.
In the circuit module, a 12 V battery is connected to three resistors: a 6 ohm and a 3 ohm resistor wired in parallel with each other, and that combination wired in series with a 4 ohm resistor. An ammeter reads the current leaving the battery. The students compute the equivalent resistance, the current, and the power the battery delivers, treating the battery as an ideal source with negligible internal resistance and the wires as resistanceless.

passage.title: psg-bb-6
passage.body:
A cell-biology group compared how three different solutes cross the plasma membrane of cultured cells. For each solute they measured the initial rate of uptake into the cell as a function of the solute's external concentration, under conditions where metabolic ATP could be depleted with an inhibitor when desired.
Solute X, a small hydrophobic steroid, entered at a rate that increased linearly with external concentration and did not plateau even at very high concentrations; depleting ATP had no effect on its uptake. Solute Y, a polar sugar, entered at a rate that rose with concentration and then leveled off at a maximum, tracing a curve resembling enzyme saturation; adding a structurally similar sugar reduced Y's uptake, but ATP depletion did not. Solute Z, an ion, was accumulated inside the cell to a concentration far higher than outside, against its concentration gradient; this uptake collapsed when ATP was depleted.
The researchers interpreted the linear, nonsaturable, ATP-independent uptake of X as simple diffusion directly through the lipid bilayer. The saturable, competable, but ATP-independent uptake of Y indicated a finite number of specific membrane transport proteins moving the sugar down its gradient. The accumulation of Z against its gradient, abolished by ATP depletion, indicated a pump doing work at the expense of cellular energy. The experiment thus separated three transport modes using two simple criteria: whether the rate saturates, and whether it requires cellular energy.

items.stem: The nucleophilic serine of a serine protease is mutated to alanine. Steady-state kinetics show that kcat falls by about six orders of magnitude while Km for a peptide substrate is nearly unchanged. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

choices.text: The serine hydroxyl is required for covalent catalysis but contributes little to ground-state substrate binding
The mutation destroys the S1 specificity pocket, so substrate can no longer bind
Serine was a diffusible cofactor rather than a residue in the polypeptide, and dialysis had already removed it
Km is numerically equal to kcat for hydrolases, so both parameters must fall together; the data are impossible

items.explanation: In the catalytic triad the serine hydroxyl attacks the scissile carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate and then an acyl-enzyme. Replacing that oxygen with alanine’s methyl group removes the nucleophile and collapses kcat. Km, which for many proteases is dominated by substrate binding to the specificity pockets, can remain similar if those pockets are intact—exactly the pattern reported. A destroyed binding pocket would raise Km substantially. Serine is an amino-acid residue, not a cofactor, and Km is not equal to kcat; they are independent kinetic parameters.

distractorRationales.B: An unchanged Km argues that ground-state binding is largely intact; the defect is chemical step(s), not docking.
distractorRationales.C: The nucleophilic serine is part of the protein sequence; it is not a small-molecule cofactor that dialyzes away.
distractorRationales.D: Km and kcat are independent. A selective kcat drop is the expected signature of a catalytic-residue mutation.

passage.title: The Archive Test (1979)
passage.body: Elena Rossi published “The Archive Test” in 1979 after a season in vaccine campaigns. The argument is that institutions remember procedures better than people. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: Aesthetics — why originals matter
passage.body:
Suppose a forger produces a copy of a painting so exact that no expert, however equipped, could tell it from the original. Most of us would still prefer to own the original, and would pay vastly more for it. This preference is easy to mock as mere snobbery — a fetish for provenance that adds nothing to what the eye receives. If two canvases are visually identical, the skeptic asks, how can one be aesthetically superior to the other? Whatever we are paying for, it cannot be the look of the thing.

The skeptic assumes that the value of a painting must reside entirely in its present visual surface. But this assumption is far from obvious. When I stand before a canvas that Rembrandt himself touched, I am in physical, causal contact with the very object his hand shaped. The forgery, however exquisite, offers no such contact; it is the terminus of a different causal chain, one that runs back not to Rembrandt but to a clever imitator in a rented studio. To value the original is to value that lineage, and there is nothing irrational about caring where a thing comes from.

An analogy makes the point. A letter in a beloved's handwriting is treasured over a flawless photocopy, though the copy conveys every word. We do not think the person who keeps the original has made a perceptual error, as though they had failed to notice that the words are the same. They are responding to something the photocopy lacks: a direct trace of the writer's presence. Paintings, on this view, are less like texts, whose value is exhausted by their content, and more like relics, whose value depends on their history.

Yet the analogy should not be pressed too far. Relics are valued almost wholly for contact and hardly at all for how they look; the point of a saint's bone is not its appearance. Great paintings are not like this. Their history matters, but so, undeniably, does what they show — the very composition and color the forger has reproduced. A defender of originals need not deny that appearance carries much of a painting's worth. The claim is only that appearance does not carry all of it, and that the remainder, however hard to name, is not nothing.

This more modest thesis is also the more defensible one. It grants the skeptic everything plausible in the skeptical position — that the visible work is most of what we prize — while denying the further, unargued step from "most" to "all." The forger's triumph, if it is one, is to have captured the larger share of a painting's value. It is not to have shown that the smaller share was an illusion all along.

items.stem: Patient S.M. has bilateral amygdala calcification. In delay fear conditioning she shows little potentiation of startle to a colored light that predicts a blast of noise, yet she can later describe the light–noise pairing. A comparison patient with hippocampal damage shows the reverse: intact startle potentiation but no declarative memory of the pairing. Which mapping is best?

choices.text: The amygdala is required for implicit fear learning; the hippocampus is required for declarative memory of the episode
The amygdala stores the explicit narrative; the hippocampus stores the conditioned fear reflex
Either lesion abolishes all emotion, so the double dissociation must be a measurement artifact
An amygdala lesion should spare fear conditioning and impair only language, which is not what was found

items.explanation: The limbic amygdala is central to assigning affective value and supporting Pavlovian fear conditioning, which is expressed as startle potentiation or similar implicit measures. The hippocampus supports forming a declarative record of what happened. A double dissociation of the kind described is the standard mapping in affective neuroscience and in MCAT-level limbic-system teaching: amygdala damage hits the fear response while leaving the story intact, and hippocampal damage hits the story while leaving the conditioned response intact. Swapping those roles, or claiming that any limbic lesion wipes out all emotion and language, contradicts the split.

distractorRationales.B: This swaps the functions: narratives are hippocampal, not amygdalar, in this design; the reflex-like fear response tracks the amygdala.
distractorRationales.C: The point of the dissociation is that emotion-related learning and declarative memory can come apart; it is not evidence that both systems failed.
distractorRationales.D: Amygdala damage is predicted to impair fear conditioning, which is exactly the deficit described for S.M.

passage.title: psg-cp-7
passage.body:
The physical properties of a substance are set largely by the forces between its molecules. Consider a data set the students assemble. Among the hydrides of Group 16, hydrogen sulfide (H2S) boils at -60 C, yet water (H2O), a lighter molecule, boils at +100 C - a striking exception to the usual trend that heavier molecules boil higher. The students also compare two compounds with the identical formula C2H6O: ethanol, which boils at 78 C, and dimethyl ether, which boils at -24 C. Finally, they tabulate the boiling points of the noble gases and find a steady rise from helium through xenon.
To interpret the data they review molecular structure. Oxygen is far more electronegative than hydrogen, so each O-H bond is polar; in water the two O-H bonds and two lone pairs on oxygen arrange the electron domains tetrahedrally, giving the molecule a bent shape with an H-O-H angle near 104.5 degrees and a net dipole moment. They classify the intermolecular forces available to each substance: London dispersion forces (present in all molecules, stronger in larger and more polarizable electron clouds), dipole-dipole forces (between permanent dipoles), and hydrogen bonding (the especially strong attraction when H bonded to N, O, or F is drawn to a lone pair on another such atom).
Their goal is to connect each measured boiling point to the strongest intermolecular force a molecule can form, and to explain the anomalies - water's high boiling point, ethanol versus its isomer, and the noble-gas trend - in terms of hydrogen bonding, polarity, geometry, and polarizability.

The keyed choice holds because: Correct. SN2 needs an accessible carbon (primary, less steric hindrance); SN1 forms a carbocation, stabilized best at tertiary carbons. items.stem: A thin converging lens has focal length 10 cm. An object stands 20 cm to the left of the lens. The image is:

choices.text: real, inverted, and the same size as the object, 20 cm to the right of the lens
virtual, upright, and enlarged, 20 cm to the left of the lens
real, inverted, and half the size of the object, 10 cm to the right of the lens
real, upright, and the same size as the object, 20 cm to the right of the lens

items.explanation: The thin-lens equation is 1/f = 1/o + 1/i. With f = +10 cm (converging) and o = +20 cm, 1/10 = 1/20 + 1/i, so 1/i = 1/20 and i = +20 cm: a real image on the opposite side of the lens. Magnification m = −i/o = −20/20 = −1, so the image is inverted and the same size as the object. This is the classic object-at-2f geometry, which places the image at 2f. A single converging lens does not produce a real upright image; upright images from this lens are virtual and occur only for o < f.

distractorRationales.B: A virtual upright enlarged image is the o < f (magnifying-glass) case. Here the object is at 2f, outside the focal point, so the image is real and inverted.
distractorRationales.C: An image at f with |m| = 1/2 would require a different object distance (o = 2f is same-size, not half-size). Solving 1/f = 1/o + 1/i with these numbers gives i = 20 cm, not 10 cm.
distractorRationales.D: The location and size are right, but a real image formed by a single converging lens is inverted. Upright and real together would require a second lens or a more elaborate optical system.

passage.title: The Hiring Rubric (1977)
passage.body: Clara Voss's 1977 essay “The Hiring Rubric,” on public libraries, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that a metric can become the mission that it was supposed to measure. The piece admits that some gatekeeping keeps fraud out. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: Critical Reasoning · Philosophy of Science
passage.body: For centuries we have told the story of the solitary genius: Newton alone under his apple tree, Curie alone in her laboratory, the writer alone at her desk producing a masterpiece from nothing but personal brilliance. This narrative is comforting because it is simple, and it sells a great many biographies. It is also, historians of science increasingly argue, badly incomplete. Newton corresponded for decades with a network of mathematicians whose incremental work he built on and later minimised in his own accounts. Curie's laboratory depended on instruments, techniques and a body of prior findings assembled by dozens of researchers across Europe. Even the writer's "original" idea usually turns out, on close inspection, to be a recombination of things read, overheard, or absorbed from a wider culture. None of this makes any of these individuals less remarkable. But it does suggest that crediting a single mind for a breakthrough often erases the scaffolding — the teachers, rivals, funders and quiet collaborators — without which that mind would have had nothing to work with.

Compound | Main functional group | Relevant pKa | Dominant form at pH 8.3 | Expected layer at pH 8.3
A | carboxylic acid | 4.2 | deprotonated carboxylate | aqueous

passage.title: Care and Speed (1973)
passage.body: Leo Nyathi published “Care and Speed” in 1973 after a season in broadcast newsrooms. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: psg-ps-7
passage.body:
Researchers studied how people view themselves and explain behavior. In Study 1, community volunteers completed a scale measuring their belief that they could organize and execute the actions needed to reach specific goals. Independently, they rated how much they felt their life outcomes were controlled by their own actions versus by luck or powerful others. Volunteers high on the first measure attempted harder tasks, persisted longer after setbacks, and reported less anxiety. Those who attributed outcomes mostly to outside forces set fewer goals and gave up sooner.
In Study 2, participants read vignettes about a student who failed an exam. When explaining the student's failure, observers most often cited the student's laziness or low ability, rarely mentioning the situation (an unfair test, a family emergency). Yet when participants recalled a time they themselves had failed, they overwhelmingly cited situational causes. In a variation, participants watched a peer perform poorly under obvious time pressure; even so, most still rated the peer as low in ability.
The authors linked Study 1 to two related constructs: a person's belief in their capability to succeed at specific tasks, and a general expectancy about whether outcomes are internally or externally controlled. They interpreted Study 2 as showing a systematic bias in how observers explain others' behavior, together with a divergence between how people explain their own versus others' outcomes. They stressed that these attribution tendencies operate even when situational information is clearly available.

items.stem:
A stone is dropped from rest. Taking g = 10 m s−2 downward as positive, the velocity–time graph is a straight line from (t, v) = (0, 0) to (4.0 s, 40 m s−1).

t (s) | v (m s−1)
0 | 0
2.0 | 20
4.0 | 40

Displacement from rest is the triangular area under this v–t graph, equivalently s = (1/2) g t^2. How far has the stone fallen in 4.0 s?
items.explanation: The area of the triangle is (1/2) × 4.0 s × 40 m s−1 = 80 m. The same result is s = (1/2)×10×(4.0)^2 = 80 m. Multiplying the final speed by the elapsed time (40 × 4.0 = 160 m) would be correct only if the stone had travelled at 40 m s−1 for the whole interval; instead the average speed from rest is half of the final speed, 20 m s−1, and 20 × 4.0 = 80 m. 40 m is the numerical value of the final speed with units of metres attached. 200 m would correspond to using g = 25 m s−2 or a 5 s drop at this g. The graph’s linearity already encodes constant acceleration from rest.

distractorRationales.A: 40 m matches the final speed numerically but is not an area. Distance requires integrating v, not reading the last v value as a length.
distractorRationales.C: 160 m is v_final × t, which uses the highest speed as if it applied for all 4 s. The average velocity from rest is 20 m s−1.
distractorRationales.D: 200 m does not match either the triangular area or (1/2)gt^2 with the given g and t.

items.stem: Run R2 shows a higher pressure than Run R1 despite the same sealed headspace volume and oxygen mole fraction. Which explanation best accounts for this observation?

choices.text: The oxygen molecules have a larger molar mass at higher temperature.
The average molecular kinetic energy is greater at 310 K than at 298 K.
The number of gas molecules decreases when temperature increases.
The ideal gas pressure is independent of temperature when volume is fixed.

items.explanation: For a sealed, rigid headspace with constant moles and volume, the ideal gas law gives P proportional to T. Increasing temperature from 298 K to 310 K predicts P2/P1 = 310/298 = 1.04, matching the pressure increase in R2. Common miss: Thinking of temperature in Celsius terms rather than using absolute temperature in gas-law relationships. This correctly links higher absolute temperature to greater average kinetic energy and increased pressure at fixed n and V. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.A: Molar mass does not change with temperature.
distractorRationales.C: The headspace is sealed, so the number of gas molecules is not expected to decrease.
distractorRationales.D: At fixed n and V, ideal gas pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

passage.title: Electrochemical Monitoring of Dissolved Oxygen
passage.body:
A fictional microfluidic device is designed to monitor oxygen consumption by cultured cells. The device contains a 10.0 mL sealed gas headspace above an aqueous medium. At the working electrode, oxygen is reduced according to: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O. A 3.0 V source drives current through a variable series resistor and the electrode system. In the tested range, electrode current is approximately proportional to oxygen partial pressure unless the electrode becomes limited by oxygen diffusion from the bulk solution. A pressure sensor in the chamber acts as a parallel-plate capacitor. When gas pressure increases, a flexible membrane deflects toward the fixed plate, decreasing the plate separation d. Before each run, the headspace is sealed, and the table reports conditions just before current is measured.

Operating conditions and measured current for the oxygen sensor.
Run | Headspace O2 mole fraction | Temperature (K) | Total pressure before measurement (atm) | Series resistance (ohm) | Measured current (mA)
R1 | 0.21 | 298 | 1.00 | 1000 | 1.8
R2 | 0.21 | 310 | 1.04 | 1000 | 1.9
R3 | 0.10 | 298 | 1.00 | 1000 | 0.86
R4 | 0.21 | 298 | 1.00 | 500 | 2.4
R5 | 0.21 | 298 | 1.00 | 2000 | 0.95

Current response of the oxygen electrode. — For runs with 1000 ohm resistance, measured current increases approximately linearly with oxygen mole fraction. At lower resistance, the current increases less than expected from Ohm's law, consistent with a diffusion-limited plateau.

items.stem: A 2.00 mg mass of a drug is dissolved in 1.00 kg of water. Density of the dilute solution is 1.00 g mL−1. 1 ppm is 1 mg of solute per kg of solution. The same solution is also described in mol L−1; the drug’s molar mass is 200 g mol−1. Which pair is correct?
items.explanation: 2.00 mg in 1.00 kg is exactly 2.00 ppm by the given definition. The solution volume is 1.00 L at the stated density. Moles of drug = 2.00 × 10−3 g / 200 g mol−1 = 1.00 × 10−5 mol, so molarity is 1.00 × 10−5 mol L−1. Using 2.00 g instead of 2.00 mg would give 0.0100 M. Calling 2.00 mg in 1 kg ‘2000 ppm’ treats the solute as 2 g. 0.00200 ppm would be 2.00 µg in 1 kg.

distractorRationales.A: The ppm figure is 2.00, not 0.00200; the molarity half of the option is right but the ppm is not.
distractorRationales.C: 1.00 × 10−2 M would require 2.00 g of drug in 1 L, a thousand-fold mass error.
distractorRationales.D: 2000 ppm would be 2.00 g per kg, not 2.00 mg.

items.stem: Undocumented patients delay ED care until a surgical emergency. Link and Phelan’s fundamental-cause theory of health disparities would emphasize which point?

choices.text: Once germ theory is known, social position cannot affect infectious risk

SES and socially excluded legal status are flexible resources (money, power, knowledge, beneficial social connections, freedom to choose) that keep reproducing unequal health even as specific diseases and mechanisms change
Only genetic ancestry, not exclusion from insurance, can delay presentation
Parsons’s sick role requires undocumented patients to be blamed for symptoms

items.explanation: Link and Phelan argue that socioeconomic status is a fundamental cause of disease: it commands flexible resources that can be used to avoid risks and minimize consequences no matter which mechanisms are currently salient. Legal exclusion and social exclusion restrict those resources, producing delayed care and worse outcomes. Germ theory did not erase class gradients; mechanisms were replaced. Genetics does not exhaust presentation delay when insurance and deportation fear operate. Parsons’s sick role is a functionalist ideal, not a requirement to blame excluded patients.

distractorRationales.A: Fundamental-cause theory exists because gradients survive mechanism change, including after germ theory.
distractorRationales.C: Access barriers are exactly the sort of resource restriction the theory highlights.
distractorRationales.D: The sick role’s “not responsible” clause is not a license to blame undocumented patients.

items.stem: Erythrocytes metabolize glucose to lactate. When inorganic phosphate is replaced by arsenate, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase still oxidizes its substrate, but 1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate hydrolyzes spontaneously and 3-phosphoglycerate forms without generating ATP at phosphoglycerate kinase. What happens to the net ATP yield of anaerobic glycolysis per glucose?

choices.text: Net ATP falls to zero because the two ATP from phosphoglycerate kinase are lost while hexokinase and PFK-1 still consume two ATP
Net ATP doubles because pyruvate kinase is stimulated by arsenate
Net ATP becomes two extra from hexokinase, which now runs in reverse
ATP yield is unchanged because substrate-level phosphorylation occurs only at pyruvate kinase

items.explanation: In anaerobic glycolysis, ATP is spent at hexokinase and phosphofructokinase-1 (−2) and recouped at phosphoglycerate kinase (+2, one per triose) and pyruvate kinase (+2), for a net of +2 ATP per glucose. Arsenate allows GAPDH to proceed but bypasses the acyl-phosphate that PGK uses to make ATP, so those two ATP are lost. Pyruvate kinase still makes two ATP from two PEP, exactly canceling the two ATP invested, and net yield is zero. Hexokinase does not reverse under these conditions, and arsenate is not a PK stimulator that would raise yield. PGK is a genuine substrate-level phosphorylation step that the uncoupler removes.

distractorRationales.B: Arsenate uncouples PGK; it does not double PK flux in a way that increases net ATP above normal.
distractorRationales.C: Hexokinase remains an ATP-consuming step; it does not run in reverse to produce ATP in glycolysis.
distractorRationales.D: Phosphoglycerate kinase is also a substrate-level phosphorylation; ignoring it misses the uncoupling.

items.stem:
Solid calcium carbonate decomposes in a closed, evacuated vessel: CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g). At 1073 K the equilibrium constant is Kp = 0.22 bar, and Kp = P_CO2 because the activities of the pure solids are omitted. The vessel is already at equilibrium with P_CO2 = 0.22 bar and both solids present. An extra 12 g of CaCO3(s) is then added, T held at 1073 K.

Measured P_CO2 (bar) | Condition
0.22 | before adding extra CaCO3
? | after re-equilibration

What is P_CO2 after re-equilibration, and why?

choices.text: 0.44 bar, because doubling the carbonate mass doubles the equilibrium pressure of CO2.
0.22 bar, because Kp depends only on P_CO2 at this T, and extra solid CaCO3 does not appear in Kp.
Much less than 0.22 bar, because added CaCO3 shifts the equilibrium left by mass action on a concentration [CaCO3].
0 bar, because extra CaCO3 reabsorbs all of the CO2.

items.explanation: For this heterogeneous equilibrium the equilibrium law is Kp = P_CO2. At 1073 K that pressure is fixed at 0.22 bar as long as both CaCO3(s) and CaO(s) remain. Adding more solid carbonate does not change the activities of the solids (taken as 1 for pure phases) and does not change T, so P_CO2 is unchanged. Doubling the mass of a solid does not double a gas pressure that is set by Kp. Treating CaCO3 as if it had a molarity in Kp is the usual incorrect homogeneous-style mass-action argument.

distractorRationales.A: Equilibrium pressure of CO2 is set by Kp, not by the mass of solid carbonate, provided some solid remains.
distractorRationales.C: Pure solids are omitted from Kp; there is no [CaCO3] term that would drive the equilibrium backward when extra solid is added.
distractorRationales.D: Reabsorption of all CO2 would require Kp = 0. The given Kp is 0.22 bar, so a finite CO2 pressure remains.

items.stem: An action potential is initiated at the axon hillock of a typical multipolar neuron. Under physiologic conditions the impulse propagates:

choices.text: only backward through the dendritic tree, because axons cannot conduct toward terminals
as a standing wave occupying the entire axon in both directions indefinitely
only after the soma electrically depolarizes a skeletal muscle fiber without using an axon
toward the axon terminals; Na+ channels behind the active region are inactivated, so the spike does not reverse along that axon

items.explanation: Orthodromic conduction runs from the trigger zone toward synaptic terminals. Voltage-gated Na+ channels inactivate shortly after opening, creating a refractory wake that prevents the regenerative depolarization from turning around on the same axon under normal conditions. Dendrites are not the primary regenerative path to the output synapse, a standing wave is not the Hodgkin-Huxley picture, and a CNS neuron does not skip its axon and dump current into a muscle fiber.

distractorRationales.A: The functional output path is the axon to terminals, not exclusive antidromic invasion of dendrites.
distractorRationales.B: The AP is a traveling, self-limited wave with a refractory period, not a persistent bidirectional standing depolarization of the whole axon.
distractorRationales.C: Chemical synaptic transmission at a neuromuscular junction, when it occurs, still requires axonal conduction to the terminal; the soma does not directly pace muscle by volume conduction as the default.

passage.title: Alternative splicing and protein dimerization of LUM1
passage.body:
A fictional eukaryotic gene, LUM1, contains four exons. Exon 3 encodes a hydrophobic alpha-helical segment required for stable LUM1 dimer formation. A regulatory RNA-binding protein, RBP-K, binds an intronic splicing enhancer near exon 3 and promotes exon 3 inclusion. Skipping exon 3 preserves the reading frame but produces a mostly monomeric protein that is degraded more rapidly. A separate mutation in the 5' splice donor of intron 2 causes intron retention and introduces a premature termination codon more than 50 nucleotides upstream of the final exon-exon junction.

Effects of LUM1 expression constructs in cultured cells.
Condition | Pre-mRNA transcription rate (%) | Mature mRNA containing exon 3 (%) | Total mature LUM1 mRNA (%) | LUM1 protein (%) | Dimeric LUM1 among detected protein (%)
Wild type | 100 | 85 | 100 | 100 | 80
RBP-K knockdown | 98 | 20 | 55 | 25 | 18
Exon 3 splice acceptor weakened | 95 | 10 | 50 | 20 | 12
Intron 2 splice donor mutant | 100 | 5 | 18 | 6 | 8
Kozak sequence mutant | 100 | 82 | 95 | 22 | 78
Exon 3 hydrophobic-to-charged coding mutant | 100 | 84 | 98 | 45 | 20

Model for LUM1 isoform production. — When exon 3 is included, LUM1 contains a hydrophobic helical segment that supports dimerization. When exon 3 is skipped, the reading frame remains intact but the helical dimerization segment is absent. Intron 2 retention creates a premature stop codon predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.

items.stem: A 100 keV diagnostic X-ray photon is compared with a 2 eV visible photon, both in vacuum. The X-ray photon has:

items.explanation: Photon energy E = h f = hc / lambda, so a 100 keV photon has much higher frequency and much shorter wavelength than a 2 eV photon. In vacuum both travel at c; electromagnetic waves do not speed up because they are more energetic. Pairing short wavelength with low frequency, or long wavelength with high frequency, contradicts c = f lambda.

distractorRationales.A: Higher energy means shorter, not longer, wavelength, and vacuum speed is c for both.
distractorRationales.B: Shorter wavelength is correct, but frequency is higher, not lower, because f = c / lambda.
distractorRationales.C: Higher frequency is correct for the X-ray, but that requires a shorter wavelength, not a longer one.

items.stem:
Silica TLC (polar stationary phase, hexane/ethyl acetate 4:1). Distances from origin:

Spot | distance (cm)
Solvent front | 8.0
Compound A | 6.0
Compound B | 2.0
Compound C | 2.0, after staining also UV-active at 254 nm like B

Rf = distance(spot)/distance(front). A is a non-polar hydrocarbon; B is a phenol. Which reading is justified?

choices.text: Rf(A)=0.75, Rf(B)=0.25; A is less polar and travels farther on silica; C co-spots with B so TLC alone does not prove C ≠ B
Rf(A)=0.25 because hydrocarbons stick to silica
B is less polar than A because it moved only 2.0 cm
C must be identical to B because two compounds cannot share an Rf

items.explanation: Rf(A)=6.0/8.0=0.75 and Rf(B)=2.0/8.0=0.25. Polar silica retains the phenol (hydrogen bonding) so B lags; the hydrocarbon A interacts weakly and rides near the solvent front. Compound C has the same Rf as B, so they may be the same or merely coincidentally similar in polarity; co-spotting is necessary but not sufficient for identity. Hydrocarbons do not ‘stick’ on silica relative to phenols. Smaller distance means more polar on this phase, so B is more polar than A. Different compounds can share an Rf, which is why mixed-spot tests and a second method are used.

distractorRationales.B: A travelled 6.0 of 8.0 cm, Rf 0.75, the less retained non-polar compound.
distractorRationales.C: Shorter travel on silica means stronger adsorption, i.e. more polar, not less.
distractorRationales.D: Equal Rf is consistent with identity but does not prove it; many phenols could occupy Rf 0.25.

passage.title: psg-ps-10
passage.body:
A longitudinal study followed 8,000 adults for 15 years to examine links between social position and health. Participants were grouped by socioeconomic status (SES), a composite of income, education, and occupational prestige. Age-adjusted rates of chronic illness and mortality declined steadily at each higher step of the SES ladder - not merely a gap between rich and poor, but a graded relationship across the whole range. The pattern held after controlling for smoking and diet, and was partly explained by chronic stress, worse neighborhood conditions, and unequal access to preventive care.
Participants were also classified by the neighborhood where they lived. Lower-SES families were concentrated in areas with fewer clinics, more pollution, and less green space; researchers described these areas as products of long-standing residential segregation. Children raised in the lowest-SES neighborhoods were less likely to reach a higher SES than their parents, a pattern the authors linked to unequal schools and social networks.
Finally, the study noted a demographic shift: as the population aged and birth rates fell, the ratio of working-age adults to dependents changed, straining programs that fund elder care. The authors argued that health follows a social gradient, that place and inequality shape opportunity across generations, and that population structure interacts with these inequalities to shape a society's future needs. They emphasized that individual choices operated within, and were constrained by, these structural conditions.

passage.title: psg-ps-5
passage.body:
Researchers ran three studies of behavior in groups. In Study 1, a participant judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line, answering aloud after several confederates. On critical trials the confederates unanimously gave an obviously wrong answer. Participants conformed to the wrong answer on about 35% of critical trials, and three-quarters conformed at least once; conformity fell sharply when a single confederate broke from the majority. Most conformers later said they knew the group was wrong but did not want to stand out.
In Study 2, participants completed either a simple, well-practiced task or a complex, unfamiliar task, alone or in front of an audience. An audience improved performance on the simple task but worsened it on the complex task.
In Study 3, participants heard what sounded like a fellow participant having a medical emergency in another room. When participants believed they were the only witness, 85% sought help within a minute; when they believed four others were also present, only 31% did, and those who helped took longer. Interviews suggested that the presence of others reduced each individual's felt responsibility.
The authors distinguished going along with a group to fit in from the effect of an audience on task performance, and linked Study 3 to a well-documented reduction in helping as the number of bystanders rises. They emphasized that these effects reflect the social situation rather than stable personality differences among the participants.

passage.title: psg-cars-9
passage.body:
Classical economic theory rests on a conception of the agent as fundamentally rational: possessed of stable, consistent preferences, capable of processing available information, and motivated to maximize personal utility. This model has extraordinary analytical power. It generates precise, testable predictions and underlies the welfare theorems that have guided economic policy for generations. Yet beginning in the latter decades of the twentieth century, a body of research in behavioral economics accumulated evidence that humans deviate from this ideal in systematic, predictable, and consequential ways.
Among the most robust findings is loss aversion: people respond more strongly to losses than to equivalent gains. The discomfort of losing one hundred dollars is experienced as more intense than the pleasure of gaining the same amount. This asymmetry has significant implications. It helps explain why people hold losing financial assets far longer than rational profit-maximization would recommend — they prefer the pain of waiting to the certain loss of selling. It also explains why contract and policy framings that emphasize avoiding losses are more motivationally effective than those that emphasize equivalent gains.
A second set of findings concerns heuristic judgment under uncertainty. When people lack the time or information to calculate expected values precisely, they rely on cognitive shortcuts that usually suffice but sometimes produce systematic errors. The availability heuristic leads people to estimate the probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind: dramatic events, such as airplane crashes, are overestimated in frequency because they are memorable, while mundane but statistically commoner risks, such as car accidents, are underestimated. The representativeness heuristic leads people to assess probability by how closely an instance resembles a prototypical category member, often ignoring base-rate information entirely. A familiar illustration involves base rates. Told that a quiet, orderly person who loves books was drawn from a group made up mostly of salespeople and only a few librarians, many respondents confidently judge the person a librarian, swayed by resemblance to a stereotype while all but ignoring how rare librarians are in the sample. The mistake is not stupidity but the misfiring of an ordinarily useful strategy: resemblance is frequently a serviceable guide to category membership, and only in cases engineered to pit it against base-rate information does it lead reliably astray. The shortcuts that behavioral research exposes are, in most everyday settings, both fast and surprisingly accurate; they betray us mainly in the artificial problems constructed to reveal their inner workings.
These findings have generated debate about the appropriate policy response. Some argue that behavioral insights justify 'nudging': designing choice environments so that the default option is the one that most people would choose on reflection. Automatic enrollment in retirement savings plans, for instance, exploits the tendency to accept defaults, boosting participation without eliminating freedom of choice. Critics of nudging worry that it is paternalistic, that it manipulates rather than informs, and that it presupposes policymakers know better than individuals what those individuals' reflective preferences actually are.
The behavioral economics literature does not establish that markets always fail or that regulation is always beneficial. It establishes only that the idealized rational actor is an incomplete description of real human psychology, and that understanding how people actually decide is essential to designing institutions that work well in the world as it is.

Points P and Q lie on the perpendicular bisector and on the line joining two charges, respectively:

Charges: +4.0 μC at x = −1.0 m and +4.0 μC at x = +1.0 m.
P is at (0, 0), the midpoint.
Q is at (3.0 m, 0).

Electric field is a vector; potential V = kq/r is a scalar. Which statement is true?

choices.text: E is maximum at P and zero at Q
At P the fields cancel so E = 0 but V is 2 kq/r = 7.2 × 10^4 V; at Q the fields add in the same direction
E and V are both zero at P because it is halfway
V = 0 at P because the charges are equal

items.explanation: At the midpoint the two E vectors are equal, opposite, and cancel, so E = 0. Potentials add: each is k(4.0×10−6)/1.0 = 3.6×10^4 V, total 7.2×10^4 V. Equal like charges do not make V = 0; that would need opposite signs. At Q, both field arrows point to +x (away from both positives), so they add. E is therefore a minimum (zero) at P, not a maximum. Midpoint cancellation of E for like charges is a vector effect and does not null the scalar potential.

distractorRationales.A: The symmetric point P is where E cancels; Q is off to one side, where the arrows align.
distractorRationales.C: E = 0 at P, but V is the sum of two positive terms, 7.2 × 10^4 V.
distractorRationales.D: V = 0 on a perpendicular bisector of opposite charges, not like charges.

passage.title: Unacknowledged Method (1978)
passage.body: In “Unacknowledged Method” (1978), Clara Voss writes from inside community radio. The argument is that neutrality is a style, not an absence of interest. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: A string of length 2.0 m is fixed at both ends. Transverse waves on the string travel at 10 m/s. The frequency of the fundamental standing wave is:
items.explanation: A string fixed at both ends has a node at each end, so the fundamental fits one-half wavelength into the string: λ/2 = L, or λ = 2L = 4.0 m. Frequency and wavelength are related by v = f λ, so f = v/λ = 10 m/s / 4.0 m = 2.5 Hz. Equivalently, f_n = n v / (2 L) with n = 1 gives 10 / 4 = 2.5 Hz. A closed air column uses v/(4L) for its fundamental, which is a different boundary condition and does not apply to this string.

distractorRationales.A: This is v/(4L), the closed-pipe (node–antinode) fundamental. Both ends of the string are nodes, so the fundamental is v/(2L), not v/(4L).
distractorRationales.C: This is v/L = 5 Hz, which would be the n = 2 harmonic (one full wavelength on the string), not the fundamental.

items.stem: Nitronium ion, NO2+, is linear, whereas nitrite, NO2−, is bent. Which pair of hybridizations at nitrogen is consistent with those shapes?

choices.text: NO2+: nitrogen is sp (two electron domains); NO2−: nitrogen is sp2 (three electron domains, including a lone pair).
Both nitrogens are sp3, and the extra charge on nitrite simply compresses the bond angle below 109°.
NO2+: nitrogen is sp3d; NO2−: nitrogen is sp, so nitrite should be linear.
Both nitrogens are sp, so both ions must be linear; packing in the lattice bends nitrite.

items.explanation: Count electron domains at nitrogen. In NO2+ the nitrogen is bonded to two oxygens with no remaining lone pair (the ion is isoelectronic with CO2), so two domains imply sp hybridization and a 180° bond angle. In NO2− nitrogen has two bonding domains plus one lone pair, so three domains imply sp2 hybridization and a bent geometry. Expanding the octet to sp3d is unnecessary for these second-period nitrogen species, and a lattice cannot turn a linear isolated ion into a persistently bent one in the gas-phase or solution description used here.

distractorRationales.B: sp3 would imply four electron domains and a pyramidal or tetrahedral arrangement, which matches neither the linear cation nor the bent anion with only three domains.
distractorRationales.C: This assignment reverses the domain counts and would predict a linear nitrite, contradicting the bent structure.
distractorRationales.D: Nitrite is bent as an isolated ion because of the nitrogen lone pair, not because of crystal packing.

passage.title: psg-bb-6
passage.body:
A cell-biology group compared how three different solutes cross the plasma membrane of cultured cells. For each solute they measured the initial rate of uptake into the cell as a function of the solute's external concentration, under conditions where metabolic ATP could be depleted with an inhibitor when desired.
Solute X, a small hydrophobic steroid, entered at a rate that increased linearly with external concentration and did not plateau even at very high concentrations; depleting ATP had no effect on its uptake. Solute Y, a polar sugar, entered at a rate that rose with concentration and then leveled off at a maximum, tracing a curve resembling enzyme saturation; adding a structurally similar sugar reduced Y's uptake, but ATP depletion did not. Solute Z, an ion, was accumulated inside the cell to a concentration far higher than outside, against its concentration gradient; this uptake collapsed when ATP was depleted.
The researchers interpreted the linear, nonsaturable, ATP-independent uptake of X as simple diffusion directly through the lipid bilayer. The saturable, competable, but ATP-independent uptake of Y indicated a finite number of specific membrane transport proteins moving the sugar down its gradient. The accumulation of Z against its gradient, abolished by ATP depletion, indicated a pump doing work at the expense of cellular energy. The experiment thus separated three transport modes using two simple criteria: whether the rate saturates, and whether it requires cellular energy.

items.stem: A hospital scheduling algorithm shortens appointment slots for ZIP codes that historically overlap with redlined districts, with no individual clerk expressing hostility. Outcome data show longer waits for Black patients. This pattern is best labeled how?

choices.text: Individual discrimination only, because an algorithm cannot be institutional
Institutional discrimination: organizational rules or routines producing systematic unequal treatment, even without a bigoted actor at the desk
Prejudice without discrimination, because no clerk used a slur
Goffman stigma only, which is defined as a ZIP-code variable

items.explanation: Institutional (structural) discrimination is unequal outcomes built into policies, algorithms, or standard operating procedures, and it does not require a prejudiced individual at the moment of action. Individual discrimination is a particular person treating another unequally. The algorithm produces extra wait—discrimination in behavior/outcome—not a mere private attitude. Goffman’s stigma is interactional identity spoilage, not a geocoded slot-length rule. Carmichael and Hamilton’s discussion of institutional racism is the usual MCAT contrast with individual bias.

distractorRationales.A: Institutions can discriminate through routines and code; a smiling clerk is not required.
distractorRationales.C: Unequal waits are discriminatory outcomes, not prejudice-only.
distractorRationales.D: Stigma is not defined as a ZIP-code scheduler.

items.stem: Why is it important that HSP-70X mRNA levels were also measured under normal, non-heat conditions?

choices.text: It shows that ReguFactor B and HSP-70X are irrelevant to wheat survival.
It proves that wheat seedlings cannot survive without heat stress.
It shows that mRNA cannot be measured accurately.
It establishes a baseline showing that ReguFactor B's effect on HSP-70X is specific to heat stress, not just a constant difference between the groups.

items.explanation: Without the non-heat baseline, the mRNA differences seen under heat could just reflect a constant, pre-existing difference between the modified and normal seedlings rather than a heat-specific regulatory effect. Since all three groups look similar without heat, the heat-specific pattern can be attributed to ReguFactor B's role in the heat response specifically. A baseline measurement under "normal" conditions lets you check whether an effect is specific to the condition being tested, or just a constant difference between groups that would show up regardless. No baseline means you can't tell the two apart. Memory tip: "Same before, different after": if the groups look identical before heat but different after, you know heat — not some pre-existing quirk of the seedlings — is what triggered the difference. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: Biology · Gene Regulation
passage.body: A research group is studying a heat-shock protein gene, HSP-70X, thought to help wheat seedlings survive short bursts of extreme heat. They suspect a regulatory protein, called ReguFactor B, switches HSP-70X on when temperatures rise. To test this, they create three groups of genetically modified wheat seedlings: one where ReguFactor B is overexpressed (produced in excess), one where the gene for ReguFactor B is knocked out (disabled), and a normal (wild-type) control group. All seedlings are exposed to a two-hour heat spike, and HSP-70X mRNA levels are measured immediately afterwards. The overexpression group shows HSP-70X mRNA levels roughly four times higher than the wild-type control. The knockout group shows almost no detectable HSP-70X mRNA at all, even after the heat spike. Under normal, non-heat conditions, HSP-70X mRNA levels are low and roughly equal across all three groups.

items.stem:
Vapour pressures at 20 °C:

Liquid | Pvap (kPa) | notable IMF
Pentane | 57 | dispersion only
Propanone | 24 | dipole–dipole + dispersion
Ethanol | 5.8 | hydrogen bonding + dispersion
Water | 2.3 | hydrogen-bond network

A lower vapour pressure at a given temperature means stronger net attractions in the liquid. Which ranking of total intermolecular attraction is supported?

choices.text: Propanone > water, because a carbonyl dipole is always stronger than hydrogen bonding
Pentane > propanone > ethanol > water, following vapour pressure
All four are equal because each is a molecular liquid at 20 °C

items.explanation: Vapour pressure falls 57 → 24 → 5.8 → 2.3 kPa from pentane to water, so the liquid-phase attractions increase in that same direction: pentane (dispersion only) weakest, then polar propanone, then hydrogen-bonded ethanol, then the water network. Ranking by the vapour-pressure numbers themselves reverses the force order. Being molecular at 20 °C does not equalise escaping tendency. Propanone’s 24 kPa is an order of magnitude above water’s 2.3 kPa, so the carbonyl dipole is not stronger than water’s hydrogen-bond network.

distractorRationales.A: Propanone’s vapour pressure is much higher than water’s, so its net IMF are weaker.
distractorRationales.C: High vapour pressure means weak attractions; that list is the reverse of interaction strength.
distractorRationales.D: A 25-fold range in Pvap shows the liquids are not equivalent.

items.stem: In the trp operon leader, a short ORF contains tandem Trp codons. When charged tRNA^Trp is abundant the ribosome translates the leader without stalling and a terminator hairpin forms; when tryptophan is scarce the ribosome stalls and an antiterminator RNA structure forms. Both leader Trp codons are mutated to alanine. Which phenotype is expected when tryptophan is low but alanine is plentiful?

choices.text: Attenuation still occurs because the ribosome does not stall at alanine codons, the terminator hairpin forms, and trp structural genes remain under-expressed despite tryptophan starvation.
The operon is transcribed constitutively at high levels because the trp aporepressor can no longer bind tryptophan.
Translation of TrpE initiates at the leader alanine codons, producing a functional TrpE fusion enzyme that bypasses regulation.
Uncharged tRNA^Ala stalls the ribosome whenever tryptophan is low, fully relieving attenuation whenever the cell is starved for tryptophan.

items.explanation: trp attenuation couples translation of the leader peptide to a choice between terminator and antiterminator RNA hairpins. Tandem Trp codons stall the ribosome only when charged tRNA^Trp is scarce, favoring the antiterminator and transcription into trpEDCBA. Replacing those codons with alanine removes the tryptophan-specific stall. If alanine-tRNA is available, the ribosome translates the leader smoothly even during tryptophan starvation, the terminator hairpin still forms, and the biosynthetic genes remain attenuated—exactly when the cell needs them. The mutation is in the leader ORF, not in TrpR’s tryptophan-binding site, does not create a TrpE fusion, and does not charge or uncharge tRNA^Ala in response to tryptophan.

distractorRationales.B: TrpR corepression is a separate input; changing leader Trp codons to Ala does not prevent the repressor from binding tryptophan.
distractorRationales.C: The leader peptide is not fused in-frame to TrpE by this codon swap, and attenuation acts on transcription termination, not on creating a new enzyme.
distractorRationales.D: Alanine charging is independent of tryptophan levels, so tRNA^Ala does not stall the leader ribosome specifically when Trp is low.

items.stem:
The Abbe resolution limit is d = 0.61 λ / NA. Two fluorescent point sources are 250 nm apart. Illumination wavelength λ = 500 nm.

Objective | NA | calculated d
Air 10× | 0.25 | 1220 nm
Air 40× | 0.65 | 469 nm
Oil 100× | 1.40 | 218 nm

Which objective can resolve the two sources as separate, and why?

choices.text: The 40× and 100× equally, because both have d listed below 500 nm
Only the oil 100×, because 218 nm < 250 nm while 469 nm and 1220 nm are coarser than the spacing
All three, because 250 nm is larger than the wavelength divided by 2
Only the 10×, because lower magnification reduces diffraction

items.explanation: Two points are resolved when their separation exceeds d. For the oil lens, 250 > 218, so they are just resolved. For the 40× air lens, 250 < 469, so they merge. The 10× is far worse (d = 1.22 µm). Magnification does not appear in the Abbe formula; numerical aperture and wavelength do. Being less than 500 nm (the wavelength) is not the criterion—the 40× d of 469 nm is still larger than 250 nm. The naive λ/2 = 250 nm cutoff is an approximation at NA = 1.22, not a free pass for every lens.

distractorRationales.A: The 40× d of 469 nm still exceeds 250 nm, so that lens cannot split the pair.
distractorRationales.C: λ/2 = 250 nm would require NA ≈ 1.22; the 0.25 and 0.65 objectives do not meet that.
distractorRationales.D: Lower NA at 10× makes d worse (1220 nm), not better; magnification is not in the formula.

items.stem:
rms speed is v_rms = √(3 R T / M). Two flasks of oxygen (same M):
Flask A: 300 K
Flask B: 1200 K
A third flask C holds hydrogen at 300 K; M_H2 = M_O2 / 16. What are the rms-speed ratios vB/vA and vC/vA?

choices.text: All three rms speeds are equal because rms is a universal thermal speed

items.explanation: v_rms scales as √(T/M). Quadrupling T from 300 to 1200 K multiplies v_rms by 2, so vB/vA = 2. Hydrogen at the same T has M smaller by 16, so √(1/M) larger by 4, hence vC/vA = 4. Scaling as T or as M without the square root produces 4 and 16. Inverting the mass factor would make hydrogen slower. rms speed is not a constant; it is why H2 effuses faster and why hot molecules in a tail of the distribution escape a planet more easily.

distractorRationales.A: v_rms depends on T and M, as the formula in the stem states.
distractorRationales.C: The square root on T and on 1/M is required: √4 = 2 and √16 = 4, not 4 and 16.
distractorRationales.D: Hydrogen is lighter, so it is faster, not four times slower.

Alveolar ventilation VA = f × (VT − VD), with f the respiratory frequency, VT tidal volume, and VD anatomic dead space (150 mL here).

Pattern | f (min−1) | VT (mL)
Quiet breathing | 12 | 500
Slow deep | 6 | 1000
Panting | 24 | 250

choices.text: Slow deep (5100 mL min−1) > quiet (4200) > panting (2400)
Panting > quiet > slow deep, because frequency dominates
All three equal 4200 mL min−1 because minute ventilation f × VT is 6000 in each row
Quiet 6000; slow deep 6000; panting 6000, ignoring dead space

items.explanation: Quiet: 12 × (500 − 150) = 12 × 350 = 4200 mL min−1. Slow deep: 6 × (1000 − 150) = 6 × 850 = 5100 mL min−1. Panting: 24 × (250 − 150) = 24 × 100 = 2400 mL min−1. Minute ventilation f×VT is 6000 mL min−1 in every pattern, but a larger fraction of each pant is dead-space air, so alveolar ventilation falls. Slow deep breathing spends a larger fraction of each breath below the dead-space threshold, raising VA. Frequency alone does not rank the rows.

items.stem: Two otherwise identical eukaryotic mRNAs differ only in 3′ poly(A) length (about 250 adenosines versus about 20). In the cytosol, which difference is expected?

choices.text: The short-tailed mRNA is translated more efficiently because ribosomes bind poly(A) directly as a substitute 5′ cap.
Both mRNAs are equally stable because eukaryotic decay begins exclusively at an internal endonuclease cut that ignores the tail.
The short-tailed mRNA reaches the deadenylation threshold that triggers decapping and 5′–3′ decay more rapidly, shortening its half-life.
The long tail is spliced out in the cytosol, so tail length cannot affect cytoplasmic stability.

items.explanation: Most cytoplasmic eukaryotic mRNAs are degraded by deadenylation-dependent pathways. Poly(A)-binding protein coats a long tail, circularizes the mRNA with eIF4G/eIF4E, and hinders decapping. Once the tail is shortened below a threshold, PABP is lost, the decapping enzyme acts, and Xrn1 degrades the RNA 5′ to 3′ (a 3′–5′ exosome route also exists). An mRNA that already has only ~20 adenosines is close to that threshold and is turned over faster than a 250-A counterpart. Ribosomes do not use poly(A) as a cap substitute, and poly(A) is added after cleavage, not spliced out in the cytosol.

distractorRationales.A: A long poly(A) tail generally supports translation via PABP–eIF4G closed-loop formation. A very short tail reduces, rather than enhances, translation efficiency.
distractorRationales.B: The major decay pathways are deadenylation-dependent; tail length is a primary determinant of mRNA half-life, not an irrelevant decoration.
distractorRationales.D: Splicing removes introns in the nucleus. Poly(A) tails are not exons and are not spliced out in the cytosol.

items.stem: Laminar flow of an incompressible Newtonian fluid through a rigid cylindrical vessel obeys Poiseuille's law. If the radius is halved while pressure drop, length, and viscosity remain the same, the volume flow rate becomes:

Halving r multiplies Q by (1/2)^4 = 1/16 if every other factor is held fixed. Resistance therefore rises sixteenfold. Scaling with r, r^2 (area), or r^3 (a common incomplete product of area and a single extra r) does not match the derived r^4 dependence of laminar pipe flow.

distractorRationales.C: One-fourth is the area ratio. Flow rate for a viscous tube is not simply proportional to cross-sectional area at fixed driving pressure.
distractorRationales.D: One-half is the radius ratio. That would describe a linear geometric scale, not laminar resistance.

passage.title: psg-ps-2
passage.body:
A memory researcher tested how the way information is studied affects later recall. In Phase 1, 90 undergraduates saw a list of 30 common nouns, one every three seconds. Each word was preceded by one of three questions: whether the word was printed in capital letters (structural), whether it rhymed with a target word (phonemic), or whether it fit meaningfully into a sentence (semantic). After a filled delay, participants took a surprise free-recall test.
Recall rose steadily with the depth of processing: 18% for structural, 37% for phonemic, and 65% for semantic judgments. In addition, regardless of the processing condition, words from the beginning and end of the list were recalled better than words from the middle. When recall was delayed by 30 seconds of counting backward, the advantage for the last few items disappeared, but the advantage for the first few items remained.
In Phase 2, participants watched a short video of a car approaching an intersection. Afterward, half were asked, 'How fast was the car going when it passed the yield sign?' though the video actually showed a stop sign. A week later, participants who had received the misleading question were far more likely to report having seen a yield sign than participants asked a neutral question. The researchers argued that memory is not a faithful recording but is encoded selectively and reconstructed at retrieval, so that later information can alter what is 'remembered.'

passage.title: psg-cp-8
passage.body:
Purifying the product of a reaction is a routine but crucial task. A student runs a reaction that yields a mixture of a carboxylic acid (benzoic acid) and a neutral, nonpolar hydrocarbon, both dissolved in an organic solvent, and sets out to separate and identify them.
She first checks the mixture by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) on a silica gel plate, a polar stationary phase, developed in a relatively nonpolar solvent. After development, one spot has traveled 3.0 cm from the origin while the solvent front has advanced 5.0 cm. She records the retention factor (Rf) for the spot and notes that, on polar silica, more polar compounds cling to the plate and move less, whereas less polar compounds travel farther.
To separate the two components in bulk, she performs a liquid-liquid extraction, shaking the organic solution with aqueous sodium hydroxide in a separatory funnel. The carboxylic acid reacts with the base and is converted to its sodium carboxylate salt; the neutral hydrocarbon does not react. After the layers settle, she drains them apart and then treats the aqueous layer with hydrochloric acid to reverse the reaction and recover the purified acid.
Finally, she considers how to separate two miscible liquids that differ in boiling point and reviews simple distillation, in which the mixture is heated, the vapor is drawn off and condensed, and the collected liquid is enriched in one component. Throughout, she relies on differences in polarity, acid-base behavior, and volatility - the physical and chemical handles that separations exploit.

passage.title: psg-cp-6
passage.body:
Water's ability to dissolve ions and to resist changes in acidity underlies much of physiology. Blood plasma is held near pH 7.4 largely by the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer: dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which dissociates into a hydrogen ion and bicarbonate, H2CO3 H+ + HCO3-. The effective pKa for this equilibrium in plasma is about 6.1. Normally the concentration of bicarbonate is roughly twenty times that of dissolved carbonic acid, and the lungs and kidneys adjust the two components to hold that ratio steady. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation links the pH to the ratio of conjugate base to weak acid.
To study buffering directly, students titrate a weak acid at 25 C. They place 0.10 M acetic acid (pKa 4.74) in a flask and add sodium hydroxide from a burette while a pH meter records the curve. Early on the pH rises slowly through a buffering plateau; near the end it climbs steeply through the equivalence point, where exactly enough base has been added to neutralize all the acid. A separate reference solution at 25 C is measured to have a pH of 3.0.
The students note that at 25 C the ion product of water fixes pH + pOH = 14, and that a solution's acidity reflects the balance between hydrogen and hydroxide ions produced when water and solutes interact. They also test the buffer's resilience by adding a few drops of strong acid to the bicarbonate system and to plain water, comparing how far the pH of each moves.

passage.title: Two short poems: Ferry
passage.body:
Poem 1 — “Ticket”
I bought a ticket to the other bank
as if the river were a problem in change.
The ferryman took coins that had known other pockets.
He did not ask what I was leaving.
The water did, in small repeated questions
against the hull.

Poem 2 — “Return”
On the way back the same boat
was a different animal.
I recognised the coins by their edges
and not the faces.
Someone on the far jetty waved
at a person I had not yet become
and I, traitor, waved.

items.stem: A leucine that packs in the dehydrated core of a globular protein is mutated to asparagine. The mutant is soluble, but its thermal unfolding midpoint falls by 12 °C relative to wild type. Which thermodynamic explanation is best?

choices.text: Asparagine introduces a new disulfide that over-stabilizes a misfolded state
The mutation increases core hydrophobicity, which always lowers Tm
Placing a polar carboxamide in the hydrophobic core is energetically costly unless new hydrogen bonds fully compensate
Leucine is charged at neutral pH and asparagine neutralizes that charge, loosening the fold

items.explanation: The protein interior is a low-dielectric environment. A buried leucine contributes to the hydrophobic effect and packs with van der Waals contacts. Asparagine’s polar side chain must either satisfy its hydrogen-bonding potential inside the core or pay a large desolvation penalty; incomplete compensation destabilizes the native state and lowers Tm. Asparagine has no thiol, so it cannot make a disulfide. The substitution decreases, rather than increases, hydrophobicity. passage.title: psg-bb-5
passage.body:
To probe how mitochondria couple fuel oxidation to ATP synthesis, researchers suspended isolated mitochondria in a buffered chamber fitted with an oxygen electrode, so that the rate of oxygen consumption could be followed continuously. Because the electron transport chain uses O2 as its final electron acceptor, oxygen consumption serves as a readout of electron flow.
The team added an oxidizable substrate (to feed electrons into the chain) plus ADP and inorganic phosphate (the raw materials for ATP synthesis). Oxygen consumption rose to a brisk, steady rate, and ATP accumulated in the chamber. They then added oligomycin, a compound that blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase. Oxygen consumption fell almost to zero, and ATP synthesis stopped. Finally, they added 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), a small molecule that ferries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Oxygen consumption surged back to a high rate, yet no ATP was produced; the released energy instead appeared as heat.
The investigators explained the pattern in terms of the proton-motive force. Electron transport pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building an electrochemical gradient; ATP synthase normally lets those protons flow back into the matrix, harnessing the gradient to make ATP. Blocking ATP synthase lets the gradient build until it opposes further pumping, so electron flow (and O2 use) slows. A protonophore like DNP short-circuits the gradient, so electron transport races ahead while its energy is dissipated as heat rather than captured as ATP.

items.stem: A mitochondrial preparation is supplied with ADP and phosphate, but the inner mitochondrial membrane is mechanically ruptured. Which outcome is most likely?

Electron transfer becomes unnecessary because ADP donates electrons directly to oxygen.
ATP synthesis increases because protons can diffuse freely to ATP synthase.
The mitochondrial DNA code changes to compensate for membrane rupture.

items.explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation requires an intact inner mitochondrial membrane to maintain the proton-motive force. If the membrane is ruptured, protons cannot be compartmentalized effectively, so ATP synthesis by ATP synthase decreases. Common miss: Thinking proton access alone is sufficient for ATP synthesis, rather than recognizing the need for a gradient. This correctly identifies loss of the proton gradient as the key consequence. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.B: ADP does not donate electrons to oxygen in the electron transport chain.
distractorRationales.C: Free proton diffusion dissipates the gradient rather than improving ATP synthesis.
distractorRationales.D: Membrane damage does not alter the genetic code.

items.stem:
Mass spectrum of compound W (odd-electron molecular ion):

m/z | interpretation offered
72 | M+•
57 | M − 15 (loss of CH3)
43 | C3H7+ or CH3CO+
29 | C2H5+ or CHO+

IR of W: 1715 cm−1, no 2720 cm−1. Which molecular formula and structure are most consistent?

choices.text: C5H12, pentane: M = 72, but no carbonyl IR is then allowed
C3H4O2, with M = 72, necessarily an aldehyde because of m/z 29
C4H8O, butanal, required by m/z 29 even though 2720 cm−1 is absent
C4H8O, butan-2-one: M = 72, methyl loss to 57, acyl ion CH3CO+ at 43, and a ketone IR

Pentane is also Mr 72 but cannot produce 1715 cm−1. C3H4O2 is 72 and could be acrylic acid or similar, but the 1715 cm−1-only description without a broad acid O–H, plus the 57 methyl-loss, fits butanone better; m/z 29 is not uniquely CHO+. Butanal would show the 2720 cm−1 aldehyde C–H that is absent. The IR therefore selects the ketone over the aldehyde isomer of C4H8O.

distractorRationales.C: Butanal is C4H8O and would give M = 72, but the IR lacks 2720 cm−1, so it is not W.

passage.title: Study of Notification Cues and Attention
passage.body:
Researchers investigated how smartphone notification cues affect attention and perceived stress. Eighty undergraduate volunteers completed a computerized reaction-time task in three counterbalanced conditions: no notification, a vibration notification, and a visual banner notification. In each condition, participants pressed a key as soon as a target shape appeared. The phone was placed face down for the vibration condition and face up for the visual banner condition. Participants were told that notifications were unrelated to task performance and did not require a response. After each condition, participants rated their momentary stress on a 1 to 7 scale. The researchers also measured whether participants reported checking their phones within 30 seconds after the task.

Mean task performance and stress ratings by notification condition
Condition | Mean reaction time to target (ms) | Error rate (%) | Mean stress rating
No notification | 420 | 4 | 2.1
Vibration notification | 470 | 6 | 3.4
Visual banner notification | 445 | 5 | 2.8

Phone-checking behavior after task
Condition | Percent checking phone within 30 seconds
No notification | 12
Vibration notification | 48
Visual banner notification | 31

Design summary — Each participant completed all three notification conditions in randomized order. The primary dependent variables were reaction time, error rate, stress rating, and post-task phone checking.

items.stem:
The gas-phase equilibrium A(g) ⇌ 2 B(g) has Kc = 0.40 mol L−1 at temperature T, with Kc = [B]^2 / [A]. A 1.00 L flask at equilibrium contains the concentrations in the first data row. The mixture is then rapidly diluted to 2.00 L at the same T (concentrations instantly halved) before any reaction occurs.

Stage | [A] (mol L−1) | [B] (mol L−1)
At equilibrium in 1.00 L | 0.100 | 0.200
Immediately after dilution to 2.00 L | 0.050 | 0.100

What is Q immediately after dilution, and what net reaction restores equilibrium?

choices.text: Q = 0.40, already equal to Kc, so dilution produces no net chemical change.
Q = 0.80, greater than Kc, so B combines to form A.
Q = 0.20, less than Kc, so A dissociates net to form additional B.
Q = 0.20, less than Kc, so B is consumed because dilution always favours fewer particles.

items.explanation: Check the original row: Q = (0.200)^2 / 0.100 = 0.40 = Kc, so the flask truly started at equilibrium. After doubling the volume, Q′ = (0.100)^2 / 0.050 = 0.010 / 0.050 = 0.20, which is below Kc. The forward reaction therefore proceeds, producing more B. That direction also matches Le Chatelier for a process that increases the number of gas particles when the system is diluted. Q does not remain equal to Kc after a concentration jump of this stoichiometry, because [B] is squared.

distractorRationales.A: Halving both concentrations does not leave Q unchanged when the numerator is a square. Q falls to 0.20, so a net reaction occurs.
distractorRationales.B: Q = 0.80 would require doubling rather than halving concentrations, or inverting the dilution. The actual Q is 0.20, below Kc, so A does not form net.
distractorRationales.D: Q is 0.20, but the restoring reaction produces more particles (A → 2 B), which is the direction favoured by dilution, not consumption of B.

items.stem: A 2 kg stone is released from rest 10 m above the ground. Take g = 10 m/s^2 and neglect air resistance. The speed of the stone just before it hits the ground is closest to:

distractorRationales.D: This is 2 g h without taking the square root. Speed is the square root of 200 m^2/s^2, not 200 m/s.

passage.title: psg-cp-3
passage.body:
Students build and analyze a galvanic (voltaic) cell and then use batteries to study simple circuits. In the cell, a strip of zinc metal sits in zinc sulfate solution and a strip of copper metal sits in copper sulfate solution; a salt bridge connects the two half-cells, and a wire with a voltmeter links the metal strips. Under standard conditions the tabulated reduction potentials are Zn^2+ + 2 e- -> Zn, E = -0.76 V, and Cu^2+ + 2 e- -> Cu, E = +0.34 V. When the wire is connected, one electrode gains mass while the other slowly dissolves, and the voltmeter registers a steady potential difference. The students confirm which metal is oxidized by weighing the electrodes before and after.
They then replace the standard 1 M solutions with more dilute ones and record how the measured cell voltage shifts away from its standard value, relating the change to the reaction quotient Q for Zn + Cu^2+ -> Zn^2+ + Cu.
In the circuit module, a 12 V battery is connected to three resistors: a 6 ohm and a 3 ohm resistor wired in parallel with each other, and that combination wired in series with a 4 ohm resistor. An ammeter reads the current leaving the battery. The students compute the equivalent resistance, the current, and the power the battery delivers, treating the battery as an ideal source with negligible internal resistance and the wires as resistanceless.
