passage.title: Politeness as Gate (1980)
passage.body: Owen Blake's 1980 essay “Politeness as Gate,” on university hiring, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that neutrality is a style, not an absence of interest. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem:
The Haber equilibrium is N2(g) + 3 H2(g) ⇌ 2 NH3(g) at a fixed temperature where Kc = 0.50, with Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2][H2]^3) and concentrations in mol L−1. A reactor is sampled and the instantaneous concentrations are:

Species | Concentration (mol L−1)
N2 | 0.20
H2 | 0.60
NH3 | 0.10

What is the reaction quotient Q, and what net change occurs as the mixture returns to equilibrium?

choices.text: Q = 0.50, so the mixture is already at equilibrium and no net change occurs.
Q ≈ 0.23, which is less than Kc, so ammonia forms net until Q rises to 0.50.
Q ≈ 2.3, which is greater than Kc, so ammonia decomposes net.
Q ≈ 0.083, which is less than Kc, so the reaction shifts to produce N2 and H2.

items.explanation: Q is evaluated with the same expression as Kc but using the instantaneous concentrations: Q = (0.10)^2 / (0.20 × 0.60^3) = 0.010 / (0.20 × 0.216) = 0.010 / 0.0432 ≈ 0.231. Because Q is smaller than Kc, the forward reaction is favoured and ammonia is produced until Q = Kc. Failing to cube [H2] or to square [NH3] gives the distractor values. Kc itself is unchanged at constant temperature, so the comparison of Q with the given Kc fully determines the net direction.

distractorRationales.A: Q equals Kc only if the plugged-in concentrations already satisfy Kc. Here Q ≈ 0.23, not 0.50, so the mixture is not at equilibrium.
distractorRationales.C: Q ≈ 2.3 is obtained if [NH3] is not squared. The correctly computed Q is below Kc, so the net reaction is forward, not reverse.
distractorRationales.D: Q ≈ 0.083 comes from omitting the cube on [H2]. Even with a Q below Kc, the net change is ammonia formation, not production of N2 and H2.

items.stem: A toxin constitutively locks Gs in the GTP-bound state in hepatocytes that use Gs-coupled receptors to mobilize glucose. The expected effect is:

choices.text: persistent adenylyl cyclase activity, high cAMP, and increased glycogen breakdown
a fall in cAMP and net glycogen synthesis
cleavage of the insulin receptor as the toxin's only target
ligand-independent translocation of steroid receptors onto DNA

items.explanation: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase while GTP is bound. A lock in the active state (as in cholera toxin on Gs) keeps cAMP high. In hepatocytes, cAMP-dependent protein kinase phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase and promotes glycogenolysis (the glucagon/epinephrine Gs pathway). That is the opposite of lowering cAMP and building glycogen. The toxin is not an insulin-receptor protease, and steroid-receptor nuclear entry is a separate, ligand-regulated path.

distractorRationales.B: Active Gs raises, not lowers, cAMP. High cAMP in liver favors breakdown, not synthesis, of glycogen.
distractorRationales.C: Gs-directed toxins modify G proteins, not by default cleaving the insulin receptor as their sole action.
distractorRationales.D: Steroid receptors are not the Gs-cAMP module. Constitutive Gs does not substitute for steroid ligand in nuclear targeting.

items.stem: "He wore his humility like a medal, polished daily, displayed to anyone who would look." The literary device at work here is best described as:

passage.title: psg-cars-6
passage.body:
Social capital — broadly understood as the networks of relationships, norms of reciprocity, and trust that enable collective action — has become one of the most debated concepts in contemporary sociology. Proponents argue that it explains why some communities flourish economically and politically while others, equally well endowed in financial and physical resources, remain mired in dysfunction. Where citizens trust one another and are embedded in overlapping civic associations, cooperative ventures are easier to organize, contracts are more reliably honored, and public goods are more effectively maintained.
The concept distinguishes between two broad types. Bonding social capital refers to the dense ties within homogeneous groups — extended families, ethnic neighborhoods, religious congregations — that provide strong mutual support and a sense of belonging. Bridging social capital refers to the weaker but more diverse ties that link members of different social groups, enabling information and resources to flow across community boundaries. Theorists have argued that bridging capital is especially important for economic mobility and democratic stability, because it prevents the insularity and exclusivity that can calcify into tribal antagonism. The interplay between the two forms often matters more than either in isolation. Newcomers to a city, for example, tend to rely first on bonding ties — kin and compatriots who supply lodging, informal credit, and job referrals — and only later cultivate the bridging ties to employers, officials, and institutions beyond their original circle that permit genuine advancement. A community rich in bonding capital but starved of bridging capital may be tightly knit yet economically trapped, whereas one with abundant bridging ties but thin internal solidarity may struggle to sustain the everyday obligations on which cooperation depends. On this view the vitality of a community turns less on how much social capital it can claim than on how its bonding and bridging forms are balanced against each other.
Critics have raised several concerns. First, they argue that the concept is so capacious as to be analytically vacuous: if social capital includes trust, networks, and norms all at once, it risks becoming a label that explains everything and therefore explains nothing. Second, the emphasis on voluntary civic associations may obscure the role of institutional design and state capacity in producing the outcomes attributed to social capital. A society with strong courts, reliable public services, and enforceable property rights may achieve cooperation through formal mechanisms, regardless of the density of its associational life.
A third critique focuses on the dark side of social capital. The same dense ties that produce cohesion within a group can generate exclusion and hostility toward outsiders. Historically, tightly bonded criminal networks, nativist movements, and exclusionary professional guilds have all exhibited strong social capital while causing harm to those outside the charmed circle. If social capital is a neutral resource that amplifies whatever goals a group pursues, then celebrating it uncritically is a mistake. A community of mutual trust can be a community of mutual hostility toward all who fall outside its boundaries, and the literature on ethnic cleansing, organized crime, and racially restrictive covenants demonstrates this possibility in grim historical detail.
These debates have produced a more nuanced research agenda. Scholars now investigate not just the presence or absence of social capital but its distribution across social groups, its articulation with formal institutions, and the conditions under which it promotes rather than undermines democratic participation and social equity.

passage.title: Electron transport, proton coupling, and cytochrome c release
passage.body:
A fictional study examined isolated mitochondria from cultured liver-derived cells. Investigators supplied either pyruvate plus malate, which generate NADH for Complex I, or succinate, which donates electrons through Complex II. They then added inhibitors or a pore-forming BAX-derived peptide. Oxygen consumption, ATP synthesis, inner mitochondrial membrane potential, and cytochrome c detected outside mitochondria were measured. Values are normalized to untreated mitochondria supplied with pyruvate plus malate unless otherwise noted.

Effects of mitochondrial perturbations.
Condition | O2 consumption with pyruvate/malate (%) | O2 consumption with succinate (%) | ATP synthesis (%) | Membrane potential (%) | Cytochrome c outside mitochondria (%)
Control | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 5
Rotenone | 25 | 90 | 35 | 45 | 5
Antimycin A | 10 | 12 | 10 | 20 | 5
Oligomycin | 35 | 38 | 8 | 130 | 5
CCCP | 160 | 155 | 15 | 15 | 5
BAX-derived peptide | 70 | 72 | 60 | 70 | 65

Simplified map of oxidative phosphorylation. — Electrons from NADH enter at Complex I, electrons from succinate enter at Complex II, both pathways pass through ubiquinone to Complex III, cytochrome c, and Complex IV. Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons to create the proton-motive force used by ATP synthase.

items.stem: The author's central claim is best stated as

choices.text: Parks should be ticketed like venues so the ledger can finally close.

A park is not a leak from private order but a condition of urban inhabitability; defend it with a more complete ledger, including maintenance and the people priced off adjacent blocks, rather than with mere poetry of the unowned.
Ledgers are evil, and gardeners in winter betray the commons.
Developers are wrong that parks have any price.

items.explanation: The opening denies that a park is a leak, the middle rejects fencing-or-neglect and weak poetry, and the close demands maintenance plus the displaced neighbors. B holds those parts. A is the crude policy attacked. C inverts the adult defense. D ignores the grant that developers are not wrong about a price. Main idea answers must include both the inhabitability thesis and the incomplete-ledger politics, not only a slogan about green space.

distractorRationales.A: Ticketing until the park behaves like a venue is named as a crude refusal to count the park's effects.
distractorRationales.C: The author says planting, toilets, and a winter gardener are how openness lasts, not betrayals.
distractorRationales.D: The first paragraph says developers are not wrong that the gift has a price.

passage.title: The ledger of the commons
passage.body:
When a city puts a park on a map, it appears to have given something away: land that could have been lots, hours that could have been tolls. Developers are not wrong that the gift has a price. They are wrong when they treat the price as a leak from an otherwise watertight private order. The private order is already subsidized by streets, courts, pipes, and the patience of people who do not sue every time a stranger walks past a porch. A park is not the exception to property. It is one of the ways a dense city remains inhabitable enough for property to be worth wanting.

Accountants prefer a ledger in which every square metre has a named owner and a yield. Parks embarrass the ledger because their yield is a crowd that does not pay at the gate, a cooling that does not send an invoice, a child who learns a city can include her without a purchase. The embarrassment produces two crude policies. One is to fence and ticket until the park behaves like a venue. The other is to neglect the park until the crowd looks like a problem that only private security can solve. Both policies claim to be realistic. Both are ways of refusing to count the effects that made the park rational in the first place.

Friends of the park sometimes answer with a poetry of the unowned. The poetry is moving and strategically weak. A commons that cannot speak in maintenance budgets will lose to a spreadsheet that can. The more adult defense is to insist that the ledger is incomplete, not that ledgers are evil. Planting, lighting, toilets, and a gardener who is paid in winter are not betrayals of openness. They are how openness lasts past a ribbon-cutting.

There is a further honesty. Parks are not innocent. They have been used to raise adjacent rents, to move unhoused people out of sight, to display a city’s kindness to visitors who will never need the toilets. Naming those uses does not hand the land to the highest bidder. It prevents the park’s defenders from pretending that green on a map is already justice. Justice would be a park whose ledger includes the people who were priced off the blocks around it.

If urban politics cannot hold that thought, it will keep oscillating between the venue and the ruin, and calling the oscillation pragmatism.

items.stem: What does the terminator hairpin disruption result most strongly support about metabolite M regulation?

M changes the genetic code so that UAA encodes tryptophan.

items.explanation: In wild-type cells, M lowers full-length mRNA and protein. When the terminator hairpin is disrupted, full-length mRNA and protein remain high even with M, supporting a model in which M represses expression by promoting attenuation before the coding region. distractorRationales.D: M is described as binding the 5' untranslated region, not stabilizing an active-site residue.

passage.title: Regulation of a bacterial nucleotide-reduction operon
passage.body:
A fictional bacterial operon, nrdPQ, encodes proteins required for deoxyribonucleotide synthesis during low-oxygen growth. The operon contains a sigma-factor promoter, a 5' untranslated region with a metabolite M-sensitive attenuator, and a Shine-Dalgarno sequence upstream of the nrdP start codon. When metabolite M binds the nascent 5' untranslated region, a terminator hairpin forms before the coding sequence, reducing production of full-length mRNA. Researchers constructed mutations and measured full-length nrdP mRNA, NrdP protein, and NrdP enzyme activity.

Expression and activity of nrdP constructs.
Construct and condition | Full-length mRNA (%) | NrdP protein (%) | NrdP activity (%)
Wild type, no M | 100 | 100 | 100
Wild type, +M | 30 | 28 | 30
-10 promoter mutant, no M | 12 | 10 | 11
Terminator hairpin disrupted, +M | 95 | 92 | 90
Shine-Dalgarno mutant, no M | 105 | 15 | 14
Active-site Cys to Ser mutant, no M | 100 | 98 | 8

Model of metabolite M-dependent attenuation. — In the presence of metabolite M, the 5' untranslated region folds into a terminator hairpin that causes RNA polymerase to stop before transcribing the nrdP coding sequence. When M is absent or the hairpin is disrupted, RNA polymerase usually produces full-length mRNA.

passage.title: Critical Reasoning · Environmental Policy
passage.body: Beekeepers in the region have reported that average honey yields per hive fell by 30% over the past five years, and several have linked this decline to the increased use of a new class of pesticide introduced during the same period. Advocacy groups have used the honey yield figures to call for an immediate ban. Agricultural researchers point out that the same five years also saw two unusually dry summers and a rise in a parasitic mite known to weaken hive productivity independently of pesticide exposure. A separate long-term study, tracking the same hives annually since before the pesticide was introduced, found no significant difference in yield decline between hives in treated and untreated areas.

items.stem:
A beam of radiation is absorbed according to I = I0 e^{−μ x}. Taking the natural log gives ln I = ln I0 − μ x, so a graph of ln I versus x is linear with slope −μ. Count rates versus absorber thickness are:

x (cm) | I (counts s−1)
0.0 | 800
2.0 | 400
4.0 | 200
6.0 | 100

What is μ?

choices.text: 0.50 cm−1, using (800 − 100) / 6.0 from the raw I–x table.
2.0 cm−1, the half-thickness itself treated as μ.
0.347 cm−1, because I halves every 2.0 cm and μ = ln 2 / 2.0 cm.

items.explanation: Each additional 2.0 cm of absorber halves the count rate, so the half-thickness x1/2 = 2.0 cm. Then I / I0 = 1/2 = e^{−μ x1/2}, hence μ = ln 2 / x1/2 = 0.693 / 2.0 = 0.347 cm−1. Equivalently, from x = 0 to 6.0 cm there are three halvings, I / I0 = 1/8, ln(I0/I) = ln 8 = 2.079, μ = 2.079 / 6.0 = 0.347 cm−1. The raw I-versus-x graph is exponential, not linear, so (ΔI)/Δx is not μ. The half-thickness is 2.0 cm, which is not the value of μ. A linear fit must be performed on ln I versus x, whose slope is −0.347 cm−1.

distractorRationales.A: Subtracting raw counts and dividing by thickness treats an exponential as a straight line. μ comes from the slope of ln I versus x, not of I versus x.
distractorRationales.B: 2.0 cm is the half-thickness, whose unit is length. μ is ln 2 divided by that length, about 0.35 cm−1.
distractorRationales.D: 100/800 = 0.125 is I(6 cm)/I0, not a value of μ. Dividing that fraction by 6.0 cm also has the wrong algebra for an exponential.

passage.title: Identity, Group Membership, and Academic Feedback
passage.body:
A developmental psychology research group examined how social identity salience affects interpretation of academic feedback. High school students completed a difficult reasoning task and then received standardized written feedback stating that their score was below the sample average. Before receiving feedback, students were randomly assigned to one of two writing prompts. In the personal-values condition, students wrote about an important personal value. In the group-comparison condition, students wrote about ways their school group was viewed by students from a nearby school. After feedback, students rated perceived threat, expected future performance, and willingness to attempt a similar task.

Mean post-feedback ratings on 1 to 7 scales
Condition | Perceived threat | Expected future performance | Willingness to attempt similar task
Personal-values prompt | 3.0 | 4.9 | 5.5
Group-comparison prompt | 4.8 | 3.8 | 4.1

Interpretive note — All participants received identical task instructions and identical feedback; only the pre-feedback writing prompt differed across conditions.

passage.title: psg-cp-4
passage.body:
Diagnostic imaging often relies on how waves interact with tissue. In an ultrasound scanner, a transducer emits pulses of high-frequency sound into the body and listens for echoes returning from boundaries between tissues. A common obstetric probe operates at 2.0 MHz, and sound travels through soft tissue at about 1540 m/s. The scanner forms an image from the time delay and strength of each returning echo, and clinicians choose the probe frequency to trade off image detail against how deep the sound can penetrate.
A Doppler mode measures blood flow. When a pulse reflects from red blood cells moving relative to the transducer, the returning sound is shifted in frequency; the scanner converts this shift into a flow velocity and direction, coloring flow toward and away from the probe differently.
A second instrument, a fiber-optic endoscope, guides visible light instead of sound. Light travels along a thin glass fiber whose core has a higher refractive index (about 1.5) than its surrounding cladding (about 1.2). Rays that strike the core-cladding boundary at a large enough angle are trapped inside the core and travel the fiber's length with little loss, so the endoscope can illuminate and image tissue deep inside the body and around bends. The physicians rely on the same refraction principles when a laser beam crosses from one tissue layer into another and changes direction. Throughout, the team treats soft tissue as a uniform medium for sound and the fiber as an ideal light guide.

items.stem: A student health campaign first asks residents to sign a one-sentence hand-hygiene pledge at a table, then a week later asks them to staff a four-hour influenza-shot drive. Compliance with the large request is higher among those who signed. This is which sequential technique, as in Freedman and Fraser’s work?

choices.text: Door-in-the-face (Cialdini): a huge request first, then retreat to a smaller one
Foot-in-the-door: a small granted request raises the chance of a later larger one, often via self-perception of being “the kind of person who helps”
Low-balling: the cost is revealed only after commitment to an unchanged request
Cognitive dissonance from a $1 lie about an OSCE, which is the same operational procedure

items.explanation: Foot-in-the-door (Freedman and Fraser) is a small yes followed by a larger related request. Self-perception (Bem) or consistency motives are the usual mediators. Door-in-the-face is the reverse sequence: extreme request refused, then a moderate target. Low-ball changes the cost after a commitment. Festinger’s $1/$20 paradigm is induced compliance with a counter-attitudinal speech, not this two-request campaign.

distractorRationales.A: Door-in-the-face starts large, not with a one-sentence pledge.
distractorRationales.C: The large request is a new, openly described task, not a hidden-price change of the same deal.
distractorRationales.D: Insufficient-justification dissonance is a different experimental recipe than sequential requests.

passage.title: psg-cars-1
passage.body:
Is there any knowledge in the world so certain that no reasonable person could doubt it? This question, which at first sight might not seem difficult, is really among the most difficult that can be asked. In daily life we assume as certain many things which, on closer scrutiny, are found to be so full of apparent contradictions that only a great deal of thought enables us to know what it is that we may really believe.
Consider the plain table before me. To the eye it appears rectangular, brown, and shiny; to the touch it is smooth, cool, and hard; when I tap it, it gives out a wooden sound. Anyone else who sees, feels, and hears the table will agree with this description, so it might seem that no difficulty could arise. But the moment we try to be more precise, our troubles begin. Although I believe that the table is 'really' of one uniform brown, the parts that reflect the light look far brighter than the rest, and some parts look white because of reflected light. If I move, the parts that reflect the light change, so that the apparent distribution of colours upon the table shifts. It follows that if several people look at the table at the same moment, no two of them will see exactly the same distribution of colours, for no two can view it from precisely the same point, and any change in the point of view changes the way in which the light is reflected.
For most practical purposes these differences are unimportant, but to the painter they are all-important: the painter has to unlearn the habit of thinking that things seem to have the colour which common sense says they 'really' have, and to learn the habit of seeing things as they appear. Here we already meet with one of the distinctions that cause the most trouble in philosophy — the distinction between 'appearance' and 'reality,' between what things seem to be and what they are. The table, if it is 'real' at all, must have some real colour; yet the colour we see is not a property of the table in itself but something depending upon the table, the observer, and the way the light falls. When, in ordinary life, we speak of the colour of the table, we mean only the sort of colour which it will seem to have to a normal spectator, under ordinary conditions of light, from an ordinary point of view. But the other colours which appear under other conditions have just as good a right to be considered real; and so, to avoid favouritism, we are compelled to deny that the table has any one particular colour.
The same holds for the texture. With the naked eye the grain of the wood looks smooth and even; under a microscope it shows roughness, and hills and valleys, and all sorts of differences that are imperceptible to unaided sight. Which of these is the 'real' table? We are naturally tempted to say that what we see through the microscope is more real; yet a still more powerful instrument would reveal something different again, so that we can never rest content with what the eye alone reports. Thus confidence in the senses, which had seemed so secure, begins to desert us.
It becomes evident that the real table, if there is one, is not the same as what we immediately experience by sight or touch or hearing. The real table, if it exists, is not immediately known to us at all, but must be an inference from what is immediately known. Hence two very difficult questions at once arise: Is there a real table at all? And if so, what sort of object can it be?

items.stem: A coding (nontemplate, sense) DNA strand contains 5′-ATG GCA-3′ at the start of an open reading frame. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The mRNA in this region is 5′-AUG GCA-3′, matching the coding strand except that U replaces T.
The mRNA is 5′-UAC CGU-3′ because RNA polymerase copies the coding strand 3′ to 5′.
The template strand has 5′-ATG GCA-3′ and is copied directly into 5′-AUG GCA-3′.
tRNA, not mRNA, is transcribed from the coding strand of protein-coding genes.

items.explanation: The coding strand has the same sequence as the RNA transcript except that DNA has T where RNA has U. RNA polymerase actually uses the complementary template (antisense) strand as the substrate and polymerizes RNA 5′ to 3′. If the coding strand reads 5′-ATG GCA-3′, the template is 3′-TAC CGT-5′ and the mRNA is 5′-AUG GCA-3′. Calling the coding strand the template, reversing polarity, or asserting that protein-coding genes produce tRNA from that strand all misstate transcription. This relationship is why gene sequences are usually published as the coding strand: it can be read as the mRNA with U for T.

distractorRationales.B: 5′-UAC CGU-3′ is the reverse complement of the coding sequence, not the transcript. Polymerase synthesizes RNA 5′ to 3′ complementary to the template, yielding 5′-AUG GCA-3′.
distractorRationales.C: The template strand is complementary to the coding strand, so it cannot also be 5′-ATG GCA-3′ if the coding strand already has that sequence.
distractorRationales.D: Protein-coding genes are transcribed into mRNA (pre-mRNA in eukaryotes). tRNA genes are separate transcription units, mainly RNA polymerase III products in eukaryotes.

items.stem: A driving simulator has residents keep a car in lane while simultaneously monitoring a second screen for a rare vital-sign alarm. Lane-keeping error jumps when the alarm task is added, even though both tasks are easy alone. Kahneman’s limited-capacity account of divided attention predicts which outcome?

choices.text: Error should not change, because Broadbent’s filter fully protects the driving channel
Only late-selection theory predicts dual-task cost, and only if the alarm is physically identical to engine noise
Habituation of the orienting reflex will abolish lane error after one combined trial
The two tasks compete for a shared pool of attention, so dual-task costs appear when combined demand exceeds available capacity

items.explanation: Kahneman treated attention as a limited, allocatable capacity. Two easy tasks can still interfere when their sum exceeds that pool, which is the classic dual-task cost. Broadbent’s filter is an account of selective, not divided, attention and does not guarantee a protected driving channel. Late selection concerns how far ignored messages are processed, not this resource trade-off. Habituation would reduce responding to a repeated irrelevant stimulus, not erase capacity competition in a first dual-task block.

distractorRationales.A: A selective-attention filter does not imply cost-free divided attention between two attended tasks.
distractorRationales.B: Dual-task costs are the central prediction of capacity models, not a unique late-selection claim about physical identity.
distractorRationales.C: Habituation is non-associative waning to a repeated stimulus, not an explanation of divided-attention interference.

items.stem: In mitochondria, the intermembrane space is more acidic than the matrix during active respiration. Which movement is directly coupled to ATP synthesis by ATP synthase?

items.stem: 1-Pentanol is oxidized in two separate flasks: flask P with PCC in anhydrous CH2Cl2, and flask J with CrO3 in aqueous H2SO4 (Jones conditions). What are the principal organic products?

choices.text: P: pentanal; J: pentanoic acid, because in water the aldehyde hydrate is further oxidized by chromic acid
P: pentanoic acid; J: pentanal, because PCC is the stronger aqueous oxidant
Both flasks give pentane, because chromium reagents reduce alcohols to alkanes
Neither flask oxidizes a primary alcohol; only secondary alcohols react with Cr(VI)

items.explanation: Primary alcohols are oxidized by Cr(VI) to aldehydes. Under anhydrous PCC conditions the aldehyde is not hydrated and is not rapidly oxidized further, so pentanal is isolated. Jones reagent is aqueous: the aldehyde forms a gem-diol (hydrate) that behaves like a secondary alcohol equivalent and is oxidized to the carboxylic acid. Chromium(VI) is an oxidant, not a reductant, and it certainly oxidizes primary alcohols. The solvent, not a mysterious difference in ‘strength’ of PCC versus Jones as named reagents, is what decides aldehyde versus acid.

distractorRationales.B: This swaps the products. PCC in dry CH2Cl2 is the aldehyde reagent; aqueous chromic acid over-oxidizes to the acid.
distractorRationales.C: Cr(VI) oxidizes alcohols to carbonyls (or acids). It does not deoxygenate them to alkanes (that would be a reduction such as Wolff–Kishner).
distractorRationales.D: Primary and secondary alcohols both react with Cr(VI). Tertiary alcohols lack a C–H on the carbinol carbon and typically do not oxidize.

items.stem: A temperature-sensitive mutation blocks COPII-coated vesicle exit from the ER. Newly synthesized secretory proteins in these cells will:

choices.text: acquire mature Golgi N-glycan modifications on the normal schedule
be translated exclusively on mitochondrial ribosomes
remain in the early secretory pathway and fail to receive Golgi-specific modifications

items.explanation: COPII vesicles carry cargo from ER to Golgi. If they cannot form or fuse, secretory proteins remain ER-associated (or in an ER-Golgi intermediate) and do not encounter Golgi glycosyltransferases, so Golgi-dependent glycan maturation fails. Mitochondrial import uses different targeting peptides and translocons, and secretory proteins are made on cytosolic ribosomes docked at the ER, not on mitochondrial ribosomes. Mature Golgi sugars are precisely what should be missing.

distractorRationales.A: Golgi modifications require arrival at the Golgi. Blocking ER exit prevents that arrival.
distractorRationales.B: ER-retained secretory proteins are not rerouted through TOM/TIM as a default.
distractorRationales.C: Mitochondrial ribosomes translate a handful of OXPHOS subunits, not the cell's secretory proteome.

passage.title: psg-ps-9
passage.body:
Sociologists analyzed how a chronic illness is understood and managed in a mid-sized city. Using surveys and interviews, they documented three patterns. First, physicians and hospitals coordinated with schools and workplaces so that ill members could be temporarily excused from normal duties while being expected to seek treatment and cooperate with doctors. Second, patients with more education and income obtained diagnoses and specialist care far faster than poorer patients, who often relied on crowded clinics; the researchers traced this to differences in insurance, flexible work hours, and familiarity with medical institutions. Third, behaviors once seen as ordinary or as moral failings - such as persistent sadness or restlessness - were increasingly defined and treated as medical conditions.
The team framed each pattern with a different theoretical lens. The coordinated excusing of the sick was described as an institution maintaining social stability by managing how illness disrupts roles. The unequal access was described in terms of groups with different amounts of resources and power competing for a scarce good. The redefinition of ordinary behaviors as illnesses was described as a process by which the meaning of 'sickness' is negotiated and expanded within a society. In interviews, patients described how a formal diagnosis changed how others treated them, sometimes granting sympathy and sometimes attaching stigma. The authors noted that the fastest-growing diagnoses clustered among specific age groups, and that the city's aging population was projected to raise overall demand for chronic-disease care over the coming decades.

items.stem: A researcher needs to separate the two strands of genomic DNA for hybridization without hydrolyzing either covalent backbone. Which class of interaction must be disrupted?

choices.text: N-glycosidic bonds linking bases to deoxyribose
Disulfide bonds that covalently crosslink complementary bases
Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, together with base-stacking interactions

items.explanation: The two strands of a DNA duplex are held together by noncovalent hydrogen bonds between Watson–Crick pairs and by stacking of the aromatic bases. Heat, alkali (which titrates bases and disrupts pairing), or formamide can melt those interactions and yield intact single strands that still have covalent phosphodiester backbones. Breaking phosphodiester or glycosidic bonds would fragment or depurinate the DNA rather than produce hybridizable full-length strands. Complementary bases are not linked by disulfides; those bonds stabilize some proteins, not the DNA double helix. Strand separation for blotting or PCR denaturation therefore targets noncovalent duplex forces only.

distractorRationales.A: Phosphodiester cleavage would nick or degrade each strand. Denaturation for hybridization must leave the covalent backbones intact.
distractorRationales.B: Breaking glycosidic bonds depurinates or depyrimidinates DNA and destroys base-pairing information rather than simply unzipping the duplex.
distractorRationales.C: DNA strands are not covalently crosslinked by disulfides; disulfide bonds are a protein feature. Duplex DNA is noncovalently paired.

distractorRationales.C: Structural isomers differ in connectivity, not mirror-image relationship.
distractorRationales.D: Conformers interconvert by bond rotation; they aren't distinct configurations.

passage.title: Adult Education Centers and Health Information Navigation
passage.body:
A community research team evaluated a short workshop designed to improve adults' ability to interpret online health information. The workshop taught participants how to identify source credibility, distinguish testimonials from population-level evidence, and compare numerical risks. Participants attended one of three adult education centers located in districts that differed in occupational composition and average household income. Workshop attendance was optional, so participants were not randomly assigned to attend. All participants completed a health-information comprehension test at baseline and four weeks later.

Mean health-information comprehension scores out of 100
Center district | Baseline score | Four-week score among nonattendees | Four-week score among workshop attendees | Households with reliable broadband (%) | Mean schedule predictability, 1 to 7
Working-class district | 58 | 60 | 72 | 62 | 2.1
Mixed-income district | 64 | 65 | 75 | 78 | 3.5
Professional-class district | 75 | 76 | 82 | 94 | 5.4

Resource context — The researchers proposed that broadband access and predictable work schedules may influence the ability to practice health-information skills outside the workshop.

passage.title: Alternative splicing and protein dimerization of LUM1
passage.body:
A fictional eukaryotic gene, LUM1, contains four exons. Exon 3 encodes a hydrophobic alpha-helical segment required for stable LUM1 dimer formation. A regulatory RNA-binding protein, RBP-K, binds an intronic splicing enhancer near exon 3 and promotes exon 3 inclusion. Skipping exon 3 preserves the reading frame but produces a mostly monomeric protein that is degraded more rapidly. A separate mutation in the 5' splice donor of intron 2 causes intron retention and introduces a premature termination codon more than 50 nucleotides upstream of the final exon-exon junction.

Effects of LUM1 expression constructs in cultured cells.
Condition | Pre-mRNA transcription rate (%) | Mature mRNA containing exon 3 (%) | Total mature LUM1 mRNA (%) | LUM1 protein (%) | Dimeric LUM1 among detected protein (%)
Wild type | 100 | 85 | 100 | 100 | 80
RBP-K knockdown | 98 | 20 | 55 | 25 | 18
Exon 3 splice acceptor weakened | 95 | 10 | 50 | 20 | 12
Intron 2 splice donor mutant | 100 | 5 | 18 | 6 | 8
Kozak sequence mutant | 100 | 82 | 95 | 22 | 78
Exon 3 hydrophobic-to-charged coding mutant | 100 | 84 | 98 | 45 | 20

Model for LUM1 isoform production. — When exon 3 is included, LUM1 contains a hydrophobic helical segment that supports dimerization. When exon 3 is skipped, the reading frame remains intact but the helical dimerization segment is absent. Intron 2 retention creates a premature stop codon predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.

passage.title: Recycling Behavior and Reinforcement Schedules in Dormitory Kitchens
passage.body:
A campus sustainability team tested behavioral strategies for improving recycling accuracy in dormitory kitchens. Twenty dormitory floors were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: informational signs only, a fixed-ratio points program in which floors earned a reward after every fifth correctly sorted item, a variable-ratio points program in which floors earned rewards unpredictably after an average of five correctly sorted items, or an observational-modeling condition in which residents watched a peer demonstrate correct sorting before signs were posted. In the reward conditions, a green light on the sorting station indicated that the sensor was active and points could be earned; a red light indicated that the sensor was off. After four weeks, point rewards were removed for one week while signs remained.

Mean percentage of items correctly sorted
Condition | Baseline week | Week 4 | Reward-removal week
Informational signs only | 43 | 55 | 52
Fixed-ratio points | 42 | 68 | 50
Variable-ratio points | 44 | 75 | 63
Observational modeling plus signs | 41 | 70 | 66

Assignment unit — The dormitory floor, rather than the individual resident, was the unit of assignment because rewards and signs were shared within floor kitchens.

items.stem:
50.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl is mixed with 50.0 mL of 1.00 M NaOH in a coffee-cup calorimeter. Treat the mixture as 100.0 g of solution with c = 4.18 J g−1 °C−1. Both solutions start at 22.0 °C; the final temperature is 28.8 °C. The limiting reaction is H+ + OH− → H2O (0.0500 mol). q_solution = m c ΔT, and ΔH_rxn = −q_solution / moles.
What is ΔH for the neutralization?

choices.text: −28.4 kJ mol−1 (using 0.100 mol as the extent of reaction)

items.explanation: ΔT = 28.8 − 22.0 = 6.8 °C. Heat absorbed by the solution is 100.0 × 4.18 × 6.8 = 2842 J. The reaction released that heat, so q_rxn = −2842 J. Extent is 0.0500 mol (50.0 mL of 1.00 M of each, 1:1 stoichiometry), giving ΔH = −2842 J / 0.0500 mol = −56.8 kJ mol−1. The temperature rise shows an exothermic process, so the sign is negative. Using 0.100 mol (sum of both reagents) halves |ΔH|; using 0.500 mol divides by ten.

distractorRationales.B: Heat flowed into the solution (T rose), so the reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.
distractorRationales.C: Only 0.0500 mol of water forms; 50.0 mL of 1.00 M plus 50.0 mL of 1.00 M is not 0.100 mol of reaction.
distractorRationales.D: 0.500 mol is ten times the actual extent, which would give −5.68 kJ mol−1.

Osmotic pressure π = i c RT, with R = 0.080 L atm mol−1 K−1 and T = 300 K. Two intravenous-style solutions:

Solution | formal concentration | i
Glucose | 0.30 M | 1
NaCl | 0.15 M | 2

choices.text: Glucose 7.2 atm; NaCl 3.6 atm, ignoring i of NaCl
Glucose 0.30 atm; NaCl 0.15 atm, omitting RT
Both 2.4 atm, using R = 0.080 without T
Both 7.2 atm, because i c is 0.30 M in each

items.explanation: Particle concentration i c is 0.30 M for glucose and 0.15 × 2 = 0.30 M for NaCl, so they are iso-osmotic. π = 0.30 × 0.080 × 300 = 0.30 × 24 = 7.2 atm for both. Dropping i for NaCl halves its π incorrectly. Omitting RT leaves the molarity numbers with atm painted on. Using R but not T gives 0.30 × 0.080 = 0.024, not 2.4; a 2.4 atm figure is 0.30 × 8 without the 300/100 bookkeeping. Clinically this is why 0.15 M NaCl (half-molar salt) matches 0.30 M glucose.

distractorRationales.A: NaCl’s i = 2 doubles 0.15 M to the same 0.30 M particles as glucose.
distractorRationales.B: RT = 24 L atm mol−1 at 300 K with this R, so π is tens of atm per mole per litre, not 0.30 atm.
distractorRationales.C: Forgetting T underestimates by a factor of 300; 2.4 atm is not the correct product.

passage.title: The Creek Map (1979)
passage.body: Kwame Boateng published “The Creek Map” in 1979 after a season in broadcast newsrooms. The argument is that a caption can do the arguing the image refuses to do. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem:
A stationary observer hears a 400 Hz siren. The speed of sound in the air is 340 m s−1. When the source moves directly toward the observer at 30 m s−1, the observed frequency is given by f′ = f × v / (v − vs), where vs is the source speed toward the observer.

Quantity | Value
f | 400 Hz
v | 340 m s−1
vs toward observer | 30 m s−1

What frequency does the observer hear?
items.explanation: Substitute into the given Doppler formula: f′ = 400 × 340 / (340 − 30) = 400 × 340 / 310. First 340/310 ≈ 1.0968, then 400 × 1.0968 ≈ 439 Hz. Using v + vs in the denominator (340 + 30 = 370) is the receding-source formula and yields 400 × 340/370 ≈ 367 Hz. Leaving the frequency unchanged ignores the approaching source. Putting v + vs in the numerator and v − vs in the denominator (as if both source and observer moved) gives 400 × 370/310 ≈ 477 Hz. The stem specifies a stationary observer and a source moving toward, so only the given f′ = f v / (v − vs) applies.

distractorRationales.A: 367 Hz is 400 × 340 / 370, the formula for a source receding at 30 m s−1. The source is approaching, so the denominator is 310 m s−1.
distractorRationales.C: 400 Hz would be correct only for a source at rest relative to the air and observer. The 30 m s−1 approach is not negligible compared with 340 m s−1.
distractorRationales.D: 477 Hz is 400 × 370 / 310, which inserts an extra (v + vs) factor appropriate to a moving observer as well. The observer is stationary.

items.stem: A single slit of width a = 4.0 × 10−4 m is illuminated with λ = 5.0 × 10−7 m. The first diffraction minimum satisfies a sin θ = λ. For small θ in radians, sin θ ≈ θ ≈ λ/a. items.stem: Two antibodies bind the same hapten substrate with indistinguishable Kd. Antibody 1 is noncatalytic. Antibody 2, raised against a transition-state analog, accelerates hapten hydrolysis 10^4-fold. Relative to antibody 1, antibody 2 must additionally:

choices.text: Bind the product more tightly than the substrate so that the equilibrium constant of the reaction increases
Raise the activation free energy by straining the substrate into a less reactive geometry
Stabilize the transition state (or align catalytic groups) beyond what ground-state binding affinity reports
Convert the unimolecular reaction into a diffusion-limited bimolecular collision in bulk water

items.explanation: Equal Kd values mean the two antibodies bind the ground-state hapten similarly, so differential ground-state affinity cannot explain a 10^4 rate ratio. Catalytic antibodies selected on transition-state analogs work by binding the altered geometry of the transition state more tightly than the substrate, or by placing catalytic side chains, which lowers ΔG‡. Tighter product binding would risk product inhibition and does not change the reaction equilibrium, which is a property of free substrate and product. Raising the barrier would slow the reaction. Catalysis occurs in the binding site, not by sending the hapten into an uncatalyzed bimolecular solvent path.

distractorRationales.A: Enzymes do not change overall Keq. Excess product affinity causes inhibition, not acceleration.
distractorRationales.B: Increasing the activation energy decreases the rate; the catalytic antibody does the opposite.
distractorRationales.D: The point of a catalytic binding site is to avoid relying on the slow uncatalyzed solution reaction.

items.stem: De novo palmitate synthesis is measured in a liver fractionation experiment. Which combination of compartment, committed step, and reductant is correct?

choices.text: Mitochondrial matrix; thiolase; NADH from the citric acid cycle
Endoplasmic reticulum lumen; HMG-CoA reductase; NADPH
Cytosol; acetyl-CoA carboxylase producing malonyl-CoA; NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway and malic enzyme
Peroxisome; CPT-I; FADH2 from acyl-CoA dehydrogenase

items.explanation: De novo fatty-acid synthesis in hepatocytes occurs in the cytosol. The committed step is carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin). Fatty acid synthase then uses NADPH, not NADH or FADH2, to reduce the growing chain; NADPH comes largely from the pentose phosphate pathway and from malic enzyme. Acetyl-CoA itself is delivered from mitochondria via citrate and ATP-citrate lyase. Thiolase and FADH2 belong to β-oxidation, HMG-CoA reductase to cholesterol synthesis in the ER, and CPT-I to the mitochondrial uptake of acyl chains for oxidation, the opposite pathway.

distractorRationales.A: Mitochondrial thiolase and NADH are features of β-oxidation/ketogenesis, not of de novo palmitate synthesis, which is cytosolic and NADPH-dependent.

items.stem: Two monomeric proteins are compared by native gel electrophoresis at pH 7.0. Protein A has pI 5.0 and protein B has pI 9.0. Ignoring sieving differences, toward which electrode does each protein migrate?

choices.text: A toward the anode and B toward the cathode

The two proteins therefore run in opposite directions if the field is applied to a horizontal strip, or they enter a vertical gel only if the polarity matches their charge. This is the same pH-versus-pI logic used for amino acids.

items.stem:
Four weak acids and their pKa values in water at 25 °C are listed. Separate 0.10 M aqueous solutions of the sodium salts NaA, NaB, NaC and NaD are prepared (each salt is the conjugate base of the corresponding HA).

Acid | pKa of HA
HA | 3.80
HB | 4.90
HC | 7.20
HD | 9.10

Which 0.10 M salt solution has the highest pH?

choices.text: NaA, because HA is the strongest acid, so A− is the strongest hydrolysing base.
NaB, because pKa near 5 maximises hydrolysis of a 0.10 M salt.
NaC, because only acids with pKa > 7 give basic salts.
NaD, because HD is the weakest acid, so D− has the largest Kb and produces the most OH−.

items.explanation: The hydrolysis constant of A− is Kb = Kw / Ka = 10^−14 / 10^−pKa = 10^(pKa − 14). The largest pKa therefore gives the largest Kb. HD has pKa 9.10, so Kb of D− is 10^−4.90, much larger than Kb of A− (10^−10.20). For the same 0.10 M concentration, [OH−] ≈ √(Kb C) is therefore greatest for NaD, and that solution has the highest pH. The strongest acid (HA) has the weakest conjugate base, so NaA is the least basic of the four salts, not the most basic. All four conjugate bases hydrolyse to some extent; pKa = 7 is not a switch that turns hydrolysis on.

distractorRationales.A: The strongest acid has the weakest conjugate base. NaA therefore has the smallest Kb and the lowest pH among the four salts.
distractorRationales.B: There is no special maximum in hydrolysis at pKa 5. Hydrolysis of the conjugate base increases monotonically as pKa of HA increases.
distractorRationales.C: Even salts of acids with pKa < 7 (acetate, formate) give pH > 7. The ranking is still set by Kb, which is largest for NaD.

passage.title: psg-bb-2
passage.body:
A biochemistry lab studied how a small globular enzyme, RibN, loses activity when it unfolds. In its native state, RibN is stabilized by a hydrophobic core, numerous hydrogen bonds within its alpha-helices and beta-sheets, and a single disulfide bond linking two cysteine residues. The team monitored folding both by measuring enzyme activity and by tracking buried tryptophan residues, which fluoresce differently when the protein unfolds. Slowly heating the wild-type enzyme, they found that activity was retained up to about 55 deg C and then fell sharply, with a melting temperature (Tm, the temperature at which half the protein is unfolded) of 65 deg C.
They compared three samples. A cysteine-to-alanine mutant that cannot form the disulfide bond behaved like wild type at low temperature but had a Tm of only 52 deg C. Adding 6 M urea, a chemical denaturant, to wild-type enzyme lowered its Tm dramatically and abolished activity even at room temperature; on dialysis to remove the urea, activity slowly returned. Boiling followed by cooling left the protein inactive and aggregated, yet sequencing showed that the polypeptide's amino acid sequence was fully intact.
The investigators emphasized that all of these treatments disrupted the folded shape without breaking the peptide bonds of the backbone, and that the enzyme's function depended on maintaining its three-dimensional conformation, not merely on possessing the correct sequence.

passage.title: Anthropology — the invention of tradition
passage.body:
Many customs that present themselves as immemorial are surprisingly young. The Scottish clan tartan, worn as a badge of ancient lineage, was largely codified in the nineteenth century; the elaborate ceremonial of certain monarchies, apparently the residue of centuries, was substantially devised within living memory of those who first performed it. Historians have given such practices a name: invented traditions — rituals that claim continuity with a distant past to which their actual connection is tenuous or fabricated.

Why manufacture a past? Invented traditions tend to appear, scholars note, at moments of rapid change, when older bonds have frayed and new institutions must secure loyalty quickly. A ritual that feels ancient lends the present an air of inevitability; what looks as though it has always been done is harder to question than what is admittedly new. The invention, in other words, does work: it stabilizes, legitimizes, binds.

It would be easy to draw a cynical moral — that such traditions are frauds, and that exposing their recent origins deflates them. But this conclusion moves too fast. That a practice was invented at a datable moment does not show that it is meaningless to those who observe it. A wedding ritual devised a century ago may bind a community as tightly as one a millennium old; the bonds are real even if the pedigree is not. To confuse the falsity of a tradition's origin story with the falsity of its present function is to misjudge what such traditions are for.

Nor is the category as tidy as it first appears. Few traditions are either wholly ancient or wholly invented; most are refashioned inheritances — old materials put to new use. The nineteenth-century codifiers of tartan did not conjure it from nothing: they systematized and embellished a genuine, if looser, prior practice. "Invented" is thus better read as a matter of degree than as a verdict of pure fabrication.

The value of the concept, then, is not that it unmasks tradition as a lie. It is that it dissolves a false assumption: that the authority of a practice depends on the antiquity of its origins. Once we see how readily a sense of the ancient can be manufactured, we are freed to ask a better question — not how old a tradition is, but what work it does, and for whom.

passage.title: Who Is a Speaker (1975)
passage.body: In “Who Is a Speaker” (1975), Priya Raman writes from inside heritage listing. The argument is that fairness talk often arrives after the decision has already been made. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: During prolonged fasting, hepatic mitochondria convert acetyl-CoA to acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate, which are released to blood. Extrahepatic tissues oxidize these ketones, but the liver itself cannot use them as fuel. Which enzymatic gap explains the liver’s inability to consume the ketone bodies it produces?

choices.text: Liver lacks mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase, so it cannot make ketones in the first place.
Liver lacks succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA-transferase (thiophorase), so it cannot activate acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA.
Liver lacks 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase, so 3-hydroxybutyrate cannot be formed or reoxidized.
Liver mitochondria have no succinyl-CoA, so the citric acid cycle cannot run in hepatocytes.

items.explanation: Ketone utilization in muscle, brain, and kidney begins by activating acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA using succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA-transferase (thiophorase). Hepatocytes lack this enzyme, which prevents a futile cycle in which the liver would remake and then re-consume ketones. Liver does contain mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase (the committed ketogenic enzyme) and 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase, which is why it can produce both acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate. Succinyl-CoA is a normal citric-acid-cycle intermediate in liver; its presence is not the missing factor. Extrahepatic tissues then split acetoacetyl-CoA to acetyl-CoA for the cycle.

distractorRationales.A: Mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase is present in liver and is required for ketogenesis; its absence would prevent ketone production, contradicting the stem.
distractorRationales.C: Hepatic 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase is how liver generates 3-hydroxybutyrate from acetoacetate; the enzyme is not absent.
distractorRationales.D: Liver mitochondria operate the citric acid cycle and contain succinyl-CoA. Lack of succinyl-CoA is not the reason ketones are exported rather than oxidized locally.

items.stem: In a minimal-group experiment, strangers are randomly labeled Klee or Kandinsky fans after a coin flip. They then allocate points to unknown others identified only by label. People give more points to in-group members even though no interaction or conflicting interest exists. This result most directly supports:

choices.text: Social identity: mere categorization into a group can create in-group favoritism without a history of realistic conflict
Looking-glass self, because a mirror was required to assign the labels

passage.title: psg-cp-5
passage.body:
Nuclear medicine uses radioactive isotopes to image the body. The most widely used tracer, technetium-99m, is a metastable ('m') nuclear state that returns to its ground state by emitting a single gamma-ray photon, without changing its number of protons or neutrons. Because those gamma photons escape the body and reach a gamma camera, and because the isotope's half-life is a convenient 6.0 hours, it images well and clears quickly. A patient receives an initial activity of 800 MBq, and the staff track how the activity falls over the following day.
Positron emission tomography (PET) uses a different decay. Fluorine-18, built into a glucose analog, decays by positron emission: inside the nucleus a proton is converted into a neutron, and a positron is ejected. The positron soon annihilates with a nearby electron, producing two photons the scanner detects in coincidence.
The passage also compares decay modes. Some heavy parents decay by alpha emission, ejecting a helium-4 nucleus, while others undergo beta-minus decay. In every case the totals of mass number and charge are conserved across the nuclear equation. Finally, the team notes that alpha, beta, and especially gamma emissions are all 'ionizing': each quantum can carry enough energy to eject electrons from the atoms it strikes, which is both the basis of detection and the reason for strict dose limits. Planck's relation ties a photon's energy to its frequency, and gamma photons lie at the high-energy end of the electromagnetic spectrum.

passage.title: The Caption (1978)
passage.body: In “The Caption” (1978), Amina Okonkwo writes from inside university hiring. The argument is that a caption can do the arguing the image refuses to do. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

choices.text: It increases because NaF is a strong electrolyte that adds extra H3O+.
It decreases because the added fluoride (common ion) shifts HF ⇌ H+ + F− toward undissociated HF.
It is unchanged because Ka is a constant.

items.explanation: Le Chatelier’s principle applied to HF ⇌ H3O+ + F− says that adding F− from NaF drives the equilibrium left, lowering [H3O+] and decreasing the percent ionization of HF. After the addition, [H3O+] ≈ Ka [HF]/[F−] ≈ 6.8 × 10^−4, about an order of magnitude below the original 8.2 × 10^−3 M. Ka itself is unchanged; concentrations adjust so that the quotient again equals Ka. NaF is a salt, not a source of H3O+. Residual acid remains, so [H3O+] does not fall to zero.

distractorRationales.A: Na+ and F− are the ions of a salt; fluoride is a base, not an acid, and does not add H3O+.

items.stem: A ball is dropped from a height and falls freely (ignoring air resistance). As it falls, what happens to its total mechanical energy?

choices.text: It increases, because kinetic energy is being created from nothing.
It is entirely converted to heat immediately.
It stays constant — gravitational potential energy converts into kinetic energy, but the total stays the same.

items.explanation: With no air resistance, no energy leaves the ball-Earth system. Potential energy (mgh) converts into kinetic energy (½mv²) as it falls, but the sum of the two remains constant — conservation of mechanical energy. In a closed system with no friction/air resistance, total mechanical energy (potential + kinetic) is conserved — it just converts between forms. When friction or air resistance is present, some mechanical energy converts to heat, which is why real systems appear to "lose" energy. Memory tip: "Energy just changes outfits": in a frictionless system, energy never disappears, it just swaps from a potential "outfit" to a kinetic one and back, with the total wardrobe value unchanged. Glycogenesis stores glucose as glycogen; glycogenolysis breaks glycogen back down to glucose-1-phosphate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.A: Reversed — building is glycogenesis, breakdown is glycogenolysis.
distractorRationales.C: Gluconeogenesis/glycolysis are different pathways (new glucose / glucose breakdown).
distractorRationales.D: Lipogenesis/lipolysis concern fat, not glycogen.

items.stem:
[H+] is measured for two monoprotic acids over a range of formal concentrations C at 25 °C:

C (mol L−1) | Acid X: [H+] (mol L−1) | Acid Y: [H+] (mol L−1)
0.010 | 0.010 | 1.0 × 10^−3
0.040 | 0.040 | 2.0 × 10^−3
0.090 | 0.090 | 3.0 × 10^−3

For a weak acid, [H+] ≈ √(Ka C). Which description fits both columns?

choices.text: X and Y are both strong; the Y column must be a unit error because [H+] should always equal C.
X is weak with Ka = 1.0 × 10^−4 and Y is strong, because only Y has [H+] far below C.
X is a strong monoprotic acid ([H+] = C). Y is a weak acid with Ka = 1.0 × 10^−4, because [H+] = √(Ka C) at each row.
Y is a strong diprotic acid, because [H+] is three times larger at 0.090 M than at 0.010 M.

items.explanation: Acid X matches [H+] = C at every row, which is the hallmark of a fully dissociated monoprotic acid. Acid Y follows [H+] ∝ √C: √0.010 : √0.040 : √0.090 = 0.10 : 0.20 : 0.30, and the table is 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 × 10^−3, the same ratios. Then Ka = [H+]^2 / C. Using the first Y row, (1.0 × 10^−3)^2 / 0.010 = 1.0 × 10^−4, and the other rows give the same Ka. A strong diprotic acid would give [H+] closer to 2C, not a square-root dependence. Swapping which acid is strong contradicts the X column, where [H+] equals C.

distractorRationales.A: Y’s [H+] is far below C and scales as √C, which is incompatible with complete dissociation. The Y column is chemically consistent, not a unit error.
distractorRationales.B: X has [H+] = C, so X is the strong acid. Y is the weak one. This option reverses the assignments.
distractorRationales.D: A factor of three in [H+] when C increases ninefold is the square-root law, not evidence of two protons. A strong diprotic acid would not give [H+] = 0.0030 M from 0.090 M.

items.stem:
Relative catalytic activity of a cysteine protease is plotted against pH:

pH | relative activity (%)
4 | 8
5 | 25
6 | 70
7 | 100
8 | 80
9 | 20
10 | 4

The mechanism requires a histidine (pKa ≈ 6.2) to be deprotonated so it can accept a proton, and a cysteine (pKa ≈ 8.3) to be protonated in the resting enzyme so the thiol is available for activation. Which statement is consistent with the profile and those pKa values?

choices.text: The acidic limb (pH 4–6) tracks protonation of histidine, which removes the required base, while the alkaline limb (pH 8–10) tracks deprotonation of cysteine.
Maximum activity at pH 7 shows that both residues must be fully protonated.
The enzyme is inactive at pH 4 because the peptide substrate is uncharged only in base.
Activity collapses above pH 9 mainly because the essential histidine becomes protonated.

items.explanation: For His to act as a base it must be deprotonated, which becomes true as pH rises through 6.2, matching the climb from 8% at pH 4 to 100% at pH 7. For the thiol to remain in the activatable resting state it must stay protonated, which fails as pH exceeds 8.3, matching the fall to 20% then 4%. Peak activity at pH 7 sits between the two pKa values. The alkaline drop is therefore Cys deprotonation, not His protonation, which would occur on the acidic side.

distractorRationales.B: Fully protonated His would be the inactive acidic form; the pH 7 maximum is the mixed protonation state between the two pKa values.
distractorRationales.C: The stem assigns the pH dependence to catalytic residues, not to a requirement that the substrate be uncharged.
distractorRationales.D: Histidine protonation occurs on the low-pH side of pKa 6.2, not above pH 9.

items.stem: The author's attitude toward the chair is best described as:

choices.text: Quietly critical, conveyed through irony rather than direct statement.

items.explanation: The details — a smile that "did not reach her eyes," a pause designed to make silence uncomfortable, work assigned to everyone but herself — build a critical portrait without the author ever stating "the chair was manipulative" outright. That is irony, not neutral reporting or open hostility. Tone can build up across several small, carefully chosen details rather than one obvious clue. Add them up before judging tone — no single sentence here is hostile, but the pattern across all four is unmistakably critical. Memory tip: Death by a thousand details: no single sentence insults the chair, but stack four small unflattering details and the sarcastic verdict writes itself. Look for the pattern, not a single smoking gun. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: Critical Reasoning · Literary Tone & Inference
passage.body: The chair called the meeting to order at exactly nine, though half the room was still finding chairs. She thanked everyone for their punctuality with a smile that did not reach her eyes, then spent the next forty minutes explaining, in exhaustive detail, why the decision that mattered had already been made without them. When someone finally asked a question, she paused just long enough to make the silence uncomfortable before answering it with another question. By the time the meeting closed, three action items had been assigned, none of them to her, and everyone filed out thanking her for her time.

passage.title: psg-cars-8
passage.body:
Ritual occupies a paradoxical place in modern social thought. On one hand, it has been systematically studied as a fundamental mechanism of social solidarity: shared symbolic performances bind participants together, express and reinforce collective values, and mark the transitions — birth, initiation, marriage, death — that punctuate the human life course. On the other hand, modern societies tend to regard ritual with a degree of unease, as if elaborate ceremony were a relic of pre-rational ages unsuited to a world governed by science and voluntary choice.
Early sociological and anthropological accounts emphasized the integrative functions of ritual. Ceremonies, on this view, do not merely reflect an already-existing social order; they actively produce and sustain it. When a community gathers to mark a harvest, a coronation, or a national founding, participants do not simply observe an event — they enact membership in a collectivity that transcends any individual. The shared emotional experience generated by such occasions — what early theorists called collective effervescence — temporarily dissolves the boundaries between self and group, creating a felt sense of unity that persists in social memory long after the ceremony has concluded.
Later anthropologists complicated this functionalist picture by attending to the internal diversity and contestation that characterize real rituals. Ceremonies are rarely performed identically across time or across the different status groups within a community. The ruling class and the subjugated, men and women, elders and youth — each may experience the same ceremony quite differently, and the ritual may serve to reinforce not solidarity across the board but specific hierarchies of power. From this perspective, treating ritual purely as a mechanism of integration ignores its role in legitimating and reproducing asymmetric social arrangements.
A third approach draws attention to ritual's cognitive and communicative dimensions. Rituals encode information in a form — embodied action, sensory symbol, repeated performance — that is particularly durable and memorable. Unlike propositional statements that can be contested or forgotten, knowledge embedded in ritual is resistant to revision precisely because it is experienced rather than merely asserted. This explains why ritual tends to be invoked when other communicative resources fail: in the face of death, catastrophic loss, or radical uncertainty, shared performance provides a structure of meaning that discursive language alone cannot furnish. Grief rituals in particular demonstrate how embodied collective action can sustain communities through episodes of radical disruption that would otherwise threaten social fabric. The contrast with ordinary instruction is telling. A fact conveyed in a lecture can be doubted the moment the lecture ends; a truth rehearsed year after year in fasting, procession, or song is renewed in the body and rarely submitted to cross-examination at all. This is why communities so often entrust their most load-bearing commitments — who belongs, what is owed to the dead, which obligations the future imposes — not to argument but to observance. The very features that make ritual knowledge conservative, and sometimes an obstacle to reform, are also what allow it to hold a group together when argument alone would divide it, carrying shared meaning across generations that never meet.
Each of these accounts captures something genuine. Ritual is simultaneously a mechanism of solidarity, an arena of power and contestation, and a form of embodied knowledge. Understanding any particular ceremony requires attending to all three dimensions and to the historical context that shapes their relative salience.

Neighbouring options fail because they name a different relation, drop a required conversion, or contradict a number given in the stem (GAMSAT.S1.tone.t3#800012). distractorRationales.A: The essay criticises procedure; it does not celebrate it.
distractorRationales.C: It explicitly refuses slogans and outrage as the heat source.

passage.title: A Slow Era (1982)
passage.body: Ingrid Nilsen published “A Slow Era” in 1982 after a season in disaster mapping. The argument is that neutrality is a style, not an absence of interest. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Fatty acids are transported into the mitochondrion and broken down by beta-oxidation into ______, which enters the Krebs cycle.

The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Beta-oxidation cleaves fatty acids two carbons at a time into acetyl-CoA (generating NADH and FADH2), yielding far more ATP per gram than carbohydrate. distractorRationales.B: Beta-oxidation produces acetyl-CoA, not pyruvate.
distractorRationales.D: Lactate is a fermentation product, not a beta-oxidation product.

passage.title: Fidelity of a threonyl-tRNA synthetase
passage.body:
A fictional threonyl-tRNA synthetase, ThrRS-F, attaches threonine to tRNAThr during translation. The first active site activates threonine by forming threonyl-AMP from threonine and ATP; the amino acid is then transferred to the 3' end of tRNAThr. Because valine is structurally similar to threonine, ThrRS-F also contains an editing domain that hydrolyzes mischarged Val-tRNAThr. A reporter protein loses activity when valine is inserted at positions normally encoded by threonine codons.

Aminoacylation and editing properties of ThrRS-F.
Condition | Thr-tRNAThr charging rate (%) | Val-tRNAThr accumulation (%) | ATP-to-AMP conversion rate (%) | Active reporter protein (%)
Wild-type ThrRS-F + wild-type tRNAThr | 100 | 1 | 100 | 98
Editing-site D201A + wild-type tRNAThr | 95 | 28 | 125 | 62
Activation-site K55A + wild-type tRNAThr | 8 | 1 | 10 | 12
Wild-type ThrRS-F + acceptor-stem mutant tRNAThr | 18 | 1 | 22 | 20
Editing-site D201A + excess free valine | 90 | 45 | 140 | 45
Wild-type ThrRS-F + noncognate tRNAAla | 3 | 0.5 | 5 | 8

Two-site model of ThrRS-F specificity. — The activation site forms aminoacyl-AMP intermediates using ATP. Correct threonylated tRNA is released for translation. Incorrect Val-tRNAThr can enter an editing domain, where the aminoacyl ester bond is hydrolyzed before the tRNA reaches the ribosome.

passage.title: Identity, Group Membership, and Academic Feedback
passage.body:
A developmental psychology research group examined how social identity salience affects interpretation of academic feedback. High school students completed a difficult reasoning task and then received standardized written feedback stating that their score was below the sample average. Before receiving feedback, students were randomly assigned to one of two writing prompts. In the personal-values condition, students wrote about an important personal value. In the group-comparison condition, students wrote about ways their school group was viewed by students from a nearby school. After feedback, students rated perceived threat, expected future performance, and willingness to attempt a similar task.

Mean post-feedback ratings on 1 to 7 scales
Condition | Perceived threat | Expected future performance | Willingness to attempt similar task
Personal-values prompt | 3.0 | 4.9 | 5.5
Group-comparison prompt | 4.8 | 3.8 | 4.1

Interpretive note — All participants received identical task instructions and identical feedback; only the pre-feedback writing prompt differed across conditions.

passage.title: psg-bb-7
passage.body:
Microbiologists grew a pure culture of a rod-shaped bacterium in a closed flask of nutrient broth held at 37 deg C and tracked population size by measuring turbidity (optical density) over time. The resulting growth curve had four phases. During an initial lag phase, cell number changed little as the cells synthesized enzymes and adjusted to the medium. This was followed by an exponential (log) phase, during which the population doubled at a constant interval; the team measured a doubling time of 20 minutes. Growth then slowed into a stationary phase, in which the number of new cells produced roughly equaled the number dying, as nutrients ran low and wastes accumulated. Finally, in the death phase, viable counts declined.
To test antibiotics, the researchers exposed separate exponential-phase cultures to two drugs. Penicillin, which blocks the cross-linking step in synthesis of the peptidoglycan cell wall, killed rapidly growing cells but had little effect on cells that were not actively dividing. A second drug bound the bacterial ribosome and halted protein synthesis, stopping growth without immediately lysing the cells.
The team highlighted features that distinguish these prokaryotes from the animal cells in a companion culture: the bacteria lacked a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, divided asexually by binary fission rather than mitosis, and could acquire new genes horizontally, for example by taking up plasmids during conjugation. These traits shape both how the population grows and how drugs can target the bacteria selectively.
