passage.title: psg-cars-15
passage.body:
The concept of the unreliable narrator invites readers to question the testimony of a fictional voice that presents itself as authoritative. An unreliable narrator is one whose account of events, characters, or motives the reader has grounds to distrust -- not necessarily because the narrator lies deliberately, but because their perception is limited, their self-understanding deficient, or their emotional investment in a particular version of events distorts what they report. The detection of narrative unreliability is, accordingly, one of the more sophisticated interpretive skills literary fiction demands of its readers, requiring attention to gaps, contradictions, and moments when the narrator's self-presentation strains against the evidence the text itself provides. The concept therefore depends on a tacit collaboration between author and reader carried on over the narrator's head. Behind the speaking voice stands an implied author who arranges the evidence so that a discerning reader can measure the narrator's claims against it, catching what the narrator misses or conceals. This is why unreliability is a matter of degree and of inference rather than a property simply switched on or off: the same first-person account may strike a careless reader as candid and a careful one as riddled with evasions. Recognizing it depends less on any single tell-tale sentence than on the accumulating weight of discrepancies between what is said and what, on reflection, the text as a whole gives the reader reason to believe.
Narrative theorists have identified several sources of unreliability. The most philosophically interesting is self-deception: the narrator who sincerely believes their own account while systematically misrepresenting it, particularly with respect to their own motives and moral quality. Such narrators often generate irony at their own expense -- the gap between what they report and what the text implies about them becomes the site of the reader's critical engagement. A narrator who insists on their generosity in every paragraph while every described action suggests self-interest produces a portrait more damning than any external indictment could achieve.
A second source is cognitive limitation: the narrator who simply lacks the knowledge or experience to interpret correctly what they observe. A child narrator reporting on adult conflicts without understanding their significance, or an outsider narrator describing an unfamiliar culture through inappropriate categories, produces unreliability through innocence rather than self-interest. In such cases, the reader must supply interpretive frameworks that the narrator cannot, and the gap between the narrator's report and the reader's inference becomes the text's most productive space.
A third source, less often discussed, is structural: some narratives are built on multiple competing narrators whose accounts cannot all be true, or on a narrator who explicitly announces their own limitations and invites the reader to read against them. In the former case, unreliability is dispersed across the text; in the latter, it is ironized through self-consciousness. Both strategies challenge the assumption that narrative access to events is, even in fiction, transparent and unmediated.
The broader significance of narrative unreliability extends beyond literary technique. It models a stance of critical reading that has application outside the text: the recognition that all reported experience is shaped by the particular perspective, interests, and cognitive limitations of the reporter -- a recognition that is as relevant to journalism, autobiography, and legal testimony as it is to fiction. Learning to read unreliable narrators teaches a transferable epistemic skill: suspending credulity and attending to the conditions under which any account is produced.

items.stem: A journalist interviews five people leaving a luxury car dealership and concludes "most people in this city are wealthy." The main problem with this conclusion is:

choices.text: The sample is both too small and drawn from a location (a luxury dealership) that is not representative of the general population.
Five people is an unbiased, representative sample of the city.
The journalist should have asked ten people instead of five.
Wealth cannot be measured through interviews.

items.explanation: Beyond the small sample size, the real problem is selection bias — people at a luxury dealership are far more likely to be wealthy than the city's population as a whole. A conclusion about a whole population needs a sample that actually represents that population. Watch for two separate issues: sample size (too small to be reliable) and sample bias (drawn from an unrepresentative subgroup) — GAMSAT often tests whether you can tell these apart. Memory tip: Check both SIZE and SOURCE: a shaky sample can fail because it's too SIZE-small, drawn from the wrong SOURCE (a biased subgroup), or both — GAMSAT often hides one while flaunting the other. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

items.stem: Take hc = 1240 eV nm. Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal with work function φ = 2.0 eV. Photon energy E = hc/λ. Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is K_max = E − φ, and the stopping potential satisfies e Vs = K_max. The threshold wavelength is λ0 = hc/φ. Which set is consistent?

choices.text: E = 2.0 eV; K_max = 0; emission at every λ
E = 3.1 eV; K_max = 1.1 eV; λ0 = 400 nm, so 400 nm is already the threshold
E = 3.1 eV; K_max = 1.1 eV; Vs = 1.1 V; λ0 = 620 nm
E = 3.1 eV; K_max = 5.1 eV (adding φ); λ0 = 400 nm

items.explanation: E = 1240/400 = 3.1 eV. Then K_max = 3.1 − 2.0 = 1.1 eV, so Vs = 1.1 V. Threshold: λ0 = 1240/2.0 = 620 nm. Photons less energetic than 2.0 eV (λ > 620 nm) give no emission. Adding φ instead of subtracting would invent 5.1 eV electrons. E is not equal to φ at 400 nm. If 400 nm were threshold, φ would be 3.1 eV, contradicting the given 2.0 eV. Intensity does not appear because K_max is set by one photon’s leftover energy.

distractorRationales.A: E = 3.1 eV at 400 nm, well above φ, so K_max is not zero and emission is not possible at every λ.
distractorRationales.B: K_max = 1.1 eV is right, but that leftover proves 400 nm is above threshold; λ0 is 620 nm.
distractorRationales.D: φ is subtracted, not added; leftover energy is 1.1 eV. Threshold is 620 nm, not the illuminating 400 nm.

passage.title: The Roster (1974)
passage.body: Clara Voss's 1974 essay “The Roster,” on museum captions, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that local knowledge is treated as anecdote until a model needs it. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: Electrophoretic Separation with Optical Readout
passage.body:
A fictional capillary electrophoresis device separates carboxylate-labeled peptides. The capillary contains buffer at pH 7.4. The fluorescent carboxylate label has pKa 4.5, so labeled peptides are predominantly negatively charged. The electric field magnitude is E = V/L, where V is the applied voltage and L is electrode spacing. A higher electric field generally increases migration distance over a fixed time, but excessive current can cause Joule heating and band broadening. The fluorescent band is imaged onto a camera using a thin converging lens. For the standard optical setup, the object distance is 12 cm and the image distance is 24 cm.

Electrophoresis conditions and separation results after 3.0 min.
Run | Applied voltage (V) | Electrode spacing (cm) | Current (mA) | Relative buffer strength | Migration distance of analyte X (cm) | Band width (mm)
A | 300 | 6.0 | 1.5 | 1x | 2.4 | 0.50
B | 600 | 6.0 | 3.0 | 1x | 4.8 | 0.80
C | 600 | 6.0 | 6.0 | 2x | 4.9 | 1.40
D | 300 | 3.0 | 3.0 | 1x | 4.7 | 0.85

Optical imaging of the fluorescent band. — A real image of the fluorescent band is formed on a camera sensor. The image is inverted relative to the object in the capillary and appears larger than the object under the standard setup.

items.stem: A radiolabeled, lipid-soluble hormone accumulates in target-cell nuclei and co-immunoprecipitates with a zinc-finger DNA-binding protein that occupies hormone-response elements. The hormone is acting most like:

choices.text: Insulin, which binds a receptor tyrosine kinase at the plasma membrane
Epinephrine, which signals through a Gs-coupled adrenergic receptor
Acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors, opening a ligand-gated cation channel
Cortisol or another steroid, which binds an intracellular receptor that regulates transcription

items.explanation: Steroid hormones are lipid-derived (from cholesterol, a triterpene relative) and cross membranes to bind intracellular receptors. Liganded steroid receptors are transcription factors with zinc-finger DNA-binding domains that sit on hormone-response elements, matching the nuclear co-IP. Peptide hormones and catecholamines bind cell-surface receptors and do not accumulate as nuclear DNA-binding complexes of this type. Nicotinic ACh is an ionotropic neurotransmitter, not a nuclear lipid messenger. The slow genomic actions of steroids follow from this transcriptional mechanism, unlike seconds-scale second-messenger cascades.

distractorRationales.A: Insulin’s receptor is a membrane RTK; the hormone does not co-IP with nuclear zinc-finger receptors as the primary complex.
distractorRationales.B: Epinephrine is a hydrophilic catecholamine acting at GPCRs, not a nuclear steroid receptor ligand.
distractorRationales.C: Nicotinic ACh receptors are ligand-gated channels at membranes, not nuclear DNA-binding proteins.

passage.title: Pentose phosphate pathway flux during oxidative stress
passage.body:
A fictional erythroid cell line lacks mitochondria after differentiation and relies on glycolysis for ATP. It also uses the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) to generate NADPH for reduction of glutathione. Researchers compared wild-type cells with cells expressing a mutant glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD-M). They exposed cells to an oxidant and measured redox status, lactate release, and radiolabeled carbon dioxide production from glucose labeled at carbon 1 or carbon 6. In the oxidative PPP, carbon 1 of glucose 6-phosphate is released as CO2 while NADPH is produced.

Metabolic responses to oxidant exposure.
Cells and condition | NADPH/NADP+ | GSH/GSSG | Lactate release (%) | 14CO2 from [1-14C]glucose (%) | 14CO2 from [6-14C]glucose (%) | Viable cells (%)
Wild type, basal | 4.0 | 8.0 | 100 | 100 | 5 | 98

items.stem: A rigid, massless board is balanced on a fulcrum. A 2 kg mass sits 3 m to the left of the fulcrum. What mass placed 1 m to the right of the fulcrum produces static equilibrium? Take g = 10 m/s^2.
items.explanation: Static equilibrium of a rigid body requires zero net torque about the fulcrum (and zero net force, which the fulcrum can supply). Taking counterclockwise as positive, (2 kg)(10 m/s^2)(3 m) = m (10 m/s^2)(1 m), so m = 6 kg. Gravity cancels, leaving the lever rule m1 d1 = m2 d2. A smaller mass on a longer arm balances a larger mass on a shorter arm: 2 kg at 3 m matches 6 kg at 1 m.

distractorRationales.A: Equal masses would balance only if the lever arms were equal. The left arm is three times the right arm, so the right-hand mass must be three times 2 kg.
distractorRationales.B: This averages the given numbers or uses 2 kg times 3 m / 2 m. Torque balance uses the actual 1 m right-hand arm, not an invented 2 m.
distractorRationales.D: This adds 2 + 3 + 3 or otherwise combines the given figures without using torque = force times perpendicular lever arm.

passage.title: Fidelity of a threonyl-tRNA synthetase
passage.body:
A fictional threonyl-tRNA synthetase, ThrRS-F, attaches threonine to tRNAThr during translation. The first active site activates threonine by forming threonyl-AMP from threonine and ATP; the amino acid is then transferred to the 3' end of tRNAThr. Because valine is structurally similar to threonine, ThrRS-F also contains an editing domain that hydrolyzes mischarged Val-tRNAThr. A reporter protein loses activity when valine is inserted at positions normally encoded by threonine codons.

Aminoacylation and editing properties of ThrRS-F.
Condition | Thr-tRNAThr charging rate (%) | Val-tRNAThr accumulation (%) | ATP-to-AMP conversion rate (%) | Active reporter protein (%)
Wild-type ThrRS-F + wild-type tRNAThr | 100 | 1 | 100 | 98
Editing-site D201A + wild-type tRNAThr | 95 | 28 | 125 | 62
Activation-site K55A + wild-type tRNAThr | 8 | 1 | 10 | 12
Wild-type ThrRS-F + acceptor-stem mutant tRNAThr | 18 | 1 | 22 | 20
Editing-site D201A + excess free valine | 90 | 45 | 140 | 45
Wild-type ThrRS-F + noncognate tRNAAla | 3 | 0.5 | 5 | 8

Two-site model of ThrRS-F specificity. — The activation site forms aminoacyl-AMP intermediates using ATP. Correct threonylated tRNA is released for translation. Incorrect Val-tRNAThr can enter an editing domain, where the aminoacyl ester bond is hydrolyzed before the tRNA reaches the ribosome.

passage.title: psg-cars-2
passage.body:
Among the most contested claims in moral philosophy is the assertion that ethical judgments are irreducibly relative to the cultural frameworks that produce them. Cultural relativism, in its strongest form, holds not merely that different societies happen to endorse different moral codes, but that no standpoint outside all cultures exists from which those codes can be objectively ranked. If morality is constituted by social practice rather than discovered through reason or intuition, then condemning another culture's practices amounts to little more than projecting one's own conventions onto alien terrain.
Defenders of this position often draw strength from the anthropological record, which reveals a startling diversity of moral norms across societies separated by time and geography. Practices that one tradition regards as obligatory — ancestor veneration, dowry exchange, arranged marriage — strike others as superstitious, exploitative, or coercive. From this diversity, relativists infer that no norm enjoys a privileged status independent of its cultural home. To insist otherwise, they argue, is to mistake familiarity for objectivity.
Yet the relativist position encounters formidable internal difficulties. If moral judgments are valid only within the culture that generates them, then the reformer who criticizes her own society's practices — the abolitionist in a slave-holding nation, the suffragette in a society that bars women from public life — is simply wrong by definition. Her protest cannot be morally correct because the dominant convention of her society says otherwise. This consequence strikes many philosophers as a reductio ad absurdum: a moral theory that silences the reformer and vindicates the oppressor cannot be adequate.
Universalists reply that moral diversity, while real, does not demonstrate moral relativism any more than disagreement among scientists demonstrates that there are no scientific facts. People may disagree about the boiling point of water and still be wrong; analogously, cultures may disagree about the permissibility of torture yet one of them may be mistaken. The universalist identifies certain core norms — prohibitions on gratuitous cruelty, requirements of basic reciprocity — that appear in some form across virtually every known society, suggesting not conventional agreement but convergent recognition of genuine moral truths.
The exchange rarely ends there. Relativists counter that the universalist's alleged core norms are either too thin to settle any real dispute or are honored more in word than in deed. Nearly every society condemns killing, they concede — yet societies differ profoundly over which killings count as murder, whom the prohibition protects, and when violence becomes duty. A principle so abstract that rival cultures can all recite it while behaving in opposite ways, the relativist argues, marks no genuine agreement at all. Universalists answer that shared abstract commitments are precisely what one would expect if morality tracked real but imperfectly grasped values, and that quarrels over application no more dissolve an underlying norm than disputed measurements dissolve the quantity being measured.
A nuanced middle position distinguishes between first-order moral claims (what is right or wrong) and metaethical claims (what makes moral judgments true or false). One may acknowledge deep cultural variation in first-order norms while still holding that some metaethical framework — natural law, contractualism, or sentimentalism — provides a transcultural criterion of moral evaluation. On this view, the diversity of moral codes is evidence of human fallibility and limited information, not of the absence of any moral standard. Whether such a criterion is ultimately defensible remains among the central unresolved questions of moral philosophy.

items.stem: A researcher studying anaplerosis in liver mitochondria finds that adding pyruvate plus bicarbonate increases the oxaloacetate pool and accelerates citrate formation from acetyl-CoA. The responsible enzyme requires biotin and is allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA. Which reaction is occurring?

choices.text: Pyruvate kinase converting PEP to pyruvate, which cannot be a net gain of cycle intermediates
Pyruvate dehydrogenase running in reverse to carboxylate acetyl-CoA to pyruvate
Pyruvate carboxylase converting pyruvate plus CO2 to oxaloacetate
ATP-citrate lyase producing oxaloacetate in the mitochondrial matrix from cytosolic citrate

items.explanation: Pyruvate carboxylase is the principal anaplerotic enzyme in liver mitochondria: it carboxylates pyruvate to oxaloacetate using biotin as a CO2 carrier and is allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA, matching every experimental clue. The new four-carbon unit can condense with acetyl-CoA at citrate synthase, so citrate formation rises. Pyruvate kinase makes pyruvate, not OAA, and is not biotin-dependent. PDH is irreversible in animals and does not carboxylate acetyl-CoA. ATP-citrate lyase is cytosolic, generating acetyl-CoA for fatty-acid synthesis, not a mitochondrial biotin enzyme that fills the oxaloacetate pool.

distractorRationales.A: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate from PEP and is not a biotin-dependent carboxylase; it does not replenish oxaloacetate.
distractorRationales.B: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible under physiologic conditions and is inhibited, not reversed, by acetyl-CoA. It does not add CO2 to acetyl-CoA.
distractorRationales.D: ATP-citrate lyase is cytosolic (citrate + ATP + CoA → acetyl-CoA + OAA + ADP + Pi) and does not require biotin or reside in the matrix as the anaplerotic fill reaction described.

passage.title: psg-ps-5
passage.body:
Researchers ran three studies of behavior in groups. In Study 1, a participant judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line, answering aloud after several confederates. On critical trials the confederates unanimously gave an obviously wrong answer. Participants conformed to the wrong answer on about 35% of critical trials, and three-quarters conformed at least once; conformity fell sharply when a single confederate broke from the majority. Most conformers later said they knew the group was wrong but did not want to stand out.
In Study 2, participants completed either a simple, well-practiced task or a complex, unfamiliar task, alone or in front of an audience. An audience improved performance on the simple task but worsened it on the complex task.
In Study 3, participants heard what sounded like a fellow participant having a medical emergency in another room. When participants believed they were the only witness, 85% sought help within a minute; when they believed four others were also present, only 31% did, and those who helped took longer. Interviews suggested that the presence of others reduced each individual's felt responsibility.
The authors distinguished going along with a group to fit in from the effect of an audience on task performance, and linked Study 3 to a well-documented reduction in helping as the number of bystanders rises. They emphasized that these effects reflect the social situation rather than stable personality differences among the participants.

items.stem: HCl infused into the duodenum of a fasting animal raises plasma secretin and pancreatic bicarbonate output. Cutting the vagus does not abolish the bicarbonate response. The dominant mechanism is:

choices.text: CCK released from gastric G cells acting on pancreatic acini to secrete trypsinogen as bicarbonate
Pepsin from pancreatic duct cells, stimulated only by vagal preganglionic fibers
Secretin from duodenal S cells acting hormonally on pancreatic ductal epithelium to secrete HCO3-
Direct titration of pancreatic juice by duodenal acid without any endocrine cell involvement

items.explanation: Duodenal acid is the physiologic stimulus for S cells to release secretin. Secretin travels in blood to pancreatic duct cells, raises cAMP, and drives bicarbonate-rich secretion that neutralizes chyme. Persistence after vagotomy shows a hormonal, not solely neural, reflex. CCK is released from I cells in response to fat and protein and primarily stimulates enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction, not this acid-bicarbonate pairing. G cells make gastrin in the stomach, pepsin is a gastric protease, and duct cells do not dump pepsin. Acid does not magically become pancreatic juice without secretin.

distractorRationales.A: G cells secrete gastrin, not CCK, and CCK is not the acid-evoked bicarbonate hormone.
distractorRationales.B: Pepsin is gastric; the vagus is unnecessary here by experimental design.
distractorRationales.D: The rise in plasma secretin identifies an endocrine mediator.

passage.title: Fit and Hiring (1978)
passage.body: In “Fit and Hiring” (1978), Priya Raman writes from inside municipal archives. The argument is that a caption can do the arguing the image refuses to do. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: Identity, Group Membership, and Academic Feedback
passage.body:
A developmental psychology research group examined how social identity salience affects interpretation of academic feedback. High school students completed a difficult reasoning task and then received standardized written feedback stating that their score was below the sample average. Before receiving feedback, students were randomly assigned to one of two writing prompts. In the personal-values condition, students wrote about an important personal value. In the group-comparison condition, students wrote about ways their school group was viewed by students from a nearby school. After feedback, students rated perceived threat, expected future performance, and willingness to attempt a similar task.

Mean post-feedback ratings on 1 to 7 scales
Condition | Perceived threat | Expected future performance | Willingness to attempt similar task
Personal-values prompt | 3.0 | 4.9 | 5.5
Group-comparison prompt | 4.8 | 3.8 | 4.1

Interpretive note — All participants received identical task instructions and identical feedback; only the pre-feedback writing prompt differed across conditions.

passage.title: psg-bb-10
passage.body:
To study how blood delivers oxygen, physiologists measured the percentage of hemoglobin saturated with O2 across a range of oxygen partial pressures (PO2), generating an oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. For adult hemoglobin the curve was S-shaped (sigmoidal): saturation rose slowly at very low PO2, steeply through intermediate values, and leveled off near 100 percent at high PO2. The partial pressure at which hemoglobin is 50 percent saturated (the P50) was about 26 mmHg. For comparison, myoglobin, a single-subunit muscle protein, gave a hyperbolic curve that was left-shifted, reaching high saturation at much lower PO2.
The team then altered the conditions around adult hemoglobin. Lowering the pH (more acidic), raising the partial pressure of carbon dioxide, and raising temperature each shifted the curve to the right, increasing the P50; at any given intermediate PO2, hemoglobin then held less oxygen and released more. These effects are collectively called the Bohr effect. Conversely, fetal hemoglobin gave a left-shifted curve with a lower P50 than adult hemoglobin.
The investigators related the findings to physiology. The sigmoidal shape reflects cooperative binding among hemoglobin's four subunits: O2 binding to one subunit increases the affinity of the others. In metabolically active tissue, where CO2 and acid are high and temperature is elevated, the right shift promotes oxygen unloading exactly where it is needed. The left-shifted fetal curve lets fetal blood extract oxygen from maternal blood across the placenta.

passage.title: psg-bb-7
passage.body:
Microbiologists grew a pure culture of a rod-shaped bacterium in a closed flask of nutrient broth held at 37 deg C and tracked population size by measuring turbidity (optical density) over time. The resulting growth curve had four phases. During an initial lag phase, cell number changed little as the cells synthesized enzymes and adjusted to the medium. This was followed by an exponential (log) phase, during which the population doubled at a constant interval; the team measured a doubling time of 20 minutes. Growth then slowed into a stationary phase, in which the number of new cells produced roughly equaled the number dying, as nutrients ran low and wastes accumulated. Finally, in the death phase, viable counts declined.
To test antibiotics, the researchers exposed separate exponential-phase cultures to two drugs. Penicillin, which blocks the cross-linking step in synthesis of the peptidoglycan cell wall, killed rapidly growing cells but had little effect on cells that were not actively dividing. A second drug bound the bacterial ribosome and halted protein synthesis, stopping growth without immediately lysing the cells.
The team highlighted features that distinguish these prokaryotes from the animal cells in a companion culture: the bacteria lacked a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, divided asexually by binary fission rather than mitosis, and could acquire new genes horizontally, for example by taking up plasmids during conjugation. These traits shape both how the population grows and how drugs can target the bacteria selectively.

items.stem: Ouabain blocks Na+/K+ ATPase in a neuron that still has Na+ and K+ leak pathways. Over the following minutes, the most direct effect is that:

items.explanation: The pump continuously extrudes three Na+ ions and imports two K+ ions, maintaining steep gradients against leak. When the pump is blocked, leak is unopposed: Na+ runs down its gradient into the cell and K+ leaks out, so both gradients run down and the membrane slowly depolarizes. distractorRationales.D: Cardiac glycosides inhibit the pump protein; they do not punch nonspecific holes that dump macromolecules.

items.stem: Mock jurors who individually lean slightly toward conviction become, after deliberation, much more confident that the defendant is guilty. Stoner’s risky shift was an early case of the same family of findings. Which label and mechanism best fit?

choices.text: Groupthink: the jury must have had a mindguard and an illusion of invulnerability, which is required for any extremity shift
Normative social influence as in Asch, which always produces a moderate, never more extreme, consensus
Social facilitation (Zajonc): mere presence of co-actors multiplies the dominant conviction response without discussion
Group polarization: discussion amplifies the group’s already-favored pole via persuasive arguments and social comparison

items.explanation: Group polarization is the finding that like-minded discussion makes the average position more extreme in the initially favored direction. Persuasive-arguments and social-comparison accounts (and the older risky-shift literature Stoner began) explain it. Groupthink is defective decision quality from suppressed dissent, not the same as a lawful extremity shift. Asch conformity can yield a wrong majority, but it is not defined as extremity amplification. Zajonc’s mere-presence facilitation does not require deliberation and is not a jury-discussion theory.

items.stem: A mixed sample of purified genomic DNA and cellular RNA is incubated in dilute sodium hydroxide at room temperature and then neutralized. Only DNA polymers remain intact. Which structural feature accounts for the selective degradation of RNA?

choices.text: RNA uses uracil, which is deprotonated by hydroxide and leaves the backbone as free base.
DNA lacks a 5′-phosphate, so it cannot undergo nucleophilic cleavage of phosphodiesters.
The C5 methyl of thymine sterically blocks hydroxide attack on DNA phosphodiesters.
The 2′-OH of ribose can be deprotonated and attack the adjacent phosphodiester, forming a 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate.

items.explanation: Alkaline cleavage of RNA is an intramolecular transesterification. Hydroxide deprotonates the ribose 2′-OH, which attacks the 3′-linked phosphorus and displaces the 5′ end of the next nucleotide, producing a 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate that subsequently hydrolyzes. DNA lacks a 2′-OH, so it cannot form that cyclic intermediate and is alkali-stable under the same conditions. Uracil versus thymine and the thymine methyl group do not explain backbone scission, and both polymers have 5′-phosphates in internucleotide linkages. This chemistry is why alkaline lysis can destroy RNA while leaving plasmid DNA intact.

distractorRationales.A: Uracil versus thymine does not make the phosphodiester alkali-labile; RNA with U still requires the 2′-OH for cleavage, and DNA with T is stable because it lacks that hydroxyl.
distractorRationales.B: DNA strands are connected by 5′-phosphates in phosphodiester bonds; the absence of a 2′-OH, not absence of a 5′-phosphate, explains alkali stability.
distractorRationales.C: Thymine’s methyl group is on the base, far from the internucleotide phosphate, and does not account for DNA’s resistance to dilute base.

passage.title: Two ways of hearing a census
passage.body:
Poem (untitled, 2019)

We counted rooms as if rooms were people.
The spare one kept its coat on.
In the column for language we wrote the kettle.
Nobody asked the stairs their age.

Commentary by L. Okonkwo, catalogue essay for an exhibition of household inventories:
The poem is easy to misread as anti-data. It is not. It notices that a census already poetizes: it decides what may stand for a life (rooms, language, age) and what must remain downstairs, unasked. The coat on the spare room is not a joke about furniture. It is a figure for surplus — the part of a household that official forms cannot rent. When the poem puts a kettle in the language column, it is not claiming kettles speak. It is showing how quickly a form will accept a proxy if the proxy is small and warm.

A table printed beside the poem in the gallery listed visitors by hour and by whether they photographed the stairs:
Hour 10: 14 visitors, 2 photographed stairs
Hour 11: 31 visitors, 18 photographed stairs
Hour 12: 9 visitors, 0 photographed stairs (docent talk in progress)
The curator captioned the table: Attention is not the same as attendance.

A radio host later called the exhibition “political because it made a kettle into a citizen.” Okonkwo's essay had already refused that flattening. The political cut, for her, is not enfranchising objects. It is noticing which human details a state is willing to miss.

items.stem: A mutant citric-acid-cycle enzyme cannot generate GTP (or ATP) even though NADH can still be produced from succinate via later steps. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?

Isocitrate dehydrogenase, which reduces NAD+ but does not form GTP

Succinyl-CoA synthetase (succinyl-CoA ligase), which performs substrate-level phosphorylation

items.explanation: The only substrate-level phosphorylation in the citric acid cycle is the conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinate by succinyl-CoA synthetase, which conserves the thioester energy as GTP (or ATP, depending on isoform). Loss of isocitrate dehydrogenase would cut NADH from that step and would not be rescued in the GTP phenotype by succinate in the way described. Thus the GTP-specific defect localizes to succinyl-CoA synthetase.

items.stem: A spinal-injury clinic re-interviews adults who had complete thoracic transection years earlier. Compared with their own pre-injury descriptions, patients still classify scenes as frightening or funny, but they say the “heat” of those feelings is weaker, especially for states that used to come with a pounding heart. Autonomic recordings below the lesion are flat. Which theory most directly predicts the drop in felt intensity?

choices.text: James–Lange theory, because the feeling of emotion depends on detecting bodily change
Cannon–Bard theory, because experience is fully independent of the body, so intensity cannot fall
Schachter–Singer theory, because a missing body makes any situational label impossible
Opponent-process theory, because every emotion automatically elicits its opposite and cancels intensity

items.explanation: James–Lange theory treats conscious emotion as perception of bodily change, including visceral and autonomic feedback that travels in part through the spinal cord. Interrupting that afferent traffic should therefore blunt intensity even when the person can still identify the situation as frightening or amusing. Cannon–Bard theory instead treats the feeling as a parallel central event and does not predict this selective dulling after deafferentation. Two-factor theory emphasizes labeling of unexplained arousal rather than loss of spinal feedback. Opponent-process theory concerns sequential opposite emotions, not bodily deafferentation.

distractorRationales.B: Cannon–Bard holds that feeling and physiology are triggered together by a central process, so cutting spinal autonomic traffic should not systematically weaken the feeling.
distractorRationales.C: Two-factor theory does not claim that a spinal lesion makes labeling impossible; people can still use context. It also does not uniquely predict intensity loss after transection.
distractorRationales.D: Opponent-process theory describes a later opposite reaction (for example, relief after fear), not a requirement for intact viscera.

passage.title: psg-ps-6
passage.body:
A study examined how persuasive messages change attitudes. Undergraduates read an editorial advocating a new campus exam policy. The message was either strong (well-reasoned arguments) or weak (superficial slogans), and was attributed either to a distinguished professor or to a first-year student. Crucially, half the participants were told the policy would take effect next year (high personal relevance) and half were told it would begin in a decade (low relevance).
Among high-relevance readers, attitude change depended almost entirely on argument strength and hardly at all on the source; among low-relevance readers, the reverse held - the prestigious source mattered, but argument quality did not. A follow-up a week later showed that attitudes formed by high-relevance readers persisted and better predicted sign-up behavior than those of low-relevance readers.
In a second study, participants who volunteered to argue publicly for a position they privately opposed later shifted their private attitudes toward that position - but only when they felt they had freely chosen to do so and were paid little. Those paid a large sum, or who felt coerced, showed no attitude change.
The authors mapped the first study onto a dual-route model of persuasion: one route processes the substance of a message when motivation is high, while the other relies on surface cues when motivation is low. They explained the second study as the reduction of an uncomfortable inconsistency between behavior and belief, resolved by changing the belief when the behavior could not be justified by an external incentive.

passage.title: The Creek Map (1977)
passage.body: Jonas Berg's 1977 essay “The Creek Map,” on vaccine campaigns, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. The piece admits that some gatekeeping keeps fraud out. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: psg-cars-2
passage.body:
Among the most contested claims in moral philosophy is the assertion that ethical judgments are irreducibly relative to the cultural frameworks that produce them. Cultural relativism, in its strongest form, holds not merely that different societies happen to endorse different moral codes, but that no standpoint outside all cultures exists from which those codes can be objectively ranked. If morality is constituted by social practice rather than discovered through reason or intuition, then condemning another culture's practices amounts to little more than projecting one's own conventions onto alien terrain.
Defenders of this position often draw strength from the anthropological record, which reveals a startling diversity of moral norms across societies separated by time and geography. Practices that one tradition regards as obligatory — ancestor veneration, dowry exchange, arranged marriage — strike others as superstitious, exploitative, or coercive. From this diversity, relativists infer that no norm enjoys a privileged status independent of its cultural home. To insist otherwise, they argue, is to mistake familiarity for objectivity.
Yet the relativist position encounters formidable internal difficulties. If moral judgments are valid only within the culture that generates them, then the reformer who criticizes her own society's practices — the abolitionist in a slave-holding nation, the suffragette in a society that bars women from public life — is simply wrong by definition. Her protest cannot be morally correct because the dominant convention of her society says otherwise. This consequence strikes many philosophers as a reductio ad absurdum: a moral theory that silences the reformer and vindicates the oppressor cannot be adequate.
Universalists reply that moral diversity, while real, does not demonstrate moral relativism any more than disagreement among scientists demonstrates that there are no scientific facts. People may disagree about the boiling point of water and still be wrong; analogously, cultures may disagree about the permissibility of torture yet one of them may be mistaken. The universalist identifies certain core norms — prohibitions on gratuitous cruelty, requirements of basic reciprocity — that appear in some form across virtually every known society, suggesting not conventional agreement but convergent recognition of genuine moral truths.
The exchange rarely ends there. Relativists counter that the universalist's alleged core norms are either too thin to settle any real dispute or are honored more in word than in deed. Nearly every society condemns killing, they concede — yet societies differ profoundly over which killings count as murder, whom the prohibition protects, and when violence becomes duty. A principle so abstract that rival cultures can all recite it while behaving in opposite ways, the relativist argues, marks no genuine agreement at all. Universalists answer that shared abstract commitments are precisely what one would expect if morality tracked real but imperfectly grasped values, and that quarrels over application no more dissolve an underlying norm than disputed measurements dissolve the quantity being measured.
A nuanced middle position distinguishes between first-order moral claims (what is right or wrong) and metaethical claims (what makes moral judgments true or false). One may acknowledge deep cultural variation in first-order norms while still holding that some metaethical framework — natural law, contractualism, or sentimentalism — provides a transcultural criterion of moral evaluation. On this view, the diversity of moral codes is evidence of human fallibility and limited information, not of the absence of any moral standard. Whether such a criterion is ultimately defensible remains among the central unresolved questions of moral philosophy.

passage.title: Pentose phosphate pathway flux during oxidative stress

It also uses the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) to generate NADPH for reduction of glutathione. Students build and analyze a galvanic (voltaic) cell and then use batteries to study simple circuits. In the cell, a strip of zinc metal sits in zinc sulfate solution and a strip of copper metal sits in copper sulfate solution; a salt bridge connects the two half-cells, and a wire with a voltmeter links the metal strips. Under standard conditions the tabulated reduction potentials are Zn^2+ + 2 e- -> Zn, E = -0.76 V, and Cu^2+ + 2 e- -> Cu, E = +0.34 V. When the wire is connected, one electrode gains mass while the other slowly dissolves, and the voltmeter registers a steady potential difference. The students confirm which metal is oxidized by weighing the electrodes before and after.
They then replace the standard 1 M solutions with more dilute ones and record how the measured cell voltage shifts away from its standard value, relating the change to the reaction quotient Q for Zn + Cu^2+ -> Zn^2+ + Cu.
In the circuit module, a 12 V battery is connected to three resistors: a 6 ohm and a 3 ohm resistor wired in parallel with each other, and that combination wired in series with a 4 ohm resistor. An ammeter reads the current leaving the battery. The students compute the equivalent resistance, the current, and the power the battery delivers, treating the battery as an ideal source with negligible internal resistance and the wires as resistanceless.

passage.title: psg-bb-3
passage.body:
To dissect how mutations disrupt protein output, a lab engineered a set of Escherichia coli strains, each carrying a single defined change in a gene (galK) that encodes a metabolic enzyme. For every strain they measured two quantities: the steady-state level of galK messenger RNA (by quantitative PCR) and the amount of functional enzyme (by an activity assay). Results were expressed as a percentage of the wild-type value.
Wild type showed 100 percent mRNA and 100 percent enzyme activity. Strain 1, carrying a substitution in the promoter region upstream of the coding sequence, showed 15 percent mRNA and 14 percent activity. Strain 2, carrying a single base-pair change that converted a glutamine codon (CAG) into a stop codon (TAG) near the beginning of the coding sequence, showed 95 percent mRNA but less than 2 percent activity; the protein it produced was abnormally short. Strain 3, carrying a single-nucleotide deletion just after the start codon, showed 92 percent mRNA and less than 2 percent activity, and its protein product bore no resemblance to the wild-type sequence beyond its first few residues. Strain 4, carrying a base change that altered a codon from CTG to CTA (both of which encode leucine), showed 98 percent mRNA and 97 percent activity.
The investigators noted that a mutation's consequences depend on where in the gene it falls and how it interacts with the genetic code: some changes reduce how much mRNA is made, others corrupt translation of the message, and some have essentially no effect at all.

passage.title: psg-ps-10
passage.body:
A longitudinal study followed 8,000 adults for 15 years to examine links between social position and health. Participants were grouped by socioeconomic status (SES), a composite of income, education, and occupational prestige. Age-adjusted rates of chronic illness and mortality declined steadily at each higher step of the SES ladder - not merely a gap between rich and poor, but a graded relationship across the whole range. The pattern held after controlling for smoking and diet, and was partly explained by chronic stress, worse neighborhood conditions, and unequal access to preventive care.
Participants were also classified by the neighborhood where they lived. Lower-SES families were concentrated in areas with fewer clinics, more pollution, and less green space; researchers described these areas as products of long-standing residential segregation. Children raised in the lowest-SES neighborhoods were less likely to reach a higher SES than their parents, a pattern the authors linked to unequal schools and social networks.
Finally, the study noted a demographic shift: as the population aged and birth rates fell, the ratio of working-age adults to dependents changed, straining programs that fund elder care. The authors argued that health follows a social gradient, that place and inequality shape opportunity across generations, and that population structure interacts with these inequalities to shape a society's future needs. They emphasized that individual choices operated within, and were constrained by, these structural conditions.

A behavioral neuroscience lab examined whether ambient odors influence taste judgments. Seventy-two adults sampled the same unsweetened citrus beverage in three counterbalanced conditions: no ambient scent, a congruent lemon scent, and an incongruent coffee scent. Participants were not told that the scent condition changed across trials. After each sample, they rated perceived sweetness, perceived sourness, and purchase intention on 1 to 7 scales. Congruent lemon scent | 4.2 | 4.5 | 4.5
Incongruent coffee scent | 2.7 | 5.0 | 2.8

Odor detection threshold in arbitrary concentration units
Time point | Mean lemon odor detection threshold
Before continuous odor exposure | 2.0
Immediately after 3 minutes of exposure | 6.0
Ten minutes after exposure ended | 3.0

Study design — Each participant experienced all beverage scent conditions in randomized order. The adaptation task was completed after the beverage ratings and used a detection threshold procedure for lemon odor.

items.stem:
Oxygen evolution of a green algal suspension (relative units) is recorded at equal incident photon flux at each wavelength:

Wavelength (nm) | O2 evolution
430 | 100
480 | 85
550 | 18
650 | 72
680 | 96
700 | 12
720 | 3

Chlorophyll a absorption maxima lie near 430 and 680 nm; chlorophyll b contributes near 480 and 650 nm. Photosystem II photochemistry that splits water declines sharply beyond about 680 nm (Emerson red drop), whereas photosystem I can still absorb near 700 nm. Which conclusion follows?

choices.text: O2 evolution tracks chlorophyll absorption and collapses in far-red light even though PSI can still absorb, so water oxidation is tied to PSII.
The 700 nm point being low proves that chlorophyll does not absorb beyond 680 nm at all.
Equal photon flux at 430 and 700 nm must give equal O2 because both wavelengths are visible light.
The 550 nm trough shows that carotenoids are the main O2-evolving pigments.

items.explanation: High O2 at 430 and 680 nm matches chlorophyll a, with secondary peaks at 480 and 650 nm from chlorophyll b. Green-yellow light at 550 nm is poorly absorbed, so O2 is low. The further collapse at 700–720 nm is the red drop: PSI absorbs there but PSII, which oxidises water, does not drive non-cyclic electron flow efficiently. The action spectrum is therefore a chlorophyll-plus-PSII signature, not a statement that chlorophyll has zero absorbance at 700 nm or that all visible wavelengths are equivalent.

distractorRationales.B: PSI chlorophyll does absorb near 700 nm; the low O2 is a photochemical, not an absorption, failure of PSII.
distractorRationales.C: The table shows 100 versus 12 at those two wavelengths, so equal photon flux does not yield equal O2.
distractorRationales.D: Carotenoids absorb in the blue-green, but O2 is lowest at 550 nm and highest at the chlorophyll peaks, so they are not the O2-evolving pigments.

passage.title: Anthropology — the invention of tradition
passage.body:
Many customs that present themselves as immemorial are surprisingly young. The Scottish clan tartan, worn as a badge of ancient lineage, was largely codified in the nineteenth century; the elaborate ceremonial of certain monarchies, apparently the residue of centuries, was substantially devised within living memory of those who first performed it. Historians have given such practices a name: invented traditions — rituals that claim continuity with a distant past to which their actual connection is tenuous or fabricated.

Why manufacture a past? Invented traditions tend to appear, scholars note, at moments of rapid change, when older bonds have frayed and new institutions must secure loyalty quickly. A ritual that feels ancient lends the present an air of inevitability; what looks as though it has always been done is harder to question than what is admittedly new. The invention, in other words, does work: it stabilizes, legitimizes, binds.

It would be easy to draw a cynical moral — that such traditions are frauds, and that exposing their recent origins deflates them. But this conclusion moves too fast. That a practice was invented at a datable moment does not show that it is meaningless to those who observe it. A wedding ritual devised a century ago may bind a community as tightly as one a millennium old; the bonds are real even if the pedigree is not. To confuse the falsity of a tradition's origin story with the falsity of its present function is to misjudge what such traditions are for.

Nor is the category as tidy as it first appears. Few traditions are either wholly ancient or wholly invented; most are refashioned inheritances — old materials put to new use. The nineteenth-century codifiers of tartan did not conjure it from nothing: they systematized and embellished a genuine, if looser, prior practice. "Invented" is thus better read as a matter of degree than as a verdict of pure fabrication.

The value of the concept, then, is not that it unmasks tradition as a lie. It is that it dissolves a false assumption: that the authority of a practice depends on the antiquity of its origins. Once we see how readily a sense of the ancient can be manufactured, we are freed to ask a better question — not how old a tradition is, but what work it does, and for whom.

items.stem: Complete β-oxidation of a saturated odd-chain fatty acid (C17) yields acetyl-CoA plus a three-carbon piece. That piece can support net gluconeogenesis after biotin- and vitamin B12-dependent reactions. Which sequence is correct?

choices.text: Acetyl-CoA is carboxylated to pyruvate in mitochondria and then used for glucose.
The three-carbon piece is acetone, which is transaminated to alanine and then to glucose.
Propionyl-CoA is converted to methylmalonyl-CoA and then to succinyl-CoA, a gluconeogenic citric-acid-cycle intermediate.
Propionyl-CoA is converted to acetoacetate, which is strictly ketogenic and cannot make glucose.

items.explanation: Odd-chain fatty acids leave a terminal propionyl-CoA after the last complete two-carbon cleavage. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin) makes D-methylmalonyl-CoA, which is racemized and then rearranged by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (adenosylcobalamin, vitamin B12) to succinyl-CoA. Succinyl-CoA can proceed to oxaloacetate and, via PEPCK, to net glucose, so odd-chain fat is partially glucogenic. Animals cannot convert acetyl-CoA to pyruvate in net amounts (PDH is irreversible; two carbons enter and two leave the cycle). Acetone is a ketone body from acetoacetate decarboxylation, not the three-carbon acyl leftover of odd-chain β-oxidation, and propionyl-CoA is not converted to acetoacetate as its primary fate.

distractorRationales.A: There is no net conversion of acetyl-CoA to pyruvate in human mitochondria; PDH is irreversible, so even-chain acetyl units are not glucogenic.
distractorRationales.B: The leftover of odd-chain β-oxidation is propionyl-CoA, not acetone. Acetone is not transaminated to alanine as a major gluconeogenic path.
distractorRationales.D: Propionyl-CoA is carboxylated and rearranged to succinyl-CoA, which is glucogenic; it is not routed primarily to acetoacetate.

items.stem: Sulfur tetrafluoride, SF4, has a steric number of 5 at sulfur. What molecular geometry (the arrangement of the four fluorines) does VSEPR predict?
items.explanation: Sulfur in SF4 has four bonding pairs and one lone pair, so five electron domains occupy a trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry. The lone pair occupies an equatorial site to minimize 90° lone-pair–bond-pair repulsions. The four fluorine atoms then occupy the remaining two axial positions and two equatorial positions, which is the seesaw molecular shape. Tetrahedral describes four electron domains, square planar describes XeF4 (four bonds plus two axial lone pairs), and trigonal bipyramidal would be the molecular shape only if there were five bonding pairs and no lone pair, as in PF5.

distractorRationales.A: Tetrahedral molecular geometry requires four electron domains and no extra lone pair, as in CH4 or SiF4, not steric number 5.
distractorRationales.B: Square planar is the molecular geometry of XeF4, which has two lone pairs opposite each other, not SF4’s single lone pair.
distractorRationales.D: Trigonal bipyramidal is the electron-domain geometry of SF4 and the molecular geometry of PF5, but it is not the molecular shape once one equatorial site is a lone pair.

items.stem: Eight minutes remain on a typed Task A. The draft has a clear thesis and a half-built example. Which move best protects clarity under timed typing?

choices.text: Begin a new introduction with a dictionary definition, then hope to loop back.
Finish the example in short independent sentences, add one counterargument sentence and one delimiting close; do not open a third example or a nested clause garden.
Write one 180-word sentence so the piece looks dense.
Stop thinking and hold the shift key to add visual emphasis instead of a close.

items.explanation: Timed typing rewards finishing a thought in readable units. Short independent sentences reduce tangle when there is no leisure to recast. A second example will not be earned. Nested gardens hide the thesis. Dictionary restarts waste the remaining clock. Capitals are not a close. The taxonomy’s point is sentence control without relying on later polish: type the claim, the case, the meeting of an objection, stop. B is that sequence. Markers can follow it; they cannot follow a last-minute syntactic monument. Clarity here is a time skill, not a handwriting skill.

distractorRationales.A: A late dictionary opening doubles the unfinished middle rather than closing it.
distractorRationales.C: A giant sentence is how control is lost when there is no time to edit.
distractorRationales.D: Emphasis without a close is panic, not communication.

passage.title: Study of Notification Cues and Attention
passage.body:
Researchers investigated how smartphone notification cues affect attention and perceived stress. Eighty undergraduate volunteers completed a computerized reaction-time task in three counterbalanced conditions: no notification, a vibration notification, and a visual banner notification. In each condition, participants pressed a key as soon as a target shape appeared. The phone was placed face down for the vibration condition and face up for the visual banner condition. Participants were told that notifications were unrelated to task performance and did not require a response. After each condition, participants rated their momentary stress on a 1 to 7 scale. The researchers also measured whether participants reported checking their phones within 30 seconds after the task.

Mean task performance and stress ratings by notification condition
Condition | Mean reaction time to target (ms) | Error rate (%) | Mean stress rating
No notification | 420 | 4 | 2.1
Vibration notification | 470 | 6 | 3.4
Visual banner notification | 445 | 5 | 2.8

Phone-checking behavior after task
Condition | Percent checking phone within 30 seconds
No notification | 12
Vibration notification | 48
Visual banner notification | 31

Design summary — Each participant completed all three notification conditions in randomized order. The primary dependent variables were reaction time, error rate, stress rating, and post-task phone checking.

items.stem: A uniform electric field of 10 N/C is directed from plate L toward plate R. The plates are 2.0 m apart. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Plate R is at the higher potential, and |ΔV| between the plates is 20 V.
Plate L is at the higher potential, and |ΔV| between the plates is 20 V.
Plate L is at the higher potential, and |ΔV| between the plates is 5 V.
The plates are at equal potential because a uniform field means potential does not change with position.

items.explanation: By definition E points from higher electric potential toward lower potential, so plate L (where the field originates in this description) is at the higher V. In a uniform field the magnitude of the potential difference is |ΔV| = E d = (10 N/C)(2.0 m) = 20 V. A uniform field means E is constant, not that V is constant: V still drops linearly along the field. Dividing E by d instead of multiplying inverts the relation between field and potential difference.

distractorRationales.A: The field direction is high V to low V, so L, not R, is the high-potential plate. The 20 V magnitude is right but assigned to the wrong plate.
distractorRationales.C: L is the high-potential plate, but |ΔV| = E d = 20 V, not E/d = 5 V. Field is potential drop per meter, so you multiply by the 2 m gap.
distractorRationales.D: A uniform field is a constant slope of V versus position, not a flat potential. Only E = 0 would make the plates equipotential.

passage.title: Pentose phosphate pathway flux during oxidative stress
passage.body:
A fictional erythroid cell line lacks mitochondria after differentiation and relies on glycolysis for ATP. It also uses the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) to generate NADPH for reduction of glutathione. Researchers compared wild-type cells with cells expressing a mutant glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD-M). They exposed cells to an oxidant and measured redox status, lactate release, and radiolabeled carbon dioxide production from glucose labeled at carbon 1 or carbon 6. In the oxidative PPP, carbon 1 of glucose 6-phosphate is released as CO2 while NADPH is produced.

Metabolic responses to oxidant exposure.
Cells and condition | NADPH/NADP+ | GSH/GSSG | Lactate release (%) | 14CO2 from [1-14C]glucose (%) | 14CO2 from [6-14C]glucose (%) | Viable cells (%)
Wild type, basal | 4.0 | 8.0 | 100 | 100 | 5 | 98
Wild type, +oxidant | 2.0 | 4.5 | 120 | 180 | 8 | 92
G6PD-M, basal | 1.5 | 3.0 | 110 | 35 | 5 | 95
G6PD-M, +oxidant | 0.4 | 0.8 | 145 | 40 | 7 | 55

Purified G6PD kinetic parameters.
Enzyme | Km for glucose 6-phosphate (mM) | Relative Vmax (%)
Wild-type G6PD | 0.08 | 100
G6PD-M | 0.09 | 30

Relationship between glycolysis and the oxidative PPP. — Glucose 6-phosphate can enter glycolysis or the oxidative PPP. The oxidative PPP produces NADPH and ribulose 5-phosphate, releasing carbon 1 as CO2. Glycolysis in these differentiated erythroid cells ends mainly in lactate formation.

passage.body:
A behavioral science lab used a virtual environment to study how neutral sounds can acquire emotional significance. During acquisition, participants repeatedly heard Tone A immediately before an unpleasant but safe burst of white noise. Tone B was presented equally often but was never followed by the white noise. In a final test, participants heard Tone C, which was acoustically similar to Tone A but slightly lower in pitch.

Mean skin conductance response in arbitrary units
Phase and stimulus | Mean response
Late acquisition: Tone A | 0.78
Late acquisition: Tone B | 0.22
Late extinction: Tone A | 0.31
Late extinction: Tone B | 0.20
Final test: Tone C | 0.49

Stimulus arrangement — Tone A and Tone C were similar in pitch, whereas Tone B was clearly distinct from both.

passage.title: psg-bb-4
passage.body:
In a classic-style linkage experiment, geneticists studied two genes in a fruit fly stock: one affecting body color (B = gray, dominant; b = black) and one affecting wing shape (V = normal, dominant; v = vestigial). The two genes reside on the same chromosome. Females heterozygous for both genes, with both dominant alleles on one homolog and both recessive alleles on the other (arrangement B V / b v), were testcrossed to males that were homozygous recessive (b v / b v). Because the testcross father contributes only b and v alleles, each offspring's phenotype directly reveals which allele combination it received from the mother.
Among 1,000 offspring, the researchers counted four phenotypic classes: 425 gray, normal-winged; 415 black, vestigial-winged; 82 gray, vestigial-winged; and 78 black, normal-winged. The first two classes matched the parental (non-recombinant) allele combinations, whereas the last two classes represented new combinations that could only arise if the maternal homologs exchanged segments.
The team used the frequency of these new-combination offspring to estimate how far apart the two genes lie, applying the rule that one map unit (centimorgan) corresponds to a 1 percent recombination frequency. They noted that if the two genes had been on different chromosomes, or extremely far apart on the same one, the four classes would instead have appeared in roughly equal numbers.

items.stem:
A 4000 bp plasmid has a single EcoRI site. A 1000 bp EcoRI fragment is ligated into that site. After ligation, DNA is linearised with EcoRI (complete digestion) and run on a gel.

Sample | observed band(s)
Uncut parental plasmid | fast supercoiled band (apparent ~2500 bp)
Parental plasmid + EcoRI | 4000 bp
Ligation + EcoRI | 4000 bp and 1000 bp
Self-ligated parental recircularised + EcoRI | 4000 bp only

Which conclusion is supported?

choices.text: EcoRI linearisation of recombinants must give a single 5000 bp band because the insert lacks EcoRI ends
A 1000 bp band proves contamination with genomic DNA of that length rather than insert release
Successful recombinants release the 1000 bp insert plus the 4000 bp backbone; empty recircularised plasmid yields only 4000 bp
The uncut apparent 2500 bp band is the true recombinant size (4000 + 1000 − 2500)

items.explanation: Cloning into a unique EcoRI site recreates EcoRI sites at both insert–vector junctions. Complete EcoRI digestion of a recombinant therefore cuts out the 1000 bp insert and leaves the 4000 bp vector, two bands. An empty plasmid cut at its one EcoRI site is a 4000 bp line. Supercoiled uncut DNA migrates anomalously fast (~2500 apparent), which is not a true size and not 4000+1000−2500 arithmetic. The insert was defined as an EcoRI fragment, so it does have EcoRI ends; a 5000 bp linear would appear only if a different enzyme that cuts once in the recombinant were used.

distractorRationales.A: EcoRI ends on the insert restore two EcoRI sites, so the recombinant should fall into 4000 + 1000, not remain 5000.
distractorRationales.B: The 1000 bp band matches the insert length used in the ligation; genomic contamination would not be a single clean 1000 bp species correlated with the ligation lane.
distractorRationales.D: Supercoiled mobility is not a reliable base-pair measure; 2500 is an apparent, not physical, size.

items.stem: An aircraft flies horizontally at 80 m s−1 at a height of 45 m and releases a supply crate. g = 10 m s−2; air resistance is neglected. The crate’s initial vertical velocity is 0. Time to the ground is found from h = (1/2) g t². Horizontal velocity remains 80 m s−1. How far down-range does the crate land, and what is its vertical speed on impact?

choices.text: 45 m down-range; vertical speed 0, because it was released not thrown
240 m down-range; vertical speed 30 m s−1
80 m down-range; vertical speed 45 m s−1
240 m down-range; vertical speed 80 m s−1

items.explanation: From 45 = 5 t², t² = 9, t = 3.0 s. Horizontal distance = 80 × 3.0 = 240 m. Vertical speed vy = g t = 30 m s−1. The horizontal speed is unchanged at 80 m s−1, but that is not the vertical component. Using t = 1 s (as if s = vt with v = 45) gives only 80 m of range. A dropped object still accelerates vertically; impact vertical speed is not zero. Independence of perpendicular components is the whole point of the calculation.

distractorRationales.A: Release with uy = 0 still allows free-fall acceleration; after 3 s, vy = 30 m s−1, and the crate has travelled 240 m horizontally.
distractorRationales.C: 80 m would be the range for a 1.0 s fall; t is 3.0 s from h = 5 t². Vertical speed is gt, not the height number 45.
distractorRationales.D: The range 240 m is right, but 80 m s−1 is the unchanged horizontal speed, not vy.

items.stem: In an oxygen-electrode experiment, mitochondria oxidizing NADH-linked substrates consume O2 rapidly after ADP is added. Oligomycin then arrests O2 consumption. Adding DNP restores O2 consumption without restoring ATP synthesis. Which explanation is consistent with these data?

choices.text: Oligomycin inhibits Complex IV; DNP chemically reduces oxygen, bypassing the chain.
Oligomycin blocks proton flow through ATP synthase, stalling the chain; DNP lets protons re-enter without ATP synthase, restarting electron flow while synthase remains inhibited.
DNP reverses oligomycin binding at the F1 catalytic sites, fully restoring coupled phosphorylation.
Oligomycin uncouples the membrane, and DNP subsequently blocks ATP synthase.

items.explanation: Oligomycin binds the F0 proton channel of ATP synthase, so protons cannot re-enter the matrix through the synthase. The proton-motive force rises until electron transport is thermodynamically stalled and O2 consumption stops, even though Complex IV is intact. DNP provides an alternate proton re-entry path, collapsing the gradient and allowing the respiratory chain to run again, which restores oxygen uptake. ATP synthase remains blocked, so ATP is not restored. That pattern distinguishes ATP-synthase inhibition from Complex IV poisons such as cyanide, which DNP cannot rescue, and from true uncoupling as the primary action of oligomycin.

distractorRationales.A: Oligomycin’s target is ATP synthase, not Complex IV. DNP is a protonophore, not a chemical reductant of O2 that bypasses cytochrome oxidase.
distractorRationales.C: DNP does not competitively displace oligomycin from F1 to restore coupled ATP synthesis; phosphorylation remains inhibited in the experiment.
distractorRationales.D: This choice reverses the two drugs’ mechanisms: oligomycin is the ATP-synthase blocker and DNP is the uncoupler.

items.stem: Moving left to right across a period (row) of the periodic table, atomic radius generally:

choices.text: Decreases, because increasing nuclear charge pulls the same electron shell in more tightly.

items.explanation: Across a period, electrons are added to the same outer shell while protons (and thus positive nuclear charge) also increase. The stronger pull draws the electron cloud in closer, shrinking atomic radius. Across a period: more protons pull the same shell in tighter -> radius shrinks, ionisation energy rises. Down a group: an extra electron shell is added each row, with inner electrons shielding the pull -> radius grows, ionisation energy falls. Learn the "why" (charge vs shielding) rather than memorising each trend separately. Memory tip: Picture the nucleus in a tug of war with its electrons: across a period, more protons pull the SAME shell in tighter (radius shrinks); down a group, a whole new outer shell is added each row, further from the pull (radius grows). Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

items.stem: A reverse-phase C18 HPLC column is equilibrated in 95:5 water/acetonitrile and then eluted with a gradient of increasing acetonitrile. Two peptides are injected: KKKKK (all lysine) and FFFFF (all phenylalanine). Which elution order is expected, and why?

choices.text: FFFFF first, because reverse-phase stationary phases retain polar solutes more strongly than nonpolar ones
KKKKK first, because the hydrophobic C18 phase retains the aromatic peptide while the highly charged oligolysine prefers the aqueous mobile phase
They coelute, because HPLC cannot distinguish peptides of equal residue count
KKKKK first, because C18 silica is a cation-exchange resin that binds lysine and therefore must be eluted last

items.explanation: Reverse-phase chromatography uses a nonpolar stationary phase (typically C18-bonded silica) and a polar aqueous mobile phase. Hydrophobic solutes partition into the alkyl chains and require more organic modifier to elute. Penta-phenylalanine is aromatic and poorly hydrated, so it is retained. Penta-lysine is polycationic and highly water-soluble at acidic or near-neutral pH, so it spends little time on C18 and emerges early in a water-rich gradient. Residue count alone does not set retention. C18 is not an ion-exchange resin; sulfonated or carboxylate resins are.

distractorRationales.A: That statement describes normal-phase (polar) chromatography. Reverse-phase retains hydrophobics, not polars.
distractorRationales.C: Equal length does not imply equal hydrophobicity; lysine and phenylalanine side chains interact very differently with C18.
distractorRationales.D: C18 is a hydrophobic bonded phase, not a cation exchanger. Oligolysine elutes first because it is polar, not because it is ionically stuck.

items.stem: An atom has the ground-state valence configuration 4s^2 4p^5. This element is best classified as:
items.explanation: Valence 4s^2 4p^5 means seven valence electrons in period 4, which is the halogen configuration (group 17); the element is bromine. Alkaline earth metals are ns^2 only (here that would be 4s^2 with an empty 4p). Noble gases are ns^2 np^6 (4s^2 4p^6 would be krypton). Transition metals place electrons in (n−1)d subshells; a configuration quoted as 4s^2 4p^5 is p-block, not d-block. Group number for the p-block follows the valence count: 5 + 2 = 7 valence electrons → group 17.

distractorRationales.B: Alkaline earth atoms are ns^2 (two valence electrons), for example 4s^2 for calcium. The additional 4p^5 puts this atom in the p-block halogens.
distractorRationales.C: Noble gases have filled np^6. This configuration is one electron short of 4p^6, which is exactly the halogen pattern.
distractorRationales.D: Transition metals are d-block (incomplete (n−1)d). A 4p^5 count is a main-group p-block element, not a transition metal.

items.stem: The combination of a giant sat-upon stethoscope and a politely typeset postponement is best described as

choices.text: sincere instructional design for new clinic staff.
tragic realism without irony, because cash registers commonly appear in waiting rooms as medical equipment.
satire that uses understatement in the caption and grotesque scale in the image to evaluate whose hearing counts.
affectionate celebration of boards who multitask by listening to receipts.

items.explanation: Satire and understatement: the caption's we'll-call-you is the mild public language of triage; the image is not mild. Grotesque scale (ticket as door, patients as dotted outlines, earpieces on BOARD) evaluates without a ranting label. The tone is not a training poster, not a documentary claim that tills are auscultation devices, and not affection. Non-literal evaluative language is the polite sentence doing the work of a knife. Recognising that pairing is the skill the item tags.

distractorRationales.A: Nothing in the described frame instructs staff in a sincere protocol; the dotted patients and till make mockery, not a handbook.
distractorRationales.B: A cash register as the thing being listened to is ironic substitution, not unironic realism.
distractorRationales.D: Listening to a till while patients remain unfinished is the critique, not a compliment for multitasking.

passage.title: When your number becomes a priority
passage.body:
[Image]
A waiting-room drawn as a long, low shed. The bench is actually the tubing of a giant stethoscope, coiled so that patients must sit on the instrument that is supposed to listen to them. Two figures in dark suits, labelled BOARD, wear the earpieces. They are not facing the patients. They lean together toward a cash register whose receipt paper unspools across the floor like a white carpet. The patients are drawn in broken dotted lines, as if they were still being sketched. One solid figure is a child holding a numbered ticket as tall as a door. The ticket number is 1847. A clock on the wall has no hands.

[Caption, in a polite typeface beneath the frame]
"We'll call you when your number becomes a priority."

items.stem: The Ksp of CaF2 is 4.0 × 10^−11 at 25 °C. Solid CaF2 is stirred with 0.020 M NaF until equilibrium is reached (volume change from the solid is negligible). What is the equilibrium [Ca2+]?

choices.text: 2.2 × 10^−4 M, from 4s^3 = Ksp as if the solid dissolved in pure water

items.explanation: Calcium fluoride dissolves as CaF2(s) ⇌ Ca2+ + 2 F−, so Ksp equals [Ca2+][F−]^2. The 0.020 M fluoride supplied by NaF dwarfs the fluoride that comes from dissolving the salt, so [F−] remains 0.020 M. The dissolved calcium concentration is therefore the molar solubility: [Ca2+] = Ksp / (0.020)^2 = 4.0 × 10^−11 / 4.0 × 10^−4 = 1.0 × 10^−7 M. The pure-water 4s^3 expression ignores the common ion. Taking a square root treats CaF2 as a 1:1 salt. Dividing by [F−] only once uses the wrong stoichiometric exponent.

distractorRationales.A: 4s^3 = Ksp is the mass-action expression in pure water. Added NaF fixes [F−] near 0.020 M, so that cubic relation no longer applies.
distractorRationales.C: Ksp = [Ca2+][F−]^2, not [Ca2+][F−]. Using a single power of fluoride undercounts the common-ion suppression.
distractorRationales.D: √Ksp would be the solubility of an MX salt. CaF2 releases two fluoride ions per formula unit, and the common ion further changes the algebra.

choices.text: children who play with oversized stationery in clinics.
a governing board that uses the listening tool of medicine while actually attending to revenue, leaving patients unfinished and untimed.
the invention of the stethoscope as a nineteenth-century error.

items.explanation: Political-cartoon reading: the board wears the earpieces of a giant stethoscope but leans toward a cash register; patients are dotted, not fully drawn; the clock has no hands; the child's ticket is 1847. The satire is institutional misdirection of attention, not an attack on children, on auscultation as such, or on furniture design. Symbolism (instrument of listening, unfinished people, frozen time) and the labelled BOARD fix the target. Without the image's arrangement, a caption about priorities could mean several things; the drawing specifies whose ears and whose receipts.
