passage.title: psg-cars-4
passage.body:
History is not the past itself but a selective reconstruction of the past, assembled from fragmentary evidence by scholars whose questions, categories, and assumptions are inevitably shaped by their own time and place. This observation, often associated with the philosophy of history that emerged in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, does not reduce historical writing to fiction. Yet it does demand that historians acknowledge their craft as an interpretive one rather than a neutral transcription of what happened.
The most influential historians have always made choices: choices about which events to emphasize, which actors to foreground, and which causal chains to trace. A military historian who concentrates on battles and generals produces a different account of the same period than a social historian who foregrounds the lives of ordinary laborers, or an economic historian who treats fluctuations in grain prices as the deeper explanatory variable. None of these accounts is simply wrong; each illuminates a dimension of a complex past while necessarily leaving other dimensions in shadow.
Critics of this pluralism worry that it licenses an anything-goes relativism in which no historical account is better than any other. Defenders respond that recognizing the constructed character of historical narratives is compatible with rigorous standards of evidence, logical consistency, and fidelity to the archival record. An interpretation can be shown to be false if it contradicts well-authenticated documents, or shown to be weak if it ignores a large body of relevant evidence. The standards are not arbitrary, even if the questions that animate historical inquiry are themselves products of particular intellectual climates.
A further complication arises from the role of the historical archive itself. Archives are not neutral repositories of the past; they are collections shaped by decisions about what to preserve, who had the resources to produce written records, and which categories of information administrative systems deemed worth tracking. Consequently, the voices most abundantly represented in archives tend to be those of literate elites, state bureaucracies, and dominant institutions, while the experiences of the illiterate, the dispossessed, and the colonized are filtered through the records of those who observed or administered them from a position of power.
Contemporary historians have developed a range of techniques to recover marginalized perspectives: reading documents 'against the grain' of their intended purpose, triangulating between different types of sources, and drawing on oral traditions and material culture as complementary evidence. These methods have expanded the scope of historical knowledge considerably, even as they have deepened awareness that the gap between the past and the historian's account of it can never be fully closed.
None of this counsels despair about historical knowledge. The recognition that every history is written from somewhere, on the basis of imperfect and unevenly preserved traces, is better understood as a discipline than as a defeat. It obliges the historian to state her guiding questions openly, to weigh the silences of the record as carefully as its assertions, and to hold her conclusions as revisable in the light of new evidence or sharper questions. Readers, for their part, are invited to judge a historical account not by whether it achieves an impossible neutrality but by the range of evidence it engages, the rival explanations it takes seriously, and the candor with which it marks the limits of what it cannot know.

items.stem: Terminal alkyne C–H bonds (as in acetylene) are substantially more acidic than alkene or alkane C–H bonds. Which orbital argument best accounts for the lower pKa of the alkyne hydrogen?

choices.text: The conjugate-base lone pair of an acetylide sits in an sp orbital, which has 50% s-character and holds electron density closer to the nucleus than sp2 or sp3 orbitals.
Alkyne carbons are sp3 hybridized, so they have weaker bonds and lose hydrogen more easily.
Acetylene has London dispersion forces that stabilize the acetylide anion in water.
The alkyne hydrogen is more acidic because the C≡C bond is longer than a C–C single bond, so the H is farther from carbon.

items.explanation: Acidity of a C–H bond tracks stability of the conjugate-base anion. In an acetylide the lone pair occupies an sp hybrid (50% s-character). Greater s-character concentrates that pair closer to the carbon nucleus, lowering the energy of the anion relative to an sp2 vinyl anion (~33% s) or an sp3 alkyl anion (25% s). That is why typical pKa values run roughly 25 (alkyne), 44 (alkene), and 50 (alkane). The alkyne carbon is sp, not sp3; the C≡C bond is shorter, not longer, than a single bond; and dispersion forces do not explain the hybridization trend.

distractorRationales.B: Alkyne carbons of a terminal C–H are sp, not sp3. An sp3 description would predict the opposite acidity ranking.
distractorRationales.C: London forces are weak intermolecular attractions among neutral molecules; they do not stabilize a specific conjugate-base orbital.
distractorRationales.D: A C≡C triple bond is shorter than a C–C single bond. Bond length is not the reason the alkyne proton is more acidic.

items.stem: Cultured fibroblasts are treated with a membrane-permeable analog of latrunculin that binds G-actin with nanomolar affinity and drops free monomer below the critical concentration for barbed-end assembly. Fifteen minutes later, which structure is expected to disassemble first?

choices.text: Nuclear lamina, because lamins are actin polymers that treadmill rapidly
Keratin tonofilaments, because intermediate filaments require a high G-actin pool
Stress fibers and the cortical actin meshwork, which are F-actin arrays in equilibrium with G-actin
Centrioles, because the nine triplet blades are unstabilized actin bundles

items.explanation: Latrunculin-like ligands sequester G-actin so the monomer concentration falls below the critical concentration. Filamentous actin therefore net-depolymerizes, collapsing stress fibers, lamellipodia, and cortical F-actin within minutes. Intermediate filaments (lamins, keratins) are nonpolar coiled-coil polymers of unrelated subunits and do not require an actin monomer pool. Centrioles are highly stable microtubule-based organelles. The kinetic selectivity of the drug therefore reports which cytoskeletal polymer is actin, not which structure looks fibrous by light microscopy.

distractorRationales.A: Nuclear lamins are intermediate filaments, not actin polymers, so sequestering G-actin does not dismantle the lamina on this timescale.
distractorRationales.B: Keratin filaments are intermediate filaments assembled from keratin subunits; they are not in rapid equilibrium with G-actin.
distractorRationales.D: Centrioles are microtubule triplets plus accessory proteins, not actin bundles, and they are unusually stable.

passage.title: Note on a cancelled tram
passage.body:
In the third week of the lockout the company ran a single tram, brightly lit, along the route at dusk, with no passengers permitted. Officials called it a demonstration of service. Strikers called it a lantern on a coffin. Children ran beside it anyway, as they had when the cars were working, and were photographed. The photograph was printed in the morning paper under the heading NORMALITY RETURNS, and in an overseas paper under the heading CHILDREN MOCK THE DEAD LINE.

A clerk in the tram office, years later, wrote that he had been told to leave the lights on even if the generator complained, because darkness would look like surrender. He added, without apparent bitterness, that surrender had already occurred in the timetable. What remained was a moving argument about who owned the look of a street at evening.

Historians still disagree whether the empty tram lengthened the dispute by humiliating the men or shortened it by frightening the board with the cost of theatre. The clerk’s sentence is more useful than either camp: the fight had become, for a night, a question of illumination.

items.stem: A horizontal artery widens into an aneurysm whose cross-sectional area is twice that of the adjacent vessel. For steady incompressible flow at constant height, the pressure inside the dilated segment is:

choices.text: lower than adjacent pressure because speed is higher there
higher than adjacent pressure because speed is lower there
higher than adjacent pressure because speed is higher there
equal to adjacent pressure because the vessel is still horizontal

items.explanation: Continuity forces speed to fall where area rises, so the aneurysm is a slow region. Bernoulli's relation at constant gravitational height then requires hydrostatic pressure to rise where dynamic pressure 1/2 rho v squared falls. The elevated transmural pressure, together with Laplace's law for wall tension, is why a dilation can progress. Equal height alone does not equalize pressure if speeds differ along the streamline.

distractorRationales.A: Speed is lower, not higher, in the wider segment. A fast, low-pressure region describes a stenosis, the opposite geometry.
distractorRationales.C: This pairs the correct pressure change with the wrong speed change. Higher speed would lower pressure, not raise it.
distractorRationales.D: Horizontal flow removes the rho g h term from the comparison but does not cancel the 1/2 rho v^2 term. Pressure still tracks speed.

distractorRationales.C: Spontaneity depends on temperature in this case.
distractorRationales.D: It becomes spontaneous once T is high enough.

items.stem: A researcher titrates free histidine (pKa values: α-carboxyl 1.8, imidazole 6.0, α-ammonium 9.2) and asks at which pH the amino acid has a time-averaged net charge closest to zero. Which pH should be chosen for an isoelectric precipitation trial?
items.explanation: Fully protonated histidine carries a net charge of +2 (carboxylic acid, imidazolium, and ammonium). Loss of the carboxyl proton (pKa 1.8) yields net +1; loss of the imidazole proton (pKa 6.0) yields the zwitterion of net charge 0; loss of the ammonium proton (pKa 9.2) yields net −1. The isoelectric point of a basic amino acid is the average of the two pKa values that bound the net-zero form, here (6.0 + 9.2)/2 = 7.6. Averaging the two lowest pKa values is the rule for acidic residues such as aspartate, not for histidine, and the pI is not equal to a single pKa.

distractorRationales.A: Averaging the two lowest pKa values gives the pI of acidic amino acids (Asp, Glu), not of histidine.
distractorRationales.B: Averaging the α-carboxyl and α-ammonium pKa values is the rule for amino acids with uncharged side chains.
distractorRationales.D: At the α-ammonium pKa the side chain is already deprotonated, so the net charge is negative, not zero.

items.stem: A proliferating culture is treated with a microtubule-depolymerizing drug. Flow cytometry shows a 4C DNA peak. Live imaging shows condensed chromosomes and a disassembled nuclear envelope that persist for hours. The cells are arrested primarily in:

choices.text: G1, when unreplicated 2C nuclei wait for mitogen
Early S phase, when DNA content is still near 2C
Mitosis, because the spindle assembly checkpoint blocks anaphase until kinetochores attach to microtubules
Cytokinesis of a haploid cell, which has 1C DNA

items.explanation: After S phase, G2 and mitotic cells both have 4C DNA, so DNA content alone cannot separate them. Condensed chromosomes and nuclear-envelope breakdown are mitotic hallmarks. Without microtubules, kinetochores cannot attach, the spindle assembly checkpoint remains active, separase stays inhibited, and cells arrest in prometaphase with 4C genomes. G1 is 2C with an intact nucleus, early S is between 2C and 4C, and haploid cytokinesis is not the state of these somatic cells. Microtubule poisons used in karyotyping exploit this SAC arrest.

distractorRationales.A: G1 cells are 2C with decondensed chromatin and an intact nucleus.
distractorRationales.B: Early S is not a 4C condensed-chromosome arrest.
distractorRationales.D: These are 4C mitotic somatic cells, not 1C haploids completing cytokinesis.

passage.title: Vesicle swelling under osmotic load
passage.body:
A student prepares identical phospholipid vesicles in 300 mOsmol kg−1 sucrose, then dilutes them at t = 0 into the media below. Vesicle volume is inferred from light scatter (larger vesicles scatter less in this geometry). Temperature 25 °C. n = 6 aliquots; scatter reported as mean ± s.d. arbitrary units (higher = smaller vesicles).

Medium after dilution | 10 s | 60 s | 300 s
A: 300 mOsmol sucrose (control) | 1.00 ± 0.02 | 0.99 ± 0.03 | 1.01 ± 0.02
B: 150 mOsmol sucrose | 0.71 ± 0.04 | 0.52 ± 0.05 | 0.48 ± 0.06
C: 150 mOsmol sucrose + 0.1 mM HgCl2 (water-channel blocker in this model) | 0.92 ± 0.03 | 0.80 ± 0.04 | 0.61 ± 0.05
D: 150 mOsmol sucrose + aquaporin proteoliposomes fused at 5 mol% | 0.40 ± 0.06 | 0.33 ± 0.05 | 0.34 ± 0.04

A second table lists initial rates estimated from 0–10 s, treating scatter drop as swelling:

Condition | Δscatter / 10 s
A | ~0
B | −0.029
C | −0.008
D | −0.060

The student claims: “Swelling requires a hypotonic bath, is slowed when water pores are blocked, and is accelerated when extra water pores are added, so the membrane’s phospholipid bilayer is not the main path in B–D.”

passage.title: Multisensory Influences on Beverage Perception
passage.body:
A behavioral neuroscience lab examined whether ambient odors influence taste judgments. Seventy-two adults sampled the same unsweetened citrus beverage in three counterbalanced conditions: no ambient scent, a congruent lemon scent, and an incongruent coffee scent. Participants were not told that the scent condition changed across trials. After each sample, they rated perceived sweetness, perceived sourness, and purchase intention on 1 to 7 scales. In a separate adaptation task, participants detected faint lemon odors before and after continuous exposure to a moderate lemon scent for 3 minutes.

Mean ratings for identical beverage across ambient scent conditions
Condition | Perceived sweetness | Perceived sourness | Purchase intention
No ambient scent | 3.1 | 4.8 | 3.2
Congruent lemon scent | 4.2 | 4.5 | 4.5
Incongruent coffee scent | 2.7 | 5.0 | 2.8

Odor detection threshold in arbitrary concentration units
Time point | Mean lemon odor detection threshold
Before continuous odor exposure | 2.0
Immediately after 3 minutes of exposure | 6.0
Ten minutes after exposure ended | 3.0

Study design — Each participant experienced all beverage scent conditions in randomized order. The adaptation task was completed after the beverage ratings and used a detection threshold procedure for lemon odor.

passage.title: psg-cp-3
passage.body:
Students build and analyze a galvanic (voltaic) cell and then use batteries to study simple circuits. In the cell, a strip of zinc metal sits in zinc sulfate solution and a strip of copper metal sits in copper sulfate solution; a salt bridge connects the two half-cells, and a wire with a voltmeter links the metal strips. Under standard conditions the tabulated reduction potentials are Zn^2+ + 2 e- -> Zn, E = -0.76 V, and Cu^2+ + 2 e- -> Cu, E = +0.34 V. When the wire is connected, one electrode gains mass while the other slowly dissolves, and the voltmeter registers a steady potential difference. The students confirm which metal is oxidized by weighing the electrodes before and after.
They then replace the standard 1 M solutions with more dilute ones and record how the measured cell voltage shifts away from its standard value, relating the change to the reaction quotient Q for Zn + Cu^2+ -> Zn^2+ + Cu.
In the circuit module, a 12 V battery is connected to three resistors: a 6 ohm and a 3 ohm resistor wired in parallel with each other, and that combination wired in series with a 4 ohm resistor. An ammeter reads the current leaving the battery. The students compute the equivalent resistance, the current, and the power the battery delivers, treating the battery as an ideal source with negligible internal resistance and the wires as resistanceless.

items.stem:
Resistance is computed from R = V / I. Independent absolute uncertainties add in quadrature or, as a standard school-level rule used here, relative uncertainties add: δR/R = δV/V + δI/I.

Reading | Value | Absolute uncertainty | Relative uncertainty
V | 12.0 V | 0.3 V | 0.3/12.0 = 2.5%
I | 2.00 A | 0.10 A | 0.10/2.00 = 5.0%

What should be reported for R?

choices.text: 6.00 ± 0.15 Ω, using only the 2.5% voltage uncertainty.
6.00 ± 0.30 Ω, using only the 5.0% current uncertainty.
6.00 ± 0.75 Ω, multiplying the percentages (2.5% × 5.0% is not the combination rule).

items.explanation: R = 12.0 / 2.00 = 6.00 Ω. Adding the given relative uncertainties produces 2.5% + 5.0% = 7.5%. Then δR = 0.075 × 6.00 = 0.45 Ω, so R = 6.00 ± 0.45 Ω. Using only one of the two contributions underestimates the uncertainty. Multiplying 2.5% by 5.0% gives 0.125%, or if the percentages are multiplied as 12.5% one gets 0.75 Ω; neither is the sum rule stated in the stem. Adding the absolute 0.3 V and 0.10 A would mix volts with amperes and is not how a quotient is combined. The current’s 5% dominates, but the voltage’s 2.5% is still required in the sum.

distractorRationales.A: 2.5% of 6.00 Ω is 0.15 Ω, which ignores the larger current uncertainty. Both relative errors must be added for a quotient.
distractorRationales.B: 5.0% of 6.00 Ω is 0.30 Ω, which ignores the voltage uncertainty. The stem’s rule adds both relative contributions.
distractorRationales.D: 0.75 Ω corresponds to 12.5%, as if the percentages were multiplied. The stated rule is to add 2.5% and 5.0%.

items.stem: When percent-correct detections are plotted against stimulus intensity, the result is an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve rather than a sharp step. This shape reflects that:

choices.text: Detection is probabilistic — near threshold, the same faint stimulus is sometimes detected and sometimes missed

Stronger stimuli are detected less often
Detection is impossible below the threshold and certain above it

items.explanation: Near the threshold, a faint stimulus is detected on some trials and missed on others (and it varies across people), so detection rises gradually with intensity — an S-curve. The threshold is defined at the 50%-detection point. Takeaway: Detection near threshold is probabilistic → a sigmoidal curve. The threshold is the 50% point, not a hard cutoff. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Trial-to-trial and person-to-person variability makes detection gradual, not all-or-nothing. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.B: A fixed value would give a sharp step, not an S-curve.
distractorRationales.C: Stronger stimuli are detected more often — the curve rises.
distractorRationales.D: A true step function (impossible below, certain above) is exactly what the gradual S-curve contradicts.

choices.text: Lipid solubility (log P) dominates: testosterone is fastest despite the largest MW.
The smallest molar mass always wins, so urea (MW 60) should exceed testosterone.
Glucose is fastest because cells need sugar, and 0.05 is the largest influx.
Charge determines the order; all four solutes must be anions because they cross at all.

items.explanation: Simple diffusion through a bilayer favours hydrophobic solutes. Testosterone’s log P of +3.3 and flux 42 dwarf urea (log P −2.1, flux 0.4) and glucose (log P −3.0, flux 0.05) even though testosterone is the heaviest (MW 288). Ethanol is intermediate (log P −0.3, flux 18). Molecular weight still matters for a given polarity, but in this set polarity outranks size. Need for a metabolite is irrelevant in a protein-free bilayer, and none of the tabulated solutes is an anion.

distractorRationales.B: Urea’s influx is 0.4 versus testosterone’s 42, so smallest MW does not win here.
distractorRationales.C: Glucose has the smallest influx (0.05), not the largest, and a protein-free bilayer has no glucose carriers.
distractorRationales.D: The table gives no charges; urea, ethanol, glucose, and testosterone are not anions, yet they still show very different fluxes.

passage.title: Stress Appraisal and Working Memory During Social Evaluation
passage.body:
Researchers studied how appraisal framing affects stress responses during a brief social-evaluation task. Ninety-six adults were randomly assigned to one of three groups. In the private-reading group, participants read a neutral passage alone. In the evaluative-threat group, participants gave a short speech while being observed and were told that poor performance would indicate weak communication ability. In the evaluative-challenge group, participants gave the same speech while being observed but were told that increased arousal could help them perform effectively. Participants completed a working-memory task afterward and provided saliva samples before and after the task.

Mean outcomes by task condition
Condition | Perceived control, 1 to 7 | Heart rate increase, beats/min | Salivary cortisol increase, nmol/L | Working-memory accuracy (%)
Private reading | 5.8 | 4 | 0.7 | 86
Evaluative threat | 2.7 | 18 | 4.6 | 71
Evaluative challenge | 4.9 | 16 | 2.6 | 79

Appraisal framing — The evaluative-threat and evaluative-challenge groups completed the same speech task; only the framing statement before the task differed.

items.stem:
Glycine (pI 6.0) and lysine (pI 9.7) are spotted at the origin of an electrophoresis strip buffered at pH 6.0. A species with pI < pH is net negative and migrates to the anode; pI > pH is net positive and migrates to the cathode; pI = pH does not migrate. After 20 min the strip is:

Position (towards cathode +) | spot
+ 4 cm | one ninhydrin-positive spot
0 cm (origin) | one spot
− 4 cm | none

Which assignment is consistent?

choices.text: Both amino acids are at the origin because they are zwitterions in the solid state
Lysine is at −4 cm because pI 9.7 is larger, so it must be negative
Glycine migrates to the cathode at its isoelectric pH
The origin is glycine (net zero at pH = pI); the cathodic spot is lysine (net positive at pH 6.0 < 9.7)

items.explanation: At pH 6.0 glycine is at its pI, so its net charge is zero and it stays at the origin. Lysine’s pI is 9.7, so at pH 6 both its carboxylates and its extra side-chain ammonium are such that the net charge is positive; it moves toward the cathode (+4 cm). There is no anodic spot, matching the absence of a net-negative species. Solid-state zwitterions still acquire a net charge in a pH 6 buffer if pI ≠ 6. A higher pI means more basic, hence cationic at pH 6, not anionic. Migration of glycine at its pI would contradict the definition of pI.

distractorRationales.A: The strip shows a second spot at +4 cm, so they do not both remain at the origin.
distractorRationales.B: pI > pH produces a cation, which moves to the cathode, the +4 cm position, not the anode.
distractorRationales.C: At pH = pI the net charge is zero; glycine is the origin spot.

passage.title: Adult Education Centers and Health Information Navigation
passage.body:
A community research team evaluated a short workshop designed to improve adults' ability to interpret online health information. The workshop taught participants how to identify source credibility, distinguish testimonials from population-level evidence, and compare numerical risks. Participants attended one of three adult education centers located in districts that differed in occupational composition and average household income. Workshop attendance was optional, so participants were not randomly assigned to attend. All participants completed a health-information comprehension test at baseline and four weeks later.

Mean health-information comprehension scores out of 100
Center district | Baseline score | Four-week score among nonattendees | Four-week score among workshop attendees | Households with reliable broadband (%) | Mean schedule predictability, 1 to 7
Working-class district | 58 | 60 | 72 | 62 | 2.1
Mixed-income district | 64 | 65 | 75 | 78 | 3.5
Professional-class district | 75 | 76 | 82 | 94 | 5.4

Resource context — The researchers proposed that broadband access and predictable work schedules may influence the ability to practice health-information skills outside the workshop.

items.stem: Measured pKa values: acetic acid 4.76, chloroacetic acid 2.87, dichloroacetic acid 1.35. Which explanation accounts for the trend?

choices.text: Chlorine donates electron density by resonance into the carboxylate, making the acid weaker as more Cl is added
Each chlorine withdraws electron density inductively through the σ framework, stabilizing the conjugate base and lowering pKa
Chlorinated acids are strong mineral acids like HCl, so pKa collapses to that of hydrochloric acid
Chlorine increases the hydrophobicity of the acid, which always increases pKa in water

items.explanation: Carboxylic-acid strength in this series is controlled by inductive stabilization of the conjugate base. Electronegative chlorines pull electron density through the C–C σ bonds toward themselves, dispersing the negative charge on the carboxylate and favoring dissociation. More chlorines, or chlorines closer to the carboxyl, give a larger effect, matching the stepwise drop in pKa. Resonance donation from Cl into the carboxylate would raise pKa, which is the opposite of the data. These are still weak organic acids, not fully dissociated mineral acids, and hydrophobicity is not the parameter that tracks this halogen trend.

distractorRationales.A: Inductive withdrawal, not resonance donation, is the dominant substituent effect of alkyl chlorides on aliphatic acids. The data show stronger, not weaker, acids.
distractorRationales.C: Even dichloroacetic acid is not HCl. It remains an equilibrium weak acid, albeit a relatively strong one among carboxylic acids.
distractorRationales.D: Adding chlorines lowers pKa here. A generic ‘hydrophobic acids are weaker’ rule does not explain the observed trend.

items.stem:
An object starts from rest with constant acceleration a. Then s = (1/2) a t^2. Four timings are:

t (s) | s (m)
1.0 | 2.0
2.0 | 8.0
3.0 | 18
4.0 | 32

Which graph is linear, and what acceleration does its slope give?

choices.text: s versus t is linear with slope 8.0 m s−1, so a = 8.0 m s−2.
s versus t is linear with slope 2.0 m s−1, so a = 4.0 m s−2.
s versus t^2 is linear with slope 8.0 m s−2, so a = 8.0 m s−2.
s versus t^2 is linear with slope 2.0 m s−2, so a = 4.0 m s−2 because slope = a/2.

items.explanation: Check s / t^2: 2.0/1 = 2.0, 8.0/4 = 2.0, 18/9 = 2.0, 32/16 = 2.0 m s−2 at every row. Therefore s = 2.0 t^2, which is a straight line of slope 2.0 m s−2 when s is plotted against t^2. Comparing with s = (1/2) a t^2 gives a/2 = 2.0, so a = 4.0 m s−2. A plot of s versus t is a parabola (2, 8, 18, 32 m at equal time steps), not a straight line. Taking the last-over-first slope (32 − 2)/(4 − 1) ≈ 10 m s−1 is not a. Using slope = a instead of a/2 on the t^2 graph would report 2.0 m s−2, which is not among the options that pair the correct graph with a = 4.0 m s−2 except D.

distractorRationales.A: s versus t is not linear: the successive s values 2, 8, 18, 32 are not in arithmetic sequence. Constant a produces a parabola on an s–t graph.
distractorRationales.B: s versus t is parabolic, not linear. A slope of 2.0 m s−1 also does not match the tabulated Δs/Δt values, which increase with t.
distractorRationales.C: s versus t^2 is linear, but its slope is 2.0 m s−2, not 8.0. Even if the slope were 8, that would be a/2, implying a = 16 m s−2, not 8.

items.stem:
A heating curve for 18 g (1.00 mol) of H2O at 1 atm uses Lf = 6.0 kJ mol−1 and Lv = 41 kJ mol−1, and c = 75 J mol−1 K−1 for liquid water. The curve’s plateaux are:

Segment | T (°C) | heat absorbed (kJ) | process
AB | 0 | 6.0 | ice → water
BC | 0 → 100 | 7.5 | warming liquid
CD | 100 | 41 | water → steam

Which statement is required by the data?

choices.text: Latent-heat plateaux occur at the melting and boiling points; warming the liquid 100 °C costs 1.00 × 75 × 100 J = 7.5 kJ, matching BC
The longest energy segment is melting, because AB is drawn first
Temperature rises during AB and CD, because heat is being absorbed
BC should cost 41 kJ, the same as vaporisation

items.explanation: At 1 atm, ice melts at 0 °C and water boils at 100 °C; during those phase changes T is constant while the latent heats 6.0 and 41 kJ are absorbed. Between them, q = n c ΔT = 1.00 × 75 J K−1 × 100 K = 7500 J = 7.5 kJ, which is row BC. Vaporisation dwarfs fusion (41 versus 6.0 kJ), so CD, not AB, is the costly plateau. Heat absorbed at a phase change does not raise T; that is why they are plateaux. Equating the liquid-warming leg to Lv confuses sensible heat with latent heat.

distractorRationales.B: AB is 6.0 kJ; CD is 41 kJ, so boiling, not melting, is the largest energy step.
distractorRationales.C: The table lists constant T for AB and CD; absorbed heat there breaks intermolecular forces, not the thermometer reading.
distractorRationales.D: 41 kJ is Lv for CD; BC is the 7.5 kJ sensible-heat calculation.

passage.title: psg-bb-3
passage.body:
To dissect how mutations disrupt protein output, a lab engineered a set of Escherichia coli strains, each carrying a single defined change in a gene (galK) that encodes a metabolic enzyme. For every strain they measured two quantities: the steady-state level of galK messenger RNA (by quantitative PCR) and the amount of functional enzyme (by an activity assay). Results were expressed as a percentage of the wild-type value.
Wild type showed 100 percent mRNA and 100 percent enzyme activity. Strain 1, carrying a substitution in the promoter region upstream of the coding sequence, showed 15 percent mRNA and 14 percent activity. Strain 2, carrying a single base-pair change that converted a glutamine codon (CAG) into a stop codon (TAG) near the beginning of the coding sequence, showed 95 percent mRNA but less than 2 percent activity; the protein it produced was abnormally short. Strain 3, carrying a single-nucleotide deletion just after the start codon, showed 92 percent mRNA and less than 2 percent activity, and its protein product bore no resemblance to the wild-type sequence beyond its first few residues. Strain 4, carrying a base change that altered a codon from CTG to CTA (both of which encode leucine), showed 98 percent mRNA and 97 percent activity.
The investigators noted that a mutation's consequences depend on where in the gene it falls and how it interacts with the genetic code: some changes reduce how much mRNA is made, others corrupt translation of the message, and some have essentially no effect at all.

passage.title: psg-cars-11
passage.body:
Among the foundational distinctions in the sociology of religion is the division of the world into two mutually exclusive domains: the sacred and the profane. The sacred encompasses all things set apart and forbidden, surrounded by special prohibitions and observed with reverence; the profane designates everything else the ordinary, the utilitarian, the everyday. This distinction is not primarily about supernatural belief. A society without gods can still organize its collective life around sacred objects and practices; conversely, explicitly theistic language can be deployed in contexts so routine that nothing sacred attaches to it at all. The sacred is a structural feature of collective life, not a property of any particular theological tradition.
What makes something sacred is not its intrinsic properties but its relationship to the collective. The sacred object or practice has been designated by the community as set apart, invested with a significance that transcends individual preference and commands a distinctive emotional response. Violations of the sacred provoke not merely practical objection but moral indignation and often the collective sanction of the group. The sacred functions, in this analysis, as a boundary marker: it demarcates what the collective treats as inviolable from what can be freely negotiated, exchanged, or modified. The power of the sacred is thus inseparable from the collective from which it derives and to which it refers. A corollary is that the sacred is hedged about with rules of separation. Precisely because sacred things are set apart, they must be kept from casual contact with the profane: they are approached through prescribed gestures, handled by designated persons, and encountered on appointed occasions rather than at will. Transgression is felt less as a mistake than as a kind of pollution, calling forth rites of purification or punishment rather than simple correction. This logic of separation explains why the sacred can inspire dread as readily as devotion: what is marked off as supremely valuable is also, for that very reason, treated as perilous to handle carelessly. The boundary, in short, is enforced as much by feeling as by rule.
This framework has been applied far beyond explicitly religious contexts. National flags, war memorials, and constitutional documents can function as sacred objects in secular societies: they command a special reverence, their desecration provokes communal outrage, and they focus the collective sense of identity and shared purpose. Academic ceremonies, such as the conferral of degrees and the inauguration of presidents, likewise exhibit a ritualized formality that marks them off from ordinary transactions. The secular and the sacred are not opposites; rather, the sacred is a structural feature of collective life that may attach to entirely secular objects and occasions.
Critics of this framework have worried that extending the concept of the sacred to secular contexts dilutes it beyond usefulness. If anything sufficiently cherished by a community counts as sacred, the concept loses its explanatory precision. Moreover, the framework has been criticized for underplaying internal dissent: in any actual society, which objects are sacred and which are merely important is itself politically contested, and the boundary between the sacred and the profane is drawn by those with the social power to draw it. Sacred designations can thus serve ideological functions, naturalizing existing arrangements by placing them beyond ordinary critical scrutiny.
These tensions notwithstanding, the sacred/profane distinction continues to illuminate the emotional architecture of collective life in ways that strictly rational accounts of social organization cannot easily replicate. Communities that lack shared sacred commitments often struggle to motivate the sacrifices that sustaining collective institutions requires.

passage.title: Study of Notification Cues and Attention
passage.body:
Researchers investigated how smartphone notification cues affect attention and perceived stress. Eighty undergraduate volunteers completed a computerized reaction-time task in three counterbalanced conditions: no notification, a vibration notification, and a visual banner notification. In each condition, participants pressed a key as soon as a target shape appeared. The phone was placed face down for the vibration condition and face up for the visual banner condition. Participants were told that notifications were unrelated to task performance and did not require a response. After each condition, participants rated their momentary stress on a 1 to 7 scale. The researchers also measured whether participants reported checking their phones within 30 seconds after the task.

Mean task performance and stress ratings by notification condition
Condition | Mean reaction time to target (ms) | Error rate (%) | Mean stress rating
No notification | 420 | 4 | 2.1
Vibration notification | 470 | 6 | 3.4
Visual banner notification | 445 | 5 | 2.8

Phone-checking behavior after task
Condition | Percent checking phone within 30 seconds
No notification | 12
Vibration notification | 48
Visual banner notification | 31

Design summary — Each participant completed all three notification conditions in randomized order. The primary dependent variables were reaction time, error rate, stress rating, and post-task phone checking.

passage.title: Note on a cancelled tram
passage.body:
In the third week of the lockout the company ran a single tram, brightly lit, along the route at dusk, with no passengers permitted. Officials called it a demonstration of service. Strikers called it a lantern on a coffin. Children ran beside it anyway, as they had when the cars were working, and were photographed. The photograph was printed in the morning paper under the heading NORMALITY RETURNS, and in an overseas paper under the heading CHILDREN MOCK THE DEAD LINE.

A clerk in the tram office, years later, wrote that he had been told to leave the lights on even if the generator complained, because darkness would look like surrender. He added, without apparent bitterness, that surrender had already occurred in the timetable. What remained was a moving argument about who owned the look of a street at evening.

Historians still disagree whether the empty tram lengthened the dispute by humiliating the men or shortened it by frightening the board with the cost of theatre. The clerk’s sentence is more useful than either camp: the fight had become, for a night, a question of illumination.

A team studied what sustains effort on a task. Ninety children who already enjoyed drawing were randomly assigned to three groups. The 'expected-reward' group was promised a certificate for drawing; the 'unexpected-reward' group drew and then received the same certificate as a surprise; the 'no-reward' group simply drew. Two weeks later, during free-play periods, observers unobtrusively recorded how much each child chose to draw. Children in the expected-reward group spent about half as much free time drawing as the other two groups, whose behavior did not differ.
In a second study with adults, participants worked on solvable puzzles under one of two framings. Some were told the task measured 'innate intelligence'; others were told that effort and strategy drive success. After encountering difficult items, the 'effort' group persisted longer and reported greater interest, and this difference was largest among participants who scored high on a measure of conscientiousness.
The researchers interpreted the children's result as evidence that offering an expected tangible reward for an already-enjoyable activity can reduce later voluntary engagement, because the behavior becomes attributed to the external incentive. They connected the adult result to a framework distinguishing motivation that arises from within the person from motivation driven by external consequences, and noted that a stable personality dimension moderated persistence. They cautioned that rewards are not universally harmful: unexpected rewards, and rewards for dull tasks, did not undermine engagement.

items.stem: The claim that an interview “can be managed as tightly as a colonial gazette” plays which role in the argument?

choices.text: It is offered as evidence that official gazettes are generally more accurate than spoken testimony and should therefore remain the backbone of public history.
It blocks the inference that switching from paper to speech is by itself a democratic solution, by asserting that control can migrate into the making of the interview.
It is a concession that colonial records should be discarded because their tightness makes them unusable as historical sources.
It defines democracy as a property of recording technology, so that any taped interview counts as a democratic act.

items.explanation: The oral-history paragraph grants that interviews can admit people the file forgot, then immediately warns that the corrective is not automatic. The gazette comparison is the argumentative block: if prompting, recording, and cutting can be as tightly managed as an official publication, then orality as such does not deliver democracy. What the author wants instead is visibility of the historian in the manufacture of the record. The sentence is not a defense of gazettes, a call to throw them out, or a technological definition of democracy. Its logical job is to undercut an inference the preceding sentences might otherwise have licensed.

distractorRationales.A: The author never ranks gazette accuracy above speech; the comparison is about manageability of production, not about which genre is truer.
distractorRationales.C: The passage refuses abandonment of documents and does not argue that colonial tightness makes written sources unusable.
distractorRationales.D: Responsible oral history is distinguished by visible steering and refusal, not by the mere fact that a machine was running.

passage.title: The archive and the street
passage.body:
Historians often speak as if the past were a reluctant witness who can be coaxed into testimony if only the right box is opened. The letter, the minute-book, the trial transcript, and the parish register are treated not as remnants but as the event itself, patiently waiting to be interviewed. The metaphor is professionally convenient. It locates virtue in attentiveness and implies that an archive, handled without aggression, will speak of its own accord. Archives do not speak. They are offices that decide, usually long before a scholar arrives, which traces of life will be kept, numbered, and thereby made eligible for later recovery. To mistake a folder for a microphone is to forget that someone built the studio, invited some guests, and switched the machine off when the conversation became inconvenient.

This is not a case for abandoning documents. It is a case against a piety now common in public history: the belief that proximity to a primary source is itself a moral credential. Museum captions announce that an object was found in an attic or rescued from a demolition site, as if its later career in a glass case were a continuation of its first life rather than a conversion into evidence. Conversion is what historians do. Trouble begins when conversion is narrated as rescue, because that narration conceals the historian's power and, more consequentially, conceals the people who never generated a paper trail to be rescued.

Oral historians have pressed this objection for decades, sometimes with more hope than caution. They have offered the recorded interview as a democratic patch, a way of admitting those whom the file forgot. The patch is real; it is not automatic. An interview is also a document, made under conditions of prompting, recording, transcription, and later cutting. It can be managed as tightly as a colonial gazette. What distinguishes a responsible oral history is not orality as such, but the historian remaining visible in the manufacture of the record—visible enough that a later reader can see where a question steered, where a narrator pushed back, and where a silence was not a hole but a refusal.

The sharper problem is civic rather than technical. If the only past that can be cited is the past that was filed, public memory will go on over-representing those who employed clerks. Cities make the point more bluntly than seminars do. A demolished neighborhood deposits fewer cartons than a merchant's townhouse; a street seller deposits fewer than a chartered company. When a preservation trust then campaigns to save the townhouse because it is richly documented, the trust is not merely selecting architecture. It is ratifying a distribution of paperwork as a distribution of historical weight. The house is asked to stand for an age, and the undocumented street is invited, if at all, to supply atmosphere.

Honesty does not require the fantasy that every life can be reconstructed with equal density. Some absences are final. The decent procedure is to treat those absences as facts about power rather than as temporary vacancies that a more heroic search will fill. A history that admits what cannot be known is more public-minded than a history that performs completeness by adding still more pages to an already thick dossier. The archive will remain necessary. It need not remain innocent.

passage.title: Critical Reasoning · Health & Statistics
passage.body: A widely circulated report claims that teenagers who spend more than four hours a day on social media are twice as likely to report symptoms of anxiety as teenagers who spend less than one hour a day. Newspaper headlines quickly translated this into warnings that social media "causes" anxiety in teenagers, and several schools cited the report when introducing new phone bans. The original researchers were more cautious. They noted that their data was cross-sectional — collected at a single point in time — rather than following the same teenagers over years, and that anxious teenagers might simply be more likely to retreat into their phones, rather than phones making them anxious in the first place. They also noted that heavy social media use was more common among teenagers who already reported sleeping fewer than six hours a night, raising the possibility that disrupted sleep, not screen time itself, was doing much of the work.

passage.title: On the new memorial
passage.body:
The memorial is a corridor of rusted uprights, each the height of a person, irregularly spaced so that you must turn sideways to pass. At noon they look like a failed fence. At dusk they look like a crowd that has agreed not to face you. There are no names. A small plaque at the exit says only: THEY WERE NOT LATE. THEY WERE PREVENTED.

Tourists complain that they do not know whom to pity. School groups count the uprights and get different numbers, because some are so close they read as one. A veteran interviewed on the steps said he hated it, then stood there until the lights came on, then said he hated that he did not hate it enough.

The sculptor, in a panel discussion, refused the word healing. “If it heals,” she said, “it has failed at being a door you cannot swagger through.” Critics split between those who call this moral bullying in Cor-Ten steel and those who call the tourists’ complaint the point.

I went through twice. The second time a child asked why the fence was broken. His father said it was not a fence. The child, satisfied with a new category, ran. I was not satisfied. Prevention is a bureaucratic word. In the corridor it becomes a body insisting on its width.

items.stem: Which pair of claims does the passage hold together without treating them as a contradiction?

choices.text: Scores should be burned, and recordings are the true work.
The worry about impressionistic study without a text is real in a university, and some traditions still rightly treat the night’s playing as the work.
Jazz time is a failed metronome grid, and village dances were always in three.
Microphones are neutral, and fans who own every take therefore know what the music is for.

items.explanation: Paragraph three grants the university’s need for a shared object and immediately limits the grant: the worry is less real where the night is the work. That is a qualification, not a collapse. The last paragraph repeats the pattern with maps. A, C, and D assemble positions the author rejects. Internal consistency here is the author’s habit of granting a real institutional problem without letting it dictate ontology.

distractorRationales.A: Both burning scores and treating recordings as the true work are refused.
distractorRationales.C: Jazz time is a negotiation, not a failed grid; dances may never have been “in three.”
distractorRationales.D: Recordings smuggle politics; owning takes can multiply facts while missing purpose.

passage.title: What the metronome cannot hear
passage.body:
Musicology has a long habit of treating the score as the work and the performance as a more or less obedient copy. The habit is understandable. Paper sits still. It can be compared, edited, and taught in rooms where no instrument is present. A performance disappears as it occurs, leaving only memory, a recording, or an argument.

Yet the stillness of paper is not neutrality. Notation is a technology with a history: it captures some relations (pitch against a staff, duration against a beat) and lets others leak away (the weight of a bow, the delay before a singer accepts a consonant, the social fact of who is allowed to ornament). When a textbook says a movement is “in three,” it is reporting a notational decision that a village dance may never have made in those terms. The metronome, arriving later still, offers a fantasy that time is a ruler laid beside sound. Dancers know otherwise. So do jazz rhythm sections, whose time is a negotiation, not a grid that failed.

Scholars who defend the score-as-work often point to the composer’s authority and to the need for a shared object of study. Without a text, they say, we are left with impressions. The worry is real in a university. It is less real in a tradition that already treats the night’s playing as the work, and the paper, if paper exists, as a prompt. To call that tradition incomplete because it will not sit still is to confuse the archive’s convenience with the art’s ontology.

Recordings seemed to solve the disappearance problem. They created a new paper: a fixed take that can be looped, transcribed, and worshipped. The solution smuggles in its own politics. Which night was recorded, from which seat, with which microphone aiming at which social center of the band? A “definitive” recording can freeze a hierarchy that a living scene would have kept in motion. The fan who owns every take may know more facts than a player and still know less about what the music is for.

The practical upshot is not to burn scores. Scores are superb tools, as maps are superb tools. The upshot is to stop calling the map the territory in order to make seminars easier to grade. A pedagogy that can only hear what the metronome can hear will keep producing excellent accountants of pitch and a thin audience for everything else. If musicology wants to study music rather than the paperwork of music, it will have to tolerate objects that do not hold still, and to admit that some of the most precise information arrives as a glance between players that no staff line was built to hold.

Formation of nickel complexes in water (Ni2+ is d8):

Species | added ligand | colour | proposed formula | coordination number
aqua ion | H2O | green | [Ni(H2O)6]2+ | 6
+ excess NH3 | NH3 | blue-violet | [Ni(NH3)6]2+ | 6
+ excess CN− | CN− | yellow | [Ni(CN)4]2− | 4

Charge on the cyano complex: Ni2+ plus 4 CN−. Which statement is consistent?

choices.text: The aqua ion is [Ni(H2O)4]2+ because the cyano complex is four-coordinate
Adding NH3 oxidises Ni2+ to Ni3+, which is why the colour changes
Water and ammonia give octahedral Ni(II); cyanide, a strong-field ligand, gives a four-coordinate [Ni(CN)4]2− of charge 2−
[Ni(CN)4]2− must contain Ni(IV) because the charge is 2−

items.explanation: The aqua and ammine rows are both coordination number 6, the usual octahedral Ni(II) complexes, with ligand substitution (not a change of oxidation state) explaining the green to blue-violet shift. Four cyanide ligands on Ni2+ give overall charge 2 + 4(−1) = −2, matching [Ni(CN)4]2−, a well-known square-planar strong-field complex of d8 Ni(II). Charge 2− does not require Ni(IV) (that would be Ni4+ + 4 CN− = 0). The aqua ion is listed as six-coordinate. Colour change on adding NH3 is ligand-field substitution of H2O, not oxidation to Ni3+.

distractorRationales.A: The table assigns the aqua ion coordination number 6, [Ni(H2O)6]2+.
distractorRationales.B: The ammine formula still contains Ni2+; NH3 is not an oxidant here.
distractorRationales.D: Ni2+ + 4 CN− = −2 overall with nickel still in the +2 state.

passage.title: psg-cars-5
passage.body:
Beauty and sublimity are often treated as synonyms in everyday speech, but the aesthetic tradition has long maintained a crucial distinction between them. Beauty, on the classical account, is associated with harmony, proportion, and pleasure: the beautiful object is one whose parts cohere in a way that the observer finds immediately gratifying. Sublimity, by contrast, involves an experience of excess — of forms or magnitudes that exceed the observer's capacity to take them in all at once. The encounter with the sublime is therefore double-edged: it produces both awe and a kind of distress, a sense of being overwhelmed that coexists with exhilaration.
Eighteenth-century theorists were among the first to treat the sublime as a distinct aesthetic category. One influential account located the cause of sublimity in attributes such as vast extent, darkness, and the suggestion of danger or power. A stormy ocean, a jagged mountain range, the interior of a vast cathedral — these provoke a response that differs qualitatively from our response to a well-proportioned garden or a graceful melody. The difference lies not in mere intensity but in the character of the response: the sublime suspends our habitual sense of comfort and security.
A subsequent philosophical tradition shifted the locus of the sublime from the external object to the observer's mental activity. On this view, what is truly sublime is not the mountain itself but the mind's discovery of its own capacity to conceive of what it cannot perceive — to think totality even when the senses are overwhelmed by the magnitude before them. The initial feeling of inadequacy thus gives way to a recognition of the mind's superiority: the faculty that can frame the idea of infinity is, in this sense, greater than any finite spectacle.
These two accounts — one locating sublimity in the object's properties, the other in the observer's cognitive response — are not necessarily incompatible. Objects with certain properties may reliably trigger the cognitive response that constitutes the full experience of the sublime. What both accounts agree on, however, is that the sublime cannot be reduced to beauty: the sublime disrupts the comfortable relationship between the observer and the world, while beauty affirms and soothes it.
The distinction carries an ethical resonance that later writers were quick to draw out. Because the sublime confronts the observer with magnitudes that dwarf the human frame, it has often been tied to humility — to a chastening awareness of finitude that beauty, with its reassurances of order and fit, does not compel. Standing before a storm or an abyss, the spectator is reminded that the world is not arranged for human convenience. And yet, on the observer-centered account, the very same encounter can enlarge the self, for the mind that registers its own smallness is also the mind capacious enough to entertain the immensity that occasions the feeling. This union of abasement and elevation is what makes the sublime so stubbornly resistant to the vocabulary of ordinary pleasure.
Contemporary critics have extended the concept of the sublime to non-natural contexts. The technological sublime finds its occasion in artifacts of overwhelming scale or power: a vast suspension bridge, a particle accelerator, a data center housing more information than any mind could process. Whether such objects genuinely provoke the traditional experience of mingled awe and inadequacy, or whether they produce only spectacle and wonder, remains a live debate in aesthetic theory.

passage.title: psg-cp-5
passage.body:
Nuclear medicine uses radioactive isotopes to image the body. The most widely used tracer, technetium-99m, is a metastable ('m') nuclear state that returns to its ground state by emitting a single gamma-ray photon, without changing its number of protons or neutrons. Because those gamma photons escape the body and reach a gamma camera, and because the isotope's half-life is a convenient 6.0 hours, it images well and clears quickly. A patient receives an initial activity of 800 MBq, and the staff track how the activity falls over the following day.
Positron emission tomography (PET) uses a different decay. Fluorine-18, built into a glucose analog, decays by positron emission: inside the nucleus a proton is converted into a neutron, and a positron is ejected. The positron soon annihilates with a nearby electron, producing two photons the scanner detects in coincidence.
The passage also compares decay modes. Some heavy parents decay by alpha emission, ejecting a helium-4 nucleus, while others undergo beta-minus decay. In every case the totals of mass number and charge are conserved across the nuclear equation. Finally, the team notes that alpha, beta, and especially gamma emissions are all 'ionizing': each quantum can carry enough energy to eject electrons from the atoms it strikes, which is both the basis of detection and the reason for strict dose limits. Planck's relation ties a photon's energy to its frequency, and gamma photons lie at the high-energy end of the electromagnetic spectrum.

items.explanation: Convert ΔS to kJ: -31/1000 kJ mol^{-1} K^{-1}. Then ΔG = -61 − 298×-31/1000 ≈ -51.8 kJ mol^{-1}. The sign of the TΔS term is a minus. Leaving ΔS in joules inflates TΔS by 1000. items.stem: A draft reads: “They never understood me. They were wrong. I was right. The end.” What is the principal reflective-voice failure, and which revision begins to repair it?

choices.text: Failure: too much world, not enough self. Repair: delete every concrete table and name only “society.”
Failure: the “I” prosecutes without examining itself. Repair: “I called it misunderstanding because that word hurt less than admitting I had used silence as a weapon too.”
Failure: presence of any family. Repair: write about interest rates.
Failure: brevity. Repair: triple the length with adjectives of rage.

items.explanation: The draft’s “I” is a verdict machine. Reflection would turn the lens around: how the writer named the hurt, what the naming protected, whether silence went both ways. The repair sentence does that without cancelling the hurt. Making the piece less particular or fleeing into rates would be a task error. Lengthening rage is still prosecution. Voice here is not decoration; it is the difference between a diary dump and a piece of thought. B names the failure and a first repair that a marker could actually reward.

distractorRationales.A: The draft is already short on world; more fog is not the cure.
distractorRationales.C: Family is legitimate Task B material; the failure is unexamined verdict, not the topic.
distractorRationales.D: More rage without self-scrutiny would intensify the same failure.

passage.title: Neighborhood Resources and Stress Physiology
passage.body:
A community psychology team studied 120 adults living in three neighborhoods that differed in access to public transportation, grocery stores, and safe recreational spaces. Participants completed a perceived-stress scale, provided a morning saliva sample for cortisol measurement, and reported how often they used neighborhood recreational spaces. The investigators did not randomly assign participants to neighborhoods. They collected age, income, and employment status to use as covariates in later analyses.

Neighborhood characteristics and participant outcomes
Neighborhood resource level | Mean monthly household income | Mean perceived stress score | Mean morning cortisol, nmol/L | Mean recreational-space use, days/week
High | $5200 | 13.1 | 11.2 | 3.8
Moderate | $3900 | 17.4 | 13.9 | 2.1
Low | $2600 | 22.0 | 16.7 | 0.8

Conceptual model — The researchers hypothesized that neighborhood resource access may influence stress partly through daily opportunities for exercise, social interaction, and perceived control.

items.stem: A 10 kg crate on a rough horizontal floor is pulled by a 20 N horizontal force. Kinetic friction is 5.0 N. Newton’s second law is ΣF = ma. Starting from rest, what is the acceleration, and how far has the crate moved after 4.0 s?

choices.text: a = 2.5 m s−2; s = 20 m (adding friction to the pull)
a = 2.0 m s−2; s = 16 m (friction omitted)

items.explanation: Net force = 20 − 5.0 = 15 N, so a = 15/10 = 1.5 m s−2. From rest, s = (1/2) a t² = 0.50 × 1.5 × 16 = 12 m. Omitting friction gives a = 2.0 m s−2 and 16 m. Using only the 5 N friction as the net force gives 0.50 m s−2. Adding friction to the pull as if both acted forward gives 25 N and 2.5 m s−2. The free-body diagram has the pull forward and friction backward.

distractorRationales.A: 0.50 m s−2 would be 5.0 N / 10 kg, using friction alone and ignoring the 20 N pull.
distractorRationales.B: Friction does not add to the pull; it subtracts from it on a horizontal floor.
distractorRationales.D: Friction 5.0 N opposes the 20 N pull, so the net force is 15 N, not 20 N.

items.stem: A mutant Escherichia coli cannot synthesize meso-diaminopimelic acid, an amino acid of the peptidoglycan peptide stem. In hypotonic medium the cells swell and lyse unless 0.5 M sucrose is added as an osmotic stabilizer. Integrity of which structure has been lost?

choices.text: The 70S ribosome, which normally resists turgor by covalently cross-linking phospholipids
The peptidoglycan cell wall, whose peptide cross-links bear turgor pressure
The nuclear envelope, which is the load-bearing wall of Gram-negative bacteria
Flagellar hooks, which osmotically clamp the periplasm

items.explanation: Peptidoglycan is a mesh of glycan chains cross-linked through short peptides; meso-DAP is a stem residue used in those cross-links in E. coli. Without it the wall cannot be completed, so it cannot oppose the osmotic driving force for water influx, and the inner membrane ruptures in hypotonic medium. Sucrose outside the cell raises external osmolarity and reduces net water entry, rescuing the spheroplasts. Ribosomes do not bear turgor, bacteria have no nuclear envelope, and flagella are motility organelles rather than the hydrostatic exoskeleton.

distractorRationales.A: Ribosomes synthesize protein; they are not a pressure-bearing sac and do not cross-link membrane lipids.
distractorRationales.C: Prokaryotes lack a nuclear envelope; the wall, not a nucleus, is the turgor-resistant layer.
distractorRationales.D: Flagella propel the cell; they do not substitute for a missing peptidoglycan sacculus.

items.stem: A eukaryotic mRNA recovered from the cytosol is unusually unstable and poorly translated. The 5′ end is a free triphosphate rather than 7-methylguanosine attached by a 5′–5′ triphosphate bridge. Which nuclear processing step failed?

choices.text: Cleavage and polyadenylation at the 3′ end
Assembly of U2 snRNP on the first intron branch point

items.explanation: The eukaryotic 5′ cap is 7-methylguanosine joined to the first transcribed nucleotide by a 5′–5′ triphosphate linkage, added shortly after initiation by RNA polymerase II. The cap is bound by eIF4E, supporting scanning-dependent translation, and it protects mRNA from 5′ exonucleases. A cytosolic RNA that still ends in a 5′ triphosphate has not been capped, which explains both poor translation and rapid decay. Poly(A) status is a 3′-end event, U2 assembly is a splicing event, and tRNA charging is a translation-factor issue that would not change the chemical structure of the mRNA 5′ end.

distractorRationales.A: Defective polyadenylation would alter the 3′ tail, not replace a 5′ cap with a free 5′ triphosphate. The chemistry described is specifically the uncapped 5′ end.
distractorRationales.B: U2 snRNP functions in splicing; failure to splice would retain intron sequences but would not leave a 5′ triphosphate in place of the cap.
distractorRationales.C: Initiator tRNA charging affects translation globally but does not remodel the 5′ end of an already synthesized mRNA.

items.stem: A patient takes high-dose exogenous glucocorticoid for ten days. Endogenous hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal function is expected to show:

items.explanation: Cortisol and related glucocorticoids exert negative feedback on hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, lowering CRH and ACTH. passage.title: psg-cars-3
passage.body:
Few debates in literary theory have proved more durable than the question of authorial intent: does the meaning of a text reside primarily in what its author meant to communicate, or does meaning emerge through the activity of reading itself? At one extreme, the intentionalist holds that misreading is always possible — that interpretations diverging from the author's design are simply mistaken, however ingenious or culturally resonant they may be. At the other extreme, the anti-intentionalist insists that once a text is released into the world, the author's psychological states become strictly irrelevant: what the words mean is fixed not by biography but by the conventions of the language and genre in which they are embedded.
The anti-intentionalist position gained influential expression in mid-twentieth-century criticism, when theorists argued that treating the author's intention as the criterion of correct interpretation commits a category error. Evidence about what a poet hoped to achieve, they maintained, cannot settle what a poem achieves, because a poem is a verbal artifact that may realize meanings its creator did not foresee — meanings that become available only through the community of readers over time. The celebrated example of an ironic text serves as illustration: a writer may compose a scathing satire of nationalistic rhetoric while sincerely believing the rhetoric they are parodying; the satiric meaning is there in the text whether the author intended it or not.
Intentionalists counter that language is an intentional practice: utterances mean what speakers mean by them, and written language does not somehow escape this fundamental feature of linguistic communication. To read a text in complete disregard of what its author was trying to do, they argue, is to treat it as a natural object rather than a human creation — to decode it the way one might decode an accidental inkblot rather than a deliberate message. Moreover, intentionalists point out that appeals to 'the language and genre' still presuppose communicative conventions that are themselves constituted by the intentions of the linguistic community.
A mediating view distinguishes between actual authorial intention (the historical individual's specific psychological states) and what might be called the implied author: the authorial persona that a competent reader constructs from the textual evidence alone. On this account, interpretation aims neither at private biography nor at free-floating textual play but at the coherent communicative project that the text itself invites. The implied author is, in effect, the best hypothesis about what an ideally communicative author of this text would have intended — a construct that disciplines interpretation without requiring access to historical documents.
What unites all parties to this dispute is the recognition that texts are not transparent windows onto authors' minds or onto a language-independent reality. They are artifacts whose significance is never simply given but must always be construed — a fact that makes hermeneutics, the theory of interpretation, as much a practical as a philosophical discipline.

items.stem: A Task A thesis states that “whoever owns the clock owns the apology.” Which use of an example is weakest, and why?

choices.text: Weakest: a fully specified case of an airline keeping passengers on the tarmac without a true estimated time, then offering a voucher in lieu of an explanation of the delay’s cause.
Weakest: “Companies these days are bad.” It names no clock-owner, no delayed public, and no apology-substitute, so the thesis’s parts have nothing to inhabit.
Weakest: a hospital’s public dashboard that shows average wait while omitting the longest decile, if the essay explains how the omitted tail is the apology being owned.
Weakest: a comparison between a minister’s press conference time and a benefits helpline’s hold music, if both clocks are identified.

items.explanation: The thesis has moving parts: ownership of time, and an apology that can be captured or replaced. A, C, and D, though imperfect, still give those parts somewhere to live. “Companies these days are bad” is a mood, not a case; it cannot earn a claim about clocks or apologies. Task A examples fail most often by staying at that altitude. The question is not which story is nicest but which one leaves the thesis unemployed. B is the unemployed example. Specificity is a thinking tool, not an ornament.

distractorRationales.A: The tarmac case supplies a clock, a public, and a voucher as a substitute apology; it is usable, not weakest.

Task A — 30 minutes. Soren is writing to these comments:

“The queue is a moral document.”
“To be seen clearly is not the same as to be seen kindly.”

passage.title: psg-cp-5
passage.body:
Nuclear medicine uses radioactive isotopes to image the body. The most widely used tracer, technetium-99m, is a metastable ('m') nuclear state that returns to its ground state by emitting a single gamma-ray photon, without changing its number of protons or neutrons. Because those gamma photons escape the body and reach a gamma camera, and because the isotope's half-life is a convenient 6.0 hours, it images well and clears quickly. A patient receives an initial activity of 800 MBq, and the staff track how the activity falls over the following day.
Positron emission tomography (PET) uses a different decay. Fluorine-18, built into a glucose analog, decays by positron emission: inside the nucleus a proton is converted into a neutron, and a positron is ejected. The positron soon annihilates with a nearby electron, producing two photons the scanner detects in coincidence.
The passage also compares decay modes. Some heavy parents decay by alpha emission, ejecting a helium-4 nucleus, while others undergo beta-minus decay. In every case the totals of mass number and charge are conserved across the nuclear equation. Finally, the team notes that alpha, beta, and especially gamma emissions are all 'ionizing': each quantum can carry enough energy to eject electrons from the atoms it strikes, which is both the basis of detection and the reason for strict dose limits. Planck's relation ties a photon's energy to its frequency, and gamma photons lie at the high-energy end of the electromagnetic spectrum.

passage.title: Note on a cancelled tram
passage.body:
In the third week of the lockout the company ran a single tram, brightly lit, along the route at dusk, with no passengers permitted. Officials called it a demonstration of service. Strikers called it a lantern on a coffin. Children ran beside it anyway, as they had when the cars were working, and were photographed. The photograph was printed in the morning paper under the heading NORMALITY RETURNS, and in an overseas paper under the heading CHILDREN MOCK THE DEAD LINE.

A clerk in the tram office, years later, wrote that he had been told to leave the lights on even if the generator complained, because darkness would look like surrender. He added, without apparent bitterness, that surrender had already occurred in the timetable. What remained was a moving argument about who owned the look of a street at evening.

Historians still disagree whether the empty tram lengthened the dispute by humiliating the men or shortened it by frightening the board with the cost of theatre. The clerk’s sentence is more useful than either camp: the fight had become, for a night, a question of illumination.

passage.title: Two ways of hearing a census
passage.body:
Poem (untitled, 2019)

We counted rooms as if rooms were people.
The spare one kept its coat on.
In the column for language we wrote the kettle.
Nobody asked the stairs their age.

Commentary by L. Okonkwo, catalogue essay for an exhibition of household inventories:
The poem is easy to misread as anti-data. It is not. It notices that a census already poetizes: it decides what may stand for a life (rooms, language, age) and what must remain downstairs, unasked. The coat on the spare room is not a joke about furniture. It is a figure for surplus — the part of a household that official forms cannot rent. When the poem puts a kettle in the language column, it is not claiming kettles speak. It is showing how quickly a form will accept a proxy if the proxy is small and warm.

A table printed beside the poem in the gallery listed visitors by hour and by whether they photographed the stairs:
Hour 10: 14 visitors, 2 photographed stairs
Hour 11: 31 visitors, 18 photographed stairs
Hour 12: 9 visitors, 0 photographed stairs (docent talk in progress)
The curator captioned the table: Attention is not the same as attendance.

A radio host later called the exhibition “political because it made a kettle into a citizen.” Okonkwo's essay had already refused that flattening. The political cut, for her, is not enfranchising objects. It is noticing which human details a state is willing to miss.

passage.title: The Caption (1973)
passage.body: Kwame Boateng published “The Caption” in 1973 after a season in disaster mapping. The argument is that fairness talk often arrives after the decision has already been made. The piece admits that some gatekeeping keeps fraud out. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: A diet contains only amino acids that cannot yield net oxaloacetate or other gluconeogenic intermediates. Which pair consists of the two purely ketogenic amino acids?

choices.text: Alanine and glutamate, which are transaminated to pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate

Valine and isoleucine, both of which are exclusively ketogenic branched-chain amino acids
Leucine and lysine, which are catabolized to acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate without net glucose production

items.explanation: A purely ketogenic amino acid cannot produce net pyruvate or citric-acid-cycle intermediates that can exit to gluconeogenesis; its carbons yield acetyl-CoA or ketone bodies. Leucine and lysine are the two standard amino acids in that class. Alanine and glutamate are glucogenic (pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate). Aspartate and asparagine yield oxaloacetate. Among branched-chain amino acids, valine is glucogenic and isoleucine is mixed (both glucogenic and ketogenic), so that pair is not exclusively ketogenic. A diet of only leucine and lysine therefore cannot support net glucose synthesis from amino-acid carbon, matching the stem.

distractorRationales.A: Alanine → pyruvate and glutamate → α-ketoglutarate are classic glucogenic conversions, so this pair can make net glucose.
distractorRationales.B: Aspartate and asparagine are glucogenic via oxaloacetate, not purely ketogenic.
distractorRationales.C: Valine is glucogenic and isoleucine is mixed; they are not the two purely ketogenic amino acids.

items.stem: Hot aqueous NaOH is used in an attempt to convert each of the following lipids into water-soluble carboxylate soaps. Which compound does not yield fatty-acid soaps under those saponification conditions?

passage.title: Allosteric regulation of a glycolytic kinase
passage.body:
Researchers studied PFK-X, a fictional tetrameric phosphofructokinase isoform that catalyzes the conversion of fructose 6-phosphate (F6P) and ATP to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate and ADP in rapidly dividing cells. ATP is both a substrate and, at high concentration, a negative allosteric regulator. AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate favor the active R state, whereas citrate favors the less active T state. The investigators purified wild-type PFK-X and several variants, then measured initial velocity at pH 7.4 while varying F6P. ATP was held at 2.0 mM in all assays.

Kinetic properties of PFK-X under selected conditions.
Enzyme and condition | S0.5 for F6P (mM) | Relative Vmax (%) | Hill coefficient
Wild type | 0.80 | 100 | 2.8
Wild type + AMP | 0.25 | 105 | 1.4
Wild type + citrate | 1.60 | 95 | 3.0
R212E variant | 1.20 | 85 | 1.2
R212E variant + AMP | 1.10 | 84 | 1.2
D150N variant | Not determined | <5 | Not determined

Oligomeric state of PFK-X variants measured by native gel electrophoresis.
Protein | Tetrameric protein (%) | Dimeric protein (%)
Wild type | 92 | 8
R212E variant | 88 | 12
D150N variant | 90 | 10
C-terminal truncation | 45 | 55

Initial velocity curves for PFK-X. — Wild-type PFK-X shows a sigmoidal dependence on F6P. Addition of AMP shifts the curve left with little change in the plateau. Addition of citrate shifts the curve right. The R212E variant shows a more hyperbolic curve that changes minimally when AMP is added.

items.stem: Standard reduction potentials: Cu2+/Cu = +0.34 V; Zn2+/Zn = −0.76 V. A Daniell cell runs Zn | Zn2+ (1.0 M) || Cu2+ (1.0 M) | Cu with E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V and n = 2. The Nernst equation at 25 °C is E = E° − (0.060/n) log10 Q, with Q = [Zn2+]/[Cu2+]. If [Zn2+] = 1.0 M and [Cu2+] = 0.010 M, what is E?
items.explanation: Q = 1.0 / 0.010 = 100, log10 Q = 2.00. The correction is (0.060/2) × 2.00 = 0.060 V. E = 1.10 − 0.060 = 1.04 V. The cell is slightly less than E° because the product ion is at 1 M while the reactant Cu2+ is depleted. Omitting the log term leaves 1.10 V. Adding instead of subtracting the 0.060 V gives 1.16 V. Using 0.060 × 2 without dividing by n would subtract 0.12 V and give 0.98 V.

distractorRationales.B: 1.10 V is E° at Q = 1; here Q = 100.
distractorRationales.C: 1.16 V would be E° plus the 0.060 V term, the wrong sign in Nernst’s − (RT/nF) ln Q.
distractorRationales.D: 0.98 V subtracts 0.12 V, as if n were omitted when applying 0.060 log Q.
