passage.title: On keeping a promise to a stranger
passage.body:
When the magistrate asked why he had returned the purse, the clerk did not say honesty. He said habit. He had been taught, in a household that measured virtue by small repetitions, that a found object remains someone else's until the world has been given a fair chance to reclaim it. The purse contained little money and a letter, unsealed, beginning: I will not be there when you arrive. He did not finish it. To finish it, he thought, would convert a duty into a story, and stories have a way of making the finder important.

Philosophers like to treat this as a puzzle about property and knowledge. If he does not know the owner, is the duty weaker? If the letter would have saved a marriage, does withholding it become a harm? The clerk would have found the questions indecent. He was not refusing knowledge so much as refusing a role. The city had clerks for lost property; it did not have clerks for other people's farewells.

A later commentator, writing after the clerk was dead, praised him as a Kantian saint: he acted from a maxim he could will as universal. The praise is too clean. The clerk's maxim was local and slightly ashamed. He did not want to be the man who had read the letter. Shame, not universality, kept his eyes off the page. That is not a lesser ethics. It is an ethics that knows how quickly curiosity dresses itself as concern.

The owner collected the purse the next morning and did not thank him. In the commentary this becomes a test of whether virtue needs recognition. The clerk, if asked, would have said only that the counter was busy.

passage.title: Who Counts (1973)
passage.body: Ibrahim El-Sayed published “Who Counts” in 1973 after a season in disaster mapping. The argument is that fairness talk often arrives after the decision has already been made. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: A homodimeric extracellular protein is held together solely by one interchain disulfide and has no other covalent links between subunits. Aliquots are run on SDS-PAGE with or without β-mercaptoethanol. Which banding pattern is expected?

choices.text: A monomer band of identical apparent mass in both the reducing and nonreducing lanes
A dimer band in both lanes, because SDS alone cannot disrupt a protein–protein interface
A dimer band only in the reducing lane and a monomer band only in the nonreducing lane
A band at the dimer mass without reductant and a band at approximately half that mass with reductant

items.explanation: SDS denatures noncovalent subunit interfaces, so a dimer that is held together only by a disulfide still migrates as a covalent dimer on nonreducing SDS-PAGE. β-Mercaptoethanol reduces the cystine to two free thiols, releasing the polypeptides, which then migrate at the monomer mass—about half the dimer mass for a homodimer. The reducing lane therefore cannot show the dimer if the disulfide was the only cross-link, and the nonreducing lane cannot show free monomer as the major species. This comparison is the standard test for interchain disulfides.

distractorRationales.A: Without reductant the interchain disulfide remains, so the nonreducing lane should not collapse to monomer.
distractorRationales.B: SDS disrupts noncovalent interfaces; a disulfide-linked dimer is the exception that survives without reductant, not with it.
distractorRationales.C: This pattern reverses the chemistry: reductant breaks the disulfide, so the dimer should disappear in the reducing lane.

items.stem: Cells use the hydrolysis of ATP to drive unfavorable reactions. This strategy is called energy coupling because:

choices.text: ATP is converted permanently into DNA
ATP directly lowers activation energy like an enzyme
ATP hydrolysis absorbs energy from the surroundings
The exergonic hydrolysis of ATP is linked to an endergonic reaction so the sum is favorable

items.explanation: Energy coupling links the strongly exergonic hydrolysis of ATP (to ADP + Pi) with an endergonic process so their combined ΔG is negative and the overall reaction proceeds. ATP hydrolysis releases (not absorbs) energy, ATP is not a catalyst (that is the enzyme's role), and ATP is not turned into DNA. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. items.stem:
Water potential ψ = ψs + ψp (MPa) along a transpiring shoot at midday:

Compartment | ψs | ψp | ψ
Soil solution | −0.20 | 0.00 | −0.20
Root cortex | −0.60 | +0.20 | −0.40
Xylem sap | −0.10 | −1.10 | −1.20
Leaf cell | −1.50 | +0.20 | −1.30

Water moves toward more negative ψ. Which path is possible?

choices.text: Soil → root → xylem → leaf, because −0.20 > −0.40 > −1.20 > −1.30 (less negative to more negative)
Leaf → xylem → root → soil, following the pressure potential ψp alone
Xylem cannot contain liquid water because ψp is negative
The root is a barrier to uptake because its ψs is more negative than the soil’s

items.explanation: The summed ψ values become steadily more negative from soil (−0.20) to root (−0.40) to xylem (−1.20) to leaf (−1.30), the required downhill gradient for transpiration. Negative xylem ψp is tension in a continuous water column, not an empty pipe; liquid xylem sap is the standard cohesion–tension state. Root ψs is more negative than soil, which is how the root lowers its ψ below the soil and takes up water; that is a driving force, not a barrier. Ranking by ψp alone would send water the wrong way because it ignores solute potential.

distractorRationales.B: Using only ψp would drive water out of the pressurised root toward the soil (0.00) and miss the actual ψ gradient.
distractorRationales.C: Negative hydrostatic pressure in xylem is tension in liquid water, the cohesion–tension mechanism.
distractorRationales.D: A more negative root ψs contributes to a more negative root ψ than soil, which is required for uptake.

items.stem: Preschoolers watch an adult batter a Bobo doll. One film ends with the adult receiving praise and snacks; another ends with a scolding. Children are then left with the doll and are not themselves rewarded or punished. Imitation of the aggressive acts is highest after the rewarded model. This most directly supports:

choices.text: Classical conditioning of fear to the doll
Central-route persuasion by a two-sided statistical message
Cognitive dissonance from being forbidden to play with the doll
Social-cognitive observational learning: vicarious reinforcement changes imitation without direct operant shaping of the child

items.explanation: Bandura’s social cognitive theory holds that people can acquire and regulate behavior by observing models, and that seeing a model rewarded (vicarious reinforcement) increases later imitation even when the observer is not directly reinforced. The Bobo design is the classic demonstration. Classical conditioning would pair the doll with an aversive unconditioned stimulus to produce fear, which is not the outcome. ELM concerns message scrutiny, not filmed aggression. Dissonance from forbidden toys is a different paradigm (insufficient justification / reactance-adjacent), and the stem does not forbid play.

distractorRationales.A: The children attack the doll rather than avoiding it, which is the opposite of conditioned fear.
distractorRationales.B: No argument quality or statistical message is involved; the children watch a behavioral model.
distractorRationales.C: Play was not forbidden, and dissonance is not required to explain imitation of a rewarded model.

items.stem: A 10 V battery with negligible internal resistance is connected to two 2 Ω resistors. The current drawn from the battery is largest when the resistors are arranged so that:

choices.text: they are in series, because then Req = 4 Ω and I = 2.5 A
they are in series, because then voltages add and I = 10 A
they are in parallel, because then Req = 1 Ω and I = 10 A
they are in parallel, because then Req = 4 Ω and I = 2.5 A

items.explanation: Battery current is I = V / Req. Two equal 2 Ω resistors in series have Req = 4 Ω, so I = 10/4 = 2.5 A. In parallel, 1/Req = 1/2 + 1/2, so Req = 1 Ω and I = 10/1 = 10 A. The parallel hookup therefore draws the larger current because it presents the smaller equivalent resistance. Series resistors add; they do not produce I = V/R of a single 1 Ω or a free 10 A from 'adding voltages.' Parallel resistors combine as a reciprocal sum, which for two equal resistors is half of one resistor, not the series sum.

distractorRationales.A: The series numbers are computed correctly (Req = 4 Ω, I = 2.5 A), but that current is smaller than the parallel current, not larger.
distractorRationales.B: Series voltages across the two resistors add to 10 V, but that does not make I = 10 A. Current is V/Req = 10/4 = 2.5 A.
distractorRationales.D: Parallel combination of two 2 Ω resistors is 1 Ω, not 4 Ω. Four ohms is the series sum, which would give the smaller current.

items.stem: In aqueous solution, Li+ has a larger hydrated radius and a more negative hydration enthalpy than Cs+, even though the bare Li+ ion is smaller. Which explanation is correct?

choices.text: Li+ has higher charge density, so it orients and holds more water molecules more tightly via ion–dipole forces.
Li+ is less polarizing, so water binds more loosely and the hydrated radius expands.
Cs+ hydrolyzes water to H3O+ while Li+ does not, shrinking the cesium hydration shell.
Hydration enthalpy tracks only mass, so the heavier Cs+ must have the more negative hydration enthalpy.

items.explanation: Ion–dipole attraction scales with charge density (charge/volume). Li+ is much smaller than Cs+ at the same +1 charge, so the electric field at its surface is stronger. Water dipoles pack more tightly and in greater number around Li+, producing a larger hydrodynamic (hydrated) radius despite the smaller ionic radius, and a more exothermic hydration enthalpy. Cs+ is weakly hydrated. Hydrolysis to H3O+ is characteristic of small, highly charged metal ions such as Al3+, not of Cs+. Mass alone does not set hydration enthalpy.

distractorRationales.B: Li+ is more polarizing, not less; tighter—not looser—water binding is the point.
distractorRationales.C: Neither alkali cation is a strong hydrolyzing acid in water; that description fits Al3+ or Fe3+ aquo ions.
distractorRationales.D: Heavier Cs+ is less strongly hydrated. Hydration enthalpy correlates with charge density, not with mass in this pair.

items.stem: A clinician taps the patellar tendon, stretching the quadriceps. The shortest-latency pathway that extends the knee is:

choices.text: Golgi tendon organ to cerebellum to contralateral cortex to spinal motor neuron
cutaneous nociceptor to brainstem to gamma motor neuron only
Ia afferent from the muscle spindle to the spinal cord to an alpha motor neuron innervating the same muscle
visual startle via cranial nerve II to extraocular muscles only

items.explanation: The tendon tap stretches muscle spindles, firing Ia afferents that monosynaptically excite homonymous alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord—the phasic stretch reflex. That loop does not require cortex or cerebellum for the shortest latency, is not a nociceptive withdrawal via gamma neurons alone, and is unrelated to CN II. Golgi tendon organs are in series with extrafusal fibers and are not the primary receptors for this brief stretch-of-spindle test.

distractorRationales.A: Long-loop transcortical or cerebellar paths exist for some stretch responses but are not the shortest-latency knee jerk, which is spinal and Ia-driven.
distractorRationales.B: This is not a pain-withdrawal reflex, and gamma motor neurons alone do not extend the knee by contracting extrafusal fibers.
distractorRationales.D: Vision and extraocular muscles are irrelevant to a patellar tendon tap with the eyes uninvolved in the circuit.

items.stem: The resting membrane potential of about -70 mV is maintained largely by:

passage.title: psg-bb-9
passage.body:
Neurophysiologists used a squid giant axon and fine electrodes to record the membrane potential during a nerve impulse. At rest, the inside of the axon measured about -70 mV relative to the outside. A brief electrical stimulus that depolarized the membrane to a threshold near -55 mV triggered an all-or-none action potential: the potential shot upward to about +30 mV (the rising phase) and then rapidly returned toward rest (the falling phase), briefly overshooting to a value more negative than -70 mV before stabilizing.
The team dissected the ionic basis using two toxins. Applying tetrodotoxin (TTX), which blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, abolished the action potential entirely: stimulation no longer produced the rapid upstroke. Applying tetraethylammonium (TEA), which blocks voltage-gated potassium channels, left the upstroke intact but markedly slowed the return to rest, prolonging the action potential. Blocking the Na+/K+ ATPase with a separate agent did not abolish individual action potentials over the short term but, over many impulses, degraded the ion gradients on which they depend.
In a final experiment the researchers compared conduction along a myelinated axon with an unmyelinated one of similar diameter. The myelinated axon conducted impulses far faster, because the action potential regenerated only at the gaps in the myelin (nodes of Ranvier), jumping from node to node. The results tied each phase of the action potential to specific ion channels and showed how myelination speeds signaling without changing the underlying ionic mechanism.

items.stem: A point P is a distance 2r from a +4q charge and a distance r from a +q charge. How do the magnitudes of the electric fields at P due to the two charges compare?

items.stem:
DNA per nucleus is plotted for a cell that starts at 6.0 pg (diploid G1, 2C). The trace is: 0–8 h, DNA rises 6.0 → 12.0 pg; 8–10 h, DNA stays 12.0 pg; at 10 h the nucleus divides into two nuclei of 6.0 pg; at 11 h those two divide again into four nuclei of 3.0 pg. There is no second S-phase plateau at 12 pg after the first division.
Which process is shown?

choices.text: Mitosis, which would also finish at 3.0 pg after a single division.
Endoreduplication without nuclear division, which would leave one 12 pg nucleus.
Two S phases then one mitosis, which would require a second rise 6 → 12 pg after 10 h.
Meiosis: one S phase then two divisions, producing 3.0 pg (1C) nuclei.

items.explanation: Meiosis replicates DNA once (6 → 12 pg) and then divides twice without another S phase, so the products are 1C (3.0 pg) if G1 diploid was 6.0 pg. Mitosis would stop after the first division, leaving two 6.0 pg G1 nuclei. Endoreduplication would not split the nucleus. A second S phase would be visible as another 6 → 12 pg rise after 10 h, which the trace lacks. The four 3 pg nuclei at 11 h are therefore meiotic products.

distractorRationales.A: Mitosis yields two 6 pg nuclei, not four 3 pg nuclei.
distractorRationales.B: The plot shows divisions at 10 h and 11 h, not a single undivided 12 pg nucleus.
distractorRationales.C: After 10 h DNA falls rather than rising through a second S phase.

passage.title: psg-ps-8
passage.body:
A study tested how awareness of a negative stereotype affects performance and self-presentation. Two groups of equally qualified students took the same difficult verbal test. In the 'diagnostic' condition, the test was described as measuring underlying ability; in the 'nondiagnostic' condition, it was described as a problem-solving exercise unrelated to ability. Students from a group stereotyped as weaker in the domain scored lower than others in the diagnostic condition but scored equally in the nondiagnostic condition. Merely asking students to record their group membership before a diagnostic test reproduced the gap.
In a second study, participants prepared for a mock interview. Told the interviewer valued modesty, they described themselves cautiously; told the interviewer admired confidence, the same participants emphasized their strengths. Observers who saw only one version rated the participants accordingly, and participants reported deliberately tailoring the impression they gave.
The authors interpreted the first study as evidence that the fear of confirming a negative group stereotype can itself depress performance, independent of ability, and that subtle cues activate this fear. They interpreted the second as an example of managing the impression one presents to different audiences, comparing it to an actor shifting performances between a front region and a back region. They cautioned that persistent performance gaps in real settings may partly reflect such situational threats and unequal conditions rather than fixed differences in ability between groups.

items.stem: "Either we cut the arts budget completely, or the school will go bankrupt." This statement is an example of:

choices.text: A false dilemma — presenting only two extreme options when other possibilities (partial cuts, other savings) exist.

items.explanation: The statement ignores every middle-ground option — partial cuts, finding savings elsewhere, extra fundraising — and forces a choice between two extremes. A false dilemma presents only two options as if they were the only possibilities, when in reality a range of options exists. Whenever you see "either... or..." phrasing in a persuasive passage, check whether a middle ground has been silently excluded. Memory tip: "Door number three": whenever an argument offers only two doors ("either... or..."), your job is to go looking for the door hiding just out of sight. items.stem: A virus-infected epithelial cell presents a viral peptide on MHC class I. The lymphocyte that recognizes this complex and kills the infected cell is a:

choices.text: CD8 cytotoxic T cell, whose TCR surveys peptide-MHC I
CD4 helper T cell restricted to MHC class II on that epithelium as the sole killing receptor
Naive B cell secreting IgM without MHC restriction
Neutrophil expressing a T-cell receptor that binds MHC I

items.explanation: Almost all nucleated cells express MHC I and display cytosolic (often viral) peptides. CD8 binds the MHC I alpha-3 domain, and the CD8 T-cell receptor recognizes the peptide-MHC I complex, triggering perforin/granzyme or FasL killing. CD4 T cells recognize peptide-MHC II on professional antigen-presenting cells and are helper rather than the classic killers of infected epithelium. B cells bind native antigen with immunoglobulin and do not use MHC to see intracellular viral peptides on the epithelial surface. Neutrophils are innate phagocytes without TCRs.

distractorRationales.B: CD4 is MHC II-restricted and does not mediate the standard MHC I-restricted cytotoxic hit on infected epithelia.
distractorRationales.C: B-cell receptors see extracellular native epitopes, not MHC I-displayed peptides, as the killing mechanism here.
distractorRationales.D: Neutrophils lack TCRs and MHC-restricted clonal antigen receptors.

items.stem: A toddler who has heard only “went” and “went” nonetheless says “I goed to clinic.” Nativist accounts following Chomsky treat such overregularization as evidence for which claim?

choices.text: Skinnerian verbal behavior: every utterance is a reinforced copy of a parental exemplar
Sapir–Whorf linguistic determinism: English past-tense morphology forces the child to invent travel
Children extract abstract grammatical rules (here, add -ed) that they apply beyond the input, consistent with a language-acquisition device and poverty of the stimulus
Wernicke’s area has myelinated, so comprehension errors must produce “goed”

items.explanation: Overregularization shows children are not limited to echoing reinforced strings; they generalize a rule to irregulars they have not heard inflected that way. Chomsky argued that the input is too poor and error-riddled to explain such abstract competence without innate grammatical constraints (the LAD / universal grammar). Skinner’s account struggles with forms that were never reinforced. Whorf concerns thought following language categories, not past-tense invention. Wernicke’s area is an adult lesion story, not toddler morphology.

distractorRationales.A: “Goed” is precisely a form that was not copied from adult input or obviously reinforced.
distractorRationales.B: Whorf does not explain overregularization of inflectional rules.
distractorRationales.D: Toddler overregularization is a developmental grammar phenomenon, not Wernicke aphasia.

passage.title: psg-cars-2
passage.body:
Among the most contested claims in moral philosophy is the assertion that ethical judgments are irreducibly relative to the cultural frameworks that produce them. Cultural relativism, in its strongest form, holds not merely that different societies happen to endorse different moral codes, but that no standpoint outside all cultures exists from which those codes can be objectively ranked. If morality is constituted by social practice rather than discovered through reason or intuition, then condemning another culture's practices amounts to little more than projecting one's own conventions onto alien terrain.
Defenders of this position often draw strength from the anthropological record, which reveals a startling diversity of moral norms across societies separated by time and geography. Practices that one tradition regards as obligatory — ancestor veneration, dowry exchange, arranged marriage — strike others as superstitious, exploitative, or coercive. From this diversity, relativists infer that no norm enjoys a privileged status independent of its cultural home. To insist otherwise, they argue, is to mistake familiarity for objectivity.
Yet the relativist position encounters formidable internal difficulties. If moral judgments are valid only within the culture that generates them, then the reformer who criticizes her own society's practices — the abolitionist in a slave-holding nation, the suffragette in a society that bars women from public life — is simply wrong by definition. Her protest cannot be morally correct because the dominant convention of her society says otherwise. This consequence strikes many philosophers as a reductio ad absurdum: a moral theory that silences the reformer and vindicates the oppressor cannot be adequate.
Universalists reply that moral diversity, while real, does not demonstrate moral relativism any more than disagreement among scientists demonstrates that there are no scientific facts. People may disagree about the boiling point of water and still be wrong; analogously, cultures may disagree about the permissibility of torture yet one of them may be mistaken. The universalist identifies certain core norms — prohibitions on gratuitous cruelty, requirements of basic reciprocity — that appear in some form across virtually every known society, suggesting not conventional agreement but convergent recognition of genuine moral truths.
The exchange rarely ends there. Relativists counter that the universalist's alleged core norms are either too thin to settle any real dispute or are honored more in word than in deed. Nearly every society condemns killing, they concede — yet societies differ profoundly over which killings count as murder, whom the prohibition protects, and when violence becomes duty. A principle so abstract that rival cultures can all recite it while behaving in opposite ways, the relativist argues, marks no genuine agreement at all. Universalists answer that shared abstract commitments are precisely what one would expect if morality tracked real but imperfectly grasped values, and that quarrels over application no more dissolve an underlying norm than disputed measurements dissolve the quantity being measured.
A nuanced middle position distinguishes between first-order moral claims (what is right or wrong) and metaethical claims (what makes moral judgments true or false). One may acknowledge deep cultural variation in first-order norms while still holding that some metaethical framework — natural law, contractualism, or sentimentalism — provides a transcultural criterion of moral evaluation. On this view, the diversity of moral codes is evidence of human fallibility and limited information, not of the absence of any moral standard. Whether such a criterion is ultimately defensible remains among the central unresolved questions of moral philosophy.

passage.title: psg-bb-1
passage.body:
Researchers characterized a bacterial hydrolase, EnzA, that cleaves a colorless substrate into a yellow product, allowing the initial reaction velocity to be measured by absorbance. Working at constant enzyme concentration, saturating buffer, and 37 deg C, they varied the substrate concentration [S] and recorded the initial velocity (v0). As [S] increased, v0 rose steeply at first and then leveled off, tracing the hyperbolic curve expected for a single-active-site enzyme. From these data the team estimated a maximum velocity (Vmax) of 100 micromol/min and a Michaelis constant (Km) of 2.0 mM, where Km is the [S] at which v0 equals half of Vmax.
The team then repeated the assay in the presence of two candidate drugs. With a fixed concentration of Inhibitor A, the measured Vmax remained 100 micromol/min, but the apparent Km rose to 6.0 mM; adding excess substrate fully restored the maximal rate. With a fixed concentration of Inhibitor B, the apparent Km stayed at 2.0 mM, but Vmax fell to 50 micromol/min, and no amount of added substrate recovered the original maximal rate.
A double-reciprocal (Lineweaver-Burk) plot summarized the results: the control line and the Inhibitor A line shared the same y-intercept but differed in slope, whereas the control line and the Inhibitor B line shared the same x-intercept but differed in y-intercept. The researchers concluded that the two inhibitors act by distinct mechanisms, a distinction that matters clinically because it determines whether raising the physiological substrate concentration can overcome the drug's effect.

items.stem: Four otherwise identical E. coli cultures are grown with: (1) glucose only, (2) glucose plus lactose, (3) lactose only, or (4) no utilizable carbon source. lacZYA mRNA is quantified during exponential growth (or, for culture 4, during carbon starvation). Which culture has the highest lac transcription, and why?

choices.text: Culture 1, because glucose is the inducer that binds LacI and catabolite repression activates the operon.
Culture 2, because both sugars must occupy the operator simultaneously before RNA polymerase can bind.
Culture 3, because allolactose inactivates the lac repressor while high cAMP allows the cAMP–CAP complex to recruit RNA polymerase at the lac promoter.
Culture 4, because ppGpp alone fully induces every catabolic operon in the absence of any sugar.

items.explanation: The lac repressor binds the operator and blocks polymerase unless allolactose (from lactose) occupies LacI and lowers operator affinity. Independently, glucose starvation raises cAMP so that cAMP–CAP binds upstream of the lac promoter and strongly activates transcription. Maximal expression therefore requires lactose present (repressor off) and glucose absent (CAP on), which is culture 3. Glucose alone leaves the repressor bound. Glucose plus lactose yields only CAP-independent, lower transcription. Starvation without lactose leaves LacI on the operator; stringent-response ppGpp does not replace allolactose and CAP at lac.

distractorRationales.A: Glucose is the preferred carbon source that lowers cAMP and causes catabolite repression; it is not the lac inducer, and LacI remains bound without lactose.
distractorRationales.B: Neither sugar binds the operator DNA. Glucose plus lactose is the induced but CAP-off condition, not the expression maximum.
distractorRationales.D: Without lactose the repressor still occupies the operator; carbon starvation does not constitutively fire lacZYA via ppGpp alone.

items.stem: Which statement correctly classifies calcium and iron by block and family?

choices.text: Calcium is an alkaline-earth (s-block) metal; iron is a d-block transition metal.

items.explanation: Calcium is [Ar] 4s^2, a group 2 alkaline-earth metal in the s-block. Iron is [Ar] 4s^2 3d^6, a d-block transition metal with a partially filled d subshell and the variable oxidation states that classification implies. Calling both s-block ignores iron's 3d electrons; calling both transition metals ignores that Ca has no d electrons in its ground-state valence set. Calcium is not a halogen (halogens are p-block, group 17), and iron is not an alkali metal (alkali metals are group 1, ns^1).

distractorRationales.D: Calcium is group 2, not a halogen. Iron is group 8/d-block, not group 1. Both family assignments are swapped into the wrong columns.

passage.title: psg-ps-2
passage.body:
A memory researcher tested how the way information is studied affects later recall. In Phase 1, 90 undergraduates saw a list of 30 common nouns, one every three seconds. Each word was preceded by one of three questions: whether the word was printed in capital letters (structural), whether it rhymed with a target word (phonemic), or whether it fit meaningfully into a sentence (semantic). After a filled delay, participants took a surprise free-recall test.
Recall rose steadily with the depth of processing: 18% for structural, 37% for phonemic, and 65% for semantic judgments. In addition, regardless of the processing condition, words from the beginning and end of the list were recalled better than words from the middle. When recall was delayed by 30 seconds of counting backward, the advantage for the last few items disappeared, but the advantage for the first few items remained.
In Phase 2, participants watched a short video of a car approaching an intersection. Afterward, half were asked, 'How fast was the car going when it passed the yield sign?' though the video actually showed a stop sign. A week later, participants who had received the misleading question were far more likely to report having seen a yield sign than participants asked a neutral question. The researchers argued that memory is not a faithful recording but is encoded selectively and reconstructed at retrieval, so that later information can alter what is 'remembered.'

items.stem: An infant-cognition lab (looking-time methods in the Fantz/Baillargeon tradition) presents the same face for eight trials; looking declines. A new face restores looking. After the new face, the original face is shown again and looking briefly rises relative to the last familiar-face trial. Which pair of non-associative processes is illustrated?

choices.text: Habituation to the repeated face and dishabituation (recovery) when the stimulus changes
Classical conditioning to the face, then operant kicking for the new face
Sensory receptor fatigue only, which cannot recover to a new face that uses the same retina
Vicarious reinforcement in Bandura’s sense, because the infant watched the experimenter look

items.explanation: Habituation is a decrease in response to a repeated, unchanging stimulus that is not explained by receptor fatigue or motor exhaustion. Dishabituation is recovery when a new stimulus appears (or, in some designs, when a novel interpolating event restores responding to the original). Infant looking-time exploits that pair to ask what babies discriminate. No CS–US pairing or response–reinforcer contingency is described. Bandura’s vicarious reinforcement is observational learning of a model’s consequences, not waning looking.

distractorRationales.B: No US or reinforcer is paired with looking; this is non-associative.
distractorRationales.C: Recovery to a new face, and often to the original after a novel event, is used to argue against pure receptor fatigue.
distractorRationales.D: The infant is not learning from a model’s rewarded action.

items.stem: A protein of isoelectric point 5.4 is focused to equilibrium in an immobilized pH gradient from 3 (anode) to 10 (cathode). Separately, the same protein is dissolved in pH 7.4 buffer. Which description is correct?

choices.text: It focuses at the anode (pH 3) because acidic proteins always migrate to positive electrodes in IEF
It focuses at the cathode (pH 10) because its pI is less than 7
It focuses at pH 7.4, the pH of blood, regardless of the gradient
It focuses at the pH 5.4 zone of the gradient; in pH 7.4 buffer its net charge is negative

items.explanation: In isoelectric focusing a protein is cationic when the local pH is below its pI and anionic when the local pH is above its pI, so it migrates until pH = pI and the net charge is zero. This protein therefore stops at pH 5.4, not at either electrode and not at 7.4. At pH 7.4, which is two units above the pI, acidic side chains are deprotonated in excess of the remaining cationic groups, so the protein carries a net negative charge and would migrate toward the anode in a uniform-pH gel.

distractorRationales.A: IEF does not park every acidic protein on the anode. Migration stops where pH equals pI, here 5.4.
distractorRationales.B: A pI of 5.4 is acidic, so the protein is not driven to the basic (cathode) end. High-pI proteins focus near the cathode.
distractorRationales.C: The focusing pH is the protein’s pI, a property of its titratable groups, not the pH of a later buffer experiment.

items.stem: In SDS-PAGE, proteins are treated with sodium dodecyl sulfate before electrophoresis. What is the main reason this treatment allows separation primarily by molecular mass?

choices.text: SDS converts all proteins into neutral molecules.
SDS causes smaller proteins to have lower charge density than larger proteins.
SDS separates proteins by boiling point.
SDS gives proteins a roughly uniform negative charge-to-mass ratio.

items.explanation: SDS denatures proteins and coats them with negative charge in approximate proportion to length. This makes charge-to-mass ratios more uniform, so migration through the gel depends mainly on size, with smaller proteins moving more readily. Common miss: Assuming electrophoretic migration always reflects native charge rather than recognizing the role of SDS treatment. This correctly explains the mass-based separation principle of SDS-PAGE. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.A: SDS gives proteins negative charge rather than neutralizing them.
distractorRationales.B: The purpose is to make charge-to-mass ratios more similar, not systematically lower for smaller proteins.
distractorRationales.C: Electrophoresis separates by motion in an electric field through a matrix, not by volatility.

items.stem: Which process is most directly impaired in the Kozak sequence mutant?

choices.text: Protein dimerization by the exon 3 helix

items.explanation: The Kozak sequence helps eukaryotic ribosomes identify the start codon. The mutant has nearly normal mature mRNA and exon 3 inclusion but much lower protein, which is consistent with impaired translation initiation. Common miss: Confusing start-codon context effects with mRNA splicing defects. This matches the role of the Kozak sequence and the observed low protein with preserved mRNA. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.B: Among detected protein, dimeric LUM1 remains high, so dimerization is not the primary defect.
distractorRationales.C: Exon 3 inclusion remains high in the Kozak mutant.
distractorRationales.D: The mutation affects mRNA translation, not DNA replication.

passage.title: Alternative splicing and protein dimerization of LUM1
passage.body:
A fictional eukaryotic gene, LUM1, contains four exons. Exon 3 encodes a hydrophobic alpha-helical segment required for stable LUM1 dimer formation. A regulatory RNA-binding protein, RBP-K, binds an intronic splicing enhancer near exon 3 and promotes exon 3 inclusion. Skipping exon 3 preserves the reading frame but produces a mostly monomeric protein that is degraded more rapidly. A separate mutation in the 5' splice donor of intron 2 causes intron retention and introduces a premature termination codon more than 50 nucleotides upstream of the final exon-exon junction.

Effects of LUM1 expression constructs in cultured cells.
Condition | Pre-mRNA transcription rate (%) | Mature mRNA containing exon 3 (%) | Total mature LUM1 mRNA (%) | LUM1 protein (%) | Dimeric LUM1 among detected protein (%)
Wild type | 100 | 85 | 100 | 100 | 80
RBP-K knockdown | 98 | 20 | 55 | 25 | 18
Exon 3 splice acceptor weakened | 95 | 10 | 50 | 20 | 12
Intron 2 splice donor mutant | 100 | 5 | 18 | 6 | 8
Kozak sequence mutant | 100 | 82 | 95 | 22 | 78
Exon 3 hydrophobic-to-charged coding mutant | 100 | 84 | 98 | 45 | 20

Model for LUM1 isoform production. — When exon 3 is included, LUM1 contains a hydrophobic helical segment that supports dimerization. When exon 3 is skipped, the reading frame remains intact but the helical dimerization segment is absent. Intron 2 retention creates a premature stop codon predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.

items.stem: In a laboratory replication of the classic epinephrine waiting-room study, students receive either epinephrine or saline. Half of the epinephrine group is correctly warned about palpitations and tremor; half is told the shot is inert. Each student then waits with a confederate who acts either euphoric or angry. Which group should give emotion ratings that most closely match the confederate’s mood?

choices.text: Informed epinephrine participants, because an accurate drug label maximizes emotional matching
Uninformed epinephrine participants, because unexplained arousal is attributed using the waiting-room cue
Saline participants, because only placebo arousal can be misattributed to a social cue
All epinephrine participants equally, because catecholamine level fixes the quality of emotion

items.explanation: Schachter–Singer two-factor theory says an emotion is unexplained physiological arousal plus a cognitive label drawn from context. Uninformed epinephrine subjects have a real sympathetic surge they cannot credit to the injection, so they interpret it as euphoria or anger depending on the confederate. Informed subjects already have a sufficient explanation (the drug) and therefore have less need to use the social cue. Saline subjects lack the extra arousal. Catecholamines can intensify arousal, but they do not by themselves select the quality of the feeling.

distractorRationales.A: A correct explanation of palpitations reduces, rather than increases, the need to borrow an emotion label from the confederate.
distractorRationales.C: Saline produces little extra arousal to misattribute, so matching should be weaker, not stronger, than in the uninformed drug group.
distractorRationales.D: Two-factor theory denies that a catecholamine level by itself determines whether one feels anger versus euphoria; the cognitive label does that work.

items.stem: Which ion is amphiprotic in water, able both to donate a proton to water and to accept a proton from water?
items.explanation: Bicarbonate can act as an acid (HCO3− + H2O ⇌ CO3^2− + H3O+) or as a base (HCO3− + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 + OH−). That dual behavior is amphiprotic and is why NaHCO3 solutions are mildly basic (the Kb path is stronger than the Ka path for this ion). Cl− and ClO4− are conjugate bases of strong acids and have negligible basicity and no proton to donate. Na+ is neither a proton donor nor a meaningful proton acceptor in water; it is a spectator cation.

distractorRationales.A: Chloride has no proton to donate and is such a weak base that it does not accept protons from water to a measurable extent.
distractorRationales.C: Sodium ion is a closed-shell spectator; it is not amphiprotic.
distractorRationales.D: Perchlorate is the conjugate base of superacidic HClO4 and neither donates nor accepts protons in water.

items.stem: F+ Escherichia coli that are streptomycin-sensitive and lac+ are mixed with F- cells that are streptomycin-resistant and lac-. DNase is present in the medium throughout the 30-minute mating. Streptomycin-resistant lac+ colonies appear at high frequency. The DNA transfer mechanism is:

choices.text: Transformation with naked chromosomal DNA, which DNase would degrade in the medium
Conjugation through a pilus, which is DNase-resistant because DNA moves cell to cell inside a protected channel
Generalized transduction, which requires a lytic phage lysate that was not provided
Uptake of secreted lac mRNA and reverse transcription in the recipient

items.explanation: F plasmid conjugation transfers DNA through a conjugative pilus/pore. Because the nucleic acid never becomes free in the medium, extracellular DNase does not block the cross. Transformation is defined by uptake of naked DNA and is DNase-sensitive, so it is ruled out by the experimental design. Transduction requires phage particles to package and deliver DNA, which the stem does not supply. Recipients become F+ lac+ (here lac is on the F or cotransferred) while remaining streptomycin-resistant because that chromosomal marker was already theirs. Bacterial recipients do not reverse-transcribe environmental mRNA to gain a stable lac+ genotype.

distractorRationales.A: Transformation uses naked DNA and is blocked by DNase; the high frequency despite DNase excludes it.
distractorRationales.C: No phage was introduced; conjugation between F+ and F- is sufficient to explain the exconjugants.
distractorRationales.D: Stable bacterial alleles are DNA; there is no physiologic reverse transcription of secreted lac mRNA in E. coli.

items.stem: "To be eligible for the scholarship, an applicant must have a GPA above 3.5." A student has a GPA of 3.8 but was rejected for the scholarship. Which statement is best supported?

choices.text: The rule about GPA must be false.
The student's GPA was calculated incorrectly.
A GPA above 3.5 is necessary but was not stated to be sufficient, so other criteria may also apply.
The scholarship committee broke its own rule.

items.explanation: The original statement only establishes GPA as a minimum requirement (necessary), not as a guarantee of selection (sufficient). Rejection despite meeting the minimum is fully consistent with other unstated criteria existing. A necessary condition must be true for an outcome to happen ("you must have X"). A sufficient condition guarantees the outcome on its own ("having X is enough"). Confusing the two is one of the most common traps in GAMSAT Section I logic questions. Memory tip: N is a bouncer at the door: no ticket, no entry — but even with a ticket you might still be turned away for other reasons. S is a golden ticket that guarantees you get in, no questions asked. "Necessary = No entry without it, Sufficient = Ships you straight through." Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

items.stem: A purified tRNA^Ile bears the anticodon 5′-IAU-3′. In a reconstituted translation system it supports isoleucine incorporation in response to AUU, AUC, and AUA but not AUG. Which statement best explains this codon set?

choices.text: Inosine at the wobble (5′) position of the anticodon pairs with U, C, or A at the third position of the codon, reading the three Ile codons; AUG is Met and would require a G that inosine does not stably pair with.
The genetic code is overlapping, so a single IAU anticodon slides across a window that includes AUG as an isoleucine codon.
Inosine is attached to isoleucine by a mischarging event that converts Met-tRNA to Ile-tRNA, allowing the ribosome to skip AUG.
Each isoleucine codon is recognized only by a perfectly matched anticodon, so the IAU tRNA can read solely AUA.

items.explanation: Wobble pairing occurs between the 5′ base of the anticodon and the 3′ base of the codon. Inosine, produced by deamination of adenosine, hydrogen-bonds with U, C, or A, so anticodon 5′-IAU-3′ decodes AUU, AUC, and AUA—the three isoleucine codons. It does not decode AUG, which specifies methionine and presents a 3′ G that is not a standard inosine wobble partner. The code is nonoverlapping and commaless from a fixed start. Inosine is a tRNA nucleoside modification, not a misacylation of initiator tRNA, and degeneracy plus wobble exist precisely so that one tRNA species can read multiple synonymous codons.

distractorRationales.B: Codons are nonoverlapping triplets; the ribosome advances three nucleotides and does not slide IAU across AUG as Ile.
distractorRationales.C: Inosine is in the anticodon loop of tRNA^Ile; it is not a charging defect that converts Met-tRNA into an Ile carrier.
distractorRationales.D: Wobble exists so that a single tRNA can read several third-position variants; restriction to AUA alone contradicts the incorporation data.

items.stem: Hexokinase catalyzes glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP. To which Enzyme Commission class does this reaction belong, and why is ‘ligase’ the wrong label?

choices.text: Hydrolase, because water is the phosphoryl acceptor
Lyase, because ATP is cleaved without transferring a group to glucose

Transferase (phosphotransferase): a phosphoryl group is transferred from ATP to glucose; ligases join two substrates with concurrent NTP hydrolysis rather than transferring a preexisting group onto one of them
Oxidoreductase, because the aldehyde of glucose is oxidized to a phosphate ester

items.explanation: The six EC classes are oxidoreductase, transferase, hydrolase, lyase, isomerase, and ligase. Hexokinase moves the γ-phosphoryl of ATP onto glucose’s C6 hydroxyl, which is group transfer (EC 2.7). Ligases (EC 6) catalyze joining of two molecules coupled to NTP hydrolysis, typically forming new C–C, C–O, C–N, or C–S bonds (DNA ligase, glutamine synthetase, pyruvate carboxylase). Water is not the acceptor, so it is not a hydrolase. A lyase would add or remove groups from double bonds without ATP as a phosphoryl donor. The aldehyde of glucose is not oxidized; C6 is a primary alcohol.

distractorRationales.A: A hydrolase would transfer the phosphoryl to water (ATPase). Glucose, not water, is the acceptor in the hexokinase reaction.
distractorRationales.B: A lyase does not use ATP as a phosphoryl donor to an alcohol. The phosphoryl is transferred, not merely eliminated.
distractorRationales.D: No redox change occurs at carbon. Phosphorylation of an alcohol is not oxidation of an aldehyde.

passage.title: The Hiring Rubric (1980)
passage.body: Kwame Boateng's 1980 essay “The Hiring Rubric,” on vaccine campaigns, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that expertise without a named audience is just private language. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Simply repeating someone's name over and over to remember it is:

choices.text: Elaborative encoding — the most effective strategy

passage.title: psg-ps-6
passage.body:
A study examined how persuasive messages change attitudes. Undergraduates read an editorial advocating a new campus exam policy. The message was either strong (well-reasoned arguments) or weak (superficial slogans), and was attributed either to a distinguished professor or to a first-year student. Crucially, half the participants were told the policy would take effect next year (high personal relevance) and half were told it would begin in a decade (low relevance).
Among high-relevance readers, attitude change depended almost entirely on argument strength and hardly at all on the source; among low-relevance readers, the reverse held - the prestigious source mattered, but argument quality did not. A follow-up a week later showed that attitudes formed by high-relevance readers persisted and better predicted sign-up behavior than those of low-relevance readers.
In a second study, participants who volunteered to argue publicly for a position they privately opposed later shifted their private attitudes toward that position - but only when they felt they had freely chosen to do so and were paid little. Those paid a large sum, or who felt coerced, showed no attitude change.
The authors mapped the first study onto a dual-route model of persuasion: one route processes the substance of a message when motivation is high, while the other relies on surface cues when motivation is low. They explained the second study as the reduction of an uncomfortable inconsistency between behavior and belief, resolved by changing the belief when the behavior could not be justified by an external incentive.

passage.title: Who Counts (1976)
passage.body: Clara Voss published “Who Counts” in 1976 after a season in disaster mapping. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. The piece admits that some gatekeeping keeps fraud out. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: Mental Health Messaging, Stigma, and Help-Seeking Intentions
passage.body:
A campus research group tested how different messages influence responses to a fictional vignette about a student named R who has experienced repeated episodes of sudden intense fear, rapid heartbeat, trembling, and worry about having another episode. Participants were randomly assigned to read one of four messages before viewing the vignette: a neutral campus-services message, a biological-explanation message, a coping-continuum message emphasizing that distress varies in degree and can be managed with support, or a danger-focused message emphasizing rare extreme outcomes. Participants then rated recognition of clinically significant distress, stigma, and willingness to recommend help-seeking.

Mean outcomes by message condition

passage.title: Speed and Care (1983)
passage.body: Owen Blake's 1983 essay “Speed and Care,” on university hiring, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that expertise without a named audience is just private language. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: Gluconeogenic flux in hepatocyte-like cells
passage.body:
Researchers used fictional hepatocyte-like HGL cells to study glucose production from lactate and alanine. Pyruvate generated in the cytosol must enter mitochondria through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC). In the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate carboxylase (PC) uses ATP, bicarbonate, and a biotin cofactor to convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate. Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) then uses GTP to convert oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate. The pathway requires substantial energy input and is sensitive to cellular ATP availability.

Metabolic effects of perturbing gluconeogenesis from lactate and alanine.
Condition | Glucose output (%) | Cytosolic pyruvate (%) | Mitochondrial OAA/malate pool (%) | O2 consumption (%) | ATP/ADP ratio
Control | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 5.0
MPC inhibitor B | 20 | 190 | 35 | 90 | 4.8
PC inhibitor C | 12 | 220 | 28 | 82 | 3.9
PEPCK knockdown | 18 | 120 | 210 | 85 | 4.2
Low-dose ETC inhibitor | 44 | 115 | 82 | 34 | 1.5
Acetyl-CoA analog | 135 | 70 | 155 | 112 | 4.6

Simplified route from lactate and alanine to glucose. — Lactate and alanine are converted to cytosolic pyruvate. Pyruvate enters mitochondria through MPC and is carboxylated by PC to oxaloacetate. Oxaloacetate-derived carbon returns to the cytosol and proceeds through gluconeogenic reactions to form glucose.

passage.title: psg-cars-15
passage.body:
The concept of the unreliable narrator invites readers to question the testimony of a fictional voice that presents itself as authoritative. An unreliable narrator is one whose account of events, characters, or motives the reader has grounds to distrust -- not necessarily because the narrator lies deliberately, but because their perception is limited, their self-understanding deficient, or their emotional investment in a particular version of events distorts what they report. The detection of narrative unreliability is, accordingly, one of the more sophisticated interpretive skills literary fiction demands of its readers, requiring attention to gaps, contradictions, and moments when the narrator's self-presentation strains against the evidence the text itself provides. The concept therefore depends on a tacit collaboration between author and reader carried on over the narrator's head. Behind the speaking voice stands an implied author who arranges the evidence so that a discerning reader can measure the narrator's claims against it, catching what the narrator misses or conceals. This is why unreliability is a matter of degree and of inference rather than a property simply switched on or off: the same first-person account may strike a careless reader as candid and a careful one as riddled with evasions. Recognizing it depends less on any single tell-tale sentence than on the accumulating weight of discrepancies between what is said and what, on reflection, the text as a whole gives the reader reason to believe.
Narrative theorists have identified several sources of unreliability. The most philosophically interesting is self-deception: the narrator who sincerely believes their own account while systematically misrepresenting it, particularly with respect to their own motives and moral quality. Such narrators often generate irony at their own expense -- the gap between what they report and what the text implies about them becomes the site of the reader's critical engagement. A narrator who insists on their generosity in every paragraph while every described action suggests self-interest produces a portrait more damning than any external indictment could achieve.
A second source is cognitive limitation: the narrator who simply lacks the knowledge or experience to interpret correctly what they observe. A child narrator reporting on adult conflicts without understanding their significance, or an outsider narrator describing an unfamiliar culture through inappropriate categories, produces unreliability through innocence rather than self-interest. In such cases, the reader must supply interpretive frameworks that the narrator cannot, and the gap between the narrator's report and the reader's inference becomes the text's most productive space.
A third source, less often discussed, is structural: some narratives are built on multiple competing narrators whose accounts cannot all be true, or on a narrator who explicitly announces their own limitations and invites the reader to read against them. In the former case, unreliability is dispersed across the text; in the latter, it is ironized through self-consciousness. Both strategies challenge the assumption that narrative access to events is, even in fiction, transparent and unmediated.
The broader significance of narrative unreliability extends beyond literary technique. It models a stance of critical reading that has application outside the text: the recognition that all reported experience is shaped by the particular perspective, interests, and cognitive limitations of the reporter -- a recognition that is as relevant to journalism, autobiography, and legal testimony as it is to fiction. Learning to read unreliable narrators teaches a transferable epistemic skill: suspending credulity and attending to the conditions under which any account is produced.

items.stem: Ethanol (CH3CH2OH) and dimethyl ether (CH3OCH3) are isomers, yet ethanol boils at 78 °C while dimethyl ether boils at −24 °C. Which intermolecular-force difference is the principal reason?

choices.text: Ethanol is ionic and dimethyl ether is covalent.
Only London forces operate in ethanol, whereas dimethyl ether is hydrogen bonded at oxygen.
Dimethyl ether has a much larger surface area, so it should actually boil higher; the listed boiling points must be reversed.
Ethanol molecules form O–H···O hydrogen bonds; dimethyl ether can exert only dipole–dipole and London forces.

items.explanation: Both compounds have similar molar mass, so London forces are comparable. Ethanol has an O–H bond, so it can donate and accept hydrogen bonds, which are much stronger than the dipole–dipole contacts available to the ether. Extra thermal energy is required to separate hydrogen-bonded ethanol molecules, raising the boiling point by about 100 °C. Dimethyl ether’s oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond from water but cannot donate one to another ether molecule. Neither isomer is ionic, and the ether does not have a larger elongated surface that would reverse the boiling-point order.

distractorRationales.A: Both compounds are neutral covalent molecules; ethanol’s elevated boiling point is hydrogen bonding, not an ionic lattice.
distractorRationales.B: This reverses the hydrogen-bond donor ability: the alcohol, not the ether, has the O–H needed for H-bonding between like molecules.
distractorRationales.C: The isomers have similar size; the ether is not the higher-boiling compound. The experimental order is ethanol >> ether.

items.stem:

Isomer | bp (°C) | miscibility with water
Ethanol | 78 | miscible
Methoxymethane (dimethyl ether) | −25 | modest

choices.text: Ethanol’s higher bp shows it has the larger molecular mass
Ethanol hydrogen-bonds to itself and to water, raising bp and conferring miscibility; the ether has only dipole and dispersion forces and cannot donate a hydrogen bond
The ether has the higher boiling point because it is more volatile at −25 °C
Both isomers hydrogen-bond identically, so the 103 °C gap is packing of CH3 groups

items.explanation: Both isomers have Mr = 46, so mass is not the discriminator. Ethanol’s O–H group donates and accepts hydrogen bonds, producing a liquid that boils at 78 °C and mixes in all proportions with water. Dimethyl ether has no O–H bond: it can accept a hydrogen bond from water but cannot form an O–H···O network of its own, so it is a gas at room temperature (bp −25 °C) and only modestly soluble. Volatility is high when boiling point is low, not the reverse. Identical hydrogen bonding cannot open a 103 °C gap.

distractorRationales.A: The isomers are C2H6O, identical mass; mass cannot explain the gap.
distractorRationales.C: −25 °C is a lower boiling point, meaning weaker liquid-phase attractions and higher vapour pressure at a given T.
distractorRationales.D: The ether has no hydrogen-bond donor; the isomers are not equivalent.

items.stem: Oncogenic Ras G12V has greatly reduced GTPase activity and is insensitive to GAPs. In serum-starved fibroblasts this mutant, relative to wild-type Ras, will:

passage.title: psg-cp-10
passage.body:
A research team studies both how fast a reaction goes and whether it goes at all - kinetics and thermodynamics, two independent questions. They first examine the decomposition of a reactant, X, measuring its initial rate as they vary the starting concentration at fixed temperature. In three trials the initial concentration of X is 0.10, 0.20, and 0.30 M, and the corresponding initial rates are 2.0x10^-3, 8.0x10^-3, and 1.8x10^-2 M/s. From these data they extract the reaction order in X and the rate constant.
They then vary temperature and find, as expected, that the rate rises steeply as the sample is warmed. They interpret this with the Arrhenius picture: only molecules with at least the activation energy can react, and warming increases that fraction. Adding a catalyst speeds the reaction further, and the team is careful to note what a catalyst does and does not change.
Separately, they assess the reaction's thermodynamics. Calorimetry gives a standard enthalpy change delta_H = +50 kJ/mol, and the standard entropy change is delta_S = +100 J/(mol.K). Using the Gibbs relation delta_G = delta_H - T*delta_S, they compute the free-energy change at 298 K to judge spontaneity, and they determine the temperature above which the reaction becomes spontaneous. They stress that kinetics (how fast) and thermodynamics (how favorable) are separate: a reaction can be thermodynamically favorable yet immeasurably slow, or fast yet unfavorable. They treat delta_H and delta_S as approximately constant over the range considered.

passage.title: The ledger of the commons
passage.body:
When a city puts a park on a map, it appears to have given something away: land that could have been lots, hours that could have been tolls. Developers are not wrong that the gift has a price. They are wrong when they treat the price as a leak from an otherwise watertight private order. The private order is already subsidized by streets, courts, pipes, and the patience of people who do not sue every time a stranger walks past a porch. A park is not the exception to property. It is one of the ways a dense city remains inhabitable enough for property to be worth wanting.

Accountants prefer a ledger in which every square metre has a named owner and a yield. Parks embarrass the ledger because their yield is a crowd that does not pay at the gate, a cooling that does not send an invoice, a child who learns a city can include her without a purchase. The embarrassment produces two crude policies. One is to fence and ticket until the park behaves like a venue. The other is to neglect the park until the crowd looks like a problem that only private security can solve. Both policies claim to be realistic. Both are ways of refusing to count the effects that made the park rational in the first place.

Friends of the park sometimes answer with a poetry of the unowned. The poetry is moving and strategically weak. A commons that cannot speak in maintenance budgets will lose to a spreadsheet that can. The more adult defense is to insist that the ledger is incomplete, not that ledgers are evil. Planting, lighting, toilets, and a gardener who is paid in winter are not betrayals of openness. They are how openness lasts past a ribbon-cutting.

There is a further honesty. Parks are not innocent. They have been used to raise adjacent rents, to move unhoused people out of sight, to display a city’s kindness to visitors who will never need the toilets. Naming those uses does not hand the land to the highest bidder. It prevents the park’s defenders from pretending that green on a map is already justice. Justice would be a park whose ledger includes the people who were priced off the blocks around it.

If urban politics cannot hold that thought, it will keep oscillating between the venue and the ruin, and calling the oscillation pragmatism.

passage.title: Aesthetics — why originals matter
passage.body:
Suppose a forger produces a copy of a painting so exact that no expert, however equipped, could tell it from the original. Most of us would still prefer to own the original, and would pay vastly more for it. This preference is easy to mock as mere snobbery — a fetish for provenance that adds nothing to what the eye receives. If two canvases are visually identical, the skeptic asks, how can one be aesthetically superior to the other? Whatever we are paying for, it cannot be the look of the thing.

The skeptic assumes that the value of a painting must reside entirely in its present visual surface. But this assumption is far from obvious. When I stand before a canvas that Rembrandt himself touched, I am in physical, causal contact with the very object his hand shaped. The forgery, however exquisite, offers no such contact; it is the terminus of a different causal chain, one that runs back not to Rembrandt but to a clever imitator in a rented studio. To value the original is to value that lineage, and there is nothing irrational about caring where a thing comes from.

An analogy makes the point. A letter in a beloved's handwriting is treasured over a flawless photocopy, though the copy conveys every word. We do not think the person who keeps the original has made a perceptual error, as though they had failed to notice that the words are the same. They are responding to something the photocopy lacks: a direct trace of the writer's presence. Paintings, on this view, are less like texts, whose value is exhausted by their content, and more like relics, whose value depends on their history.

Yet the analogy should not be pressed too far. Relics are valued almost wholly for contact and hardly at all for how they look; the point of a saint's bone is not its appearance. Great paintings are not like this. Their history matters, but so, undeniably, does what they show — the very composition and color the forger has reproduced. A defender of originals need not deny that appearance carries much of a painting's worth. The claim is only that appearance does not carry all of it, and that the remainder, however hard to name, is not nothing.

This more modest thesis is also the more defensible one. It grants the skeptic everything plausible in the skeptical position — that the visible work is most of what we prize — while denying the further, unargued step from "most" to "all." The forger's triumph, if it is one, is to have captured the larger share of a painting's value. It is not to have shown that the smaller share was an illusion all along.

passage.title: History — the press and the Reformation
passage.body:
It is often said that the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation. Luther's theses, the story goes, would have died as a local academic dispute had the new technology not broadcast them across Europe within weeks. There is something to this. Print did carry Luther's words farther and faster than any scribe could, and the reformers themselves marveled at the machine — one called it "God's highest act of grace." But "the press caused the Reformation" claims more than the evidence will bear.

Consider what the same presses were printing. In the decades before Luther, Europe's workshops turned out indulgences, devotional manuals, and papal bulls in enormous numbers; the technology served the old church at least as eagerly as it later served its critics. A tool that amplifies whatever message it is given cannot, by itself, explain why one message rather than another swept the continent. To credit the press with the Reformation is to mistake a multiplier for a cause.

The point can be sharpened. Earlier reformers — Wyclif in England, Hus in Bohemia — had advanced doctrines close to Luther's a full century before movable type, and had won substantial followings without it. Their movements were contained, but by armies and inquisitions, not by any shortage of copyists. What differed in Luther's case was not merely the speed of transmission but a constellation of circumstances: a fractured German political landscape in which sympathetic princes could shield him, a literate urban public primed by grievance, and a message pitched to that public's discontents.

None of this makes the press irrelevant. Technologies shape the movements that use them, and a Reformation conducted by pamphlet was bound to differ from one conducted by sermon and manuscript. The press lowered the cost of dissent and widened the circle of those who could join it. But "shaped" is not "caused," and "made easier" is not "made inevitable." The most we can say is that print was among the conditions that allowed the Reformation to spread as it did — a necessary instrument, perhaps, but not a sufficient explanation.

The appeal of the simpler story is easy to understand. Causes that can be named and dated — a machine, an invention — are more satisfying than a tangle of politics, literacy, and timing. But history rarely obliges us with single causes, and the historian's task is often to resist the tidy explanation in favor of the true one.

passage.title: psg-ps-7
passage.body:
Researchers studied how people view themselves and explain behavior. In Study 1, community volunteers completed a scale measuring their belief that they could organize and execute the actions needed to reach specific goals. Independently, they rated how much they felt their life outcomes were controlled by their own actions versus by luck or powerful others. Volunteers high on the first measure attempted harder tasks, persisted longer after setbacks, and reported less anxiety. Those who attributed outcomes mostly to outside forces set fewer goals and gave up sooner.
In Study 2, participants read vignettes about a student who failed an exam. When explaining the student's failure, observers most often cited the student's laziness or low ability, rarely mentioning the situation (an unfair test, a family emergency). Yet when participants recalled a time they themselves had failed, they overwhelmingly cited situational causes. In a variation, participants watched a peer perform poorly under obvious time pressure; even so, most still rated the peer as low in ability.
The authors linked Study 1 to two related constructs: a person's belief in their capability to succeed at specific tasks, and a general expectancy about whether outcomes are internally or externally controlled. They interpreted Study 2 as showing a systematic bias in how observers explain others' behavior, together with a divergence between how people explain their own versus others' outcomes. They stressed that these attribution tendencies operate even when situational information is clearly available.

passage.title: psg-cars-4
passage.body:
History is not the past itself but a selective reconstruction of the past, assembled from fragmentary evidence by scholars whose questions, categories, and assumptions are inevitably shaped by their own time and place. This observation, often associated with the philosophy of history that emerged in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, does not reduce historical writing to fiction. Yet it does demand that historians acknowledge their craft as an interpretive one rather than a neutral transcription of what happened.
The most influential historians have always made choices: choices about which events to emphasize, which actors to foreground, and which causal chains to trace. A military historian who concentrates on battles and generals produces a different account of the same period than a social historian who foregrounds the lives of ordinary laborers, or an economic historian who treats fluctuations in grain prices as the deeper explanatory variable. None of these accounts is simply wrong; each illuminates a dimension of a complex past while necessarily leaving other dimensions in shadow.
Critics of this pluralism worry that it licenses an anything-goes relativism in which no historical account is better than any other. Defenders respond that recognizing the constructed character of historical narratives is compatible with rigorous standards of evidence, logical consistency, and fidelity to the archival record. An interpretation can be shown to be false if it contradicts well-authenticated documents, or shown to be weak if it ignores a large body of relevant evidence. The standards are not arbitrary, even if the questions that animate historical inquiry are themselves products of particular intellectual climates.
A further complication arises from the role of the historical archive itself. Archives are not neutral repositories of the past; they are collections shaped by decisions about what to preserve, who had the resources to produce written records, and which categories of information administrative systems deemed worth tracking. Consequently, the voices most abundantly represented in archives tend to be those of literate elites, state bureaucracies, and dominant institutions, while the experiences of the illiterate, the dispossessed, and the colonized are filtered through the records of those who observed or administered them from a position of power.
Contemporary historians have developed a range of techniques to recover marginalized perspectives: reading documents 'against the grain' of their intended purpose, triangulating between different types of sources, and drawing on oral traditions and material culture as complementary evidence. These methods have expanded the scope of historical knowledge considerably, even as they have deepened awareness that the gap between the past and the historian's account of it can never be fully closed.
None of this counsels despair about historical knowledge. The recognition that every history is written from somewhere, on the basis of imperfect and unevenly preserved traces, is better understood as a discipline than as a defeat. It obliges the historian to state her guiding questions openly, to weigh the silences of the record as carefully as its assertions, and to hold her conclusions as revisable in the light of new evidence or sharper questions. Readers, for their part, are invited to judge a historical account not by whether it achieves an impossible neutrality but by the range of evidence it engages, the rival explanations it takes seriously, and the candor with which it marks the limits of what it cannot know.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most defensible limitation of the author's argument as written?

items.explanation: The passage is strong on a diagnostic implication: legitimacy-by-photograph and coerced averages are not consent. It is modest on substance. The recommended sentence admits a choice; it does not tell a reader how to judge whether the reasons are good. That is a real limitation, not a hole in the conversion mechanism, which is specified through minutes, themes, and ratings. The text also refuses the implication that portals must be abandoned or that recordings exhaust duty. Naming what the argument does not establish is the task; C tracks that gap without inventing a stronger legal claim than the author makes.

distractorRationales.A: The mechanism is specified: crowded-hall photographs, recoding into themes, and averaged stars. The limitation is not absence of mechanism.
