passage.title: psg-bb-11
passage.body:
To characterize kidney function, a renal-physiology team infused test substances into volunteers and measured how the kidneys handled each, using the concept of clearance: the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute. They relied on three markers.
Inulin, a plant polysaccharide, is freely filtered at the glomerulus but neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the tubules. Its clearance therefore equals the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which averaged 125 mL/min in the study. Para-aminohippurate (PAH) is both filtered and actively secreted into the tubule, so nearly all PAH is removed in a single pass; its clearance (about 600 mL/min) approximated the renal plasma flow, a value much larger than GFR. Glucose, by contrast, is freely filtered but then almost completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by carrier proteins; at normal plasma glucose levels its clearance was essentially zero, and none appeared in the urine.
The team then raised plasma glucose experimentally. Below a threshold, urine remained glucose-free. Above the threshold, the reabsorptive carriers became saturated (their transport maximum, or Tm, was exceeded), and glucose spilled into the urine. Because the unreabsorbed glucose held water osmotically within the tubule, urine volume also rose.
The investigators noted that comparing a substance's clearance with the inulin clearance reveals its tubular handling: a clearance below GFR implies net reabsorption, a clearance above GFR implies net secretion, and a clearance equal to GFR implies filtration only.

Blocking the pump lets Na+ accumulate inside, the inward Na+ driving force falls, and concentrative glucose uptake falls even though SGLT is not an ATPase. The trap is to treat 'no ATP hydrolysis at SGLT' as 'insensitive to pump blockade.' Secondary active transport is energetically parasitic on the primary pump.

distractorRationales.A: SGLT does not hydrolyze ATP, so spare ATP is irrelevant, and the pump's inhibition removes the real driving gradient rather than helping uptake.

distractorRationales.D: Pump blockade does not magically insert apical glucose channels as the mechanism of reversal. The SGLT cycle simply loses its Na+ driving force.

items.stem: X-ray intensity follows I = I0 e−μx. The half-value layer satisfies μ x½ = ln 2 ≈ 0.69. A beam has μ = 0.10 cm−1 in soft tissue. What is x½, and what fraction of I0 remains after 6.9 cm?

choices.text: x½ ≈ 6.9 cm; after 6.9 cm, I / I0 = 1/2
x½ ≈ 6.9 cm; after 6.9 cm, I = 0 because one HVL absorbs everything
x½ ≈ 69 cm; after 6.9 cm, I / I0 = 0.90

items.explanation: x½ = ln 2 / μ = 0.69 / 0.10 = 6.9 cm. By definition, one half-value layer leaves half the intensity, so 6.9 cm yields I/I0 = 1/2. The linear attenuation coefficient 0.10 cm−1 is not itself the HVL. One HVL does not zero the beam; it halves it (two HVLs would leave 1/4, and so on). Inverting μ without ln 2, or dropping a factor of ten, produces 69 cm and a 10% attenuation guess (e−0.1 ≈ 0.90 would be 1.0 cm of this tissue, not 6.9 cm). Exponential attenuation is therefore a repeated-halving process at the HVL scale.

distractorRationales.B: 0.10 cm−1 is μ, not x½; x½ = 0.69/μ = 6.9 cm.
distractorRationales.C: Half-value means half remains, not zero; the exponential never drops to exactly zero at finite x.
distractorRationales.D: 69 cm would be 1/μ without the 0.10 placement; e−μx at 6.9 cm is e−0.69 = 1/2, not 0.90.

Premature concurrence-seeking under high cohesion, directive leadership, and insulation, with self-censorship and an illusion of unanimity
Deindividuation in a crowd, which requires anonymity and arousal in a street mob

items.explanation: Janis defined groupthink as concurrence-seeking that suppresses realistic appraisal in cohesive, insulated groups with directive leaders. Symptoms include self-censorship, mindguards, and an illusion of unanimity—the silence after the chair’s cue. Group polarization is a different phenomenon: the group mean becomes more extreme after discussion. Social loafing is reduced effort on additive tasks. Deindividuation is loss of self-awareness in aroused anonymous crowds, not a boardroom consensus failure.

distractorRationales.A: Polarization is an extremity shift after discussion, not the suppressed dissent Janis named.
distractorRationales.B: The stem does not describe unidentifiable additive effort; it describes concurrence-seeking.
distractorRationales.D: Deindividuation is a crowd-anonymity process, not credentials-committee insulation.

passage.title: psg-cars-1
passage.body:
Is there any knowledge in the world so certain that no reasonable person could doubt it? This question, which at first sight might not seem difficult, is really among the most difficult that can be asked. In daily life we assume as certain many things which, on closer scrutiny, are found to be so full of apparent contradictions that only a great deal of thought enables us to know what it is that we may really believe.
Consider the plain table before me. To the eye it appears rectangular, brown, and shiny; to the touch it is smooth, cool, and hard; when I tap it, it gives out a wooden sound. Anyone else who sees, feels, and hears the table will agree with this description, so it might seem that no difficulty could arise. But the moment we try to be more precise, our troubles begin. Although I believe that the table is 'really' of one uniform brown, the parts that reflect the light look far brighter than the rest, and some parts look white because of reflected light. If I move, the parts that reflect the light change, so that the apparent distribution of colours upon the table shifts. It follows that if several people look at the table at the same moment, no two of them will see exactly the same distribution of colours, for no two can view it from precisely the same point, and any change in the point of view changes the way in which the light is reflected.
For most practical purposes these differences are unimportant, but to the painter they are all-important: the painter has to unlearn the habit of thinking that things seem to have the colour which common sense says they 'really' have, and to learn the habit of seeing things as they appear. Here we already meet with one of the distinctions that cause the most trouble in philosophy — the distinction between 'appearance' and 'reality,' between what things seem to be and what they are. The table, if it is 'real' at all, must have some real colour; yet the colour we see is not a property of the table in itself but something depending upon the table, the observer, and the way the light falls. When, in ordinary life, we speak of the colour of the table, we mean only the sort of colour which it will seem to have to a normal spectator, under ordinary conditions of light, from an ordinary point of view. But the other colours which appear under other conditions have just as good a right to be considered real; and so, to avoid favouritism, we are compelled to deny that the table has any one particular colour.
The same holds for the texture. With the naked eye the grain of the wood looks smooth and even; under a microscope it shows roughness, and hills and valleys, and all sorts of differences that are imperceptible to unaided sight. Which of these is the 'real' table? We are naturally tempted to say that what we see through the microscope is more real; yet a still more powerful instrument would reveal something different again, so that we can never rest content with what the eye alone reports. Thus confidence in the senses, which had seemed so secure, begins to desert us.
It becomes evident that the real table, if there is one, is not the same as what we immediately experience by sight or touch or hearing. The real table, if it exists, is not immediately known to us at all, but must be an inference from what is immediately known. Hence two very difficult questions at once arise: Is there a real table at all? And if so, what sort of object can it be?

items.stem: The claim that dropping a person from a census “is often a theory of the state” most nearly implies that

items.explanation: The third paragraph says dropping looks like a mishap and then reclassifies it as a theory: some lives are too expensive, mobile, or inconvenient. The implication is that omission can embody a judgment, not that every omission is a petition or that surveys signal abolition. A restates the appearance the author is rejecting. C invents a formal opt-out. D confuses later remarks about coverage estimates with a motive to abolish boxes.

passage.title: The census of the uncounted
passage.body:
Political arithmetic began as a courtly hobby: a way of estimating how many subjects a prince could tax, feed, or send to war. Its early practitioners treated people as a kind of harvest. What could be enumerated could be extracted. What could not be enumerated was, for administrative purposes, a rumor.

The modern census inherited the appetite and dressed it as representation. To be counted is now advertised as a civic right, a way of appearing in the distribution of schools, clinics, and parliamentary seats. The advertisement is not false. Under-counted neighborhoods do lose clinics. The advertisement is incomplete. A census is also a machine for deciding which kinds of life will be treated as facts and which will remain anecdotes told to a volunteer with a clipboard.

Consider the category. Every census must invent boxes. The boxes are not discovered in nature; they are negotiated among ministries, churches, and, later, identity movements. A person who lives in two houses, or in none, or who works in a language the form does not print, must be forced into a box or dropped. Dropping looks like a clerical mishap. It is often a theory of the state: some lives are too expensive to verify, too mobile to locate, too politically inconvenient to add to a total that will be used against the ministry next year.

Statisticians reply that they already know this, that they publish coverage estimates and post-enumeration surveys, that the professional ethic is to name the error. Naming the error is not the same as refusing the uses of the total. A coverage estimate can become a footnote that licenses the headline number. The public hears fifty million; the appendix whispers that the fifty million is a compromise among several less flattering models. Compromise is not a crime. Treating the compromise as a photograph is.

There is a further twist. Groups that have been historically erased often demand better counting, and they are right to. Visibility in a dataset can be a precondition of funds. Yet the same groups may later discover that a sharper count is also a sharper target: for policing, for debt collection, for the allocation of blame when a service fails. The census does not choose the policy. It does make the policy cheaper to aim.

None of this is an argument for ignorance. A state that refuses to count will invent its numbers in the back room and call the invention common sense. The argument is for a less enchanted relationship to the table. Read the boxes as arguments. Read the missing as a constituency. And when a politician says the numbers speak for themselves, notice that speech is exactly what numbers cannot do until someone supplies a sentence.

passage.title: psg-cars-11
passage.body:
Among the foundational distinctions in the sociology of religion is the division of the world into two mutually exclusive domains: the sacred and the profane. The sacred encompasses all things set apart and forbidden, surrounded by special prohibitions and observed with reverence; the profane designates everything else the ordinary, the utilitarian, the everyday. This distinction is not primarily about supernatural belief. A society without gods can still organize its collective life around sacred objects and practices; conversely, explicitly theistic language can be deployed in contexts so routine that nothing sacred attaches to it at all. The sacred is a structural feature of collective life, not a property of any particular theological tradition.
What makes something sacred is not its intrinsic properties but its relationship to the collective. The sacred object or practice has been designated by the community as set apart, invested with a significance that transcends individual preference and commands a distinctive emotional response. Violations of the sacred provoke not merely practical objection but moral indignation and often the collective sanction of the group. The sacred functions, in this analysis, as a boundary marker: it demarcates what the collective treats as inviolable from what can be freely negotiated, exchanged, or modified. The power of the sacred is thus inseparable from the collective from which it derives and to which it refers. A corollary is that the sacred is hedged about with rules of separation. Precisely because sacred things are set apart, they must be kept from casual contact with the profane: they are approached through prescribed gestures, handled by designated persons, and encountered on appointed occasions rather than at will. Transgression is felt less as a mistake than as a kind of pollution, calling forth rites of purification or punishment rather than simple correction. This logic of separation explains why the sacred can inspire dread as readily as devotion: what is marked off as supremely valuable is also, for that very reason, treated as perilous to handle carelessly. The boundary, in short, is enforced as much by feeling as by rule.
This framework has been applied far beyond explicitly religious contexts. National flags, war memorials, and constitutional documents can function as sacred objects in secular societies: they command a special reverence, their desecration provokes communal outrage, and they focus the collective sense of identity and shared purpose. Academic ceremonies, such as the conferral of degrees and the inauguration of presidents, likewise exhibit a ritualized formality that marks them off from ordinary transactions. The secular and the sacred are not opposites; rather, the sacred is a structural feature of collective life that may attach to entirely secular objects and occasions.
Critics of this framework have worried that extending the concept of the sacred to secular contexts dilutes it beyond usefulness. If anything sufficiently cherished by a community counts as sacred, the concept loses its explanatory precision. Moreover, the framework has been criticized for underplaying internal dissent: in any actual society, which objects are sacred and which are merely important is itself politically contested, and the boundary between the sacred and the profane is drawn by those with the social power to draw it. Sacred designations can thus serve ideological functions, naturalizing existing arrangements by placing them beyond ordinary critical scrutiny.
These tensions notwithstanding, the sacred/profane distinction continues to illuminate the emotional architecture of collective life in ways that strictly rational accounts of social organization cannot easily replicate. Communities that lack shared sacred commitments often struggle to motivate the sacrifices that sustaining collective institutions requires.

items.stem: Among the isoelectronic species O2-, F-, Na+, and Mg2+, the ionic radius is largest for:

choices.text: Mg2+, because it has the most protons pulling on the electron cloud
Na+, because sodium is an alkali metal and alkali cations are always the largest isoelectronic species
O2-, because it has the smallest nuclear charge acting on the same number of electrons
F-, because fluorine is the most electronegative element

items.explanation: These four ions all have 10 electrons (the neon configuration). For a fixed electron count, radius decreases as nuclear charge Z increases, because the same cloud is pulled inward more strongly. Oxygen (Z = 8) has the fewest protons of the set, so O2- is the largest; then F- (Z = 9), then Na+ (Z = 11), then Mg2+ (Z = 12), which is the smallest. Electronegativity of the neutral atom is not the ranking tool for isoelectronic ionic radii, and extra protons shrink rather than expand the ion.

distractorRationales.A: More protons at fixed electron number shrink the ion. Mg2+ is the smallest member of this isoelectronic series, not the largest.
distractorRationales.B: Alkali-metal parentage does not override Zeff. Na+ is smaller than both O2- and F- because sodium has more protons (11) than O or F.
distractorRationales.D: Fluorine's high electronegativity describes the atom's pull on bonding electrons; it does not make F- the largest 10-electron ion. O2- has still fewer protons.

passage.title: The Metric (1975)
passage.body: In “The Metric” (1975), Yuki Tanaka writes from inside public libraries. The argument is that a caption can do the arguing the image refuses to do. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem:
A student mixes 30.0 mL of 0.250 M HCl with 30.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. Both solutes are strong. Amounts before mixing and the total volume afterwards are:

Species | Amount (mmol) | After mixing
HCl | 7.50 | excess H+ remains
NaOH | 3.00 | fully consumed
Total volume | — | 60.0 mL

What is the pH of the final solution?
items.explanation: HCl supplies 30.0 mL × 0.250 M = 7.50 mmol of H+. NaOH supplies 30.0 mL × 0.100 M = 3.00 mmol of OH−. After neutralization, 4.50 mmol of H+ remains in 60.0 mL, so [H+] = 4.50 mmol / 60.0 mL = 0.0750 M. Then pH = −log10(0.0750) = 1.12. Equal volumes do not imply a neutral mixture because the acid is more concentrated. The leftover solute is a strong acid, so the pH is acidic, not 14 minus 1.12. Using the leftover millimoles in only 30.0 mL would give [H+] = 0.150 M and pH 0.82, which ignores dilution by the other aliquot.

distractorRationales.A: 0.82 is −log10(0.150), which uses leftover H+ in 30.0 mL instead of the combined 60.0 mL volume.
distractorRationales.C: pH 7 would require equal millimoles of strong acid and strong base. Here acid millimoles are larger (7.50 versus 3.00).
distractorRationales.D: 12.88 is what one would obtain if the leftover reagent were treated as OH− (pOH = 1.12). The leftover reagent is H+, so the solution is acidic.

passage.title: Electron transport, proton coupling, and cytochrome c release
passage.body:
A fictional study examined isolated mitochondria from cultured liver-derived cells. Investigators supplied either pyruvate plus malate, which generate NADH for Complex I, or succinate, which donates electrons through Complex II. They then added inhibitors or a pore-forming BAX-derived peptide. Oxygen consumption, ATP synthesis, inner mitochondrial membrane potential, and cytochrome c detected outside mitochondria were measured. Values are normalized to untreated mitochondria supplied with pyruvate plus malate unless otherwise noted.

Effects of mitochondrial perturbations.
Condition | O2 consumption with pyruvate/malate (%) | O2 consumption with succinate (%) | ATP synthesis (%) | Membrane potential (%) | Cytochrome c outside mitochondria (%)
Control | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 5
Rotenone | 25 | 90 | 35 | 45 | 5
Antimycin A | 10 | 12 | 10 | 20 | 5
Oligomycin | 35 | 38 | 8 | 130 | 5
CCCP | 160 | 155 | 15 | 15 | 5
BAX-derived peptide | 70 | 72 | 60 | 70 | 65

Simplified map of oxidative phosphorylation. — Electrons from NADH enter at Complex I, electrons from succinate enter at Complex II, both pathways pass through ubiquinone to Complex III, cytochrome c, and Complex IV. Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons to create the proton-motive force used by ATP synthase.

passage.title: psg-cars-8
passage.body:
Ritual occupies a paradoxical place in modern social thought. On one hand, it has been systematically studied as a fundamental mechanism of social solidarity: shared symbolic performances bind participants together, express and reinforce collective values, and mark the transitions — birth, initiation, marriage, death — that punctuate the human life course. On the other hand, modern societies tend to regard ritual with a degree of unease, as if elaborate ceremony were a relic of pre-rational ages unsuited to a world governed by science and voluntary choice.
Early sociological and anthropological accounts emphasized the integrative functions of ritual. Ceremonies, on this view, do not merely reflect an already-existing social order; they actively produce and sustain it. When a community gathers to mark a harvest, a coronation, or a national founding, participants do not simply observe an event — they enact membership in a collectivity that transcends any individual. The shared emotional experience generated by such occasions — what early theorists called collective effervescence — temporarily dissolves the boundaries between self and group, creating a felt sense of unity that persists in social memory long after the ceremony has concluded.
Later anthropologists complicated this functionalist picture by attending to the internal diversity and contestation that characterize real rituals. Ceremonies are rarely performed identically across time or across the different status groups within a community. The ruling class and the subjugated, men and women, elders and youth — each may experience the same ceremony quite differently, and the ritual may serve to reinforce not solidarity across the board but specific hierarchies of power. From this perspective, treating ritual purely as a mechanism of integration ignores its role in legitimating and reproducing asymmetric social arrangements.
A third approach draws attention to ritual's cognitive and communicative dimensions. Rituals encode information in a form — embodied action, sensory symbol, repeated performance — that is particularly durable and memorable. Unlike propositional statements that can be contested or forgotten, knowledge embedded in ritual is resistant to revision precisely because it is experienced rather than merely asserted. This explains why ritual tends to be invoked when other communicative resources fail: in the face of death, catastrophic loss, or radical uncertainty, shared performance provides a structure of meaning that discursive language alone cannot furnish. Grief rituals in particular demonstrate how embodied collective action can sustain communities through episodes of radical disruption that would otherwise threaten social fabric. The contrast with ordinary instruction is telling. A fact conveyed in a lecture can be doubted the moment the lecture ends; a truth rehearsed year after year in fasting, procession, or song is renewed in the body and rarely submitted to cross-examination at all. This is why communities so often entrust their most load-bearing commitments — who belongs, what is owed to the dead, which obligations the future imposes — not to argument but to observance. The very features that make ritual knowledge conservative, and sometimes an obstacle to reform, are also what allow it to hold a group together when argument alone would divide it, carrying shared meaning across generations that never meet.
Each of these accounts captures something genuine. Ritual is simultaneously a mechanism of solidarity, an arena of power and contestation, and a form of embodied knowledge. Understanding any particular ceremony requires attending to all three dimensions and to the historical context that shapes their relative salience.

items.stem: Two cities have the same citywide percentage of Black residents. In City A those residents are evenly spread across tracts; in City B nearly all live in three tracts. The index of dissimilarity is much higher in B. Asthma hospitalizations cluster in B’s segregated tracts despite similar citywide income. Which conclusion is most warranted?

choices.text: Evenness of groups across tracts cannot affect health if citywide composition is matched
Segregation can be measured only in majority-Black cities, so B’s index is invalid
The dissimilarity index measures income inequality only and cannot be computed for race
Residential segregation—the uneven spatial distribution of groups—can concentrate hazards and limit resources even when citywide composition is held constant

items.explanation: Spatial inequality includes how groups are arranged in space, not only each group’s citywide share. The index of dissimilarity quantifies how unevenly two groups are spread across neighborhoods; City B is more segregated despite an identical overall percentage. Segregated tracts can concentrate pollution, poor housing, and weak services, producing clustered asthma that a citywide average conceals. Dissimilarity is routinely computed for race and does not require a majority-Black city. Matching citywide composition is what makes the spatial arrangement the remaining explanation.

distractorRationales.A: The point of comparing A and B is that evenness can differ—and can track health—when composition is matched.
distractorRationales.B: Dissimilarity is defined for any pair of group shares; majority status is not a requirement.
distractorRationales.C: Dissimilarity is a segregation statistic for any two groups, including racial groups, not an income-Gini by another name.

items.explanation: Enterocytes package long-chain fatty acids into chylomicrons that enter lacteals, not blood capillaries, and reach the circulation via the thoracic duct at the left subclavian vein. Nuclear processes are written as parent (Z, A) → daughter (Z, A):

Process 2: (90, 234) → (91, 234)
Process 3: (91, 234) → (92, 234)
Process 4: (92, 234) → (90, 230)
Alpha emission decreases Z by 2 and A by 4. Beta-minus emission increases Z by 1 and leaves A unchanged.
Which processes are alpha emissions?
items.explanation: Process 1 drops Z by 2 and A by 4 (92 → 90, 238 → 234), the alpha signature. Process 4 does the same (92 → 90, 234 → 230). Processes 2 and 3 keep A = 234 while Z increases by 1 (90 → 91, then 91 → 92), which is beta-minus decay (a neutron converting to a proton). Mixing an alpha with a beta, or pairing the two betas, does not match the ΔZ, ΔA rules given in the stem.

items.stem:
Two spherical cells are compared. Cell L has diameter 20 µm (radius 10 µm). Cell S has diameter 10 µm (radius 5 µm). Surface area = 4πr² and volume = (4/3)πr³, so the surface-to-volume ratio equals 3/r. Membrane transport capacity scales with surface area; metabolic demand scales with volume.
Which statement follows?

choices.text: Cell S is more transport-limited because its SA/V is 0.60 µm−1 versus 0.30 µm−1 for L.
The two cells are equally transport-limited because both are spheres with the same 3/r formula.
Cell L is more transport-limited because its SA/V is 0.30 µm−1, half that of cell S (0.60 µm−1).
Cell L is more transport-limited because it has the larger SA/V of 0.60 µm−1.

items.explanation: For a sphere, SA/V = 3/r. Cell L has r = 10 µm so SA/V = 0.30 µm−1; cell S has r = 5 µm so SA/V = 0.60 µm−1. The larger cell therefore has only half as much membrane per unit cytoplasm. Nutrient import, gas exchange, and waste export are more likely to limit L than S. Being spherical does not equalise the ratios, and 0.60 µm−1 belongs to the smaller cell, not L.

distractorRationales.A: A higher SA/V eases, rather than limits, membrane transport relative to volume; S is less limited.
distractorRationales.B: The same geometric formula still yields different numerical ratios when r differs.
distractorRationales.D: L’s SA/V is 0.30 µm−1, not 0.60 µm−1; the larger value belongs to S.

passage.title: Courtesy at the checkpoint
passage.body:
A border official is trained in courtesy as if courtesy were a disinfectant. Smile, use the family name, apologize for the wait. The training manuals are not cynical. They are trying to prevent the obvious cruelty of a raised voice. What they cannot prevent is the deeper grammar of the encounter: one person may leave, the other must persuade a stranger that her life is plausible.

Liberal theory likes to treat this grammar as an unfortunate delay on the way to a principle. In the principle, the stranger is already a rights-bearer; the checkpoint is a bureaucratic remainder. On the ground, the remainder is the event. Rights that must be performed as a story—complete, sequential, tearful at the approved moments—are rights as an audition. The official who says “help me to help you” is not necessarily a villain. He is naming the price of entry into a language that pretends it is only asking for facts.

Scholars of hospitality distinguish welcome from inspection. The distinction is cleaner on the page than in a queue. Inspection can dress as welcome, and welcome can become inspection the moment a detail fails to match a database. A cup of tea in an interview room is not the opposite of a file. It can be the file’s most efficient instrument, loosening speech until it can be contradicted.

None of this requires pretending that states have no legitimate interest in knowing who crosses. It requires noticing that “legitimate interest” is not a measuring cup. It expands. Yesterday’s emergency power is today’s ordinary form. Tomorrow’s form will be justified by the person who told her story too well, or too badly, last year. The archive of interviews becomes a training set for suspicion.

The courteous checkpoint is therefore not a milder politics. It is a politics that has learned to sound like a service. If we want a different politics, we will need a different distribution of who must be plausible to whom—not a warmer script for the same audition.

items.stem: A loud sound triggers a small muscle in the ear to contract and dampen the vibrations reaching the inner ear (the acoustic reflex). Because this reflex takes up to a fraction of a second to engage, it:

choices.text: Protects against a sudden gunshot but not sustained noise
Works equally well for sudden and sustained sounds
Makes the ear more sensitive to loud sounds
Protects hearing during sustained loud noise, like a concert, but not a sudden gunshot

items.explanation: The acoustic reflex is too slow to react to an abrupt, impulsive sound like a gunshot, but it can dampen sustained loud noise once engaged — which is why a prolonged concert is attenuated while a sudden blast is not. Takeaway: The acoustic reflex is protective but slow — it guards against sustained loud noise, not sudden impulse sounds like a gunshot. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Slow onset → useless for an instantaneous blast, useful for prolonged loud sound. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.A: Reversed — the delay means it can't protect against a sudden gunshot.
distractorRationales.B: Its latency makes it selective for sustained sound, not equal for both.
distractorRationales.C: It dampens vibration to protect the ear; it doesn't increase sensitivity.

items.stem: A ball is launched from level ground at 20 m s−1 and 45° in a region where g = 10 m s−2 and air resistance is neglected. Take sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2, so the initial components are each 10√2 m s−1. Maximum height H = uy² / (2g), range R = u² sin 2θ / g, and time of flight T = 2 uy / g. Which set is correct?

Using uy = 20 m s−1 as if the launch were vertical would give H = 20 m and T = 4 s. Halving the range to 20 m confuses H with R/2 or uses only one velocity component in R = u t. Swapping 10 m and 40 m mixes height with range.

items.stem:
Initial uptake rates (nmol min−1 per milligram protein) versus external concentration [S]:
[S] = 0.5 mM: glucose 18, urea 2.1.
1.0 mM: glucose 32, urea 4.0.
2.0 mM: glucose 48, urea 8.1.
8.0 mM: glucose 58, urea 32.
16 mM: glucose 60, urea 64.
Which kinetic reading is correct?

choices.text: Both solutes cross by unsaturable simple diffusion, because both rates increase with [S].
Glucose uses a saturable facilitated carrier; urea crosses by unsaturable simple diffusion.
Urea uses an ATP pump, because its rate at 16 mM (64) exceeds that of glucose (60).
Glucose uses simple diffusion, because a plateau means the bilayer has become infinitely permeable.

items.explanation: Facilitated transporters saturate when binding sites are occupied. Glucose rises from 18 to 58 between 0.5 and 8 mM but only to 60 at 16 mM, so Vmax is about 60 nmol min−1 and Km is near 1 mM (rate 32 ≈ Vmax/2). Urea doubles whenever [S] doubles (2.1, 4.0, 8.1, 32, 64), a linear relation with no plateau, as expected for simple diffusion. A higher urea rate at 16 mM does not imply a pump; pumps would still saturate and would require an energy source, which is not indicated.

distractorRationales.A: Glucose clearly plateaus (58 then 60) while urea does not; an increase with [S] at low concentration occurs for both mechanisms.
distractorRationales.C: Simple diffusion can outrun a saturated carrier at high [S]; rate 64 versus 60 is not evidence of active pumping.
distractorRationales.D: A plateau is the signature of a limited number of carriers, not of infinite bilayer permeability.

passage.title: History — the press and the Reformation
passage.body:
It is often said that the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation. Luther's theses, the story goes, would have died as a local academic dispute had the new technology not broadcast them across Europe within weeks. There is something to this. Print did carry Luther's words farther and faster than any scribe could, and the reformers themselves marveled at the machine — one called it "God's highest act of grace." But "the press caused the Reformation" claims more than the evidence will bear.

Consider what the same presses were printing. In the decades before Luther, Europe's workshops turned out indulgences, devotional manuals, and papal bulls in enormous numbers; the technology served the old church at least as eagerly as it later served its critics. A tool that amplifies whatever message it is given cannot, by itself, explain why one message rather than another swept the continent. To credit the press with the Reformation is to mistake a multiplier for a cause.

The point can be sharpened. Earlier reformers — Wyclif in England, Hus in Bohemia — had advanced doctrines close to Luther's a full century before movable type, and had won substantial followings without it. Their movements were contained, but by armies and inquisitions, not by any shortage of copyists. What differed in Luther's case was not merely the speed of transmission but a constellation of circumstances: a fractured German political landscape in which sympathetic princes could shield him, a literate urban public primed by grievance, and a message pitched to that public's discontents.

None of this makes the press irrelevant. Technologies shape the movements that use them, and a Reformation conducted by pamphlet was bound to differ from one conducted by sermon and manuscript. The press lowered the cost of dissent and widened the circle of those who could join it. But "shaped" is not "caused," and "made easier" is not "made inevitable." The most we can say is that print was among the conditions that allowed the Reformation to spread as it did — a necessary instrument, perhaps, but not a sufficient explanation.

The appeal of the simpler story is easy to understand. Causes that can be named and dated — a machine, an invention — are more satisfying than a tangle of politics, literacy, and timing. But history rarely obliges us with single causes, and the historian's task is often to resist the tidy explanation in favor of the true one.

Alignment at the metaphase plate happens in metaphase, nuclear envelope reformation happens in telophase, and pairing/crossing over of homologs is a feature of meiosis I, not mitosis. items.stem: Starling filtration slightly exceeds venous reabsorption in most capillary beds; lymphatics return the difference plus leaked plasma protein. If lymphatics draining a limb are obliterated, the limb most likely develops:

passage.title: The Caption (1977)
passage.body: Diego Ferreira's 1977 essay “The Caption,” on public libraries, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that expertise without a named audience is just private language. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem:
Acidified dichromate (orange Cr2O7 2− → green Cr3+) is used in excess, then the organic product is characterised.

Alcohol | dichromate colour | product IR after oxidation
CH3CH2OH | orange → green | 1710 cm−1 plus broad 3000 cm−1 (carboxylic acid)
(CH3)2CHOH | orange → green | 1715 cm−1 only (ketone)
(CH3)3COH | orange remains | unchanged 3300 cm−1 alcohol

Which oxidation-level account is correct?

choices.text: Primary ethanol oxidises through aldehyde to carboxylic acid; secondary propan-2-ol stops at the ketone; tertiary 2-methylpropan-2-ol has no C–H on the carbinol carbon and does not oxidise
Tertiary alcohols oxidise most easily, so the orange colour should have vanished
Secondary alcohols give carboxylic acids, matching the 1715 cm−1-only row
All three alcohols are at the same oxidation level because each contains one oxygen

items.explanation: Dichromate decolourisation (orange to green) means the alcohol reduced Cr(VI). Ethanol, primary, is oxidised all the way to ethanoic acid (carbonyl plus very broad O–H). Propan-2-ol, secondary, can lose its one carbinol hydrogen and stops at acetone (carbonyl, no acid O–H). tert-Butanol has no hydrogen on the carbon bearing OH, so Cr(VI) remains orange. Tertiary is therefore the least, not most, oxidisable under these conditions. A ketone IR without the broad acid band is not a carboxylic acid. One oxygen atom does not equalise oxidation levels: RCH2OH, R2CHOH and R3COH sit at different levels.

distractorRationales.B: The tertiary row keeps orange dichromate, experimental proof of no oxidation.
distractorRationales.C: The secondary product is a ketone (1715 cm−1 only), not an acid.
distractorRationales.D: The three different outcomes show three different oxidisabilities.

items.stem: A hydrolase exhibits a bell-shaped kcat versus pH profile with apparent pKa values near 4.5 and 6.5. Mutating a conserved active-site glutamate to glutamine collapses kcat across pH 5–8 to near the uncatalyzed baseline. The glutamate is most likely required as:

choices.text: A residue whose hydrogen-bond donor pattern is identical to glutamine, so the activity loss must be steric only
A carboxylate that must be deprotonated in the active enzyme and cannot ionize after the Gln substitution
The organic substrate itself, meaning the enzyme had been catalyzing glutamate conversion rather than peptide hydrolysis
A residue that sets the pKa of solvent water to 14, without participating in proton transfer

items.explanation: A bell-shaped kcat–pH curve implies that two ionizable groups must occupy specific protonation states during the rate-limiting step. An apparent pKa near 4.5 is in the carboxylic-acid range. Glutamate in the deprotonated form can act as a general base or stabilize a cation; glutamine is isosteric but cannot ionize, so it cannot supply that carboxylate and kcat collapses at all assay pH values. Gln still donates and accepts hydrogen bonds, so a purely H-bond-identical substitution would not explain total loss. The conserved residue is in the enzyme, not the substrate, and water’s pKa in bulk is already ~15.7; the data specifically implicate an ionizable carboxylate.

distractorRationales.A: Gln can mimic some H-bonds but not the negative charge or proton-shuttling of Glu; the activity collapse indicates ionization is essential.
distractorRationales.C: A conserved active-site glutamate is a catalytic residue of the hydrolase, not evidence that glutamate was the substrate.
distractorRationales.D: Bulk water already has a high pKa; the pH profile and the Glu→Gln phenotype point to a catalytic carboxylate.

items.stem: A homodimer is stabilized by an interfacial salt bridge between Arg80 and Glu120. The Glu120Lys mutant remains a single 30 kDa band on SDS-PAGE, but sedimentation equilibrium in native buffer shifts from a 60 kDa dimer toward a 30 kDa monomer. Which interpretation is most accurate?

SDS-PAGE would show a 60 kDa band if the interface were real, so the wild-type dimer assignment was an artifact
Lysine cannot occupy a primary-structure position, so the mutant protein cannot be synthesized

items.explanation: SDS-PAGE reports covalent polypeptide mass after denaturation. An unchanged 30 kDa band means the backbone is intact and the substitution is a simple point mutant. Sedimentation in native buffer reports oligomeric state: loss of the attractive Arg–Glu pair in favor of Arg–Lys repulsion destabilizes the dimer, shifting the equilibrium toward monomer. That is a quaternary-structure defect. SDS always dissociates noncovalent dimers, so wild-type SDS-PAGE is also 30 kDa and does not refute the native dimer. Lysine is a standard encoded amino acid.

distractorRationales.C: Noncovalent dimers routinely run as monomers on SDS-PAGE; native methods are required to see the oligomer.
distractorRationales.D: Lysine is genetically encoded and is commonly introduced by mutagenesis.

passage.title: psg-cars-11
passage.body:
Among the foundational distinctions in the sociology of religion is the division of the world into two mutually exclusive domains: the sacred and the profane. The sacred encompasses all things set apart and forbidden, surrounded by special prohibitions and observed with reverence; the profane designates everything else the ordinary, the utilitarian, the everyday. This distinction is not primarily about supernatural belief. A society without gods can still organize its collective life around sacred objects and practices; conversely, explicitly theistic language can be deployed in contexts so routine that nothing sacred attaches to it at all. The sacred is a structural feature of collective life, not a property of any particular theological tradition.
What makes something sacred is not its intrinsic properties but its relationship to the collective. The sacred object or practice has been designated by the community as set apart, invested with a significance that transcends individual preference and commands a distinctive emotional response. Violations of the sacred provoke not merely practical objection but moral indignation and often the collective sanction of the group. The sacred functions, in this analysis, as a boundary marker: it demarcates what the collective treats as inviolable from what can be freely negotiated, exchanged, or modified. The power of the sacred is thus inseparable from the collective from which it derives and to which it refers. A corollary is that the sacred is hedged about with rules of separation. Precisely because sacred things are set apart, they must be kept from casual contact with the profane: they are approached through prescribed gestures, handled by designated persons, and encountered on appointed occasions rather than at will. Transgression is felt less as a mistake than as a kind of pollution, calling forth rites of purification or punishment rather than simple correction. This logic of separation explains why the sacred can inspire dread as readily as devotion: what is marked off as supremely valuable is also, for that very reason, treated as perilous to handle carelessly. The boundary, in short, is enforced as much by feeling as by rule.
This framework has been applied far beyond explicitly religious contexts. National flags, war memorials, and constitutional documents can function as sacred objects in secular societies: they command a special reverence, their desecration provokes communal outrage, and they focus the collective sense of identity and shared purpose. Academic ceremonies, such as the conferral of degrees and the inauguration of presidents, likewise exhibit a ritualized formality that marks them off from ordinary transactions. The secular and the sacred are not opposites; rather, the sacred is a structural feature of collective life that may attach to entirely secular objects and occasions.
Critics of this framework have worried that extending the concept of the sacred to secular contexts dilutes it beyond usefulness. If anything sufficiently cherished by a community counts as sacred, the concept loses its explanatory precision. Moreover, the framework has been criticized for underplaying internal dissent: in any actual society, which objects are sacred and which are merely important is itself politically contested, and the boundary between the sacred and the profane is drawn by those with the social power to draw it. Sacred designations can thus serve ideological functions, naturalizing existing arrangements by placing them beyond ordinary critical scrutiny.
These tensions notwithstanding, the sacred/profane distinction continues to illuminate the emotional architecture of collective life in ways that strictly rational accounts of social organization cannot easily replicate. Communities that lack shared sacred commitments often struggle to motivate the sacrifices that sustaining collective institutions requires.

passage.title: Who Counts (1977)
passage.body: Diego Ferreira's 1977 essay “Who Counts,” on community radio, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that institutions remember procedures better than people. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: psg-cars-7
passage.body:
Democratic legitimacy, on one influential account, does not derive from the mere aggregation of pre-formed preferences through voting. Rather, it emerges from the quality of the public reasoning that precedes and informs collective decisions. This deliberative ideal holds that citizens who engage in open, reciprocal, and reasoned discourse — genuinely considering one another's arguments rather than simply advocating for prior commitments — are more likely to reach outcomes that are justifiable to all affected parties, regardless of who ultimately wins the vote.
The deliberative model places considerable demands on participants. It requires a willingness to offer reasons that others can evaluate on their merits, not just expressions of passion or assertions of power. It requires a disposition to revise one's views in response to compelling counter-arguments. And it requires conditions of rough equality: if some participants lack the resources, time, or rhetorical confidence to engage effectively, the deliberation is skewed in ways that may reproduce rather than remedy existing inequalities of power.
Critics have challenged the deliberative ideal on several grounds. The most fundamental challenge concerns the status of passionate advocacy. Much of what moves democratic politics — the eloquence of a civil-rights speech, the moral urgency communicated by a protest march, the experiential testimony of those who have suffered injustice — does not take the form of a reasoned argument that invites calm evaluation. To require that all democratic communication conform to deliberative norms risks excluding the voices of the marginalized, whose experiences may be most authentically expressed through modes other than academic debate.
A second critique concerns the domain of the reasonable. Deliberative theory assumes that despite deep disagreements, a set of publicly acceptable reasons can be identified that citizens holding different moral and religious convictions can endorse. Critics argue this assumption is empirically dubious in societies characterized by deep moral pluralism: when citizens disagree not just about policies but about the very framework within which policies should be evaluated, appeals to 'public reason' may function to privilege particular substantive views disguised as neutral procedural ones. The point can be sharpened with an example. When a legislature debates whether assisted dying should be permitted, one citizen may argue from the sanctity of life and another from the primacy of individual autonomy. A demand that each set aside these 'sectarian' premises and reason only from what everyone can accept may sound even-handed, yet in practice it tends to favor whichever background outlook already resembles the supposedly neutral default — often a secular, individualist one. What presents itself as a ground rule for fair discussion, the critics contend, can thus operate as a substantive thesis smuggled in under procedural dress, settling in advance the very questions it claims only to referee.
Defenders of deliberative democracy acknowledge these tensions but argue they point to the need for a more expansive and less rationalist conception of deliberation — one that includes narrative, testimony, and emotional appeal alongside discursive argument — rather than an abandonment of the deliberative ideal itself. If the goal is collective decision-making that citizens can recognize as fair, some approximation of reasoned exchange remains indispensable, even if the form that exchange takes must be more capacious than classical deliberative theory imagined.

items.stem: Teachers are told, randomly, that certain pupils are “late bloomers.” Those children later gain more on an IQ test. Rosenthal and Jacobson’s Pygmalion study is a classroom instance of which process Merton named?

Fundamental attribution error about the teachers’ essays

items.explanation: Merton’s self-fulfilling prophecy (building on the Thomas theorem) is a false public definition that elicits behavior confirming it. Rosenthal and Jacobson randomly labeled children; teachers’ expectancies then altered interaction and measured IQ—the prophecy fulfilled. distractorRationales.D: Faculty concurrence-seeking is not the Pygmalion mechanism.

Effects of mitochondrial perturbations.

Control | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 5
Rotenone | 25 | 90 | 35 | 45 | 5

Simplified map of oxidative phosphorylation. — Electrons from NADH enter at Complex I, electrons from succinate enter at Complex II, both pathways pass through ubiquinone to Complex III, cytochrome c, and Complex IV. items.stem: On a weak-acid + strong-base titration curve, which region is nearly flat (small ΔpH per mL of titrant) and why?

choices.text: The initial point only, because no acid has reacted yet.
The far-basic plateau after equivalence, which is flat because the solution is a perfect buffer of NaOH and water.
The vertical equivalence jump, which is flat by definition.
The buffer region around the half-equivalence point, where added OH− converts HA to A− without large pH change while both species remain.

items.explanation: Buffer action is maximal when [HA] and [A−] are both substantial, which occurs between the start and the equivalence point and is centered at half-equivalence (pH = pKa). Added strong base is consumed by HA, so pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]) changes only as the log ratio changes—slowly. The equivalence region is the opposite: a tiny increment of titrant swings the pH through many units (steep, not flat). After equivalence the curve tracks excess NaOH and rises, but that is not the HA/A− buffer. The initial weak-acid point is not a buffer until some A− has been generated.

distractorRationales.A: The starting weak-acid solution has almost no A− and is not well buffered; the first additions of base change pH faster than in the mid-buffer region.
distractorRationales.B: Excess strong base is not a conventional buffer; pH still changes with each added milliliter, though more slowly than at equivalence.
distractorRationales.C: The equivalence jump is the steepest part of the curve, used to locate the endpoint, not a flat region.

passage.title: What the metronome cannot hear
passage.body:
Musicology has a long habit of treating the score as the work and the performance as a more or less obedient copy. The habit is understandable. Paper sits still. It can be compared, edited, and taught in rooms where no instrument is present. A performance disappears as it occurs, leaving only memory, a recording, or an argument.

Yet the stillness of paper is not neutrality. Notation is a technology with a history: it captures some relations (pitch against a staff, duration against a beat) and lets others leak away (the weight of a bow, the delay before a singer accepts a consonant, the social fact of who is allowed to ornament). When a textbook says a movement is “in three,” it is reporting a notational decision that a village dance may never have made in those terms. The metronome, arriving later still, offers a fantasy that time is a ruler laid beside sound. Dancers know otherwise. So do jazz rhythm sections, whose time is a negotiation, not a grid that failed.

Scholars who defend the score-as-work often point to the composer’s authority and to the need for a shared object of study. Without a text, they say, we are left with impressions. The worry is real in a university. It is less real in a tradition that already treats the night’s playing as the work, and the paper, if paper exists, as a prompt. To call that tradition incomplete because it will not sit still is to confuse the archive’s convenience with the art’s ontology.

Recordings seemed to solve the disappearance problem. They created a new paper: a fixed take that can be looped, transcribed, and worshipped. The solution smuggles in its own politics. Which night was recorded, from which seat, with which microphone aiming at which social center of the band? A “definitive” recording can freeze a hierarchy that a living scene would have kept in motion. The fan who owns every take may know more facts than a player and still know less about what the music is for.

The practical upshot is not to burn scores. Scores are superb tools, as maps are superb tools. The upshot is to stop calling the map the territory in order to make seminars easier to grade. A pedagogy that can only hear what the metronome can hear will keep producing excellent accountants of pitch and a thin audience for everything else. If musicology wants to study music rather than the paperwork of music, it will have to tolerate objects that do not hold still, and to admit that some of the most precise information arrives as a glance between players that no staff line was built to hold.

passage.title: Electrochemical Monitoring of Dissolved Oxygen
passage.body:
A fictional microfluidic device is designed to monitor oxygen consumption by cultured cells. The device contains a 10.0 mL sealed gas headspace above an aqueous medium. At the working electrode, oxygen is reduced according to: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O. A 3.0 V source drives current through a variable series resistor and the electrode system. In the tested range, electrode current is approximately proportional to oxygen partial pressure unless the electrode becomes limited by oxygen diffusion from the bulk solution. A pressure sensor in the chamber acts as a parallel-plate capacitor. When gas pressure increases, a flexible membrane deflects toward the fixed plate, decreasing the plate separation d. Before each run, the headspace is sealed, and the table reports conditions just before current is measured.

Operating conditions and measured current for the oxygen sensor.
Run | Headspace O2 mole fraction | Temperature (K) | Total pressure before measurement (atm) | Series resistance (ohm) | Measured current (mA)
R1 | 0.21 | 298 | 1.00 | 1000 | 1.8
R2 | 0.21 | 310 | 1.04 | 1000 | 1.9
R3 | 0.10 | 298 | 1.00 | 1000 | 0.86
R4 | 0.21 | 298 | 1.00 | 500 | 2.4
R5 | 0.21 | 298 | 1.00 | 2000 | 0.95

Current response of the oxygen electrode. — For runs with 1000 ohm resistance, measured current increases approximately linearly with oxygen mole fraction. At lower resistance, the current increases less than expected from Ohm's law, consistent with a diffusion-limited plateau.

passage.body:
A fictional arylpropionic acid, compound C, has two enantiomers labeled R-C and S-C. The carboxylic acid group has pKa = 4.4. A chiral stationary phase contains hydrophobic binding pockets and protonated amine sites. Neutral analytes interact mainly through hydrophobic contacts, while carboxylate forms can also interact electrostatically. Very high salt concentrations can screen electrostatic interactions. items.stem: In a coffee-cup calorimeter, 2.00 g of KNO3 (101.1 g mol−1) dissolves in 50.0 g of water. The temperature falls from 25.00 °C to 22.60 °C. Take the solution mass as 52.0 g and c = 4.18 J g−1 °C−1. What is ΔH_soln per mole of KNO3?

choices.text: −26.4 kJ mol−1, because any temperature change in a calorimeter is reported as a negative enthalpy
+52.2 kJ mol−1, using q = m c ΔT without dividing by moles
+26.4 kJ mol−1, because dissolution absorbed heat from the solution (endothermic) and q_rxn = −q_solution
+13.2 kJ mol−1, from accidentally doubling the number of moles

items.explanation: A coffee-cup calorimeter operates at constant pressure, so q_p = ΔH for the process inside. The solution’s temperature drop means the solution lost heat: q_solution = (52.0 g)(4.18 J g−1 °C−1)(−2.40 °C) = −522 J. Heat conservation requires q_rxn = −q_solution = +522 J, so dissolution is endothermic. Dividing by n = 2.00/101.1 = 0.0198 mol gives ΔH = +26.4 kJ mol−1. The sign tracks the observed cooling; omitting the mole conversion or doubling n produces the numeric traps.

distractorRationales.A: The calorimeter cools, which means the chemical process absorbed heat. ΔH_soln is positive, not negative.
distractorRationales.B: q_rxn ≈ +522 J is the enthalpy change for 2.00 g, not for one mole. Molar ΔH requires division by 0.0198 mol.
distractorRationales.D: Using n = 0.0396 mol (as if the formula weight were applied twice) halves the molar enthalpy to 13.2 kJ mol−1.

items.stem:
A microphone records the superposition of two nearby pure tones. A Fourier analysis of a 2.00 s recording lists:

Component | Frequency (Hz)
Tone 1 | 440
Tone 2 | 436

The beat frequency is |f1 − f2|. Intensity maxima occur once per beat period. How many loud intensity maxima occur in the 2.00 s recording, and what is the beat frequency?

choices.text: Beat frequency 4 Hz, so 8 maxima in 2.00 s.
Beat frequency 4 Hz, so 4 maxima in 2.00 s.
Beat frequency 438 Hz, so 876 maxima in 2.00 s.
Beat frequency 876 Hz, so 1752 maxima in 2.00 s.

items.explanation: The beat frequency is |440 − 436| = 4 Hz, so the intensity envelope repeats 4 times each second. In 2.00 s there are 4 × 2.00 = 8 loud maxima. Counting only 4 maxima in 2 s confuses the beat frequency with the number of events in 2 s (forgetting to multiply by the duration). The arithmetic mean 438 Hz is the average of the two tones, not the beat rate. The sum 876 Hz is an upper sideband of a nonlinear mixer, not the slow envelope. The table’s two frequencies are close, which is exactly the condition under which beats are heard as a slow wavering of loudness at the difference frequency.

distractorRationales.B: The beat frequency is 4 Hz, but 4 Hz means 4 maxima per second, hence 8 in 2.00 s, not 4. Duration must be multiplied in.
distractorRationales.C: 438 Hz is the mean of 440 and 436. Beats are heard at the difference, not at the average pitch.
distractorRationales.D: 876 Hz is the sum of the two frequencies. The slow loudness variation is the difference 4 Hz, not the sum.

items.stem: A hand-therapy clinic maps just-noticeable differences for hidden grip-weights. Against a 200 g standard, patients first report a change when the increment is 6 g. Weber’s law is assumed to hold over this range. Which increment should be just noticeable against a 500 g standard?

choices.text: 15 g, because the ratio of increment to standard intensity is constant
6 g, because the just-noticeable difference is a fixed mass independent of the standard
2.4 g, because sensitivity improves linearly as the standard grows
500 g, because the comparison must equal the standard before a difference can be felt

items.explanation: Weber’s law states that the just-noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the standing intensity, ΔI/I = k. Here k = 6/200 = 0.03, so a 500 g standard requires about 15 g. Fechner later integrated that ratio into a logarithmic sensation scale, but the clinic’s prediction is the Weber fraction itself. Absolute threshold is detection from zero, not a difference from a standing weight. Signal-detection theory concerns hits and false alarms, not this ratio.

distractorRationales.B: A constant absolute increment is the opposite of Weber’s law; the increment must scale with the standard.
distractorRationales.C: Weber’s law makes the absolute increment larger, not smaller, as intensity rises (k held constant).
distractorRationales.D: Equality with the standard would be a 100 percent change, far above a typical Weber fraction.

items.stem: Which statement best captures what the extract as a whole is saying?

choices.text: Estate agents are uniquely cruel, and carpet cleaning is a form of theft from the bereaved.
Legal vacancy and a cleared rental can coexist with objects and habits that still assign tasks, so grief here is less a passing weather than an unanswered list.
The speaker decides that buying milk will bring her father back, and the poem proves supernatural continuance.
Poetry taped in cupboards is always a confession of a secret literary career the family refused to honour.

items.explanation: The piece moves from the agent's tidy phrase through remaining marks, a list, a poem about a week that never arrived, and a daughter who almost ticks milk. Its claim is that emptiness in law is not emptiness in the present tense of objects and unfinished care. It does not prosecute agents as thieves, promise resurrection by shopping, or unmask a hidden career. A main-claim answer must sit inside that modest, exact complaint about vacant possession and assigned tasks, which only B does.

distractorRationales.A: The speaker says the agent is not unkind and is on a clock; the target is a legal sentence, not a morality play about cruelty.
distractorRationales.C: Ticking milk is called a joke at her own expense and a ridiculous want, not a magical program; the poem addresses a week that never arrived.
distractorRationales.D: He is explicitly not a man who announced poems; the scrap is intimate remainder, not evidence of a suppressed vocation.

passage.title: Vacant possession
passage.body:
The rental had been emptied with the efficiency of people who did not live there. I arrived after the skip had gone. What remained were the marks of remaining: a paler rectangle on the wall where a calendar had blocked the sun, a screw in the kitchen plaster that had held nothing I could remember, a ring on the lino where a bin had sat long enough to become a climate. The agent called it "vacant possession." The phrase was legally tidy. It treated my father as a tenancy that had concluded.

I opened the cupboard above the kettle. Inside, taped to the wood, was a shopping list in his slanted capitals, and beneath it a scrap of verse I had never seen. He was not a man who announced poems. He had been a man who boiled water at the same hour, as if the day were a machine that required a particular ignition. The list wanted milk, soap, and a cheaper brand of tea. The last item was written twice, then crossed out, then written again, as if indecision were a kind of company.

The kettle still knew his hour.
I did not.
The cupboard kept a shopping list
addressed to a week that never arrived.
I ticked the milk as if the ticking
could make a future stand up.

I stood with a pen I had not meant to bring and put a mark beside milk, then stopped, because the gesture had the shape of care and the content of a joke at my own expense. Grief, in the pamphlets, is supposed to be a weather that passes over a landscape. In the cupboard it was more like a task left in a shared kitchen: unclaimed, slightly shameful, still assigned. I wanted, ridiculously, to buy the milk. I wanted not to be the kind of daughter who leaves a list unanswered.

The agent coughed in the hallway and mentioned carpet cleaning, then the bond, then the need to "move on" as if the room were a queue. I heard myself thank him. Courtesy was easier than explaining that the room was not empty, only unpopulated. He was not unkind. He was on a clock I did not share. Vacant possession, I thought, is a legal sentence that cannot conjugate the present tense of objects. The kettle, if it could speak, would not have used it. It would have asked why the hour had been cancelled without notice.

items.stem: Each time a normal human somatic cell divides, its telomeres (repetitive DNA caps on chromosome ends) tend to:

choices.text: Shorten, eventually contributing to replicative senescence when they become too short

items.explanation: Because DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate the ends of linear chromosomes (the end-replication problem), telomeres shorten with each division; when they become critically short, the cell stops dividing (replicative senescence). passage.title: Care and Speed (1977)
passage.body: Pavel Hrdlička's 1977 essay “Care and Speed,” on vaccine campaigns, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that fairness talk often arrives after the decision has already been made. The piece admits that some gatekeeping keeps fraud out. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: From Table 2, the initial velocity estimated from the 0 s and 20 s product concentrations is closest to which value?
items.explanation: Table 2 reports 19.6 μM product at 20 s and 0.0 μM at 0 s, so the early-time rate is 19.6/20 = 0.98 μM s^{-1}. That window is the one the experimenters would treat as an initial rate: Table 2 is still nearly linear through 20–30 s, whereas averaging to 120 s (102.4/120 ≈ 0.85 μM s^{-1}) already shows curvature from substrate depletion. The value 2.0 μM s^{-1} is the assay V_max expected from 80 nmol s^{-1} mg^{-1} times 0.025 mg in 1.00 mL at saturating S, not the rate at [S]_0 = K_m. 0.16 μM s^{-1} would follow if 2 μg rather than 25 μg of enzyme had been used. Only the 0 s and 20 s pair in Table 2 yields 0.98.

distractorRationales.A: 0.16 μM s^{-1} matches an assay loaded with 2 μg of enzyme at the Table 1 specific activity, not the 25 μg progress curve actually described.
distractorRationales.B: 0.85 μM s^{-1} is 102.4 μM divided by 120 s, an average over a curved progress trace rather than an initial slope from the 0–20 s points.
distractorRationales.D: 2.0 μM s^{-1} is the saturating-S assay V_max in the 1.00 mL cuvette (80 nmol s^{-1} mg^{-1} × 0.025 mg); Table 2 starts at [S] = K_m, so the initial rate should be near half of that ceiling.

passage.title: Reversible inhibitors of a cytosolic dehydrogenase
passage.body:
Investigators purified a cytosolic NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase that oxidizes a small-molecule metabolite S. Initial velocities were measured at 25 °C by following NADH formation in 1.00 mL assays. Nonlinear fits of v versus [S] produced the apparent Michaelis constants and maximal velocities in Table 1. When an inhibitor was present, its concentration was 2.0 μM in the assay mix. Dialysis that removed unbound compound restored full catalytic activity after incubation with P, Q, or R, indicating reversible binding rather than covalent inactivation. Active-site titration with a tight-binding stoichiometric inactivator found 4.0 nmol of catalytic sites per milligram of protein.

Table 1. Apparent kinetic parameters from initial-rate fits

| Condition | Apparent K_m (mM) | Apparent V_max (nmol s^{-1} mg^{-1}) |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------------------------|
| No inhibitor | 0.50 | 80 |
| Compound P (2.0 μM) | 0.50 | 40 |
| Compound Q (2.0 μM) | 1.50 | 80 |
| Compound R (2.0 μM) | 0.25 | 40 |

In a separate progress-curve experiment, 25 μg of the same enzyme protein was mixed with 0.50 mM S and no inhibitor in a 1.00 mL reaction. Product concentration was recorded as a function of time (Table 2).

Table 2. Product appearance at [S]_0 = 0.50 mM without inhibitor

| Time (s) | [Product] (μM) |
|----------|----------------|
| 0 | 0.0 |
| 10 | 9.9 |
| 20 | 19.6 |
| 30 | 29.1 |
| 60 | 56.2 |
| 120 | 102.4 |

items.explanation: The analogy has to map same intensity, different moral labels, tracking prestige. Dress codes that rename the same scuff according to who wears it preserve that structure. A physics classroom that refuses the distinction is the meter the author says officials are not; a total ban is the unlimited-noise opposite the fourth paragraph declines; compressor studies are the genuine public-health work the first paragraph grants. Hypothetical mapping fails if it erases the double uniform or if it substitutes the health concession for the hypocrisy claim. A keeps the hypocrisy without denying that some health measurements are real.

distractorRationales.C: The author rejects both unlimited noise and the romance of the unregulated street; a total ban is not the analogue of two uniforms.

passage.title: Who may be loud
passage.body:
Noise ordinances are written as if they were thermometers. A number of decibels is named; a clock hour is named; a fine is attached. The language of public health does real work here: sleep is not a luxury, and a child whose window faces a compressor is not being precious. But the thermometer conceals a second instrument, which is a social sorting device. Cities do not merely suppress loudness. They decide which kinds of loudness will be classified as vitality and which as nuisance, and the decision tracks, with embarrassing regularity, the prestige of the people making the sound.

Walk a mixed street after dark and the taxonomy is audible. A licensed terrace with heaters and a playlist is "activation of the night-time economy." A storefront church whose singing lasts past the same hour is a complaint waiting to be logged. A terrace is a business; a congregation is a disturbance that happens to own a building. Street vendors packing ice and calling prices are "chaos"; a restaurant's Friday overflow onto the pavement is "vibrancy," provided the overflow has paid for a permit. The ear that writes the ordinance has already been trained to hear money as atmosphere and unpaid sound as aggression.

Defenders of the ordinances will say that the issue is volume, not culture. Sometimes it is. A speaker stack aimed at a bedroom is a harm whether the music is sacred or commercial. The author's claim is narrower and more awkward: when two sounds of similar intensity are sorted differently, the sorting is not acoustics. It is a theory of who belongs in the air. "Quiet" is then sold as a natural baseline, like clean water, when it is often an aesthetic associated with certain housing and certain hours of salaried rest. Night-shift workers returning at dawn, whose rest is real, rarely get to define the city's sonic morals. People who sleep when the ordinance writers sleep do.

None of this is a brief for unlimited noise, or for the romance of the unregulated street. A city that cannot protect sleep will punish the poorest first, because they cannot buy distance from compressors. The decent aim is not a louder city but a less hypocritical one: a city that admits that permission to be loud is a scarce good, distributed by licensing, policing, and taste, and that "quality of life" is never only a medical phrase. It is also a claim about whose life is the measure.

The rhetorical trick is hygiene. Once noise is framed as dirt, opposition to a particular sound can wear the costume of sanitation rather than of preference. Dirt, unlike preference, does not have to justify itself at a public meeting. It only has to be pointed at. That is why a campaign against a night market can speak the idiom of rats and refuse even when the photographs show swept stones, and why a campaign for a waterfront festival can speak the idiom of civic joy even when the sound spill is identical. The same wave-form, two moral uniforms.

If the argument holds, then reform is not a new app for logging complaints. It is a requirement that like sounds be given like reasons, and that exemptions be named as political choices rather than as nature. A hospital generator may deserve its exemption. So, perhaps, does a funeral that spills into a street. What cannot be defended is the pretense that the ordinance is only a meter reading. Meters do not know the difference between a hymn and a brand. Officials do, and they should have to say so.

passage.title: Construction Site (1981)
passage.body: In “Construction Site” (1981), Priya Raman writes from inside a coastal fishery. The argument is that local knowledge is treated as anecdote until a model needs it. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. items.stem:
A runner’s velocity–time graph consists of three straight-line segments:

Interval | v(t)
0 to 4.0 s | v increases linearly from 0 to 8.0 m s−1
4.0 to 10.0 s | v is constant at 8.0 m s−1
10.0 to 12.0 s | v decreases linearly from 8.0 m s−1 to 0

Displacement equals the signed area under a v–t graph. What is the runner’s displacement from t = 0 to t = 12.0 s?
items.explanation: The area is a triangle of base 4.0 s and height 8.0 m s−1, plus a rectangle 6.0 s by 8.0 m s−1, plus a triangle of base 2.0 s and height 8.0 m s−1. Those areas are (1/2)×4.0×8.0 = 16 m, 6.0×8.0 = 48 m, and (1/2)×2.0×8.0 = 8 m, which sum to 72 m. Using only the constant-speed rectangle gives 48 m. Omitting the final triangle gives 64 m. Multiplying the peak speed by the total time (8.0 × 12) gives 96 m, which would be valid only if v were 8.0 m s−1 for the whole 12 s. All three segments contribute positive area because v never reverses.

distractorRationales.A: 48 m is only the rectangular middle segment. The two triangular areas (16 m and 8 m) must be added.
distractorRationales.B: 64 m is the first triangle plus the rectangle, omitting the 8 m triangle during deceleration from 10 s to 12 s.
distractorRationales.D: 96 m is (8.0 m s−1)×(12 s), as if the runner held peak speed for the entire interval instead of accelerating and then stopping.

items.stem:
A sealed respirometer records gas exchange of isolated muscle fibres. Complete oxidation of glucose is C6H12O6 + 6 O2 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O (respiratory quotient RQ = CO2 produced / O2 consumed = 1.00). Complete oxidation of palmitate is C16H32O2 + 23 O2 → 16 CO2 + 16 H2O (RQ = 16/23 ≈ 0.70).
Run 1: 12 mmol O2 consumed, 12 mmol CO2 produced.
Run 2: 10 mmol O2 consumed, 7 mmol CO2 produced.
Which fuel use is consistent with the two runs?

choices.text: Run 1 is carbohydrate oxidation (RQ = 1.00); Run 2 is close to fatty-acid oxidation (RQ = 0.70).
Run 1 is fatty-acid oxidation because equal moles of the two gases always indicate fat.
Run 2 is carbohydrate oxidation because more O2 than CO2 always indicates sugar.
Both runs have RQ = 1.00 once the 23 and 6 stoichiometric coefficients are ignored.

items.explanation: RQ is the measured mole ratio, not a count of carbons alone. Run 1 gives 12/12 = 1.00, matching glucose. Run 2 gives 7/10 = 0.70, matching the palmitate stoichiometry 16/23. Fat oxidation consumes extra O2 to oxidise the more reduced hydrocarbon chain, so CO2 < O2. Equal gas volumes do not diagnose fat; that pattern is carbohydrate. The coefficients 6 and 23 are exactly what generate the two distinctive RQ values.

distractorRationales.B: Equal moles of CO2 and O2 give RQ = 1, the carbohydrate signature, not the fat signature of ~0.70.
distractorRationales.C: Carbohydrate has RQ = 1, so O2 and CO2 match; Run 2’s excess O2 consumption is the fat pattern.
distractorRationales.D: Dropping the stoichiometric coefficients would erase the definition of RQ; the data already give 1.00 and 0.70.
