passage.title: Gas Collection During Electrolysis of a Buffer
passage.body:
A fictional laboratory exercise uses water electrolysis to calibrate a gas-volume sensor. At the cathode, hydrogen gas forms according to: 2H2O + 2e- -> H2 + 2OH-. At the anode, oxygen gas forms separately and is not collected in the cathode tube. The cathode gas is collected over water. At 298 K, the vapor pressure of water is 0.031 atm. The gas collection tube is adjusted so that the total pressure of the collected gas equals 1.031 atm. The Faraday constant is 96500 C/mol e-. A 6.0 V source supplies the cell through external circuit elements.

Electrolysis trials and collected cathode gas.
Trial | Current (A) | Time (s) | Total gas pressure (atm) | Temperature (K) | Collected cathode gas volume (mL)
1 | 0.100 | 1930 | 1.031 | 298 | 24.0
2 | 0.100 | 3860 | 1.031 | 298 | 48.0
3 | 0.200 | 1930 | 1.031 | 298 | 46.5
4 | 0.100 | 1930 | 1.031 | 310 | 25.0

Cathode gas collection apparatus. — Hydrogen produced at the cathode bubbles into an inverted graduated tube filled with water. The gas volume is read after equalizing the water levels inside and outside the tube.

items.stem: How is the author's admission that “some rooms change designs” best reconciled with the critique of participation rituals?

choices.text: It is a contradiction the passage never notices, because any revision would make attendance identical with consent.
It is a sarcastic aside that the author immediately withdraws by calling all ramps imaginary.

items.explanation: Internal consistency turns on whether the concession cancels the thesis. The third paragraph says revisions matter and that a different piety would deny them, then names the actual target: the theory that any revision proves the process and that remaining grievance is leftover noise from people who had their chance. Attendance made to do the work of consent can coexist with occasional ramps. There is no later withdrawal of the ramp example, and the closing preference is for attributable 'proceeding anyway' over the listening-face photograph. The concession is therefore a scope limit, not a hidden reversal.

passage.title: Minutes as consent
passage.body:
City governments have learned to speak the language of invitation. A new waterfront, a bus garage, a night-time licensing scheme: each arrives with a room, a facilitator, sticky notes, and a promise that "your voice will be heard." The promise is not empty in the way cynics assume. People do speak. Minutes are taken. A summary slide later reports that the community was "engaged." What the ritual converts, with almost chemical reliability, is dissent into attendance. The fact of having been in the room is then cited as evidence that the decision which followed was shared.

This conversion is the point, not an accidental side-effect. A planning authority that can display a photograph of a crowded hall has already performed legitimacy. The photograph does not record what was refused, only that refusal was given a chair. Once refusal has a chair, it can be filed. The file then travels upward as proof of consultation, and the project proceeds under the borrowed moral credit of those who came to object. Objectors discover, sometimes only at the groundbreaking, that they were extras in a scene titled participation.

The objection is not that consultation is a trick in every case. Some rooms change designs. A ramp is added; a tree is spared; a night bus is rerouted. Those revisions matter, and it would be a different piety to pretend they never occur. The trouble is the ambient theory that treats any revision as proof that the process is sound, and any remaining grievance as leftover noise from people who "had their chance." Attendance is thereby made to do the work of consent. Consent, if the word still means anything civic, is not the same as having been scheduled.

Oral comments at a microphone illustrate the substitution with painful clarity. Three minutes are allotted. A timer is visible. The speaker is thanked. The next speaker is invited. The form is courteous and the structure is a funnel: complexity is shaved to fit the slot, and what cannot be shaved is classified as repetition. Staff later write that "themes" emerged. Themes are what survive the funnel. They are not necessarily what the speakers thought they had said. A person who came to argue that the garage should not be built at all finds herself listed under "requests for mitigation." The minutes have translated abolition into upholstery.

Digital portals repeat the same conversion with a friendlier interface. A comment box invites "feedback." Character limits and dropdown menus decide in advance which kinds of sentence will count as input. The resident who types a structural objection is asked, before submitting, to rate the project from one to five stars. The rating is the datum that will be averaged; the paragraph is optional texture. When officials later announce that the "average rating was 3.7," they are not lying about the arithmetic. They are treating a coerced metric as a public will.

A more honest practice would not abandon rooms or portals. It would stop narrating them as consent machines. It would publish the unedited record beside the decision, including the proposals that were not adopted, and it would say plainly: we heard you and we are proceeding anyway, for these reasons. That sentence is politically expensive, which is why the photograph of the hall is preferred. The photograph allows a government to be seen listening without being seen choosing. Democracy, however, is not a listening face. It is the willingness to let a choice remain attributable, especially when the choice disappoints the people who were invited to speak.

items.stem: Participants hold a pen either in the teeth, which recruits smile muscles, or in the lips, which prevents a smile, while rating cartoons. They cannot see their own faces, and autonomic recordings do not differ between conditions. Cartoon ratings are higher in the teeth condition. The result most directly implicates which claim about emotion’s components?

choices.text: Pure autonomic arousal is sufficient, because a pen cannot affect the face
The behavioral/expressive component can feed back onto the subjective component, as in a facial-feedback account
Unexplained epinephrine was labeled using a confederate, as required by Schachter–Singer theory
Universal-emotion recognition of another person’s face is required, so an audience must have been present

items.explanation: Emotion is typically parsed into physiological, behavioral/expressive, and cognitive/subjective components that can influence one another. Forcing a smile-like contraction without a visible audience and without a change in autonomic arousal isolates the expressive component. Higher amusement ratings then indicate feedback from face to feeling, the facial-feedback hypothesis. The design does not manipulate epinephrine or a confederate, and it does not require recognizing someone else’s expression. Autonomic sufficiency is ruled out if recordings are matched across conditions.

distractorRationales.D: Participants could not see their own faces and no audience is required for a facial-feedback effect on one’s own ratings.

items.stem: The polite caption “We'll call you when your number becomes a priority” relates to the image most accurately as

items.explanation: Caption-versus-image items ask whether words soothe, ironise, or duplicate the drawing. The typeface is described as polite; the sentence is the familiar postponement of waiting rooms. The image refuses the courtesy: patients are not fully drawn, time has no hands, the ticket is monstrous, the board's ears point at money. That is tension, not illustration without friction. The caption does not promise immediacy, and the board is explicitly not facing patients. The joke is the mismatch between civilised delay and what the picture shows delay is for.

passage.title: psg-cars-6
passage.body:
Social capital — broadly understood as the networks of relationships, norms of reciprocity, and trust that enable collective action — has become one of the most debated concepts in contemporary sociology. Proponents argue that it explains why some communities flourish economically and politically while others, equally well endowed in financial and physical resources, remain mired in dysfunction. Where citizens trust one another and are embedded in overlapping civic associations, cooperative ventures are easier to organize, contracts are more reliably honored, and public goods are more effectively maintained.
The concept distinguishes between two broad types. Bonding social capital refers to the dense ties within homogeneous groups — extended families, ethnic neighborhoods, religious congregations — that provide strong mutual support and a sense of belonging. Bridging social capital refers to the weaker but more diverse ties that link members of different social groups, enabling information and resources to flow across community boundaries. Theorists have argued that bridging capital is especially important for economic mobility and democratic stability, because it prevents the insularity and exclusivity that can calcify into tribal antagonism. The interplay between the two forms often matters more than either in isolation. Newcomers to a city, for example, tend to rely first on bonding ties — kin and compatriots who supply lodging, informal credit, and job referrals — and only later cultivate the bridging ties to employers, officials, and institutions beyond their original circle that permit genuine advancement. A community rich in bonding capital but starved of bridging capital may be tightly knit yet economically trapped, whereas one with abundant bridging ties but thin internal solidarity may struggle to sustain the everyday obligations on which cooperation depends. On this view the vitality of a community turns less on how much social capital it can claim than on how its bonding and bridging forms are balanced against each other.
Critics have raised several concerns. First, they argue that the concept is so capacious as to be analytically vacuous: if social capital includes trust, networks, and norms all at once, it risks becoming a label that explains everything and therefore explains nothing. Second, the emphasis on voluntary civic associations may obscure the role of institutional design and state capacity in producing the outcomes attributed to social capital. A society with strong courts, reliable public services, and enforceable property rights may achieve cooperation through formal mechanisms, regardless of the density of its associational life.
A third critique focuses on the dark side of social capital. The same dense ties that produce cohesion within a group can generate exclusion and hostility toward outsiders. Historically, tightly bonded criminal networks, nativist movements, and exclusionary professional guilds have all exhibited strong social capital while causing harm to those outside the charmed circle. If social capital is a neutral resource that amplifies whatever goals a group pursues, then celebrating it uncritically is a mistake. A community of mutual trust can be a community of mutual hostility toward all who fall outside its boundaries, and the literature on ethnic cleansing, organized crime, and racially restrictive covenants demonstrates this possibility in grim historical detail.
These debates have produced a more nuanced research agenda. Scholars now investigate not just the presence or absence of social capital but its distribution across social groups, its articulation with formal institutions, and the conditions under which it promotes rather than undermines democratic participation and social equity.

passage.title: Anthropology — the invention of tradition
passage.body:
Many customs that present themselves as immemorial are surprisingly young. The Scottish clan tartan, worn as a badge of ancient lineage, was largely codified in the nineteenth century; the elaborate ceremonial of certain monarchies, apparently the residue of centuries, was substantially devised within living memory of those who first performed it. Historians have given such practices a name: invented traditions — rituals that claim continuity with a distant past to which their actual connection is tenuous or fabricated.

Why manufacture a past? Invented traditions tend to appear, scholars note, at moments of rapid change, when older bonds have frayed and new institutions must secure loyalty quickly. A ritual that feels ancient lends the present an air of inevitability; what looks as though it has always been done is harder to question than what is admittedly new. The invention, in other words, does work: it stabilizes, legitimizes, binds.

It would be easy to draw a cynical moral — that such traditions are frauds, and that exposing their recent origins deflates them. But this conclusion moves too fast. That a practice was invented at a datable moment does not show that it is meaningless to those who observe it. A wedding ritual devised a century ago may bind a community as tightly as one a millennium old; the bonds are real even if the pedigree is not. To confuse the falsity of a tradition's origin story with the falsity of its present function is to misjudge what such traditions are for.

Nor is the category as tidy as it first appears. Few traditions are either wholly ancient or wholly invented; most are refashioned inheritances — old materials put to new use. The nineteenth-century codifiers of tartan did not conjure it from nothing: they systematized and embellished a genuine, if looser, prior practice. "Invented" is thus better read as a matter of degree than as a verdict of pure fabrication.

The value of the concept, then, is not that it unmasks tradition as a lie. It is that it dissolves a false assumption: that the authority of a practice depends on the antiquity of its origins. Once we see how readily a sense of the ancient can be manufactured, we are freed to ask a better question — not how old a tradition is, but what work it does, and for whom.

items.stem:
Hydrogen and iodine reach the equilibrium H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g). After a long wait at constant volume and temperature, the equilibrium concentrations are:

Species | Equilibrium concentration (mol L−1)
H2 | 0.20
I2 | 0.20
HI | 1.60

Using Kc = [HI]^2 / ([H2][I2]), what is Kc for this reaction at this temperature?
items.explanation: Kc uses equilibrium concentrations in the mass-action expression. Substituting the table values gives Kc = (1.60)^2 / (0.20 × 0.20) = 2.56 / 0.040 = 64. The numerical value is unitless for this equal-mole reaction. Omitting a concentration in the denominator, forgetting to square [HI], or squaring incorrectly produces 8, 16, or 256. Because the system is stated to be at equilibrium, these table entries are the values that belong in Kc, not in a nonequilibrium Q.

distractorRationales.A: 8.0 is [HI] / ([H2][I2]) or a similar expression that fails to square the product concentration.
distractorRationales.B: 16 is (1.60)^2 / 0.20, which drops one of the two reactant concentrations from the denominator.
distractorRationales.D: 256 would require an extra factor of 4 in the numerator or an erroneously small denominator such as (0.10)^2.

items.explanation: Particularity is not a thesaurus and not a costume of theory. The mug, the rack, and the fear that a drying object looks like a claim turn sadness into a decision in a kitchen—thought plus scene. Synonyms stall. Borrowing a famous memoir’s life as if it were yours is both generic and a integrity problem; this bank uses original scenes only. passage.title: A Slow Era (1979)
passage.body: Owen Blake published “A Slow Era” in 1979 after a season in disaster mapping. The argument is that expertise without a named audience is just private language. The piece admits that some gatekeeping keeps fraud out. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: A high-poverty tract is cut off by a highway from a job corridor. Survey networks show few overlapping ties with higher-opportunity tracts. Citywide employment rises in a boom year, but unemployment in the isolated tract barely moves. Which spatial-inequality mechanism is most consistent with this pattern?

choices.text: A pure individual self-efficacy deficit with no role for place
Concentrated disadvantage and spatial mismatch/isolation that can trap residents out of labor markets even when the wider city adds jobs
Social loafing inside factories, which built the highway to reduce effort
Cannon–Bard emotion theory as a predictor of unemployment

items.explanation: Spatial inequality is not only pollution; it is also isolation from jobs, schools, and bridging social networks. Spatial mismatch and concentrated poverty describe neighborhoods physically and socially cut off from opportunity, so a citywide boom need not reach them. That is a place-level mechanism, not a claim that self-efficacy is irrelevant, but it cannot be reduced to self-efficacy alone. Factory loafing and Cannon–Bard theory do not explain highway barriers or truncated networks.

distractorRationales.A: A tract-level failure to share in a citywide boom, with a physical barrier and thin bridging ties, is a spatial pattern rather than a lone personality score.
distractorRationales.C: Highways are infrastructure, not a loafing strategy by workers.
distractorRationales.D: Simultaneity of feeling and arousal does not place jobs on the far side of a highway.

items.stem:
A randomly mating population of 10 000 diploid adults is genotyped at an autosomal locus:

Genotype | Number
AA | 6400
Aa | 3200
aa | 400

Allele frequency of A is counted as (2×AA + Aa) / 20 000. Are the data consistent with Hardy–Weinberg proportions, and what is p(A)?

choices.text: p = 0.80, but HWE requires 8000 AA : 1800 Aa : 200 aa
p = 0.32, the heterozygote frequency, which already equals Hardy–Weinberg
p = 0.64, and the population is not in HWE because 6400 ≠ 0.80² × 10 000
p = 0.80, expected counts are 6400 : 3200 : 400, so the sample matches HWE

items.explanation: p = (2×6400 + 3200) / 20 000 = 16 000 / 20 000 = 0.80, so q = 0.20. Hardy–Weinberg expectations are p²N = 0.64 × 10 000 = 6400, 2pqN = 0.32 × 10 000 = 3200, q²N = 0.04 × 10 000 = 400, identical to the counts. Using p = 0.64 confuses the AA genotype frequency with the allele frequency. The 8000:1800:200 split would correspond to different p or to a selection-distorted sample, not to p = 0.80.

distractorRationales.A: Those counts would require a much higher p or a deficit of heterozygotes; they are not the HWE prediction for p = 0.80.
distractorRationales.B: Heterozygote frequency 0.32 equals 2pq only after p is known; p itself is 0.80, not 0.32.
distractorRationales.C: 0.64 is the frequency of AA, not of allele A; with p = 0.80 the 6400 AA individuals are exactly p²N.

items.stem: Isolated mitochondria are given pyruvate plus ADP. When matrix NADH and acetyl-CoA are raised experimentally, pyruvate consumption falls. Which enzyme is the principal site of this feedback, and which reaction does it catalyze?

choices.text: Citrate synthase; condensation of two acetyl-CoA molecules to acetoacetate
Pyruvate carboxylase; decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetaldehyde
The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex; oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA
Malate dehydrogenase; oxidation of malate that is stimulated by NADH

items.explanation: Pyruvate enters mitochondrial oxidative metabolism through the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, which converts pyruvate, CoA, and NAD+ to acetyl-CoA, CO2, and NADH. High NADH and acetyl-CoA are the immediate products of that reaction and inhibit PDH (product inhibition and, via PDH kinase, phosphorylation). That feedback slows pyruvate consumption when the cell is already reduced and acetyl-CoA-rich. Citrate synthase does not consume pyruvate and does not condense two acetyl-CoA units to acetoacetate. Pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate, not acetaldehyde. NADH inhibits, rather than stimulates, NAD+-dependent malate oxidation.

distractorRationales.A: Citrate synthase condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to citrate, not two acetyl-CoA molecules to acetoacetate. It also does not consume pyruvate, so it is not the site that explains falling pyruvate use.
distractorRationales.B: Pyruvate carboxylase carboxylates pyruvate to oxaloacetate and is activated, not inhibited, by acetyl-CoA. It does not produce acetaldehyde.
distractorRationales.D: Malate dehydrogenase uses NAD+; a high NADH/NAD+ ratio drives the reaction toward malate, so NADH does not stimulate malate oxidation or explain reduced pyruvate uptake as the primary gate.

items.stem: 25.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl is titrated with 0.10 M NaOH. At the equivalence point the pH is 7.0, and the curve is nearly vertical from about pH 4 to 10. Which statement correctly contrasts this curve with the acetic acid titration curve?

choices.text: Both curves have a half-equivalence buffer plateau at pH = pKa of the acid being titrated; for HCl that pKa is 7.
The strong-acid curve starts near pH 1, has no weak-acid buffer region, and the equivalence pH is 7 because the salt is NaCl, which does not hydrolyze.
The strong-acid curve starts near pH 5 and is identical to the weak-acid curve after the first 1 mL of base.
Strong-acid titrations have two equivalence points because HCl is diprotic.

items.explanation: 0.10 M HCl has pH 1.0 at the start. As NaOH is added, [H3O+] falls, but there is no HA/A− buffer plateau because HCl is fully dissociated. At equivalence the solute is NaCl; Cl− is the conjugate of a strong acid and Na+ is the conjugate of a strong base, so the pH is 7. The vertical region is wider than for a weak acid, which is why many indicators work. HCl is monoprotic and has no aqueous pKa near 7. The acetic acid curve, by contrast, starts near pH 3, buffers around pH 4.7, and ends basic at equivalence.

distractorRationales.A: HCl has no useful weak-acid pKa in water and no half-equivalence buffer at pH 7. pH 7 is the equivalence point, not a pKa.
distractorRationales.C: The strong-acid start is pH 1, not 5, and the early part of the curve is not a weak-acid buffer.
distractorRationales.D: HCl donates one proton; diprotic curves (H2SO4, H2CO3) are a different class.

items.stem: 3-Oxobutanoic acid (acetoacetic acid) evolves CO2 on gentle warming and leaves acetone. Hexanoic acid is unchanged under the same conditions. Which mechanistic feature explains the difference?

choices.text: Every carboxylic acid decarboxylates below 100 °C; hexanoic acid is simply slower for steric reasons
Only acids with a quaternary α-carbon can lose CO2, and hexanoic acid is secondary at C2
The β-ketone permits a six-membered cyclic transition state that transfers the carboxyl proton to the ketone oxygen as C–C cleavage releases CO2, giving an enol that tautomerizes to acetone
The ketone is reduced to an alcohol by the departing CO2, a redox decarboxylation unique to fatty acids

items.explanation: β-Keto acids decarboxylate thermally through a cyclic, concerted transition state: the carboxyl hydrogen hydrogen-bonds to the β-carbonyl oxygen as the Cα–CO2H bond breaks, producing CO2 and a ketone enol that tautomerizes to acetone. Hexanoic acid lacks a β-carbonyl and cannot form that six-membered array, so it does not lose CO2 on gentle heating. Ordinary fatty acids require much harsher conditions or enzymatic activation (as in metabolic decarboxylations) to lose carbon dioxide. The α-carbon need not be quaternary, and the process is not a reduction of the ketone by CO2.

distractorRationales.A: Simple alkanoic acids do not decarboxylate on a steam bath. The β-keto functional group is essential for the mild thermal reaction.
distractorRationales.B: Malonic acid and acetoacetic acid decarboxylate with primary or secondary α-carbons. Quaternary substitution is not the requirement.
distractorRationales.D: The ketone oxidation state is preserved: the product is acetone, not an alcohol. CO2 is not a reductant in this reaction.

passage.title: psg-bb-2
passage.body:
A biochemistry lab studied how a small globular enzyme, RibN, loses activity when it unfolds. In its native state, RibN is stabilized by a hydrophobic core, numerous hydrogen bonds within its alpha-helices and beta-sheets, and a single disulfide bond linking two cysteine residues. The team monitored folding both by measuring enzyme activity and by tracking buried tryptophan residues, which fluoresce differently when the protein unfolds. Slowly heating the wild-type enzyme, they found that activity was retained up to about 55 deg C and then fell sharply, with a melting temperature (Tm, the temperature at which half the protein is unfolded) of 65 deg C.
They compared three samples. A cysteine-to-alanine mutant that cannot form the disulfide bond behaved like wild type at low temperature but had a Tm of only 52 deg C. Adding 6 M urea, a chemical denaturant, to wild-type enzyme lowered its Tm dramatically and abolished activity even at room temperature; on dialysis to remove the urea, activity slowly returned. Boiling followed by cooling left the protein inactive and aggregated, yet sequencing showed that the polypeptide's amino acid sequence was fully intact.
The investigators emphasized that all of these treatments disrupted the folded shape without breaking the peptide bonds of the backbone, and that the enzyme's function depended on maintaining its three-dimensional conformation, not merely on possessing the correct sequence.

choices.text: correctly identified the only kind of knowledge there is

items.explanation: The last paragraph: asking a novel for general laws "is to misunderstand the kind of knowledge it offers," and concluding from that failure that it offers none "is to make the same mistake twice." Takeaway: Watch for "wrong standard" inferences, where an author faults a critic for demanding what the thing was never meant to supply. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. It is a category error — judging fiction by a standard it does not aim at. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.C: The author argues fiction does cognitive work, not that it is mere entertainment.
distractorRationales.D: The critique concerns misjudging fiction, not misunderstanding science.

passage.title: Philosophy — can we learn from fiction?
passage.body:
Can a novel teach us anything true about the world? The doubt is old and not unserious. A novel, after all, is by definition a made-up story; its characters never lived, its events never happened. Whatever a novelist asserts through the tale is unsupported by evidence — the author simply stipulates that things are so within the fiction. If I want to know how grief works, or how power corrupts, it seems I should consult a psychologist or a historian, not a storyteller who has invented her data.

This objection has force against one kind of knowledge but not another. It is true that fiction cannot establish general facts: no number of novels about ambitious men could prove that ambition corrupts, since the novelist controls the outcome. But not all knowledge is knowledge of general facts. There is also knowing what something is like — what it would be to face a certain choice, to bear a certain loss. And here fiction has resources the treatise lacks: it can place us, in imagination, inside a situation and let us try it on.

Consider the difference between being told that jealousy distorts perception and following, page by page, a character's jealous misreadings of an innocent scene. The first hands us a proposition to file away; the second rehearses the experience, and may leave us better able to recognize the distortion in ourselves. The novelist need not prove that jealousy works this way. It is enough that she renders it so vividly that we recognize it — the recognition, not the proof, is the point.

A skeptic may reply that this "knowledge" is merely emotional, not cognitive — that we have been moved, not taught. But the line is not so clean. To grasp what a situation is like is often a precondition for judging it well; the person who cannot imagine another's suffering will reason poorly about how to treat them. If fiction cultivates that imaginative grasp, it is doing cognitive work, even if it proves no theorems.

The modest conclusion is that fiction and science divide the labor of understanding rather than compete for it. Science tells us that things are so and why; fiction shows us what their being so is like from the inside. To ask a novel to furnish general laws is to misunderstand the kind of knowledge it offers — and to conclude, from its failure to do so, that it offers none, is to make the same mistake twice.

Successive ionisation energies (kJ mol−1) of element Q in period 3:

IE1 590 | IE2 1150 | IE3 4910 | IE4 6480 | IE5 8110

A large jump marks removal of an electron from a new, much more stable shell. Which inference is justified, and what is the most likely ground-state valence configuration of the neutral atom?

choices.text: The jump after IE2 shows two valence electrons; Q is a group-2 metal with valence ns2
The jump after IE2 shows Q is a halogen with valence ns2 np5
IE values increase smoothly, so Q is a noble gas with ns2 np6
The jump after IE5 shows five valence electrons, so Q is group 15 with ns2 np3

items.explanation: IE3 is more than four times IE2 (4910 versus 1150), while IE1 and IE2 are comparable. That pattern means the third electron comes from a complete inner shell, so only two electrons are valence electrons: a group-2 configuration ns2 (Mg-like in period 3). A halogen would show a jump after seven valence ionisations. A noble-gas atom would have a very high IE1. A jump after IE5 is not present; IE3 is already the cliff. The configuration therefore cannot be np5, np6, or np3.

distractorRationales.B: A halogen has seven valence electrons, so the first large jump would appear after IE7, not after IE2.
distractorRationales.C: IE1 of Q is only 590 kJ mol−1, far too low for a noble gas, and the series is not smooth: IE3 is a cliff.
distractorRationales.D: The cliff is at IE3, not after five electrons; group 15 would jump after IE5.

passage.title: Official Adjectives (1981)
passage.body: In “Official Adjectives” (1981), Amina Okonkwo writes from inside court translation. The argument is that a metric can become the mission that it was supposed to measure. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: After a meal, blood glucose rises. Insulin is released, causing cells to take up glucose and lowering blood sugar back toward normal. This is an example of:

choices.text: Positive feedback, amplifying the original change.
Negative feedback, counteracting the original change to restore a stable set point.

items.explanation: The rise in glucose triggers a response (insulin release) that pushes glucose back down — the response opposes the original change, which is the hallmark of negative feedback. Most homeostatic systems (blood sugar, body temperature, blood pressure) use negative feedback: a deviation from the set point triggers a corrective response in the opposite direction. Positive feedback (e.g. childbirth contractions, blood clotting) instead amplifies change — much rarer in the body. Memory tip: Thermostat rule: negative feedback works like a thermostat correcting back toward a set point (blood sugar too high -> insulin brings it down). Positive feedback is the rare exception that amplifies change, like a snowball rolling downhill (e.g. childbirth contractions). Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

choices.text: ATP hydrolysis at a dynein-like ATPase built into the basal body, identical to the axoneme
GTP hydrolysis by FtsZ rings at the pole, which turn the filament
Actin polymerization against the cell wall, which pushes the hook
Proton (or in some species sodium) flux through Mot proteins of the rotary motor in the envelope

items.explanation: The bacterial flagellum is a rotary motor. Torque is generated by ion flow, usually protons, through MotA/MotB stator complexes in the inner membrane, dissipating the proton motive force. An uncoupler therefore stops rotation even while ATP is still abundant, proving the motor is not an ATP-burning dynein. Eukaryotic cilia and flagella are different machines: axonemal dynein hydrolyzes ATP to slide microtubule doublets. FtsZ is a tubulin homolog used in cytokinesis, and bacteria do not rotate flagella by polymerizing actin at the pole.

distractorRationales.A: Axonemal beating is ATP-driven dynein sliding; the uncoupler result shows the bacterial motor is PMF-driven, not an ATP ATPase like dynein.
distractorRationales.B: FtsZ GTP hydrolysis assembles the division ring; it does not power flagellar rotation.
distractorRationales.C: Some pathogens use actin polymerization for intracellular motility, not for rotating a Gram-negative flagellum.

passage.title: Critical Reasoning · Environmental Policy
passage.body: Beekeepers in the region have reported that average honey yields per hive fell by 30% over the past five years, and several have linked this decline to the increased use of a new class of pesticide introduced during the same period. Advocacy groups have used the honey yield figures to call for an immediate ban. Agricultural researchers point out that the same five years also saw two unusually dry summers and a rise in a parasitic mite known to weaken hive productivity independently of pesticide exposure. A separate long-term study, tracking the same hives annually since before the pesticide was introduced, found no significant difference in yield decline between hives in treated and untreated areas.

passage.title: psg-cp-2
passage.body:
Atherosclerotic plaque narrows an artery and changes how blood moves through it. In a benchtop model of a coronary artery, a pump drives an incompressible fluid with the density of blood (1050 kg/m^3) through a rigid tube at a steady volume flow rate. Midway along the tube a molded plaque reduces the internal radius to half its normal value over a short segment before the tube widens again. Pressure sensors record the fluid's lateral (static) pressure against the wall upstream of, within, and downstream of the narrowing, while a Doppler probe measures flow speed at the same locations.
Away from the narrowing the fluid moves at 0.20 m/s. Because the fluid is incompressible and the flow is steady, the same volume per second must cross every section, so the fluid accelerates as it enters the constricted segment. The investigators also compare the pump pressure needed to maintain the flow rate before and after the plaque forms, and they note that the vessel's resistance is extremely sensitive to its radius.
A second module models gas exchange. Air in an alveolus is held at an oxygen partial pressure of about 100 mmHg, while blood entering the surrounding pulmonary capillary has an oxygen partial pressure of about 40 mmHg. A thin, moist membrane separates the two compartments, and the team measures how quickly oxygen crosses as they vary the partial-pressure difference, the membrane thickness, and its area. Height differences in the standing circulation are represented by raising or lowering the capillary bed relative to the pump. Take g = 10 m/s^2.

items.stem: Suppose a government publishes a real-time mobility dashboard, updated from phone pings, with no category boxes, and uses it to send clinics to whichever grid cell shows density. How would the author most likely respond?

choices.text: This dissolves the problem, because the absence of boxes means no political decisions remain.
The dashboard still decides which lives become facts; a ping is another invented trace, and aiming services (or blame) can become cheaper still.
The author would refuse to comment, having limited the critique to paper forms printed by churches.
Phone pings would be praised as the photograph the passage wants totals to become.

items.explanation: The thesis is that counting systems decide which lives are facts and make policy cheaper to aim, not that paper boxes are the only sin. A ping without boxes still selects a trace and a grid. The author already says the census does not choose the policy but makes aiming cheaper; a density dashboard is that logic intensified. A treats missing boxes as missing politics. C is false: ministries and identity movements already sit beside churches. D inverts the warning against treating totals as photographs.

distractorRationales.A: The author treats boxes as one invented instrument, not as the sole site of political decision.
distractorRationales.C: The passage's actors already include ministries and movements, not only churches.
distractorRationales.D: Photograph-like faith in a number is exactly what the author wants to disenchant.

passage.title: The census of the uncounted
passage.body:
Political arithmetic began as a courtly hobby: a way of estimating how many subjects a prince could tax, feed, or send to war. Its early practitioners treated people as a kind of harvest. What could be enumerated could be extracted. What could not be enumerated was, for administrative purposes, a rumor.

The modern census inherited the appetite and dressed it as representation. To be counted is now advertised as a civic right, a way of appearing in the distribution of schools, clinics, and parliamentary seats. The advertisement is not false. Under-counted neighborhoods do lose clinics. The advertisement is incomplete. A census is also a machine for deciding which kinds of life will be treated as facts and which will remain anecdotes told to a volunteer with a clipboard.

Consider the category. Every census must invent boxes. The boxes are not discovered in nature; they are negotiated among ministries, churches, and, later, identity movements. A person who lives in two houses, or in none, or who works in a language the form does not print, must be forced into a box or dropped. Dropping looks like a clerical mishap. It is often a theory of the state: some lives are too expensive to verify, too mobile to locate, too politically inconvenient to add to a total that will be used against the ministry next year.

Statisticians reply that they already know this, that they publish coverage estimates and post-enumeration surveys, that the professional ethic is to name the error. Naming the error is not the same as refusing the uses of the total. A coverage estimate can become a footnote that licenses the headline number. The public hears fifty million; the appendix whispers that the fifty million is a compromise among several less flattering models. Compromise is not a crime. Treating the compromise as a photograph is.

There is a further twist. Groups that have been historically erased often demand better counting, and they are right to. Visibility in a dataset can be a precondition of funds. Yet the same groups may later discover that a sharper count is also a sharper target: for policing, for debt collection, for the allocation of blame when a service fails. The census does not choose the policy. It does make the policy cheaper to aim.

None of this is an argument for ignorance. A state that refuses to count will invent its numbers in the back room and call the invention common sense. The argument is for a less enchanted relationship to the table. Read the boxes as arguments. Read the missing as a constituency. And when a politician says the numbers speak for themselves, notice that speech is exactly what numbers cannot do until someone supplies a sentence.

items.stem: If adjacent rents rise after a park is planted, the author implies that defenders should

choices.text: admit the park is therefore not justice yet, without handing the land to the highest bidder.
immediately convert the park to lots, since rents prove the ledger was right all along.
stop paying gardeners, because maintenance caused the rents.
deny that parks have ever been used to raise rents.

items.explanation: The further-honesty paragraph says parks raise adjacent rents and that naming those uses does not hand land to the bidder; justice would include people priced off surrounding blocks. The implication for defenders is to drop the pretense that green is already justice. B takes the fact as a deed transfer. C blames maintenance, which the author treats as how openness lasts. D contradicts the named use. Implications stay inside that honesty-without-surrender move.

distractorRationales.B: Naming rent effects is explicitly not a transfer to the highest bidder.
distractorRationales.C: Winter gardeners are part of the adult defense, not the cause to be punished.
distractorRationales.D: The passage states that parks have been used to raise adjacent rents.

passage.title: The ledger of the commons
passage.body:
When a city puts a park on a map, it appears to have given something away: land that could have been lots, hours that could have been tolls. Developers are not wrong that the gift has a price. They are wrong when they treat the price as a leak from an otherwise watertight private order. The private order is already subsidized by streets, courts, pipes, and the patience of people who do not sue every time a stranger walks past a porch. A park is not the exception to property. It is one of the ways a dense city remains inhabitable enough for property to be worth wanting.

Accountants prefer a ledger in which every square metre has a named owner and a yield. Parks embarrass the ledger because their yield is a crowd that does not pay at the gate, a cooling that does not send an invoice, a child who learns a city can include her without a purchase. The embarrassment produces two crude policies. One is to fence and ticket until the park behaves like a venue. The other is to neglect the park until the crowd looks like a problem that only private security can solve. Both policies claim to be realistic. Both are ways of refusing to count the effects that made the park rational in the first place.

Friends of the park sometimes answer with a poetry of the unowned. The poetry is moving and strategically weak. A commons that cannot speak in maintenance budgets will lose to a spreadsheet that can. The more adult defense is to insist that the ledger is incomplete, not that ledgers are evil. Planting, lighting, toilets, and a gardener who is paid in winter are not betrayals of openness. They are how openness lasts past a ribbon-cutting.

There is a further honesty. Parks are not innocent. They have been used to raise adjacent rents, to move unhoused people out of sight, to display a city’s kindness to visitors who will never need the toilets. Naming those uses does not hand the land to the highest bidder. It prevents the park’s defenders from pretending that green on a map is already justice. Justice would be a park whose ledger includes the people who were priced off the blocks around it.

If urban politics cannot hold that thought, it will keep oscillating between the venue and the ruin, and calling the oscillation pragmatism.

items.stem: A pathogenic mtDNA mutation is heteroplasmic. An affected mother has both affected and unaffected sons and daughters; an affected father has no affected children. Which statement is most accurate?

choices.text: Mitochondrial genomes in humans are transmitted through sperm mitochondria that dominate the zygote, so fathers should transmit the trait.
mtDNA is maternally inherited; random partitioning of heteroplasmic mitochondria during oogenesis can produce different mutant loads among offspring, and paternal mtDNA is typically not transmitted.
The pedigree is X-linked recessive, which also spares all children of affected fathers and affects sons and daughters of affected mothers equally.
Crossing over between mitochondrial chromosomes during paternal meiosis eliminates the mutation from sperm, which is why fathers do not transmit it.

items.explanation: Human mtDNA is transmitted through the oocyte; sperm mitochondria are generally eliminated and do not set the child’s mtDNA genotype, so fathers do not transmit the trait. Heteroplasmy is a mixture of mutant and wild-type genomes. During oogenesis, random partitioning of mitochondria (vegetative segregation) can produce eggs with different mutant loads and thus both affected and unaffected sons and daughters. X-linked recessive inheritance can spare children of affected fathers in some respects, but affected mothers typically produce affected sons and carrier daughters rather than both sexes affected by a cytoplasmic genome. Paternal meiotic crossing over is not how mtDNA transmission is blocked.

distractorRationales.A: Paternal mitochondria do not determine the zygote’s mtDNA in humans; the observed pattern is maternal transmission.
distractorRationales.C: X-linked recessive disease in children of a heterozygous mother predominantly affects sons, not sons and daughters similarly, and does not explain heteroplasmic mtDNA genetics.
distractorRationales.D: Absence of paternal transmission reflects destruction or exclusion of sperm mitochondria, not meiotic recombination that ‘cleanses’ mtDNA in sperm.

passage.title: psg-ps-3
passage.body:
Investigators examined how bodily arousal and its interpretation combine to produce emotion. In Study 1, 120 volunteers received an injection described as a vitamin; half actually received a mild dose of adrenaline (epinephrine), which raises heart rate and produces jitteriness, and half received saline. Within each group, some were accurately told to expect arousal symptoms and others were told nothing. Each participant then waited with a confederate who acted either euphoric or irritated. Aroused participants who had not been warned about the symptoms reported emotions matching the confederate's mood - euphoria or anger - more strongly than warned participants or saline controls. Participants who could attribute their arousal to the injection were less swayed by the confederate.
In Study 2, the same volunteers completed a stressful mental-arithmetic task while salivary cortisol was sampled. Cortisol rose within 20 minutes, peaked, and then declined once the task ended. Participants who appraised the task as a 'challenge' showed a smaller cortisol response than those who appraised it as a 'threat,' despite identical task difficulty. Reported stress correlated with threat appraisal, not with objective performance.
The authors linked Study 1 to a theory holding that emotion requires both physiological arousal and a cognitive label for that arousal, and linked Study 2 to a model in which the same stressor produces different physiological responses depending on how it is appraised. They noted that the cortisol time course mirrored the mobilize-then-recover pattern of the body's general response to stressors.

passage.title: Courtesy at the checkpoint
passage.body:
A border official is trained in courtesy as if courtesy were a disinfectant. Smile, use the family name, apologize for the wait. The training manuals are not cynical. They are trying to prevent the obvious cruelty of a raised voice. What they cannot prevent is the deeper grammar of the encounter: one person may leave, the other must persuade a stranger that her life is plausible.

Liberal theory likes to treat this grammar as an unfortunate delay on the way to a principle. In the principle, the stranger is already a rights-bearer; the checkpoint is a bureaucratic remainder. On the ground, the remainder is the event. Rights that must be performed as a story—complete, sequential, tearful at the approved moments—are rights as an audition. The official who says “help me to help you” is not necessarily a villain. He is naming the price of entry into a language that pretends it is only asking for facts.

Scholars of hospitality distinguish welcome from inspection. The distinction is cleaner on the page than in a queue. Inspection can dress as welcome, and welcome can become inspection the moment a detail fails to match a database. A cup of tea in an interview room is not the opposite of a file. It can be the file’s most efficient instrument, loosening speech until it can be contradicted.

None of this requires pretending that states have no legitimate interest in knowing who crosses. It requires noticing that “legitimate interest” is not a measuring cup. It expands. Yesterday’s emergency power is today’s ordinary form. Tomorrow’s form will be justified by the person who told her story too well, or too badly, last year. The archive of interviews becomes a training set for suspicion.

The courteous checkpoint is therefore not a milder politics. It is a politics that has learned to sound like a service. If we want a different politics, we will need a different distribution of who must be plausible to whom—not a warmer script for the same audition.

F (1681) versus O (1314), a drop from O to F
C (1086) versus B (801), a drop from C to B that does not occur

Electron–electron repulsion in that pair lowers IE1: 1314 kJ mol−1 for O versus 1402 for N, against the general left-to-right rise. Skeletal-muscle fibres are treated with ouabain, which blocks Na+/K+ ATPase. Intracellular concentrations (mM) versus time:
0 min: [Na+] 12, [K+] 140.
20 min: [Na+] 28, [K+] 118.
60 min: [Na+] 61, [K+] 82.
Which mechanism explains the table?

choices.text: [Na+]in falls because the pump is the only pathway for sodium to enter.
[K+]in rises because potassium is trapped once the pump stops.
Sodium leaks in and potassium leaks out down their gradients, so [Na+]in rises and [K+]in falls.
Concentrations are unchanged at 60 min (still 12 and 140 mM).

items.explanation: The pump continuously extrudes Na+ and imports K+ to offset passive leaks. Blocking it with ouabain leaves those leaks unopposed: [Na+]in climbs from 12 to 61 mM while [K+]in falls from 140 to 82 mM. Sodium is more concentrated outside, so it cannot fall inside when its active export stops. Potassium is more concentrated inside, so it cannot rise when its active import stops. The 60 min row is clearly not the t = 0 pair.

distractorRationales.A: [Na+]in increases (12 → 61), so sodium is entering through leak channels, not leaving.
distractorRationales.B: [K+]in decreases (140 → 82); K+ leaves through K+ channels rather than being trapped.
distractorRationales.D: By 60 min the values are 61 and 82 mM, not the original 12 and 140 mM.

items.stem:
Combustion and unsaturation data:

Hydrocarbon | combustion: mol O2 per mol hydrocarbon | mol H2 absorbed over Pt | formula
P | 8.0 | 0 | C5H12
Q | 7.5 | 1.0 | C5H10
R | 7.0 | 2.0 | C5H8

Complete combustion of CnHm is CnHm + (n + m/4) O2 → n CO2 + (m/2) H2O. Which structural conclusion follows?

choices.text: R is more saturated than P because it absorbs more H2
Q must be an alkyne, because 7.5 is half-integral
P is an alkane; Q has one double bond or ring; R has two double-bond equivalents (diene, alkyne, or cycloalkene)
All three are alkanes, because each contains only C and H

items.explanation: For C5H12, n + m/4 = 5 + 3 = 8, matching P, and zero H2 uptake is a saturated alkane. C5H10 is one degree of unsaturation (double bond or ring): 5 + 2.5 = 7.5 mol O2 and 1 mol H2. C5H8 has two degrees of unsaturation, 7.0 mol O2 and 2 mol H2. Hydrocarbons include unsaturated series. Absorbing H2 diagnoses unsaturation, so R is less, not more, saturated than P. A half-integral O2 coefficient is normal for odd hydrogen counts, not an alkyne fingerprint (C5H8 would be the alkyne formula, which is R, not Q).

distractorRationales.A: H2 absorption measures unsaturation; R absorbing 2 mol is less saturated than P absorbing 0.
distractorRationales.B: Q is C5H10, one DUE, typically an alkene or cycloalkane; the alkyne formula C5H8 is R.
distractorRationales.D: Q and R absorb H2 and match C5H10 and C5H8, the unsaturated formulae.

items.stem:
A resonance tube of length 0.42 m is driven in air of speed 336 m s−1. A spectrum analyser shows intensity peaks only at the frequencies below (no peak is detected at 400 Hz or 800 Hz):

Observed peak (Hz)
200
600
1000
1400

Which conclusion is consistent with the data and with v = f λ?

choices.text: The tube is open at both ends with fundamental 200 Hz, so even harmonics should appear at 400 Hz and 800 Hz.
The tube is closed at one end with fundamental 400 Hz; 200 Hz is an artefact.
The tube is open at both ends with fundamental 100 Hz; the missing 100 Hz is below the speaker range.
The tube is closed at one end: f1 = v / (4L) = 200 Hz, and only odd harmonics 3f1, 5f1, 7f1 appear.

items.explanation: For a pipe closed at one end, L = λ/4 at the fundamental, so f1 = v / (4L) = 336 / (4 × 0.42) = 336 / 1.68 = 200 Hz. Allowed frequencies are the odd multiples 200, 600, 1000, 1400 Hz, matching the table and explaining the absent 400 Hz and 800 Hz. An open pipe with f1 = 200 Hz would have shown 400 Hz and 800 Hz. Treating 400 Hz as the fundamental contradicts both the 200 Hz peak and L = 0.42 m. An open-pipe fundamental of 100 Hz would produce 200, 300, 400, … including the missing even values. The missing even harmonics are therefore diagnostic of a closed pipe of this length.

distractorRationales.A: An open pipe would display the even harmonics 400 Hz and 800 Hz. The analyser found none of those peaks, so the open-pipe assignment is inconsistent with the table.
distractorRationales.B: A closed-pipe fundamental of 400 Hz would give L = v / (4 × 400) = 0.21 m, not 0.42 m, and would not produce a real 200 Hz resonance.
distractorRationales.C: An open pipe with f1 = 100 Hz would still produce 300 Hz, 400 Hz, 500 Hz and so on. The spectrum is only odd multiples of 200 Hz.

items.stem: In a Festinger and Carlsmith-style design, students complete a dull spool-turning task and then tell a waiting participant that the task was interesting. One group is paid $1 for the lie; another is paid $20. A control group does not lie. On a later private rating, which group should describe the original task as most enjoyable?

choices.text: The $20 group, because a larger reinforcer stamps in a new positive attitude
The $1 group: counterattitudinal speech with insufficient external justification creates dissonance, reduced by deciding the task really was enjoyable
Both lie groups equally, because any public statement rewires attitude regardless of pay
Neither lie group; cognitive dissonance theory predicts that behavior never feeds back on attitude

items.explanation: Cognitive dissonance theory says holding two inconsistent cognitions is aversive and motivates change. Saying a boring task was fun conflicts with the belief that it was boring. Twenty dollars is ample external justification for the lie, so little dissonance remains and the original attitude can stand. One dollar is insufficient justification, so people reduce dissonance by shifting the attitude: the task must have been somewhat interesting. Simple reinforcement would predict the opposite ($20 produces more liking). Dissonance theory is precisely a behavior-to-attitude path, not a ban on that path.

distractorRationales.A: Large payment supplies justification and should reduce, not increase, the need to change the attitude. Reinforcement is the competing prediction that the classic result contradicts.
distractorRationales.C: Pay magnitude matters; the theory’s point is that insufficient, not any, justification produces the attitude shift.
distractorRationales.D: Dissonance theory’s central claim is that counterattitudinal behavior can change attitude when justification is low.

passage.title: Biology · Exercise Physiology
passage.body: Researchers measure blood lactate concentration in athletes performing exercise at increasing intensity on a stationary bike. At low to moderate intensity, blood lactate stays low and roughly stable. Above a certain intensity — different for each athlete, but typically around 70–80% of their maximum effort — blood lactate concentration begins rising sharply and continues to climb the longer the athlete sustains that intensity. items.stem: The potassium Nernst potential is EK = 60 log10([K+]o / [K+]i) mV. A neuron has [K+]i = 140 mM. Resting [K+]o = 5.0 mM. During ischaemia [K+]o rises to 10 mM. (log10 28 ≈ 1.45; log10 14 ≈ 1.15.) How does EK change?

EK remains −87 mV because [K+]i is unchanged

items.explanation: At rest EK = 60 log10(5/140) = 60 log10(1/28) = −60 × 1.45 = −87 mV. After the rise, EK = 60 log10(10/140) = 60 log10(1/14) = −60 × 1.15 = −69 mV. Raising extracellular potassium therefore moves EK toward 0 mV (depolarisation), which is why ischaemic hyperkalaemia can inactivate sodium channels. The inward concentration ratio shrank, so the magnitude of the negative potential must fall, not increase. Doubling [K+]o does not reverse the gradient, which is still 14-fold inward.

passage.title: psg-bb-10
passage.body:
To study how blood delivers oxygen, physiologists measured the percentage of hemoglobin saturated with O2 across a range of oxygen partial pressures (PO2), generating an oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. For adult hemoglobin the curve was S-shaped (sigmoidal): saturation rose slowly at very low PO2, steeply through intermediate values, and leveled off near 100 percent at high PO2. The partial pressure at which hemoglobin is 50 percent saturated (the P50) was about 26 mmHg. For comparison, myoglobin, a single-subunit muscle protein, gave a hyperbolic curve that was left-shifted, reaching high saturation at much lower PO2.
The team then altered the conditions around adult hemoglobin. Lowering the pH (more acidic), raising the partial pressure of carbon dioxide, and raising temperature each shifted the curve to the right, increasing the P50; at any given intermediate PO2, hemoglobin then held less oxygen and released more. These effects are collectively called the Bohr effect. Conversely, fetal hemoglobin gave a left-shifted curve with a lower P50 than adult hemoglobin.
The investigators related the findings to physiology. The sigmoidal shape reflects cooperative binding among hemoglobin's four subunits: O2 binding to one subunit increases the affinity of the others. In metabolically active tissue, where CO2 and acid are high and temperature is elevated, the right shift promotes oxygen unloading exactly where it is needed. The left-shifted fetal curve lets fetal blood extract oxygen from maternal blood across the placenta.

items.stem: Three 6.0 Ω resistors are combined. Network X is all three in series. Network Y is all three in parallel. Network Z is one resistor in series with a parallel pair of the other two. A 12 V ideal battery is applied to each network in turn. What are the three currents drawn from the battery?

choices.text: All three draw 2.0 A, because each network still contains three 6 Ω resistors

items.explanation: Series: Req = 18 Ω, I = 12/18 = 0.67 A. Parallel: 1/Req = 3/6.0, Req = 2.0 Ω, I = 12/2.0 = 6.0 A. For Z, the parallel pair is 3.0 Ω, plus 6.0 Ω in series gives 9.0 Ω, I = 12/9.0 = 1.33 A. Reversing series and parallel swaps 0.67 with 6.0. Identical resistor counts do not imply identical Req. A current of 2.0 A would be 12 V across a single 6 Ω resistor, not three in parallel. The three currents therefore rank Y > Z > X, matching decreasing equivalent resistance.

distractorRationales.A: Series adds resistance (small current); parallel cuts resistance (large current).

distractorRationales.C: Y draws 6.0 A, not 2.0 A; 2.0 A would be a single 6 Ω across 12 V.

passage.title: psg-bb-3
passage.body:
To dissect how mutations disrupt protein output, a lab engineered a set of Escherichia coli strains, each carrying a single defined change in a gene (galK) that encodes a metabolic enzyme. For every strain they measured two quantities: the steady-state level of galK messenger RNA (by quantitative PCR) and the amount of functional enzyme (by an activity assay). Results were expressed as a percentage of the wild-type value.
Wild type showed 100 percent mRNA and 100 percent enzyme activity. Strain 1, carrying a substitution in the promoter region upstream of the coding sequence, showed 15 percent mRNA and 14 percent activity. Strain 2, carrying a single base-pair change that converted a glutamine codon (CAG) into a stop codon (TAG) near the beginning of the coding sequence, showed 95 percent mRNA but less than 2 percent activity; the protein it produced was abnormally short. Strain 3, carrying a single-nucleotide deletion just after the start codon, showed 92 percent mRNA and less than 2 percent activity, and its protein product bore no resemblance to the wild-type sequence beyond its first few residues. Strain 4, carrying a base change that altered a codon from CTG to CTA (both of which encode leucine), showed 98 percent mRNA and 97 percent activity.
The investigators noted that a mutation's consequences depend on where in the gene it falls and how it interacts with the genetic code: some changes reduce how much mRNA is made, others corrupt translation of the message, and some have essentially no effect at all.

passage.title: What the metronome cannot hear
passage.body:
Musicology has a long habit of treating the score as the work and the performance as a more or less obedient copy. The habit is understandable. Paper sits still. It can be compared, edited, and taught in rooms where no instrument is present. A performance disappears as it occurs, leaving only memory, a recording, or an argument.

Yet the stillness of paper is not neutrality. Notation is a technology with a history: it captures some relations (pitch against a staff, duration against a beat) and lets others leak away (the weight of a bow, the delay before a singer accepts a consonant, the social fact of who is allowed to ornament). When a textbook says a movement is “in three,” it is reporting a notational decision that a village dance may never have made in those terms. The metronome, arriving later still, offers a fantasy that time is a ruler laid beside sound. Dancers know otherwise. So do jazz rhythm sections, whose time is a negotiation, not a grid that failed.

Scholars who defend the score-as-work often point to the composer’s authority and to the need for a shared object of study. Without a text, they say, we are left with impressions. The worry is real in a university. It is less real in a tradition that already treats the night’s playing as the work, and the paper, if paper exists, as a prompt. To call that tradition incomplete because it will not sit still is to confuse the archive’s convenience with the art’s ontology.

Recordings seemed to solve the disappearance problem. They created a new paper: a fixed take that can be looped, transcribed, and worshipped. The solution smuggles in its own politics. Which night was recorded, from which seat, with which microphone aiming at which social center of the band? A “definitive” recording can freeze a hierarchy that a living scene would have kept in motion. The fan who owns every take may know more facts than a player and still know less about what the music is for.

The practical upshot is not to burn scores. Scores are superb tools, as maps are superb tools. The upshot is to stop calling the map the territory in order to make seminars easier to grade. A pedagogy that can only hear what the metronome can hear will keep producing excellent accountants of pitch and a thin audience for everything else. If musicology wants to study music rather than the paperwork of music, it will have to tolerate objects that do not hold still, and to admit that some of the most precise information arrives as a glance between players that no staff line was built to hold.

passage.title: The borrowed coat
passage.body:
He wore other people's sentences the way some men wear coats: against weather, and with the labels left in. At the seminar he began, "One might argue," and then produced, almost unaltered, a paragraph his supervisor had emailed at midnight to save him. The room nodded. He felt the coat settle on his shoulders, warm and slightly too large in the sleeves.

Afterward a friend said, "That was the first time you sounded like yourself." He laughed too quickly. In the bathroom mirror the coat was still on. He tried to take it off by telling the truth to the glass: I do not know whether I think this. The glass, being a glass, offered his mouth moving.

Ethics talks as if authenticity were a mineral you either contain or fake. The evening suggested something cheaper and more ordinary. A borrowed argument can keep you from freezing. It can also teach your arms the wrong length. The crime, if there is one, is not the borrowing. It is the nod you collect as if the sleeves had always been yours.

He sent the supervisor a note: Thank you. I sounded like myself. He deleted it. He sent: Thank you. I used your paragraph. He left that one in the outbox until morning, which is a kind of cowardice that still knows the difference.

passage.title: Recycling Behavior and Reinforcement Schedules in Dormitory Kitchens
passage.body:
A campus sustainability team tested behavioral strategies for improving recycling accuracy in dormitory kitchens. Twenty dormitory floors were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: informational signs only, a fixed-ratio points program in which floors earned a reward after every fifth correctly sorted item, a variable-ratio points program in which floors earned rewards unpredictably after an average of five correctly sorted items, or an observational-modeling condition in which residents watched a peer demonstrate correct sorting before signs were posted. In the reward conditions, a green light on the sorting station indicated that the sensor was active and points could be earned; a red light indicated that the sensor was off. After four weeks, point rewards were removed for one week while signs remained.

Mean percentage of items correctly sorted
Condition | Baseline week | Week 4 | Reward-removal week
Informational signs only | 43 | 55 | 52
Fixed-ratio points | 42 | 68 | 50
Variable-ratio points | 44 | 75 | 63
Observational modeling plus signs | 41 | 70 | 66

Assignment unit — The dormitory floor, rather than the individual resident, was the unit of assignment because rewards and signs were shared within floor kitchens.

passage.title: psg-cars-5
passage.body:
Beauty and sublimity are often treated as synonyms in everyday speech, but the aesthetic tradition has long maintained a crucial distinction between them. Beauty, on the classical account, is associated with harmony, proportion, and pleasure: the beautiful object is one whose parts cohere in a way that the observer finds immediately gratifying. Sublimity, by contrast, involves an experience of excess — of forms or magnitudes that exceed the observer's capacity to take them in all at once. The encounter with the sublime is therefore double-edged: it produces both awe and a kind of distress, a sense of being overwhelmed that coexists with exhilaration.
Eighteenth-century theorists were among the first to treat the sublime as a distinct aesthetic category. One influential account located the cause of sublimity in attributes such as vast extent, darkness, and the suggestion of danger or power. A stormy ocean, a jagged mountain range, the interior of a vast cathedral — these provoke a response that differs qualitatively from our response to a well-proportioned garden or a graceful melody. The difference lies not in mere intensity but in the character of the response: the sublime suspends our habitual sense of comfort and security.
A subsequent philosophical tradition shifted the locus of the sublime from the external object to the observer's mental activity. On this view, what is truly sublime is not the mountain itself but the mind's discovery of its own capacity to conceive of what it cannot perceive — to think totality even when the senses are overwhelmed by the magnitude before them. The initial feeling of inadequacy thus gives way to a recognition of the mind's superiority: the faculty that can frame the idea of infinity is, in this sense, greater than any finite spectacle.
These two accounts — one locating sublimity in the object's properties, the other in the observer's cognitive response — are not necessarily incompatible. Objects with certain properties may reliably trigger the cognitive response that constitutes the full experience of the sublime. What both accounts agree on, however, is that the sublime cannot be reduced to beauty: the sublime disrupts the comfortable relationship between the observer and the world, while beauty affirms and soothes it.
The distinction carries an ethical resonance that later writers were quick to draw out. Because the sublime confronts the observer with magnitudes that dwarf the human frame, it has often been tied to humility — to a chastening awareness of finitude that beauty, with its reassurances of order and fit, does not compel. Standing before a storm or an abyss, the spectator is reminded that the world is not arranged for human convenience. And yet, on the observer-centered account, the very same encounter can enlarge the self, for the mind that registers its own smallness is also the mind capacious enough to entertain the immensity that occasions the feeling. This union of abasement and elevation is what makes the sublime so stubbornly resistant to the vocabulary of ordinary pleasure.
Contemporary critics have extended the concept of the sublime to non-natural contexts. The technological sublime finds its occasion in artifacts of overwhelming scale or power: a vast suspension bridge, a particle accelerator, a data center housing more information than any mind could process. Whether such objects genuinely provoke the traditional experience of mingled awe and inadequacy, or whether they produce only spectacle and wonder, remains a live debate in aesthetic theory.

passage.title: Gluconeogenic flux in hepatocyte-like cells
passage.body:
Researchers used fictional hepatocyte-like HGL cells to study glucose production from lactate and alanine. Pyruvate generated in the cytosol must enter mitochondria through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC). In the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate carboxylase (PC) uses ATP, bicarbonate, and a biotin cofactor to convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate. Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) then uses GTP to convert oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate. The pathway requires substantial energy input and is sensitive to cellular ATP availability.

Metabolic effects of perturbing gluconeogenesis from lactate and alanine.
Condition | Glucose output (%) | Cytosolic pyruvate (%) | Mitochondrial OAA/malate pool (%) | O2 consumption (%) | ATP/ADP ratio
Control | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 5.0
MPC inhibitor B | 20 | 190 | 35 | 90 | 4.8
PC inhibitor C | 12 | 220 | 28 | 82 | 3.9
PEPCK knockdown | 18 | 120 | 210 | 85 | 4.2
Low-dose ETC inhibitor | 44 | 115 | 82 | 34 | 1.5
Acetyl-CoA analog | 135 | 70 | 155 | 112 | 4.6

Simplified route from lactate and alanine to glucose. — Lactate and alanine are converted to cytosolic pyruvate. Pyruvate enters mitochondria through MPC and is carboxylated by PC to oxaloacetate. Oxaloacetate-derived carbon returns to the cytosol and proceeds through gluconeogenic reactions to form glucose.

passage.title: psg-bb-8
passage.body:
A cancer-biology lab used flow cytometry to measure the DNA content of individual cells in a proliferating culture. A fluorescent dye that binds DNA in proportion to its amount let the instrument sort cells by how much DNA each contained. Cells in G1 phase, before DNA replication, showed a baseline amount of DNA (call it 2n). Cells in S phase, actively replicating, showed intermediate amounts between 2n and 4n. Cells in G2 and M, having completed replication, showed 4n. A normal asynchronous culture therefore produced two peaks (at 2n and 4n) with cells spread in between.
The team then treated cells with Drug Q. Afterward, nearly all cells piled up in the 2n peak, with almost none at 4n, indicating an arrest before DNA replication began. In a separate experiment, they examined a cell line carrying a nonfunctional version of a checkpoint protein that normally halts cells with damaged DNA. When these mutant cells were irradiated to damage their DNA, they continued through the cycle and divided anyway, accumulating chromosomal abnormalities over successive generations. Unlike normal cells, the mutant cells also kept dividing after covering the surface of the culture dish, having lost contact inhibition.
The investigators connected these observations to tumor formation: checkpoints normally verify that conditions are correct before a cell commits to replication and division, and loss of these controls allows damaged cells to proliferate, a hallmark of cancer.

items.stem: In a lab shock-noise study, students wearing identical hoods in a dim room deliver longer white-noise bursts to a stranger than students who wear large name tags under bright lights, even though each student decides the burst length alone. Which process best explains the increase?

choices.text: Deindividuation: anonymity and reduced self-awareness disinhibit behavior that is usually constrained
Social loafing on a motor task whose output is individually recorded
Social facilitation of a well-learned skilled performance
Diffusion of responsibility for a medical emergency unfolding in another room

items.explanation: Deindividuation occurs when people are anonymous, aroused, and less self-aware, so personal standards exert less control and behavior can become more impulsive or aggressive. Hoods plus darkness are a standard anonymity manipulation; name tags plus lights restore identifiability. The dependent measure is disinhibited harm, not reduced effort on a pooled task (loafing) and not improved skilled performance (facilitation). Diffusion of responsibility is the bystander explanation for not helping when others are thought to be present; no emergency and no co-helpers are described.

distractorRationales.B: Burst length is an individual, recorded act, so loafing’s unidentifiable-pooled-effort logic does not apply.
distractorRationales.C: Delivering noise is not a well-learned skilled task being improved by an audience; it is disinhibited aggression.
distractorRationales.D: There is no emergency and no set of potential helpers among whom responsibility is split.

items.stem: A pain clinic places transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation pads over a painful lumbar dermatome and records a drop in reported intensity without a change in the noxious heat on the skin. Melzack and Wall’s gate-control theory locates the critical interaction where?

choices.text: Only in the anterior cingulate, because gating is purely a cognitive relabeling of heat
At the free nerve ending, where TENS chemically destroys C-fiber peptides
In the olivary cochlea, because pain and hearing share a single thalamic nucleus
In the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn, where large-fiber (Aβ) input can inhibit transmission of small-fiber nociceptive signals

items.explanation: Gate-control theory (Melzack and Wall) proposes that the spinal dorsal horn, especially substantia gelatinosa, is a gate: large-diameter Aβ activity can close it and reduce projection of C and Aδ nociceptive traffic, while small-fiber activity opens it. TENS is taught as a clinical use of that large-fiber inhibition. Anterior cingulate modulates affect but is not the named spinal gate. TENS does not ablate peripheral peptides as its primary mechanism. Hearing pathways are anatomically separate.

distractorRationales.A: Affective cortex can modulate pain, but Melzack and Wall located the gate in the dorsal horn, not only cingulate relabeling.
distractorRationales.B: TENS is not a chemical lesion of C-fiber terminals.
distractorRationales.C: Auditory olives are irrelevant to lumbar nociceptive gating.

items.stem: A neutralizing monoclonal IgG binds a repeating viral glycoprotein with Kd = 2 nM. Limited papain digestion yields Fab fragments that still bind the same epitope with a nearly identical Kd in a monovalent ELISA, yet they neither agglutinate virions nor fix C1q. Which conclusion is most consistent with antibody structure?

choices.text: Antigen specificity resides in the Fc domain, so an intact Fc is required for the observed nanomolar Kd.
Each Fab retains the original combining site, so monovalent affinity is largely unchanged, but bivalent avidity, agglutination, and Fc-dependent effector functions are lost.
Papain destroys complementarity-determining loops, so the Kd in the ELISA must have increased by several orders of magnitude.
C1q binds the antigen-combining site; without intact IgG the viral epitope itself is chemically altered and can no longer be recognized.

items.explanation: Papain cleaves IgG above the hinge, releasing two monovalent Fab fragments and an Fc fragment. The variable domains that form the paratope remain in each Fab, so the intrinsic Kd for a single epitope is essentially unchanged, matching the ELISA. What is lost is simultaneous engagement of two epitopes on one particle (avidity), lattice formation that produces agglutination, and Fc clustering that recruits C1q. Specificity is not encoded in Fc, an unchanged Kd shows that CDRs were not destroyed, and C1q binds Fc rather than the combining site or the viral antigen itself.

distractorRationales.A: The antigen-binding site is formed by VH and VL CDRs in Fab, not by Fc; Fc is dispensable for monovalent Kd.
distractorRationales.C: The stem states that monovalent Kd is nearly identical, so the combining site survived papain cleavage.
distractorRationales.D: C1q docks on clustered Fc regions; it does not occupy the paratope or chemically modify the viral epitope.

distractorRationales.C: Unattended info is weakened, not amplified above attended info.
distractorRationales.D: Physical features are still processed; attenuation acts on the unattended channel.
