passage.title: psg-cars-1
passage.body:
Is there any knowledge in the world so certain that no reasonable person could doubt it? This question, which at first sight might not seem difficult, is really among the most difficult that can be asked. In daily life we assume as certain many things which, on closer scrutiny, are found to be so full of apparent contradictions that only a great deal of thought enables us to know what it is that we may really believe.
Consider the plain table before me. To the eye it appears rectangular, brown, and shiny; to the touch it is smooth, cool, and hard; when I tap it, it gives out a wooden sound. Anyone else who sees, feels, and hears the table will agree with this description, so it might seem that no difficulty could arise. But the moment we try to be more precise, our troubles begin. Although I believe that the table is 'really' of one uniform brown, the parts that reflect the light look far brighter than the rest, and some parts look white because of reflected light. If I move, the parts that reflect the light change, so that the apparent distribution of colours upon the table shifts. It follows that if several people look at the table at the same moment, no two of them will see exactly the same distribution of colours, for no two can view it from precisely the same point, and any change in the point of view changes the way in which the light is reflected.
For most practical purposes these differences are unimportant, but to the painter they are all-important: the painter has to unlearn the habit of thinking that things seem to have the colour which common sense says they 'really' have, and to learn the habit of seeing things as they appear. Here we already meet with one of the distinctions that cause the most trouble in philosophy — the distinction between 'appearance' and 'reality,' between what things seem to be and what they are. The table, if it is 'real' at all, must have some real colour; yet the colour we see is not a property of the table in itself but something depending upon the table, the observer, and the way the light falls. When, in ordinary life, we speak of the colour of the table, we mean only the sort of colour which it will seem to have to a normal spectator, under ordinary conditions of light, from an ordinary point of view. But the other colours which appear under other conditions have just as good a right to be considered real; and so, to avoid favouritism, we are compelled to deny that the table has any one particular colour.
The same holds for the texture. With the naked eye the grain of the wood looks smooth and even; under a microscope it shows roughness, and hills and valleys, and all sorts of differences that are imperceptible to unaided sight. Which of these is the 'real' table? We are naturally tempted to say that what we see through the microscope is more real; yet a still more powerful instrument would reveal something different again, so that we can never rest content with what the eye alone reports. Thus confidence in the senses, which had seemed so secure, begins to desert us.
It becomes evident that the real table, if there is one, is not the same as what we immediately experience by sight or touch or hearing. The real table, if it exists, is not immediately known to us at all, but must be an inference from what is immediately known. Hence two very difficult questions at once arise: Is there a real table at all? And if so, what sort of object can it be?

passage.title: History — the press and the Reformation
passage.body:
It is often said that the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation. Luther's theses, the story goes, would have died as a local academic dispute had the new technology not broadcast them across Europe within weeks. There is something to this. Print did carry Luther's words farther and faster than any scribe could, and the reformers themselves marveled at the machine — one called it "God's highest act of grace." But "the press caused the Reformation" claims more than the evidence will bear.

Consider what the same presses were printing. In the decades before Luther, Europe's workshops turned out indulgences, devotional manuals, and papal bulls in enormous numbers; the technology served the old church at least as eagerly as it later served its critics. A tool that amplifies whatever message it is given cannot, by itself, explain why one message rather than another swept the continent. To credit the press with the Reformation is to mistake a multiplier for a cause.

The point can be sharpened. Earlier reformers — Wyclif in England, Hus in Bohemia — had advanced doctrines close to Luther's a full century before movable type, and had won substantial followings without it. Their movements were contained, but by armies and inquisitions, not by any shortage of copyists. What differed in Luther's case was not merely the speed of transmission but a constellation of circumstances: a fractured German political landscape in which sympathetic princes could shield him, a literate urban public primed by grievance, and a message pitched to that public's discontents.

None of this makes the press irrelevant. Technologies shape the movements that use them, and a Reformation conducted by pamphlet was bound to differ from one conducted by sermon and manuscript. The press lowered the cost of dissent and widened the circle of those who could join it. But "shaped" is not "caused," and "made easier" is not "made inevitable." The most we can say is that print was among the conditions that allowed the Reformation to spread as it did — a necessary instrument, perhaps, but not a sufficient explanation.

The appeal of the simpler story is easy to understand. Causes that can be named and dated — a machine, an invention — are more satisfying than a tangle of politics, literacy, and timing. But history rarely obliges us with single causes, and the historian's task is often to resist the tidy explanation in favor of the true one.

items.stem: Blindfolded participants pull a rope, believing they are alone or on a two- or six-person team. Force per person falls as believed team size rises. When a screen displays each person’s force in real time, the drop disappears. Which process is illustrated?

choices.text: Social facilitation of a complex novel task
Deindividuation that requires costumes and darkness
Normative peer pressure to pull harder in larger teams
Social loafing: effort drops when individual output is not identifiable, and identifiability restores effort

items.explanation: Social loafing is reduced individual effort on a collective task when contributions are pooled and hard to monitor. The rope-pull (Ringelmann) pattern—less force per person as the believed team grows—is the classic case. Making each person’s output identifiable removes the incentive to hide, so loafing shrinks. Facilitation would predict better performance of a simple, well-learned pull in front of others, not a drop. Deindividuation is about anonymity and disinhibition of usually restrained acts, not a dynamometer. Peer pressure to pull harder predicts the opposite slope.

distractorRationales.A: A simple maximal pull getting worse in a group is loafing, not facilitation of a complex skill.
distractorRationales.B: No costumes or darkness are required for loafing; the manipulation is identifiability of force.
distractorRationales.C: If peers pressured harder pulling, per-person force should rise, not fall, with team size.

items.stem:
A Task A set reads:
1. “We outsourced judgment to whoever had the thickest lamination on a name badge.”
2. “Ignorance is not a crime; pretending we do not need teachers is.”
3. “A society that cannot tell a specialist from a loud amateur will pay for the confusion in waiting rooms.”
4. “Democracy is not a refusal of knowledge.”
5. “Humility before evidence is not elitism.”
A student writes that the theme is “the importance of university.” Why is that identification weak, and which theme is tighter?

choices.text: It is weak because none of the comments mention universities; a tighter theme is the civic status of expertise versus the flattening of knowledge into mere opinion.
It is weak because Task A forbids any theme involving knowledge; the only legal theme is sport.
It is strong; “teachers” in comment 2 proves the set is about campus funding formulas.
It is weak because the real theme is name-badge stationery, which must be discussed as industrial design.

items.explanation: “University” is a nearby institution, not the shared object. The comments concern judgment, specialists, amateurs, democracy, evidence, and humility—expertise as a public good, not a budget line for campuses. Teachers appear as a figure for needed knowledge, not as a prompt to rehearse HECS policy. Theme identification fails when a student substitutes a familiar essay they have memorised. A is the correction. Sport as the only legal theme is invented; stationery is a metaphor in comment 1, not the issue.

distractorRationales.B: Task A has no banned-knowledge rule and no sport requirement; that answer invents exam law.
distractorRationales.C: One mention of teachers does not convert the set into a funding-formula essay; the other four comments would become decoration.
distractorRationales.D: Lamination is a metaphor for hollow credential theatre, not an industrial-design brief.

passage.title: Fraud Control (1977)
passage.body: Ingrid Nilsen's 1977 essay “Fraud Control,” on museum captions, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that expertise without a named audience is just private language. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Country X publishes vital statistics after a national vaccine and sanitation campaign. Crude death rate falls from 30 to 12 per 1,000 over twenty years, while crude birth rate stays near 40. The age pyramid is wide at the base and total population is rising fast. Which demographic-transition stage is this?

choices.text: Stage 2: mortality decline precedes fertility decline, producing rapid natural increase
Stage 1: high birth and high death rates in approximate equilibrium
Stage 4: low birth and low death rates with a stable size
Stage 3: fertility has already fallen to match the new death rate

items.explanation: In the demographic transition, stage 1 has high fertility and high mortality and little growth. Stage 2 begins when death rates fall—typically from public health—while birth rates remain high, so the population booms and the pyramid stays youthful. Stage 3 is when fertility falls in response to urbanization, education, and contraception. Stage 4 is the later low-low equilibrium. Country X has a mortality drop without a birth-rate drop, which is the definition of stage 2, not stages 1, 3, or 4.

distractorRationales.B: Stage 1 would still show a high death rate near 30, not a fall to 12, and would not produce a boom.
distractorRationales.C: Stage 4 requires low fertility as well as low mortality; CBR near 40 is incompatible.
distractorRationales.D: Stage 3 is the fertility decline; the stem says births remain high.

items.stem: A globular protein is unfolded in 8 M urea plus a thiol reductant so that all disulfides are broken and secondary structure is lost. Both urea and reductant are then removed by dialysis in air, and catalytic activity spontaneously returns to near-wild-type levels. Which conclusion is best supported?

items.stem: A cuvette of double-stranded DNA is heated through its melting transition while absorbance at 260 nm is recorded. Absorbance rises as the sample denatures. Which molecular explanation is best?

choices.text: Heat hydrolyzes phosphodiester bonds, releasing free nucleotides that absorb more strongly than polymers.

items.explanation: Stacked bases in a duplex have hypochromic UV absorbance relative to the same nucleotides in a random coil. When heat melts hydrogen bonds and stacking, the bases become more exposed to solvent and electronic coupling between stacked rings is lost, so A260 rises. That hyperchromic shift is the experimental readout of a melting curve and is reversible upon cooling if strands can reanneal. Melting temperatures used in the experiment are far below those needed to hydrolyze phosphodiesters, and pairing does not create a special 260 nm chromophore in the hydrogen-bond donors; unpaired bases absorb more, not less.

distractorRationales.A: Thermal melting at typical Tm values does not hydrolyze the backbone; oligonucleotides remain intact and can reanneal, which would be impossible if phosphodiesters were cleaved.
distractorRationales.B: The absorbance jump tracks the cooperative helix-to-coil transition, not a bulk protonation of bases as temperature rises.
distractorRationales.D: Paired, stacked bases absorb less at 260 nm than unpaired bases; hydrogen-bond donors do not become chromophores only when paired.

items.stem: A 20-residue alanine-based peptide that is highly α-helical in water is redesigned by placing proline at the central position. Far-UV circular dichroism then shows a marked loss of the 222 nm helical minimum. Which property of proline best accounts for the helix disruption?

items.explanation: sin θ2 = (1.00/1.50) × 0.50 = 1/3, so θ2 ≈ 19.5°. Light bends toward the normal on entering glass, so the angle must drop below 30°, not rise to 45°. The critical angle is measured inside glass: sin θc = n_air/n_glass = 2/3, θc ≈ 42°. Using sin 60° = √3/2 with n_g would not equal 1. The critical angle applies to the dense-to-rare direction; a 30° air ray is well able to enter. Total internal reflection is not an issue on this first interface.

passage.title: Return-of-service bond: two letters
passage.body:
Two letters appeared in the same metropolitan daily after the health minister proposed a "return-of-service" bond: new doctors whose training was publicly subsidised would owe three years in designated underserved clinics before they could take an unrestricted urban post.

Letter A
A public scholarship is not a gift ribbon. It is a wager the public makes on a scarce skill. If the graduate then sells that skill immediately to the densest private market, the wager has been privatised without a receipt. Three years is not indenture; it is the time in which a clinic learns a name and a name learns a clinic. Those who call the bond a "mobility tax" speak as if mobility were a natural right unpolluted by the taxes that built the teaching hospitals. Rights that forget their invoices are just appetites with better stationery. Underserved towns are not a lifestyle choice the profession may decline, like a sport. They are the other half of the ledger.

Letter B
The minister has misdiagnosed a staffing failure as a character failure in the young. Clinics are empty of doctors for the same reasons they are empty of radiographers and nurses: housing costs, school deserts, professional isolation, and locum markets that pay more for a weekend than a bonded year pays for a winter. A bond does not staff a town; it parks a resentful beginner there and calls the parking "justice." Meanwhile the budget that should have made the posting liveable is spared the embarrassment of being seen. Coercion is cheaper than housing. If the public wants doctors in those rooms, it should furnish the rooms, not hostage the people it trained. A ledger that counts only the graduate's debt, and never the state's, is not a ledger. It is a sermon.

Editor's note: Letter A was signed by a retired regional physician; Letter B by a recent graduate now in a metropolitan hospital.

passage.title: psg-cp-2
passage.body:
Atherosclerotic plaque narrows an artery and changes how blood moves through it. In a benchtop model of a coronary artery, a pump drives an incompressible fluid with the density of blood (1050 kg/m^3) through a rigid tube at a steady volume flow rate. Midway along the tube a molded plaque reduces the internal radius to half its normal value over a short segment before the tube widens again. Pressure sensors record the fluid's lateral (static) pressure against the wall upstream of, within, and downstream of the narrowing, while a Doppler probe measures flow speed at the same locations.
Away from the narrowing the fluid moves at 0.20 m/s. Because the fluid is incompressible and the flow is steady, the same volume per second must cross every section, so the fluid accelerates as it enters the constricted segment. The investigators also compare the pump pressure needed to maintain the flow rate before and after the plaque forms, and they note that the vessel's resistance is extremely sensitive to its radius.
A second module models gas exchange. Air in an alveolus is held at an oxygen partial pressure of about 100 mmHg, while blood entering the surrounding pulmonary capillary has an oxygen partial pressure of about 40 mmHg. A thin, moist membrane separates the two compartments, and the team measures how quickly oxygen crosses as they vary the partial-pressure difference, the membrane thickness, and its area. Height differences in the standing circulation are represented by raising or lowering the capillary bed relative to the pump. Take g = 10 m/s^2.

items.explanation: Osmosis moves water from an area of lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration across a semi-permeable membrane. In a hypotonic (more dilute) solution, water flows into the cell, which can cause it to swell or lyse. Water moves to dilute the more concentrated side. Hypotonic outside = water rushes in (cell swells). Hypertonic outside = water rushes out (cell shrinks). Isotonic = no net movement. This single rule covers most osmosis questions. items.stem: A chemist needs one enantiomer of 2-phenylpropanoic acid from a racemate. Which procedure can produce an enantioenriched free acid?

choices.text: Simple distillation, because the R and S acids have different boiling points

Pass plane-polarized light through the melt so that only one enantiomer crystallizes
Extract with achiral diethyl ether and water, because enantiomers have different partition coefficients

items.explanation: Enantiomers are identical in an achiral environment, so they share boiling point, ordinary solubility, and ether/water partition. They cannot be separated by simple distillation or by achiral extraction, and a polarimeter measures rotation rather than physically sorting molecules. Reaction with an enantiopure amine creates two diastereomeric salts, which differ in lattice energy and solubility. Crystallizing one salt and then protonating the carboxylate returns an enantioenriched acid. This is classical resolution via diastereomers.

distractorRationales.A: Enantiomers have identical boiling points. Distillation does not resolve a racemate.
distractorRationales.C: Polarized light is an analytical tool for optical rotation; it does not selectively crystallize one enantiomer under ordinary laboratory conditions.
distractorRationales.D: Partition coefficients in achiral solvent pairs are identical for enantiomers, so the extraction does not enrich either isomer.

items.stem: A vestibular lab spins a seated patient at constant angular velocity about a vertical axis for 30 seconds, then stops the chair abruptly. For several seconds the patient reports rotation in the opposite direction and shows post-rotary nystagmus. Which receptors, and which physical lag, produce that after-sensation?

choices.text: Otolith organs of the utricle and saccule detecting linear acceleration of the chair rails
Cochlear inner hair cells, because angular motion is encoded as a Doppler shift on the basilar membrane
Cristae in the horizontal semicircular canals, because endolymph inertia keeps the cupula deflected after the canal itself has stopped
Muscle spindles in the neck, because they are the only sensors that fire after motion ceases

items.explanation: Semicircular-canal cristae encode angular acceleration via cupula deflection. During a sudden stop, the canal wall halts but endolymph continues, bending the cupula opposite the original spin and driving a false sense of counter-rotation plus nystagmus. Otolith maculae sense linear acceleration and head tilt, not this angular after-effect. Cochlear hair cells encode sound. Neck spindles contribute to proprioception but are not the mechanism of post-rotary nystagmus in this chair test.

distractorRationales.A: Otoliths detect linear acceleration and gravity, not the angular after-sensation of a stopped yaw spin.
distractorRationales.B: The cochlea is not a gyroscope; it does not encode chair yaw as a traveling-wave Doppler shift.
distractorRationales.D: Cervical proprioception is not the generator of classic post-rotary nystagmus after an abrupt stop.

items.explanation: Photosynthesis (in chloroplasts) uses light energy to convert CO2 and water into glucose and oxygen. This is essentially the reverse of cellular respiration, which breaks glucose + oxygen back down into CO2 + water + usable energy (ATP). Cellular respiration (all living cells, including plants) breaks glucose back down using oxygen, releasing CO2, water and ATP. Learn them as reverses of each other and you'll never mix up inputs/outputs again. Memory tip: Mirror image: photosynthesis and respiration are exact opposites. Learn one equation and flip the arrow to get the other — CO2 + water + light -> glucose + oxygen, reversed, is glucose + oxygen -> CO2 + water + energy. items.stem: An α-helix in a soluble protein is probed by mutating a solvent-exposed internal alanine to proline. The magnitude of the negative circular-dichroism band at 222 nm decreases, while the peptide covalent mass is unchanged. The most direct structural interpretation is that:

choices.text: Proline increases helical hydrogen bonding, so the CD change must reflect aggregation rather than helix loss
The mutation oxidizes nearby cysteines and the CD change reports new disulfides
Helical secondary structure is reduced because proline kinks the helix and cannot donate an amide hydrogen bond
Alanine cannot occur in helices, so the starting protein had no helix and the mutation has no structural meaning

items.explanation: Far-UV ellipticity at 222 nm is a standard reporter of α-helix content. Proline’s pyrrolidine ring constrains the backbone and removes the amide NH that would donate a hydrogen bond to the carbonyl four residues earlier, so an internal proline typically breaks or kinks a helix. Loss of helix is therefore the most parsimonious reading of a smaller 222 nm signal at constant covalent mass. Alanine is in fact helix-favoring, proline does not create disulfides, and increased helix would deepen—not shrink—the 222 nm minimum.

distractorRationales.A: Proline is a helix breaker, not a helix stabilizer; a smaller 222 nm signal is the opposite of increased helicity.
distractorRationales.B: Proline has no thiol. Disulfide formation is a cysteine chemistry and is not implied by this substitution.
distractorRationales.D: Alanine has high helix propensity and is common in helices; the starting CD signal already indicated helix.

passage.title: The Roster (1977)
passage.body: Elena Rossi's 1977 essay “The Roster,” on urban cycling, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that local knowledge is treated as anecdote until a model needs it. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

An asynchronous culture has a measured generation time of 20.0 h. A snapshot of 360 cells shows:
interphase 324, prophase 18, metaphase 12, anaphase 4, telophase 2.
The duration of a phase is (fraction of cells in that phase) × generation time.

As a check, interphase is 324/360 × 20 = 18 h, the expected long gap phase, and prophase is 18/360 × 20 = 1.0 h.

passage.title: Chiral Chromatography of Arylpropionic Acid Analogs
passage.body:
A fictional arylpropionic acid, compound C, has two enantiomers labeled R-C and S-C. The carboxylic acid group has pKa = 4.4. A chiral stationary phase contains hydrophobic binding pockets and protonated amine sites. Neutral analytes interact mainly through hydrophobic contacts, while carboxylate forms can also interact electrostatically. Very high salt concentrations can screen electrostatic interactions. An achiral column cannot directly distinguish enantiomers unless the compounds are converted into diastereomeric derivatives or salts.

Chromatographic performance under different conditions.
Condition | Column type | Mobile phase pH | Salt level | Retention time R-C (min) | Retention time S-C (min) | Resolution
1 | Achiral silica | 2.5 | low | 5.1 | 5.1 | 0.0
2 | Chiral | 2.5 | low | 6.2 | 7.0 | 1.1
3 | Chiral | 7.5 | low | 12.8 | 16.4 | 2.4
4 | Chiral | 7.5 | high | 8.0 | 9.0 | 0.8
5 | Chiral | 9.5 | low | 13.0 | 16.2 | 2.3

Peak areas for a mixture analyzed under Condition 3.
Peak identity | Peak area
R-C | 300
S-C | 100

Conceptual chiral recognition model. — One enantiomer fits more deeply into the chiral pocket while simultaneously orienting its carboxylate toward a protonated amine site. The other enantiomer has a less favorable alignment and elutes earlier.

items.stem: A CpG island at a tumor-suppressor promoter is densely methylated on cytosine. A DNA methyltransferase inhibitor reduces 5-methylcytosine at this island, increases local histone acetylation, and restores mRNA. Which mechanism is most consistent?

choices.text: Cytosine methylation is required for RNA polymerase II binding at CpG islands, so removing it should silence rather than activate the gene.
Methylated CpG is recognized by complexes that recruit histone acetyltransferases, so demethylation would decrease acetylation.
Methyl-CpG-binding proteins recruit histone deacetylases and compacting factors; demethylation releases this silencing, permitting HAT activity and transcription-factor access.
DNA methylation in animals occurs only on adenine; the drug must therefore be acting on contaminating bacteria rather than the tumor-suppressor gene.

items.explanation: In vertebrates, methylation of cytosine in promoter CpG islands is a stable silencing mark. Methyl-CpG-binding proteins recruit histone deacetylases and other corepressors, compacting chromatin and blocking transcription-factor and polymerase access. Inhibiting DNA methyltransferase allows passive loss of 5-methylcytosine through replication, dissociation of the silencing complex, histone acetylation by HATs, and restoration of tumor-suppressor mRNA, matching the experiment. Methylation does not promote Pol II recruitment at these promoters, and it does not primarily recruit HATs. Cytosine, not adenine, is the predominant DNA methylation target in mammalian genomes.

distractorRationales.A: Promoter CpG methylation correlates with silencing, not with obligatory Pol II recruitment; demethylation restored mRNA in the stem.
distractorRationales.B: Methyl-CpG readers typically recruit deacetylases, not acetyltransferases; acetylation rose after demethylation, the opposite of this prediction.
distractorRationales.D: Mammalian DNA methylation is primarily 5-methylcytosine at CpG dinucleotides, not N6-methyladenine as the dominant gene-silencing mark.

passage.title: psg-cars-12
passage.body:
One of the most consequential shifts in twentieth-century philosophy of language was the move away from the view that words get their meaning by standing for objects in the world. On the referentialist picture, to know the meaning of a term like 'gold' is to know which substance the term picks out; to know the meaning of 'Julius Caesar' is to know which historical individual the name refers to. The attractions of this view are obvious: it grounds meaning in something outside language itself, connecting our words to the world they describe and offering a clear criterion for distinguishing correct from incorrect usage.
Yet referentialism encounters serious difficulties when applied to expressions whose meaning does not seem to consist in any reference at all. Words like 'and,' 'perhaps,' 'nevertheless,' and 'of' do not pick out objects, properties, or relations in any obvious sense. Equally problematic are terms whose reference appears to shift depending on context: 'here' refers to wherever the speaker happens to be, 'now' to whenever the utterance is made, and 'I' to whoever is speaking. The meaning of these expressions cannot be their reference, since their reference changes while their meaning remains constant across every ordinary use of the word.
An alternative tradition proposed that meaning is constituted by use. On this view, to know the meaning of a word is not to know what it refers to but to know how to use it -- in what contexts it is appropriately deployed, what inferences it licenses, how it interacts with the meanings of other expressions. This account handles the problematic cases naturally: logical connectives like 'and' are explained by the inferential rules governing their use (the conjunction of P and Q implies both P and Q separately); indexical expressions like 'here' are explained by specifying the rule that they refer to the context of utterance. Knowing the meaning of 'here' means knowing that it picks out the speaker's location, not knowing any particular location.
Critics of the use theory worry that it leaves too little stable content in meaning. If meaning is just use, and use can vary between individual speakers or across historical periods, then there seems to be no fact of the matter about whether two speakers mean the same thing by a word, or whether we mean the same thing by 'democracy' as people in ancient Athens did. Some philosophers have sought to address this by distinguishing between the linguistic meaning of an expression (shared by competent speakers of a language) and speaker meaning (what a particular individual intends to convey in a specific utterance). Semantic theory can then concern itself with the former -- a stable, shared content -- while acknowledging the latter's irreducibly contextual character and the inevitable gap between what a speaker means and what a sentence means.
None of this need force an exclusive choice between the two pictures. A mature semantics may well be pluralistic, allowing that proper names and natural-kind terms lean heavily on reference while connectives, indexicals, and evaluative vocabulary are better explained by the rules governing their use. What the twentieth-century debate established is less the triumph of one theory than the inadequacy of assuming that a single mechanism must underwrite meaning across the whole of a language. The more durable lesson is methodological: before asking what a word means, one does well to ask what kind of word it is, since expressions of different types may secure their significance in quite different ways.

items.stem: Marmot’s Whitehall studies found a stepwise gradient in coronary mortality across British civil-service grades, even though all groups had access to the National Health Service. Which conclusion about class and health is most justified?

choices.text: Only the unemployed are unhealthy; employed grades should be identical
Weber denied that status can affect the body, so Whitehall refutes Weber
The gradient proves Davis–Moore meritocracy causes infarctions by justice
A socioeconomic gradient in health can persist above poverty and despite universal access, implicating status, control, and related class-linked conditions—not access alone

items.explanation: The socioeconomic gradient in health is the graded, not binary, association of SES with morbidity and mortality. Whitehall is famous because it appears among employed, NHS-covered civil servants, so “no insurance” and “absolute destitution” cannot be the whole story. Control, hierarchy, and other class-linked exposures are implicated. Weber actually made status a distinct stratification dimension, compatible with a gradient. Davis–Moore does not claim justice of infarcts as functional necessity.

distractorRationales.B: Weber included status and life chances; Whitehall does not refute him.

items.stem: A city has a large 0–14 population and relatively few 15–64 workers after a baby boom, straining pediatric clinics. Forty years later the same boom cohort is 65+, pension outlays spike, and the youth share is smaller. Which demographic-structure claim is best?

choices.text: Sex ratio, not age structure, explains both clinic crowding and pensions
Only international immigration can change a population’s age distribution
Birth cohorts move through the age pyramid, so a high youth-dependency ratio can later become a high aged-dependency ratio
Gender identity determines how many pediatric versus geriatric beds are needed

items.explanation: Age is a core axis of demographic structure. A birth cohort is a set of people born in the same interval; they occupy successive bands of the pyramid as they age. Dependency ratios compare non-working-age groups (children, elderly) to working-age adults. A baby boom therefore presents first as youth dependency and later as old-age dependency without any change in the identity of the cohort. Sex ratio and gender identity do not replace that age-cohort mechanism. Fertility, mortality, and migration all can reshape age structure; immigration is not the only path.

distractorRationales.A: The timeline is an aging cohort, not a change in males per females.
distractorRationales.B: Fertility waves change age structure even with zero migration, which is the baby-boom story.
distractorRationales.D: Need for pediatric versus geriatric services tracks age composition, not gender identity.

items.stem: Chloroquine is used to raise the pH of macrophage lysosomes. Acid hydrolases in the lysosomal lumen are expected to:

choices.text: become more active, because they are optimized for alkaline pH
relocate to the nucleus and degrade genomic DNA as their primary effect
lose activity, because they are adapted to an acidic lumen
synthesize ATP by running the vacuolar ATPase in reverse as a synthase

items.explanation: Lysosomal hydrolases have acidic pH optima matching the V-ATPase-acidified lumen. Raising pH moves them off their optimum, impairing degradation of endocytosed cargo (the basis of chloroquine's effect in this assay). They are not alkaline enzymes, they are not nuclear DNases as a first consequence of chloroquine, and the vacuolar ATPase is a proton pump that consumes ATP; it is not an ATP synthase in this setting.

distractorRationales.A: Lysosomal enzymes are acid hydrolases. Alkalinization reduces, not increases, their activity.
distractorRationales.B: These enzymes are sequestered in lysosomes. Raising luminal pH does not retarget them to chromatin as the primary mechanism.
distractorRationales.D: V-ATPase hydrolyzes ATP to pump H+ in. Uncoupling or pH collapse does not turn it into the cell's ATP source.

passage.title: Critical Reasoning · Health & Statistics
passage.body: A widely circulated report claims that teenagers who spend more than four hours a day on social media are twice as likely to report symptoms of anxiety as teenagers who spend less than one hour a day. Newspaper headlines quickly translated this into warnings that social media "causes" anxiety in teenagers, and several schools cited the report when introducing new phone bans. The original researchers were more cautious. They noted that their data was cross-sectional — collected at a single point in time — rather than following the same teenagers over years, and that anxious teenagers might simply be more likely to retreat into their phones, rather than phones making them anxious in the first place. They also noted that heavy social media use was more common among teenagers who already reported sleeping fewer than six hours a night, raising the possibility that disrupted sleep, not screen time itself, was doing much of the work.

items.stem:
Two isomers of octahedral [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ are isolated.

Isomer | colour | measured dipole moment | Cl–Co–Cl angle from diffraction
Violet | polar (μ > 0) | 90°
Green | μ = 0 | 180°

MA4B2 octahedra have a cis isomer (adjacent X ligands) and a trans isomer (opposite X ligands). Which assignment follows?

choices.text: Green is cis because a 180° angle means the chlorides are neighbours
Both must be the same isomer because the formula is [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ in each case
Violet is tetrahedral CoCl2(NH3)2, which is why it is polar
Violet is cis (90° Cl–Co–Cl, net dipole); green is trans (180° Cl–Co–Cl, dipoles cancel)

items.explanation: Adjacent chlorides in cis-[Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ give a 90° Cl–Co–Cl angle, so the Co–Cl bond dipoles cannot cancel and the ion is polar: the violet isomer. Opposite chlorides in the trans isomer sit 180° apart, the dipoles cancel (μ = 0), and that is the green isomer. A 180° angle is the definition of trans, not of neighbouring (cis) ligands. The same formula with two geometries is stereoisomerism, not identity. Four ammines plus two chlorides is coordination number 6, octahedral Co(III), not a tetrahedral CoCl2(NH3)2 species.

distractorRationales.A: Neighbouring chlorides are 90° apart (cis). 180° is trans.
distractorRationales.B: Cis and trans share a formula by definition; polarity and the Cl–Co–Cl angle distinguish them.
distractorRationales.C: The formula [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+ already contains six ligands, so the geometry is octahedral.

items.stem:
Two cell types are characterised:
Cell P: ribosomes sediment at 70S; 100% of 3H-thymidine autoradiographic grains over a nucleoid with no nuclear envelope; internal membrane area 0.2 µm² per cell; diameter 1.2 µm.
Cell E: cytoplasmic ribosomes 80S, plus 70S ribosomes inside double-membrane organelles; 94% of DNA grains inside a nuclear envelope; internal membrane area 48 µm² per cell; diameter 18 µm.
Which classification is supported?

choices.text: Cell P is prokaryotic: 70S ribosomes, nucleoid DNA, and almost no endomembrane.
Cell E is prokaryotic, because some of its ribosomes are 70S.
Cell P is eukaryotic, because a diameter of 1.2 µm is typical of animal cells.
Both are eukaryotic, because both contain DNA.

items.explanation: Prokaryotes lack a nuclear envelope, use 70S ribosomes, and have little internal membrane; those are exactly the measurements for cell P (nucleoid grains 100%, 0.2 µm² membranes, 1.2 µm diameter). Cell E has a nucleus, 80S cytosolic ribosomes, and extensive endomembrane (48 µm²), so it is eukaryotic. The 70S ribosomes inside E’s organelles are the bacterial-descended mitochondrial or chloroplast ribosomes, not evidence that E itself is a prokaryote. DNA is present in both domains.

distractorRationales.B: 70S ribosomes inside organelles of a nucleated 80S cell are expected in eukaryotes; they do not make E prokaryotic.
distractorRationales.C: 1.2 µm is bacterial-scale; typical animal cells are an order of magnitude larger, matching E at 18 µm.
distractorRationales.D: Prokaryotes also contain DNA; the distinguishing features are the nucleus and endomembrane system.

passage.title: Philosophy — can we learn from fiction?
passage.body:
Can a novel teach us anything true about the world? The doubt is old and not unserious. A novel, after all, is by definition a made-up story; its characters never lived, its events never happened. Whatever a novelist asserts through the tale is unsupported by evidence — the author simply stipulates that things are so within the fiction. If I want to know how grief works, or how power corrupts, it seems I should consult a psychologist or a historian, not a storyteller who has invented her data.

This objection has force against one kind of knowledge but not another. It is true that fiction cannot establish general facts: no number of novels about ambitious men could prove that ambition corrupts, since the novelist controls the outcome. But not all knowledge is knowledge of general facts. There is also knowing what something is like — what it would be to face a certain choice, to bear a certain loss. And here fiction has resources the treatise lacks: it can place us, in imagination, inside a situation and let us try it on.

Consider the difference between being told that jealousy distorts perception and following, page by page, a character's jealous misreadings of an innocent scene. The first hands us a proposition to file away; the second rehearses the experience, and may leave us better able to recognize the distortion in ourselves. The novelist need not prove that jealousy works this way. It is enough that she renders it so vividly that we recognize it — the recognition, not the proof, is the point.

A skeptic may reply that this "knowledge" is merely emotional, not cognitive — that we have been moved, not taught. But the line is not so clean. To grasp what a situation is like is often a precondition for judging it well; the person who cannot imagine another's suffering will reason poorly about how to treat them. If fiction cultivates that imaginative grasp, it is doing cognitive work, even if it proves no theorems.

The modest conclusion is that fiction and science divide the labor of understanding rather than compete for it. Science tells us that things are so and why; fiction shows us what their being so is like from the inside. To ask a novel to furnish general laws is to misunderstand the kind of knowledge it offers — and to conclude, from its failure to do so, that it offers none, is to make the same mistake twice.

passage.title: psg-cp-9
passage.body:
Nucleophilic substitution is central to organic and biochemical reactivity, from laboratory synthesis to the alkylation of DNA. A class studies how two bromoalkanes react with hydroxide ion, which acts as the nucleophile, in a hydroxylic solvent.
The first substrate is 1-bromobutane, a primary alkyl halide in which the carbon bearing bromine is attached to only one other carbon. With a good nucleophile it reacts by a one-step, concerted mechanism (SN2): hydroxide attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving bromide, and as bromide departs the other three groups invert like an umbrella in the wind. The measured rate depends on the concentrations of both the substrate and the hydroxide.
The second substrate is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide), a tertiary halide whose brominated carbon is attached to three other carbons. It reacts by a two-step mechanism (SN1): the carbon-bromine bond breaks first to give a carbocation, which the nucleophile then captures. The measured rate depends only on the concentration of the substrate, and because the carbocation is trigonal planar, a nucleophile can approach from either face.
The class also revisits structure. They note that a carbon bonded to four different groups is a stereocenter and examine 2-bromobutane as an example. They track how the functional group changes when hydroxide replaces bromide, and they rank the stability of primary, secondary, and tertiary carbocations to explain why substrate structure dictates the mechanism. The instructor stresses that the same electronic and steric principles govern reactions of biological molecules such as the phosphate esters of nucleotides.

items.stem: A neuronal membrane is modeled as a K+ concentration cell. Extracellular K+ is raised tenfold (for example 5 mM to 50 mM) while intracellular K+ is unchanged. The K+ Nernst potential EK:

choices.text: Shifts in the positive direction by about 61 mV (depolarizes), because EK = (RT/F) ln([K+]o/[K+]i) and the concentration ratio falls tenfold
Shifts negative by about 61 mV (hyperpolarizes), because more external K+ increases the outward driving force
Is independent of [K+]o and remains at the sodium Nernst potential
Reverses the sign of ENa without affecting EK

items.explanation: The Nernst equation for a monovalent cation is E = (RT/zF) ln(out/in), about 61 mV * log10(out/in) at mammalian temperature with z = +1. Increasing [K+]o tenfold multiplies the argument of the log by 10, adding +61 mV to EK regardless of the starting ratio. EK therefore becomes less negative. Resting membranes are largely K+-permeable, so Vm follows EK and the cell depolarizes (the basis of hyperkalemic excitability changes). Raising external K+ decreases, not increases, the outward chemical gradient. ENa depends on sodium concentrations and is not slaved to this K+ change.

distractorRationales.B: A smaller out-to-in K+ gradient reduces the magnitude of the negative EK; the shift is depolarizing.
distractorRationales.C: EK is defined by the K+ gradient; it is not a constant and is not ENa.
distractorRationales.D: Changing only K+ concentrations moves EK, not ENa.

passage.title: psg-cars-10
passage.body:
The relationship between mind and body has occupied Western philosophy since antiquity, but the specific problem of consciousness has acquired a new urgency in an era when neuroscience can map the brain in unprecedented detail. Even if we knew the complete physical state of every neuron in a human brain at a given moment, would that knowledge exhaust our understanding of what it is like for the person whose brain it is to be having the experiences they are having? Many philosophers believe the answer is no — and they argue that this gap between complete physical description and subjective experience reveals something fundamental about the nature of mind.
This 'hard problem' — why any physical process should be accompanied by subjective experience at all — is distinguished from the 'easy problems' of consciousness, such as how the brain integrates information, controls attention, or generates verbal reports about mental states. The easy problems are not trivial; they may require decades of research to solve. But they are, in principle, amenable to explanation in functional and computational terms. The hard problem seems to resist this treatment: even a complete functional account of how a system processes information leaves unexplained why processing should feel like anything at all. To feel the force of the puzzle, imagine two systems that process a stimulus in functionally identical ways — the same inputs, the same discriminations, the same outputs — and ask whether it follows that there is something it is like to be each of them, and, if so, whether it must be the same something. Nothing in the functional story, defenders of the hard problem insist, settles the matter: one could in principle specify every computational step by which an auditory system registers a rising tone without thereby explaining why those steps are accompanied by any felt quality at all. It is this apparent slack between function and feeling — not mere complexity — that makes the problem look hard rather than merely unsolved.
Physicalists respond in several ways. Some deny that there is a genuine explanatory gap: what seems like an inexplicable residue is, they argue, an artifact of our limited cognitive access to neural processes rather than evidence of a non-physical dimension of reality. Once neuroscience matures sufficiently, the sense that something has been left out will dissolve, just as vitalism — the doctrine that life requires a special non-physical force — dissolved when biochemistry revealed the mechanisms of metabolism. Others accept that qualia — the intrinsic qualitative character of experience — are real but argue that they are identical with, or constituted by, physical brain states in ways we do not yet fully understand.
Dualists, by contrast, maintain that the hard problem reflects a genuine ontological gap: minds and physical processes belong to categorically different orders of being. This position preserves the intuition that experience is irreducibly subjective but faces the difficulty of explaining how non-physical minds causally interact with physical brains — a puzzle that has shadowed substance dualism since its classical formulation. To say that minds and brains interact is plausible as ordinary description; to explain the mechanism of that interaction without smuggling physical causation back in is a philosophical challenge that has resisted resolution for centuries.
The hard problem of consciousness thus sits at the intersection of metaphysics, philosophy of mind, and neuroscience. Whether it admits of a naturalistic solution remains one of the deepest unresolved questions in intellectual life.

items.stem: In 3-methyl-2-pentene the double-bond carbons are C2 (attached to CH3 and H) and C3 (attached to CH2CH3 and CH3). If the C2 methyl and the C3 ethyl group lie on the same side of the double bond, the isomer is designated:
items.explanation: E/Z assignment uses CIP priorities at each alkene carbon, not whether the identical-looking alkyl groups happen to be trans in a casual sense. At C2, CH3 outranks H. At C3, CH2CH3 outranks CH3 because the first point of difference is a carbon versus hydrogen. The two higher-priority groups are therefore the C2 methyl and the C3 ethyl. When those two groups are on the same side, the isomer is Z (from zusammen). E would require those higher-priority groups on opposite sides. R/S and meso do not describe this alkene geometry.

items.stem: A buffer is prepared from acetic acid (pKa = 4.74) with [CH3CO2−] = 0.30 M and [CH3CO2H] = 0.030 M. What is the pH?
items.explanation: Henderson–Hasselbalch gives pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]). The ratio 0.30/0.030 = 10, and log10(10) = 1, so pH = 4.74 + 1 = 5.74. Equal concentrations would have given pH = pKa = 4.74. The value 3.74 would correspond to inverting the ratio (tenfold excess acid). Neutrality (pH 7) is not required for a buffer; this acetate buffer is mildly acidic, as expected near pKa 4.74 with excess conjugate base pulling the pH one unit above pKa.

distractorRationales.A: 3.74 is pKa − 1, which would apply if [HA]/[A−] were 10 rather than [A−]/[HA] = 10. The logarithm was inverted.
distractorRationales.B: 4.74 is the pKa and is the pH only when [A−] = [HA], which is not the case here.
distractorRationales.D: pH 7 is neutrality of pure water, not the pH of a carboxylate buffer with pKa 4.74.

passage.title: The ledger of the commons
passage.body:
When a city puts a park on a map, it appears to have given something away: land that could have been lots, hours that could have been tolls. Developers are not wrong that the gift has a price. They are wrong when they treat the price as a leak from an otherwise watertight private order. The private order is already subsidized by streets, courts, pipes, and the patience of people who do not sue every time a stranger walks past a porch. A park is not the exception to property. It is one of the ways a dense city remains inhabitable enough for property to be worth wanting.

Accountants prefer a ledger in which every square metre has a named owner and a yield. Parks embarrass the ledger because their yield is a crowd that does not pay at the gate, a cooling that does not send an invoice, a child who learns a city can include her without a purchase. The embarrassment produces two crude policies. One is to fence and ticket until the park behaves like a venue. The other is to neglect the park until the crowd looks like a problem that only private security can solve. Both policies claim to be realistic. Both are ways of refusing to count the effects that made the park rational in the first place.

Friends of the park sometimes answer with a poetry of the unowned. The poetry is moving and strategically weak. A commons that cannot speak in maintenance budgets will lose to a spreadsheet that can. The more adult defense is to insist that the ledger is incomplete, not that ledgers are evil. Planting, lighting, toilets, and a gardener who is paid in winter are not betrayals of openness. They are how openness lasts past a ribbon-cutting.

There is a further honesty. Parks are not innocent. They have been used to raise adjacent rents, to move unhoused people out of sight, to display a city’s kindness to visitors who will never need the toilets. Naming those uses does not hand the land to the highest bidder. It prevents the park’s defenders from pretending that green on a map is already justice. Justice would be a park whose ledger includes the people who were priced off the blocks around it.

If urban politics cannot hold that thought, it will keep oscillating between the venue and the ruin, and calling the oscillation pragmatism.

items.stem:
At the experimental temperature the Nernst equation is given as E = (58 mV / z) log10([ion]out / [ion]in). Concentrations (mM) are:
K+: out 4, in 140 (z = +1).
Na+: out 145, in 12 (z = +1).
Cl−: out 116, in 4 (z = −1).
If the membrane were permeable only to K+, the resting potential would be closest to which value?

choices.text: 0 mV, because unequal concentrations cannot produce a voltage until pumps run.
+90 mV, using log10(140/4) with a positive sign.
+58 mV, assuming a ten-fold K+ gradient.

items.explanation: For K+, z = +1 and [out]/[in] = 4/140 = 0.0286. log10(0.0286) ≈ −1.54, so E_K = 58 × (−1.54) ≈ −89 mV, about −90 mV. A membrane permeable only to K+ rests at that equilibrium potential: K+ efflux leaves unmatched negative charge inside until the electrical pull balances the concentration gradient. Inverting the concentration ratio gives +90 mV, which would be the potential if the inside were the reference for a cation gradient in the opposite direction. A ten-fold gradient would be −58 mV, but 140/4 is 35-fold, not 10-fold.

distractorRationales.A: A concentration gradient of a permeant ion is sufficient to set E_K; pumps maintain the gradient but are not required in the Nernst formula itself.
distractorRationales.B: Using [in]/[out] flips the sign; cations leaving a K+-rich cell make the interior negative.
distractorRationales.C: The gradient is 35-fold (log10 ≈ 1.54), not 10-fold, and the sign must be negative.

items.stem: A Northern blot probed for a rare mRNA shows high background from imperfect RNA–DNA hybrids. The researcher wants to increase hybridization stringency without changing the probe sequence. Which change is most appropriate?

choices.text: Raise hybridization temperature and lower the NaCl concentration.
Lower hybridization temperature and raise the NaCl concentration.
Keep temperature fixed and raise NaCl to 2 M so that only G–C pairs remain paired.
Decrease temperature to 25 °C at unchanged salt so that mismatches are kinetically trapped.

items.explanation: Stringency is the degree to which hybridization conditions require perfect complementarity. Raising temperature approaches the Tm of imperfect duplexes first, so mismatched hybrids melt while matched hybrids remain. Lowering monovalent salt reduces shielding of the phosphate backbone, which destabilizes duplexes and likewise disfavors mismatches. The combination therefore increases specificity of a Northern or Southern hybridization. Cooling and adding salt do the opposite: they stabilize even poorly matched hybrids and raise background, which is the problem the blot already shows.

distractorRationales.B: Lower temperature and higher salt decrease stringency by stabilizing mismatched hybrids, which would worsen the background the blot already shows.
distractorRationales.C: High salt stabilizes nucleic acid duplexes, including imperfect ones; it does not selectively preserve only G–C pairs in a way that raises specificity.
distractorRationales.D: Dropping to 25 °C far below typical probe Tm allows nonspecific annealing; mismatches are not ‘trapped’ in a way that improves signal-to-noise.

passage.title: Construction Site (1974)
passage.body: Amina Okonkwo's 1974 essay “Construction Site,” on broadcast newsrooms, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that speed of publication is being mistaken for care. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: What is the most likely explanation for the reaction being slower at 50°C than at 40°C, despite 50°C being the higher temperature?

choices.text: The higher temperature likely began denaturing the amylase, disrupting its active site and reducing its ability to bind starch.
There was less starch available at 50°C.
Amylase works better in cold conditions in general.
The timer used to measure the reaction was faulty only at 50°C.

items.explanation: Since starch and amylase concentrations were held constant across all trials, the drop in rate at 50°C is best explained by heat-induced denaturation disrupting the enzyme's active site, not by a change in the amount of substrate or a measurement fault. Denaturation does not remove the enzyme molecules — it distorts their 3D shape, especially the active site, so they can no longer bind their substrate effectively. The enzyme is still present, just non-functional. Memory tip: Same wax-figure image as before: the amylase is still physically there at 50°C, it's just melted out of the shape it needs to grip starch. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: Chemistry · Enzyme Kinetics
passage.body: A student investigates how temperature affects the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction, using an enzyme called amylase to break down starch into sugar. They measure the time taken for a fixed amount of starch to be fully broken down at five different temperatures: 10°C, 20°C, 30°C, 40°C and 50°C, keeping the amylase concentration and starch concentration constant in every trial. The reaction is fastest at 40°C. At 50°C, the reaction is slower than at 40°C, and even slower than at 30°C, despite the higher temperature. At 10°C, the reaction is very slow but still eventually completes.

items.stem: A monoclonal IgG stored at pH 8 slowly deamidates a buried asparagine to aspartate. Isoelectric focusing of the aged sample is compared with fresh antibody. How should the pI of the major new species change, and why?

choices.text: pI increases because aspartate is more basic than asparagine
pI is unchanged because deamidation does not alter covalent charge
pI becomes undefined because proteins have no isoelectric point after mutation
pI decreases because a neutral carboxamide is converted to an ionizable carboxylate

items.explanation: Asparagine’s side chain is a nonionizable carboxamide. Deamidation replaces it with aspartic acid, whose carboxylic acid is negatively charged at the mildly alkaline pH of typical IEF sample buffers and throughout most of a focusing gradient above ~pH 4. Adding a new acidic group lowers the pH at which the protein’s net charge is zero, so the focused band shifts toward a lower pI. Aspartate is not a base, the covalent charge table does change, and every protein still has a pI defined by the pH of zero net charge.

distractorRationales.A: Aspartate is acidic, not basic; adding a carboxylate cannot raise pI.
distractorRationales.B: Converting Asn to Asp adds an ionizable group, so the charge versus pH curve and the pI both change.
distractorRationales.C: Mutations shift pI but do not abolish the concept; IEF still focuses the new species at a new pH.

items.stem: The commentator who calls the clerk a “Kantian saint” is presented as

choices.text: faithfully capturing the clerk's own account of his motive
imposing a tidy philosophical costume on a more local, shame-based restraint
proving that the clerk acted to save a marriage
arguing that unsealed letters are public documents

items.explanation: The narrator says the Kantian praise is too clean and contrasts universality with the clerk's local, slightly ashamed maxim: he did not want to be the man who had read the letter. Shame, not a universal law, kept his eyes off the page. The passage therefore treats the commentator as dressing a smaller ethics in a grand theory. The clerk never claims Kant; he did not finish the letter, so he cannot be saving a marriage; and the text does not make the letter public.

distractorRationales.A: The clerk's motive is habit and shame, not the commentator's Kantian maxim.
distractorRationales.C: He refused to finish the letter; the marriage-saving hypothesis is exactly what he will not test.
distractorRationales.D: The passage never treats the letter as a public document; he withholds it.

passage.title: On keeping a promise to a stranger
passage.body:
When the magistrate asked why he had returned the purse, the clerk did not say honesty. He said habit. He had been taught, in a household that measured virtue by small repetitions, that a found object remains someone else's until the world has been given a fair chance to reclaim it. The purse contained little money and a letter, unsealed, beginning: I will not be there when you arrive. He did not finish it. To finish it, he thought, would convert a duty into a story, and stories have a way of making the finder important.

Philosophers like to treat this as a puzzle about property and knowledge. If he does not know the owner, is the duty weaker? If the letter would have saved a marriage, does withholding it become a harm? The clerk would have found the questions indecent. He was not refusing knowledge so much as refusing a role. The city had clerks for lost property; it did not have clerks for other people's farewells.

A later commentator, writing after the clerk was dead, praised him as a Kantian saint: he acted from a maxim he could will as universal. The praise is too clean. The clerk's maxim was local and slightly ashamed. He did not want to be the man who had read the letter. Shame, not universality, kept his eyes off the page. That is not a lesser ethics. It is an ethics that knows how quickly curiosity dresses itself as concern.

The owner collected the purse the next morning and did not thank him. In the commentary this becomes a test of whether virtue needs recognition. The clerk, if asked, would have said only that the counter was busy.

items.stem: Demyelination of a central axon, as in multiple sclerosis, is most likely to:

choices.text: raise internodal membrane resistance and thereby increase conduction velocity
leave membrane capacitance unchanged but permanently eliminate nodes of Ranvier, which speeds continuous conduction
increase internodal capacitance and ionic leak, slowing or blocking saltatory propagation
increase axon diameter enough that continuous unmyelinated conduction becomes faster than the original myelinated fiber

items.explanation: Losing myelin strips away the high-resistance, low-capacitance internodal wrapping. Exposed internodal membrane then behaves more like a leaky capacitor: more current is lost across the membrane and more charge is required to change membrane potential, so the local-circuit current may fail to bring the next node to threshold. The result is slowed or blocked saltatory conduction, which is the physiologic basis of many MS deficits. Demyelination does not raise Rm, does not remove the anatomic nodes in a way that helps, and does not enlarge axon diameter as a compensatory speed mechanism.

distractorRationales.A: Myelin is what raises internodal Rm. Removing it lowers resistance to leak and slows conduction rather than speeding it.
distractorRationales.B: Nodes remain as specialized axonal domains; the problem is the internodes. Capacitance of the denuded membrane increases, which is not 'unchanged,' and conduction does not speed up.
distractorRationales.D: Demyelination does not hypertrophy the axon into a giant unmyelinated fiber. Even if diameter were unchanged, losing myelin slows the impulse relative to the myelinated state.

items.stem: n-Pentane (bp 36 °C) boils higher than its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane, bp 9 °C). Which statement correctly links shape to intermolecular forces?

choices.text: The more spherical neopentane has less surface contact, so London forces are weaker and the boiling point is lower.
n-Pentane hydrogen-bonds through its terminal methyl groups, while neopentane cannot.
Neopentane is ionic; n-pentane is covalent.
Branching always raises boiling point because branched isomers pack more tightly in the liquid.

items.explanation: Both isomers are nonpolar hydrocarbons, so the only significant intermolecular forces are London dispersions. Dispersion strength increases with polarizable surface area in contact. The compact, nearly spherical neopentane molecule presents less surface to neighbors than the elongated n-pentane chain, so the attractions are weaker and less heat is needed to vaporize it. Hydrocarbons do not hydrogen-bond, neither isomer is ionic, and branching generally lowers boiling points of alkanes for this surface-area reason (while often raising melting points because of packing in the solid).

distractorRationales.B: C–H bonds are not hydrogen-bond donors; alkane boiling-point trends are dispersion, not hydrogen bonding.
distractorRationales.C: Both compounds are neutral hydrocarbons.
distractorRationales.D: Branching typically lowers alkane boiling points by reducing surface contact. Tight crystal packing can raise melting points, which is a different phase change.

passage.title: Electrodialysis Removal of Lactate
passage.body:
A fictional electrodialysis device removes lactate from a small waste stream. Lactic acid has pKa = 3.9, and lactate carries a -1 charge. The feed chamber initially contains 100 mL of 0.100 mM total lactate species. An anion-exchange membrane separates the feed chamber from a collection chamber near the positive anode. Each run lasts 300 s. Current can be carried by lactate and by other ions in the buffer. Joule heating may broaden concentration gradients and reduce separation efficiency.

Electrodialysis conditions and lactate removal.
Run | Feed pH | Voltage (V) | Current (mA) | Temperature rise (C) | Salt condition | Total lactate removed from feed (%)
1 | 3.0 | 20 | 2.0 | 0.2 | low salt | 8
2 | 7.0 | 20 | 10.0 | 1.0 | low salt | 45
3 | 7.0 | 40 | 20.0 | 4.5 | low salt | 70
4 | 7.0 | 40 | 20.0 | 1.0 with cooling | low salt | 78
5 | 7.0 | 20 | 25.0 | 5.0 | high salt | 30

Electrodialysis chamber arrangement. — Negatively charged lactate migrates through an anion-exchange membrane toward the positive anode. Neutral lactic acid is much less efficiently transported by the electric field.

items.stem: Inserting a gene of interest into a plasmid vector and introducing it into bacteria to produce many copies (or a protein product) is:
items.explanation: Molecular cloning: insert a gene into a plasmid vector → bacteria make copies/protein. Takeaway: Cloning = gene into plasmid → bacteria copy it (recombinant DNA). items.stem: A heritage board awards restoration funds to a nineteenth-century bank whose ledgers, portraits, and blueprints fill a municipal archive, while a demolished riverside market—attested only by a few photographs—is marked with a single plaque. The author’s analysis most strongly supports which evaluation?

choices.text: The board has measured historical importance correctly, because importance is proportional to the quantity of surviving paperwork.
The plaque is already the more democratic monument, because photographs do not count as documents and so cannot distort public memory.
Interviews with former stallholders would automatically cancel the imbalance, since speech cannot be managed the way a gazette can.
The funding choice treats a surviving paper trail as a measure of historical weight, thereby letting the distribution of clerks and cartons decide which urban past is monumentalized.

items.explanation: The civic paragraph maps directly onto the bank-versus-market case: a preservation campaign that “saves” the richly documented building is not merely picking architecture; it ratifies a distribution of paperwork as a distribution of historical weight, and the undocumented street is left as atmosphere. The bank’s ledgers are the merchant-townhouse carton pile; the market is the demolished neighborhood. The author denies that quantity of files equals importance, denies that non-paper traces are simply non-documents, and denies that oral history automatically undoes archival bias. Applying that principle yields D rather than a celebration of the archive’s bulk.

distractorRationales.A: The author treats that proportionality as the error to be named, not as a valid public standard of importance.
distractorRationales.B: Photographs are still traces; the author’s worry is over-representation of what was filed, not a claim that images lie outside documentation.
distractorRationales.C: The oral-history section insists that an interview can be managed as tightly as a colonial gazette, so speech is not an automatic democratic solvent.

passage.title: The archive and the street
passage.body:
Historians often speak as if the past were a reluctant witness who can be coaxed into testimony if only the right box is opened. The letter, the minute-book, the trial transcript, and the parish register are treated not as remnants but as the event itself, patiently waiting to be interviewed. The metaphor is professionally convenient. It locates virtue in attentiveness and implies that an archive, handled without aggression, will speak of its own accord. Archives do not speak. They are offices that decide, usually long before a scholar arrives, which traces of life will be kept, numbered, and thereby made eligible for later recovery. To mistake a folder for a microphone is to forget that someone built the studio, invited some guests, and switched the machine off when the conversation became inconvenient.

This is not a case for abandoning documents. It is a case against a piety now common in public history: the belief that proximity to a primary source is itself a moral credential. Museum captions announce that an object was found in an attic or rescued from a demolition site, as if its later career in a glass case were a continuation of its first life rather than a conversion into evidence. Conversion is what historians do. Trouble begins when conversion is narrated as rescue, because that narration conceals the historian's power and, more consequentially, conceals the people who never generated a paper trail to be rescued.

Oral historians have pressed this objection for decades, sometimes with more hope than caution. They have offered the recorded interview as a democratic patch, a way of admitting those whom the file forgot. The patch is real; it is not automatic. An interview is also a document, made under conditions of prompting, recording, transcription, and later cutting. It can be managed as tightly as a colonial gazette. What distinguishes a responsible oral history is not orality as such, but the historian remaining visible in the manufacture of the record—visible enough that a later reader can see where a question steered, where a narrator pushed back, and where a silence was not a hole but a refusal.

The sharper problem is civic rather than technical. If the only past that can be cited is the past that was filed, public memory will go on over-representing those who employed clerks. Cities make the point more bluntly than seminars do. A demolished neighborhood deposits fewer cartons than a merchant's townhouse; a street seller deposits fewer than a chartered company. When a preservation trust then campaigns to save the townhouse because it is richly documented, the trust is not merely selecting architecture. It is ratifying a distribution of paperwork as a distribution of historical weight. The house is asked to stand for an age, and the undocumented street is invited, if at all, to supply atmosphere.

Honesty does not require the fantasy that every life can be reconstructed with equal density. Some absences are final. The decent procedure is to treat those absences as facts about power rather than as temporary vacancies that a more heroic search will fill. A history that admits what cannot be known is more public-minded than a history that performs completeness by adding still more pages to an already thick dossier. The archive will remain necessary. It need not remain innocent.

passage.title: psg-bb-1
passage.body:
Researchers characterized a bacterial hydrolase, EnzA, that cleaves a colorless substrate into a yellow product, allowing the initial reaction velocity to be measured by absorbance. Working at constant enzyme concentration, saturating buffer, and 37 deg C, they varied the substrate concentration [S] and recorded the initial velocity (v0). As [S] increased, v0 rose steeply at first and then leveled off, tracing the hyperbolic curve expected for a single-active-site enzyme. From these data the team estimated a maximum velocity (Vmax) of 100 micromol/min and a Michaelis constant (Km) of 2.0 mM, where Km is the [S] at which v0 equals half of Vmax.
The team then repeated the assay in the presence of two candidate drugs. With a fixed concentration of Inhibitor A, the measured Vmax remained 100 micromol/min, but the apparent Km rose to 6.0 mM; adding excess substrate fully restored the maximal rate. With a fixed concentration of Inhibitor B, the apparent Km stayed at 2.0 mM, but Vmax fell to 50 micromol/min, and no amount of added substrate recovered the original maximal rate.
A double-reciprocal (Lineweaver-Burk) plot summarized the results: the control line and the Inhibitor A line shared the same y-intercept but differed in slope, whereas the control line and the Inhibitor B line shared the same x-intercept but differed in y-intercept. The researchers concluded that the two inhibitors act by distinct mechanisms, a distinction that matters clinically because it determines whether raising the physiological substrate concentration can overcome the drug's effect.

passage.title: The Caption (1973)
passage.body: Mei-Ling Vargas published “The Caption” in 1973 after a season in disaster mapping. The argument is that fairness talk often arrives after the decision has already been made. The piece admits that some gatekeeping keeps fraud out. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: psg-bb-9
passage.body:
Neurophysiologists used a squid giant axon and fine electrodes to record the membrane potential during a nerve impulse. At rest, the inside of the axon measured about -70 mV relative to the outside. A brief electrical stimulus that depolarized the membrane to a threshold near -55 mV triggered an all-or-none action potential: the potential shot upward to about +30 mV (the rising phase) and then rapidly returned toward rest (the falling phase), briefly overshooting to a value more negative than -70 mV before stabilizing.
The team dissected the ionic basis using two toxins. Applying tetrodotoxin (TTX), which blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, abolished the action potential entirely: stimulation no longer produced the rapid upstroke. Applying tetraethylammonium (TEA), which blocks voltage-gated potassium channels, left the upstroke intact but markedly slowed the return to rest, prolonging the action potential. Blocking the Na+/K+ ATPase with a separate agent did not abolish individual action potentials over the short term but, over many impulses, degraded the ion gradients on which they depend.
In a final experiment the researchers compared conduction along a myelinated axon with an unmyelinated one of similar diameter. The myelinated axon conducted impulses far faster, because the action potential regenerated only at the gaps in the myelin (nodes of Ranvier), jumping from node to node. The results tied each phase of the action potential to specific ion channels and showed how myelination speeds signaling without changing the underlying ionic mechanism.

items.stem: Limited micrococcal nuclease digestion of eukaryotic chromatin, followed by deproteinization, yields a DNA ladder with a ~147 bp core and, under milder cutting, a ~200 bp repeat. Extraction of histone H1 converts 30-nm-scale fibers toward a beads-on-a-string 10-nm filament without changing 147 bp core protection.
