choices.text: An H2A/H2B/H3/H4 octamer wraps ~147 bp; H1 binds linker DNA and stabilizes higher-order folding, so H1 removal lengthens nuclease-accessible linker without unwrapping the core particle.
H1 is the sole histone in the octamer; its extraction must destroy 147 bp protection, contradicting the data unless the assay failed.
Micrococcal nuclease cuts inside the nucleosome core first, so the 147 bp fragment is unprotected linker DNA rather than histone-bound DNA.
Telomeric DNA uniquely lacks nucleosomes, so the ladder can arise only from centromeric satellite repeats.

items.explanation: The nucleosome core particle is an H3/H4 tetramer plus two H2A/H2B dimers wrapping 147 bp of DNA. Linker histone H1 binds DNA at the entry and exit of the core and stabilizes folding toward 30-nm-scale fibers. Micrococcal nuclease first cleaves accessible linker DNA, producing ~200 bp repeats that include linker, then trims to the nuclease-resistant 147 bp core. Removing H1 increases linker accessibility and unfolds higher-order structure without dismantling the octamer, so core protection persists. H1 is not an octamer histone, the enzyme does not preferentially cut inside the core first, and nucleosome ladders are genome-wide.

distractorRationales.B: The octamer is H2A, H2B, H3, and H4; H1 is the linker histone, and the stem shows that 147 bp protection survives H1 extraction.
distractorRationales.C: The core DNA is protected from nuclease; 147 bp is the wrapped core fragment, not naked linker.
distractorRationales.D: Nucleosomes package most of the nuclear genome, including euchromatin; telomeres and centromeres are not the sole source of the ladder.

passage.title: Fraud Control (1977)
passage.body: Samir Haddad's 1977 essay “Fraud Control,” on community radio, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that speed of publication is being mistaken for care. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem:
A pulse of 3H-leucine labels a secretory protein in cultured cells. Radioactivity in the immunoprecipitated protein (counts min−1) is:
5 min: rough ER 820, Golgi 40, secretory vesicles 10, extracellular medium 5.
20 min: RER 210, Golgi 640, vesicles 80, medium 15.
45 min: RER 50, Golgi 180, vesicles 520, medium 90.
90 min: RER 20, Golgi 40, vesicles 110, medium 710.
Which route do the counts support?

choices.text: Golgi → rough ER → secretory vesicles → medium
Rough ER → Golgi → secretory vesicles → extracellular medium
Medium → vesicles → Golgi → rough ER (endocytosis of the labelled protein)
Rough ER → secretory vesicles → Golgi → medium

items.explanation: The radioactivity peak moves in time: 820 counts in the rough ER at 5 min, 640 in the Golgi at 20 min, 520 in secretory vesicles at 45 min, and 710 in the medium at 90 min. That order is the classical secretory pathway (synthesis into the RER, processing in the Golgi, packaging into vesicles, then exocytosis). The reverse order would require the earliest counts in the medium, which are only 5. Skipping the Golgi would not produce the 640-count Golgi peak at 20 min before the vesicular peak.

distractorRationales.A: The 5 min maximum is in the RER (820), not the Golgi (40), so the path cannot start at the Golgi.
distractorRationales.C: Extracellular counts rise last (5 then 710), so the protein is being secreted, not taken up.
distractorRationales.D: Vesicles peak at 45 min after the Golgi peak at 20 min, so vesicles follow the Golgi rather than precede it.

A fictional electrodialysis device removes lactate from a small waste stream. Lactic acid has pKa = 3.9, and lactate carries a -1 charge. The feed chamber initially contains 100 mL of 0.100 mM total lactate species. An anion-exchange membrane separates the feed chamber from a collection chamber near the positive anode. Each run lasts 300 s. Current can be carried by lactate and by other ions in the buffer. Joule heating may broaden concentration gradients and reduce separation efficiency.

Electrodialysis conditions and lactate removal.
Run | Feed pH | Voltage (V) | Current (mA) | Temperature rise (C) | Salt condition | Total lactate removed from feed (%)

passage.title: Biology · Gene Regulation
passage.body: A research group is studying a heat-shock protein gene, HSP-70X, thought to help wheat seedlings survive short bursts of extreme heat. They suspect a regulatory protein, called ReguFactor B, switches HSP-70X on when temperatures rise. To test this, they create three groups of genetically modified wheat seedlings: one where ReguFactor B is overexpressed (produced in excess), one where the gene for ReguFactor B is knocked out (disabled), and a normal (wild-type) control group. All seedlings are exposed to a two-hour heat spike, and HSP-70X mRNA levels are measured immediately afterwards. The overexpression group shows HSP-70X mRNA levels roughly four times higher than the wild-type control. The knockout group shows almost no detectable HSP-70X mRNA at all, even after the heat spike. Under normal, non-heat conditions, HSP-70X mRNA levels are low and roughly equal across all three groups.

items.stem:
A spring is stretched by hanging masses. Force F is plotted against extension x. Hooke’s law is F = k x, so the slope of a graph of F (N) versus x (m) is the spring constant k.

x (m) | F (N)
0.000 | 0.02 ± 0.04
0.020 | 1.02 ± 0.04
0.040 | 2.02 ± 0.04
0.060 | 3.02 ± 0.04

Using the change from the first to the last reliable point, what is k?

choices.text: 0.050 N m−1, if x were left in millimetres in the denominator.
3.0 N m−1, using ΔF / 1 rather than Δx.
50 N m−1, because ΔF / Δx = 3.00 N / 0.060 m = 50 N m−1.
0.020 m N−1, the reciprocal of the slope (the compliance).

items.explanation: From x = 0.000 to 0.060 m, F rises from 0.02 N to 3.02 N, so ΔF = 3.00 N and Δx = 0.060 m. Then k = 3.00 / 0.060 = 50 N m−1. The same slope is (1.02 − 0.02)/0.020 = 50 N m−1 between neighbouring points, so the graph is linear. The intercept 0.02 N is consistent with zero within the ±0.04 N error, so there is no significant preload. If millimetres were used accidentally (Δx = 60), k would appear 1000 times too small (0.050). The reciprocal 0.020 m N−1 is 1/k, which is not what the question asked. ΔF without dividing by Δx is not a spring constant.

distractorRationales.A: 0.050 N m−1 is 3.00 / 60, i.e. treating 0.060 m as 60 (millimetres) without converting. SI units require metres in F = k x.
distractorRationales.B: 3.0 N is a force difference, not a slope. Spring constant is force per unit extension.
distractorRationales.D: 0.020 m N−1 is 1/k. That is the compliance, useful in some analyses, but the question asked for k from the F–x slope.

passage.title: Nuclear genes required for Complex IV assembly in a model alga
passage.body:
A fictional unicellular alga uses nuclear genes E and F to assemble functional mitochondrial Complex IV. Gene E encodes a copper-delivery chaperone, and gene F encodes a Complex IV structural subunit. Loss of either gene produces a slow-respiration phenotype, and loss of both genes is not more severe than loss of either single gene. The genes are autosomal and assort independently. Researchers crossed EEFF algae with eeff algae, selfed the EeFf F1, and measured F2 respiration phenotypes. Biochemical assays were performed on representative genotypes.

F2 respiration phenotypes after EeFf selfing.
Phenotype | Observed colonies
Normal respiration | 166
Slow respiration | 126

Respiratory measurements in representative strains.
Strain or condition | Complex I activity (%) | Complex IV activity (%) | O2 consumption (%) | NADH/NAD+ ratio | Growth on fermentable carbon
E_F_ | 100 | 100 | 100 | 0.5 | Robust
eeF_ | 95 | 18 | 22 | 3.2 | Slow but viable
E_ff | 100 | 20 | 25 | 3.0 | Slow but viable
eeff | 93 | 15 | 20 | 3.4 | Slow but viable
E_F_ + Complex IV inhibitor | 98 | 5 | 8 | 4.0 | Poor

Electron flow to Complex IV. — Electrons from NADH enter through Complex I and are transferred through ubiquinone, Complex III, cytochrome c, and Complex IV. Complex IV transfers electrons to oxygen. When Complex IV activity is low, upstream electron carriers become more reduced and oxygen consumption falls.

items.stem: An inhibitor of a Michaelis-Menten enzyme increases the apparent Km from 4 micromolar to 12 micromolar but does not change Vmax when substrate is saturating. Which mechanism is most consistent with these data?

choices.text: Pure noncompetitive inhibition at a separate site
Competitive inhibition at or near the active site
Irreversible covalent inactivation of half the enzyme molecules
Uncompetitive inhibition that binds only the enzyme-substrate complex

items.explanation: Competitive inhibitors reduce apparent substrate affinity, increasing apparent Km, but their effect can be overcome by sufficiently high substrate concentration, so Vmax is unchanged. Common miss: Reversing how competitive and noncompetitive inhibitors affect Km and Vmax. This matches the increase in apparent Km with unchanged Vmax. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.A: Pure noncompetitive inhibition decreases Vmax without changing Km in the simple model.
distractorRationales.C: Irreversible loss of active enzyme would lower Vmax.
distractorRationales.D: Uncompetitive inhibition lowers both apparent Km and Vmax.

items.stem: A microRNA is complementary to the 3′ UTR of a growth-factor receptor mRNA. Overexpression of the miRNA decreases receptor protein with little change in pre-mRNA transcription. Argonaute immunoprecipitation recovers the mature receptor mRNA. Which mechanism is most likely?

choices.text: The miRNA is reverse-transcribed into repressor DNA that methylates the receptor promoter as its sole mode of action.
The miRNA guides an RNA-induced silencing complex to the 3′ UTR, causing translational repression and/or mRNA destabilization without requiring a change in transcription initiation.
The miRNA splices the receptor’s signal sequence out of the pre-mRNA as a nuclear intron, so no protein is made.
The miRNA aminoacylates tRNA so that the receptor’s codons cannot be translated because of a global charging defect.

items.explanation: Animal microRNAs are processed to ~22-nt RNAs loaded onto Argonaute in the RNA-induced silencing complex. Partial complementarity to a 3′ UTR represses translation and often destabilizes the mRNA via deadenylation, lowering protein output without a required change in transcription initiation. Recovery of the receptor mRNA in Argonaute immunoprecipitates supports this cytoplasmic, post-transcriptional mechanism and fits the unchanged pre-mRNA transcription. miRNAs are not routinely reverse-transcribed into promoter-methylating DNA as their primary mode, they do not act as spliceosomes for signal peptides, and they do not aminoacylate tRNAs.

distractorRationales.A: Unchanged pre-mRNA transcription and Argonaute recovery of the mature mRNA point to cytoplasmic RISC action, not promoter methylation as the sole mechanism.
distractorRationales.C: miRNAs do not catalyze nuclear splicing of signal-sequence exons; RISC acts on mature mRNAs, consistent with the IP result.
distractorRationales.D: A global charging defect would collapse translation of many proteins, not specifically the receptor whose 3′ UTR matches the miRNA.

items.stem: The agent’s “vacant possession,” called “legally tidy,” is later set against the speaker’s “not empty, only unpopulated.” The diction most nearly implies that

choices.text: legal vacancy-language treats a concluded tenancy as a blank, while “unpopulated” concedes missing persons without declaring the remaining objects finished.
the agent is quoting a poem, and “unpopulated” is a zoological term for a kettle.
the speaker now agrees that the room is legally and emotionally identical to a vacant lot.
“tidy” means the skip workers folded the calendar, which is why the wall is paler.

items.explanation: Implication from diction: vacant possession is praised as tidy because it ends a tenancy; empty would complete that blankness. Unpopulated keeps a distinction the law’s word flattens—people gone, things and hours not. The later grammatical metaphor (present tense of objects) confirms the contrast. Nothing supports a zoological kettle, an agreement that the room is a lot, or tidy as a claim about folded calendars. Word choice is doing the ethical work, which is why this is an inference-from-diction item rather than a mere restatement.

distractorRationales.B: Unpopulated is the speaker’s correction of empty, not a biology joke, and vacant possession is the agent’s legal phrase, not a poem.
distractorRationales.C: The whole point of the correction is that she does not accept identity between legal vacancy and the room’s remaining assignments.
distractorRationales.D: Tidy characterises the legal phrase, not the skip’s handling of a calendar; the paler rectangle is a mark of remaining, not a definition of tidy.

passage.title: Vacant possession
passage.body:
The rental had been emptied with the efficiency of people who did not live there. I arrived after the skip had gone. What remained were the marks of remaining: a paler rectangle on the wall where a calendar had blocked the sun, a screw in the kitchen plaster that had held nothing I could remember, a ring on the lino where a bin had sat long enough to become a climate. The agent called it "vacant possession." The phrase was legally tidy. It treated my father as a tenancy that had concluded.

I opened the cupboard above the kettle. Inside, taped to the wood, was a shopping list in his slanted capitals, and beneath it a scrap of verse I had never seen. He was not a man who announced poems. He had been a man who boiled water at the same hour, as if the day were a machine that required a particular ignition. The list wanted milk, soap, and a cheaper brand of tea. The last item was written twice, then crossed out, then written again, as if indecision were a kind of company.

The kettle still knew his hour.
I did not.
The cupboard kept a shopping list
addressed to a week that never arrived.
I ticked the milk as if the ticking
could make a future stand up.

I stood with a pen I had not meant to bring and put a mark beside milk, then stopped, because the gesture had the shape of care and the content of a joke at my own expense. Grief, in the pamphlets, is supposed to be a weather that passes over a landscape. In the cupboard it was more like a task left in a shared kitchen: unclaimed, slightly shameful, still assigned. I wanted, ridiculously, to buy the milk. I wanted not to be the kind of daughter who leaves a list unanswered.

The agent coughed in the hallway and mentioned carpet cleaning, then the bond, then the need to "move on" as if the room were a queue. I heard myself thank him. Courtesy was easier than explaining that the room was not empty, only unpopulated. He was not unkind. He was on a clock I did not share. Vacant possession, I thought, is a legal sentence that cannot conjugate the present tense of objects. The kettle, if it could speak, would not have used it. It would have asked why the hour had been cancelled without notice.

items.stem: Which new case is most analogous to the test in Hanae Morioka’s “The Roster” (1983), vol. 200015, no. 2?

choices.text: A proof in Euclidean geometry that names every axiom
A recipe that lists oven temperature
Hanae Morioka winning a literary prize
A hospital checklist that cannot be described without the word “quality,” yet quality is never defined

items.explanation: Apply-to-new-context: the analog is a practice that depends on an undefined official word. Geometry and recipes are explicit; a prize is off-axis. Changing names does not change the analog. Neighbouring options fail because they name a different relation, drop a required conversion, or contradict a number given in the stem (GAMSAT.S1.humanities.t3#800013). Those traps are not a second live key.

distractorRationales.A: Named axioms are the opposite of hidden adjectives.
distractorRationales.B: A temperature is an operational instruction, not an official perfume.
distractorRationales.C: A prize is biographical, not analogical.

passage.title: The Roster (1983)
passage.body: Hanae Morioka's 1983 essay “The Roster,” on court translation, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that fairness talk often arrives after the decision has already been made. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: One reason sensory adaptation is useful is that it:

choices.text: Amplifies weak signals for the brain
Filters out constant, unchanging stimuli — and can protect receptors from damaging overexcitation

Takeaway: Adaptation = ignore constant stimuli + protect receptors from overexcitation. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Adaptation lets us ignore constant, uninformative input and spares receptors from overexcitation (persistent intense signaling can damage cells). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

items.stem: Unfolding of a small protein is characterized by ΔH = +160 kJ mol−1 and ΔS = +400 J mol−1 K−1, both approximately temperature-independent in this range. At which temperatures is unfolding spontaneous (ΔG < 0)?

choices.text: At all temperatures, because ΔS is positive
Only above 400 K, where TΔS exceeds ΔH so that ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative
Only below 400 K, because endothermic processes are spontaneous at low temperature
Never, because a positive ΔH forbids spontaneity at any T

items.explanation: Spontaneity is decided by ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not by ΔH or ΔS alone. Here both signs are positive (endothermic unfolding that increases disorder), so −TΔS becomes more negative as temperature rises. Setting ΔG = 0 gives T = ΔH/ΔS = 160 kJ mol−1 / 0.400 kJ mol−1 K−1 = 400 K. Above 400 K, TΔS > ΔH and unfolding is spontaneous; below 400 K the folded state is favored. A positive ΔS does not guarantee spontaneity at low T, and a positive ΔH does not forbid it at high T. This is the same pattern as ice melting or N2O4 dissociating to NO2.

distractorRationales.A: At low T the ΔH term dominates a ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0 process. Positive entropy does not override enthalpy at every temperature.
distractorRationales.C: Endothermic, entropy-increasing reactions are the high-temperature-spontaneous class, not the low-temperature class (that class is ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0).
distractorRationales.D: Positive ΔH forbids spontaneity only if ΔS is also negative. Here ΔS > 0 opens a high-T window.

items.stem:
Arterial blood gases and electrolytes:

Patient | pH | PCO2 (mmHg) | [HCO3−] (mM) | Na+ | Cl−
A | 7.32 | 60 | 30 | 140 | 100
B | 7.20 | 25 | 9 | 140 | 100
C | 7.20 | 25 | 9 | 140 | 116

Anion gap AG = [Na+] − ([Cl−] + [HCO3−]); a normal gap is about 12 mM. Which classification is consistent?

choices.text: All three are the same disorder because each pH is below 7.40
A chronic respiratory acidosis (high PCO2 with compensatory HCO3− 30); B high-gap metabolic acidosis (AG 31); C hyperchloraemic normal-gap metabolic acidosis (AG 15)
A metabolic alkalosis, because HCO3− is 30
B and C are respiratory alkaloses, because PCO2 is 25

items.explanation: Patient A has acidaemia with PCO2 60 mmHg, so the primary process is respiratory acidosis; bicarbonate has risen to 30 mM, a renal compensation seen in chronic CO2 retention, not a metabolic alkalosis as the primary. Patients B and C share pH 7.20 and low bicarbonate, i.e. metabolic acidosis, with PCO2 25 mmHg as respiratory compensation (not a primary respiratory alkalosis, which would raise pH). AG for B is 140 − (100+9) = 31, a high-gap (e.g. lactate/ketoacid) acidosis. AG for C is 140 − (116+9) = 15, essentially normal, with hyperchloraemia filling the gap. Shared acidaemia does not unify the three mechanisms.

distractorRationales.A: pH < 7.40 only says acidaemia; the PCO2, HCO3− and AG patterns distinguish three disorders.
distractorRationales.C: A high bicarbonate with low pH and high PCO2 is compensated respiratory acidosis; primary metabolic alkalosis would raise pH.
distractorRationales.D: Low PCO2 with low pH is compensation for a metabolic acidosis; a primary respiratory alkalosis alkalinises.

items.stem:
Valence electron counts and VSEPR conclusions for three molecules:

Molecule | valence e− | electron domains on central atom | predicted shape | measured dipole
CO2 | 16 | 2 (two C=O) | linear | 0 D
SO2 | 18 | 3 (two S–O bonding regions + 1 lone pair) | bent | 1.6 D
BF3 | 24 | 3 bonding, 0 lone pairs | trigonal planar | 0 D

Which statement is consistent?

choices.text: BF3 is polar because fluorine is electronegative, so the dipole cannot be 0 D
Any molecule with an 18-electron count must be linear like CO2
SO2 is polar because the lone pair bends the molecule so the S–O bond dipoles do not cancel, unlike linear CO2 and trigonal BF3
CO2 is bent like SO2, which is why both have 16–18 electrons

items.explanation: CO2’s two domains lie 180° apart and the C=O dipoles cancel (0 D). SO2 has three domains, so the observed shape is bent and a net dipole remains (1.6 D). BF3’s three identical B–F bonds at 120° cancel despite polar bonds (0 D). Electron count 16 versus 18 is why CO2 is not bent. Electronegative fluorines do not create a dipole when the vector sum is zero by symmetry. Eighteen electrons is the SO2 count, and SO2 is bent, not linear.

distractorRationales.A: The table gives BF3 a 0 D dipole; symmetry cancellation overrides bond polarity.
distractorRationales.B: SO2 has 18 electrons and is bent with a 1.6 D dipole.
distractorRationales.D: CO2 is listed as linear with dipole 0 D; sharing a similar electron count with SO2 does not make it bent.

passage.title: Mental Health Messaging, Stigma, and Help-Seeking Intentions
passage.body:
A campus research group tested how different messages influence responses to a fictional vignette about a student named R who has experienced repeated episodes of sudden intense fear, rapid heartbeat, trembling, and worry about having another episode. Participants were randomly assigned to read one of four messages before viewing the vignette: a neutral campus-services message, a biological-explanation message, a coping-continuum message emphasizing that distress varies in degree and can be managed with support, or a danger-focused message emphasizing rare extreme outcomes. Participants then rated recognition of clinically significant distress, stigma, and willingness to recommend help-seeking.

Mean outcomes by message condition
Message condition | Recognized clinically significant distress (%) | Stigma rating, 1 to 7 | Willingness to recommend help-seeking, 1 to 7
Neutral campus-services message | 62 | 3.8 | 3.9
Biological-explanation message | 76 | 3.5 | 4.4
Coping-continuum message | 72 | 2.7 | 5.1
Danger-focused message | 80 | 5.2 | 3.1

Ethical note — The researchers debriefed participants after the study and provided a list of campus and community support resources. The vignette was fictional and was not used to diagnose participants.

items.stem: The inner ear houses both the vestibular organs and one structure devoted to hearing rather than balance. That structure is the:
items.explanation: The cochlea is the organ of hearing. The semicircular canals, utricle, and saccule are all vestibular (balance) structures. They share the inner ear but serve different senses. Takeaway: Inner ear: cochlea = HEARING; semicircular canals + utricle + saccule = BALANCE (vestibular). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The cochlea is the auditory organ; the others are vestibular (balance). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.A: The utricle is a vestibular (balance) organ — linear acceleration and tilt.
distractorRationales.B: The semicircular canals are vestibular — rotational sensing.
distractorRationales.D: The saccule is a vestibular organ — vertical linear acceleration.

items.stem: In a photograph, a car partially blocks a building behind it, and the viewer judges the car to be closer. Which cue is operating, and what is its key limitation vs. binocular cues?

choices.text: Retinal disparity; it yields precise absolute distance
Interposition; it yields only relative depth order, not absolute distance
Linear perspective; it requires input from both eyes
Accommodation; it operates only for objects several meters away

items.explanation: Interposition: an occluding object is seen as nearer. It reliably tells you the order of objects but not how far apart they are — relative, not absolute, depth. Monocular. Takeaway: Interposition ranks objects front-to-back without quantifying the gap. Disparity is prized because it approaches absolute depth up close. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Overlap establishes near/far ordering only. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.A: The cue described is overlap, not disparity; disparity is binocular.
distractorRationales.C: Linear perspective is monocular and isn't described here.
distractorRationales.D: Accommodation is monocular and works for near objects, opposite of the claim.

items.stem: A four-year-old fails a Sally–Anne false-belief task, saying Sally will look where the child knows a marble was moved. The same afternoon, after a teacher frowns at the child’s drawing, the child tells a parent “I’m bad at art.” A classmate shows the reverse: passes false-belief but does not change self-ratings after the frown. Which distinction is best?

choices.text: Both children lack any self-concept, so neither report can be interpreted
Theory of mind (false-belief) and Cooley’s looking-glass self can dissociate: attributing another’s belief about an object is not the same as internalizing another’s evaluation into self-concept
Looking-glass self cannot operate until false-belief is passed, so the first child’s report is theoretically impossible
Theory of mind is only a theory of in-group identity and does not concern beliefs about objects

items.explanation: Theory of mind, indexed here by false-belief, is the ability to represent that another person can hold a belief one knows to be false. The looking-glass self is Cooley’s claim that self-concept is built from how we imagine others judge us. A child can take a frown as a verdict on the self without passing a marble false-belief task, and another child can track beliefs without using social evaluation to revise self-worth. Treating the two as identical, or declaring self-concept absent, is not required by either construct. ToM is not restricted to in-group identity.

distractorRationales.A: Saying “I’m bad at art” is a self-concept statement; failing false-belief does not erase it.
distractorRationales.C: The stem’s first child is the existence proof that reflected appraisal can appear without laboratory false-belief success.
distractorRationales.D: False-belief tasks are explicitly about others’ beliefs regarding objects and locations.

items.stem: Genes located close together on the SAME chromosome tend to be inherited together and are called:
items.explanation: Linked genes sit close on the same chromosome and are usually inherited together. Takeaway: Linked genes = close on same chromosome, inherited together. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Linked genes are near each other on one chromosome, so they're usually inherited together (violating independent assortment unless crossing over separates them). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.A: Unlinked genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
distractorRationales.B: Homologous refers to matching chromosome pairs, not linkage.
distractorRationales.D: Pleiotropy is one gene affecting many traits.

items.stem: Average bond enthalpies (kJ mol−1): H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432. For H2 + Cl2 → 2 HCl, ΔH = Σ bonds broken − Σ bonds formed. What is ΔH?
items.explanation: Bonds broken: one H–H and one Cl–Cl, 436 + 243 = 679 kJ absorbed. Bonds formed: two H–Cl, 2 × 432 = 864 kJ released. ΔH = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ per mole of reaction as written. The negative sign means the H–Cl bonds are stronger in total than the bonds they replace, matching an exothermic hydrogen–chlorine combination. Counting only broken bonds leaves the endothermic half. Forming two H–Cl molecules requires twice 432, not once.

distractorRationales.A: The arithmetic 864 − 679 = 185 kJ is the magnitude of heat released; ΔH carries a minus sign.
distractorRationales.B: 679 kJ is only the break term; the 864 kJ of H–Cl formation must be subtracted.
distractorRationales.D: The balanced equation produces two moles of HCl, so two H–Cl bonds form.

items.stem: Dermal fibroblasts from a patient with dietary ascorbate deficiency are labeled with 14C-proline. Secreted type I collagen has a sharply reduced hydroxyproline content and a lower thermal unfolding temperature than collagen from ascorbate-replete cultures. The most direct biochemical explanation is that vitamin C:

choices.text: Is an essential cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase; without 4-hydroxyproline the collagen triple helix is thermally unstable
Is the reductant required to form desmosine cross-links in elastin, which then templates collagen folding
Provides the ATP for ribosomal translation of collagen mRNA, so chains are truncated
Converts fibroblasts into polarized epithelial cells that no longer secrete fibrillar collagen

items.explanation: Collagen prolyl hydroxylase uses Fe2+, 2-oxoglutarate, O2, and ascorbate to form 4-hydroxyproline. The hydroxyl groups stabilize the triple helix through stereoelectronic effects and hydrogen bonding, raising the melting temperature above body temperature. When ascorbate is absent, underhydroxylated tropocollagen is secreted but unfolds more readily, which is the molecular basis of scurvy and of the thermal shift in this labeling experiment. Desmosine is an elastin cross-link, ascorbate is not the energy source for translation, and vitamin C does not transdifferentiate fibroblasts into epithelium.

distractorRationales.B: Desmosine cross-links elastin via lysyl oxidase, not prolyl hydroxylase, and does not explain a hydroxyproline deficit in collagen.
distractorRationales.C: Translation is GTP/ATP-dependent at the ribosome; ascorbate is not the stoichiometric energy donor for collagen synthesis.
distractorRationales.D: Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen modification; it does not reprogram fibroblasts into epithelial cells.

passage.title: Vesicle swelling under osmotic load
passage.body:
A student prepares identical phospholipid vesicles in 300 mOsmol kg−1 sucrose, then dilutes them at t = 0 into the media below. Vesicle volume is inferred from light scatter (larger vesicles scatter less in this geometry). Temperature 25 °C. n = 6 aliquots; scatter reported as mean ± s.d. arbitrary units (higher = smaller vesicles).

Medium after dilution | 10 s | 60 s | 300 s
A: 300 mOsmol sucrose (control) | 1.00 ± 0.02 | 0.99 ± 0.03 | 1.01 ± 0.02
B: 150 mOsmol sucrose | 0.71 ± 0.04 | 0.52 ± 0.05 | 0.48 ± 0.06
C: 150 mOsmol sucrose + 0.1 mM HgCl2 (water-channel blocker in this model) | 0.92 ± 0.03 | 0.80 ± 0.04 | 0.61 ± 0.05
D: 150 mOsmol sucrose + aquaporin proteoliposomes fused at 5 mol% | 0.40 ± 0.06 | 0.33 ± 0.05 | 0.34 ± 0.04

A second table lists initial rates estimated from 0–10 s, treating scatter drop as swelling:

Condition | Δscatter / 10 s
A | ~0
B | −0.029
C | −0.008
D | −0.060

The student claims: “Swelling requires a hypotonic bath, is slowed when water pores are blocked, and is accelerated when extra water pores are added, so the membrane’s phospholipid bilayer is not the main path in B–D.”

items.stem: Which piece of evidence in the passage provides the strongest test of whether the pesticide is actually responsible for the yield decline?

choices.text: The long-term study comparing yield decline in treated versus untreated hives over time.
Beekeepers' reports of a 30% decline in average yield.
The two unusually dry summers occurring in the same period.
Advocacy groups' call for an immediate ban.

items.explanation: Comparing treated versus untreated hives directly isolates the pesticide's specific contribution from the drought and mite factors, which would affect both groups roughly equally — this is the only piece of evidence in the passage that actually controls for the confounds. If a suspected cause is compared against a group not exposed to it, while other factors (weather, pests) affect both groups equally, any remaining difference between the groups can be attributed to the suspected cause specifically. Memory tip: Same drought, same mites, different pesticide exposure: what's left over between the two hive groups is the pesticide's fingerprint, precisely because everything else was shared. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: Critical Reasoning · Environmental Policy
passage.body: Beekeepers in the region have reported that average honey yields per hive fell by 30% over the past five years, and several have linked this decline to the increased use of a new class of pesticide introduced during the same period. Advocacy groups have used the honey yield figures to call for an immediate ban. Agricultural researchers point out that the same five years also saw two unusually dry summers and a rise in a parasitic mite known to weaken hive productivity independently of pesticide exposure. A separate long-term study, tracking the same hives annually since before the pesticide was introduced, found no significant difference in yield decline between hives in treated and untreated areas.

items.stem: Which paragraph best integrates ideas rather than treating comments as a checklist?

choices.text: Comment 1 is true. Comment 2 is also true. Comment 3 is interesting. Comment 4 exists. Comment 5 concludes.
If speed can be care when delay is neglect, then the people who never wait are in a poor position to define neglect; their clock is not a medical instrument, even when they borrow triage words.
I will now integrate by numbering my sentences 1a, 1b, 1c to match the prompt.
Integration means quoting a philosopher at random between each comment.

items.explanation: Integration is ideas in relation: a conditional that uses one comment to limit another, producing a claim neither line stated alone. B does that with speed-as-care and owned clocks. A is a roll-call. Numbering as a display of matching is fake structure. Random authority quotes are name-dropping, not relation. ACER’s “quality of thinking” is visible in that relational sentence. The comments become a springboard because the writer’s claim needed both. That is the craft. Under time, one such sentence is worth five restatements.

distractorRationales.A: Serial true-true-interesting is the checklist the topic forbids.
distractorRationales.C: Cosmetic numbering is not relation; it is inventory with decimals.
distractorRationales.D: Unrelated authorities do not put the set’s ideas into contact.

items.stem: The oxidation number of chromium in dichromate, Cr2O7^2-, is:
items.explanation: Oxygen is assigned −2 in this oxide, and the ion's net charge is −2. For two chromium atoms, 2x + 7(−2) = −2, so 2x − 14 = −2, 2x = 12, and x = +6. Each Cr is +6, which matches the usual assignment in dichromate and chromate. The value +7 is permanganate's manganese, not chromium here. Leaving the result as +12 counts the total chromium oxidation contribution without dividing by the two Cr atoms. Chromium(III) is +3, the product of dichromate reduction in acid, not the oxidation number in Cr2O7^2- itself.

distractorRationales.A: +3 is Cr in Cr3+ or in many reduced chromium products. In dichromate before reduction, the algebra gives +6, not +3.
distractorRationales.C: +7 is the oxidation number of Mn in MnO4-. Chromium in Cr2O7^2- is +6; do not import the permanganate count.
distractorRationales.D: +12 is the combined contribution of both chromium atoms (2x = 12). The oxidation number is the per-atom value +6.

items.stem: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygenated blood out to the rest of the body?
items.explanation: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium, passes into the left ventricle, which is the most muscular chamber and pumps blood at high pressure out through the aorta to the whole body. Simplify the heart into two pumps in series: the right side receives deoxygenated blood from the body and sends it to the lungs; the left side receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and sends it to the body. The left ventricle is thickest because it pumps against the greatest resistance (the whole body). Memory tip: "Right to lungs, left to limbs": the right side of the heart sends blood on a short trip to the lungs; the thicker, stronger left side pumps it the long way round the whole body. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

items.stem: In a Bandura Bobo-doll replication, preschoolers watch an adult punch and verbally insult the doll. Children who saw the adult rewarded later produce more of those acts, including some novel aggressive variants, than children who saw the adult punished. Which process is essential to Bandura’s account?

choices.text: Observational learning plus vicarious reinforcement, so the model’s consequences change the child’s performance
Direct classical pairing of the doll with a US in the child’s own skin
A fixed instinct to aggress that is independent of modeled consequences
Habituation of startle to the doll, which looks like punching

items.explanation: Bandura’s social-learning theory holds that people acquire responses by watching models (attention, retention, reproduction, motivation) and that seeing the model rewarded or punished alters performance (vicarious reinforcement/punishment). Novel aggressive variants show that children learned a script, not a single reinforced muscle twitch. No CS–US pairing with the child as the subject is required. Instinct theories do not predict the reward-versus-punishment split. Habituation is response waning, not imitative punching.

distractorRationales.B: The child did not receive the adult’s US; learning was vicarious.
distractorRationales.C: An invariant instinct cannot explain more copying after a rewarded model.
distractorRationales.D: Habituation decreases responding; the children increased modeled aggression.

items.stem: A motor neuron innervating a skeletal-muscle motor unit is stimulated at increasing frequency. Twitches fuse into fused tetanus. The summation occurs because:

choices.text: Each action potential halves sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ so force falls then rebounds
ATP concentration doubles between spikes, independently of calcium
SERCA cannot sequester Ca2+ fully between closely spaced action potentials, so cytosolic Ca2+ and active force remain elevated
The muscle fiber converts into a neuron and fires its own regenerative tetanus without calcium

items.explanation: A single twitch is brief because Ca2+ is released and then pumped back into the SR by SERCA, tropomyosin reblocks myosin-binding sites, and force falls. When stimuli arrive before sequestration is complete, Ca2+ remains bound to troponin C, more cross-bridges stay attached, and force sums into tetanus. This is temporal summation of the calcium transient, not a doubling of ATP as the causal variable. Action potentials increase, not halve, SR release per unit time. Muscle remains a contractile cell using Ca2+; it does not become a calcium-free neuron.

distractorRationales.A: High-frequency stimulation increases, rather than halves, time-averaged Ca2+ release.
distractorRationales.B: ATP is the energy source but is not the integrator that produces tetanic summation.
distractorRationales.D: Tetanus is fused contractile force in muscle, still Ca2+/troponin-dependent.

items.stem: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency, given by:
items.explanation: Photon energy E = hf (higher frequency = higher energy). Takeaway: E = hf (photon energy ∝ frequency). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. items.stem: A mutation prevents U1 snRNP from recognizing the 5′ splice site of an intron in a two-exon pre-mRNA. No cryptic splice sites are used. Which statement about splicing chemistry is most accurate?

choices.text: The two exons are joined by a cytoplasmic RNA ligase that bypasses the spliceosome.
The lariat still forms normally because the branch-point adenosine is unchanged.
The first transesterification cannot initiate, so the intron is not removed.
Polyadenylation fails because the 5′ cap cannot be added until splicing is finished.

items.explanation: Nuclear pre-mRNA splicing is two sequential transesterifications catalyzed by the spliceosome. U1 snRNP recognizes the invariant GU at the 5′ splice site; that recognition is required for the branch-point 2′-OH to attack the 5′ splice-site phosphorus (the first transesterification). If U1 cannot bind and no cryptic 5′ site is activated, that attack does not occur, the lariat does not form, and the intron remains in the transcript. A free cytoplasmic ligase does not replace the spliceosome for GT–AG introns. Capping and cleavage/polyadenylation are mechanistically distinct from U1 recognition, even though the events are often coordinated.

distractorRationales.A: Standard GT–AG introns are removed by the spliceosome, not by a backup cytoplasmic RNA ligase. Without splicing, the intron stays in the RNA.
distractorRationales.B: Lariat formation is the first transesterification at the 5′ splice site. An unrecognized 5′ site means the branch-point A has no proper target, so the lariat does not form normally.
distractorRationales.D: The 5′ cap is added co-transcriptionally by capping enzymes on the nascent 5′ end and does not require that this intron first be spliced.

passage.title: psg-ps-8
passage.body:
A study tested how awareness of a negative stereotype affects performance and self-presentation. Two groups of equally qualified students took the same difficult verbal test. In the 'diagnostic' condition, the test was described as measuring underlying ability; in the 'nondiagnostic' condition, it was described as a problem-solving exercise unrelated to ability. Students from a group stereotyped as weaker in the domain scored lower than others in the diagnostic condition but scored equally in the nondiagnostic condition. Merely asking students to record their group membership before a diagnostic test reproduced the gap.
In a second study, participants prepared for a mock interview. Told the interviewer valued modesty, they described themselves cautiously; told the interviewer admired confidence, the same participants emphasized their strengths. Observers who saw only one version rated the participants accordingly, and participants reported deliberately tailoring the impression they gave.
The authors interpreted the first study as evidence that the fear of confirming a negative group stereotype can itself depress performance, independent of ability, and that subtle cues activate this fear. They interpreted the second as an example of managing the impression one presents to different audiences, comparing it to an actor shifting performances between a front region and a back region. They cautioned that persistent performance gaps in real settings may partly reflect such situational threats and unequal conditions rather than fixed differences in ability between groups.

items.stem: Lactate dehydrogenase is passed over a gel-filtration column that separates protein from small molecules. The eluted polypeptide has no activity in a lactate-plus-buffer assay until NAD+ is added back, after which NADH production resumes. How is NAD+ best classified in this experiment?

choices.text: A tightly bound prosthetic group that remains covalently attached throughout gel filtration
A dissociable coenzyme (cosubstrate) required for the hydride-transfer reaction
A competitive inhibitor that was removed so that lactate could finally bind
The enzyme’s true substrate, with lactate serving only as an allosteric activator

items.explanation: LDH catalyzes hydride transfer from lactate to NAD+, producing pyruvate and NADH. NAD+ is a small, dissociable coenzyme that occupies a Rossmann fold and leaves with the product as NADH; gel filtration therefore strips it from the protein and activity vanishes until NAD+ is restored. A covalently attached prosthetic group would not be removed by a desalting column. NAD+ is a substrate analog of the redox pair, not an inhibitor, and lactate is the hydride donor, not merely an allosteric ligand. The restoration experiment is the operational definition of a dissociable coenzyme.

distractorRationales.A: If NAD+ remained covalently attached, gel filtration would not have abolished activity.
distractorRationales.C: Adding NAD+ restores catalysis; that is the opposite of removing an inhibitor.
distractorRationales.D: Both lactate and NAD+ are substrates of the bisubstrate reaction; lactate is not only a regulator.

items.stem: What is the most reasonable explanation for why more highly trained endurance athletes reach their lactate threshold at a higher percentage of maximum effort?

choices.text: Trained athletes' muscles and cardiovascular systems are likely better able to supply and use oxygen at higher intensities, delaying the shift toward anaerobic respiration.
Trained athletes do not produce lactate at all.
Training makes muscles heavier, which lowers the intensity needed to reach the threshold.
The lactate threshold is unrelated to oxygen supply.

items.explanation: Since the lactate threshold is explained by oxygen supply failing to meet demand, a trained athlete reaching threshold later (at higher relative intensity) is best explained by an improved capacity to supply and use oxygen, delaying the point at which anaerobic respiration must take over. When a passage gives you a mechanism for a phenomenon, use that same mechanism to explain differences between groups, rather than inventing an unrelated new explanation. The strongest answer usually extends the logic already established, not a new one. Memory tip: "Same engine, better fuel line": training doesn't change the underlying mechanism (oxygen vs anaerobic switch) — it just improves how much oxygen can be delivered before the switch has to happen. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: Biology · Exercise Physiology
passage.body: Researchers measure blood lactate concentration in athletes performing exercise at increasing intensity on a stationary bike. At low to moderate intensity, blood lactate stays low and roughly stable. Above a certain intensity — different for each athlete, but typically around 70–80% of their maximum effort — blood lactate concentration begins rising sharply and continues to climb the longer the athlete sustains that intensity. Athletes who report more years of endurance training tend to reach this "lactate threshold" at a higher percentage of their maximum effort than less-trained athletes.

passage.title: psg-ps-3
passage.body:
Investigators examined how bodily arousal and its interpretation combine to produce emotion. In Study 1, 120 volunteers received an injection described as a vitamin; half actually received a mild dose of adrenaline (epinephrine), which raises heart rate and produces jitteriness, and half received saline. Within each group, some were accurately told to expect arousal symptoms and others were told nothing. Each participant then waited with a confederate who acted either euphoric or irritated. Aroused participants who had not been warned about the symptoms reported emotions matching the confederate's mood - euphoria or anger - more strongly than warned participants or saline controls. Participants who could attribute their arousal to the injection were less swayed by the confederate.
In Study 2, the same volunteers completed a stressful mental-arithmetic task while salivary cortisol was sampled. Cortisol rose within 20 minutes, peaked, and then declined once the task ended. Participants who appraised the task as a 'challenge' showed a smaller cortisol response than those who appraised it as a 'threat,' despite identical task difficulty. Reported stress correlated with threat appraisal, not with objective performance.
The authors linked Study 1 to a theory holding that emotion requires both physiological arousal and a cognitive label for that arousal, and linked Study 2 to a model in which the same stressor produces different physiological responses depending on how it is appraised. They noted that the cortisol time course mirrored the mobilize-then-recover pattern of the body's general response to stressors.

passage.title: The Creek Map (1977)
passage.body: Samir Haddad's 1977 essay “The Creek Map,” on vaccine campaigns, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: History — the press and the Reformation
passage.body:
It is often said that the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation. Luther's theses, the story goes, would have died as a local academic dispute had the new technology not broadcast them across Europe within weeks. There is something to this. Print did carry Luther's words farther and faster than any scribe could, and the reformers themselves marveled at the machine — one called it "God's highest act of grace." But "the press caused the Reformation" claims more than the evidence will bear.

Consider what the same presses were printing. In the decades before Luther, Europe's workshops turned out indulgences, devotional manuals, and papal bulls in enormous numbers; the technology served the old church at least as eagerly as it later served its critics. A tool that amplifies whatever message it is given cannot, by itself, explain why one message rather than another swept the continent. To credit the press with the Reformation is to mistake a multiplier for a cause.

The point can be sharpened. Earlier reformers — Wyclif in England, Hus in Bohemia — had advanced doctrines close to Luther's a full century before movable type, and had won substantial followings without it. Their movements were contained, but by armies and inquisitions, not by any shortage of copyists. What differed in Luther's case was not merely the speed of transmission but a constellation of circumstances: a fractured German political landscape in which sympathetic princes could shield him, a literate urban public primed by grievance, and a message pitched to that public's discontents.

None of this makes the press irrelevant. Technologies shape the movements that use them, and a Reformation conducted by pamphlet was bound to differ from one conducted by sermon and manuscript. The press lowered the cost of dissent and widened the circle of those who could join it. But "shaped" is not "caused," and "made easier" is not "made inevitable." The most we can say is that print was among the conditions that allowed the Reformation to spread as it did — a necessary instrument, perhaps, but not a sufficient explanation.

The appeal of the simpler story is easy to understand. Causes that can be named and dated — a machine, an invention — are more satisfying than a tangle of politics, literacy, and timing. But history rarely obliges us with single causes, and the historian's task is often to resist the tidy explanation in favor of the true one.

passage.title: The Standard (1979)
passage.body: Yuki Tanaka published “The Standard” in 1979 after a season in a coastal fishery. The argument is that a caption can do the arguing the image refuses to do. The piece admits that some gatekeeping keeps fraud out. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: psg-cp-8
passage.body:
Purifying the product of a reaction is a routine but crucial task. A student runs a reaction that yields a mixture of a carboxylic acid (benzoic acid) and a neutral, nonpolar hydrocarbon, both dissolved in an organic solvent, and sets out to separate and identify them.
She first checks the mixture by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) on a silica gel plate, a polar stationary phase, developed in a relatively nonpolar solvent. After development, one spot has traveled 3.0 cm from the origin while the solvent front has advanced 5.0 cm. She records the retention factor (Rf) for the spot and notes that, on polar silica, more polar compounds cling to the plate and move less, whereas less polar compounds travel farther.
To separate the two components in bulk, she performs a liquid-liquid extraction, shaking the organic solution with aqueous sodium hydroxide in a separatory funnel. The carboxylic acid reacts with the base and is converted to its sodium carboxylate salt; the neutral hydrocarbon does not react. After the layers settle, she drains them apart and then treats the aqueous layer with hydrochloric acid to reverse the reaction and recover the purified acid.
Finally, she considers how to separate two miscible liquids that differ in boiling point and reviews simple distillation, in which the mixture is heated, the vapor is drawn off and condensed, and the collected liquid is enriched in one component. Throughout, she relies on differences in polarity, acid-base behavior, and volatility - the physical and chemical handles that separations exploit.

items.stem: A 12 V battery with internal resistance r = 1.0 Ω is connected to an external resistor R = 5.0 Ω. The current is I = emf / (R+r). Terminal voltage is V = I R = emf − I r. Power in R is I² R. Which set is correct?

choices.text: I = 2.4 A; V = 12 V (internal resistance ignored)

items.explanation: Total resistance 6.0 Ω, so I = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A. Terminal voltage is the drop across R: 2.0 × 5.0 = 10 V, equivalently 12 − 2.0 × 1.0 = 10 V. Power in R is 4.0 × 5.0 = 20 W. Ignoring r gives 2.4 A and a false 12 V at the terminals under load. Keeping I = 2.0 A but quoting V = 12 V forgets the internal drop. I = 12 A would be emf/r or emf with 1 Ω total. Loaded terminal voltage is always below emf when r > 0 and I > 0.

distractorRationales.A: I = 2.0 A is right, but 2.0 A through r wastes 2.0 V, leaving 10 V at the terminals.
distractorRationales.B: 12 A would require a 1.0 Ω total loop; the loop is 6.0 Ω.
distractorRationales.D: The 1.0 Ω internal resistance sits in series, so I is 2.0 A not 12/5 = 2.4 A, and V_terminal < 12 V.

items.stem: Racemic 1-phenylethanol shows a single spot on ordinary silica TLC and a single peak on an achiral GC column. Which statement best explains those observations and how the enantiomers can still be separated?

choices.text: The sample is actually a meso compound, so there are not two stereoisomers to separate
Enantiomers have different Rf values on silica but identical GC retention; only GC can fail
Enantiomers interact identically with achiral silica and achiral GC phases; a chiral stationary phase or a chiral derivatizing agent is required
Racemates always decompose on silica, so the single spot is a decomposition product

items.explanation: Ordinary silica and ordinary GC stationary phases are achiral. Each enantiomer of 1-phenylethanol therefore experiences the same adsorption energy and the same vapor pressure, giving one TLC spot and one GC peak. The molecule has a single stereocenter and is not meso. Separation requires a chiral environment: a chiral GC or HPLC stationary phase, or conversion to diastereomeric esters with an enantiopure acid chloride that then differ in Rf or retention. A single spot is the intact racemate, not a decomposition artifact.

distractorRationales.A: 1-Phenylethanol has one stereocenter and no internal mirror plane; a racemate is a 1:1 mixture of enantiomers, not a meso form.
distractorRationales.B: Achiral silica does not distinguish enantiomers any more than an achiral GC column does; both methods fail for the same reason.
distractorRationales.D: A racemic alcohol is chromatographically stable on silica under standard TLC conditions; a single spot is the expected, not decomposed, result.

passage.title: Alternative splicing and protein dimerization of LUM1
passage.body:
A fictional eukaryotic gene, LUM1, contains four exons. Exon 3 encodes a hydrophobic alpha-helical segment required for stable LUM1 dimer formation. A regulatory RNA-binding protein, RBP-K, binds an intronic splicing enhancer near exon 3 and promotes exon 3 inclusion. Skipping exon 3 preserves the reading frame but produces a mostly monomeric protein that is degraded more rapidly. A separate mutation in the 5' splice donor of intron 2 causes intron retention and introduces a premature termination codon more than 50 nucleotides upstream of the final exon-exon junction.

Effects of LUM1 expression constructs in cultured cells.
Condition | Pre-mRNA transcription rate (%) | Mature mRNA containing exon 3 (%) | Total mature LUM1 mRNA (%) | LUM1 protein (%) | Dimeric LUM1 among detected protein (%)
Wild type | 100 | 85 | 100 | 100 | 80
RBP-K knockdown | 98 | 20 | 55 | 25 | 18
Exon 3 splice acceptor weakened | 95 | 10 | 50 | 20 | 12
Intron 2 splice donor mutant | 100 | 5 | 18 | 6 | 8
Kozak sequence mutant | 100 | 82 | 95 | 22 | 78
Exon 3 hydrophobic-to-charged coding mutant | 100 | 84 | 98 | 45 | 20

Model for LUM1 isoform production. — When exon 3 is included, LUM1 contains a hydrophobic helical segment that supports dimerization. When exon 3 is skipped, the reading frame remains intact but the helical dimerization segment is absent. Intron 2 retention creates a premature stop codon predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.

Bureaucracy (Weber) replaces all socialization agents once someone enters a hospital
Family is typically the primary agent; school is a major secondary agent that also transmits a hidden curriculum of punctuality and deference

items.explanation: Primary socialization, usually in the family, lays down language, manners, and basic identities. Secondary agents—school, peers, media, workplace—continue the process. Schools famously transmit a hidden curriculum of time-discipline and authority relations (later emphasized by Bowles and Gintis). Peers matter, especially in adolescence, but they do not erase family and school. Mead did not make mass media the sole primary agent. Weberian bureaucracy structures organizations; it does not cancel prior socialization.

distractorRationales.A: Peer influence is real but not exclusive after age 6.
distractorRationales.B: Mead’s primary social world is significant others and the generalized other, not “media only.”
distractorRationales.C: Entering a bureaucracy does not nullify family and school as agents.

items.stem: After a hurricane, Cohort H reports acute terror during the storm. Cohort D reports a divorce in the same month and no storm exposure. Cohort N reports years of traffic, noisy neighbors, and crowding with no discrete disaster. All three complete the same allostatic-load battery. Which statement is most accurate?

choices.text: Only catastrophes engage the HPA axis; daily hassles are opinions without physiology
Catastrophes, significant life changes, and chronic daily hassles can all raise allostatic load; persistent hassles often track symptoms as strongly as major events
Chosen life changes cannot be stressors, so Cohort D should look like unstressed controls
Ambient noise is ignored by sympathetic systems unless it is first labeled a challenge

items.explanation: MCAT-level stress taxonomy groups stressors as catastrophes, significant life changes, and daily hassles (including ambient strains). Each class can activate sympathetic and HPA systems and accumulate as allostatic load. Chronic hassles are not physiologically trivial; they often predict somatic symptoms as well as or better than a single dramatic event because of their duration. Appraising a divorce as chosen does not remove it from the life-change category. Ambient stressors can drive physiology even when they are not framed as an exciting challenge.

distractorRationales.A: Hassles can activate stress physiology; they are not merely cognitive opinions.
distractorRationales.C: Even intended transitions (divorce, job change) are classic significant life-change stressors.
distractorRationales.D: Challenge is one primary-appraisal outcome, not a gate that ambient stressors must pass before the SAM axis can respond.

passage.title: psg-ps-3
passage.body:
Investigators examined how bodily arousal and its interpretation combine to produce emotion. In Study 1, 120 volunteers received an injection described as a vitamin; half actually received a mild dose of adrenaline (epinephrine), which raises heart rate and produces jitteriness, and half received saline. Within each group, some were accurately told to expect arousal symptoms and others were told nothing. Each participant then waited with a confederate who acted either euphoric or irritated. Aroused participants who had not been warned about the symptoms reported emotions matching the confederate's mood - euphoria or anger - more strongly than warned participants or saline controls. Participants who could attribute their arousal to the injection were less swayed by the confederate.
In Study 2, the same volunteers completed a stressful mental-arithmetic task while salivary cortisol was sampled. Cortisol rose within 20 minutes, peaked, and then declined once the task ended. Participants who appraised the task as a 'challenge' showed a smaller cortisol response than those who appraised it as a 'threat,' despite identical task difficulty. Reported stress correlated with threat appraisal, not with objective performance.
The authors linked Study 1 to a theory holding that emotion requires both physiological arousal and a cognitive label for that arousal, and linked Study 2 to a model in which the same stressor produces different physiological responses depending on how it is appraised. They noted that the cortisol time course mirrored the mobilize-then-recover pattern of the body's general response to stressors.

items.stem: An Hfr donor transfers chromosomal markers in the time-of-entry order thr at 8 min, azi at 9 min, ton at 11 min, and lac at 18 min. Mating is interrupted at 10 minutes. Among streptomycin-counterselected recipients, thr+ azi+ recombinants are common but lac+ recombinants are essentially absent. This pattern indicates that:

choices.text: All four genes are on a small plasmid that always transfers as a unit in under 2 minutes
Transformation equalizes every marker by 10 minutes regardless of map position
The integrated F plasmid mobilizes the chromosome linearly from a fixed origin, so 10 minutes of contact transfers thr and azi but not the later lac locus
The recipient was already F+, which blocks all chromosomal recombination after 8 minutes

items.explanation: In Hfr strains the F plasmid is integrated into the chromosome. Conjugation nicks at oriT and transfers chromosomal DNA in a linear, time-dependent order set by the site and orientation of integration. Interrupted-mating clocks that order: markers that have already entered can recombine into the recipient, while markers still upstream of the transfer fork cannot. At 10 minutes thr and azi have entered and lac has not, matching the 8-9 versus 18 minute map. A small plasmid would not show a 10-minute lag between markers, and ordinary transformation does not produce a time-of-entry gradient.

distractorRationales.A: Unit transfer of a tiny plasmid would not generate a several-minute time-of-entry series.
distractorRationales.B: Transformation does not create a conjugation clock; marker frequency would not follow this ordered delay.
distractorRationales.D: F+ recipients can show surface exclusion, but that would reduce transfer globally, not spare early markers and exclude only lac.

items.stem:
Task B — 30 minutes. Clara is writing to these comments:

“Translation is never only a linguistic problem.”
“A metric can become the mission.”
“The first person to leave a room is not always the least loyal.”

Which approach is most likely to score?

choices.text: Inventory every comment in order so the marker sees completeness.
Write a generic paragraph that could fit any prompt this century.
Spend the first twenty minutes outlining and the last two typing.
Tone control; avoid sentimentality. Do that with particular examples; do not inventory the comments.

items.explanation: GAMSAT S2 is production under a clock. What scores is: Tone control; avoid sentimentality. Use a clear position or a precise personal scene; comments are pressure, not a checklist. Inventory, generic filler, and outline-without-prose are the three ways this hour fails to raise a mark. Clara's comments only change the prompt pairing.

distractorRationales.A: Comment inventory is the named failure mode for S2.
distractorRationales.B: Generic voice is the opposite of particular/theme precision.
distractorRationales.C: Under time, an unused outline does not score.

items.stem: A biopsy taken immediately after a 10-second maximal sprint shows depleted phosphocreatine, elevated creatine and Pi, and a rise in lactate. The fastest initial buffer that regenerated ATP during the sprint is:

choices.text: The creatine kinase reaction (PCr + ADP -> Cr + ATP)
Mitochondrial beta-oxidation of fatty acids as the sole 10-second ATP source
De novo AMP biosynthesis, which produces ATP on a millisecond timescale
Oxidative phosphorylation reaching maximal flux in the first 50 milliseconds, before PCr is used

items.explanation: Cytosolic creatine kinase equilibrates phosphocreatine with ATP, providing an immediate high-energy phosphate buffer for brief maximal efforts. The biopsy pattern (PCr down, Cr and Pi up) is the fingerprint of that reaction. Anaerobic glycolysis then contributes lactate when the sprint lasts several seconds. Fatty-acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation are too slow to be the first ATP source in a 10-second all-out effort, and they would not uniquely deplete PCr. Nucleotide de novo synthesis is a slow biosynthetic pathway, not a millisecond ATP buffer. Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption later restores PCr and oxidizes lactate.

distractorRationales.B: Beta-oxidation cannot meet the instantaneous ATP demand of a 10-second sprint as the primary buffer.
distractorRationales.C: Purine biosynthesis does not regenerate ATP on the timescale of a sprint.
distractorRationales.D: Oxidative phosphorylation ramps more slowly; PCr is the immediate buffer, consistent with its depletion.

items.stem: How does the student recover the purified benzoic acid from the aqueous layer?

choices.text: Add hydrochloric acid to reprotonate the carboxylate, regenerating neutral, water-insoluble benzoic acid.
Add more sodium hydroxide to the aqueous layer.
Boil the aqueous layer to drive off the acid as vapor.
Add a nonpolar solvent to dissolve the sodium ions.

items.explanation: In the aqueous layer the acid exists as the benzoate ion; adding a strong acid (HCl) restores the proton, regenerating neutral benzoic acid, which is only sparingly soluble in water and precipitates (or can be re-extracted) as the purified product. Adding more base (2) keeps it ionized; boiling (3) will not vaporize the salt; option 4 targets the wrong species. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passage.title: psg-cp-8
passage.body:
Purifying the product of a reaction is a routine but crucial task. A student runs a reaction that yields a mixture of a carboxylic acid (benzoic acid) and a neutral, nonpolar hydrocarbon, both dissolved in an organic solvent, and sets out to separate and identify them.
She first checks the mixture by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) on a silica gel plate, a polar stationary phase, developed in a relatively nonpolar solvent. After development, one spot has traveled 3.0 cm from the origin while the solvent front has advanced 5.0 cm. She records the retention factor (Rf) for the spot and notes that, on polar silica, more polar compounds cling to the plate and move less, whereas less polar compounds travel farther.
To separate the two components in bulk, she performs a liquid-liquid extraction, shaking the organic solution with aqueous sodium hydroxide in a separatory funnel. The carboxylic acid reacts with the base and is converted to its sodium carboxylate salt; the neutral hydrocarbon does not react. After the layers settle, she drains them apart and then treats the aqueous layer with hydrochloric acid to reverse the reaction and recover the purified acid.
Finally, she considers how to separate two miscible liquids that differ in boiling point and reviews simple distillation, in which the mixture is heated, the vapor is drawn off and condensed, and the collected liquid is enriched in one component. Throughout, she relies on differences in polarity, acid-base behavior, and volatility - the physical and chemical handles that separations exploit.

items.stem: The H177Q variant has nearly normal pyruvate and NADH Km values but very low Vmax. Which interpretation is most directly supported?

choices.text: His177 forms the entire NADH-binding pocket.
His177 contributes to catalytic chemistry after substrate binding.
His177 is required for LDH-R tetramer assembly.
His177 prevents pyruvate from binding to the active site.

items.explanation: H177Q remains mostly tetrameric and retains near-normal Km values for pyruvate and NADH, but its Vmax falls to 6%. This supports a defect in catalytic turnover, such as acid-base chemistry or transition-state stabilization, rather than a major substrate-binding or assembly defect. Common miss: Assuming that low activity must reflect poor substrate binding rather than impaired catalytic turnover. This best fits preserved binding and assembly with severely impaired catalysis. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.A: The NADH Km is nearly unchanged, so His177 is unlikely to form the entire NADH-binding pocket.
distractorRationales.C: Tetrameric protein is 92%, which argues against a tetramer assembly requirement.
distractorRationales.D: The pyruvate Km is nearly unchanged, so pyruvate binding is not the main defect.

passage.title: Kinetic analysis of a cytosolic lactate dehydrogenase variant
passage.body:
Researchers studied LDH-R, a fictional homotetrameric cytosolic lactate dehydrogenase that catalyzes the reversible reaction pyruvate + NADH + H+ -> lactate + NAD+. LDH-R helps maintain cytosolic redox balance when oxidative metabolism is limited. The investigators purified wild-type LDH-R, two point variants, and one truncation variant. Initial velocity was measured at saturating NADH unless NADH affinity was being assessed. PYA is a pyruvate analog that does not undergo reduction.

Properties of LDH-R proteins under selected assay conditions.
Protein or condition | Km for pyruvate (mM) | Relative Vmax (%) | Tetrameric protein (%) | Km for NADH (micromolar)
Wild type, pH 7.4 | 0.10 | 100 | 94 | 25
Wild type + PYA, pH 7.4 | 0.55 | 96 | 93 | 25
H177Q, pH 7.4 | 0.11 | 6 | 92 | 27
L246D, pH 7.4 | 0.12 | 38 | 35 | 26
Wild type, pH 6.6 | 0.08 | 125 | 94 | 22
C-terminal tail deletion, pH 7.4 | 0.28 | 70 | 90 | 80

Initial velocity curves for LDH-R. — At saturating NADH, wild-type LDH-R shows a hyperbolic increase in velocity with increasing pyruvate. PYA shifts the wild-type curve to the right without lowering the plateau. H177Q has a very low plateau. L246D has a lower plateau than wild type. At pH 6.6, the wild-type curve shifts slightly left and reaches a higher plateau.

items.stem:
An object’s velocity–time graph consists of two horizontal segments:

Interval | v (m s−1)
0 to 3.0 s | +4.0
3.0 to 9.0 s | −2.0

Net displacement is the signed area; path length (distance travelled) is the sum of absolute areas. Which pair is correct for 0–9.0 s?
items.explanation: The first rectangle has area (+4.0)×3.0 = +12 m. The second has area (−2.0)×6.0 = −12 m. Net displacement is 12 − 12 = 0 m. Path length is |12| + |12| = 24 m. The object goes out 12 m and back 12 m. A zero path length would mean it never moved. If both segments were taken as positive without reversing, both displacement and path would be quoted as 24 m. Keeping only the outbound 12 m as both quantities ignores the return. Signed area and absolute area must be computed separately whenever v changes sign.

distractorRationales.A: 24 m would be the path length if both areas were added as positive, but then the displacement would still be 0, not 24 m. This option sets both quantities to 24 m.
distractorRationales.B: Displacement is 0, but the object moved 24 m along its path. Path length is not zero.
distractorRationales.C: 12 m is only the outbound (or only the return) distance. Neither the net displacement nor the full path equals 12 m for the whole 9 s.

passage.title: A Slow Era (1979)
passage.body: Diego Ferreira published “A Slow Era” in 1979 after a season in university hiring. The argument is that speed of publication is being mistaken for care. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: Two short poems: Ferry
passage.body:
Poem 1 — “Ticket”
I bought a ticket to the other bank
as if the river were a problem in change.
The ferryman took coins that had known other pockets.
He did not ask what I was leaving.
The water did, in small repeated questions
against the hull.

Poem 2 — “Return”
On the way back the same boat
was a different animal.
I recognised the coins by their edges
and not the faces.
Someone on the far jetty waved
at a person I had not yet become
and I, traitor, waved.

passage.title: psg-cp-4
passage.body:
Diagnostic imaging often relies on how waves interact with tissue. In an ultrasound scanner, a transducer emits pulses of high-frequency sound into the body and listens for echoes returning from boundaries between tissues. A common obstetric probe operates at 2.0 MHz, and sound travels through soft tissue at about 1540 m/s. The scanner forms an image from the time delay and strength of each returning echo, and clinicians choose the probe frequency to trade off image detail against how deep the sound can penetrate.
A Doppler mode measures blood flow. When a pulse reflects from red blood cells moving relative to the transducer, the returning sound is shifted in frequency; the scanner converts this shift into a flow velocity and direction, coloring flow toward and away from the probe differently.
A second instrument, a fiber-optic endoscope, guides visible light instead of sound. Light travels along a thin glass fiber whose core has a higher refractive index (about 1.5) than its surrounding cladding (about 1.2). Rays that strike the core-cladding boundary at a large enough angle are trapped inside the core and travel the fiber's length with little loss, so the endoscope can illuminate and image tissue deep inside the body and around bends. The physicians rely on the same refraction principles when a laser beam crosses from one tissue layer into another and changes direction. Throughout, the team treats soft tissue as a uniform medium for sound and the fiber as an ideal light guide.
