passage.title: Official Adjectives (1976)
passage.body: Amina Okonkwo published “Official Adjectives” in 1976 after a season in municipal archives. The argument is that a caption can do the arguing the image refuses to do. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: On the new memorial
passage.body:
The memorial is a corridor of rusted uprights, each the height of a person, irregularly spaced so that you must turn sideways to pass. At noon they look like a failed fence. At dusk they look like a crowd that has agreed not to face you. There are no names. A small plaque at the exit says only: THEY WERE NOT LATE. THEY WERE PREVENTED.

Tourists complain that they do not know whom to pity. School groups count the uprights and get different numbers, because some are so close they read as one. A veteran interviewed on the steps said he hated it, then stood there until the lights came on, then said he hated that he did not hate it enough.

The sculptor, in a panel discussion, refused the word healing. “If it heals,” she said, “it has failed at being a door you cannot swagger through.” Critics split between those who call this moral bullying in Cor-Ten steel and those who call the tourists’ complaint the point.

I went through twice. The second time a child asked why the fence was broken. His father said it was not a fence. The child, satisfied with a new category, ran. I was not satisfied. Prevention is a bureaucratic word. In the corridor it becomes a body insisting on its width.

passage.title: Philosophy — can we learn from fiction?
passage.body:
Can a novel teach us anything true about the world? The doubt is old and not unserious. A novel, after all, is by definition a made-up story; its characters never lived, its events never happened. Whatever a novelist asserts through the tale is unsupported by evidence — the author simply stipulates that things are so within the fiction. If I want to know how grief works, or how power corrupts, it seems I should consult a psychologist or a historian, not a storyteller who has invented her data.

This objection has force against one kind of knowledge but not another. It is true that fiction cannot establish general facts: no number of novels about ambitious men could prove that ambition corrupts, since the novelist controls the outcome. But not all knowledge is knowledge of general facts. There is also knowing what something is like — what it would be to face a certain choice, to bear a certain loss. And here fiction has resources the treatise lacks: it can place us, in imagination, inside a situation and let us try it on.

Consider the difference between being told that jealousy distorts perception and following, page by page, a character's jealous misreadings of an innocent scene. The first hands us a proposition to file away; the second rehearses the experience, and may leave us better able to recognize the distortion in ourselves. The novelist need not prove that jealousy works this way. It is enough that she renders it so vividly that we recognize it — the recognition, not the proof, is the point.

A skeptic may reply that this "knowledge" is merely emotional, not cognitive — that we have been moved, not taught. But the line is not so clean. To grasp what a situation is like is often a precondition for judging it well; the person who cannot imagine another's suffering will reason poorly about how to treat them. If fiction cultivates that imaginative grasp, it is doing cognitive work, even if it proves no theorems.

The modest conclusion is that fiction and science divide the labor of understanding rather than compete for it. Science tells us that things are so and why; fiction shows us what their being so is like from the inside. To ask a novel to furnish general laws is to misunderstand the kind of knowledge it offers — and to conclude, from its failure to do so, that it offers none, is to make the same mistake twice.

Fines-as-venue versus neglect are the crude pair. A library without fines plus staffing maps onto maintenance; the postcode table maps onto including the people the old ledger harmed. C fetishizes a technology of tracking. D repeats the mistake of treating honesty as surrender. Apply the park principles to another public good rather than importing property slogans.

distractorRationales.A: Paid winter work is explicitly not a betrayal of openness.
distractorRationales.C: Barcodes do not decide whether a good is a commons in this argument; inhabitability and incomplete ledgers do.
distractorRationales.D: Naming uses “does not hand the land to the highest bidder.”

passage.title: The ledger of the commons
passage.body:
When a city puts a park on a map, it appears to have given something away: land that could have been lots, hours that could have been tolls. Developers are not wrong that the gift has a price. They are wrong when they treat the price as a leak from an otherwise watertight private order. The private order is already subsidized by streets, courts, pipes, and the patience of people who do not sue every time a stranger walks past a porch. A park is not the exception to property. It is one of the ways a dense city remains inhabitable enough for property to be worth wanting.

Accountants prefer a ledger in which every square metre has a named owner and a yield. Parks embarrass the ledger because their yield is a crowd that does not pay at the gate, a cooling that does not send an invoice, a child who learns a city can include her without a purchase. The embarrassment produces two crude policies. One is to fence and ticket until the park behaves like a venue. The other is to neglect the park until the crowd looks like a problem that only private security can solve. Both policies claim to be realistic. Both are ways of refusing to count the effects that made the park rational in the first place.

Friends of the park sometimes answer with a poetry of the unowned. The poetry is moving and strategically weak. A commons that cannot speak in maintenance budgets will lose to a spreadsheet that can. The more adult defense is to insist that the ledger is incomplete, not that ledgers are evil. Planting, lighting, toilets, and a gardener who is paid in winter are not betrayals of openness. They are how openness lasts past a ribbon-cutting.

There is a further honesty. Parks are not innocent. They have been used to raise adjacent rents, to move unhoused people out of sight, to display a city’s kindness to visitors who will never need the toilets. Naming those uses does not hand the land to the highest bidder. It prevents the park’s defenders from pretending that green on a map is already justice. Justice would be a park whose ledger includes the people who were priced off the blocks around it.

If urban politics cannot hold that thought, it will keep oscillating between the venue and the ruin, and calling the oscillation pragmatism.

items.stem: Which 0.10 M salt solution is expected to be acidic because the cation hydrolyzes coordinated water?
items.explanation: Al3+ in water exists as [Al(H2O)6]3+. The high charge density of Al3+ withdraws electron density from coordinated water, making those O–H bonds acidic: [Al(H2O)6]3+ ⇌ [Al(H2O)5OH]2+ + H3O+. A 0.10 M Al(NO3)3 solution is therefore acidic. Na+ and K+ are weakly polarizing and do not hydrolyze water; NO3− and Cl− are conjugate bases of strong acids and are pH-neutral spectators. Acetate is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so NaCH3CO2 is basic, not acidic.

distractorRationales.A: Na+ does not hydrolyze water and NO3− is the conjugate base of strong HNO3, so NaNO3 is pH-neutral.
distractorRationales.B: KCl is a salt of a strong acid and a strong base and is pH-neutral.
distractorRationales.D: Acetate hydrolyzes as a weak base (CH3CO2− + H2O ⇌ CH3CO2H + OH−), so this solution is basic.

passage.title: psg-ps-4
passage.body:
A team studied what sustains effort on a task. Ninety children who already enjoyed drawing were randomly assigned to three groups. The 'expected-reward' group was promised a certificate for drawing; the 'unexpected-reward' group drew and then received the same certificate as a surprise; the 'no-reward' group simply drew. Two weeks later, during free-play periods, observers unobtrusively recorded how much each child chose to draw. Children in the expected-reward group spent about half as much free time drawing as the other two groups, whose behavior did not differ.
In a second study with adults, participants worked on solvable puzzles under one of two framings. Some were told the task measured 'innate intelligence'; others were told that effort and strategy drive success. After encountering difficult items, the 'effort' group persisted longer and reported greater interest, and this difference was largest among participants who scored high on a measure of conscientiousness.
The researchers interpreted the children's result as evidence that offering an expected tangible reward for an already-enjoyable activity can reduce later voluntary engagement, because the behavior becomes attributed to the external incentive. They connected the adult result to a framework distinguishing motivation that arises from within the person from motivation driven by external consequences, and noted that a stable personality dimension moderated persistence. They cautioned that rewards are not universally harmful: unexpected rewards, and rewards for dull tasks, did not undermine engagement.

items.stem: Which of the following best states the author's central claim?

choices.text: Written documents should be discarded in favor of interviews, because only speech can represent lives that clerks ignored.

Treating archived traces as unmediated testimony conceals how record-keeping decides whose past can be cited, so documentary absences should be read as facts about power rather than as temporary vacancies.
Museum conservation is unethical whenever an object is removed from the setting in which it was found.
Every past life can be reconstructed at equal density if historians search long enough and interview enough descendants.

items.explanation: The passage repeatedly denies that folders and objects speak by themselves: archives are offices that select what will later count as recoverable, and public memory therefore over-represents those who generated files. The author refuses both archive-abandonment and the fantasy of complete reconstruction, and instead asks that conversion into evidence be named as conversion and that silences be treated as facts about power. Choice B compresses that through-line without converting a local example (museums, oral history, townhouses) into the whole thesis. The rejected options each inflate a qualification or an illustration into a program the author explicitly declines.

distractorRationales.A: The second paragraph opens by denying a case for abandoning documents; oral history is offered as a limited patch, not a replacement that makes paper dispensable.
distractorRationales.C: The author says conversion is what historians do and is not itself a crime; the objection is to narrating conversion as rescue, not to moving objects.
distractorRationales.D: The closing paragraph states that some absences are final and that performing completeness by thickening an already thick file is the undemocratic option.

passage.title: The archive and the street
passage.body:
Historians often speak as if the past were a reluctant witness who can be coaxed into testimony if only the right box is opened. The letter, the minute-book, the trial transcript, and the parish register are treated not as remnants but as the event itself, patiently waiting to be interviewed. The metaphor is professionally convenient. It locates virtue in attentiveness and implies that an archive, handled without aggression, will speak of its own accord. Archives do not speak. They are offices that decide, usually long before a scholar arrives, which traces of life will be kept, numbered, and thereby made eligible for later recovery. To mistake a folder for a microphone is to forget that someone built the studio, invited some guests, and switched the machine off when the conversation became inconvenient.

This is not a case for abandoning documents. It is a case against a piety now common in public history: the belief that proximity to a primary source is itself a moral credential. Museum captions announce that an object was found in an attic or rescued from a demolition site, as if its later career in a glass case were a continuation of its first life rather than a conversion into evidence. Conversion is what historians do. Trouble begins when conversion is narrated as rescue, because that narration conceals the historian's power and, more consequentially, conceals the people who never generated a paper trail to be rescued.

Oral historians have pressed this objection for decades, sometimes with more hope than caution. They have offered the recorded interview as a democratic patch, a way of admitting those whom the file forgot. The patch is real; it is not automatic. An interview is also a document, made under conditions of prompting, recording, transcription, and later cutting. It can be managed as tightly as a colonial gazette. What distinguishes a responsible oral history is not orality as such, but the historian remaining visible in the manufacture of the record—visible enough that a later reader can see where a question steered, where a narrator pushed back, and where a silence was not a hole but a refusal.

The sharper problem is civic rather than technical. If the only past that can be cited is the past that was filed, public memory will go on over-representing those who employed clerks. Cities make the point more bluntly than seminars do. A demolished neighborhood deposits fewer cartons than a merchant's townhouse; a street seller deposits fewer than a chartered company. When a preservation trust then campaigns to save the townhouse because it is richly documented, the trust is not merely selecting architecture. It is ratifying a distribution of paperwork as a distribution of historical weight. The house is asked to stand for an age, and the undocumented street is invited, if at all, to supply atmosphere.

Honesty does not require the fantasy that every life can be reconstructed with equal density. Some absences are final. The decent procedure is to treat those absences as facts about power rather than as temporary vacancies that a more heroic search will fill. A history that admits what cannot be known is more public-minded than a history that performs completeness by adding still more pages to an already thick dossier. The archive will remain necessary. It need not remain innocent.

passage.title: Vacant possession
passage.body:
The rental had been emptied with the efficiency of people who did not live there. I arrived after the skip had gone. What remained were the marks of remaining: a paler rectangle on the wall where a calendar had blocked the sun, a screw in the kitchen plaster that had held nothing I could remember, a ring on the lino where a bin had sat long enough to become a climate. The agent called it "vacant possession." The phrase was legally tidy. It treated my father as a tenancy that had concluded.

I opened the cupboard above the kettle. Inside, taped to the wood, was a shopping list in his slanted capitals, and beneath it a scrap of verse I had never seen. He was not a man who announced poems. He had been a man who boiled water at the same hour, as if the day were a machine that required a particular ignition. The list wanted milk, soap, and a cheaper brand of tea. The last item was written twice, then crossed out, then written again, as if indecision were a kind of company.

The kettle still knew his hour.
I did not.
The cupboard kept a shopping list
addressed to a week that never arrived.
I ticked the milk as if the ticking
could make a future stand up.

I stood with a pen I had not meant to bring and put a mark beside milk, then stopped, because the gesture had the shape of care and the content of a joke at my own expense. Grief, in the pamphlets, is supposed to be a weather that passes over a landscape. In the cupboard it was more like a task left in a shared kitchen: unclaimed, slightly shameful, still assigned. I wanted, ridiculously, to buy the milk. I wanted not to be the kind of daughter who leaves a list unanswered.

The agent coughed in the hallway and mentioned carpet cleaning, then the bond, then the need to "move on" as if the room were a queue. I heard myself thank him. Courtesy was easier than explaining that the room was not empty, only unpopulated. He was not unkind. He was on a clock I did not share. Vacant possession, I thought, is a legal sentence that cannot conjugate the present tense of objects. The kettle, if it could speak, would not have used it. It would have asked why the hour had been cancelled without notice.

items.stem: In the photoelectric effect, monochromatic light already above the metal's threshold frequency has its intensity doubled while frequency is held fixed. The principal result is that:

choices.text: the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons doubles
the number of electrons ejected per second doubles, while KE_max is unchanged
the work function of the metal is halved
KE_max drops to zero because intensity, not frequency, now governs the effect

items.explanation: Each photoelectron's maximum kinetic energy is KE_max = h f − φ, which depends on photon frequency and the metal's work function, not on intensity. Intensity at fixed frequency is photon flux, so doubling intensity doubles the number of photons arriving per second and therefore doubles the number of electrons ejected per second (above threshold). The work function is a property of the metal surface; shining brighter light does not change φ. Below threshold, raising intensity still ejects no electrons, but this beam is already above threshold, so rate scales with intensity and KE_max does not.

distractorRationales.A: KE_max is set by photon energy h f minus φ. Intensity does not appear in that equation, so doubling brightness does not double electron kinetic energy.
distractorRationales.C: The work function is characteristic of the metal (and its surface condition), not of the lamp brightness. Intensity does not retune φ.
distractorRationales.D: Above threshold, intensity controls rate, not whether electrons have kinetic energy. KE_max remains h f − φ and is unchanged at fixed f.

passage.title: Chemistry · Enzyme Kinetics
passage.body: A student investigates how temperature affects the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction, using an enzyme called amylase to break down starch into sugar. They measure the time taken for a fixed amount of starch to be fully broken down at five different temperatures: 10°C, 20°C, 30°C, 40°C and 50°C, keeping the amylase concentration and starch concentration constant in every trial. The reaction is fastest at 40°C. At 50°C, the reaction is slower than at 40°C, and even slower than at 30°C, despite the higher temperature. At 10°C, the reaction is very slow but still eventually completes.

items.stem: Benzaldehyde is treated with NH4Cl and KCN, and the isolated aminonitrile is heated in aqueous acid. What is the organic product, and what is its stereochemical character?

choices.text: Enantiopure (S)-phenylglycine, because cyanide approaches only the Re face of the imine
Racemic phenylglycine (2-amino-2-phenylacetic acid), because the uncatalyzed Strecker sequence generates a new stereocenter without facial control
A β-amino acid, because cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon that becomes C3
Benzylamine, because the nitrile is reduced rather than hydrolyzed in acid

items.explanation: In the Strecker synthesis an aldehyde is converted to an imine (or iminium), which is attacked by cyanide to give an α-aminonitrile. Acidic hydrolysis then converts the nitrile into a carboxylic acid, producing an α-amino acid whose side chain was the aldehyde’s R group—here phenylglycine. The imine is achiral, and cyanide adds to both faces equally, so the product is racemic unless a chiral catalyst or auxiliary is introduced. The new carbon is the α-carbon, not a β-carbon, and aqueous acid hydrolyzes nitriles rather than reducing them to amines.

distractorRationales.A: Without a chiral catalyst or enzyme, both faces of the imine are equivalent. Classic Strecker chemistry is racemic.
distractorRationales.C: Cyanide adds to the imine carbon that becomes C2 (the α-carbon) of the amino acid, not C3.
distractorRationales.D: Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the nitrile to a carboxylic acid. Reduction to an amine would require a reductant such as LiAlH4, which is not present.

passage.title: psg-bb-2
passage.body:
A biochemistry lab studied how a small globular enzyme, RibN, loses activity when it unfolds. In its native state, RibN is stabilized by a hydrophobic core, numerous hydrogen bonds within its alpha-helices and beta-sheets, and a single disulfide bond linking two cysteine residues. The team monitored folding both by measuring enzyme activity and by tracking buried tryptophan residues, which fluoresce differently when the protein unfolds. Slowly heating the wild-type enzyme, they found that activity was retained up to about 55 deg C and then fell sharply, with a melting temperature (Tm, the temperature at which half the protein is unfolded) of 65 deg C.
They compared three samples. A cysteine-to-alanine mutant that cannot form the disulfide bond behaved like wild type at low temperature but had a Tm of only 52 deg C. Adding 6 M urea, a chemical denaturant, to wild-type enzyme lowered its Tm dramatically and abolished activity even at room temperature; on dialysis to remove the urea, activity slowly returned. Boiling followed by cooling left the protein inactive and aggregated, yet sequencing showed that the polypeptide's amino acid sequence was fully intact.
The investigators emphasized that all of these treatments disrupted the folded shape without breaking the peptide bonds of the backbone, and that the enzyme's function depended on maintaining its three-dimensional conformation, not merely on possessing the correct sequence.

passage.title: psg-cars-13
passage.body:
The global spread of American popular culture -- film, music, fast food, digital platforms -- has prompted a long-running debate about whether this constitutes cultural imperialism: the imposition of one civilization's values and forms of life on peoples who have not chosen them. Critics of globalization in this register argue that the sheer economic asymmetry between media corporations based in wealthy nations and the domestic cultural industries of smaller, poorer societies creates a structural disadvantage. When production costs and distribution networks favor global products over local ones, communities find their own cultural expressions marginalized not by legal prohibition but by market logic. The displacement is quiet, cumulative, and often more thoroughgoing than any direct act of censorship could achieve.
The cultural imperialism thesis has been challenged on several grounds. The most telling challenge is empirical: audiences in different societies do not passively absorb global content but actively interpret it through their own cultural frameworks, adapting, subverting, and hybridizing imported forms in ways that produce genuinely new cultural expressions. The global spread of hip-hop, for instance, has generated distinctive local variants -- from Algerian rai-inflected rap to Japanese-language hip-hop -- that bear the unmistakable imprint of their cultural contexts. Reception is not passive consumption, and the audience is not an empty vessel waiting to be filled.
A second challenge concerns the directionality of cultural flows. While American products dominate certain global markets, cultural influence runs in multiple directions: South Korean popular music has captured youth audiences worldwide, Indian cinema occupies an outsized position in African and diaspora markets, and African musical rhythms have profoundly shaped what is recognized as American popular music in the first place. To speak of unidirectional cultural imperialism flattens a more complex and multi-directional reality in which no single center fully controls the terms of global cultural exchange. Nor is the traffic confined to entertainment. Telenovelas produced in Latin America command devoted audiences from Eastern Europe to the Philippines; Nigeria's prolific film industry circulates across the African continent and its diasporas; culinary forms, religious movements, and styles of dress migrate along routes that begin far from the wealthy media capitals. None of this shows that the largest studios and platforms have ceased to enjoy real advantages of scale and reach. It shows, rather, that 'flow' is the wrong picture if it implies a single faucet and a passive drain: global culture is better imagined as a dense weave of currents, some far stronger than others, but none issuing from a lone source.
Yet critics of the critique resist premature optimism. They argue that hybrid cultural forms, however creative, may still be produced and distributed through infrastructure owned by global corporations, whose financial interests shape which hybrids achieve wide distribution and which remain marginal. The creative agency of local audiences does not by itself dismantle the structural power asymmetries that determine which voices are amplified and which are muffled in global cultural markets.
This debate resists tidy resolution because it operates at two levels that its participants often conflate: the empirical level of how people actually engage with global cultural content, and the structural level of which actors control the conditions under which such engagement occurs. Progress requires holding both levels in view simultaneously.

passage.title: Two short poems: Ferry
passage.body:
Poem 1 — “Ticket”
I bought a ticket to the other bank
as if the river were a problem in change.
The ferryman took coins that had known other pockets.
He did not ask what I was leaving.
The water did, in small repeated questions
against the hull.

Poem 2 — “Return”
On the way back the same boat
was a different animal.
I recognised the coins by their edges
and not the faces.
Someone on the far jetty waved
at a person I had not yet become
and I, traitor, waved.

passage.title: A Form of Fairness (1978)
passage.body: In “A Form of Fairness” (1978), Samir Haddad writes from inside urban cycling. The argument is that a caption can do the arguing the image refuses to do. The piece admits that some gatekeeping keeps fraud out. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Suppose the student had measured each L to the bottom of the bob rather than to its centre. On a plot of T² against that recorded length, how would the intercept change relative to the Table 1 procedure?

choices.text: The vertical intercept would remain zero, because a constant length error cannot affect a T² versus L graph.
The vertical intercept would become positive and equal in magnitude to T² at L = 0.400 m, because the whole data set would shift upward.
The vertical intercept would become negative (approximately −0.060 s²), because each recorded L is 0.015 m larger than the length that belongs in T² = (4π²/g) L_centre.
The vertical intercept would become positive and the gradient would double, because diameter rather than radius would now be the length unit.

items.explanation: The bob diameter is 3.0 cm, so the radius is 0.015 m. Length to the bottom is L_centre + 0.015 m. The physical relation is T² = k L_centre with k = 4π²/g ≈ 4.03 s² m^{-1} from Table 1. Substituting L_recorded = L_centre + 0.015 m gives T² = k L_recorded − 0.015k, a line of unchanged slope with vertical intercept −0.015 × 4.03 ≈ −0.060 s². Table 1, measured to the centre, is consistent with a near-zero intercept; measuring to the bottom systematically overstates L and slides every point to the right. A constant length offset is a classic intercept error, not a doubling of gradient and not an upward shift in T².

distractorRationales.A: A systematic additive error in the abscissa is precisely what produces a nonzero intercept; Table 1’s near-origin behaviour would not survive that mis-measure.
distractorRationales.B: T² does not increase when L is overstated; the points move right along the L axis, which makes the intercept more negative, not equal to the first T² value.
distractorRationales.D: Using the bottom rather than the centre adds one radius, not a change of units to diameters, and it does not double 4π²/g.

passage.title: Cartoon: Clinic time
passage.body:
A single-panel cartoon, unsigned, published on a letters page.

Foreground: a waiting-room bench. Four people sit. Above each head a small clock; the hands are at 1:10, 2:40, 4:15, and 9:50. None of the clocks match the large wall clock, which has no hands.

On the wall, a framed motto: WE VALUE YOUR TIME. The frame is gold. The glass is cracked.

To the right, a receptionist window. The receptionist smiles with many teeth and holds a clipboard titled TRIAGE (PRIVATE). On the clipboard the only visible line is: “Can they still sit up?” A potted plant on the sill is fake; its price tag remains.

Under the bench, a fifth clock, face-down.

Caption, in small type: “The system is coping.”

A letter printed beneath, from “Concerned, Upper Shore”: “Cartoons like this undermine dedicated staff. If people arrived on time and did not bring relatives, clocks would match.”

passage.title: psg-bb-1
passage.body:
Researchers characterized a bacterial hydrolase, EnzA, that cleaves a colorless substrate into a yellow product, allowing the initial reaction velocity to be measured by absorbance. Working at constant enzyme concentration, saturating buffer, and 37 deg C, they varied the substrate concentration [S] and recorded the initial velocity (v0). As [S] increased, v0 rose steeply at first and then leveled off, tracing the hyperbolic curve expected for a single-active-site enzyme. From these data the team estimated a maximum velocity (Vmax) of 100 micromol/min and a Michaelis constant (Km) of 2.0 mM, where Km is the [S] at which v0 equals half of Vmax.
The team then repeated the assay in the presence of two candidate drugs. With a fixed concentration of Inhibitor A, the measured Vmax remained 100 micromol/min, but the apparent Km rose to 6.0 mM; adding excess substrate fully restored the maximal rate. With a fixed concentration of Inhibitor B, the apparent Km stayed at 2.0 mM, but Vmax fell to 50 micromol/min, and no amount of added substrate recovered the original maximal rate.
A double-reciprocal (Lineweaver-Burk) plot summarized the results: the control line and the Inhibitor A line shared the same y-intercept but differed in slope, whereas the control line and the Inhibitor B line shared the same x-intercept but differed in y-intercept. The researchers concluded that the two inhibitors act by distinct mechanisms, a distinction that matters clinically because it determines whether raising the physiological substrate concentration can overcome the drug's effect.

items.stem: An investigator inserts a single extra nucleotide immediately after the AUG start codon of a bacterial ORF that previously encoded a 300-residue protein. No compensating mutation is present. Which outcome is most likely?

choices.text: Every amino acid remains identical because degeneracy lets the ribosome skip extra bases at wobble positions.
Translation initiates at the next in-frame AUG, producing a protein that lacks only the N-terminal residue.
The insertion is spliced out of the bacterial transcript as a nuclear intron, restoring the original frame.
The reading frame shifts by one nucleotide, so downstream codons are systematically misread until a stop is encountered, typically yielding a truncated nonfunctional polypeptide.

items.explanation: The genetic code is read as nonoverlapping triplets from a fixed initiation codon. Inserting one nucleotide immediately after AUG regroups every subsequent base, so all downstream codons differ from the original frame. Premature stop codons appear frequently in the new frame, truncating the chain well before 300 residues. Degeneracy does not authorize skipping nucleotides. There is no general mechanism that simply reinitiates at the next AUG to rescue a one-base frameshift across a long ORF, and typical bacterial protein-coding sequences are not spliced by a nuclear spliceosome.

distractorRationales.A: Degeneracy and wobble affect synonymous third-position pairing; they do not cause the ribosome to ignore an inserted nucleotide.
distractorRationales.B: A +1 insertion after the start does not leave the remainder of the original ORF in frame, so the product is not a single-residue N-terminal truncation.
distractorRationales.C: Bacteria lack the nuclear spliceosome that removes eukaryotic introns from pre-mRNA; a genomic +1 insertion remains in the mRNA.

items.stem: An enzyme is assayed with lactate as the only organic substrate. No product forms unless NAD+ is present; the organic product is pyruvate and the dinucleotide is reduced to NADH. According to enzyme classification by reaction type, the protein is:

choices.text: A hydrolase that adds water across the C–C bond of lactate
A ligase that condenses two lactates with concomitant ATP hydrolysis
An isomerase that rearranges lactate to pyruvate without a redox cofactor
An oxidoreductase that uses NAD+ as the electron acceptor

items.explanation: Oxidoreductases catalyze electron transfer. Conversion of lactate (a secondary alcohol) to pyruvate (a ketone) with stoichiometric reduction of NAD+ to NADH is hydride transfer to a nicotinamide cofactor, the defining LDH reaction and EC class 1. Hydrolases add water and do not require NAD+. Ligases join two molecules using NTP hydrolysis, which is not described. An isomerase would rearrange atoms within one molecule without a net redox change or a requirement for NAD+. The obligatory NAD+ dependence and NADH production assign the enzyme as an oxidoreductase.

distractorRationales.A: No water is added, and NAD+ would be unnecessary for a hydrolase.
distractorRationales.B: ATP is not mentioned, and two lactates are not condensed.
distractorRationales.C: Isomerases do not reduce NAD+; the observed cofactor change is a redox signature.

passage.title: The Standard (1983)
passage.body: Clara Voss's 1983 essay “The Standard,” on museum captions, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that speed of publication is being mistaken for care. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: psg-ps-8
passage.body:
A study tested how awareness of a negative stereotype affects performance and self-presentation. Two groups of equally qualified students took the same difficult verbal test. In the 'diagnostic' condition, the test was described as measuring underlying ability; in the 'nondiagnostic' condition, it was described as a problem-solving exercise unrelated to ability. Students from a group stereotyped as weaker in the domain scored lower than others in the diagnostic condition but scored equally in the nondiagnostic condition. Merely asking students to record their group membership before a diagnostic test reproduced the gap.
In a second study, participants prepared for a mock interview. Told the interviewer valued modesty, they described themselves cautiously; told the interviewer admired confidence, the same participants emphasized their strengths. Observers who saw only one version rated the participants accordingly, and participants reported deliberately tailoring the impression they gave.
The authors interpreted the first study as evidence that the fear of confirming a negative group stereotype can itself depress performance, independent of ability, and that subtle cues activate this fear. They interpreted the second as an example of managing the impression one presents to different audiences, comparing it to an actor shifting performances between a front region and a back region. They cautioned that persistent performance gaps in real settings may partly reflect such situational threats and unequal conditions rather than fixed differences in ability between groups.

passage.title: psg-cp-9
passage.body:
Nucleophilic substitution is central to organic and biochemical reactivity, from laboratory synthesis to the alkylation of DNA. A class studies how two bromoalkanes react with hydroxide ion, which acts as the nucleophile, in a hydroxylic solvent.
The first substrate is 1-bromobutane, a primary alkyl halide in which the carbon bearing bromine is attached to only one other carbon. With a good nucleophile it reacts by a one-step, concerted mechanism (SN2): hydroxide attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving bromide, and as bromide departs the other three groups invert like an umbrella in the wind. The measured rate depends on the concentrations of both the substrate and the hydroxide.
The second substrate is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide), a tertiary halide whose brominated carbon is attached to three other carbons. It reacts by a two-step mechanism (SN1): the carbon-bromine bond breaks first to give a carbocation, which the nucleophile then captures. The measured rate depends only on the concentration of the substrate, and because the carbocation is trigonal planar, a nucleophile can approach from either face.
The class also revisits structure. They note that a carbon bonded to four different groups is a stereocenter and examine 2-bromobutane as an example. They track how the functional group changes when hydroxide replaces bromide, and they rank the stability of primary, secondary, and tertiary carbocations to explain why substrate structure dictates the mechanism. The instructor stresses that the same electronic and steric principles govern reactions of biological molecules such as the phosphate esters of nucleotides.

items.stem: An experimenter depolarizes the middle of an unmyelinated axon to threshold with an extracellular electrode. Action potentials:

choices.text: travel only toward the synaptic terminal
fail to start, because spikes can be initiated only in dendrites
propagate in both directions away from the stimulus site

items.explanation: A patch of axon brought to threshold opens local voltage-gated Na+ channels and depolarizes both neighboring regions. There is no refractory wake yet on either side, so two action potentials travel away from the artificial site, one orthodromic and one antidromic. Physiologic initiation at the hillock looks unidirectional only because the soma/dendrite side is a poor regenerative axon and because a refractory region develops behind a naturally traveling spike. Dendrites are not the unique legal site of spike initiation, and the axon membrane itself is fully excitable.

distractorRationales.A: Nothing about a mid-axon shock forbids the terminal-directed spike. Both directions are available at the instant of stimulation.
distractorRationales.B: The soma-directed (antidromic) spike also propagates on that axon; unidirectionality is not an intrinsic one-way valve in the membrane.
distractorRationales.C: Axons, especially the hillock and nodes, are the usual spike-initiation zones. Dendrites are not required to start this experimentally evoked AP.

items.stem: A 2.0 kg cart travelling at 6.0 m s−1 collides with a stationary 4.0 kg cart. For a perfectly inelastic collision they move together at v = (m1 u1) / (m1 + m2). Kinetic energies: KE = (1/2) m v². What is the common speed, and how much KE is lost?

choices.text: v = 2.0 m s−1; KE is conserved at 36 J
v = 3.0 m s−1; KE lost is 0
v = 2.0 m s−1; KE falls from 36 J to 12 J, so 24 J is lost
v = 6.0 m s−1; KE is conserved at 36 J

items.explanation: Momentum conservation: 2.0 × 6.0 = (6.0) v, so v = 2.0 m s−1. Initial KE = 0.50 × 2.0 × 36 = 36 J. Final KE = 0.50 × 6.0 × 4.0 = 12 J. The missing 24 J is dissipated as heat and deformation, which is allowed in a perfectly inelastic collision. Speed is not unchanged, and KE is not conserved for the inelastic case. A 3.0 m s−1 guess is the mean of 6 and 0 without mass weighting. Elastic formulae would give a rebound of the light cart, not a common 2.0 m s−1.

distractorRationales.A: The common speed 2.0 m s−1 is right, but (1/2)×6×4 = 12 J, not 36 J, so KE is not conserved.
distractorRationales.B: Mass-weighted momentum gives 2.0 m s−1, not the unweighted average 3.0 m s−1, and inelastic collisions do lose KE.
distractorRationales.D: The 4.0 kg cart must gain momentum, so the 2.0 kg cart must slow; v cannot stay 6.0 m s−1 if they stick.

items.stem: Malonate, a competitive analog of succinate, is added to respiring mitochondria supplied with pyruvate. Which pair of matrix changes is most likely?

choices.text: Succinate falls and fumarate rises because the block is after fumarase.
Succinate accumulates and conversion of succinate to fumarate decreases.
Isocitrate is depleted because aconitase is the malonate target.
α-Ketoglutarate is converted exclusively to glutamate, fully bypassing the cycle.

items.explanation: Malonate is a classic competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase, occupying the succinate-binding site so that succinate cannot be oxidized to fumarate. The substrate of the blocked step therefore accumulates, and the product fumarate (and downstream malate/oxaloacetate) declines. Upstream cycle intermediates can also back up. Aconitase is not the malonate target, so isocitrate depletion as a primary event is wrong. Fumarase is downstream of SDH; blocking SDH cannot raise fumarate while lowering succinate. Transamination of α-ketoglutarate may increase if the cycle stalls, but that is not a complete enzymatic bypass of the malonate block.

distractorRationales.A: Malonate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase, which is before fumarase. Succinate should rise and fumarate from that step should fall, not the reverse.
distractorRationales.C: Malonate is a succinate analog aimed at SDH, not aconitase. Isocitrate would not be the depleted substrate of the inhibited enzyme.
distractorRationales.D: Glutamate formation from α-ketoglutarate can increase when the cycle backs up, but it does not ‘exclusively’ replace the cycle or remove the SDH block.

items.stem: Pyridine is readily protonated by dilute aqueous acid (pKa of pyridinium ≈ 5.2), whereas pyrrole is not (pKa of the conjugate acid ≈ −4). Which orbital analysis explains the difference?

choices.text: Pyridine’s nitrogen lone pair occupies an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring and is not part of the 6π aromatic sextet, so it can bind H+ without destroying aromaticity; pyrrole’s lone pair is part of the sextet
Pyrrole is more basic because its nitrogen is sp3 and has a higher-energy lone pair
Neither heterocycle is aromatic, so basicity tracks only the electronegativity of nitrogen
Pyridine is not aromatic; protonation creates aromaticity, which is why it is basic

items.explanation: Both rings are aromatic with 6π electrons (Hückel 4n+2). In pyridine the nitrogen contributes one electron to the π system from its p orbital, exactly as a CH group would; the lone pair sits in an sp2 orbital in the plane and is available for protonation. In pyrrole the nitrogen already contributes two electrons (the lone pair) to the π sextet. Protonating pyrrole on nitrogen would remove those two electrons from conjugation and destroy aromaticity, so pyrrole is an extremely weak base (and is instead weakly acidic at N–H). Pyrrole’s nitrogen is not sp3 in the aromatic structure.

distractorRationales.B: Pyrrole is far less basic than pyridine. Its nitrogen is planar and sp2, with the lone pair in the aromatic π system.
distractorRationales.C: Both are aromatic. Electronegativity alone cannot explain a ~9-unit pKa gap between two azine/azole nitrogens.
distractorRationales.D: Pyridine is already aromatic before protonation. Aromaticity is preserved, not created, when the in-plane lone pair binds H+.

passage.title: psg-cars-6
passage.body:
Social capital — broadly understood as the networks of relationships, norms of reciprocity, and trust that enable collective action — has become one of the most debated concepts in contemporary sociology. Proponents argue that it explains why some communities flourish economically and politically while others, equally well endowed in financial and physical resources, remain mired in dysfunction. Where citizens trust one another and are embedded in overlapping civic associations, cooperative ventures are easier to organize, contracts are more reliably honored, and public goods are more effectively maintained.
The concept distinguishes between two broad types. Bonding social capital refers to the dense ties within homogeneous groups — extended families, ethnic neighborhoods, religious congregations — that provide strong mutual support and a sense of belonging. Bridging social capital refers to the weaker but more diverse ties that link members of different social groups, enabling information and resources to flow across community boundaries. Theorists have argued that bridging capital is especially important for economic mobility and democratic stability, because it prevents the insularity and exclusivity that can calcify into tribal antagonism. The interplay between the two forms often matters more than either in isolation. Newcomers to a city, for example, tend to rely first on bonding ties — kin and compatriots who supply lodging, informal credit, and job referrals — and only later cultivate the bridging ties to employers, officials, and institutions beyond their original circle that permit genuine advancement. A community rich in bonding capital but starved of bridging capital may be tightly knit yet economically trapped, whereas one with abundant bridging ties but thin internal solidarity may struggle to sustain the everyday obligations on which cooperation depends. On this view the vitality of a community turns less on how much social capital it can claim than on how its bonding and bridging forms are balanced against each other.
Critics have raised several concerns. First, they argue that the concept is so capacious as to be analytically vacuous: if social capital includes trust, networks, and norms all at once, it risks becoming a label that explains everything and therefore explains nothing. Second, the emphasis on voluntary civic associations may obscure the role of institutional design and state capacity in producing the outcomes attributed to social capital. A society with strong courts, reliable public services, and enforceable property rights may achieve cooperation through formal mechanisms, regardless of the density of its associational life.
A third critique focuses on the dark side of social capital. The same dense ties that produce cohesion within a group can generate exclusion and hostility toward outsiders. Historically, tightly bonded criminal networks, nativist movements, and exclusionary professional guilds have all exhibited strong social capital while causing harm to those outside the charmed circle. If social capital is a neutral resource that amplifies whatever goals a group pursues, then celebrating it uncritically is a mistake. A community of mutual trust can be a community of mutual hostility toward all who fall outside its boundaries, and the literature on ethnic cleansing, organized crime, and racially restrictive covenants demonstrates this possibility in grim historical detail.
These debates have produced a more nuanced research agenda. Scholars now investigate not just the presence or absence of social capital but its distribution across social groups, its articulation with formal institutions, and the conditions under which it promotes rather than undermines democratic participation and social equity.

Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the ES complex, lowering both apparent Km and Vmax (their ratio stays roughly constant). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.B: Increased Km with unchanged Vmax describes competitive inhibition.
distractorRationales.C: Decreased Vmax with unchanged Km describes noncompetitive inhibition.
distractorRationales.D: No inhibitor increases Vmax.

items.stem: In the pigment pathway, which genetic interaction best describes the effect of aa on colony color?

choices.text: X-linked inheritance, because both genes are autosomal
Recessive epistasis, because aa masks the phenotypic effect of the B locus
Codominance, because A and B are both expressed equally in heterozygotes
Genomic imprinting, because phenotype depends on the parent of origin

items.explanation: The passage states that loss of enzyme A produces white colonies regardless of enzyme B genotype. Thus the homozygous recessive aa genotype masks B-locus variation, which is recessive epistasis. Common miss: Calling any two-gene interaction incomplete dominance rather than identifying masking across loci. This correctly describes aa masking the B locus. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.A: The passage states the genes are autosomal, not X-linked.
distractorRationales.C: Codominance involves simultaneous expression of different alleles at one locus, not masking across loci.
distractorRationales.D: No parent-of-origin effect is described.

passage.title: Pigment inheritance and enzyme oligomerization in a model yeast
passage.body:
A fictional yeast synthesizes a purple pigment in two steps. Enzyme A converts a colorless precursor to a blue intermediate, and enzyme B converts the blue intermediate to the purple product. Loss of enzyme A prevents blue intermediate formation and produces white colonies regardless of enzyme B genotype. Loss of enzyme B in a strain with functional enzyme A produces blue colonies. The genes A and B are autosomal and are hypothesized to assort independently. Researchers crossed AABB yeast to aabb yeast, then selfed the AaBb F1 progeny.

Observed F2 colony phenotypes from AaBb selfing.
Phenotype | Observed colonies
Purple | 178
Blue | 59
White | 83

Biochemical characterization of enzyme B variants.
Enzyme B protein | Dimeric protein (%) | Km for blue intermediate (mM) | Relative Vmax (%)
B wild type | 95 | 0.10 | 100
b Gly45Asp variant | 25 | 0.12 | 20
b Gly45Asp + stabilizing osmolyte | 70 | 0.11 | 65

Native gel analysis of enzyme B. — Wild-type enzyme B migrates mainly as a dimer. The Gly45Asp variant shows a stronger monomer band and weaker dimer band. Adding a stabilizing osmolyte partially restores the dimer band.

items.stem: Blood is modeled as an ideal incompressible fluid in a horizontal artery that enters a stenosis with half the upstream cross-sectional area. Compared with the wide segment, the stenosis has:

choices.text: lower speed and higher hydrostatic pressure
higher speed and lower hydrostatic pressure
higher speed and higher hydrostatic pressure
lower speed and lower hydrostatic pressure

items.explanation: Continuity requires the product of area and speed to stay constant, so halving area doubles speed. Bernoulli's equation at constant height then says that an increase in dynamic pressure 1/2 rho v squared must be paid for by a decrease in hydrostatic pressure. The stenosis is therefore the fast, low-pressure region. The opposite pairing of speed and pressure would violate either continuity or energy conservation along a streamline.

distractorRationales.A: Lower speed would require a larger area, not a stenosis. Higher pressure with lower speed can occur in a dilation, not a narrowing.
distractorRationales.C: Speed does rise in the stenosis, but Bernoulli then requires hydrostatic pressure to fall, not rise, at the same height.
distractorRationales.D: Speed does not fall where area falls. Continuity forces the opposite speed change.

items.stem: Light enters glass with refractive index 1.50 from air at an incident angle of 30 degrees from the normal. What is the approximate refracted angle?
items.explanation: Snell's law gives n1 sin theta1 = n2 sin theta2. With n1 = 1.00, theta1 = 30 degrees, and n2 = 1.50, sin theta2 = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333, so theta2 is about 19 degrees. The ray bends toward the normal in the higher-index medium. Common miss: Forgetting that entering a higher-index medium bends light toward the normal. This correctly applies Snell's law. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.A: This would occur only if the refractive indices were equal.
distractorRationales.B: This bends the ray away from the normal, opposite the expected direction.
distractorRationales.D: This confuses the angle from the normal with an angle from the surface.

items.stem: Two climbers of equal skill fall on the same pitch. The one who had rated “I can complete this route if I persist” returns to practice the move the next day. The one who had rated “I am just not a lead-climbing person” avoids the wall for weeks. Which construct most directly predicts the difference in persistence?

choices.text: Global self-esteem (overall worth) rather than any task belief
External locus of control, which always increases practice after failure
Self-efficacy: belief in capability for this task predicts practice and persistence after failure
Social identity as “climber” must be absent in anyone who falls

items.explanation: Bandura’s self-efficacy is a judgment that one can organize and execute the actions required in a specific domain. High efficacy after a fall supports return to practice; a trait-like “I am not that kind of person” statement functions as low efficacy and predicts withdrawal. Global self-esteem may not differ between the two climbers. External locus (“outcomes are luck”) would not uniquely predict more practice. A fall does not strip a social identity; identities can include being a climber who is currently struggling.

distractorRationales.A: The ratings in the stem are about completing this route, not about being a worthy person in general.
distractorRationales.B: External locus typically reduces, rather than increases, instrumental practice, because effort is seen as irrelevant.
distractorRationales.D: Identity categories survive setbacks; the predictor here is capability belief, not deletion of the climber identity.

items.stem:
A liver homogenate is fractionated by differential centrifugation. Marker quantities are reported per milligram of protein:
1000 g nuclear pellet: succinate dehydrogenase 4 units, acid phosphatase 3 units, NADPH–cytochrome c reductase 5 units, DNA 82 µg.
10 000 g pellet: SDH 96, acid phosphatase 8, reductase 6, DNA 4.
20 000 g pellet: SDH 7, acid phosphatase 88, reductase 9, DNA 2.
100 000 g microsomal pellet: SDH 3, acid phosphatase 6, reductase 91, DNA 1.
Final supernatant: SDH 2, acid phosphatase 5, reductase 4, DNA 0.
Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.text: The 10 000 g pellet is enriched in mitochondria, because succinate dehydrogenase peaks there.
The 20 000 g pellet is nuclei, because acid phosphatase is a nuclear-envelope marker.
The microsomal pellet is nuclei, because it has the highest DNA (91 units of reductase).
The supernatant contains the mitochondria, because succinate dehydrogenase is a soluble cytosolic enzyme.

items.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane, so its specific activity traces mitochondria. That activity is 96 units mg−1 in the 10 000 g pellet and only 2–7 in the other fractions, so mitochondria sediment there. Acid phosphatase at 88 units marks lysosomes in the 20 000 g pellet; NADPH–cytochrome c reductase at 91 units marks endoplasmic reticulum microsomes; DNA at 82 µg mg−1 marks nuclei. The cytosol is not the mitochondrial compartment. The table therefore assigns mitochondria to the 10 000 g fraction.

distractorRationales.B: Acid phosphatase is a lysosomal hydrolase, not a nuclear marker; nuclei track with DNA in the 1000 g pellet.
distractorRationales.C: The 91-unit peak is the ER reductase, not DNA; microsomal DNA is only 1 µg mg−1.
distractorRationales.D: Succinate dehydrogenase is membrane-bound in mitochondria; the supernatant has only 2 units.

items.stem: During prolonged fasting or very low carbohydrate intake, the liver produces ketone bodies. These are made from:

choices.text: Amino acids converted directly into glucose

items.stem: A surgical skills lab finds that a simple interrupted suture is performed fastest under high evaluative arousal, whereas a delicate microvascular anastomosis is most accurate at moderate arousal and degrades when the attending stares. This pattern is the Yerkes–Dodson law. Which statement captures it?

choices.text: Performance is a strictly rising linear function of arousal for every task
Hull’s drive reduction predicts that only hunger, not evaluative arousal, can change skill
Performance follows an inverted U with arousal, and the optimal point is lower for more difficult tasks
Maslow’s hierarchy forbids any arousal effect until self-actualization is complete

items.explanation: Yerkes and Dodson described an inverted-U relation between arousal and performance, with complex tasks peaking at lower arousal than simple ones. That matches fast simple suturing under high arousal and fragile fine anastomosis under an audience. A strictly linear “more arousal is always better” rule is the common trap. Hull’s drive-reduction theory concerns tissue deficits and habit strength, not this arousal–complexity interaction. Maslow’s need hierarchy does not ban arousal effects on motor skill.

distractorRationales.A: The law is an inverted U, not a monotonic rise, especially for hard tasks.
distractorRationales.B: Drive reduction is a different motivational theory and does not uniquely own skill-arousal curves.
distractorRationales.D: Maslow does not prohibit Yerkes–Dodson effects in a skills lab.

items.stem: In a Trier Social Stress Test, salivary α-amylase, a sympathetic marker, peaks within minutes of a judged speech, whereas salivary cortisol peaks about twenty minutes after the speech ends. Which physiological account is best?

choices.text: Cortisol is always released first because the adrenal cortex fires before the medulla
Both peaks are produced by the same postganglionic acetylcholine release at the heart, so they must coincide
The sympathetic–adrenal-medullary axis releases catecholamines rapidly, while the HPA axis releases cortisol more slowly after CRH and ACTH
The cortisol lag proves the speech was appraised as irrelevant and therefore not a stressor

items.explanation: Acute psychosocial threat rapidly engages the sympathetic–adrenal-medullary axis, raising catecholamines and markers such as salivary α-amylase within minutes. The hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal cascade requires hypothalamic CRH, pituitary ACTH, and then adrenocortical cortisol, so the glucocorticoid peak is slower, often on the order of tens of minutes in saliva. The cortex-first claim reverses adrenal anatomy and timing. Cardiac acetylcholine does not generate the cortisol curve. A cortisol rise is evidence that the HPA axis treated the speech as a stressor, not as an irrelevant event.

distractorRationales.A: Medullary catecholamines are faster than cortical cortisol; the stem’s amylase-then-cortisol order matches that, not a cortex-first rule.
distractorRationales.B: Cortisol is an endocrine HPA product, not a burst of cardiac acetylcholine, so the peaks need not coincide.
distractorRationales.D: A delayed cortisol peak is the expected HPA time course for a stressor, not a sign that the event was appraised as irrelevant.

items.stem: A focal demyelinating lesion increases internodal membrane capacitance and decreases internodal transmembrane resistance. Compared with adjacent myelinated axon, action potential propagation through the plaque is most likely to:

choices.text: Speed up, because saltatory jumps become longer when myelin is lost
Convert the axon into an electrical synapse with no need for voltage-gated sodium channels
Increase the density of internodal sodium channels above nodal levels within minutes as the only repair
Slow or fail, because local-circuit current leaks across internodal membrane instead of depolarizing the next node to threshold

items.explanation: Myelin increases effective membrane resistance and decreases capacitance, so internodal membrane does not waste depolarizing current. Voltage-gated Na+ channels are concentrated at nodes of Ranvier; the action potential jumps from node to node. Demyelination lets current leak through internodes, lowering the length constant and slowing charging of the next node, which can block conduction. Saltatory conduction is not faster without myelin. Loss of myelin does not create a gap junction, and internodal Na-channel redistribution, when it occurs, is a slow plastic response rather than an immediate rescue that speeds conduction above normal.

distractorRationales.A: Myelin loss shortens the effective jump and slows conduction; it does not lengthen saltatory steps.
distractorRationales.B: The axon remains a chemically/electrically excitable cable with Na channels; it does not become a gap-junction synapse.
distractorRationales.C: Channel redistribution is not an instantaneous, complete replacement of myelin, and internodes do not immediately exceed nodal Na-channel density to speed spikes.

items.stem: Light traveling in glass (n = 2.0) strikes a glass–air interface. The critical angle for total internal reflection is:
items.explanation: Total internal reflection can occur only when light in a higher-index medium meets a lower-index medium, as in glass to air. The critical angle satisfies n1 sin θc = n2 sin 90°, so sin θc = n2 / n1 = 1.0 / 2.0 = 1/2 and θc = 30°. At angles of incidence larger than 30° there is no transmitted ray in air. The 45° value is the critical angle for n = √2, a common memorized special case that does not match n = 2. Sixty degrees would be 90° minus 30° or arcsin(√3/2), not arcsin(1/2).

distractorRationales.A: This is half of 30° without a physical basis. The inverse sine of 1/2 is 30°, not 15°.
distractorRationales.C: sin 45° = 1/√2, which would be θc if n1 were √2. For n = 2 the sine of the critical angle is 1/2, not 1/√2.
distractorRationales.D: This is 90° − 30° or the angle whose sine is √3/2. Snell's law at the critical angle uses sin θc = n2/n1 = 1/2, which is 30°.

items.stem: A human primary spermatocyte has 46 chromosomes and 4C DNA. Immediately after meiosis I, each secondary spermatocyte has:

items.stem: How many stereoisomers exist for 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane, CH3CHBrCHClCH3?
items.explanation: C2 and C3 are both stereocenters, and they are not identically substituted (one bears Br, the other Cl). The 2^n rule therefore gives 2^2 = 4 stereoisomers: a pair of enantiomers with the (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) relative configuration and a second diastereomeric pair (2R,3S)/(2S,3R). There is no meso form because the two centers are different, so none of the four is achiral. Two would describe a single stereocenter; three is the count for a molecule such as 2,3-dibromobutane that has a meso isomer; eight would require three independent stereocenters.

distractorRationales.A: Two stereoisomers would be expected for a molecule with only one stereocenter (a single enantiomeric pair).
distractorRationales.B: Three is the stereoisomer count for 2,3-dibromobutane, which has two identically substituted centers and therefore one meso form plus one enantiomeric pair.
distractorRationales.D: Eight stereoisomers would require three unrelated stereocenters (2^3). This chain has only two.

items.stem: A mutant HIV-1 reverse transcriptase has kcat for dNTP incorporation reduced 80-fold with an unaltered Km for dNTPs. In newly infected CD4 T cells, compared with wild-type virus, synthesis of full-length proviral DNA is expected to be:

Replaced by integrase polymerization, which does not require reverse transcriptase

items.explanation: Retroviruses package reverse transcriptase so that the single-stranded RNA genome can be converted into double-stranded DNA before integrase inserts a provirus. The enzyme's kcat is the catalytic turnover per active site; dropping it 80-fold slows chain elongation even when dNTP binding (Km) is normal and dNTP pools are saturating. Fidelity can change with some RT mutants, but a pure kcat drop does not make DNA synthesis faster.

distractorRationales.B: Cellular DNA polymerases act on DNA templates; reverse transcription is the viral enzyme's job.
distractorRationales.C: Integrase cannot substitute for DNA polymerization from RNA.

items.stem: A linear double-stranded DNA viral genome is hydrolyzed completely to mononucleotides. Adenine accounts for 18% of all bases. A student reports that guanine must also be 18% because ‘purines are equal.’ Which value is the actual percentage of guanine, and why was the student wrong?

passage.title: psg-cars-6
passage.body:
Social capital — broadly understood as the networks of relationships, norms of reciprocity, and trust that enable collective action — has become one of the most debated concepts in contemporary sociology. Proponents argue that it explains why some communities flourish economically and politically while others, equally well endowed in financial and physical resources, remain mired in dysfunction. Where citizens trust one another and are embedded in overlapping civic associations, cooperative ventures are easier to organize, contracts are more reliably honored, and public goods are more effectively maintained.
The concept distinguishes between two broad types. Bonding social capital refers to the dense ties within homogeneous groups — extended families, ethnic neighborhoods, religious congregations — that provide strong mutual support and a sense of belonging. Bridging social capital refers to the weaker but more diverse ties that link members of different social groups, enabling information and resources to flow across community boundaries. Theorists have argued that bridging capital is especially important for economic mobility and democratic stability, because it prevents the insularity and exclusivity that can calcify into tribal antagonism. The interplay between the two forms often matters more than either in isolation. Newcomers to a city, for example, tend to rely first on bonding ties — kin and compatriots who supply lodging, informal credit, and job referrals — and only later cultivate the bridging ties to employers, officials, and institutions beyond their original circle that permit genuine advancement. A community rich in bonding capital but starved of bridging capital may be tightly knit yet economically trapped, whereas one with abundant bridging ties but thin internal solidarity may struggle to sustain the everyday obligations on which cooperation depends. On this view the vitality of a community turns less on how much social capital it can claim than on how its bonding and bridging forms are balanced against each other.
Critics have raised several concerns. First, they argue that the concept is so capacious as to be analytically vacuous: if social capital includes trust, networks, and norms all at once, it risks becoming a label that explains everything and therefore explains nothing. Second, the emphasis on voluntary civic associations may obscure the role of institutional design and state capacity in producing the outcomes attributed to social capital. A society with strong courts, reliable public services, and enforceable property rights may achieve cooperation through formal mechanisms, regardless of the density of its associational life.
A third critique focuses on the dark side of social capital. The same dense ties that produce cohesion within a group can generate exclusion and hostility toward outsiders. Historically, tightly bonded criminal networks, nativist movements, and exclusionary professional guilds have all exhibited strong social capital while causing harm to those outside the charmed circle. If social capital is a neutral resource that amplifies whatever goals a group pursues, then celebrating it uncritically is a mistake. A community of mutual trust can be a community of mutual hostility toward all who fall outside its boundaries, and the literature on ethnic cleansing, organized crime, and racially restrictive covenants demonstrates this possibility in grim historical detail.
These debates have produced a more nuanced research agenda. Scholars now investigate not just the presence or absence of social capital but its distribution across social groups, its articulation with formal institutions, and the conditions under which it promotes rather than undermines democratic participation and social equity.

passage.title: Tone as Rule (1976)
passage.body: Kwame Boateng published “Tone as Rule” in 1976 after a season in heritage listing. The argument is that neutrality is a style, not an absence of interest. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

Random assignment is the strongest listed feature for causal inference. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.A: Using two memory tests provides more information about retrieval but does not by itself establish causality.

distractorRationales.D: Motivation ratings help evaluate a possible alternative explanation but do not create equivalent groups.

passage.title: Working Memory, Sleep Restriction, and Retrieval Cues
passage.body:
A fictional laboratory study examined how one night of sleep restriction affects memory performance. Participants were randomly assigned to either a normal-sleep group or a restricted-sleep group. The next morning, all participants studied 30 neutral word pairs. After a 20-minute filler task, they completed two tests. In the free-recall test, participants wrote down as many target words as possible. In the cued-recall test, participants were shown the first word of each pair and attempted to retrieve the associated target word. Participants also completed a 2-back task as a measure of working memory updating.

Memory and working-memory performance
Group | Free recall: mean words recalled | Cued recall: mean words recalled | 2-back accuracy (%)
Normal sleep | 18.4 | 24.1 | 87
Restricted sleep | 13.2 | 20.2 | 73

Self-reported fatigue and motivation
Group | Fatigue rating, 1 to 7 | Motivation rating, 1 to 7
Normal sleep | 2.3 | 5.8
Restricted sleep | 5.9 | 5.6

Retrieval benefit — Both groups recalled more words on cued recall than on free recall, but the restricted-sleep group performed worse than the normal-sleep group on both tests.

The truncation has no kinase, so it cannot hyperphosphorylate STATs, it is not a Ras GAP, and RTKs are not nuclear steroid receptors.

items.stem: In the sentence “A coverage estimate can become a footnote that licenses the headline number,” the author is primarily

items.explanation: The paragraph grants that professionals name error, then shows the public-facing split: fifty million in the ear, a compromise in the appendix. Licensing is rhetorical permission, not a charge of invention from nothing. The photograph metaphor is the author's name for that misuse. A ignores the grant that compromise is not a crime. passage.title: The census of the uncounted
passage.body:
Political arithmetic began as a courtly hobby: a way of estimating how many subjects a prince could tax, feed, or send to war. Its early practitioners treated people as a kind of harvest. What could be enumerated could be extracted. What could not be enumerated was, for administrative purposes, a rumor.

The modern census inherited the appetite and dressed it as representation. To be counted is now advertised as a civic right, a way of appearing in the distribution of schools, clinics, and parliamentary seats. The advertisement is not false. Under-counted neighborhoods do lose clinics. The advertisement is incomplete. A census is also a machine for deciding which kinds of life will be treated as facts and which will remain anecdotes told to a volunteer with a clipboard.

Consider the category. Every census must invent boxes. The boxes are not discovered in nature; they are negotiated among ministries, churches, and, later, identity movements. A person who lives in two houses, or in none, or who works in a language the form does not print, must be forced into a box or dropped. Dropping looks like a clerical mishap. It is often a theory of the state: some lives are too expensive to verify, too mobile to locate, too politically inconvenient to add to a total that will be used against the ministry next year.

Statisticians reply that they already know this, that they publish coverage estimates and post-enumeration surveys, that the professional ethic is to name the error. Naming the error is not the same as refusing the uses of the total. A coverage estimate can become a footnote that licenses the headline number. The public hears fifty million; the appendix whispers that the fifty million is a compromise among several less flattering models. Compromise is not a crime. Treating the compromise as a photograph is.

There is a further twist. Groups that have been historically erased often demand better counting, and they are right to. Visibility in a dataset can be a precondition of funds. Yet the same groups may later discover that a sharper count is also a sharper target: for policing, for debt collection, for the allocation of blame when a service fails. The census does not choose the policy. It does make the policy cheaper to aim.

None of this is an argument for ignorance. A state that refuses to count will invent its numbers in the back room and call the invention common sense. The argument is for a less enchanted relationship to the table. Read the boxes as arguments. Read the missing as a constituency. And when a politician says the numbers speak for themselves, notice that speech is exactly what numbers cannot do until someone supplies a sentence.

items.stem: Groups brainstorm uses for a brick. When ideas are pooled anonymously, unique ideas per person fall relative to working alone. When each idea is tagged with a name on a shared screen, per-person output matches the alone condition. The identifiability effect is best explained as:

choices.text: Social loafing that shrinks when contributions are identifiable
Social facilitation of a novel creative task, which should always rise in groups
Deindividuation causing more ideas when people are anonymous
Bystander apathy toward a medical crisis

items.explanation: Brainstorming in a pool is a collective task. When credit is anonymous, individuals can hide, and unique output per person drops—social loafing. Tagging names restores accountability, so effort returns to the alone baseline. Facilitation of a poorly learned or complex generative task would, if anything, predict impairment from an audience, not a benefit of anonymity. Deindividuation would predict more unrestrained output when anonymous, which is the opposite of fewer ideas. No emergency is present.

distractorRationales.B: Idea generation is not a well-learned dominant response that an audience should automatically improve; the drop when anonymous is loafing.
distractorRationales.C: Anonymity reduced, rather than increased, idea counts, which is not a deindividuation-disinhibition pattern.
distractorRationales.D: The task is idea listing, not helping a victim.
