passage.title: psg-ps-7
passage.body:
Researchers studied how people view themselves and explain behavior. In Study 1, community volunteers completed a scale measuring their belief that they could organize and execute the actions needed to reach specific goals. Independently, they rated how much they felt their life outcomes were controlled by their own actions versus by luck or powerful others. Volunteers high on the first measure attempted harder tasks, persisted longer after setbacks, and reported less anxiety. Those who attributed outcomes mostly to outside forces set fewer goals and gave up sooner.
In Study 2, participants read vignettes about a student who failed an exam. When explaining the student's failure, observers most often cited the student's laziness or low ability, rarely mentioning the situation (an unfair test, a family emergency). Yet when participants recalled a time they themselves had failed, they overwhelmingly cited situational causes. In a variation, participants watched a peer perform poorly under obvious time pressure; even so, most still rated the peer as low in ability.
The authors linked Study 1 to two related constructs: a person's belief in their capability to succeed at specific tasks, and a general expectancy about whether outcomes are internally or externally controlled. They interpreted Study 2 as showing a systematic bias in how observers explain others' behavior, together with a divergence between how people explain their own versus others' outcomes. They stressed that these attribution tendencies operate even when situational information is clearly available.

items.stem:
Three C6 hydrocarbons are treated with bromine in the dark in CCl4, then with Br2/FeBr3.

Sample | Br2/CCl4 (dark) | Br2/FeBr3
Cyclohexane | orange persists | orange persists (very slow)
Cyclohexene | orange decolourises instantly | (already reacted)
Benzene | orange persists | substitution, HBr fumes, pale product

Which bonding description is supported?

choices.text: Benzene is a typical alkene, because it eventually reacts with bromine
Cyclohexane is unsaturated, which is why FeBr3 is required
All three are aromatic, differing only in colour
Cyclohexene undergoes rapid electrophilic addition; benzene’s delocalised π system resists addition and instead substitutes under Lewis-acid catalysis; cyclohexane has no π bond

items.explanation: Instant decolourisation in the dark is addition to an isolated C=C, the cyclohexene row. Benzene leaves Br2/CCl4 untouched, proving it does not add like an alkene, but does undergo catalysed substitution with FeBr3, the aromatic electrophilic-substitution signature. Cyclohexane, with only σ bonds, does neither on this timescale. Reaction of benzene under forcing catalytic conditions is substitution, not evidence that benzene is ‘a typical alkene’. Cyclohexane’s inertness in both tests is the saturated-alkane pattern. Aromaticity is unique to benzene in this set.

distractorRationales.A: A typical alkene would decolourise Br2 in the dark, which benzene does not.
distractorRationales.B: Cyclohexane fails both tests; FeBr3 is the aromatic-substitution catalyst for benzene.
distractorRationales.C: Cyclohexane and cyclohexene are not aromatic; their Br2 behaviour differs sharply from benzene.

passage.title: Unacknowledged Method (1977)
passage.body: Naomi Kline's 1977 essay “Unacknowledged Method,” on urban cycling, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that local knowledge is treated as anecdote until a model needs it. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

proves consultation is always theater and should stop.

items.explanation: The colonial paragraph says cleaning into a style that makes objects readable as art in the receiving capital completes the seizure in a gentler font, especially without a right of refusal. Concert-hall equalization and a “world music” file are that readability. A denies the paragraph. C analogizes to a different editorial aesthetic without the colonial mechanism. D overreads the theater warning into abolition of consultation. Application should carry the seizure-and-readability principle, not a random conservation technique.

distractorRationales.A: The author treats technical rescue without restored refusal as completion of seizure, font or no font.
distractorRationales.C: Leaving a lacuna is an editorial honesty example, not the colonial-readability mechanism.
distractorRationales.D: Consultation may be theater and is still called a different verb from rescue; the author does not end it.

passage.title: The museum as a verb
passage.body:
Conservation used to mean stopping time. A painting was a patient; varnish was a bandage; the ideal was to return the object to a single authentic hour and then prevent further hours from occurring. That ideal had a hidden historiography. It assumed the authentic hour was already known, usually as the artist’s last brushstroke, and that later repairs, soot, liturgy, and even damage were noise.

A newer conservation talk prefers verbs. To museum an object is to keep choosing which traces will remain legible. Cleaning is not the removal of history; it is the promotion of one history over another. The nineteenth-century restorer who “completed” a medieval panel was not more ideological than the twenty-first-century restorer who leaves the lacuna as a paler mute. Both are editors. They differ in which audience they imagine and in how proudly they sign the edit.

Critics of reversible methods sometimes complain that visible fills and honest seams break the spell. They want the old miracle: an untouched past that happens to hang at eye level under LEDs. The complaint is aesthetically sincere and philosophically confused. The spell was always produced with scaffolding, attributions, and lighting. Reversibility is not a refusal of beauty. It is a refusal to trap the next generation inside today’s certainty about what the object “really” was.

There is a colonial edge. Objects that arrived by seizure were often cleaned into a style that made them readable as art in the receiving capital, which is to say, cleaned of the uses that had made them un-museumlike. To restore the pigment without restoring the right of refusal is to complete the seizure in a gentler font. Some institutions now consult source communities about smoke, wear, and whether an object should be seen at all. Consultation is slow and can be theater. It is still a different verb from rescue.

If this sounds like relativism, notice what it does not say. It does not say that all edits are equal, or that pigment chemistry is a matter of taste. It says that technical competence cannot supply the missing decision about which past is being kept available. The decision will be made. Calling it science does not make it less a decision. Calling it care does not either. The more honest museum is the one that can show its verbs.

items.stem: A lambda lysogen is exposed to UV doses that activate RecA. RecA stimulates autocleavage of the lambda cI repressor. The expected immediate outcome for the prophage is:

choices.text: Permanent silencing of all phage genes with no virion production, because cI cleavage locks lysogeny
Excision of the prophage and induction of the lytic cycle, producing progeny phage and usually lysing the host
Conversion of the phage genome into a prion that seeds in the cytoplasm without DNA replication
Immediate reverse transcription of lambda DNA into an RNA provirus that integrates at a new site

items.explanation: In lysogeny, cI repressor occupies operators and prevents lytic transcription while the prophage rides along in the bacterial chromosome. DNA damage activates RecA, which facilitates cI autocleavage, dropping repressor occupancy. Lytic genes including excisionases then fire, the prophage excises, and the phage replicates, packages, and lyses the cell. Cleavage of cI is the switch out of lysogeny, not a lock into it. Lambda is a dsDNA phage and does not reverse-transcribe, and induction is not prion conversion.

distractorRationales.A: cI cleavage removes repression; it does not deepen lysogeny.
distractorRationales.C: Prophage induction is a DNA recombination and transcription program, not a prion disease.
distractorRationales.D: Reverse transcription is a retrovirus strategy; lambda replicates as DNA.

passage.title: Who Counts (1976)
passage.body: Diego Ferreira published “Who Counts” in 1976 after a season in court translation. The argument is that a metric can become the mission that it was supposed to measure. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem:
The water–gas shift reaction CO(g) + H2O(g) ⇌ CO2(g) + H2(g) has Kc = 10.0 at 800 K, with Kc = ([CO2][H2]) / ([CO][H2O]). A 1.0 L vessel at 800 K is at equilibrium with the first row of the table. A pulse of extra CO2 then raises [CO2] instantly to the second-row value; the other three concentrations are unchanged at that instant.

Stage | [CO] | [H2O] | [CO2] | [H2]  (all mol L−1)
Equilibrium | 0.50 | 0.50 | 1.58 | 1.58
Immediately after adding CO2 | 0.50 | 0.50 | 3.16 | 1.58

What is Q after the pulse, and what net reaction restores equilibrium?

choices.text: Q remains 10.0, so adding a product cannot shift a system that is already at equilibrium.
Q = 5.0, less than Kc, so the forward reaction produces still more CO2 and H2.
Q = 20, greater than Kc, so the reverse reaction consumes CO2 and H2 and forms CO and H2O.
Q = 20, greater than Kc, so the forward reaction continues because Kc must rise to match the new Q.

items.explanation: The equilibrium row satisfies Kc: (1.58 × 1.58) / (0.50 × 0.50) = 2.496 / 0.25 ≈ 10.0. After the CO2 pulse, Q = (3.16 × 1.58) / 0.25 = 4.993 / 0.25 ≈ 20, which is greater than Kc. The reverse reaction therefore proceeds, consuming CO2 and H2. That is Le Chatelier’s response to adding a product. Kc is unchanged at 800 K; Q, not Kc, is what jumps when a concentration is suddenly altered.

distractorRationales.A: Adding CO2 changes the numerator of Q immediately. Q is then 20, not 10, so a net reverse reaction occurs.
distractorRationales.B: Q after the pulse is about 20, not 5. Q > Kc drives the reverse reaction, which consumes CO2 rather than producing more of it.
distractorRationales.D: Q is 20, but Kc does not chase Q. Temperature is still 800 K, so Kc stays 10 and the reverse reaction lowers Q back to 10.

items.stem: A seizure is staged over an intercom. Help is faster and more likely when the participant believes they are the only listener than when they believe four other students also hear the seizure. Which mechanism is the best explanation?

choices.text: Social facilitation of helping as a dominant well-learned response that should increase in a group
Bystander effect via diffusion of responsibility: more co-witnesses reduce each person’s sense of personal obligation
Deindividuation from wearing a mask, which was not part of the procedure
Normative peer pressure to match a helpful in-group, which predicts more helping when more peers are present

items.explanation: Darley and Latané’s seizure study is the textbook bystander effect: the presence of other witnesses lowers helping. The proposed mediator is diffusion of responsibility—each person feels less uniquely accountable when others could act. Facilitation would predict better performance of a dominant helping response in a group, which is the wrong direction. Deindividuation was not manipulated with anonymity costumes. A helpful peer-pressure account predicts the opposite of what the intercom design finds.

distractorRationales.A: Helping fell, not rose, as the believed audience of co-helpers grew, which is the opposite of facilitation of a dominant help response.
distractorRationales.C: No mask or anonymity costume is described; the variable is believed number of witnesses.
distractorRationales.D: Normative pressure to be helpful in a group would increase helping with more peers, not decrease it.

passage.title: Identity, Group Membership, and Academic Feedback
passage.body:
A developmental psychology research group examined how social identity salience affects interpretation of academic feedback. High school students completed a difficult reasoning task and then received standardized written feedback stating that their score was below the sample average. Before receiving feedback, students were randomly assigned to one of two writing prompts. In the personal-values condition, students wrote about an important personal value. In the group-comparison condition, students wrote about ways their school group was viewed by students from a nearby school. After feedback, students rated perceived threat, expected future performance, and willingness to attempt a similar task.

Mean post-feedback ratings on 1 to 7 scales
Condition | Perceived threat | Expected future performance | Willingness to attempt similar task
Personal-values prompt | 3.0 | 4.9 | 5.5
Group-comparison prompt | 4.8 | 3.8 | 4.1

Interpretive note — All participants received identical task instructions and identical feedback; only the pre-feedback writing prompt differed across conditions.

items.stem: A keto ester must have its ketone preserved while the ester is reduced to a primary alcohol with LiAlH4. Which protecting-group sequence succeeds, and why?

choices.text: Use 0.5 equivalent of LiAlH4; ketones always reduce more slowly than esters, so the ketone survives
Convert the ketone to a cyclic acetal with ethylene glycol and acid, reduce the ester with LiAlH4, then hydrolyze the acetal with aqueous acid
Use NaBH4 in methanol, because borohydride reduces esters rapidly and leaves ketones untouched
Form the acetal, then reduce with LiAlH4, which also cleaves acetals, simultaneously freeing the ketone as an alcohol

items.explanation: LiAlH4 reduces both ketones and esters, so an unprotected ketone would be destroyed. A cyclic acetal (1,3-dioxolane) is formed under acid catalysis from the ketone and ethylene glycol. Acetals are stable to hydride and to basic nucleophiles, so LiAlH4 then reduces only the ester to the alcohol. Mild aqueous acid hydrolyzes the acetal back to the ketone. NaBH4 actually shows the opposite chemoselectivity: it reduces ketones much faster than esters. Acetals are not cleaved by LiAlH4; that is why they are useful protecting groups.

distractorRationales.A: Ketones are generally more electrophilic than esters and are reduced at least as readily by LiAlH4. Half an equivalent will not spare the ketone.
distractorRationales.C: NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones, not ordinary esters. That reagent would destroy the ketone and leave the ester.
distractorRationales.D: Hydride does not hydrolyze acetals. Acidic water, not LiAlH4, is what restores the ketone after reduction.

distractorRationales.C: Ligase seals nicks; it doesn't excise mismatches.

items.stem: A lab presents a sudden loud noise while recording a startle blink and a continuous self-report dial of fear. Felt fear and the blink both begin within a few hundred milliseconds, and neither measure reliably precedes the other. Palmar skin-conductance change lags by one to two seconds. Which theory is most consistent with near-simultaneity of feeling and the fast motor sign, and with the slowness of the viscera?

choices.text: James–Lange theory, which requires that visceral change be perceived before any feeling can start
Opponent-process theory, which requires a delayed opposite emotion before fear is reported
Cannon–Bard theory, which holds that a central process triggers experience and bodily responses together, so slow viscera cannot be the source of the feeling
Schachter–Singer theory, which requires a waiting-room confederate to assign a label before feeling can start

items.explanation: Cannon argued that the viscera are too slow and too undifferentiated to be the origin of distinct, rapidly felt emotions. Cannon–Bard theory therefore places a central (thalamic) process that simultaneously generates the conscious feeling and the bodily pattern. Fast coincidence of reported fear and a motor sign, with skin conductance trailing, matches that architecture and undercuts a strictly visceral James–Lange sequence. Opponent-process theory is about a later opposite state, not latency of the first feeling. Two-factor theory is an arousal-plus-label account and does not require a confederate for every fear episode.

distractorRationales.A: A visceral-first James–Lange sequence is strained when feeling begins before, or without waiting for, the slow skin-conductance change.
distractorRationales.B: Opponent-process theory predicts a subsequent opposite feeling (for example, relief), not that fear itself must be delayed until an opposite appears.
distractorRationales.D: Schachter–Singer theory uses context to label unexplained arousal; it does not require a confederate before any fear can be felt in a startle paradigm.

items.stem: The p53 protein is often called the 'guardian of the genome.' In response to DNA damage, normal p53:

choices.text: Forces the damaged cell to divide immediately
Permanently silences all of the cell's genes
Halts the cell cycle to allow repair, or triggers apoptosis if the damage is severe

Dipole moments and boiling points of 1,2-dichloroethene isomers:

Isomer | μ (D) | bp (°C)

passage.title: On the new memorial
passage.body:
The memorial is a corridor of rusted uprights, each the height of a person, irregularly spaced so that you must turn sideways to pass. At noon they look like a failed fence. At dusk they look like a crowd that has agreed not to face you. There are no names. A small plaque at the exit says only: THEY WERE NOT LATE. THEY WERE PREVENTED.

Tourists complain that they do not know whom to pity. School groups count the uprights and get different numbers, because some are so close they read as one. A veteran interviewed on the steps said he hated it, then stood there until the lights came on, then said he hated that he did not hate it enough.

The sculptor, in a panel discussion, refused the word healing. “If it heals,” she said, “it has failed at being a door you cannot swagger through.” Critics split between those who call this moral bullying in Cor-Ten steel and those who call the tourists’ complaint the point.

I went through twice. The second time a child asked why the fence was broken. His father said it was not a fence. The child, satisfied with a new category, ran. I was not satisfied. Prevention is a bureaucratic word. In the corridor it becomes a body insisting on its width.

items.stem: Which of the following situations is most analogous to the author's contrast between receiving a text and recruiting it?

choices.text: A kitchen that only 'hosts' a visiting cook after rewriting every recipe until guests cannot tell the food was ever foreign, then advertises the guest's name as proof of cosmopolitan taste.

A publisher that refuses to print any translation, on the ground that all rendering is recruitment.
A teacher who requires students to look up every word in a bilingual dictionary before class, treating the dictionary as a moral test.

items.explanation: Receiving, in the passage, would leave a trace of the guest; recruiting makes the page a mirror with a foreign name attached, using prestige to ratify what the host already believed. The kitchen that erases every foreign mark and then sells the guest's name maps that structure: hospitality is advertised while the guest's difference is removed. Bilingual editions, a ban on translation, and dictionary-as-moral-test each invert or ignore a local claim (delay can be honest; translation remains necessary; dictionaries are not moral instruments). The analogy must preserve both the erasure and the prestige-borrowing, which only A does.

distractorRationales.B: The author values some delay as information; an edition designed to make delay impossible would be closer to the fluency ideal being criticized, not an analogue of receiving.
distractorRationales.C: The author refuses abandonment of translation and the calque museum alike; a ban would not model receiving.
distractorRationales.D: That teacher is the figure the closing paragraph tells us to stop being; it is an analogue of a rejected piety, not of receiving-versus-recruiting.

passage.title: The courtesy of untranslatability
passage.body:
Historians of language like to treat translation as a pipe: meaning enters one end, equivalent wording exits the other, and any turbulence is a defect in the plumber. The figure is flattering to publishers, who can then sell fluency as fidelity, and it is flattering to readers, who can then consume a foreign argument as if it had always been written in their kitchen. The figure is also false. A translation is not a transfer of a stable cargo. It is a series of decisions about which silences will remain audible and which will be paved over so that a page turns without snagging.

Consider the ordinary boast that a novel has been rendered into "perfectly natural" English. Natural for whom? The boast treats the target language as a climate rather than as a historically specific set of habits, class markers, and tolerated opacities. When a rural insult is recast as a metropolitan joke, or a liturgical cadence is recast as a magazine paragraph, the text has not been rescued from awkwardness. It has been enrolled in a local etiquette. The reader who thanks the translator for making the book "not feel translated" is thanking the translator for hiding the fact that hospitality occurred. Hospitality, if it is more than a smile, leaves a trace of the guest.

This is not an argument for wooden calques or for the museum of untranslated words left standing like exhibits. Those tactics can become their own piety, a performance of difficulty that congratulates the reader for enduring it. The more serious failure is the opposite one: the belief that a text which does not delay us has therefore been understood. Delay is sometimes the only honest report of a conceptual mismatch. A legal term that organizes a whole civic world cannot be swapped for a near-synonym without smuggling in the civic world of the synonym. To refuse the delay is to pretend that the two worlds already agreed.

Publishers will object that readers abandon books that snag. They are not wrong about the market. They are wrong to treat the market as a theory of meaning. A culture that will only receive what has already been made to sound like itself is not receiving; it is recruiting. The translated page then becomes a mirror with a foreign name on the title page, and the prestige of the foreign name is used to ratify what the reader already believed. That is why "accessible" can function as a political adjective. It names not a reading level but a refusal of conceptual immigration.

None of this requires contempt for the reader. It requires a different courtesy: the courtesy of letting a sentence remain slightly foreign so that the reader can notice the foreignness as information rather than as a stain. The translator's invisibility, long praised as professionalism, is in this light a kind of disappearance of evidence. We might instead want translators to be visibly responsible for their choices, not as celebrities, but as people who can be asked why a silence was kept or filled.

The practical consequence is modest and severe. Reviewers should stop treating smoothness as a synonym for accuracy. Teachers should stop treating a bilingual dictionary as a moral instrument. And readers who want to be hosts rather than consumers should learn to tolerate, even to prize, the small resistances that prove a text has not been entirely naturalized. What cannot be made to sound like us is often the part that most needed to travel.

passage.title: psg-cars-3
passage.body:
Few debates in literary theory have proved more durable than the question of authorial intent: does the meaning of a text reside primarily in what its author meant to communicate, or does meaning emerge through the activity of reading itself? At one extreme, the intentionalist holds that misreading is always possible — that interpretations diverging from the author's design are simply mistaken, however ingenious or culturally resonant they may be. At the other extreme, the anti-intentionalist insists that once a text is released into the world, the author's psychological states become strictly irrelevant: what the words mean is fixed not by biography but by the conventions of the language and genre in which they are embedded.
The anti-intentionalist position gained influential expression in mid-twentieth-century criticism, when theorists argued that treating the author's intention as the criterion of correct interpretation commits a category error. Evidence about what a poet hoped to achieve, they maintained, cannot settle what a poem achieves, because a poem is a verbal artifact that may realize meanings its creator did not foresee — meanings that become available only through the community of readers over time. The celebrated example of an ironic text serves as illustration: a writer may compose a scathing satire of nationalistic rhetoric while sincerely believing the rhetoric they are parodying; the satiric meaning is there in the text whether the author intended it or not.
Intentionalists counter that language is an intentional practice: utterances mean what speakers mean by them, and written language does not somehow escape this fundamental feature of linguistic communication. To read a text in complete disregard of what its author was trying to do, they argue, is to treat it as a natural object rather than a human creation — to decode it the way one might decode an accidental inkblot rather than a deliberate message. Moreover, intentionalists point out that appeals to 'the language and genre' still presuppose communicative conventions that are themselves constituted by the intentions of the linguistic community.
A mediating view distinguishes between actual authorial intention (the historical individual's specific psychological states) and what might be called the implied author: the authorial persona that a competent reader constructs from the textual evidence alone. On this account, interpretation aims neither at private biography nor at free-floating textual play but at the coherent communicative project that the text itself invites. The implied author is, in effect, the best hypothesis about what an ideally communicative author of this text would have intended — a construct that disciplines interpretation without requiring access to historical documents.
What unites all parties to this dispute is the recognition that texts are not transparent windows onto authors' minds or onto a language-independent reality. They are artifacts whose significance is never simply given but must always be construed — a fact that makes hermeneutics, the theory of interpretation, as much a practical as a philosophical discipline.

items.stem: Nascent RNA chains isolated from a rapidly growing bacterial culture are still hydrogen-bonded to the DNA template and are also bound to ribosomes. Which conclusion fits bacterial gene expression?

choices.text: A spliceosome must finish removing introns before any ribosome can bind bacterial mRNA.
Bacterial mRNA is fully capped and exported from a nucleus before translation begins.
Transcription and translation are spatially separated, so ribosomes cannot occupy an incomplete RNA.
Ribosomes can initiate on the 5′ end of a bacterial mRNA while RNA polymerase is still elongating the 3′ end.

items.explanation: Bacteria lack a nuclear envelope, and their primary transcripts generally lack spliceosomal introns and 5′ caps of the eukaryotic type. The experimental observation in the stem is therefore diagnostic of prokaryotic expression and is not explained by nuclear capping, spliceosome dependence, or spatial separation of the two processes.

items.stem: Relative rates of hydrolysis (neutral water, 25 °C) decrease in the order acetyl chloride ≫ acetic anhydride > ethyl acetate ≫ acetamide. Which analysis best explains that ranking?

choices.text: Better leaving groups and less n→π* donation into the carbonyl make the acyl carbon more electrophilic: Cl− > RCO2− > RO− > R2N−
Amides hydrolyze fastest because nitrogen is more electronegative than chlorine
Esters cannot undergo nucleophilic acyl substitution at all, so the ranking is an artifact
Acid chlorides are the least electrophilic because chlorine is a π donor as strong as NH2

items.explanation: Nucleophilic acyl substitution rate tracks two coupled effects. First, resonance donation from the heteroatom into the carbonyl (n→π*) is strongest for nitrogen, weaker for oxygen, and weakest for chlorine, so the acyl carbon of an amide is the least electrophilic. Second, the leaving group in the tetrahedral intermediate must depart: Cl− is an excellent leaving group, carboxylate is fair, alkoxide is poor, and amide anion is very poor. Those trends place acid chlorides at the top of the reactivity scale and amides at the bottom. Esters do hydrolyze, just more slowly than anhydrides and chlorides. Nitrogen is less electronegative than chlorine, not more.

distractorRationales.B: Nitrogen is less electronegative than chlorine and donates more strongly by resonance. Amides are the least, not most, reactive common carboxylic derivatives.
distractorRationales.C: Esters undergo nucleophilic acyl substitution (saponification, acid hydrolysis, transesterification); they are simply slower than anhydrides and acid chlorides.
distractorRationales.D: Chlorine is a weak resonance donor compared with NH2. Acid chlorides are the most, not least, electrophilic in this series.

passage.title: Aesthetics — why originals matter
passage.body:
Suppose a forger produces a copy of a painting so exact that no expert, however equipped, could tell it from the original. Most of us would still prefer to own the original, and would pay vastly more for it. This preference is easy to mock as mere snobbery — a fetish for provenance that adds nothing to what the eye receives. If two canvases are visually identical, the skeptic asks, how can one be aesthetically superior to the other? Whatever we are paying for, it cannot be the look of the thing.

The skeptic assumes that the value of a painting must reside entirely in its present visual surface. But this assumption is far from obvious. When I stand before a canvas that Rembrandt himself touched, I am in physical, causal contact with the very object his hand shaped. The forgery, however exquisite, offers no such contact; it is the terminus of a different causal chain, one that runs back not to Rembrandt but to a clever imitator in a rented studio. To value the original is to value that lineage, and there is nothing irrational about caring where a thing comes from.

An analogy makes the point. A letter in a beloved's handwriting is treasured over a flawless photocopy, though the copy conveys every word. We do not think the person who keeps the original has made a perceptual error, as though they had failed to notice that the words are the same. They are responding to something the photocopy lacks: a direct trace of the writer's presence. Paintings, on this view, are less like texts, whose value is exhausted by their content, and more like relics, whose value depends on their history.

Yet the analogy should not be pressed too far. Relics are valued almost wholly for contact and hardly at all for how they look; the point of a saint's bone is not its appearance. Great paintings are not like this. Their history matters, but so, undeniably, does what they show — the very composition and color the forger has reproduced. A defender of originals need not deny that appearance carries much of a painting's worth. The claim is only that appearance does not carry all of it, and that the remainder, however hard to name, is not nothing.

This more modest thesis is also the more defensible one. It grants the skeptic everything plausible in the skeptical position — that the visible work is most of what we prize — while denying the further, unargued step from "most" to "all." The forger's triumph, if it is one, is to have captured the larger share of a painting's value. It is not to have shown that the smaller share was an illusion all along.

passage.title: Official Adjectives (1973)
passage.body: Kwame Boateng published “Official Adjectives” in 1973 after a season in municipal archives. The argument is that expertise without a named audience is just private language. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: A point mutation in the Shine–Dalgarno sequence of a bacterial mRNA reduces complementarity to the 3′ end of 16S rRNA. Ribosome profiling shows fewer 30S subunits at the authentic AUG and increased use of a downstream AUG in a different frame. Which explanation is best?

choices.text: Bacteria use 5′-cap scanning as the default mechanism; the mutation merely shortens the 5′ UTR so the first AUG is skipped.
The Shine–Dalgarno sequence encodes N-formylmethionine; mutating it changes the initiator amino acid without affecting initiation frequency.

Base-pairing between the Shine–Dalgarno sequence and 16S rRNA positions the 30S subunit so that fMet-tRNA^fMet can bind the start codon in the P site; weaker pairing permits alternative AUG selection.
Elongation factor EF-G requires the Shine–Dalgarno sequence to translocate after every peptide bond, so elongation rather than initiation is primarily affected.

items.explanation: The 3′ end of 16S rRNA base-pairs with the Shine–Dalgarno motif in the 5′ UTR, docking the 30S subunit so that the start AUG occupies the P site for fMet-tRNA^fMet. Weakening that pairing reduces authentic initiation and allows 30S subunits to occupy other AUGs, including out-of-frame starts, matching the profiling result. Bacteria do not rely on eukaryotic 5′-cap scanning as the default. The Shine–Dalgarno sequence is a ribosome-binding RNA motif, not a codon for fMet. EF-G drives translocation during elongation and does not reread the initiation Shine–Dalgarno sequence at every codon.

distractorRationales.A: Cap-dependent scanning is eukaryotic; bacterial start-site selection is driven by 16S–Shine–Dalgarno pairing and initiator tRNA, not by 5′ cap recognition.

distractorRationales.D: The phenotype is altered start-codon occupancy by 30S subunits, an initiation defect, not an EF-G translocation requirement at each codon.

passage.title: psg-ps-3
passage.body:
Investigators examined how bodily arousal and its interpretation combine to produce emotion. In Study 1, 120 volunteers received an injection described as a vitamin; half actually received a mild dose of adrenaline (epinephrine), which raises heart rate and produces jitteriness, and half received saline. Within each group, some were accurately told to expect arousal symptoms and others were told nothing. Each participant then waited with a confederate who acted either euphoric or irritated. Aroused participants who had not been warned about the symptoms reported emotions matching the confederate's mood - euphoria or anger - more strongly than warned participants or saline controls. Participants who could attribute their arousal to the injection were less swayed by the confederate.
In Study 2, the same volunteers completed a stressful mental-arithmetic task while salivary cortisol was sampled. Cortisol rose within 20 minutes, peaked, and then declined once the task ended. Participants who appraised the task as a 'challenge' showed a smaller cortisol response than those who appraised it as a 'threat,' despite identical task difficulty. Reported stress correlated with threat appraisal, not with objective performance.
The authors linked Study 1 to a theory holding that emotion requires both physiological arousal and a cognitive label for that arousal, and linked Study 2 to a model in which the same stressor produces different physiological responses depending on how it is appraised. They noted that the cortisol time course mirrored the mobilize-then-recover pattern of the body's general response to stressors.

A fictional unicellular alga uses nuclear genes E and F to assemble functional mitochondrial Complex IV. Gene E encodes a copper-delivery chaperone, and gene F encodes a Complex IV structural subunit. Loss of either gene produces a slow-respiration phenotype, and loss of both genes is not more severe than loss of either single gene. The genes are autosomal and assort independently. Researchers crossed EEFF algae with eeff algae, selfed the EeFf F1, and measured F2 respiration phenotypes. Biochemical assays were performed on representative genotypes.

F2 respiration phenotypes after EeFf selfing.
Phenotype | Observed colonies
Normal respiration | 166
Slow respiration | 126

Respiratory measurements in representative strains.
Strain or condition | Complex I activity (%) | Complex IV activity (%) | O2 consumption (%) | NADH/NAD+ ratio | Growth on fermentable carbon
E_F_ | 100 | 100 | 100 | 0.5 | Robust
eeF_ | 95 | 18 | 22 | 3.2 | Slow but viable
E_ff | 100 | 20 | 25 | 3.0 | Slow but viable

items.stem: A polar, water-soluble alkaloid has a boiling point of 255 °C at 1 atm and begins to polymerize above 190 °C. It is contaminated only with nonvolatile inorganic salts. Which purification method is most appropriate?

Steam distillation, because every high-boiling organic is carried over with water near 100 °C
Vacuum distillation, because lowering the external pressure lowers the boiling temperature below the decomposition threshold

items.explanation: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the applied pressure. Reducing the pressure therefore lowers the boiling temperature (Clausius–Clapeyron), so the alkaloid can distill below 190 °C and avoid polymerization. Atmospheric simple or fractional distillation still requires the flask to reach 255 °C. Steam distillation relies on two immiscible liquids each contributing vapor pressure; a water-soluble polar alkaloid does not form that two-phase system, so steam is the wrong tool here. The nonvolatile salts remain in the pot under reduced pressure as well.

distractorRationales.A: Atmospheric simple distillation still boils the compound at 255 °C, well above the 190 °C decomposition onset.
distractorRationales.B: A fractionating column improves separation of close-boiling volatiles; it does not lower the boiling temperature of a single compound at 1 atm.

passage.title: psg-bb-1
passage.body:
Researchers characterized a bacterial hydrolase, EnzA, that cleaves a colorless substrate into a yellow product, allowing the initial reaction velocity to be measured by absorbance. Working at constant enzyme concentration, saturating buffer, and 37 deg C, they varied the substrate concentration [S] and recorded the initial velocity (v0). As [S] increased, v0 rose steeply at first and then leveled off, tracing the hyperbolic curve expected for a single-active-site enzyme. From these data the team estimated a maximum velocity (Vmax) of 100 micromol/min and a Michaelis constant (Km) of 2.0 mM, where Km is the [S] at which v0 equals half of Vmax.
The team then repeated the assay in the presence of two candidate drugs. With a fixed concentration of Inhibitor A, the measured Vmax remained 100 micromol/min, but the apparent Km rose to 6.0 mM; adding excess substrate fully restored the maximal rate. With a fixed concentration of Inhibitor B, the apparent Km stayed at 2.0 mM, but Vmax fell to 50 micromol/min, and no amount of added substrate recovered the original maximal rate.
A double-reciprocal (Lineweaver-Burk) plot summarized the results: the control line and the Inhibitor A line shared the same y-intercept but differed in slope, whereas the control line and the Inhibitor B line shared the same x-intercept but differed in y-intercept. The researchers concluded that the two inhibitors act by distinct mechanisms, a distinction that matters clinically because it determines whether raising the physiological substrate concentration can overcome the drug's effect.

items.stem: A student-athlete bombs a chemistry quiz in the locker room and later bricks a free throw during lecture. In a twenty-statements task, self-description after the quiz emphasizes “athlete”; after the miss it emphasizes “pre-med.” Which identity claim does this pattern best support?

choices.text: People have only one self-concept, so the shift must be a scoring error
This is demographic transition of the self from stage 2 to stage 4
Looking-glass self requires a one-way mirror, which was not present, so identity cannot change
People hold multiple social identities whose salience shifts with context, sometimes protecting self-concept after a threat to one identity

items.explanation: Self-concept is a working collection of identities (student, athlete, friend) rather than a single static list. Self-categorization and social-identity approaches predict that the identity made salient will track cues and motives, including the motive to downplay a just-threatened identity and foreground an intact one. That is compatible with the quiz-then-athlete and miss-then-pre-med switch. It is not a population fertility model, not dependent on laboratory mirrors, and not evidence that only one identity exists.

distractorRationales.A: The twenty-statements shift is evidence for multiple, context-weighted identities, not for a single frozen list.
distractorRationales.B: Demographic transition refers to national birth and death rates, not to which identity is listed first.
distractorRationales.C: Reflected appraisals can occur without a piece of glass; the stem is about identity salience, not about mirrors.

items.stem: Penicillin’s antibacterial activity depends on acylation of a serine in bacterial D-alanine transpeptidase. Ordinary unstrained amides do not acylate that serine at a useful rate. Which property of the β-lactam is most responsible?

choices.text: The β-lactam is actually an ester, and esters always outrun amides in nucleophilic acyl substitution
The four-membered ring is aromatic (4n+2), so it behaves like an acid chloride
The lactam nitrogen is so basic that it deprotonates serine before any acyl transfer
Ring strain and reduced amide resonance (the nitrogen cannot be fully coplanar with the carbonyl) make the lactam carbonyl unusually electrophilic

items.explanation: A normal amide is unreactive because the nitrogen lone pair conjugates with the carbonyl, lowering electrophilicity and making R2N− a terrible leaving group. In a fused β-lactam the four-membered ring prevents that geometry: the N–C(O) system cannot be fully planar, resonance is diminished, and opening the ring relieves angle strain. The serine hydroxyl can therefore perform nucleophilic acyl substitution, covalently inactivating the transpeptidase. The functional group remains an amide, not an ester; it is not aromatic (4 π electrons would be 4n, anti-aromatic if planar); and the chemistry is acyl transfer, not a preliminary deprotonation of serine by the lactam nitrogen as a base.

distractorRationales.A: Penicillin’s reactive carbonyl is a cyclic amide (β-lactam), not an ester. Strain, not a change of functional-group class to ester, is the key.
distractorRationales.B: Hückel aromaticity requires 4n+2 π electrons in a planar conjugated loop. A saturated β-lactam is not an aromatic ring.
distractorRationales.C: Amide nitrogens are poor bases (the lone pair is tied up, even if less so in a β-lactam). The lethal step is acylation of serine, not acid–base deprotonation.

passage.title: Electrodialysis Removal of Lactate
passage.body:
A fictional electrodialysis device removes lactate from a small waste stream. Lactic acid has pKa = 3.9, and lactate carries a -1 charge. The feed chamber initially contains 100 mL of 0.100 mM total lactate species. An anion-exchange membrane separates the feed chamber from a collection chamber near the positive anode. Each run lasts 300 s. Current can be carried by lactate and by other ions in the buffer. Joule heating may broaden concentration gradients and reduce separation efficiency.

Electrodialysis conditions and lactate removal.
Run | Feed pH | Voltage (V) | Current (mA) | Temperature rise (C) | Salt condition | Total lactate removed from feed (%)
1 | 3.0 | 20 | 2.0 | 0.2 | low salt | 8
2 | 7.0 | 20 | 10.0 | 1.0 | low salt | 45
3 | 7.0 | 40 | 20.0 | 4.5 | low salt | 70
4 | 7.0 | 40 | 20.0 | 1.0 with cooling | low salt | 78
5 | 7.0 | 20 | 25.0 | 5.0 | high salt | 30

Electrodialysis chamber arrangement. — Negatively charged lactate migrates through an anion-exchange membrane toward the positive anode. Neutral lactic acid is much less efficiently transported by the electric field.

passage.title: Stress Appraisal and Working Memory During Social Evaluation
passage.body:
Researchers studied how appraisal framing affects stress responses during a brief social-evaluation task. Ninety-six adults were randomly assigned to one of three groups. In the private-reading group, participants read a neutral passage alone. In the evaluative-threat group, participants gave a short speech while being observed and were told that poor performance would indicate weak communication ability. In the evaluative-challenge group, participants gave the same speech while being observed but were told that increased arousal could help them perform effectively. Participants completed a working-memory task afterward and provided saliva samples before and after the task.

Mean outcomes by task condition
Condition | Perceived control, 1 to 7 | Heart rate increase, beats/min | Salivary cortisol increase, nmol/L | Working-memory accuracy (%)
Private reading | 5.8 | 4 | 0.7 | 86
Evaluative threat | 2.7 | 18 | 4.6 | 71
Evaluative challenge | 4.9 | 16 | 2.6 | 79

Appraisal framing — The evaluative-threat and evaluative-challenge groups completed the same speech task; only the framing statement before the task differed.

items.stem: In the intrinsic apoptotic pathway, mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization allows a heme protein of the intermembrane space to enter the cytosol, where it helps assemble the apoptosome with Apaf-1 and procaspase-9. Which protein is released, and where does it normally function in respiration?

The F1 domain of ATP synthase, which normally synthesizes ATP in the cytosol
Ubiquinone, a peripheral protein of the outer membrane that donates electrons to oxygen
Cytochrome c, which normally shuttles electrons from Complex III to Complex IV

items.explanation: Cytochrome c is a small soluble heme protein in the intermembrane space. In healthy mitochondria it carries electrons from the cytochrome bc1 complex (Complex III) to cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV). After Bax/Bak-dependent outer-membrane permeabilization, cytosolic cytochrome c binds Apaf-1, enabling apoptosome assembly and caspase-9 activation. Complex I subunits are integral/matrix-facing and reduce ubiquinone from NADH rather than reduce NAD+. ATP is made in the matrix by inner-membrane ATP synthase, not by cytosolic F1. Ubiquinone is a lipid-soluble inner-membrane carrier, not an outer-membrane protein that reduces oxygen.

distractorRationales.A: Complex I oxidizes NADH and is not the IMS heme protein that nucleates the apoptosome. It also reduces Q, rather than reducing NAD+.
distractorRationales.B: ATP synthase is inner-membrane/matrix-facing; F1 does not synthesize ATP in the cytosol, and it is not the canonical apoptosome trigger.
distractorRationales.C: Ubiquinone is a hydrophobic inner-membrane pool, not a peripheral outer-membrane protein, and it does not reduce O2 (Complex IV does).

Osmolality (mOsm kg−1) along a long-looped nephron with and without ADH:

Site | with ADH | without ADH
Bowman’s capsule | 300 | 300
Hairpin of loop | 1200 | 1200
Early distal tubule | 100 | 100
Final urine | 1200 | 100

The thick ascending limb actively exports NaCl and is impermeable to water. Which statement follows?

choices.text: Without ADH the loop cannot concentrate the hairpin, because the table would then show 300 at the hairpin
ADH is required to dilute the early distal fluid to 100 mOsm kg−1
Final urine is always 1200 mOsm kg−1 in a long-looped nephron
The loop still generates a medullary gradient without ADH, but only ADH makes the collecting duct water-permeable so urine can equilibrate to 1200 mOsm kg−1

items.explanation: The hairpin is 1200 in both columns, so countercurrent multiplication does not require ADH. Early distal fluid is 100 in both columns, the signature of salt extraction without water in the ascending limb (diluting segment). The columns diverge only at the collecting duct: with ADH, water follows the medullary gradient to 1200; without ADH the duct stays impermeable and urine remains as dilute as the distal load (100). Therefore ADH gates water permeability of the collecting duct, not loop function or distal dilution.

distractorRationales.A: The hairpin is 1200 with and without ADH, so the gradient is intact.
distractorRationales.B: Early distal osmolality is already 100 in the no-ADH column, so dilution is ADH-independent.
distractorRationales.C: The no-ADH urine is 100 mOsm kg−1, so long loops do not force concentrated urine without ADH.

items.stem: A simple pendulum has length 1.0 m. Take g = 10 m s−2 so T = 2π √(L/g) = 2π √0.10. √0.10 ≈ 0.32, hence T ≈ 2.0 s. The same pendulum is taken to a planet where g' = 2.5 m s−2, and a second pendulum of length 4.0 m is left on Earth. Which period pairing is correct?

choices.text: Both remain 2.0 s, because a pendulum’s period is a universal constant
Planet: about 4.0 s; 4.0 m Earth pendulum: about 4.0 s
Planet: about 1.0 s; 4.0 m Earth pendulum: about 1.0 s
Planet: about 4.0 s; 4.0 m Earth pendulum: about 2.0 s

items.explanation: T scales as √(L/g). Reducing g from 10 to 2.5 is a factor of 1/4, so √(1/g) grows by 2 and T doubles to ~4.0 s. Lengthening L from 1.0 to 4.0 m at fixed g also multiplies T by 2, giving ~4.0 s. The two changes are therefore equivalent. If T scaled as g or as 1/L, the planet pendulum would be faster. The 4.0 m Earth pendulum is not still 2.0 s. Period is not a universal constant independent of L and g; that is why pendulums measure g.

distractorRationales.A: T = 2π√(L/g) depends on both length and gravity; neither change can be ignored.
distractorRationales.C: Weaker gravity lengthens, not shortens, T; a longer pendulum is also slower, not faster.
distractorRationales.D: The planet value is right, but √4 = 2 so the 4.0 m Earth pendulum is ~4.0 s, not ~2.0 s.

passage.title: psg-ps-8
passage.body:
A study tested how awareness of a negative stereotype affects performance and self-presentation. Two groups of equally qualified students took the same difficult verbal test. In the 'diagnostic' condition, the test was described as measuring underlying ability; in the 'nondiagnostic' condition, it was described as a problem-solving exercise unrelated to ability. Students from a group stereotyped as weaker in the domain scored lower than others in the diagnostic condition but scored equally in the nondiagnostic condition. Merely asking students to record their group membership before a diagnostic test reproduced the gap.
In a second study, participants prepared for a mock interview. Told the interviewer valued modesty, they described themselves cautiously; told the interviewer admired confidence, the same participants emphasized their strengths. Observers who saw only one version rated the participants accordingly, and participants reported deliberately tailoring the impression they gave.
The authors interpreted the first study as evidence that the fear of confirming a negative group stereotype can itself depress performance, independent of ability, and that subtle cues activate this fear. They interpreted the second as an example of managing the impression one presents to different audiences, comparing it to an actor shifting performances between a front region and a back region. They cautioned that persistent performance gaps in real settings may partly reflect such situational threats and unequal conditions rather than fixed differences in ability between groups.

The 9:3:3:1 ratio is an F2 dihybrid ratio, and 3:1 is a monohybrid F2 ratio, neither of which applies to this testcross. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. passage.title: psg-bb-4
passage.body:
In a classic-style linkage experiment, geneticists studied two genes in a fruit fly stock: one affecting body color (B = gray, dominant; b = black) and one affecting wing shape (V = normal, dominant; v = vestigial). The two genes reside on the same chromosome. Females heterozygous for both genes, with both dominant alleles on one homolog and both recessive alleles on the other (arrangement B V / b v), were testcrossed to males that were homozygous recessive (b v / b v). Because the testcross father contributes only b and v alleles, each offspring's phenotype directly reveals which allele combination it received from the mother.
Among 1,000 offspring, the researchers counted four phenotypic classes: 425 gray, normal-winged; 415 black, vestigial-winged; 82 gray, vestigial-winged; and 78 black, normal-winged. The first two classes matched the parental (non-recombinant) allele combinations, whereas the last two classes represented new combinations that could only arise if the maternal homologs exchanged segments.
The team used the frequency of these new-combination offspring to estimate how far apart the two genes lie, applying the rule that one map unit (centimorgan) corresponds to a 1 percent recombination frequency. They noted that if the two genes had been on different chromosomes, or extremely far apart on the same one, the four classes would instead have appeared in roughly equal numbers.

passage.title: psg-ps-4
passage.body:
A team studied what sustains effort on a task. Ninety children who already enjoyed drawing were randomly assigned to three groups. The 'expected-reward' group was promised a certificate for drawing; the 'unexpected-reward' group drew and then received the same certificate as a surprise; the 'no-reward' group simply drew. Two weeks later, during free-play periods, observers unobtrusively recorded how much each child chose to draw. Children in the expected-reward group spent about half as much free time drawing as the other two groups, whose behavior did not differ.
In a second study with adults, participants worked on solvable puzzles under one of two framings. Some were told the task measured 'innate intelligence'; others were told that effort and strategy drive success. After encountering difficult items, the 'effort' group persisted longer and reported greater interest, and this difference was largest among participants who scored high on a measure of conscientiousness.
The researchers interpreted the children's result as evidence that offering an expected tangible reward for an already-enjoyable activity can reduce later voluntary engagement, because the behavior becomes attributed to the external incentive. They connected the adult result to a framework distinguishing motivation that arises from within the person from motivation driven by external consequences, and noted that a stable personality dimension moderated persistence. They cautioned that rewards are not universally harmful: unexpected rewards, and rewards for dull tasks, did not undermine engagement.

passage.title: Multisensory Influences on Beverage Perception
passage.body:
A behavioral neuroscience lab examined whether ambient odors influence taste judgments. Seventy-two adults sampled the same unsweetened citrus beverage in three counterbalanced conditions: no ambient scent, a congruent lemon scent, and an incongruent coffee scent. Participants were not told that the scent condition changed across trials. After each sample, they rated perceived sweetness, perceived sourness, and purchase intention on 1 to 7 scales. In a separate adaptation task, participants detected faint lemon odors before and after continuous exposure to a moderate lemon scent for 3 minutes.

Mean ratings for identical beverage across ambient scent conditions
Condition | Perceived sweetness | Perceived sourness | Purchase intention
No ambient scent | 3.1 | 4.8 | 3.2
Congruent lemon scent | 4.2 | 4.5 | 4.5
Incongruent coffee scent | 2.7 | 5.0 | 2.8

Odor detection threshold in arbitrary concentration units
Time point | Mean lemon odor detection threshold
Before continuous odor exposure | 2.0
Immediately after 3 minutes of exposure | 6.0
Ten minutes after exposure ended | 3.0

Study design — Each participant experienced all beverage scent conditions in randomized order. The adaptation task was completed after the beverage ratings and used a detection threshold procedure for lemon odor.

passage.title: psg-bb-7
passage.body:
Microbiologists grew a pure culture of a rod-shaped bacterium in a closed flask of nutrient broth held at 37 deg C and tracked population size by measuring turbidity (optical density) over time. The resulting growth curve had four phases. During an initial lag phase, cell number changed little as the cells synthesized enzymes and adjusted to the medium. This was followed by an exponential (log) phase, during which the population doubled at a constant interval; the team measured a doubling time of 20 minutes. Growth then slowed into a stationary phase, in which the number of new cells produced roughly equaled the number dying, as nutrients ran low and wastes accumulated. Finally, in the death phase, viable counts declined.
To test antibiotics, the researchers exposed separate exponential-phase cultures to two drugs. Penicillin, which blocks the cross-linking step in synthesis of the peptidoglycan cell wall, killed rapidly growing cells but had little effect on cells that were not actively dividing. A second drug bound the bacterial ribosome and halted protein synthesis, stopping growth without immediately lysing the cells.
The team highlighted features that distinguish these prokaryotes from the animal cells in a companion culture: the bacteria lacked a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, divided asexually by binary fission rather than mitosis, and could acquire new genes horizontally, for example by taking up plasmids during conjugation. These traits shape both how the population grows and how drugs can target the bacteria selectively.

passage.title: On the new memorial
passage.body:
The memorial is a corridor of rusted uprights, each the height of a person, irregularly spaced so that you must turn sideways to pass. At noon they look like a failed fence. At dusk they look like a crowd that has agreed not to face you. There are no names. A small plaque at the exit says only: THEY WERE NOT LATE. THEY WERE PREVENTED.

Tourists complain that they do not know whom to pity. School groups count the uprights and get different numbers, because some are so close they read as one. A veteran interviewed on the steps said he hated it, then stood there until the lights came on, then said he hated that he did not hate it enough.

The sculptor, in a panel discussion, refused the word healing. “If it heals,” she said, “it has failed at being a door you cannot swagger through.” Critics split between those who call this moral bullying in Cor-Ten steel and those who call the tourists’ complaint the point.

I went through twice. The second time a child asked why the fence was broken. His father said it was not a fence. The child, satisfied with a new category, ran. I was not satisfied. Prevention is a bureaucratic word. In the corridor it becomes a body insisting on its width.

items.stem: Which evaluation of Letter B's reasoning is most accurate?

choices.text: It is airtight, because any policy that mentions graduates' duties is by definition a sermon rather than an argument.
It usefully relocates staffing failure from character to conditions, but it overreaches if it treats a bond and liveable postings as mutually exclusive rather than as possibly joint instruments.
It has no empirical suggestions at all, because housing and isolation are not conditions.
It secretly agrees with Letter A that towns are a lifestyle choice doctors may decline.

items.explanation: B's strongest move is the misdiagnosis claim: empty clinics share causes with other missing staff, so a character story about the young is a convenient error. “Coercion is cheaper than housing” names a political incentive. The reasoning thins where a bond is identified with hostage-taking as such, as if furnishing rooms and some recoupment could not be combined. False dichotomy is the gap; it is not the case that B offers no conditions, nor that B accepts A's lifestyle-choice line. Evaluating strength means keeping the good causal relocation and naming the overreach.

distractorRationales.A: Calling all duty-language a sermon is itself a dismissal, not an evaluation of B's actual causal claims.
distractorRationales.C: Housing costs, school deserts, isolation, and locum markets are empirical-type conditions B explicitly lists.
distractorRationales.D: B rejects parking a resentful beginner as justice; it does not adopt A's claim that towns are a sport one may decline.

passage.title: Return-of-service bond: two letters
passage.body:
Two letters appeared in the same metropolitan daily after the health minister proposed a "return-of-service" bond: new doctors whose training was publicly subsidised would owe three years in designated underserved clinics before they could take an unrestricted urban post.

Letter A
A public scholarship is not a gift ribbon. It is a wager the public makes on a scarce skill. If the graduate then sells that skill immediately to the densest private market, the wager has been privatised without a receipt. Three years is not indenture; it is the time in which a clinic learns a name and a name learns a clinic. Those who call the bond a "mobility tax" speak as if mobility were a natural right unpolluted by the taxes that built the teaching hospitals. Rights that forget their invoices are just appetites with better stationery. Underserved towns are not a lifestyle choice the profession may decline, like a sport. They are the other half of the ledger.

Letter B
The minister has misdiagnosed a staffing failure as a character failure in the young. Clinics are empty of doctors for the same reasons they are empty of radiographers and nurses: housing costs, school deserts, professional isolation, and locum markets that pay more for a weekend than a bonded year pays for a winter. A bond does not staff a town; it parks a resentful beginner there and calls the parking "justice." Meanwhile the budget that should have made the posting liveable is spared the embarrassment of being seen. Coercion is cheaper than housing. If the public wants doctors in those rooms, it should furnish the rooms, not hostage the people it trained. A ledger that counts only the graduate's debt, and never the state's, is not a ledger. It is a sermon.

Editor's note: Letter A was signed by a retired regional physician; Letter B by a recent graduate now in a metropolitan hospital.

passage.title: psg-cp-11
passage.body: The following six questions are discrete and passage-independent: each stands alone and is not based on a shared passage, mirroring the freestanding question groups that appear between passages on the MCAT Chemical and Physical Foundations of Biological Systems section. Each question tests a single core physics principle - statics and torque, buoyancy, electrostatics, sound intensity, periodic atomic properties, or momentum conservation - and should be answered from fundamental principles rather than any preceding text. Constants are stated where needed; take g = 10 m/s^2.

items.stem: A five-year-old watches juice poured from a short wide beaker into a tall thin cylinder and insists there is now “more to drink.” Piaget’s stage account attributes the error to which limitation of the preoperational period?

choices.text: Centration and irreversibility, so height is attended and the transformation cannot be mentally reversed
Failure of object permanence, as in the sensorimotor A-not-B error
Lack of hypothetical-deductive reasoning that defines the formal operational stage
An already-intact conservation operation that the child simply refuses to verbalize

items.explanation: Conservation of liquid is a concrete-operational achievement (about 7–11 years). Preoperational children (about 2–7) fail it because they center on a salient dimension (height) and cannot reverse the pour in thought. Object permanence is a sensorimotor issue in infants, not this liquid task. Formal operations concern abstract hypothesis testing in adolescence, not beaker conservation. The child’s explicit “more” is a genuine conservation failure, not a hidden competence they decline to state.

distractorRationales.B: Object permanence is a sensorimotor milestone; this is a conservation failure years later.
distractorRationales.C: Formal operations are not required for liquid conservation; concrete operations suffice.
distractorRationales.D: Piaget treats the typical five-year-old’s judgment as a real operational gap, not mere tacit knowledge.

passage.title: Alternative splicing and protein dimerization of LUM1
passage.body:
A fictional eukaryotic gene, LUM1, contains four exons. Exon 3 encodes a hydrophobic alpha-helical segment required for stable LUM1 dimer formation. A regulatory RNA-binding protein, RBP-K, binds an intronic splicing enhancer near exon 3 and promotes exon 3 inclusion. Skipping exon 3 preserves the reading frame but produces a mostly monomeric protein that is degraded more rapidly. A separate mutation in the 5' splice donor of intron 2 causes intron retention and introduces a premature termination codon more than 50 nucleotides upstream of the final exon-exon junction.

Effects of LUM1 expression constructs in cultured cells.
Condition | Pre-mRNA transcription rate (%) | Mature mRNA containing exon 3 (%) | Total mature LUM1 mRNA (%) | LUM1 protein (%) | Dimeric LUM1 among detected protein (%)
Wild type | 100 | 85 | 100 | 100 | 80
RBP-K knockdown | 98 | 20 | 55 | 25 | 18
Exon 3 splice acceptor weakened | 95 | 10 | 50 | 20 | 12
Intron 2 splice donor mutant | 100 | 5 | 18 | 6 | 8
Kozak sequence mutant | 100 | 82 | 95 | 22 | 78
Exon 3 hydrophobic-to-charged coding mutant | 100 | 84 | 98 | 45 | 20

Model for LUM1 isoform production. — When exon 3 is included, LUM1 contains a hydrophobic helical segment that supports dimerization. When exon 3 is skipped, the reading frame remains intact but the helical dimerization segment is absent. Intron 2 retention creates a premature stop codon predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.

items.stem: A sleep-lab montage 12 minutes after lights-out shows 12–14 Hz bursts, occasional high-amplitude biphasic waves, mixed-frequency EEG, moderate EMG, and no rapid eye movements. Which stage of non-REM sleep, in the standard Rechtschaffen–Kales / AASM mapping, is this?

choices.text: N1, defined by vertex waves and a purely theta background without spindles
N3 slow-wave sleep, defined by high-voltage delta occupying much of the epoch
N2, defined by sleep spindles and K-complexes
REM sleep, defined by low EMG, sawtooth EEG, and bursts of rapid eye movements

items.explanation: Sleep spindles (about 12–14 Hz) and K-complexes are the defining graphoelements of N2 (formerly stage 2). N1 is light theta without those markers. N3 requires abundant delta. REM requires atonia, a wake-like low-voltage EEG, and REMs—the opposite of moderate EMG and no eye movements. Aserinsky and Kleitman described REM as a distinct state; this epoch is still non-REM N2, the stage that occupies much of a typical night after sleep onset.

distractorRationales.A: N1 lacks the spindles and K-complexes listed in the montage.
distractorRationales.B: N3 is scored on delta percentage, not on spindles as the main features.
distractorRationales.D: REM requires eye movements and atonia, both absent here.

passage.title: psg-ps-9
passage.body:
Sociologists analyzed how a chronic illness is understood and managed in a mid-sized city. Using surveys and interviews, they documented three patterns. First, physicians and hospitals coordinated with schools and workplaces so that ill members could be temporarily excused from normal duties while being expected to seek treatment and cooperate with doctors. Second, patients with more education and income obtained diagnoses and specialist care far faster than poorer patients, who often relied on crowded clinics; the researchers traced this to differences in insurance, flexible work hours, and familiarity with medical institutions. Third, behaviors once seen as ordinary or as moral failings - such as persistent sadness or restlessness - were increasingly defined and treated as medical conditions.
The team framed each pattern with a different theoretical lens. The coordinated excusing of the sick was described as an institution maintaining social stability by managing how illness disrupts roles. The unequal access was described in terms of groups with different amounts of resources and power competing for a scarce good. The redefinition of ordinary behaviors as illnesses was described as a process by which the meaning of 'sickness' is negotiated and expanded within a society. In interviews, patients described how a formal diagnosis changed how others treated them, sometimes granting sympathy and sometimes attaching stigma. The authors noted that the fastest-growing diagnoses clustered among specific age groups, and that the city's aging population was projected to raise overall demand for chronic-disease care over the coming decades.

passage.title: Neutral Style (1978)
passage.body: In “Neutral Style” (1978), Leo Nyathi writes from inside museum captions. The argument is that fairness talk often arrives after the decision has already been made. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: psg-ps-10
passage.body:
A longitudinal study followed 8,000 adults for 15 years to examine links between social position and health. Participants were grouped by socioeconomic status (SES), a composite of income, education, and occupational prestige. Age-adjusted rates of chronic illness and mortality declined steadily at each higher step of the SES ladder - not merely a gap between rich and poor, but a graded relationship across the whole range. The pattern held after controlling for smoking and diet, and was partly explained by chronic stress, worse neighborhood conditions, and unequal access to preventive care.
Participants were also classified by the neighborhood where they lived. Lower-SES families were concentrated in areas with fewer clinics, more pollution, and less green space; researchers described these areas as products of long-standing residential segregation. Children raised in the lowest-SES neighborhoods were less likely to reach a higher SES than their parents, a pattern the authors linked to unequal schools and social networks.
Finally, the study noted a demographic shift: as the population aged and birth rates fell, the ratio of working-age adults to dependents changed, straining programs that fund elder care. The authors argued that health follows a social gradient, that place and inequality shape opportunity across generations, and that population structure interacts with these inequalities to shape a society's future needs. They emphasized that individual choices operated within, and were constrained by, these structural conditions.

items.stem: Two patients with the same diabetes regimen and similar household income differ in neighborhood. Patient N lives where street lighting is poor and violent crime after dark is high; accelerometer counts are low and HbA1c is higher. Patient S lives on well-lit streets with active night sports fields and has the reverse pattern. Which spatial-inequality claim is best?

choices.text: Only genetics can explain the HbA1c gap, because both patients have the same prescription
Neighborhood safety is a spatial constraint on health behavior and can therefore shape clinical outcomes
Social facilitation by potential offenders improves exercise, so N should have been more active
The difference is a looking-glass-self illusion with no behavioral pathway

items.explanation: Neighborhood safety is a standard spatial-inequality topic because the local risk of violence and the quality of public space constrain whether people walk, play, or travel for care. If two similar patients differ in those exposures, activity and a behavior-sensitive marker such as HbA1c can diverge without any change in the written regimen. Genetics-only and “illusion” accounts ignore the measured activity gap. An audience of potential offenders is not a social-facilitation helper that improves a well-learned exercise skill.

distractorRationales.A: A matched prescription does not cancel differences in whether the neighborhood makes activity feasible.
distractorRationales.C: Fear of crime reduces, rather than facilitates, outdoor activity in this design.

items.stem: A clean lesion of the ventral root of a spinal nerve, with the dorsal root left intact, most directly:

choices.text: blocks motor outflow in the corresponding myotome while sparing sensory inflow through that spinal level
blocks sensory inflow from the dermatome while sparing motor outflow
severs the dorsal-column nuclei in the medulla
destroys the contralateral primary motor cortex

items.explanation: Ventral roots carry efferent axons (somatic motor and some autonomic) out of the cord. Dorsal roots carry afferents in. Cutting only the ventral root therefore weakens or paralyzes the myotome while leaving sensation from the dorsal root intact (a pattern historically associated with ventral-root lesions). The lesion is peripheral to the cord and does not ablate medullary nuclei or cerebral cortex.

distractorRationales.B: This describes a dorsal-root lesion, the opposite root.
distractorRationales.C: Dorsal-column nuclei (gracile and cuneate) sit in the caudal medulla, not in a spinal ventral root.
distractorRationales.D: Motor cortex is intracranial. A spinal ventral root is a lower-motor-neuron outflow, not a cortical lesion.

passage.title: Two short poems: Ferry
passage.body:
Poem 1 — “Ticket”
I bought a ticket to the other bank
as if the river were a problem in change.
The ferryman took coins that had known other pockets.
He did not ask what I was leaving.
The water did, in small repeated questions
against the hull.

Poem 2 — “Return”
On the way back the same boat
was a different animal.
I recognised the coins by their edges
and not the faces.
Someone on the far jetty waved
at a person I had not yet become
and I, traitor, waved.

passage.title: Regulation of a bacterial nucleotide-reduction operon
passage.body:
A fictional bacterial operon, nrdPQ, encodes proteins required for deoxyribonucleotide synthesis during low-oxygen growth. The operon contains a sigma-factor promoter, a 5' untranslated region with a metabolite M-sensitive attenuator, and a Shine-Dalgarno sequence upstream of the nrdP start codon. When metabolite M binds the nascent 5' untranslated region, a terminator hairpin forms before the coding sequence, reducing production of full-length mRNA. Researchers constructed mutations and measured full-length nrdP mRNA, NrdP protein, and NrdP enzyme activity.

Expression and activity of nrdP constructs.
Construct and condition | Full-length mRNA (%) | NrdP protein (%) | NrdP activity (%)
Wild type, no M | 100 | 100 | 100
Wild type, +M | 30 | 28 | 30
-10 promoter mutant, no M | 12 | 10 | 11
Terminator hairpin disrupted, +M | 95 | 92 | 90
Shine-Dalgarno mutant, no M | 105 | 15 | 14
Active-site Cys to Ser mutant, no M | 100 | 98 | 8

Model of metabolite M-dependent attenuation. — In the presence of metabolite M, the 5' untranslated region folds into a terminator hairpin that causes RNA polymerase to stop before transcribing the nrdP coding sequence. When M is absent or the hairpin is disrupted, RNA polymerase usually produces full-length mRNA.
