passage.title: psg-bb-10
passage.body:
To study how blood delivers oxygen, physiologists measured the percentage of hemoglobin saturated with O2 across a range of oxygen partial pressures (PO2), generating an oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. For adult hemoglobin the curve was S-shaped (sigmoidal): saturation rose slowly at very low PO2, steeply through intermediate values, and leveled off near 100 percent at high PO2. The partial pressure at which hemoglobin is 50 percent saturated (the P50) was about 26 mmHg. For comparison, myoglobin, a single-subunit muscle protein, gave a hyperbolic curve that was left-shifted, reaching high saturation at much lower PO2.
The team then altered the conditions around adult hemoglobin. Lowering the pH (more acidic), raising the partial pressure of carbon dioxide, and raising temperature each shifted the curve to the right, increasing the P50; at any given intermediate PO2, hemoglobin then held less oxygen and released more. These effects are collectively called the Bohr effect. Conversely, fetal hemoglobin gave a left-shifted curve with a lower P50 than adult hemoglobin.
The investigators related the findings to physiology. The sigmoidal shape reflects cooperative binding among hemoglobin's four subunits: O2 binding to one subunit increases the affinity of the others. In metabolically active tissue, where CO2 and acid are high and temperature is elevated, the right shift promotes oxygen unloading exactly where it is needed. The left-shifted fetal curve lets fetal blood extract oxygen from maternal blood across the placenta.

items.stem: When crystalline NaCl dissolves in water, the process is driven largely by interactions that replace the Na+···Cl− lattice contacts. Which solute–solvent interaction is the principal stabilizing force for the separated ions?

choices.text: Covalent Na–O bonds that destroy the identity of the sodium ion
London forces between uncharged NaCl molecules and water
Ion–dipole attractions between Na+ or Cl− and the partial charges on water

items.explanation: Dissolution of an ionic solid in water is a competition between lattice energy and hydration. Water is polar: the oxygen (δ−) orients toward Na+ and the hydrogens (δ+) toward Cl−. Those ion–dipole contacts, plus the hydrogen-bond network among water molecules in the hydration shells, stabilize free ions enough to overcome much of the lattice energy. Na+ ions do not hydrogen-bond to each other. Solid NaCl is ionic, not a lattice of covalent NaCl molecules held by London forces. Hydration is electrostatic, not formation of covalent Na–O bonds that would reduce sodium’s oxidation state.

distractorRationales.A: Hydrogen bonding requires H attached to N, O, or F. Bare Na+ ions cannot hydrogen-bond to one another.
distractorRationales.B: Aqueous sodium remains Na+; water ligands are coordinated electrostatically, not by covalent neutralization of the ion.
distractorRationales.C: NaCl does not dissolve as intact nonpolar molecules; it separates into ions. London forces are secondary for this salt.

items.stem: Lineweaver–Burk plots recorded at several concentrations of a reversible inhibitor are parallel. Both apparent Km and Vmax decrease as inhibitor rises. Mechanistically the inhibitor:

choices.text: Binds only free enzyme and is displaced by substrate (competitive)
Binds the ES complex preferentially, diverting it into a nonproductive ESI complex
Binds E and ES equally, leaving Km unchanged
Increases cooperativity so that the Hill coefficient rises above 4

items.explanation: Parallel Lineweaver–Burk lines are the hallmark of uncompetitive inhibition: inhibitor binds ES (or a downstream complex) rather than free E. Removing ES pulls more substrate onto enzyme (lower apparent Km) while the ESI complex cannot yield product (lower Vmax). Competitive inhibitors intersect on the y-axis and raise Km. Equal binding to E and ES is noncompetitive and keeps Km constant. The vignette does not describe sigmoidal cooperative kinetics or a Hill coefficient. Preferential ES binding is therefore the mechanism that simultaneously lowers both kinetic constants and produces parallel reciprocal plots.

distractorRationales.A: Competitive inhibition increases Km and shares a Vmax intercept; the lines would not be parallel with decreasing Km.
distractorRationales.C: Equal E and ES binding does not change Km and is not associated with parallel LB plots.
distractorRationales.D: Parallel MM reciprocal plots do not report cooperativity; Hill coefficients are obtained from sigmoidal v versus [S] curves.

passage.title: Critical Reasoning · Health & Statistics
passage.body: A widely circulated report claims that teenagers who spend more than four hours a day on social media are twice as likely to report symptoms of anxiety as teenagers who spend less than one hour a day. Newspaper headlines quickly translated this into warnings that social media "causes" anxiety in teenagers, and several schools cited the report when introducing new phone bans. The original researchers were more cautious. They noted that their data was cross-sectional — collected at a single point in time — rather than following the same teenagers over years, and that anxious teenagers might simply be more likely to retreat into their phones, rather than phones making them anxious in the first place. They also noted that heavy social media use was more common among teenagers who already reported sleeping fewer than six hours a night, raising the possibility that disrupted sleep, not screen time itself, was doing much of the work.

passage.title: Official Adjectives (1977)
passage.body: Ibrahim El-Sayed's 1977 essay “Official Adjectives,” on public libraries, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: In an E. coli transcription–translation coupling experiment, RNA polymerase elongates at 50 nucleotides s−1 and ribosomes elongate at 15 amino acids s−1. A small loudspeaker behaves as a point source. Intensity obeys I ∝ 1/r^2. Measurements along a radial line are:

Distance from source r | Intensity I
2.0 m | 1.80 × 10^−4 W m−2
6.0 m | (to be determined)

choices.text: 5.40 × 10^−4 W m−2, multiplying by the distance ratio 3.
6.00 × 10^−5 W m−2, dividing by the distance ratio 3.
1.62 × 10^−3 W m−2, multiplying by 9 as if intensity increased with r^2.

items.explanation: The radial factor is 6.0/2.0 = 3, so intensity falls by 3^2 = 9. Then I(6 m) = 1.80 × 10^−4 / 9 = 2.00 × 10^−5 W m−2. Inverse-square, not inverse-linear, is the geometric spreading law for a point source in three dimensions. Dividing by 3 instead of 9 leaves I too large by a factor of three (6.00 × 10^−5). Multiplying by 3 would describe intensity increasing with r, and multiplying by 9 would describe intensity growing with area. Both contradict energy conservation for a spherical wave. The stem states I ∝ 1/r^2, so the squared ratio of the tabulated distances is the only scale factor required.

distractorRationales.D: Intensity of a free spherical wave decreases with r^2; it does not increase. Multiplying by 9 goes in the wrong direction.

passage.title: psg-cars-3
passage.body:
Few debates in literary theory have proved more durable than the question of authorial intent: does the meaning of a text reside primarily in what its author meant to communicate, or does meaning emerge through the activity of reading itself? At one extreme, the intentionalist holds that misreading is always possible — that interpretations diverging from the author's design are simply mistaken, however ingenious or culturally resonant they may be. At the other extreme, the anti-intentionalist insists that once a text is released into the world, the author's psychological states become strictly irrelevant: what the words mean is fixed not by biography but by the conventions of the language and genre in which they are embedded.
The anti-intentionalist position gained influential expression in mid-twentieth-century criticism, when theorists argued that treating the author's intention as the criterion of correct interpretation commits a category error. Evidence about what a poet hoped to achieve, they maintained, cannot settle what a poem achieves, because a poem is a verbal artifact that may realize meanings its creator did not foresee — meanings that become available only through the community of readers over time. The celebrated example of an ironic text serves as illustration: a writer may compose a scathing satire of nationalistic rhetoric while sincerely believing the rhetoric they are parodying; the satiric meaning is there in the text whether the author intended it or not.
Intentionalists counter that language is an intentional practice: utterances mean what speakers mean by them, and written language does not somehow escape this fundamental feature of linguistic communication. To read a text in complete disregard of what its author was trying to do, they argue, is to treat it as a natural object rather than a human creation — to decode it the way one might decode an accidental inkblot rather than a deliberate message. Moreover, intentionalists point out that appeals to 'the language and genre' still presuppose communicative conventions that are themselves constituted by the intentions of the linguistic community.
A mediating view distinguishes between actual authorial intention (the historical individual's specific psychological states) and what might be called the implied author: the authorial persona that a competent reader constructs from the textual evidence alone. On this account, interpretation aims neither at private biography nor at free-floating textual play but at the coherent communicative project that the text itself invites. The implied author is, in effect, the best hypothesis about what an ideally communicative author of this text would have intended — a construct that disciplines interpretation without requiring access to historical documents.
What unites all parties to this dispute is the recognition that texts are not transparent windows onto authors' minds or onto a language-independent reality. They are artifacts whose significance is never simply given but must always be construed — a fact that makes hermeneutics, the theory of interpretation, as much a practical as a philosophical discipline.

items.stem: The gas-phase equilibrium A ⇌ B is exothermic and has a substantial activation energy in both directions. The mixture is already at equilibrium at temperature T1. The flask is then rapidly heated to a higher T2 and held there. Which pair of statements is correct once the new equilibrium is reached?

choices.text: Keq increases and the time required to re-equilibrate increases, because heat always favors products and slows motion
Keq is unchanged; only the Arrhenius rate constants change, because equilibrium constants never depend on temperature
A catalyst must have been produced by heating, so Keq increases while rates stay the same

Keq decreases (Le Chatelier / van ’t Hoff: heat is a product of an exothermic reaction) while both forward and reverse rate constants increase (Arrhenius), so the new, less product-rich equilibrium is reached faster

items.explanation: Thermodynamics and kinetics must be separated. For an exothermic reaction van ’t Hoff and Le Chatelier agree that raising T shifts the equilibrium toward reactants, so Keq falls. Independently, Arrhenius behavior says k = A e^(−Ea/RT) increases with T for both the forward and reverse elementary rates (the reverse Ea is larger by |ΔH|, so k_reverse grows more, which is how K = k_f/k_r falls). The system therefore re-equilibrates more quickly to a composition that contains less B. Heating does not invent a catalyst, and Keq is temperature-dependent whenever ΔH ≠ 0.

distractorRationales.A: Heat favors reactants for an exothermic equilibrium, so Keq decreases. Rates increase with T; they do not slow.
distractorRationales.B: Keq depends on T through ΔH (van ’t Hoff: d ln K / dT = ΔH / RT^2). Keq is temperature-independent only when ΔH = 0, not for this exothermic reaction.
distractorRationales.C: Temperature is not a catalyst. A catalyst would speed both directions without changing Keq; here Keq itself changes.

passage.title: Local Knowledge (1974)
passage.body: Elena Rossi's 1974 essay “Local Knowledge,” on disaster mapping, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that fairness talk often arrives after the decision has already been made. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

Using 0.15 mm drops a factor of 1000 from 0.15 m. Range finding with ultrasound is therefore a timing problem, and PET coincidence imaging is a rest-energy problem; both belong in medical physics as given.

items.stem: Which of the following is the best paraphrase of the author's claim that the ritual converts “dissent into attendance”?

choices.text: People who come to object are later counted as having jointly authored the decision, because their presence is filed as engagement while their refusal is no longer visible as a no.

items.explanation: The opening argument is that speaking and being minuted are real, yet the fact of having been in the room is later cited as evidence that the decision was shared. Conversion of dissent into attendance means presence is stored as legitimacy while refusal is filed, not that staff must fabricate praise or that revision never occurs. The author later grants that some rooms add ramps or spare trees. A faithful paraphrase must keep that conversion mechanism and must not upgrade it into a claim of universal theatrical fraud or of literal forgery of praise. Only A stays inside those bounds.

distractorRationales.B: The author describes structural conversion (photographs, themes, ratings), not a charge that facilitators secretly replace objections with praise.
distractorRationales.C: Sticky notes belong to the opening inventory of ritual props; they are not ranked as a superior record, and timed microphones are the later funnel example.
distractorRationales.D: The third paragraph insists some rooms do change designs; treating every invitation as fraud would contradict that qualification.

passage.title: Minutes as consent
passage.body:
City governments have learned to speak the language of invitation. A new waterfront, a bus garage, a night-time licensing scheme: each arrives with a room, a facilitator, sticky notes, and a promise that "your voice will be heard." The promise is not empty in the way cynics assume. People do speak. Minutes are taken. A summary slide later reports that the community was "engaged." What the ritual converts, with almost chemical reliability, is dissent into attendance. The fact of having been in the room is then cited as evidence that the decision which followed was shared.

This conversion is the point, not an accidental side-effect. A planning authority that can display a photograph of a crowded hall has already performed legitimacy. The photograph does not record what was refused, only that refusal was given a chair. Once refusal has a chair, it can be filed. The file then travels upward as proof of consultation, and the project proceeds under the borrowed moral credit of those who came to object. Objectors discover, sometimes only at the groundbreaking, that they were extras in a scene titled participation.

The objection is not that consultation is a trick in every case. Some rooms change designs. A ramp is added; a tree is spared; a night bus is rerouted. Those revisions matter, and it would be a different piety to pretend they never occur. The trouble is the ambient theory that treats any revision as proof that the process is sound, and any remaining grievance as leftover noise from people who "had their chance." Attendance is thereby made to do the work of consent. Consent, if the word still means anything civic, is not the same as having been scheduled.

Oral comments at a microphone illustrate the substitution with painful clarity. Three minutes are allotted. A timer is visible. The speaker is thanked. The next speaker is invited. The form is courteous and the structure is a funnel: complexity is shaved to fit the slot, and what cannot be shaved is classified as repetition. Staff later write that "themes" emerged. Themes are what survive the funnel. They are not necessarily what the speakers thought they had said. A person who came to argue that the garage should not be built at all finds herself listed under "requests for mitigation." The minutes have translated abolition into upholstery.

Digital portals repeat the same conversion with a friendlier interface. A comment box invites "feedback." Character limits and dropdown menus decide in advance which kinds of sentence will count as input. The resident who types a structural objection is asked, before submitting, to rate the project from one to five stars. The rating is the datum that will be averaged; the paragraph is optional texture. When officials later announce that the "average rating was 3.7," they are not lying about the arithmetic. They are treating a coerced metric as a public will.

A more honest practice would not abandon rooms or portals. It would stop narrating them as consent machines. It would publish the unedited record beside the decision, including the proposals that were not adopted, and it would say plainly: we heard you and we are proceeding anyway, for these reasons. That sentence is politically expensive, which is why the photograph of the hall is preferred. The photograph allows a government to be seen listening without being seen choosing. Democracy, however, is not a listening face. It is the willingness to let a choice remain attributable, especially when the choice disappoints the people who were invited to speak.

items.stem: A eukaryotic gene is cloned in two forms, each placed downstream of a lac promoter in a plasmid: (i) a cDNA prepared from poly(A)+ mRNA with reverse transcriptase and oligo(dT), and (ii) the corresponding genomic interval containing all introns. Only the cDNA construct yields the authentic protein in E. coli. Which explanation is best?

choices.text: Bacteria lack a spliceosome, so intron-containing genomic DNA cannot produce a continuous ORF; cDNA is reverse-transcribed from already spliced mRNA and can be translated as one coding sequence.
Reverse transcriptase automatically adds a Shine–Dalgarno sequence and fMet codon to every cDNA, whereas genomic DNA can never be transcribed from a lac promoter.
cDNA remains double-stranded RNA that bacterial ribosomes translate directly, bypassing transcription.
Genomic inserts are degraded by restriction enzymes that are chemically unable to cleave cDNA of the same sequence.

items.explanation: Eukaryotic primary transcripts contain introns that are removed in the nucleus by the spliceosome. E. coli has no spliceosome, so a genomic clone that retains those introns cannot produce a correct continuous open reading frame even when a lac promoter drives transcription. cDNA is reverse-transcribed from mature poly(A)+ mRNA and therefore already lacks introns; the continuous coding sequence can be transcribed and translated if bacterial expression signals are supplied. Reverse transcriptase does not install a Shine–Dalgarno sequence, cloning cDNA is DNA not ribosome-translated dsRNA, and type II restriction enzymes cut specific DNA sequences regardless of whether the insert originated as cDNA or genomic DNA.

distractorRationales.B: cDNA cloning does not automatically furnish bacterial ribosome-binding sites, and a lac promoter can transcribe a genomic insert; the block is splicing, not an absolute inability to transcribe DNA.
distractorRationales.C: Reverse transcriptase produces DNA; expression in this experiment is from a DNA plasmid via transcription, not direct translation of dsRNA.
distractorRationales.D: Restriction endonucleases recognize DNA palindromes independently of whether the molecule was copied from mRNA or from a chromosome.

items.stem: An anemic patient has hemoglobin 7 g/dL (about half of normal) but arterial PO2 = 100 mmHg and oxyhemoglobin saturation of the remaining hemoglobin is ~97%. Compared with a normal person at the same PO2, which statement is correct? (Henry's law: dissolved [O2] = kH * PO2.)

choices.text: Dissolved arterial O2 is halved because Henry's constant depends on hemoglobin concentration
Arterial PO2 must be ~50 mmHg because content and partial pressure are the same variable
The remaining hemoglobin must be only 50% saturated to match the anemia
Arterial O2 content is substantially reduced because most O2 is hemoglobin-bound, while dissolved O2 (hence PaO2) is nearly unchanged

items.explanation: Partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood is a property of dissolved O2 in plasma and is set by alveolar gas exchange. Henry's law relates that dissolved concentration to PO2 with a small kH; hemoglobin concentration does not appear in kH. The vast majority of arterial O2 content is bound to hemoglobin, so halving Hb halves bound O2 and thus total content even when PaO2 and saturation of whatever Hb remains are normal. Confusing content with PO2, or assuming saturation must fall to 50% in anemia, are classic traps. Dissolved O2 stays ~0.3 mL/dL at 100 mmHg either way.

distractorRationales.A: Henry's law constant is a solubility coefficient for O2 in plasma, not a function of Hb.
distractorRationales.B: PaO2 can be normal in anemia; it is not numerically equal to O2 content.
distractorRationales.C: Saturation is occupancy of available hemes; remaining tetramers still saturate normally at PaO2 100 mmHg.

The tRNA anticodon base-pairs with the mRNA codon, ensuring the correct amino acid is delivered. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

items.stem: HgCl2 in C is best interpreted, given the design, as

choices.text: a purported inhibitor of water channels, slowing but not abolishing swell relative to B.
proof the bilayer cannot admit any water, because scatter never changes.

items.explanation: The stem calls HgCl2 a water-channel blocker in this model. C is slower than B at every time but still falls by 300 s (0.61), so block is partial relative to B, not a total seal, and D is the extra-pore arm. Hypotheses: the student’s “slowed when blocked” is supported; “bilayer is not the main path” is a stronger claim that residual swell in C could still allow. The best interpretation of C is the intended inhibitor arm.

distractorRationales.A: C and B share 150 mOsmol sucrose; mercury is the extra variable.
distractorRationales.C: Scatter in C does change; residual path remains.

passage.title: Vesicle swelling under osmotic load
passage.body:
A student prepares identical phospholipid vesicles in 300 mOsmol kg−1 sucrose, then dilutes them at t = 0 into the media below. Vesicle volume is inferred from light scatter (larger vesicles scatter less in this geometry). Temperature 25 °C. n = 6 aliquots; scatter reported as mean ± s.d. arbitrary units (higher = smaller vesicles).

Medium after dilution | 10 s | 60 s | 300 s
A: 300 mOsmol sucrose (control) | 1.00 ± 0.02 | 0.99 ± 0.03 | 1.01 ± 0.02
B: 150 mOsmol sucrose | 0.71 ± 0.04 | 0.52 ± 0.05 | 0.48 ± 0.06
C: 150 mOsmol sucrose + 0.1 mM HgCl2 (water-channel blocker in this model) | 0.92 ± 0.03 | 0.80 ± 0.04 | 0.61 ± 0.05
D: 150 mOsmol sucrose + aquaporin proteoliposomes fused at 5 mol% | 0.40 ± 0.06 | 0.33 ± 0.05 | 0.34 ± 0.04

A second table lists initial rates estimated from 0–10 s, treating scatter drop as swelling:

Condition | Δscatter / 10 s
A | ~0
B | −0.029
C | −0.008
D | −0.060

The student claims: “Swelling requires a hypotonic bath, is slowed when water pores are blocked, and is accelerated when extra water pores are added, so the membrane’s phospholipid bilayer is not the main path in B–D.”

items.stem: A bacterial growth curve typically follows the order:
items.explanation: Bacterial growth: lag → log → stationary → death. Takeaway: Growth curve: lag → log → stationary → death. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Growth proceeds through lag (adjusting), log/exponential (rapid division), stationary (nutrients limiting), and death phases. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.A: Lag precedes log; the order is scrambled.
distractorRationales.C: Lag comes first, not stationary.
distractorRationales.D: That is roughly the reverse order.

items.stem:
Simultaneous plasma values during an oral glucose series in a healthy volunteer:

Time (min) | glucose (mM) | insulin (mU L−1) | glucagon (ng L−1)
0 | 4.5 | 8 | 80
30 | 8.0 | 40 | 25
60 | 6.0 | 22 | 40
120 | 4.6 | 9 | 75

Which regulatory pattern is illustrated?

choices.text: Insulin is secreted only after glucose has already returned to 4.6 mM
The three concentrations are independent, because 60 min values are intermediate by chance
Rising glucose stimulates insulin and suppresses glucagon; as glucose returns to baseline the two hormones reverse
Glucagon rises with glucose, amplifying hyperglycaemia

items.explanation: At 30 min glucose has risen to 8.0 mM, insulin has jumped fivefold, and glucagon has fallen from 80 to 25, the classic reciprocal islet response that stores the load. By 120 min glucose is back near 4.5 mM and both hormones have returned toward fasting values. Glucagon does not rise with glucose; it is suppressed. Insulin peaks while glucose is still high, not after euglycaemia is restored. The ordered rise-and-fall across three variables is coordinated negative-feedback control, not coincidence.

distractorRationales.A: Insulin is already 40 mU L−1 at 30 min, when glucose is 8.0 mM.
distractorRationales.B: The hormones move in opposite directions locked to glucose, which is the definition of coordinated regulation.
distractorRationales.D: Glucagon falls from 80 to 25 as glucose rises, the opposite of amplification.

items.stem: The initial treatment step of separating the person from the drug and managing the body's withdrawal is called:
items.explanation: Detoxification (detox) = separating the person from the drug and managing withdrawal (sometimes with medication). Takeaway: Detox = clearing the drug + managing withdrawal (first treatment step). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Detoxification is the process of clearing the drug and managing withdrawal, sometimes requiring medication. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.B: Relapse is a return to use, not the treatment step.
distractorRationales.C: Tolerance is a physiological adaptation, not a treatment.
distractorRationales.D: Intoxication is the drug's active effect, not detox.

items.stem: Soren Adeyemi’s “The Unlabeled Scale” (1979), vol. 200014, no. 2: which option best paraphrases the author’s warning without adding a policy list?

choices.text: Every institution should be defunded immediately
Soren Adeyemi wants amateurs to replace experts
If you cannot describe the practice without its official adjectives, those adjectives were doing the work

items.explanation: Paraphrase must stay inside the closing test. Defund, amateur takeover, and “tone never becomes a rule” all leave the passage. The essay’s title does not loosen that constraint. Neighbouring options fail because they name a different relation, drop a required conversion, or contradict a number given in the stem (GAMSAT.S1.understand.t2#800009). Those traps are not a second live key.

distractorRationales.A: Defunding is an outside leap.
distractorRationales.B: The essay does not replace experts with amateurs.
distractorRationales.C: The passage says tone can become a rule.

passage.title: The Unlabeled Scale (1979)
passage.body: Soren Adeyemi published “The Unlabeled Scale” in 1979 after a season in heritage listing. The argument is that neutrality is a style, not an absence of interest. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: In treating addiction, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works mainly by:

choices.text: Helping people recognize problematic thought/behavior patterns and build coping strategies (durable after therapy)
Replacing the drug with a medication only
Using hypnosis to erase cravings instantly

items.explanation: CBT addresses the thoughts/behaviors behind addiction — recognizing triggers and building coping strategies that endure after treatment. Takeaway: CBT = recognize triggers + build lasting coping skills (psychological treatment). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. CBT targets the cognitive and behavioral components of addiction — spotting triggers, building coping skills that last beyond therapy. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.B: CBT is psychological, distinct from medication substitution.
distractorRationales.C: CBT is often outpatient; hospitalization isn't required.
distractorRationales.D: CBT builds skills over time; it isn't instant hypnosis.

items.stem: Distressing physical symptoms with disproportionate thoughts/anxiety about them — without a fully explanatory medical cause — characterize:
items.explanation: Somatic symptom disorder = excessive distress about physical symptoms without a full medical explanation. Takeaway: Somatic symptom disorder = outsized distress about bodily symptoms. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Somatic symptom disorders involve real distress about bodily symptoms out of proportion to any medical findings. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.B: A phobia is fear of a specific object/situation.
distractorRationales.C: A manic episode is a mood state.
distractorRationales.D: A delusion is a fixed false belief (psychosis).

items.stem: In experiment 800006, a 6 kg crate rests on level ground. Take g = 10 m s^{-2} and μ_s = 0.3. If the normal force is just the weight, the maximum static-friction magnitude is
items.explanation: On level ground N = m g = 6×10 = 60 N. The friction ceiling is μN = 0.3×60 = 18 N. Omitting g leaves μ m; quoting N ignores the coefficient. Neighbouring options fail because they name a different relation, drop a required conversion, or contradict a number given in the stem (GAMSAT.S3.phys.t6#800005). Those traps are not a second live key.

distractorRationales.B: Reports the normal force, not μN.

items.stem: Within the otolithic organs, the utricle and saccule specialize for different directions of linear acceleration. Which pairing is correct?

choices.text: Utricle → horizontal acceleration; saccule → vertical acceleration

items.explanation: The otolithic organs split linear motion by axis: the utricle detects horizontal acceleration and head tilt; the saccule detects vertical acceleration (like an elevator). Takeaway: Utricle = horizontal linear acceleration + tilt. Saccule = vertical linear acceleration (elevator). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The utricle senses horizontal linear acceleration (and head tilt); the saccule senses vertical (e.g., an elevator). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.A: Reversed.
distractorRationales.C: Rotation is the semicircular canals' job, not the otolithic organs'.
distractorRationales.D: They cover different axes — one horizontal, one vertical — not both vertical.

items.stem: Apoptosis is best described as:

choices.text: Programmed, controlled cell death that is a normal part of development and tissue maintenance
The fusion of two cells into one
Accidental cell death from injury that causes inflammation

items.explanation: Apoptosis is regulated, programmed cell death in which the cell is dismantled in an orderly way (membrane blebbing, DNA fragmentation) without spilling contents or causing inflammation; it shapes tissues during development and removes damaged cells. Necrosis is the uncontrolled, inflammatory death from injury; the other options describe unrelated processes. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified. OpenStax Biology 2e ch.9 (Cell Communication: apoptosis) https://openstax.org/details/books/biology-2e

items.stem: In the accessory olfactory system, pheromone signals pass from the accessory olfactory bulb, via mitral/tufted cells, to which emotion-related brain region?
items.explanation: Pheromone signals reach the amygdala (emotion, aggression, mating) — fitting pheromones' role in innate social behavior. Takeaway: Pheromone pathway → accessory olfactory bulb → amygdala (emotion/mating/aggression). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Pheromone signals project to the amygdala, which handles emotion, aggression, and mating behavior. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

items.stem:
Vapour-pressure data (kPa) and a sketch of the H2O and CO2 phase diagrams are described.
Water: Pvap(100 °C)=101 kPa; the solid–liquid line slopes slightly left (ice denser as liquid).
CO2: Pvap(−78 °C) at 101 kPa is already on the sublimation curve; the triple point is 5.1 atm and −57 °C.
Which everyday consequence follows?

choices.text: Water boils at 100 °C at any pressure, because 101 kPa is listed
Dry ice sublimes at 1 atm because 1 atm lies below the CO2 triple-point pressure; ice melts under pressure (skate-blade) because water’s melting line leans to lower T at higher P
CO2 must melt at −78 °C and 1 atm, like water at 0 °C
Raising pressure on ice always raises its melting point, as for CO2

items.explanation: CO2’s triple point at 5.1 atm means that at 1 atm there is no liquid region: heating solid CO2 crosses the sublimation curve at −78 °C. Water’s triple point is well below 1 atm, so 1 atm heating melts then boils. The negative slope of water’s melting curve means higher pressure lowers the melting temperature, the qualitative ice-skate argument. CO2 does not melt at 1 atm. Water’s melting line is the unusual left-leaning one, not CO2’s. Boiling temperature tracks Pvap = external P, so it is 100 °C only when that pressure is 101 kPa.

distractorRationales.A: The 101 kPa row fixes the normal boiling point; at other pressures water boils at other temperatures.
distractorRationales.C: 1 atm is below the 5.1 atm triple point, so liquid CO2 is not stable and dry ice sublimes.
distractorRationales.D: Water’s solid–liquid line slopes the opposite way to most substances, lowering Tm with P.

items.stem: A bacteriophage that immediately replicates and bursts (lyses) the host cell follows the ______ cycle; one that integrates its DNA into the host genome and lies dormant follows the ______ cycle.
items.explanation: Lytic = replicate + burst the cell; lysogenic = integrate + lie dormant (prophage). Takeaway: Lytic = burst now. Lysogenic = integrate + hide (prophage). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Lytic = immediate replication and cell lysis; lysogenic = viral DNA integrates (as a prophage) and replicates passively until induced. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.A: Reversed — immediate lysis is the lytic cycle.
distractorRationales.C: Lag/log are bacterial growth phases, not phage cycles.
distractorRationales.D: Aerobic/anaerobic describe metabolism, not phage cycles.

items.stem: The visitor table, read with its caption, most nearly supports which claim?

choices.text: Hour 11 had both more people and more photographs of stairs than hour 10, while hour 12's talk coincides with zero stair photographs
The docent talk caused the 31 visitors at hour 11

items.explanation: Hour 10: 14 and 2; hour 11: 31 and 18; hour 12: 9 and 0 with a talk. That is what the table states. Photography does not always rise with attendance if we only have three rows, but hour 12 already breaks a naive monotone if someone claimed more people always means more photos — actually 12 has fewer people. The key is the accurate reading. B overgeneralizes. C reverses time. D contradicts 9 visitors.

distractorRationales.B: Three points do not establish always; hour 12 complicates any simple rule.
distractorRationales.C: The talk is listed at hour 12, not as the cause of hour 11's crowd.
distractorRationales.D: Nine visitors came at hour 12.

passage.title: Two ways of hearing a census
passage.body:
Poem (untitled, 2019)

We counted rooms as if rooms were people.
The spare one kept its coat on.
In the column for language we wrote the kettle.
Nobody asked the stairs their age.

Commentary by L. Okonkwo, catalogue essay for an exhibition of household inventories:
The poem is easy to misread as anti-data. It is not. It notices that a census already poetizes: it decides what may stand for a life (rooms, language, age) and what must remain downstairs, unasked. The coat on the spare room is not a joke about furniture. It is a figure for surplus — the part of a household that official forms cannot rent. When the poem puts a kettle in the language column, it is not claiming kettles speak. It is showing how quickly a form will accept a proxy if the proxy is small and warm.

A table printed beside the poem in the gallery listed visitors by hour and by whether they photographed the stairs:
Hour 10: 14 visitors, 2 photographed stairs
Hour 11: 31 visitors, 18 photographed stairs
Hour 12: 9 visitors, 0 photographed stairs (docent talk in progress)
The curator captioned the table: Attention is not the same as attendance.

A radio host later called the exhibition “political because it made a kettle into a citizen.” Okonkwo's essay had already refused that flattening. The political cut, for her, is not enfranchising objects. It is noticing which human details a state is willing to miss.

items.stem:
Three C3H6O isomers give these data:

Compound | IR (cm−1) | 13C environments | Tollens’ reagent
X | 1715 (strong) | 2 | negative
Y | 1725 and 2720 | 3 | silver mirror
Z | 1650 and 3300 (broad) | 3 | negative

1715–1725 cm−1 is C=O; 2720 cm−1 is aldehyde C–H; 1650 cm−1 is C=C; 3300 cm−1 is O–H. Which identification is consistent?

choices.text: X propanone; Y propanal; Z prop-2-en-1-ol (allyl alcohol)
X propanal; Y propanone; Z propanone enol only
X cyclopropanol; Y acetone; Z propanal
All three are propanone, because the formula is C3H6O

items.explanation: X has a ketone carbonyl (1715 cm−1), only two carbon environments (CH3 and C=O of acetone), and no aldehyde hydrogen, so Tollens’ is negative: propanone. Y has an aldehyde C–H stretch at 2720 cm−1, three carbon environments, and a silver mirror: propanal. Z lacks a carbonyl IR, shows alkene plus alcohol stretches, and is Tollens’-negative: an unsaturated alcohol C3H6O, i.e. prop-2-en-1-ol. Swapping X and Y contradicts both the 2720 cm−1 band and Tollens’. Cyclopropanol would show O–H, not 1715 cm−1. The shared molecular formula does not make the spectra identical.

distractorRationales.B: Propanal, not propanone, gives Tollens’ silver and the 2720 cm−1 band, so Y is the aldehyde.
distractorRationales.C: X has no O–H stretch; Y is Tollens’-positive, hence not acetone; Z has no carbonyl.
distractorRationales.D: Three different IR/NMR/Tollens patterns cannot be one compound.

items.stem: Which metal is oxidized here (loses mass / dissolves)?
items.explanation: Zinc's more negative reduction potential means it is preferentially oxidized; the passage notes the dissolving electrode. Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified. OpenStax Chemistry 2e, ch. 16 (electrochemistry: galvanic cells, standard reduction potentials, Nernst equation); OpenStax College Physics 2e, ch. 20-21 (current, resistance, DC circuits, power) https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e

distractorRationales.B: This option names a different relation or drops a constraint in the stem.
distractorRationales.D: This option names a different relation or drops a constraint in the stem.

items.stem: Cockroaches run a simple straight runway faster when other cockroaches are visible in adjacent boxes, but they run a complex maze more slowly with the same audience (a classic Zajonc demonstration). Which inference is most justified?

choices.text: Only humans show social facilitation, so the insect data must be a recording error
Audiences impair solely via evaluation apprehension; because cockroaches lack that concern, the simple-runway speeding is impossible
The runner is social loafing by letting the audience complete the maze
Mere presence can potentiate the dominant response even in a species for which evaluation apprehension is implausible, supporting Zajonc’s arousal account

items.explanation: If facilitation required worrying about being judged, cockroaches should not show it. The finding that a simple, well-practiced run speeds up and a difficult maze slows down with an audience matches the dominant-response rule and supports mere-presence arousal rather than a uniquely human self-presentational mechanism. Humans are not the only species in the literature. Loafing would require a shared task in which the subject’s effort is hidden among others actually running; the audience boxes do not run the maze for the subject.

distractorRationales.A: Comparative studies exist precisely because facilitation is not defined as human-only.
distractorRationales.B: Evaluation apprehension is one human mediator; the cockroach pattern is evidence that it is not required for the basic effect.
distractorRationales.C: The audience is not pulling a collective load; each runner’s time is individual.

items.stem:
Task A — 30 minutes. Kwame is writing to these comments:

“Hunger is a better critic than taste.”
“A metric can become the mission.”
“What we call realism is often only the furniture of the last war.”

Which approach is most likely to score?

choices.text: Inventory every comment in order so the marker sees completeness.
Write a generic paragraph that could fit any prompt this century.
Spend the first twenty minutes outlining and the last two typing.
Concrete cases that earn the claim. Do that with particular examples; do not inventory the comments.

items.explanation: GAMSAT S2 is production under a clock. What scores is: Concrete cases that earn the claim. Use a clear position or a precise personal scene; comments are pressure, not a checklist. Inventory, generic filler, and outline-without-prose are the three ways this hour fails to raise a mark. Kwame's comments only change the prompt pairing.

distractorRationales.A: Comment inventory is the named failure mode for S2.
distractorRationales.B: Generic voice is the opposite of particular/theme precision.
distractorRationales.C: Under time, an unused outline does not score.

items.stem: A GIS study finds that, after statistical control for household income, census tracts with higher Black and Latino shares are closer to Superfund sites and have more extreme urban heat. Which concept does this pattern best illustrate?

choices.text: Environmental injustice: unequal exposure to environmental hazards by race and place that is not fully reducible to class
Demographic transition stage 4, which eliminates toxic siting
Social loafing by residents, which causes regulators to place Superfund sites
James–Lange theory of emotion as the cause of facility siting

items.explanation: Environmental justice (and the related idea of environmental racism) concerns the disproportionate siting of hazards and the unequal distribution of environmental goods across communities defined by race, class, and place. Persisting proximity gaps after income control are the usual empirical signature that class alone does not exhaust the spatial inequality. Stage 4 of the demographic transition is a vital-rate regime, not a siting rule. Loafing and James–Lange theory are individual behavioral and emotion models; they do not explain why toxic facilities cluster in particular tracts.

passage.title: psg-cars-7
passage.body:
Democratic legitimacy, on one influential account, does not derive from the mere aggregation of pre-formed preferences through voting. Rather, it emerges from the quality of the public reasoning that precedes and informs collective decisions. This deliberative ideal holds that citizens who engage in open, reciprocal, and reasoned discourse — genuinely considering one another's arguments rather than simply advocating for prior commitments — are more likely to reach outcomes that are justifiable to all affected parties, regardless of who ultimately wins the vote.
The deliberative model places considerable demands on participants. It requires a willingness to offer reasons that others can evaluate on their merits, not just expressions of passion or assertions of power. It requires a disposition to revise one's views in response to compelling counter-arguments. And it requires conditions of rough equality: if some participants lack the resources, time, or rhetorical confidence to engage effectively, the deliberation is skewed in ways that may reproduce rather than remedy existing inequalities of power.
Critics have challenged the deliberative ideal on several grounds. The most fundamental challenge concerns the status of passionate advocacy. Much of what moves democratic politics — the eloquence of a civil-rights speech, the moral urgency communicated by a protest march, the experiential testimony of those who have suffered injustice — does not take the form of a reasoned argument that invites calm evaluation. To require that all democratic communication conform to deliberative norms risks excluding the voices of the marginalized, whose experiences may be most authentically expressed through modes other than academic debate.
A second critique concerns the domain of the reasonable. Deliberative theory assumes that despite deep disagreements, a set of publicly acceptable reasons can be identified that citizens holding different moral and religious convictions can endorse. Critics argue this assumption is empirically dubious in societies characterized by deep moral pluralism: when citizens disagree not just about policies but about the very framework within which policies should be evaluated, appeals to 'public reason' may function to privilege particular substantive views disguised as neutral procedural ones. The point can be sharpened with an example. When a legislature debates whether assisted dying should be permitted, one citizen may argue from the sanctity of life and another from the primacy of individual autonomy. A demand that each set aside these 'sectarian' premises and reason only from what everyone can accept may sound even-handed, yet in practice it tends to favor whichever background outlook already resembles the supposedly neutral default — often a secular, individualist one. What presents itself as a ground rule for fair discussion, the critics contend, can thus operate as a substantive thesis smuggled in under procedural dress, settling in advance the very questions it claims only to referee.
Defenders of deliberative democracy acknowledge these tensions but argue they point to the need for a more expansive and less rationalist conception of deliberation — one that includes narrative, testimony, and emotional appeal alongside discursive argument — rather than an abandonment of the deliberative ideal itself. If the goal is collective decision-making that citizens can recognize as fair, some approximation of reasoned exchange remains indispensable, even if the form that exchange takes must be more capacious than classical deliberative theory imagined.

passage.title: Electrochemical Monitoring of Dissolved Oxygen
passage.body:
A fictional microfluidic device is designed to monitor oxygen consumption by cultured cells. The device contains a 10.0 mL sealed gas headspace above an aqueous medium. At the working electrode, oxygen is reduced according to: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O. A 3.0 V source drives current through a variable series resistor and the electrode system. In the tested range, electrode current is approximately proportional to oxygen partial pressure unless the electrode becomes limited by oxygen diffusion from the bulk solution. A pressure sensor in the chamber acts as a parallel-plate capacitor. When gas pressure increases, a flexible membrane deflects toward the fixed plate, decreasing the plate separation d. Before each run, the headspace is sealed, and the table reports conditions just before current is measured.

Operating conditions and measured current for the oxygen sensor.
Run | Headspace O2 mole fraction | Temperature (K) | Total pressure before measurement (atm) | Series resistance (ohm) | Measured current (mA)
R1 | 0.21 | 298 | 1.00 | 1000 | 1.8
R2 | 0.21 | 310 | 1.04 | 1000 | 1.9
R3 | 0.10 | 298 | 1.00 | 1000 | 0.86
R4 | 0.21 | 298 | 1.00 | 500 | 2.4
R5 | 0.21 | 298 | 1.00 | 2000 | 0.95

Current response of the oxygen electrode. — For runs with 1000 ohm resistance, measured current increases approximately linearly with oxygen mole fraction. At lower resistance, the current increases less than expected from Ohm's law, consistent with a diffusion-limited plateau.

passage.title: psg-cars-10
passage.body:
The relationship between mind and body has occupied Western philosophy since antiquity, but the specific problem of consciousness has acquired a new urgency in an era when neuroscience can map the brain in unprecedented detail. Even if we knew the complete physical state of every neuron in a human brain at a given moment, would that knowledge exhaust our understanding of what it is like for the person whose brain it is to be having the experiences they are having? Many philosophers believe the answer is no — and they argue that this gap between complete physical description and subjective experience reveals something fundamental about the nature of mind.
This 'hard problem' — why any physical process should be accompanied by subjective experience at all — is distinguished from the 'easy problems' of consciousness, such as how the brain integrates information, controls attention, or generates verbal reports about mental states. The easy problems are not trivial; they may require decades of research to solve. But they are, in principle, amenable to explanation in functional and computational terms. The hard problem seems to resist this treatment: even a complete functional account of how a system processes information leaves unexplained why processing should feel like anything at all. To feel the force of the puzzle, imagine two systems that process a stimulus in functionally identical ways — the same inputs, the same discriminations, the same outputs — and ask whether it follows that there is something it is like to be each of them, and, if so, whether it must be the same something. Nothing in the functional story, defenders of the hard problem insist, settles the matter: one could in principle specify every computational step by which an auditory system registers a rising tone without thereby explaining why those steps are accompanied by any felt quality at all. It is this apparent slack between function and feeling — not mere complexity — that makes the problem look hard rather than merely unsolved.
Physicalists respond in several ways. Some deny that there is a genuine explanatory gap: what seems like an inexplicable residue is, they argue, an artifact of our limited cognitive access to neural processes rather than evidence of a non-physical dimension of reality. Once neuroscience matures sufficiently, the sense that something has been left out will dissolve, just as vitalism — the doctrine that life requires a special non-physical force — dissolved when biochemistry revealed the mechanisms of metabolism. Others accept that qualia — the intrinsic qualitative character of experience — are real but argue that they are identical with, or constituted by, physical brain states in ways we do not yet fully understand.
Dualists, by contrast, maintain that the hard problem reflects a genuine ontological gap: minds and physical processes belong to categorically different orders of being. This position preserves the intuition that experience is irreducibly subjective but faces the difficulty of explaining how non-physical minds causally interact with physical brains — a puzzle that has shadowed substance dualism since its classical formulation. To say that minds and brains interact is plausible as ordinary description; to explain the mechanism of that interaction without smuggling physical causation back in is a philosophical challenge that has resisted resolution for centuries.
The hard problem of consciousness thus sits at the intersection of metaphysics, philosophy of mind, and neuroscience. Whether it admits of a naturalistic solution remains one of the deepest unresolved questions in intellectual life.

items.stem: Aspartic acid has approximate pKa values 2.0 (α-COOH), 4.0 (side-chain COOH), and 10.0 (α-NH3+). What is the net charge of aspartic acid at pH 7.0?
items.explanation: At a given pH, each group is deprotonated if pH > pKa and protonated if pH < pKa. At pH 7 both carboxylic acids (pKa 2 and 4) are deprotonated (−1 each) while the ammonium (pKa 10) is still protonated (+1). The net charge is −1. The fully protonated form (+1) exists only far below pKa 2. The zwitterion with net 0 is not the major form at pH 7 because the side-chain acid is also deprotonated. Net −2 requires deprotonating the ammonium as well, which occurs only above pH ~10.

distractorRationales.A: +1 is the charge of fully protonated aspartic acid (both COOH and NH3+), which dominates only at very low pH.
distractorRationales.B: Net 0 would describe a form with one carboxylate and one ammonium and a still-protonated side chain, which is not favored at pH 7 (two units above the side-chain pKa).
distractorRationales.D: −2 is the fully deprotonated form (two carboxylates and NH2), major only when pH exceeds the ammonium pKa.

items.stem: Potassium phthalimide is alkylated with 1-bromobutane, and the product is then cleaved with hydrazine (Ing–Manske). Why does this Gabriel sequence give butan-1-amine without substantial di- and trialkylamine contamination that plagues the reaction of 1-bromobutane with ammonia?

choices.text: The phthalimide nitrogen can be alkylated only once; hydrazinolysis then releases a primary amine and leaves no nucleophilic nitrogen on the alkyl chain to react further
Phthalimide is so nucleophilic that it performs E2 exclusively, so no substitution products form until hydrazine is added
The method works only with tertiary alkyl halides, which cannot be dialkylated
Hydrazine reduces the alkyl halide to butane and the amine arises from phthalimide hydrolysis alone

items.explanation: Phthalimide’s N–H is acidic, and the imide anion is an excellent nucleophile for SN2 on a primary alkyl halide. After that single alkylation the nitrogen has no remaining hydrogen and is no longer nucleophilic toward a second equivalent of alkyl halide. Hydrazine (or strong acid/base hydrolysis) then opens the imide and releases a primary amine. Direct alkylation of NH3 fails because the 1° amine product is more nucleophilic than ammonia and continues to 2° and 3° amines. The halide here is primary, as required for SN2; tertiary halides would eliminate.

distractorRationales.B: The imide anion undergoes SN2 at a primary carbon, not exclusive E2. The N-butylphthalimide is an isolable substitution product.
distractorRationales.C: Gabriel alkylation requires an SN2-active (usually primary) halide. Tertiary halides favor elimination and are the wrong substrates.
distractorRationales.D: Hydrazine cleaves the imide C–N bonds (Ing–Manske); it does not reduce 1-bromobutane to butane as the source of the amine carbon.

items.stem: Which additional result would most strengthen the interpretation that notifications disrupted selective attention rather than only increasing motor slowing?

It links the notification effect specifically to distractor processing and attentional control. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

passage.title: Study of Notification Cues and Attention
passage.body:
Researchers investigated how smartphone notification cues affect attention and perceived stress. Eighty undergraduate volunteers completed a computerized reaction-time task in three counterbalanced conditions: no notification, a vibration notification, and a visual banner notification. In each condition, participants pressed a key as soon as a target shape appeared. The phone was placed face down for the vibration condition and face up for the visual banner condition. Participants were told that notifications were unrelated to task performance and did not require a response. After each condition, participants rated their momentary stress on a 1 to 7 scale. The researchers also measured whether participants reported checking their phones within 30 seconds after the task.

Mean task performance and stress ratings by notification condition
Condition | Mean reaction time to target (ms) | Error rate (%) | Mean stress rating
No notification | 420 | 4 | 2.1
Vibration notification | 470 | 6 | 3.4
Visual banner notification | 445 | 5 | 2.8

Phone-checking behavior after task
Condition | Percent checking phone within 30 seconds
No notification | 12
Vibration notification | 48
Visual banner notification | 31

Design summary — Each participant completed all three notification conditions in randomized order. The primary dependent variables were reaction time, error rate, stress rating, and post-task phone checking.

items.stem: Surface gravity on a spherical planet is g = GM / R² = 10 m s−2. Two locations are compared: (i) at r = 2R from the centre (above the surface), (ii) a planet of the same density with radius 2R. Density ρ is constant, and M = (4/3)π R³ ρ, so g ∝ ρ R at the surface. What is g at (i), and what is surface g on the larger planet (ii)?
items.explanation: Outside a sphere, g(r) = GM/r². At r = 2R, g = g_surface / 4 = 2.5 m s−2. For a same-density planet, M scales as R³, so surface g = GM/R² scales as R: doubling R doubles surface g to 20 m s−2. Using 1/r instead of 1/r² gives 5.0 m s−2 for (i). Applying the 1/4 factor to the larger planet as well confuses an exterior point with a new surface. Increasing g with R² without the mass scaling would overshoot. The two questions therefore use different dependencies: 1/r² off-surface versus ρR on a new world.

distractorRationales.A: g does not increase when you go farther from the original planet; (i) is weaker, not 20 m s−2.
distractorRationales.C: At 2R from the original centre, g falls as 1/r² not 1/r, so 2.5 not 5.0 m s−2. The larger same-density planet has greater surface g, not 5.0.
distractorRationales.D: 2.5 m s−2 is correct for (i) but not for the surface of a same-density world with twice the radius.

passage.title: psg-cars-15
passage.body:
The concept of the unreliable narrator invites readers to question the testimony of a fictional voice that presents itself as authoritative. An unreliable narrator is one whose account of events, characters, or motives the reader has grounds to distrust -- not necessarily because the narrator lies deliberately, but because their perception is limited, their self-understanding deficient, or their emotional investment in a particular version of events distorts what they report. The detection of narrative unreliability is, accordingly, one of the more sophisticated interpretive skills literary fiction demands of its readers, requiring attention to gaps, contradictions, and moments when the narrator's self-presentation strains against the evidence the text itself provides. The concept therefore depends on a tacit collaboration between author and reader carried on over the narrator's head. Behind the speaking voice stands an implied author who arranges the evidence so that a discerning reader can measure the narrator's claims against it, catching what the narrator misses or conceals. This is why unreliability is a matter of degree and of inference rather than a property simply switched on or off: the same first-person account may strike a careless reader as candid and a careful one as riddled with evasions. Recognizing it depends less on any single tell-tale sentence than on the accumulating weight of discrepancies between what is said and what, on reflection, the text as a whole gives the reader reason to believe.
Narrative theorists have identified several sources of unreliability. The most philosophically interesting is self-deception: the narrator who sincerely believes their own account while systematically misrepresenting it, particularly with respect to their own motives and moral quality. Such narrators often generate irony at their own expense -- the gap between what they report and what the text implies about them becomes the site of the reader's critical engagement. A narrator who insists on their generosity in every paragraph while every described action suggests self-interest produces a portrait more damning than any external indictment could achieve.
A second source is cognitive limitation: the narrator who simply lacks the knowledge or experience to interpret correctly what they observe. A child narrator reporting on adult conflicts without understanding their significance, or an outsider narrator describing an unfamiliar culture through inappropriate categories, produces unreliability through innocence rather than self-interest. In such cases, the reader must supply interpretive frameworks that the narrator cannot, and the gap between the narrator's report and the reader's inference becomes the text's most productive space.
A third source, less often discussed, is structural: some narratives are built on multiple competing narrators whose accounts cannot all be true, or on a narrator who explicitly announces their own limitations and invites the reader to read against them. In the former case, unreliability is dispersed across the text; in the latter, it is ironized through self-consciousness. Both strategies challenge the assumption that narrative access to events is, even in fiction, transparent and unmediated.
The broader significance of narrative unreliability extends beyond literary technique. It models a stance of critical reading that has application outside the text: the recognition that all reported experience is shaped by the particular perspective, interests, and cognitive limitations of the reporter -- a recognition that is as relevant to journalism, autobiography, and legal testimony as it is to fiction. Learning to read unreliable narrators teaches a transferable epistemic skill: suspending credulity and attending to the conditions under which any account is produced.

A velocity–time graph is a single straight line passing through (0 s, 3.0 m s−1) and (10.0 s, 7.0 m s−1).

Point | t (s) | v (m s−1)
Start | 0 | 3.0
End | 10.0 | 7.0

Displacement is the trapezoidal area under the line. What is the displacement during these 10.0 s?
items.explanation: For linear v(t) the area is a trapezoid: [(v_i + v_f)/2] × Δt = [(3.0 + 7.0)/2] × 10.0 = 5.0 × 10.0 = 50 m. Equivalently, a = (7.0 − 3.0)/10.0 = 0.40 m s−2 and s = v_i t + (1/2) a t^2 = 3.0×10.0 + 0.5×0.40×100 = 30 + 20 = 50 m. Using only the initial speed gives 30 m. Using only the final speed gives 70 m. Averaging incorrectly as (7 − 3) × 10 or taking 4.0 × 10 = 40 m confuses the change in velocity with the average velocity. Because v stays positive, the displacement equals the path length in this interval.

distractorRationales.A: 30 m is v_i × t, which would be correct only for constant v = 3.0 m s−1. The object speeds up, adding another 20 m.
distractorRationales.B: 40 m is (Δv) × t or 4.0 × 10, which is not an area under the v–t graph. Average velocity is 5.0 m s−1, not 4.0.
distractorRationales.D: 70 m is v_f × t. That overestimates the area because the object was slower than 7.0 m s−1 for the whole interval.

items.stem: In a conceptual replication of Seligman’s inescapable-shock work, undergraduates first face either solvable or unsolvable anagrams. Later, both groups receive a new set of solvable puzzles. The unsolvable-first group initiates fewer attempts and quits sooner even though escape is now possible. This behavioral pattern is best classified as:

choices.text: Learned helplessness, a behavioral response to uncontrollable stress
Problem-focused coping that conserves energy for a later, better task
Resistance-stage adaptation that should improve subsequent performance
Social loafing, because another student sits in the same room

items.explanation: Learned helplessness is the finding that organisms exposed to outcomes they cannot control later fail to use control when it becomes available. Unsolvable anagrams are an uncontrollable cognitive stressor; reduced later effort on solvable items is the transfer of that expectancy. It is a maladaptive behavioral stress response, not an efficient problem-focused strategy and not Selye’s resistance stage, which is associated with coping that maintains function. Social loafing is reduced effort when individual output is pooled in a group task, which is not the design here.

distractorRationales.B: Quitting on now-solvable items is not an instrumental attempt to solve the stressor; it is passivity after uncontrollability.
distractorRationales.C: Resistance is a period of continued physiological coping, not a prediction that performance will collapse on a new controllable task.
distractorRationales.D: Mere presence of another student does not define loafing; loafing requires a collective task with diluted individual accountability.

A radioactive isotope is counted in a fixed geometry:
t = 0 h, 800 min−1; 3 h, 400 min−1; 6 h, 200 min−1; 9 h, 102 min−1.
Assuming exponential decay with a constant half-life, the count rate at 12 h is closest to which value?

choices.text: 800 min−1, because total atoms are conserved
200 min−1, reading the 6 h row as the 12 h prediction
12 min−1, setting the rate equal to the elapsed time

items.explanation: The count halves every 3 h (800 → 400 → 200), so t½ = 3 h. Twelve hours is four half-lives from t = 0, and 800 / 2^4 = 800 / 16 = 50 min−1. From the 9 h point (≈100 min−1) one more half-life also gives ≈50 min−1; the 102 rather than 100 at 9 h is ordinary counting scatter. Nuclei are not conserved as the parent species: each decay removes a parent. The 6 h value is 200, which would be wrong at 12 h, and rate is not numerically equal to time in hours.

distractorRationales.B: Parent nuclei disappear as they decay; activity falls rather than staying at 800 min−1.
distractorRationales.C: 200 min−1 is the 6 h observation, only two half-lives from the start, not four.
distractorRationales.D: Elapsed hours and counts per minute are different quantities; 12 h does not force 12 min−1.

items.stem:
Human 2n = 46, so a normal gamete has 23 chromosomes. Four sperm are karyotyped:
W: 23 chromosomes; X: 24; Y: 22; Z: 46.
Each fertilises a normal 23-chromosome egg. Which pairing yields a 47-chromosome (trisomic) zygote?
items.explanation: A trisomic zygote has 2n + 1 = 47 chromosomes. That is 24 + 23, so the n + 1 sperm X. Sperm W is euploid (23 + 23 = 46). Sperm Y is n − 1 and gives monosomy (22 + 23 = 45). Sperm Z is an unreduced 46-chromosome gamete and would give triploidy (46 + 23 = 69), not 46 and not trisomy. Nondisjunction in meiosis is the usual source of the 24- and 22-chromosome sperm.

distractorRationales.A: 23 + 23 = 46, a normal diploid, not 47.
distractorRationales.B: 22 + 23 = 45, a monosomy, not trisomy.
distractorRationales.D: 46 + 23 = 69 (triploid); the sum is not 46, and triploidy is not trisomy.

items.stem: The phrase “with embarrassing regularity” in the claim that the vitality/nuisance decision tracks the prestige of the people making the sound most nearly signals

choices.text: neutral statistical caution, as if the author were merely reporting an accidental correlation without evaluating it.
amused affection for city officials, who are portrayed as lovable bunglers.
an evaluative stance: the pattern is presented as socially awkward to admit because it contradicts the ordinances' thermometer posture.
a comic retraction, inviting the reader not to take the sorting claim seriously.

items.explanation: Embarrassing evaluates. Regularity claims a pattern, not a one-off. Together they mark stance: the tracking of prestige is something a thermometer vocabulary should make hard to confess. The rest of the passage—hypocrisy, costume, meters that do not know hymns from brands—confirms a critical, not affectionate or retracted, tone. Rhetoric here is the gap between the ordinances' claimed neutrality and the author's insistence that officials already hear money as atmosphere. The adjective's job is to name that awkwardness, which is why C, not a claim of statistical humility or of comedy, fits.

distractorRationales.A: Embarrassing is not a hedge; it judges the pattern as something that ought to cause shame relative to the hygiene posture.
distractorRationales.B: Officials are said to hear money as atmosphere and unpaid sound as aggression; that is indictment, not fondness for bunglers.
distractorRationales.D: The argument proceeds to reform demands (like sounds, like reasons); it does not invite the reader to treat sorting as a joke.

passage.title: Who may be loud
passage.body:
Noise ordinances are written as if they were thermometers. A number of decibels is named; a clock hour is named; a fine is attached. The language of public health does real work here: sleep is not a luxury, and a child whose window faces a compressor is not being precious. But the thermometer conceals a second instrument, which is a social sorting device. Cities do not merely suppress loudness. They decide which kinds of loudness will be classified as vitality and which as nuisance, and the decision tracks, with embarrassing regularity, the prestige of the people making the sound.

Walk a mixed street after dark and the taxonomy is audible. A licensed terrace with heaters and a playlist is "activation of the night-time economy." A storefront church whose singing lasts past the same hour is a complaint waiting to be logged. A terrace is a business; a congregation is a disturbance that happens to own a building. Street vendors packing ice and calling prices are "chaos"; a restaurant's Friday overflow onto the pavement is "vibrancy," provided the overflow has paid for a permit. The ear that writes the ordinance has already been trained to hear money as atmosphere and unpaid sound as aggression.

Defenders of the ordinances will say that the issue is volume, not culture. Sometimes it is. A speaker stack aimed at a bedroom is a harm whether the music is sacred or commercial. The author's claim is narrower and more awkward: when two sounds of similar intensity are sorted differently, the sorting is not acoustics. It is a theory of who belongs in the air. "Quiet" is then sold as a natural baseline, like clean water, when it is often an aesthetic associated with certain housing and certain hours of salaried rest. Night-shift workers returning at dawn, whose rest is real, rarely get to define the city's sonic morals. People who sleep when the ordinance writers sleep do.

None of this is a brief for unlimited noise, or for the romance of the unregulated street. A city that cannot protect sleep will punish the poorest first, because they cannot buy distance from compressors. The decent aim is not a louder city but a less hypocritical one: a city that admits that permission to be loud is a scarce good, distributed by licensing, policing, and taste, and that "quality of life" is never only a medical phrase. It is also a claim about whose life is the measure.

The rhetorical trick is hygiene. Once noise is framed as dirt, opposition to a particular sound can wear the costume of sanitation rather than of preference. Dirt, unlike preference, does not have to justify itself at a public meeting. It only has to be pointed at. That is why a campaign against a night market can speak the idiom of rats and refuse even when the photographs show swept stones, and why a campaign for a waterfront festival can speak the idiom of civic joy even when the sound spill is identical. The same wave-form, two moral uniforms.

If the argument holds, then reform is not a new app for logging complaints. It is a requirement that like sounds be given like reasons, and that exemptions be named as political choices rather than as nature. A hospital generator may deserve its exemption. So, perhaps, does a funeral that spills into a street. What cannot be defended is the pretense that the ordinance is only a meter reading. Meters do not know the difference between a hymn and a brand. Officials do, and they should have to say so.

A monoprotic weak acid HA is prepared at 0.10 mol L−1. Its acid-dissociation constant is Ka = 1.0 × 10^−5, and Ka = [H+][A−] / [HA]. The dissociation is slight, so [H+] ≈ √(Ka × 0.10).

Trial | Method used to estimate pH | Result
1 | −log10 of the nominal 0.10 M concentration | 1.00
2 | −log10(Ka) | 5.00
3 | −log10 of √(Ka × 0.10) | 3.00

Which trial gives the correct pH of the 0.10 M HA solution?

choices.text: Trial 1, because every monoprotic acid contributes [H+] equal to its formal concentration.
Trial 2, because pH of a weak acid equals pKa.
None of the trials; water sets pH = 7.00 whenever the acid is weak.

items.explanation: For a dilute weak acid with Ka C >> Kw and x << C, [H+] = √(Ka C) = √(1.0 × 10^−6) = 1.0 × 10^−3 M, so pH = 3.00. That is Trial 3. Treating HA as strong (Trial 1) uses [H+] = 0.10 M and underestimates pH. Equating pH to pKa (Trial 2) would be appropriate near the half-neutralization point of a buffer, not for a solution of HA alone. Water’s pH of 7 is irrelevant once [H+] from the acid is 10^−3 M. The approximation x << C holds because 0.0010 is 1% of 0.10 M.

distractorRationales.A: Trial 1 is the strong-acid formula. It would apply to 0.10 M HCl, not to a weak acid with Ka = 10^−5.
distractorRationales.C: pH = pKa only when [HA] = [A−], as in a 1:1 buffer. A solution of HA alone has [A−] ≈ [H+] << [HA].
distractorRationales.D: A weak acid still produces [H+] well above 10^−7 M here. The solution is acidic with pH 3, not 7.

At the stated temperature, sucrose solute potential is Ψs = −2.50 MPa × molarity. Water potential is Ψ = Ψs + Ψp. A plant cell has sap equivalent to 0.30 M sucrose and turgor Ψp = +0.40 MPa. It is placed in an open 0.10 M sucrose bath (Ψp_bath = 0).
Ψ_cell = (−2.50 × 0.30) + 0.40 = −0.35 MPa; Ψ_bath = −2.50 × 0.10 = −0.25 MPa.
What is the direction of net water flow?

choices.text: Water leaves the cell because −0.35 MPa is higher than −0.25 MPa.
Water enters the cell because Ψ_bath (−0.25 MPa) is higher than Ψ_cell (−0.35 MPa).
There is no net flow because turgor is already +0.40 MPa.
Water leaves the cell because bath sucrose (0.10 M) exceeds cell sucrose (0.30 M).

items.explanation: Water moves from higher (less negative) water potential to lower. The bath at −0.25 MPa is higher than the cell at −0.35 MPa, so water enters. That matches the concentration comparison as well: 0.10 M outside is more dilute than 0.30 M sap, so osmosis is inward, and the +0.40 MPa turgor is not yet large enough to cancel Ψs_cell (−0.75 MPa). Turgor alone does not prove equilibrium; equilibrium would require Ψ_cell = Ψ_bath.

distractorRationales.A: On the number line −0.35 is lower, not higher, than −0.25; water does not flow up the Ψ gradient.
distractorRationales.C: Turgor is part of Ψ but equilibrium needs Ψ_cell = Ψ_bath; here they differ by 0.10 MPa.
distractorRationales.D: 0.10 M is lower, not higher, than 0.30 M; that comparison would drive water in, not out.
