items.stem: The sound intensity level at a point rises from 20 dB to 40 dB. The sound intensity I (in W/m^2) is multiplied by a factor of:
items.explanation: Sound intensity level is β = 10 log10(I / I0), so a change is Δβ = 10 log10(I2 / I1). Here Δβ = 20 dB, therefore log10(I2 / I1) = 2 and I2 / I1 = 10^2 = 100. Each +10 dB is a tenfold intensity increase, so +20 dB is a hundredfold increase. The decibel is logarithmic; a 20 dB rise is not a factor of 20 in I, nor a factor of 2. Squaring 20 to get 400 confuses the 10 log relation with an amplitude-squared identity applied to the decibel number itself.

distractorRationales.A: A factor of 2 would be only about +3 dB, not +20 dB. Linear doubling of intensity is a small step on the decibel scale.
distractorRationales.B: The decibel difference is 20, but I2/I1 is 10^(Δβ/10) = 10^2, not 20. The 10 in 10 log10 is what converts 20 dB into two factors of ten.
distractorRationales.D: This squares 20, perhaps mixing I ∝ amplitude^2 with the dB number. The correct map is 10 dB → ×10 in I, hence 20 dB → ×100.

Conduction measurements on two axons of length 1.0 m:

Axon | internodal distance | time per node | continuous conduction speed
Myelinated A | 1.0 mm | 0.10 ms | (saltatory)
Unmyelinated C | — | — | 1.0 m s−1

choices.text: A fibre 1.0 s; C fibre 0.10 s; C arrives first
A fibre 0.10 s; C fibre 1.0 s; A arrives first

Saltatory hopping therefore wins by a factor of ten, not a factor of 10 000. Using 0.10 ms (the nodal delay) as the whole-nerve time forgets that 1000 nodes must be crossed in 1.0 m (1.0 m / 1.0 mm). Equal length does not equalise time when speeds differ tenfold. The unmyelinated fibre is the slow one.

distractorRationales.A: That pair swaps the two speeds; internodal arithmetic gives 10 m s−1 for A, faster than C.
distractorRationales.C: 0.10 ms is the delay at one node, not the 1 m travel time; there are 1000 such nodes.
distractorRationales.D: Time = distance/speed; the speeds are 10 versus 1 m s−1, so times differ.

passage.title: psg-ps-9
passage.body:
Sociologists analyzed how a chronic illness is understood and managed in a mid-sized city. Using surveys and interviews, they documented three patterns. First, physicians and hospitals coordinated with schools and workplaces so that ill members could be temporarily excused from normal duties while being expected to seek treatment and cooperate with doctors. Second, patients with more education and income obtained diagnoses and specialist care far faster than poorer patients, who often relied on crowded clinics; the researchers traced this to differences in insurance, flexible work hours, and familiarity with medical institutions. Third, behaviors once seen as ordinary or as moral failings - such as persistent sadness or restlessness - were increasingly defined and treated as medical conditions.
The team framed each pattern with a different theoretical lens. The coordinated excusing of the sick was described as an institution maintaining social stability by managing how illness disrupts roles. The unequal access was described in terms of groups with different amounts of resources and power competing for a scarce good. The redefinition of ordinary behaviors as illnesses was described as a process by which the meaning of 'sickness' is negotiated and expanded within a society. In interviews, patients described how a formal diagnosis changed how others treated them, sometimes granting sympathy and sometimes attaching stigma. The authors noted that the fastest-growing diagnoses clustered among specific age groups, and that the city's aging population was projected to raise overall demand for chronic-disease care over the coming decades.

passage.title: psg-cp-4
passage.body:
Diagnostic imaging often relies on how waves interact with tissue. In an ultrasound scanner, a transducer emits pulses of high-frequency sound into the body and listens for echoes returning from boundaries between tissues. A common obstetric probe operates at 2.0 MHz, and sound travels through soft tissue at about 1540 m/s. The scanner forms an image from the time delay and strength of each returning echo, and clinicians choose the probe frequency to trade off image detail against how deep the sound can penetrate.
A Doppler mode measures blood flow. When a pulse reflects from red blood cells moving relative to the transducer, the returning sound is shifted in frequency; the scanner converts this shift into a flow velocity and direction, coloring flow toward and away from the probe differently.
A second instrument, a fiber-optic endoscope, guides visible light instead of sound. Light travels along a thin glass fiber whose core has a higher refractive index (about 1.5) than its surrounding cladding (about 1.2). Rays that strike the core-cladding boundary at a large enough angle are trapped inside the core and travel the fiber's length with little loss, so the endoscope can illuminate and image tissue deep inside the body and around bends. The physicians rely on the same refraction principles when a laser beam crosses from one tissue layer into another and changes direction. Throughout, the team treats soft tissue as a uniform medium for sound and the fiber as an ideal light guide.

items.stem: A student proposes to reverse the pyruvate kinase step in cytosol so that pyruvate plus ATP directly yields PEP and ADP, as a shortcut for gluconeogenesis. Measurements of ΔG in hepatocytes show the pyruvate kinase reaction is strongly negative. Which statement best explains why gluconeogenesis uses a two-enzyme bypass instead?

choices.text: Pyruvate kinase is freely reversible at cellular metabolite ratios, so the bypass is chemically unnecessary
PEP has a lower phosphoryl-transfer potential than pyruvate, so ATP cannot be involved
The bypass exists only to consume biotin; PEPCK alone could reverse pyruvate kinase
The pyruvate kinase reaction is too exergonic to reverse, so pyruvate carboxylase plus PEPCK provide an exergonic detour

items.explanation: Irreversible glycolytic steps are those with large negative ΔG in the cell. Pyruvate kinase is one of them: PEP’s high phosphoryl-transfer potential drives ATP formation, and the reverse reaction is strongly endergonic. Gluconeogenesis therefore spends extra free energy—ATP in the pyruvate carboxylase step (biotin-dependent formation of OAA) and GTP in PEPCK—to produce PEP by a different route whose overall ΔG can be negative. The bypass is not optional thermodynamics, PEP is the higher-energy phosphate donor relative to pyruvate’s enol, and PEPCK cannot act on pyruvate directly without the carboxylation detour through oxaloacetate.

distractorRationales.A: A strongly negative ΔG means the reaction is not freely reversible under cellular conditions.
distractorRationales.B: PEP has a higher, not lower, phosphoryl-transfer potential than ATP or pyruvate; that is why PK makes ATP.
distractorRationales.C: PEPCK uses oxaloacetate, not pyruvate; biotin-dependent carboxylation is required to make that OAA from pyruvate.

passage.title: Speed and Care (1981)
passage.body: In “Speed and Care” (1981), Ingrid Nilsen writes from inside broadcast newsrooms. The argument is that neutrality is a style, not an absence of interest. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Phenol (pKa ≈ 10.0) is insoluble in water and in aqueous NaHCO3 but dissolves in aqueous NaOH. Benzoic acid (pKa ≈ 4.2) dissolves in both NaHCO3 and NaOH. Which acid–base analysis is correct?

choices.text: Phenol is a stronger acid than benzoic acid, so only NaOH, the weaker base, can deprotonate it
Bicarbonate is a stronger base than hydroxide, which is why it fails with phenol
Hydroxide (pKa of H2O ≈ 15.7) deprotonates phenol, but bicarbonate (pKa of H2CO3 ≈ 6.4) does not; benzoic acid is strong enough to be deprotonated by either base
Phenol dissolves in NaOH because it is reduced to phenoxide by hydride transfer, not because of a proton transfer

items.explanation: An acid is deprotonated by a base when the conjugate acid of that base is a weaker acid (higher pKa) than the substrate. Water’s pKa near 16 lies above phenol’s pKa of 10, so hydroxide generates phenoxide and pulls phenol into water as a salt. Carbonic acid’s pKa near 6.4 lies below 10, so the equilibrium PhOH + HCO3− ⇌ PhO− + H2CO3 lies far to the left and phenol remains neutral and ether-soluble. Benzoic acid’s pKa of 4.2 lies below both 6.4 and 16, so both bases extract it. Phenol is the weaker acid, not the stronger, and the process is proton transfer, not reduction.

distractorRationales.A: Carboxylic acids (pKa ~4–5) are stronger than phenols (pKa ~10). That is why bicarbonate distinguishes them.
distractorRationales.B: Hydroxide is a far stronger base than bicarbonate. If the ranking were reversed, NaHCO3 would deprotonate phenol and NaOH would not.
distractorRationales.D: NaOH is not a hydride donor. Solubility tracks formation of ionic phenoxide by Brønsted deprotonation.

passage.title: On the new memorial
passage.body:
The memorial is a corridor of rusted uprights, each the height of a person, irregularly spaced so that you must turn sideways to pass. At noon they look like a failed fence. At dusk they look like a crowd that has agreed not to face you. There are no names. A small plaque at the exit says only: THEY WERE NOT LATE. THEY WERE PREVENTED.

Tourists complain that they do not know whom to pity. School groups count the uprights and get different numbers, because some are so close they read as one. A veteran interviewed on the steps said he hated it, then stood there until the lights came on, then said he hated that he did not hate it enough.

The sculptor, in a panel discussion, refused the word healing. “If it heals,” she said, “it has failed at being a door you cannot swagger through.” Critics split between those who call this moral bullying in Cor-Ten steel and those who call the tourists’ complaint the point.

I went through twice. The second time a child asked why the fence was broken. His father said it was not a fence. The child, satisfied with a new category, ran. I was not satisfied. Prevention is a bureaucratic word. In the corridor it becomes a body insisting on its width.

items.stem: A passage opens by stating that public libraries are "the last truly free public space," then spends three paragraphs describing free wifi, warm shelter, and no obligation to buy anything. What is the main idea, and what are the paragraphs?

Main idea: libraries are a uniquely unconditional public space. Supporting details: specific free, no-obligation features that illustrate this.
Main idea and supporting detail are the same thing here.
The passage has no identifiable main idea.

items.explanation: The opening sentence is the claim (main idea); everything after it is evidence supporting that specific claim, not separate ideas of equal weight. The main idea is the claim the whole passage serves; supporting details are the specific evidence, examples or reasons offered for that claim. A quick test: could you delete this sentence and still have the passage's core point survive? If yes, it's a detail, not the main idea. Memory tip: Trunk and branches: the main idea is the tree trunk holding everything up; supporting details are branches growing off it. Saw off a branch and the trunk still stands — that's the "delete it" test. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: Stress Appraisal and Working Memory During Social Evaluation
passage.body:
Researchers studied how appraisal framing affects stress responses during a brief social-evaluation task. Ninety-six adults were randomly assigned to one of three groups. In the private-reading group, participants read a neutral passage alone. In the evaluative-threat group, participants gave a short speech while being observed and were told that poor performance would indicate weak communication ability. In the evaluative-challenge group, participants gave the same speech while being observed but were told that increased arousal could help them perform effectively. Participants completed a working-memory task afterward and provided saliva samples before and after the task.

Mean outcomes by task condition
Condition | Perceived control, 1 to 7 | Heart rate increase, beats/min | Salivary cortisol increase, nmol/L | Working-memory accuracy (%)
Private reading | 5.8 | 4 | 0.7 | 86
Evaluative threat | 2.7 | 18 | 4.6 | 71
Evaluative challenge | 4.9 | 16 | 2.6 | 79

Appraisal framing — The evaluative-threat and evaluative-challenge groups completed the same speech task; only the framing statement before the task differed.

items.stem: A constant 10 N force acts on an object that undergoes a 2 m displacement. The force is directed at 60° to the displacement. The work done by this force is:
items.explanation: Work by a constant force is W = F d cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement. Cos 60° = 1/2, so W = (10 N)(2 m)(1/2) = 10 J. Only the component of force along the displacement, F cos 60° = 5 N, does work; 5 N through 2 m is 10 J. Work is zero only for a perpendicular force (θ = 90°, cos 90° = 0), not for 60°. Using sine in place of cosine is the complementary-angle trap.

distractorRationales.A: This is F d with the cosine omitted, as if the force were parallel to the displacement (θ = 0°, cos 0° = 1).
distractorRationales.B: Work is zero when force is perpendicular to displacement. Sixty degrees is not 90 degrees, so a nonzero parallel component remains.
distractorRationales.C: This is F d sin 60° (or F d cos 30°), swapping sine and cosine. The work formula uses the cosine of the given angle between F and d.

passage.title: psg-cp-10
passage.body:
A research team studies both how fast a reaction goes and whether it goes at all - kinetics and thermodynamics, two independent questions. They first examine the decomposition of a reactant, X, measuring its initial rate as they vary the starting concentration at fixed temperature. In three trials the initial concentration of X is 0.10, 0.20, and 0.30 M, and the corresponding initial rates are 2.0x10^-3, 8.0x10^-3, and 1.8x10^-2 M/s. From these data they extract the reaction order in X and the rate constant.
They then vary temperature and find, as expected, that the rate rises steeply as the sample is warmed. They interpret this with the Arrhenius picture: only molecules with at least the activation energy can react, and warming increases that fraction. Adding a catalyst speeds the reaction further, and the team is careful to note what a catalyst does and does not change.
Separately, they assess the reaction's thermodynamics. Calorimetry gives a standard enthalpy change delta_H = +50 kJ/mol, and the standard entropy change is delta_S = +100 J/(mol.K). Using the Gibbs relation delta_G = delta_H - T*delta_S, they compute the free-energy change at 298 K to judge spontaneity, and they determine the temperature above which the reaction becomes spontaneous. They stress that kinetics (how fast) and thermodynamics (how favorable) are separate: a reaction can be thermodynamically favorable yet immeasurably slow, or fast yet unfavorable. They treat delta_H and delta_S as approximately constant over the range considered.

items.stem: In this problem take L_fusion(ice) = 400 kJ kg−1 and c_water = 4.0 kJ kg−1 K−1. 0.10 kg of ice at 0 °C is dropped into 0.20 kg of water at 50 °C in an insulating cup. Heat to melt all the ice is m L. Heat the water can supply if it cools to 0 °C is m c ΔT. What is the final equilibrium?

Some ice remains, because 400 kJ is needed and only 40 kJ is available

items.explanation: Melting 0.10 kg needs 0.10 × 400 = 40 kJ. Cooling 0.20 kg of water from 50 °C to 0 °C releases 0.20 × 4.0 × 50 = 40 kJ. The two energies match, so every gram of ice melts and the water is brought exactly to 0 °C, with no leftover heat to raise the 0.30 kg of liquid above 0 °C. A 25 °C mean ignores latent heat. Using L as 400 kJ without multiplying by 0.10 kg overstates the demand 10-fold. Ice at 0 °C certainly exchanges heat until the 40 kJ balance is reached.

distractorRationales.A: The 50 °C water’s entire 40 kJ surplus is consumed as latent heat, leaving T = 0 °C, not an average of the starting temperatures.

passage.title: psg-cp-9
passage.body:
Nucleophilic substitution is central to organic and biochemical reactivity, from laboratory synthesis to the alkylation of DNA. A class studies how two bromoalkanes react with hydroxide ion, which acts as the nucleophile, in a hydroxylic solvent.
The first substrate is 1-bromobutane, a primary alkyl halide in which the carbon bearing bromine is attached to only one other carbon. With a good nucleophile it reacts by a one-step, concerted mechanism (SN2): hydroxide attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving bromide, and as bromide departs the other three groups invert like an umbrella in the wind. The measured rate depends on the concentrations of both the substrate and the hydroxide.
The second substrate is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide), a tertiary halide whose brominated carbon is attached to three other carbons. It reacts by a two-step mechanism (SN1): the carbon-bromine bond breaks first to give a carbocation, which the nucleophile then captures. The measured rate depends only on the concentration of the substrate, and because the carbocation is trigonal planar, a nucleophile can approach from either face.
The class also revisits structure. They note that a carbon bonded to four different groups is a stereocenter and examine 2-bromobutane as an example. They track how the functional group changes when hydroxide replaces bromide, and they rank the stability of primary, secondary, and tertiary carbocations to explain why substrate structure dictates the mechanism. The instructor stresses that the same electronic and steric principles govern reactions of biological molecules such as the phosphate esters of nucleotides.

items.stem: Among the hydrogen halides, HF boils at 20 °C while HCl boils at −85 °C, even though HCl has the larger molar mass. What is the best explanation?

choices.text: HCl is ionic in the liquid, so it should boil higher; the data are anomalous and unexplained.
London forces increase from HF to HCl enough to invert the boiling points, so HF is expected to boil lower.
HF forms strong hydrogen bonds (H attached to highly electronegative F); HCl’s intermolecular attractions are mainly dipole and London forces, which are weaker despite HCl’s greater polarizability.
HF has a larger molecular surface area than HCl, increasing dispersion forces.

items.explanation: Boiling point among similar covalent hydrides usually tracks polarizability (London forces), which is why HCl, HBr, and HI increase in boiling point with molar mass. HF is the exception: fluorine’s high electronegativity and small size make HF···HF hydrogen bonds unusually strong, so liquid HF is more associated than liquid HCl. That extra cohesive energy outweighs HCl’s larger London forces. Neither liquid is an ionic melt, and HF is smaller than HCl, so surface area cannot explain HF’s higher boiling point.

distractorRationales.A: Hydrogen chloride is a covalent molecular liquid, not an ionic melt. The HF/HCl inversion is a standard hydrogen-bonding effect.
distractorRationales.B: London forces do increase down the group, which is why HCl < HBr < HI, but they do not overcome HF’s hydrogen bonding.
distractorRationales.D: HF is smaller than HCl, so it has less surface area and weaker dispersion; hydrogen bonding, not surface area, raises HF’s boiling point.

passage.title: Recycling Behavior and Reinforcement Schedules in Dormitory Kitchens
passage.body:
A campus sustainability team tested behavioral strategies for improving recycling accuracy in dormitory kitchens. Twenty dormitory floors were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: informational signs only, a fixed-ratio points program in which floors earned a reward after every fifth correctly sorted item, a variable-ratio points program in which floors earned rewards unpredictably after an average of five correctly sorted items, or an observational-modeling condition in which residents watched a peer demonstrate correct sorting before signs were posted. In the reward conditions, a green light on the sorting station indicated that the sensor was active and points could be earned; a red light indicated that the sensor was off. passage.title: Critical Reasoning · Philosophy of Science
passage.body: For centuries we have told the story of the solitary genius: Newton alone under his apple tree, Curie alone in her laboratory, the writer alone at her desk producing a masterpiece from nothing but personal brilliance. This narrative is comforting because it is simple, and it sells a great many biographies. It is also, historians of science increasingly argue, badly incomplete. Newton corresponded for decades with a network of mathematicians whose incremental work he built on and later minimised in his own accounts. Curie's laboratory depended on instruments, techniques and a body of prior findings assembled by dozens of researchers across Europe. Even the writer's "original" idea usually turns out, on close inspection, to be a recombination of things read, overheard, or absorbed from a wider culture. None of this makes any of these individuals less remarkable. But it does suggest that crediting a single mind for a breakthrough often erases the scaffolding — the teachers, rivals, funders and quiet collaborators — without which that mind would have had nothing to work with.

items.stem: One molecule of acetyl-CoA is oxidized by one turn of the citric acid cycle. Ignoring subsequent oxidative phosphorylation, which set of products is generated directly by the cycle reactions?

choices.text: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP (or ATP), and 2 CO2

Counting four NADH would incorrectly include pyruvate dehydrogenase, which is not a cycle enzyme and is excluded by starting from acetyl-CoA. The FADH2:NADH ratio is not 3:1, and there is a single substrate-level phosphorylation per turn, not two. These stoichiometries are the starting point for later ATP tallies from oxidative phosphorylation.

distractorRationales.A: The cycle produces three NADH and only one FADH2 per acetyl-CoA, not the reverse. This option inverts the reduced-cofactor counts.
distractorRationales.B: Starting from acetyl-CoA there are three NADH, not four, and two CO2, not one. The extra NADH would be from PDH, which is outside the cycle.
distractorRationales.C: There is one FADH2 and one GTP per turn, not two of each, and NADH production is three, not two.

passage.title: psg-cars-14
passage.body:
Social contract theory attempts to ground the legitimacy of political authority in the hypothetical or actual consent of those who are governed. If the state can be understood as an agreement among free and equal individuals to submit to common rules in exchange for mutual protection and the benefits of social cooperation, then political obligations are not arbitrary impositions but self-incurred commitments. The theory has its roots in early modern political philosophy and was given its most rigorous contemporary formulation through the thought experiment of choosing principles of justice from behind a veil of ignorance about one's place in society.
The veil of ignorance is designed to neutralize the effects of morally arbitrary advantages. Behind this veil, contractors do not know their natural talents, social class, or the particular conception of the good that they happen to hold. Because they must choose principles without knowing whether they will turn out to be among the advantaged or the disadvantaged, the argument holds that they will prefer principles that make the situation of the worst-off members of society as good as possible -- the so-called difference principle. Rational self-interest, operating behind the veil, converges on an egalitarian outcome not through altruism but through prudent risk-avoidance. The reasoning is a form of maximin: facing a choice under radical uncertainty, one does best to make the worst available position as tolerable as it can be made, since for all one knows that worst position will turn out to be one's own. It is worth being precise about what the argument does and does not claim. It does not assert that inequality is inherently wrong, nor that talent may never be rewarded; it permits inequalities precisely insofar as they improve the prospects of those at the bottom. What it refuses to countenance is an arrangement that leaves the least advantaged worse off merely so that the already fortunate may gain still more. Equality functions here as a baseline from which any departure must earn its keep.
Libertarian critics have challenged this argument on two fronts. First, they deny that the veil of ignorance is a neutral device: by requiring contractors to ignore their distinctive identities and life plans, it smuggles in a particular egalitarian assumption about what matters morally. Second, they argue that the difference principle violates individuals' entitlements by requiring redistribution from those who have acquired their holdings through legitimate means. On this view, just distributions are determined by the history of how holdings were acquired and transferred, not by any end-state principle about the pattern of distribution. Taxing the talented to benefit the worst-off, on this account, is no different in principle from forced labor.
Communitarian critics raise a different objection: the veil of ignorance presupposes a conception of persons as atomistic, self-sufficient choosers whose identities and commitments are separable from their social contexts. This picture, they argue, is a philosophical fiction. Actual persons are constituted by their particular communities, traditions, and relationships; the self that chooses behind a veil of ignorance is an abstraction too thin to generate substantive principles of justice. A more adequate theory would begin not with hypothetical individuals stripped of their particulars but with the historically situated communities that persons actually inhabit.
The social contract tradition, despite these challenges, remains influential because it takes seriously two commitments that are difficult to honor simultaneously: the idea that political authority must be justifiable to each individual governed, and the idea that just social arrangements must be insensitive to morally arbitrary differences in natural talent and social fortune.

items.explanation: Both ketones and carboxylic acids contain a carbonyl, so both show a strong C=O stretch near 1700 cm^-1; that peak does not uniquely identify either family. An N–H stretch would indicate an amide or amine, not a carboxylic acid. Acids certainly absorb above 1500 cm^-1: they have both the carbonyl and the broad hydroxyl envelope. The paired broad O–H plus C=O pattern is the standard IR signature used to call an acid.

distractorRationales.A: Ketones and acids both have C=O stretches near 1700 cm^-1. A carbonyl peak by itself does not distinguish them.
distractorRationales.C: Carboxylic acids have O–H, not N–H. An N–H stretch would suggest an amide or amine instead of an acid-versus-ketone contrast.
distractorRationales.D: Acids absorb strongly above 1500 cm^-1 (C=O and the broad O–H). Absence of high-wavenumber bands would argue against an acid, not for one.

passage.title: psg-bb-8
passage.body:
A cancer-biology lab used flow cytometry to measure the DNA content of individual cells in a proliferating culture. A fluorescent dye that binds DNA in proportion to its amount let the instrument sort cells by how much DNA each contained. Cells in G1 phase, before DNA replication, showed a baseline amount of DNA (call it 2n). Cells in S phase, actively replicating, showed intermediate amounts between 2n and 4n. Cells in G2 and M, having completed replication, showed 4n. A normal asynchronous culture therefore produced two peaks (at 2n and 4n) with cells spread in between.
The team then treated cells with Drug Q. Afterward, nearly all cells piled up in the 2n peak, with almost none at 4n, indicating an arrest before DNA replication began. In a separate experiment, they examined a cell line carrying a nonfunctional version of a checkpoint protein that normally halts cells with damaged DNA. When these mutant cells were irradiated to damage their DNA, they continued through the cycle and divided anyway, accumulating chromosomal abnormalities over successive generations. Unlike normal cells, the mutant cells also kept dividing after covering the surface of the culture dish, having lost contact inhibition.
The investigators connected these observations to tumor formation: checkpoints normally verify that conditions are correct before a cell commits to replication and division, and loss of these controls allows damaged cells to proliferate, a hallmark of cancer.

items.stem: Enantiopure (R)-butan-2-ol is treated with TsCl and pyridine, and the isolated tosylate is then heated with NaCN in DMSO. What is the stereochemical outcome at the stereocenter?

choices.text: Retention in both steps, giving (R)-2-methylbutanenitrile as if the C–O bond never changed
Inversion in the tosylation and inversion in the cyanide step, returning the R nitrile
Racemization in the tosylation because TsCl ionizes the alcohol to a planar carbocation
Retention during tosylate formation (S–Cl, not C–O, is broken) followed by SN2 inversion by cyanide, yielding the S nitrile

items.explanation: Tosyl chloride activates alcohols by forming an S–O bond; the C–O bond of the alcohol is not broken, so the stereocenter retains its configuration in the tosylate. Cyanide in dipolar aprotic DMSO is a good nucleophile and displaces tosylate, an excellent leaving group, by SN2, which inverts the stereocenter. For 2-butyl derivatives both the OH/OTs oxygen and the CN carbon are the highest CIP priority, so R alcohol maps to S nitrile. Secondary 2-butyl cations are not formed under TsCl/pyridine conditions, so the first step is not a racemizing SN1.

distractorRationales.A: The second step is SN2 at carbon and must invert. Two retentions would describe a process that never breaks the C–O/C–X bond at the stereocenter.
distractorRationales.B: Tosylation does not invert carbon. Two inversions would return R, but only the displacement inverts.
distractorRationales.C: Pyridine/TsCl is not an SN1 ionization of a secondary alcohol. The tosylate is formed with retention and remains optically active.

passage.title: psg-ps-10
passage.body:
A longitudinal study followed 8,000 adults for 15 years to examine links between social position and health. Participants were grouped by socioeconomic status (SES), a composite of income, education, and occupational prestige. Age-adjusted rates of chronic illness and mortality declined steadily at each higher step of the SES ladder - not merely a gap between rich and poor, but a graded relationship across the whole range. The pattern held after controlling for smoking and diet, and was partly explained by chronic stress, worse neighborhood conditions, and unequal access to preventive care.
Participants were also classified by the neighborhood where they lived. Lower-SES families were concentrated in areas with fewer clinics, more pollution, and less green space; researchers described these areas as products of long-standing residential segregation. Children raised in the lowest-SES neighborhoods were less likely to reach a higher SES than their parents, a pattern the authors linked to unequal schools and social networks.
Finally, the study noted a demographic shift: as the population aged and birth rates fell, the ratio of working-age adults to dependents changed, straining programs that fund elder care. The authors argued that health follows a social gradient, that place and inequality shape opportunity across generations, and that population structure interacts with these inequalities to shape a society's future needs. They emphasized that individual choices operated within, and were constrained by, these structural conditions.

Glucose inhibition of liver phosphorylase causes muscle to export glucose-6-phosphate into blood as the sprint’s fuel.

Muscle glycogenolysis is stimulated independently of glucagon by AMP and by Ca2+-activated phosphorylase kinase, supplying G6P for glycolysis in situ; muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so free glucose is not released to blood.

Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it does not export free glucose. Glucagon receptors are not required for this local response. Liver-specific glucose inhibition of phosphorylase does not cause muscle to dump G6P into the circulation, and Ca2+ activation of phosphorylase kinase is a central feature of muscle, not an exclusively hepatic mechanism.

passage.title: psg-bb-7
passage.body:
Microbiologists grew a pure culture of a rod-shaped bacterium in a closed flask of nutrient broth held at 37 deg C and tracked population size by measuring turbidity (optical density) over time. The resulting growth curve had four phases. During an initial lag phase, cell number changed little as the cells synthesized enzymes and adjusted to the medium. This was followed by an exponential (log) phase, during which the population doubled at a constant interval; the team measured a doubling time of 20 minutes. Growth then slowed into a stationary phase, in which the number of new cells produced roughly equaled the number dying, as nutrients ran low and wastes accumulated. Finally, in the death phase, viable counts declined.
To test antibiotics, the researchers exposed separate exponential-phase cultures to two drugs. Penicillin, which blocks the cross-linking step in synthesis of the peptidoglycan cell wall, killed rapidly growing cells but had little effect on cells that were not actively dividing. A second drug bound the bacterial ribosome and halted protein synthesis, stopping growth without immediately lysing the cells.
The team highlighted features that distinguish these prokaryotes from the animal cells in a companion culture: the bacteria lacked a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, divided asexually by binary fission rather than mitosis, and could acquire new genes horizontally, for example by taking up plasmids during conjugation. These traits shape both how the population grows and how drugs can target the bacteria selectively.

passage.title: psg-bb-11
passage.body:
To characterize kidney function, a renal-physiology team infused test substances into volunteers and measured how the kidneys handled each, using the concept of clearance: the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute. They relied on three markers.
Inulin, a plant polysaccharide, is freely filtered at the glomerulus but neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the tubules. Its clearance therefore equals the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which averaged 125 mL/min in the study. Para-aminohippurate (PAH) is both filtered and actively secreted into the tubule, so nearly all PAH is removed in a single pass; its clearance (about 600 mL/min) approximated the renal plasma flow, a value much larger than GFR. Glucose, by contrast, is freely filtered but then almost completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by carrier proteins; at normal plasma glucose levels its clearance was essentially zero, and none appeared in the urine.
The team then raised plasma glucose experimentally. Below a threshold, urine remained glucose-free. Above the threshold, the reabsorptive carriers became saturated (their transport maximum, or Tm, was exceeded), and glucose spilled into the urine. Because the unreabsorbed glucose held water osmotically within the tubule, urine volume also rose.
The investigators noted that comparing a substance's clearance with the inulin clearance reveals its tubular handling: a clearance below GFR implies net reabsorption, a clearance above GFR implies net secretion, and a clearance equal to GFR implies filtration only.

items.stem: Ammonia synthesis: N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3. A reactor is loaded with 2.0 mol N2 and 3.0 mol H2. After the limiting reagent is exhausted, a student recovers 1.6 mol NH3. What is the percent yield?
items.explanation: Hydrogen is limiting: 3.0 mol H2 would consume 1.0 mol N2 and produce 2.0 mol NH3 (the 3:2 stoichiometry). Nitrogen is in excess by 1.0 mol. Theoretical yield is therefore 2.0 mol NH3. Percent yield = 1.6/2.0 × 100% = 80%. Using N2 as limiting would predict 4.0 mol NH3 and a 40% yield, but that calculation spends 6.0 mol H2 that were never loaded. 1.6/3.0 is an unmotivated 53%. The reaction did not go to the theoretical 2.0 mol, so the yield is not 100%.

distractorRationales.A: 40% comes from taking N2 as limiting (4.0 mol theoretical) despite insufficient H2.
distractorRationales.B: 53% is 1.6/3.0, mixing product moles with H2 moles.
distractorRationales.C: 1.6 mol recovered is less than the 2.0 mol theoretical ceiling.

passage.title: psg-ps-6
passage.body:
A study examined how persuasive messages change attitudes. Undergraduates read an editorial advocating a new campus exam policy. The message was either strong (well-reasoned arguments) or weak (superficial slogans), and was attributed either to a distinguished professor or to a first-year student. Crucially, half the participants were told the policy would take effect next year (high personal relevance) and half were told it would begin in a decade (low relevance).
Among high-relevance readers, attitude change depended almost entirely on argument strength and hardly at all on the source; among low-relevance readers, the reverse held - the prestigious source mattered, but argument quality did not. A follow-up a week later showed that attitudes formed by high-relevance readers persisted and better predicted sign-up behavior than those of low-relevance readers.
In a second study, participants who volunteered to argue publicly for a position they privately opposed later shifted their private attitudes toward that position - but only when they felt they had freely chosen to do so and were paid little. Those paid a large sum, or who felt coerced, showed no attitude change.
The authors mapped the first study onto a dual-route model of persuasion: one route processes the substance of a message when motivation is high, while the other relies on surface cues when motivation is low. They explained the second study as the reduction of an uncomfortable inconsistency between behavior and belief, resolved by changing the belief when the behavior could not be justified by an external incentive.

items.stem:
A simple pendulum obeys T = 2π √(L/g), which rearranges to T^2 = (4π^2 / g) L. Students plot T^2 (s^2) against L (m) and obtain a straight line through the origin. Their best-fit slope is 4.02 s^2 m−1. Take 4π^2 = 39.5.

L (m) | T^2 (s^2)
0.200 | 0.805
0.400 | 1.61
0.600 | 2.41
0.800 | 3.22

What value of g follows from the stated slope?

choices.text: 4.02 m s−2, reading the slope as g.
39.5 m s−2, quoting 4π^2 as if it were g.

items.explanation: The slope of T^2 versus L is 4π^2 / g. Solving for g gives g = 4π^2 / slope = 39.5 / 4.02. Compute 39.5 / 4.00 = 9.875 and adjust slightly: 39.5 / 4.02 ≈ 9.83 m s−2, which rounds to 9.8 m s−2 at the precision of these options. The tabulated T^2 / L ratios are 4.03, 4.03, 4.02 and 4.03 s^2 m−1, confirming the quoted slope. Identifying g with the slope ignores the 4π^2 factor. Inverting the algebra (slope / 4π^2) gives about 0.10, which is not an acceleration. The intercept is consistent with zero, as required when T = 0 at L = 0.

distractorRationales.B: The slope equals 4π^2 / g, approximately 4.0 s^2 m−1 on Earth, not g itself. g is about 9.8 m s−2.
distractorRationales.C: 39.5 is 4π^2 (dimensionless here as s^2 m−1 × m s−2). It is not an experimental value of g.
distractorRationales.D: g = 4π^2 / slope, not slope / 4π^2. The latter is about 0.102 s^4 m−1, which is not an acceleration.

items.stem: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v versus 1/[S]), which compound in Table 1 produces a line parallel to the uninhibited enzyme, and why?

choices.text: Compound P, because a halved V_max doubles both the slope and the y-intercept.
Compound Q, because a larger K_m increases the x-intercept magnitude while V_max, and therefore the y-intercept, is fixed.
None of the compounds, because any reversible inhibitor must change the slope K_m/V_max.
Compound R, because apparent K_m and V_max both fall by a factor of two, so the slope K_m/V_max is unchanged.

items.explanation: The Lineweaver–Burk slope equals K_m/V_max. From Table 1 the uninhibited slope is 0.50/80 = 0.00625 mM per (nmol s^{-1} mg^{-1}). Compound R gives 0.25/40 = 0.00625, the same ratio, which is the geometric meaning of parallel lines and the kinetic signature of uncompetitive inhibition (both parameters scaled by 1 + [I]/K_i'). Compound P doubles the slope to 0.50/40 = 0.0125, and Compound Q raises it to 1.50/80 = 0.01875; neither is parallel to the control. The parallelism cannot be read off without the paired K_m and V_max entries for R.

distractorRationales.A: P’s doubled slope means a steeper, not parallel, Lineweaver–Burk line; noncompetitive inhibition pivots about the x-intercept.
distractorRationales.B: Q’s increased K_m at fixed V_max steepens the slope and moves the x-intercept; competitive lines share a y-intercept, not a slope.
distractorRationales.C: Uncompetitive inhibition is the standard reversible case that leaves K_m/V_max unchanged; Table 1 shows R doing exactly that.

passage.title: Reversible inhibitors of a cytosolic dehydrogenase
passage.body:
Investigators purified a cytosolic NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase that oxidizes a small-molecule metabolite S. Initial velocities were measured at 25 °C by following NADH formation in 1.00 mL assays. Nonlinear fits of v versus [S] produced the apparent Michaelis constants and maximal velocities in Table 1. When an inhibitor was present, its concentration was 2.0 μM in the assay mix. Dialysis that removed unbound compound restored full catalytic activity after incubation with P, Q, or R, indicating reversible binding rather than covalent inactivation. Active-site titration with a tight-binding stoichiometric inactivator found 4.0 nmol of catalytic sites per milligram of protein.

| No inhibitor | 0.50 | 80 |
| Compound P (2.0 μM) | 0.50 | 40 |
| Compound Q (2.0 μM) | 1.50 | 80 |
| Compound R (2.0 μM) | 0.25 | 40 |

In a separate progress-curve experiment, 25 μg of the same enzyme protein was mixed with 0.50 mM S and no inhibitor in a 1.00 mL reaction. Product concentration was recorded as a function of time (Table 2).

items.stem: Glycerol (HOCH2CH(OH)CH2OH) is a viscous liquid with a boiling point near 290 °C, far above that of 1-propanol (bp 97 °C). What is the best explanation?

choices.text: Glycerol has three hydroxyl groups, so it forms an extensive hydrogen-bond network; 1-propanol has only one hydroxyl group.
Glycerol is a salt; 1-propanol is a molecular liquid.
Glycerol has a much smaller molar mass, so it should be a gas; viscosity is unrelated to intermolecular forces.
Only London forces operate in glycerol because the OH groups are intramolecularly satisfied.

items.explanation: Each glycerol molecule can donate three hydrogen bonds and accept several more, producing a three-dimensional hydrogen-bond network in the liquid. That network both raises the enthalpy of vaporization (high boiling point) and resists flow (high viscosity). 1-Propanol, with a single OH, forms only linear or loosely associated hydrogen-bonded chains and is far less associated. Glycerol is a neutral triol, not a salt, and its molar mass is larger than 1-propanol’s, not smaller. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds, if present, do not eliminate the many remaining intermolecular OH contacts.

distractorRationales.B: Glycerol is a covalent polyol, not an ionic compound.
distractorRationales.C: Glycerol’s molar mass is higher than 1-propanol’s, and viscosity is a direct macroscopic consequence of strong intermolecular attractions.
distractorRationales.D: The three OH groups are the hydrogen-bond sites; they are not “used up” intramolecularly to the exclusion of intermolecular bonding.

passage.title: The Archive Test (1983)
passage.body: Hanae Morioka's 1983 essay “The Archive Test,” on court translation, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that institutions remember procedures better than people. The piece admits that some gatekeeping keeps fraud out. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: Cartoon: Clinic time
passage.body:
A single-panel cartoon, unsigned, published on a letters page.

Foreground: a waiting-room bench. Four people sit. Above each head a small clock; the hands are at 1:10, 2:40, 4:15, and 9:50. None of the clocks match the large wall clock, which has no hands.

On the wall, a framed motto: WE VALUE YOUR TIME. The frame is gold. The glass is cracked.

To the right, a receptionist window. The receptionist smiles with many teeth and holds a clipboard titled TRIAGE (PRIVATE). On the clipboard the only visible line is: “Can they still sit up?” A potted plant on the sill is fake; its price tag remains.

Under the bench, a fifth clock, face-down.

Caption, in small type: “The system is coping.”

A letter printed beneath, from “Concerned, Upper Shore”: “Cartoons like this undermine dedicated staff. If people arrived on time and did not bring relatives, clocks would match.”

passage.title: Period of a simple pendulum and the value of g
passage.body:
A student determines the gravitational field strength g from the small-angle period of a simple pendulum. Length L is measured from the support to the centre of a spherical bob of diameter 3.0 cm. For each length the student times 20 oscillations and divides by 20 to obtain the period T; the procedure is repeated three times and the mean is recorded. The timing uncertainty on each 20-oscillation interval is estimated as ±0.20 s from reaction time, so the uncertainty in a single mean T is about ±0.010 s. All runs in Table 1 used a maximum angular displacement of about 5°. Take 4π² = 39.48. For an ideal simple pendulum, T² = (4π²/g) L, so a graph of T² against L should be a straight line through the origin with gradient 4π²/g.

Table 1. Mean period versus length (θ ≈ 5°)

| L (m) | Mean T (s) | T² (s²) |

passage.title: psg-cars-7
passage.body:
Democratic legitimacy, on one influential account, does not derive from the mere aggregation of pre-formed preferences through voting. Rather, it emerges from the quality of the public reasoning that precedes and informs collective decisions. This deliberative ideal holds that citizens who engage in open, reciprocal, and reasoned discourse — genuinely considering one another's arguments rather than simply advocating for prior commitments — are more likely to reach outcomes that are justifiable to all affected parties, regardless of who ultimately wins the vote.
The deliberative model places considerable demands on participants. It requires a willingness to offer reasons that others can evaluate on their merits, not just expressions of passion or assertions of power. It requires a disposition to revise one's views in response to compelling counter-arguments. And it requires conditions of rough equality: if some participants lack the resources, time, or rhetorical confidence to engage effectively, the deliberation is skewed in ways that may reproduce rather than remedy existing inequalities of power.
Critics have challenged the deliberative ideal on several grounds. The most fundamental challenge concerns the status of passionate advocacy. Much of what moves democratic politics — the eloquence of a civil-rights speech, the moral urgency communicated by a protest march, the experiential testimony of those who have suffered injustice — does not take the form of a reasoned argument that invites calm evaluation. To require that all democratic communication conform to deliberative norms risks excluding the voices of the marginalized, whose experiences may be most authentically expressed through modes other than academic debate.
A second critique concerns the domain of the reasonable. Deliberative theory assumes that despite deep disagreements, a set of publicly acceptable reasons can be identified that citizens holding different moral and religious convictions can endorse. Critics argue this assumption is empirically dubious in societies characterized by deep moral pluralism: when citizens disagree not just about policies but about the very framework within which policies should be evaluated, appeals to 'public reason' may function to privilege particular substantive views disguised as neutral procedural ones. The point can be sharpened with an example. When a legislature debates whether assisted dying should be permitted, one citizen may argue from the sanctity of life and another from the primacy of individual autonomy. A demand that each set aside these 'sectarian' premises and reason only from what everyone can accept may sound even-handed, yet in practice it tends to favor whichever background outlook already resembles the supposedly neutral default — often a secular, individualist one. What presents itself as a ground rule for fair discussion, the critics contend, can thus operate as a substantive thesis smuggled in under procedural dress, settling in advance the very questions it claims only to referee.
Defenders of deliberative democracy acknowledge these tensions but argue they point to the need for a more expansive and less rationalist conception of deliberation — one that includes narrative, testimony, and emotional appeal alongside discursive argument — rather than an abandonment of the deliberative ideal itself. If the goal is collective decision-making that citizens can recognize as fair, some approximation of reasoned exchange remains indispensable, even if the form that exchange takes must be more capacious than classical deliberative theory imagined.

passage.title: psg-cp-8
passage.body:
Purifying the product of a reaction is a routine but crucial task. A student runs a reaction that yields a mixture of a carboxylic acid (benzoic acid) and a neutral, nonpolar hydrocarbon, both dissolved in an organic solvent, and sets out to separate and identify them.
She first checks the mixture by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) on a silica gel plate, a polar stationary phase, developed in a relatively nonpolar solvent. After development, one spot has traveled 3.0 cm from the origin while the solvent front has advanced 5.0 cm. She records the retention factor (Rf) for the spot and notes that, on polar silica, more polar compounds cling to the plate and move less, whereas less polar compounds travel farther.
To separate the two components in bulk, she performs a liquid-liquid extraction, shaking the organic solution with aqueous sodium hydroxide in a separatory funnel. The carboxylic acid reacts with the base and is converted to its sodium carboxylate salt; the neutral hydrocarbon does not react. After the layers settle, she drains them apart and then treats the aqueous layer with hydrochloric acid to reverse the reaction and recover the purified acid.
Finally, she considers how to separate two miscible liquids that differ in boiling point and reviews simple distillation, in which the mixture is heated, the vapor is drawn off and condensed, and the collected liquid is enriched in one component. Throughout, she relies on differences in polarity, acid-base behavior, and volatility - the physical and chemical handles that separations exploit.

items.stem: A real gas is compressed to moderate pressure at a temperature near but above its boiling point. The compressibility factor Z = PV / nRT is less than 1. The dominant reason is:

choices.text: finite molecular volume, which makes the measured volume larger than the ideal prediction
inelastic collisions that permanently lower the kinetic temperature of the sample
attractive intermolecular forces, which pull molecules closer together than the ideal model assumes
complete conversion of the sample to a solid, so that Z is identically zero

items.explanation: Z < 1 means the product PV is smaller than nRT, so the gas is more compressible than ideal. Attractive forces (the van der Waals a term) reduce the pressure (or the volume at a given P) relative to the non-interacting model and are the usual cause of Z dipping below 1 at moderate density. Finite molecular volume (the b term) has the opposite sign and drives Z above 1 at very high density. Inelastic collisions do not steadily drain thermal energy from an isolated equilibrium sample, and a true solid would not be described as a compressed gas with a modest Z deficit.

distractorRationales.A: Excluded volume increases the effective volume and tends to make Z > 1, the opposite of the observation.
distractorRationales.B: Equilibrium molecular collisions are elastic in the kinetic-theory energy-bookkeeping sense; they do not provide a continuing heat sink that would redefine T in PV = nRT.
distractorRationales.D: Z slightly below 1 is a real-gas correction, not evidence that the entire sample has frozen into a solid with vanishing gas volume.

items.stem: On the question of public money and professional mobility, the letters most clearly

choices.text: agree that invoices exist and disagree about which unpaid bill—the graduate's or the state's—should be presented as the moral centre.
agree that three years is indenture and disagree only about the size of urban salaries.

items.explanation: A speaks of rights that forget their invoices and of the other half of the ledger. B says a ledger that counts only the graduate's debt and never the state's is a sermon. Shared: public money, debt imagery, underserved work. Conflict: whose unpaid bill is the scandal. Paired-prose comparison should not flatten A into B's indenture language (A denies indenture) or invent a locum-existence dispute. Purpose differs too: A defends the bond as recoupment; B unmasks it as cheaper than housing. A is the comparison that keeps the shared ledger metaphor and the forked addressee of the bill.

distractorRationales.C: Both write about publicly trained doctors and underserved rooms; clinic/hospital is not a vocabulary rupture.
distractorRationales.D: “Coercion is cheaper than housing” is B's line; A does not grant it, and locum existence is not the fork.

passage.title: Return-of-service bond: two letters
passage.body:
Two letters appeared in the same metropolitan daily after the health minister proposed a "return-of-service" bond: new doctors whose training was publicly subsidised would owe three years in designated underserved clinics before they could take an unrestricted urban post.

Letter A
A public scholarship is not a gift ribbon. It is a wager the public makes on a scarce skill. If the graduate then sells that skill immediately to the densest private market, the wager has been privatised without a receipt. Three years is not indenture; it is the time in which a clinic learns a name and a name learns a clinic. Those who call the bond a "mobility tax" speak as if mobility were a natural right unpolluted by the taxes that built the teaching hospitals. Rights that forget their invoices are just appetites with better stationery. Underserved towns are not a lifestyle choice the profession may decline, like a sport. They are the other half of the ledger.

Letter B
The minister has misdiagnosed a staffing failure as a character failure in the young. Clinics are empty of doctors for the same reasons they are empty of radiographers and nurses: housing costs, school deserts, professional isolation, and locum markets that pay more for a weekend than a bonded year pays for a winter. A bond does not staff a town; it parks a resentful beginner there and calls the parking "justice." Meanwhile the budget that should have made the posting liveable is spared the embarrassment of being seen. Coercion is cheaper than housing. If the public wants doctors in those rooms, it should furnish the rooms, not hostage the people it trained. A ledger that counts only the graduate's debt, and never the state's, is not a ledger. It is a sermon.

Editor's note: Letter A was signed by a retired regional physician; Letter B by a recent graduate now in a metropolitan hospital.

items.stem:
A resonance tube open at both ends is driven by a loudspeaker. Sound speed in the laboratory air is 340 m s−1. Intensity versus driving frequency shows peaks at:

Frequency of intensity peak (Hz)
200
400
600
800

For an open pipe, standing-wave frequencies are n v / (2L) with n = 1, 2, 3, … . For a pipe closed at one end they are the odd multiples (2n − 1) v / (4L). What is the length of the tube?

choices.text: 0.85 m, an open pipe whose fundamental is 200 Hz.
0.43 m, an open pipe whose fundamental is 400 Hz.
0.43 m, a closed pipe whose fundamental is 200 Hz.
1.70 m, a closed pipe whose fundamental is 100 Hz.

items.explanation: The spectrum contains 200, 400, 600, 800 Hz, i.e. consecutive integer multiples of 200 Hz, including the even harmonics. That pattern is an open pipe with f1 = 200 Hz, so L = v / (2 f1) = 340 / 400 = 0.85 m. A closed pipe of fundamental 200 Hz would show 200, 600, 1000 Hz and would miss 400 and 800. Taking 400 Hz as the fundamental would ignore the observed 200 Hz peak and would give L = 340 / 800 = 0.43 m. A 1.70 m closed pipe would have f1 = v / (4L) = 50 Hz, which is not the observed spacing. The even-harmonic presence is the diagnostic that the tube is open.

distractorRationales.B: 0.43 m would be L = v / (2 × 400). That treats 400 Hz as the fundamental and cannot account for the 200 Hz peak.
distractorRationales.C: A closed pipe with f1 = 200 Hz has L = v / (4 × 200) = 0.43 m, but then 400 Hz and 800 Hz would be absent. The table includes those even harmonics.
distractorRationales.D: 1.70 m is v / (200 Hz), which is 2L for an open pipe, not L, and a closed pipe of that length would not produce this harmonic list.

items.stem: What is the purpose of acidifying the bicarbonate extract to pH 2 before re-extracting it with ethyl acetate?

To deprotonate the carboxylic acid further, increasing its water solubility
To oxidize the aromatic ring into a more volatile compound
To convert the ester N into a charged salt under mild acidic conditions

items.explanation: Acidification shifts the carboxylate/carboxylic acid equilibrium toward the neutral carboxylic acid. Neutral organic acids are much more soluble in ethyl acetate than their charged carboxylate salts. Common miss: Forgetting that the desired compound must often be converted back to its neutral form before organic extraction. This correctly describes the acid-base step that enables recovery of A into an organic solvent. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.B: Acidification protonates, rather than further deprotonates, the carboxylate.
distractorRationales.C: No oxidation step is described or needed.
distractorRationales.D: Mild acidification is not used to convert a neutral ester into a water-soluble salt.

passage.title: Extraction of Substituted Benzoic Acids
passage.body:
A student separates a fictional mixture containing compound A, a substituted benzoic acid; compound P, a substituted phenol; and compound N, a neutral aromatic ester. The mixture is dissolved in ethyl acetate and extracted with aqueous base. Charged species partition strongly into the aqueous layer, whereas neutral species remain mostly in the organic layer. Sodium bicarbonate solution has pH 8.3, and sodium hydroxide solution has pH 12.0. After aqueous extracts are acidified, neutral acidic compounds can be recovered by extraction into fresh ethyl acetate. Prolonged heating of esters in strong aqueous base may hydrolyze ester bonds.

Properties of compounds in the mixture.
Compound | Main functional group | Relevant pKa | Dominant form at pH 8.3 | Expected layer at pH 8.3
A | carboxylic acid | 4.2 | deprotonated carboxylate | aqueous
P | phenol | 10.0 | mostly neutral phenol | organic
N | ester | none in this range | neutral ester | organic

TLC results on silica gel after workup.
Fraction analyzed | Observed spots by Rf
Organic layer after bicarbonate extraction | 0.62 and 0.35
Acidified bicarbonate extract re-extracted into ethyl acetate | 0.12
Strong-base extract after prolonged heating and acidification | 0.12 and a new spot at 0.18

Acid-base extraction workflow. — The original organic solution is first shaken with aqueous sodium bicarbonate. The aqueous bicarbonate layer is separated, acidified to pH 2, and extracted with fresh ethyl acetate. The remaining organic layer contains compounds that were not appreciably deprotonated by bicarbonate.

items.stem: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. What is its speed?
items.explanation: Wave speed = frequency x wavelength = 5 Hz x 2 m = 10 m/s. This one equation (v = fλ) governs sound, light, and water waves alike. Frequency (waves per second) and wavelength (distance between wave peaks) trade off against each other for a wave of fixed speed — e.g. for light in a vacuum, higher frequency always means shorter wavelength. Memory tip: "Very fast lambdas": v = fλ — wave speed equals frequency times wavelength (lambda). For a fixed speed, frequency and wavelength see-saw against each other: one up, the other down. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

items.stem:
Period-3 atomic radius and first ionisation energy:

Element | radius (pm) | IE1 (kJ mol−1)
Na | 186 | 496
Mg | 160 | 738
Al | 143 | 577
Si | 118 | 787

Which statement is consistent with both columns?

choices.text: Al has a higher IE1 than Mg because it has more protons
Na has the smallest radius, which is why its IE1 is the lowest
Radius falls Na→Si as Zeff rises, but Al’s IE1 dips below Mg because Al loses a 3p electron that is higher in energy and more shielded than Mg’s 3s electron
Radius increases across the period, matching the IE1 dip at Al

items.explanation: Radius decreases steadily from 186 to 118 pm as nuclear charge rises while the valence shell stays n=3, so Zeff climbs. IE1 generally climbs too (496 → 738 → 787) but Al is the well-known exception (577): the electron removed is 3p1, not 3s2, so it is easier to remove than Mg’s paired 3s electron despite Al’s extra proton. The radius column does not increase, Al’s IE1 is not higher than Mg, and Na has the largest, not smallest, radius.

distractorRationales.A: The table shows Al IE1 = 577, lower than Mg 738, so extra protons do not dominate here.
distractorRationales.B: Na has the largest radius (186 pm); a large radius and low Zeff together explain the low IE1.
distractorRationales.D: Radius falls from 186 to 118 pm; it does not increase.

items.stem: A city closes bilingual clinics and posts English-only wayfinding so that “everyone uses the same system.” Advocates of multiculturalism object. Which contrast is most accurate?

The policy is a subculture of hospital engineers, which is the definition of assimilation
Sapir–Whorf linguistic determinism requires English-only signs for thought to occur
The policy is assimilation (melting-pot pressure toward a dominant pattern); multiculturalism would maintain legitimate cultural pluralism in institutions

items.explanation: Assimilation is the process of taking on the dominant group’s language and institutions, historically imaged as a melting pot. Multiculturalism (cultural pluralism) values persistence of distinct cultural streams within a shared polity. English-only clinics are assimilationist. Culture shock is individual strain abroad. A subculture is a group with distinct norms inside a larger culture, not the definition of this city policy. Sapir–Whorf concerns language shaping thought, not a requirement for monolingual signage to think.

distractorRationales.A: Culture shock is not the name of an English-only ordinance.
distractorRationales.B: Subculture ≠ assimilationist city policy.
distractorRationales.C: Whorf does not legislate English-only wayfinding as a condition of thought.

passage.title: The Metric (1981)
passage.body: In “The Metric” (1981), Mei-Ling Vargas writes from inside museum captions. The argument is that fairness talk often arrives after the decision has already been made. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: psg-cars-12
passage.body:
One of the most consequential shifts in twentieth-century philosophy of language was the move away from the view that words get their meaning by standing for objects in the world. On the referentialist picture, to know the meaning of a term like 'gold' is to know which substance the term picks out; to know the meaning of 'Julius Caesar' is to know which historical individual the name refers to. The attractions of this view are obvious: it grounds meaning in something outside language itself, connecting our words to the world they describe and offering a clear criterion for distinguishing correct from incorrect usage.
Yet referentialism encounters serious difficulties when applied to expressions whose meaning does not seem to consist in any reference at all. Words like 'and,' 'perhaps,' 'nevertheless,' and 'of' do not pick out objects, properties, or relations in any obvious sense. Equally problematic are terms whose reference appears to shift depending on context: 'here' refers to wherever the speaker happens to be, 'now' to whenever the utterance is made, and 'I' to whoever is speaking. The meaning of these expressions cannot be their reference, since their reference changes while their meaning remains constant across every ordinary use of the word.
An alternative tradition proposed that meaning is constituted by use. On this view, to know the meaning of a word is not to know what it refers to but to know how to use it -- in what contexts it is appropriately deployed, what inferences it licenses, how it interacts with the meanings of other expressions. This account handles the problematic cases naturally: logical connectives like 'and' are explained by the inferential rules governing their use (the conjunction of P and Q implies both P and Q separately); indexical expressions like 'here' are explained by specifying the rule that they refer to the context of utterance. Knowing the meaning of 'here' means knowing that it picks out the speaker's location, not knowing any particular location.
Critics of the use theory worry that it leaves too little stable content in meaning. If meaning is just use, and use can vary between individual speakers or across historical periods, then there seems to be no fact of the matter about whether two speakers mean the same thing by a word, or whether we mean the same thing by 'democracy' as people in ancient Athens did. Some philosophers have sought to address this by distinguishing between the linguistic meaning of an expression (shared by competent speakers of a language) and speaker meaning (what a particular individual intends to convey in a specific utterance). Semantic theory can then concern itself with the former -- a stable, shared content -- while acknowledging the latter's irreducibly contextual character and the inevitable gap between what a speaker means and what a sentence means.
None of this need force an exclusive choice between the two pictures. A mature semantics may well be pluralistic, allowing that proper names and natural-kind terms lean heavily on reference while connectives, indexicals, and evaluative vocabulary are better explained by the rules governing their use. What the twentieth-century debate established is less the triumph of one theory than the inadequacy of assuming that a single mechanism must underwrite meaning across the whole of a language. The more durable lesson is methodological: before asking what a word means, one does well to ask what kind of word it is, since expressions of different types may secure their significance in quite different ways.

items.stem: A chromosomal domain is marked by histone H3 lysine-9 trimethylation, HP1 binding, late replication, and low RNA polymerase II occupancy. Forced histone hyperacetylation of the same domain increases DNase I sensitivity and nascent transcription. Which statement best describes the original state?

choices.text: The domain is euchromatin packaged with acetylated histones that recruit HP1 to activate transcription.
The domain is a nucleosome-free enhancer; H3K9me3 is a canonical mark of active promoters.
The domain is a prokaryotic nucleoid region, and HP1 functions there as a sigma initiation factor.
The domain is heterochromatin; H3K9me3 and HP1 compact chromatin and silence transcription, whereas acetylation loosens histone–DNA contacts and favors expression.

items.explanation: Constitutive and many facultative heterochromatic regions carry H3K9me3, which is read by HP1 proteins that oligomerize, compact chromatin, delay replication timing, and exclude RNA polymerase II. Histone acetylation neutralizes lysine charge, weakens histone–DNA interaction, and correlates with DNase-sensitive euchromatin and transcription. Forced hyperacetylation therefore switches the domain toward an open, transcribed state, matching the experiment. HP1 is not recruited by acetylation as an activator, H3K9me3 is a silencing mark rather than an active-promoter modification, and this histone code is a feature of eukaryotic nuclei, not of a bacterial nucleoid.

distractorRationales.A: Acetylated euchromatin is transcriptionally permissive and does not use H3K9me3–HP1 as an activation module.
distractorRationales.B: H3K9me3 is associated with compact, late-replicating heterochromatin, not with nucleosome-free active enhancers or promoters.

items.stem: In a Sperry–Gazzaniga split-brain examination, a key is flashed briefly in the left visual field of a patient with complete callosotomy. Speech is left-lateralized. Which outcome is expected?

items.stem: A cell-free liver extract can synthesize glucose from several precursors. Avidin is added to inactivate biotin-dependent carboxylases, including pyruvate carboxylase. Which 14C-labeled precursor can still yield [14C]glucose in this system?
items.explanation: Gluconeogenesis from pyruvate, lactate, or alanine all funnel through pyruvate and therefore require pyruvate carboxylase to form oxaloacetate before PEPCK can make PEP. Pyruvate carboxylase uses biotin; avidin binds biotin extremely tightly and blocks that step. Glycerol is phosphorylated to glycerol-3-phosphate and oxidized to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, which enters the pathway at the triose-phosphate level, bypassing the pyruvate carboxylase/PEPCK bypass of pyruvate kinase. From DHAP, aldolase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose-6-phosphatase can still produce glucose. Hence only labeled glycerol remains a competent glucogenic precursor in the avidin-treated extract.

distractorRationales.A: Pyruvate must be carboxylated by the biotin enzyme pyruvate carboxylase before it can form PEP.
distractorRationales.B: Lactate is oxidized to pyruvate and then faces the same biotin-dependent carboxylation block.
distractorRationales.D: Alanine transaminates to pyruvate and likewise requires pyruvate carboxylase.

passage.title: psg-cars-14
passage.body:
Social contract theory attempts to ground the legitimacy of political authority in the hypothetical or actual consent of those who are governed. If the state can be understood as an agreement among free and equal individuals to submit to common rules in exchange for mutual protection and the benefits of social cooperation, then political obligations are not arbitrary impositions but self-incurred commitments. The theory has its roots in early modern political philosophy and was given its most rigorous contemporary formulation through the thought experiment of choosing principles of justice from behind a veil of ignorance about one's place in society.
The veil of ignorance is designed to neutralize the effects of morally arbitrary advantages. Behind this veil, contractors do not know their natural talents, social class, or the particular conception of the good that they happen to hold. Because they must choose principles without knowing whether they will turn out to be among the advantaged or the disadvantaged, the argument holds that they will prefer principles that make the situation of the worst-off members of society as good as possible -- the so-called difference principle. Rational self-interest, operating behind the veil, converges on an egalitarian outcome not through altruism but through prudent risk-avoidance. The reasoning is a form of maximin: facing a choice under radical uncertainty, one does best to make the worst available position as tolerable as it can be made, since for all one knows that worst position will turn out to be one's own. It is worth being precise about what the argument does and does not claim. It does not assert that inequality is inherently wrong, nor that talent may never be rewarded; it permits inequalities precisely insofar as they improve the prospects of those at the bottom. What it refuses to countenance is an arrangement that leaves the least advantaged worse off merely so that the already fortunate may gain still more. Equality functions here as a baseline from which any departure must earn its keep.
Libertarian critics have challenged this argument on two fronts. First, they deny that the veil of ignorance is a neutral device: by requiring contractors to ignore their distinctive identities and life plans, it smuggles in a particular egalitarian assumption about what matters morally. Second, they argue that the difference principle violates individuals' entitlements by requiring redistribution from those who have acquired their holdings through legitimate means. On this view, just distributions are determined by the history of how holdings were acquired and transferred, not by any end-state principle about the pattern of distribution. Taxing the talented to benefit the worst-off, on this account, is no different in principle from forced labor.
Communitarian critics raise a different objection: the veil of ignorance presupposes a conception of persons as atomistic, self-sufficient choosers whose identities and commitments are separable from their social contexts. This picture, they argue, is a philosophical fiction. Actual persons are constituted by their particular communities, traditions, and relationships; the self that chooses behind a veil of ignorance is an abstraction too thin to generate substantive principles of justice. A more adequate theory would begin not with hypothetical individuals stripped of their particulars but with the historically situated communities that persons actually inhabit.
The social contract tradition, despite these challenges, remains influential because it takes seriously two commitments that are difficult to honor simultaneously: the idea that political authority must be justifiable to each individual governed, and the idea that just social arrangements must be insensitive to morally arbitrary differences in natural talent and social fortune.
