passage.title: The census of the uncounted
passage.body:
Political arithmetic began as a courtly hobby: a way of estimating how many subjects a prince could tax, feed, or send to war. Its early practitioners treated people as a kind of harvest. What could be enumerated could be extracted. What could not be enumerated was, for administrative purposes, a rumor.

The modern census inherited the appetite and dressed it as representation. To be counted is now advertised as a civic right, a way of appearing in the distribution of schools, clinics, and parliamentary seats. The advertisement is not false. Under-counted neighborhoods do lose clinics. The advertisement is incomplete. A census is also a machine for deciding which kinds of life will be treated as facts and which will remain anecdotes told to a volunteer with a clipboard.

Consider the category. Every census must invent boxes. The boxes are not discovered in nature; they are negotiated among ministries, churches, and, later, identity movements. A person who lives in two houses, or in none, or who works in a language the form does not print, must be forced into a box or dropped. Dropping looks like a clerical mishap. It is often a theory of the state: some lives are too expensive to verify, too mobile to locate, too politically inconvenient to add to a total that will be used against the ministry next year.

Statisticians reply that they already know this, that they publish coverage estimates and post-enumeration surveys, that the professional ethic is to name the error. Naming the error is not the same as refusing the uses of the total. A coverage estimate can become a footnote that licenses the headline number. The public hears fifty million; the appendix whispers that the fifty million is a compromise among several less flattering models. Compromise is not a crime. Treating the compromise as a photograph is.

There is a further twist. Groups that have been historically erased often demand better counting, and they are right to. Visibility in a dataset can be a precondition of funds. Yet the same groups may later discover that a sharper count is also a sharper target: for policing, for debt collection, for the allocation of blame when a service fails. The census does not choose the policy. It does make the policy cheaper to aim.

None of this is an argument for ignorance. A state that refuses to count will invent its numbers in the back room and call the invention common sense. The argument is for a less enchanted relationship to the table. Read the boxes as arguments. Read the missing as a constituency. And when a politician says the numbers speak for themselves, notice that speech is exactly what numbers cannot do until someone supplies a sentence.

TLC results on silica gel after workup.
Fraction analyzed | Observed spots by Rf
Organic layer after bicarbonate extraction | 0.62 and 0.35

passage.title: psg-cars-4
passage.body:
History is not the past itself but a selective reconstruction of the past, assembled from fragmentary evidence by scholars whose questions, categories, and assumptions are inevitably shaped by their own time and place. This observation, often associated with the philosophy of history that emerged in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, does not reduce historical writing to fiction. Yet it does demand that historians acknowledge their craft as an interpretive one rather than a neutral transcription of what happened.
The most influential historians have always made choices: choices about which events to emphasize, which actors to foreground, and which causal chains to trace. A military historian who concentrates on battles and generals produces a different account of the same period than a social historian who foregrounds the lives of ordinary laborers, or an economic historian who treats fluctuations in grain prices as the deeper explanatory variable. None of these accounts is simply wrong; each illuminates a dimension of a complex past while necessarily leaving other dimensions in shadow.
Critics of this pluralism worry that it licenses an anything-goes relativism in which no historical account is better than any other. Defenders respond that recognizing the constructed character of historical narratives is compatible with rigorous standards of evidence, logical consistency, and fidelity to the archival record. An interpretation can be shown to be false if it contradicts well-authenticated documents, or shown to be weak if it ignores a large body of relevant evidence. The standards are not arbitrary, even if the questions that animate historical inquiry are themselves products of particular intellectual climates.
A further complication arises from the role of the historical archive itself. Archives are not neutral repositories of the past; they are collections shaped by decisions about what to preserve, who had the resources to produce written records, and which categories of information administrative systems deemed worth tracking. Consequently, the voices most abundantly represented in archives tend to be those of literate elites, state bureaucracies, and dominant institutions, while the experiences of the illiterate, the dispossessed, and the colonized are filtered through the records of those who observed or administered them from a position of power.
Contemporary historians have developed a range of techniques to recover marginalized perspectives: reading documents 'against the grain' of their intended purpose, triangulating between different types of sources, and drawing on oral traditions and material culture as complementary evidence. These methods have expanded the scope of historical knowledge considerably, even as they have deepened awareness that the gap between the past and the historian's account of it can never be fully closed.
None of this counsels despair about historical knowledge. The recognition that every history is written from somewhere, on the basis of imperfect and unevenly preserved traces, is better understood as a discipline than as a defeat. It obliges the historian to state her guiding questions openly, to weigh the silences of the record as carefully as its assertions, and to hold her conclusions as revisable in the light of new evidence or sharper questions. Readers, for their part, are invited to judge a historical account not by whether it achieves an impossible neutrality but by the range of evidence it engages, the rival explanations it takes seriously, and the candor with which it marks the limits of what it cannot know.

passage.title: psg-bb-8
passage.body:
A cancer-biology lab used flow cytometry to measure the DNA content of individual cells in a proliferating culture. A fluorescent dye that binds DNA in proportion to its amount let the instrument sort cells by how much DNA each contained. Cells in G1 phase, before DNA replication, showed a baseline amount of DNA (call it 2n). Cells in S phase, actively replicating, showed intermediate amounts between 2n and 4n. Cells in G2 and M, having completed replication, showed 4n. A normal asynchronous culture therefore produced two peaks (at 2n and 4n) with cells spread in between.
The team then treated cells with Drug Q. Afterward, nearly all cells piled up in the 2n peak, with almost none at 4n, indicating an arrest before DNA replication began. In a separate experiment, they examined a cell line carrying a nonfunctional version of a checkpoint protein that normally halts cells with damaged DNA. When these mutant cells were irradiated to damage their DNA, they continued through the cycle and divided anyway, accumulating chromosomal abnormalities over successive generations. Unlike normal cells, the mutant cells also kept dividing after covering the surface of the culture dish, having lost contact inhibition.
The investigators connected these observations to tumor formation: checkpoints normally verify that conditions are correct before a cell commits to replication and division, and loss of these controls allows damaged cells to proliferate, a hallmark of cancer.

items.stem:
Iron is atomic number 26. A photoelectron experiment and chemical evidence are summarised:

Species | 4s occupancy | 3d occupancy | unpaired 3d electrons (high-spin)
Fe | 2 | 6 | 4
Fe2+ | 0 | 6 | 4
Fe3+ | 0 | 5 | 5

Neutral Fe is [Ar] 4s2 3d6. Which statement about ionisation and the Aufbau/exchange pattern is supported?

choices.text: Fe and Fe2+ cannot both have four unpaired 3d electrons because ionisation always pairs remaining electrons
The 4s electrons are lost first, so Fe2+ is 3d6; Fe3+ is 3d5, a half-filled high-spin set with five unpaired electrons
3d electrons are always lost before 4s, so Fe2+ would be 4s2 3d4
Fe3+ must be 4s1 3d4 to keep a 4s electron

items.explanation: Cations of the first transition series are formed by emptying 4s before 3d, matching the table: Fe2+ is 4s0 3d6 and Fe3+ is 4s0 3d5. High-spin 3d6 still has four unpaired electrons (↑↑↑↑↑ plus one pair), so Fe and Fe2+ share that count. High-spin 3d5 is five unpaired, the half-filled advantage of Fe3+. Removing 3d before 4s would give Fe2+ as 4s2 3d4, contradicting the occupancy column. There is no requirement to retain a 4s electron in Fe3+, and ionisation does not force pairing of the remaining 3d set.

distractorRationales.A: The unpaired-electron column is 4 for both Fe and Fe2+, which is the high-spin 3d6 count.

passage.title: psg-cars-12
passage.body:
One of the most consequential shifts in twentieth-century philosophy of language was the move away from the view that words get their meaning by standing for objects in the world. On the referentialist picture, to know the meaning of a term like 'gold' is to know which substance the term picks out; to know the meaning of 'Julius Caesar' is to know which historical individual the name refers to. The attractions of this view are obvious: it grounds meaning in something outside language itself, connecting our words to the world they describe and offering a clear criterion for distinguishing correct from incorrect usage.
Yet referentialism encounters serious difficulties when applied to expressions whose meaning does not seem to consist in any reference at all. Words like 'and,' 'perhaps,' 'nevertheless,' and 'of' do not pick out objects, properties, or relations in any obvious sense. Equally problematic are terms whose reference appears to shift depending on context: 'here' refers to wherever the speaker happens to be, 'now' to whenever the utterance is made, and 'I' to whoever is speaking. The meaning of these expressions cannot be their reference, since their reference changes while their meaning remains constant across every ordinary use of the word.
An alternative tradition proposed that meaning is constituted by use. On this view, to know the meaning of a word is not to know what it refers to but to know how to use it -- in what contexts it is appropriately deployed, what inferences it licenses, how it interacts with the meanings of other expressions. This account handles the problematic cases naturally: logical connectives like 'and' are explained by the inferential rules governing their use (the conjunction of P and Q implies both P and Q separately); indexical expressions like 'here' are explained by specifying the rule that they refer to the context of utterance. Knowing the meaning of 'here' means knowing that it picks out the speaker's location, not knowing any particular location.
Critics of the use theory worry that it leaves too little stable content in meaning. If meaning is just use, and use can vary between individual speakers or across historical periods, then there seems to be no fact of the matter about whether two speakers mean the same thing by a word, or whether we mean the same thing by 'democracy' as people in ancient Athens did. Some philosophers have sought to address this by distinguishing between the linguistic meaning of an expression (shared by competent speakers of a language) and speaker meaning (what a particular individual intends to convey in a specific utterance). Semantic theory can then concern itself with the former -- a stable, shared content -- while acknowledging the latter's irreducibly contextual character and the inevitable gap between what a speaker means and what a sentence means.
None of this need force an exclusive choice between the two pictures. A mature semantics may well be pluralistic, allowing that proper names and natural-kind terms lean heavily on reference while connectives, indexicals, and evaluative vocabulary are better explained by the rules governing their use. What the twentieth-century debate established is less the triumph of one theory than the inadequacy of assuming that a single mechanism must underwrite meaning across the whole of a language. The more durable lesson is methodological: before asking what a word means, one does well to ask what kind of word it is, since expressions of different types may secure their significance in quite different ways.

passage.title: psg-cars-15
passage.body:
The concept of the unreliable narrator invites readers to question the testimony of a fictional voice that presents itself as authoritative. An unreliable narrator is one whose account of events, characters, or motives the reader has grounds to distrust -- not necessarily because the narrator lies deliberately, but because their perception is limited, their self-understanding deficient, or their emotional investment in a particular version of events distorts what they report. The detection of narrative unreliability is, accordingly, one of the more sophisticated interpretive skills literary fiction demands of its readers, requiring attention to gaps, contradictions, and moments when the narrator's self-presentation strains against the evidence the text itself provides. The concept therefore depends on a tacit collaboration between author and reader carried on over the narrator's head. Behind the speaking voice stands an implied author who arranges the evidence so that a discerning reader can measure the narrator's claims against it, catching what the narrator misses or conceals. This is why unreliability is a matter of degree and of inference rather than a property simply switched on or off: the same first-person account may strike a careless reader as candid and a careful one as riddled with evasions. Recognizing it depends less on any single tell-tale sentence than on the accumulating weight of discrepancies between what is said and what, on reflection, the text as a whole gives the reader reason to believe.
Narrative theorists have identified several sources of unreliability. The most philosophically interesting is self-deception: the narrator who sincerely believes their own account while systematically misrepresenting it, particularly with respect to their own motives and moral quality. Such narrators often generate irony at their own expense -- the gap between what they report and what the text implies about them becomes the site of the reader's critical engagement. A narrator who insists on their generosity in every paragraph while every described action suggests self-interest produces a portrait more damning than any external indictment could achieve.
A second source is cognitive limitation: the narrator who simply lacks the knowledge or experience to interpret correctly what they observe. A child narrator reporting on adult conflicts without understanding their significance, or an outsider narrator describing an unfamiliar culture through inappropriate categories, produces unreliability through innocence rather than self-interest. In such cases, the reader must supply interpretive frameworks that the narrator cannot, and the gap between the narrator's report and the reader's inference becomes the text's most productive space.
A third source, less often discussed, is structural: some narratives are built on multiple competing narrators whose accounts cannot all be true, or on a narrator who explicitly announces their own limitations and invites the reader to read against them. In the former case, unreliability is dispersed across the text; in the latter, it is ironized through self-consciousness. Both strategies challenge the assumption that narrative access to events is, even in fiction, transparent and unmediated.
The broader significance of narrative unreliability extends beyond literary technique. It models a stance of critical reading that has application outside the text: the recognition that all reported experience is shaped by the particular perspective, interests, and cognitive limitations of the reporter -- a recognition that is as relevant to journalism, autobiography, and legal testimony as it is to fiction. Learning to read unreliable narrators teaches a transferable epistemic skill: suspending credulity and attending to the conditions under which any account is produced.

passage.title: psg-cars-9
passage.body:
Classical economic theory rests on a conception of the agent as fundamentally rational: possessed of stable, consistent preferences, capable of processing available information, and motivated to maximize personal utility. This model has extraordinary analytical power. It generates precise, testable predictions and underlies the welfare theorems that have guided economic policy for generations. Yet beginning in the latter decades of the twentieth century, a body of research in behavioral economics accumulated evidence that humans deviate from this ideal in systematic, predictable, and consequential ways.
Among the most robust findings is loss aversion: people respond more strongly to losses than to equivalent gains. The discomfort of losing one hundred dollars is experienced as more intense than the pleasure of gaining the same amount. This asymmetry has significant implications. It helps explain why people hold losing financial assets far longer than rational profit-maximization would recommend — they prefer the pain of waiting to the certain loss of selling. It also explains why contract and policy framings that emphasize avoiding losses are more motivationally effective than those that emphasize equivalent gains.
A second set of findings concerns heuristic judgment under uncertainty. When people lack the time or information to calculate expected values precisely, they rely on cognitive shortcuts that usually suffice but sometimes produce systematic errors. The availability heuristic leads people to estimate the probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind: dramatic events, such as airplane crashes, are overestimated in frequency because they are memorable, while mundane but statistically commoner risks, such as car accidents, are underestimated. The representativeness heuristic leads people to assess probability by how closely an instance resembles a prototypical category member, often ignoring base-rate information entirely. A familiar illustration involves base rates. Told that a quiet, orderly person who loves books was drawn from a group made up mostly of salespeople and only a few librarians, many respondents confidently judge the person a librarian, swayed by resemblance to a stereotype while all but ignoring how rare librarians are in the sample. The mistake is not stupidity but the misfiring of an ordinarily useful strategy: resemblance is frequently a serviceable guide to category membership, and only in cases engineered to pit it against base-rate information does it lead reliably astray. The shortcuts that behavioral research exposes are, in most everyday settings, both fast and surprisingly accurate; they betray us mainly in the artificial problems constructed to reveal their inner workings.
These findings have generated debate about the appropriate policy response. Some argue that behavioral insights justify 'nudging': designing choice environments so that the default option is the one that most people would choose on reflection. Automatic enrollment in retirement savings plans, for instance, exploits the tendency to accept defaults, boosting participation without eliminating freedom of choice. Critics of nudging worry that it is paternalistic, that it manipulates rather than informs, and that it presupposes policymakers know better than individuals what those individuals' reflective preferences actually are.
The behavioral economics literature does not establish that markets always fail or that regulation is always beneficial. It establishes only that the idealized rational actor is an incomplete description of real human psychology, and that understanding how people actually decide is essential to designing institutions that work well in the world as it is.

passage.title: Official Adjectives (1976)
passage.body: Ibrahim El-Sayed published “Official Adjectives” in 1976 after a season in court translation. The argument is that local knowledge is treated as anecdote until a model needs it. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Xenon difluoride is analysed. Xe contributes 8 valence electrons and each F contributes 7, total 22. The Lewis structure places 3 lone pairs and 2 bonding pairs on Xe (5 electron domains). Five domains adopt a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement; lone pairs occupy equatorial sites. What is the F–Xe–F shape, and is the molecule polar if the two Xe–F bonds are equivalent?

choices.text: Bent and polar, because any molecule with lone pairs is bent
Trigonal planar, using only three of the five domains
Square planar and polar, the 4-domain parentage of XeF4 applied to XeF2
Linear and non-polar, because the two fluorines occupy axial sites 180° apart and the equatorial lone pairs cancel by symmetry

items.explanation: Five electron domains are trigonal bipyramidal. Three lone pairs take the 120° equatorial belt, leaving the two fluorines axial, so the observed molecular shape is linear (F–Xe–F = 180°). Equivalent axial bond dipoles cancel, and the three equatorial lone pairs are symmetrically disposed, so the molecule is non-polar. The presence of lone pairs does not force a bent molecular shape when those lone pairs are equatorial in a TBP. XeF2 is not a three-domain or four-domain problem; that would describe BF3 or XeF4, not 22-electron XeF2.

distractorRationales.A: Lone pairs here occupy equatorial TBP sites, yielding a linear molecular shape, not a bent one.
distractorRationales.B: All five domains around Xe count in VSEPR; ignoring two of them is not justified.
distractorRationales.C: XeF4 is the square-planar 12-electron-on-Xe case (6 domains); XeF2 has only two fluorines.

items.stem: A missense mutation replaces a glycine in a collagen Gly–X–Y repeat with arginine. The mutant chains are still hydroxylated and secreted, but the triple helix melts below 37 °C. Why is glycine uniquely required at every third residue?

choices.text: Glycine’s side-chain carboxylate forms salt bridges that lock the three chains together
Only glycine can be hydroxylated by prolyl hydroxylase, so arginine blocks all Hyp formation
Glycine is the only residue that forms disulfide-bonded collagen dimers
Glycine has no β-carbon, so it fits the sterically crowded interior of the triple helix; arginine’s bulky side chain clashes and unscrews the helix

items.explanation: In tropocollagen each chain is a left-handed polyproline-II-type helix, and three chains wrap into a right-handed triple helix. The residue at every third position packs against the other two chains in a space that can accommodate only hydrogen as a side chain. Glycine uniquely lacks a β-carbon and occupies that interior site. Arginine’s long, charged side chain sterically and electrostatically disrupts packing, lowering the melting temperature even if hydroxylation of Pro/Lys at X and Y still occurs. Glycine is not a carboxylate, is not the substrate of prolyl hydroxylase, and does not form disulfides.

distractorRationales.A: Glycine’s side chain is a hydrogen, not a carboxylate. Salt-bridge chemistry belongs to residues such as Glu, Asp, Lys, and Arg at other positions.
distractorRationales.B: Prolyl hydroxylase acts on proline (and lysyl hydroxylase on lysine) in the Y (and X) positions, not on glycine.
distractorRationales.C: Glycine has no thiol. Collagen’s covalent cross-links after secretion are derived mainly from lysine/hydroxylysine, not from glycine disulfides.

items.stem: Sterile nutrient broth in a swan-neck flask remains clear for months. After the curved neck is broken so that airborne dust can fall into the broth, turbidity appears within a day and microscopy shows rods that are dividing by binary fission. The result most directly supports which statement of cell theory?

choices.text: New cells arise only from preexisting cells; microbial growth here depends on inoculation, not spontaneous generation from the broth
Every cell contains a membrane-bound nucleus, demonstrated by the appearance of turbidity
Mitochondria are the only source of new bacteria when a flask is opened
Broth macromolecules polymerize directly into living cells once oxygen is admitted

items.explanation: Pasteur's swan-neck design showed that sterilized medium does not spawn life on its own: as long as dust and microbes are trapped in the neck, the broth stays sterile. Breaking the neck allows preexisting airborne cells to enter, after which they proliferate by division, producing turbidity. That is experimental support for omnis cellula e cellula and against spontaneous generation. Turbidity does not demonstrate nuclei (these are prokaryotes), mitochondria do not generate free-living bacteria in the flask, and oxygen alone does not polymerize nutrients into cells.

distractorRationales.B: The dividing rods are bacteria, which lack nuclei; turbidity is biomass, not a nuclear envelope.
distractorRationales.C: Mitochondria are organelles inside eukaryotic cells, not a reservoir of bacteria that inoculates broth.
distractorRationales.D: This is spontaneous generation, the hypothesis the experiment refutes.

passage.title: Electron transport, proton coupling, and cytochrome c release
passage.body:
A fictional study examined isolated mitochondria from cultured liver-derived cells. Investigators supplied either pyruvate plus malate, which generate NADH for Complex I, or succinate, which donates electrons through Complex II. They then added inhibitors or a pore-forming BAX-derived peptide. Oxygen consumption, ATP synthesis, inner mitochondrial membrane potential, and cytochrome c detected outside mitochondria were measured. Values are normalized to untreated mitochondria supplied with pyruvate plus malate unless otherwise noted.

Effects of mitochondrial perturbations.
Condition | O2 consumption with pyruvate/malate (%) | O2 consumption with succinate (%) | ATP synthesis (%) | Membrane potential (%) | Cytochrome c outside mitochondria (%)
Control | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 5
Rotenone | 25 | 90 | 35 | 45 | 5
Antimycin A | 10 | 12 | 10 | 20 | 5
Oligomycin | 35 | 38 | 8 | 130 | 5
CCCP | 160 | 155 | 15 | 15 | 5
BAX-derived peptide | 70 | 72 | 60 | 70 | 65

Simplified map of oxidative phosphorylation. — Electrons from NADH enter at Complex I, electrons from succinate enter at Complex II, both pathways pass through ubiquinone to Complex III, cytochrome c, and Complex IV. Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons to create the proton-motive force used by ATP synthase.

items.stem: A secreted enzyme’s native fold contains two disulfides that are required for activity. The protein is unfolded in 6 M guanidinium chloride plus 5 mM DTT. The guanidinium is then dialyzed away at pH 8 while 5 mM DTT remains and oxygen is excluded. What is the most likely outcome?

choices.text: Fully native, active enzyme, because sequence alone always rebuilds native cystines once the chaotrope is gone
Noncovalent collapse can occur, but the cystines remain reduced, so the disulfide-locked native active structure cannot be completed
The backbone is hydrolyzed by DTT, yielding free amino acids
Random incorrect disulfides form immediately because DTT is an oxidant

items.explanation: Guanidinium chloride disrupts noncovalent structure (hydrophobic effect and hydrogen bonds). DTT reduces cystines to thiols. Removing only the chaotrope allows hydrophobic collapse and secondary-structure formation encoded by the sequence, but as long as excess DTT is present and O2 is excluded the thiols cannot oxidize to disulfides. For a secreted enzyme that needs those cystines, the active native fold is therefore not completed. DTT is a reductant, not an oxidant or a protease, so it neither creates random disulfides nor hydrolyzes peptide bonds under these conditions.

distractorRationales.A: Anfinsen’s experiment required removal of reductant and air oxidation (or a reshuffling catalyst) to form the native disulfides. Excess DTT blocks that step.
distractorRationales.C: DTT is a thiol reductant. It does not hydrolyze the polypeptide backbone to amino acids.
distractorRationales.D: DTT keeps cysteines reduced. Random disulfides appear when thiols are oxidized in denaturant without kinetic control, the opposite of this anaerobic DTT setup.

passage.title: Electrochemical Monitoring of Dissolved Oxygen
passage.body:
A fictional microfluidic device is designed to monitor oxygen consumption by cultured cells. The device contains a 10.0 mL sealed gas headspace above an aqueous medium. At the working electrode, oxygen is reduced according to: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O. A 3.0 V source drives current through a variable series resistor and the electrode system. In the tested range, electrode current is approximately proportional to oxygen partial pressure unless the electrode becomes limited by oxygen diffusion from the bulk solution. A pressure sensor in the chamber acts as a parallel-plate capacitor. When gas pressure increases, a flexible membrane deflects toward the fixed plate, decreasing the plate separation d. Before each run, the headspace is sealed, and the table reports conditions just before current is measured.

Operating conditions and measured current for the oxygen sensor.
Run | Headspace O2 mole fraction | Temperature (K) | Total pressure before measurement (atm) | Series resistance (ohm) | Measured current (mA)
R1 | 0.21 | 298 | 1.00 | 1000 | 1.8
R2 | 0.21 | 310 | 1.04 | 1000 | 1.9
R3 | 0.10 | 298 | 1.00 | 1000 | 0.86
R4 | 0.21 | 298 | 1.00 | 500 | 2.4
R5 | 0.21 | 298 | 1.00 | 2000 | 0.95

Current response of the oxygen electrode. — For runs with 1000 ohm resistance, measured current increases approximately linearly with oxygen mole fraction. At lower resistance, the current increases less than expected from Ohm's law, consistent with a diffusion-limited plateau.

items.stem: A homotetrameric allosteric enzyme displays a sigmoidal v versus [S] curve (Hill coefficient ≈ 2.4). A mutation locks every subunit in the high-affinity R conformation. Which change in the saturation curve is most likely?

choices.text: The curve becomes more sigmoidal and the Hill coefficient increases toward the number of subunits
Catalysis is abolished because T-state residues are required for chemistry
The curve becomes more hyperbolic with a lower half-saturation concentration for substrate
Vmax falls to zero while Km is unchanged, as in noncompetitive inhibition by substrate

items.explanation: In the concerted MWC model, cooperativity arises from a T ⇌ R equilibrium in which substrate pulls the ensemble toward R. If a mutation pre-stabilizes R, that equilibrium is already shifted, subunits no longer switch in a concerted way, and the v versus [S] plot loses sigmoidicity (Hill n approaches 1). The R state binds substrate more tightly, so K0.5 decreases. Chemistry can still occur in R—that is the high-activity state—so Vmax need not collapse. The phenotype is the opposite of increased cooperativity and is not described by noncompetitive inhibition.

distractorRationales.A: Locking R removes the T/R switch that generates cooperativity, so the Hill coefficient falls rather than rises.
distractorRationales.B: R is the catalytically competent high-affinity state in the standard model; locking R should preserve catalysis.
distractorRationales.D: Noncompetitive inhibition is a different mechanistic class and would not specifically hyperbolicize a cooperative enzyme.

passage.title: psg-ps-2
passage.body:
A memory researcher tested how the way information is studied affects later recall. In Phase 1, 90 undergraduates saw a list of 30 common nouns, one every three seconds. Each word was preceded by one of three questions: whether the word was printed in capital letters (structural), whether it rhymed with a target word (phonemic), or whether it fit meaningfully into a sentence (semantic). After a filled delay, participants took a surprise free-recall test.
Recall rose steadily with the depth of processing: 18% for structural, 37% for phonemic, and 65% for semantic judgments. In addition, regardless of the processing condition, words from the beginning and end of the list were recalled better than words from the middle. When recall was delayed by 30 seconds of counting backward, the advantage for the last few items disappeared, but the advantage for the first few items remained.
In Phase 2, participants watched a short video of a car approaching an intersection. Afterward, half were asked, 'How fast was the car going when it passed the yield sign?' though the video actually showed a stop sign. A week later, participants who had received the misleading question were far more likely to report having seen a yield sign than participants asked a neutral question. The researchers argued that memory is not a faithful recording but is encoded selectively and reconstructed at retrieval, so that later information can alter what is 'remembered.'

items.stem: In the systemic circulation, the mean speed of blood is lowest in the capillaries. The best physical reason is that capillaries, taken as a bed:

choices.text: have the smallest individual radii, and Poiseuille's law then forces speed to be lowest in the narrowest tubes
have the largest total cross-sectional area, so continuity (Q = A v) requires the lowest mean speed
have the highest hydrostatic pressure, which stalls erythrocytes between heartbeats
contain one-way valves that bring flow to zero in diastole

items.explanation: Cardiac output is the volume flow rate through the systemic circuit as a whole. Continuity then says Q = A_total v_mean is the same (in series-averaged terms) along the circuit, so the bed with the largest total cross-sectional area has the smallest mean speed. Millions of capillaries in parallel give that maximum area, even though each capillary is individually narrow. Hydrostatic pressure is highest in the aorta, not the capillaries, and one-way valves are a venous feature, not a capillary one. Poiseuille's r^4 law governs resistance of a single tube; it does not by itself set the speed ranking across the vascular tree.

distractorRationales.A: An individual capillary is narrow, but the capillary bed is a huge parallel network. Continuity uses total area, which is largest—not smallest—at the capillaries, so mean speed is lowest there.
distractorRationales.C: Hydrostatic pressure falls along the arterial tree and is not highest in capillaries; the aorta is the high-pressure vessel. High pressure would not by itself minimize speed.
distractorRationales.D: Valves that prevent retrograde flow sit in veins, not capillaries. Capillary flow is slow and relatively steady; it is not gated to zero each diastole by valves.

passage.title: psg-cp-5
passage.body:
Nuclear medicine uses radioactive isotopes to image the body. The most widely used tracer, technetium-99m, is a metastable ('m') nuclear state that returns to its ground state by emitting a single gamma-ray photon, without changing its number of protons or neutrons. Because those gamma photons escape the body and reach a gamma camera, and because the isotope's half-life is a convenient 6.0 hours, it images well and clears quickly. A patient receives an initial activity of 800 MBq, and the staff track how the activity falls over the following day.
Positron emission tomography (PET) uses a different decay. Fluorine-18, built into a glucose analog, decays by positron emission: inside the nucleus a proton is converted into a neutron, and a positron is ejected. The positron soon annihilates with a nearby electron, producing two photons the scanner detects in coincidence.
The passage also compares decay modes. Some heavy parents decay by alpha emission, ejecting a helium-4 nucleus, while others undergo beta-minus decay. In every case the totals of mass number and charge are conserved across the nuclear equation. Finally, the team notes that alpha, beta, and especially gamma emissions are all 'ionizing': each quantum can carry enough energy to eject electrons from the atoms it strikes, which is both the basis of detection and the reason for strict dose limits. Planck's relation ties a photon's energy to its frequency, and gamma photons lie at the high-energy end of the electromagnetic spectrum.

passage.title: Allosteric regulation of a glycolytic kinase
passage.body:
Researchers studied PFK-X, a fictional tetrameric phosphofructokinase isoform that catalyzes the conversion of fructose 6-phosphate (F6P) and ATP to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate and ADP in rapidly dividing cells. ATP is both a substrate and, at high concentration, a negative allosteric regulator. AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate favor the active R state, whereas citrate favors the less active T state. The investigators purified wild-type PFK-X and several variants, then measured initial velocity at pH 7.4 while varying F6P. ATP was held at 2.0 mM in all assays.

Kinetic properties of PFK-X under selected conditions.
Enzyme and condition | S0.5 for F6P (mM) | Relative Vmax (%) | Hill coefficient
Wild type | 0.80 | 100 | 2.8
Wild type + AMP | 0.25 | 105 | 1.4
Wild type + citrate | 1.60 | 95 | 3.0
R212E variant | 1.20 | 85 | 1.2
R212E variant + AMP | 1.10 | 84 | 1.2
D150N variant | Not determined | <5 | Not determined

Oligomeric state of PFK-X variants measured by native gel electrophoresis.
Protein | Tetrameric protein (%) | Dimeric protein (%)
Wild type | 92 | 8
R212E variant | 88 | 12
D150N variant | 90 | 10
C-terminal truncation | 45 | 55

Initial velocity curves for PFK-X. — Wild-type PFK-X shows a sigmoidal dependence on F6P. Addition of AMP shifts the curve left with little change in the plateau. Addition of citrate shifts the curve right. The R212E variant shows a more hyperbolic curve that changes minimally when AMP is added.

The pH is greater than 7 because leftover ammonia dominates.

items.explanation: Equivalence converts NH3 completely to NH4+. The flask holds an aqueous ammonium salt, a weak acid. Ka(NH4+) = Kw/Kb = 5.6 × 10^−10, so [H3O+] ≈ √(Ka C) = √(5.6 × 10^−10 × 0.050) ≈ 5.3 × 10^−6 and pH ≈ 5.3, acidic. Equal moles do not imply pH 7 when the product ion hydrolyzes. pH = pKa = 9.26 is the half-equivalence point of this titration (buffer NH3/NH4+), not equivalence. Leftover NH3 would make the solution basic only before equivalence.

distractorRationales.A: Neutralization to NH4Cl does not yield a pH-neutral solution; ammonium is acidic.
distractorRationales.C: 9.26 is pKa of NH4+ and is the pH at half-equivalence, where [NH3] = [NH4+].

Experiment | [A]0 (M) | rate (M s−1)

passage.title: Courtesy at the checkpoint
passage.body:
A border official is trained in courtesy as if courtesy were a disinfectant. Smile, use the family name, apologize for the wait. The training manuals are not cynical. They are trying to prevent the obvious cruelty of a raised voice. What they cannot prevent is the deeper grammar of the encounter: one person may leave, the other must persuade a stranger that her life is plausible.

Liberal theory likes to treat this grammar as an unfortunate delay on the way to a principle. In the principle, the stranger is already a rights-bearer; the checkpoint is a bureaucratic remainder. On the ground, the remainder is the event. Rights that must be performed as a story—complete, sequential, tearful at the approved moments—are rights as an audition. The official who says “help me to help you” is not necessarily a villain. He is naming the price of entry into a language that pretends it is only asking for facts.

Scholars of hospitality distinguish welcome from inspection. The distinction is cleaner on the page than in a queue. Inspection can dress as welcome, and welcome can become inspection the moment a detail fails to match a database. A cup of tea in an interview room is not the opposite of a file. It can be the file’s most efficient instrument, loosening speech until it can be contradicted.

None of this requires pretending that states have no legitimate interest in knowing who crosses. It requires noticing that “legitimate interest” is not a measuring cup. It expands. Yesterday’s emergency power is today’s ordinary form. Tomorrow’s form will be justified by the person who told her story too well, or too badly, last year. The archive of interviews becomes a training set for suspicion.

The courteous checkpoint is therefore not a milder politics. It is a politics that has learned to sound like a service. If we want a different politics, we will need a different distribution of who must be plausible to whom—not a warmer script for the same audition.

passage.title: The Archive Test (1977)
passage.body: Kwame Boateng's 1977 essay “The Archive Test,” on university hiring, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that expertise without a named audience is just private language. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem:
Equal volumes of 0.20 M HCl and 0.20 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10^−5) are mixed. After mixing, each solute is diluted by two:

Species | Concentration after mixing (mol L−1)
HCl (strong) | 0.10
CH3COOH | 0.10

Four estimates of the mixture pH are offered. Which is defensible?

choices.text: pH ≈ 1.00, because the strong acid sets [H+] ≈ 0.10 M and suppresses ionization of acetic acid.
pH ≈ 2.87, the weak-acid formula √(Ka × 0.10) applied as if HCl were absent.
pH = 4.74, equal to pKa of acetic acid, as if the mixture were an equimolar buffer of HA and A−.
pH = 7.00, because equal molar amounts of two acids cancel.

items.explanation: HCl is fully dissociated, so after the twofold dilution [H+] from HCl is 0.10 M and pH = 1.00. Acetic acid’s additional contribution is tiny: Ka = [H+][A−]/[HA] ≈ (0.10)[A−]/0.10, so [A−] ≈ Ka = 1.8 × 10^−5 M, which does not change [H+] at the precision of these options. The mixture is not a buffer, because no acetate salt was added and HCl does not convert HA into A−; HCl actually protonates any A−. Two acids cannot neutralize each other to pH 7. Ignoring HCl and using only the acetic-acid square-root formula yields pH ≈ 2.87, which contradicts the presence of 0.10 M strong acid.

distractorRationales.B: The √(Ka C) estimate is for a solution containing only the weak acid. Here 0.10 M HCl already supplies [H+] = 0.10 M, so pH cannot be 2.87.
distractorRationales.C: pH = pKa requires a comparable amount of A−, as in a buffer. This mixture contains HA and HCl, not a 1:1 HA/A− pair.
distractorRationales.D: Acids do not neutralize other acids. There is no base present in stoichiometric amount, so the mixture remains strongly acidic.

items.stem: A preschooler “plays doctor” by putting on a coat and giving a stuffed animal a shot (one role at a time). A year later she plays a clinic game in which she coordinates nurse, parent, and patient and refers to “what the doctor is supposed to do.” Mead’s stages of self development treat the later game as the emergence of which structure?

choices.text: The preparatory stage of mere imitation, which already contains the generalized other
The play stage only, because multiple roles still mean there is no “me”
The game stage, in which the child takes the organized perspective of the generalized other
Freud’s superego, which Mead defined as identical to the I

items.explanation: Mead distinguished preparatory imitation, play (taking one significant other’s role), and the game (organizing multiple roles into the generalized other—the attitude of the community). The clinic game with “what the doctor is supposed to do” is that organized perspective, which becomes the “me.” The “I” is the spontaneous subject responding to the “me.” Freud’s superego is a different architecture; Mead did not equate it with the I. Preparatory imitation lacks this coordination.

distractorRationales.A: Preparatory imitation is earlier and does not yet hold the generalized other.
distractorRationales.B: Play is single-role; coordinating a clinic is Mead’s game.
distractorRationales.D: Mead’s I is not Freud’s superego.

items.stem: A motor-nerve terminal is bathed in cadmium, which blocks voltage-gated calcium channels. Sodium-dependent action potentials still invade the terminal, but end-plate potentials disappear. The missing step is:

choices.text: Calcium-triggered fusion of synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic membrane, releasing acetylcholine
Potassium leak through resting channels, which is the sole requirement for transmitter release
Myelination of the muscle fiber, without which ACh cannot bind nicotinic receptors
Retrograde spikes in T-tubules that pump ACh out of the muscle into the cleft

items.explanation: Presynaptic depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels at active zones. The local Ca2+ rise binds synaptotagmin and drives SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion, dumping ACh into the cleft to open muscle nicotinic receptors. Cadmium blocks those Ca2+ channels, so spikes still occur (Na+-dependent) but exocytosis fails and EPPs vanish. Resting K+ leak sets resting potential; it does not substitute for the Ca2+ trigger. Muscle is unmyelinated at the end plate, and T-tubules conduct muscle APs after, not before, ACh binding; they do not secrete ACh.

distractorRationales.B: K+ leak influences excitability but is not the exocytotic trigger; Ca2+ is.
distractorRationales.C: Skeletal muscle fibers are not myelinated; receptor binding does not require myelin.
distractorRationales.D: ACh is released from the nerve terminal, not pumped out of T-tubules.

items.stem: In the presence of a reversible inhibitor, Vmax of an enzyme decreases but Km is unchanged. Increasing substrate concentration cannot restore the original Vmax. The inhibitor most likely:

choices.text: Binds equally well to E and ES at a site distinct from the substrate, lowering the population of functional catalytic cycles
Competes directly for the active site, which would have increased Km at constant Vmax
Is actually a second substrate that is turned over faster than the assayed substrate
Binds only ES (uncompetitive), which would have decreased apparent Km as well as Vmax

items.explanation: When inhibitor affinity for E and ES is equal (α = α′ in the general mixed scheme), the Michaelis constant is unaltered because substrate binding is not biased, but a fraction of enzyme is sequestered in nonproductive EI and ESI complexes, so Vmax falls. Saturating substrate cannot displace an inhibitor that still binds ES. That is classic noncompetitive inhibition and matches the vignette. Competitive inhibition would raise Km and spare Vmax. A better alternative substrate would be a competing reaction, not a simple Vmax drop at constant Km. Uncompetitive inhibition decreases apparent Km.

distractorRationales.B: Direct active-site competition is competitive inhibition: Vmax unchanged, Km increased—the opposite pattern.
distractorRationales.C: A faster alternative substrate would consume enzyme in another reaction; it is not the definition of this inhibitor pattern.
distractorRationales.D: Uncompetitive inhibitors lower apparent Km (higher apparent affinity) together with Vmax; Km was said to be unchanged.

passage.title: Mental Health Messaging, Stigma, and Help-Seeking Intentions
passage.body:
A campus research group tested how different messages influence responses to a fictional vignette about a student named R who has experienced repeated episodes of sudden intense fear, rapid heartbeat, trembling, and worry about having another episode. Participants were randomly assigned to read one of four messages before viewing the vignette: a neutral campus-services message, a biological-explanation message, a coping-continuum message emphasizing that distress varies in degree and can be managed with support, or a danger-focused message emphasizing rare extreme outcomes. Participants then rated recognition of clinically significant distress, stigma, and willingness to recommend help-seeking.

Mean outcomes by message condition
Message condition | Recognized clinically significant distress (%) | Stigma rating, 1 to 7 | Willingness to recommend help-seeking, 1 to 7
Neutral campus-services message | 62 | 3.8 | 3.9
Biological-explanation message | 76 | 3.5 | 4.4
Coping-continuum message | 72 | 2.7 | 5.1
Danger-focused message | 80 | 5.2 | 3.1

Ethical note — The researchers debriefed participants after the study and provided a list of campus and community support resources. The vignette was fictional and was not used to diagnose participants.

passage.title: Working Memory, Sleep Restriction, and Retrieval Cues
passage.body:
A fictional laboratory study examined how one night of sleep restriction affects memory performance. Participants were randomly assigned to either a normal-sleep group or a restricted-sleep group. The next morning, all participants studied 30 neutral word pairs. After a 20-minute filler task, they completed two tests. In the free-recall test, participants wrote down as many target words as possible. In the cued-recall test, participants were shown the first word of each pair and attempted to retrieve the associated target word. Participants also completed a 2-back task as a measure of working memory updating.

Memory and working-memory performance
Group | Free recall: mean words recalled | Cued recall: mean words recalled | 2-back accuracy (%)
Normal sleep | 18.4 | 24.1 | 87
Restricted sleep | 13.2 | 20.2 | 73

Self-reported fatigue and motivation
Group | Fatigue rating, 1 to 7 | Motivation rating, 1 to 7
Normal sleep | 2.3 | 5.8
Restricted sleep | 5.9 | 5.6

Retrieval benefit — Both groups recalled more words on cued recall than on free recall, but the restricted-sleep group performed worse than the normal-sleep group on both tests.

passage.title: psg-cars-1
passage.body:
Is there any knowledge in the world so certain that no reasonable person could doubt it? This question, which at first sight might not seem difficult, is really among the most difficult that can be asked. In daily life we assume as certain many things which, on closer scrutiny, are found to be so full of apparent contradictions that only a great deal of thought enables us to know what it is that we may really believe.
Consider the plain table before me. To the eye it appears rectangular, brown, and shiny; to the touch it is smooth, cool, and hard; when I tap it, it gives out a wooden sound. Anyone else who sees, feels, and hears the table will agree with this description, so it might seem that no difficulty could arise. But the moment we try to be more precise, our troubles begin. Although I believe that the table is 'really' of one uniform brown, the parts that reflect the light look far brighter than the rest, and some parts look white because of reflected light. If I move, the parts that reflect the light change, so that the apparent distribution of colours upon the table shifts. It follows that if several people look at the table at the same moment, no two of them will see exactly the same distribution of colours, for no two can view it from precisely the same point, and any change in the point of view changes the way in which the light is reflected.
For most practical purposes these differences are unimportant, but to the painter they are all-important: the painter has to unlearn the habit of thinking that things seem to have the colour which common sense says they 'really' have, and to learn the habit of seeing things as they appear. Here we already meet with one of the distinctions that cause the most trouble in philosophy — the distinction between 'appearance' and 'reality,' between what things seem to be and what they are. The table, if it is 'real' at all, must have some real colour; yet the colour we see is not a property of the table in itself but something depending upon the table, the observer, and the way the light falls. When, in ordinary life, we speak of the colour of the table, we mean only the sort of colour which it will seem to have to a normal spectator, under ordinary conditions of light, from an ordinary point of view. But the other colours which appear under other conditions have just as good a right to be considered real; and so, to avoid favouritism, we are compelled to deny that the table has any one particular colour.
The same holds for the texture. With the naked eye the grain of the wood looks smooth and even; under a microscope it shows roughness, and hills and valleys, and all sorts of differences that are imperceptible to unaided sight. Which of these is the 'real' table? We are naturally tempted to say that what we see through the microscope is more real; yet a still more powerful instrument would reveal something different again, so that we can never rest content with what the eye alone reports. Thus confidence in the senses, which had seemed so secure, begins to desert us.
It becomes evident that the real table, if there is one, is not the same as what we immediately experience by sight or touch or hearing. The real table, if it exists, is not immediately known to us at all, but must be an inference from what is immediately known. Hence two very difficult questions at once arise: Is there a real table at all? And if so, what sort of object can it be?

passage.title: psg-cp-1
passage.body:
A biomechanics laboratory studies vertical jumping with a force platform, a rigid plate that records the force a person exerts on it as a function of time. A 60 kg athlete stands motionless on the platform and then performs a maximal jump: she dips down, drives upward, and leaves the plate. High-speed video tracks a marker on her hip to follow the vertical motion of her center of mass.
While the athlete stands still, the platform reads a steady value equal to her weight. During the propulsion phase the reading rises well above this baseline, climbs to a peak, and then drops abruptly to zero at the instant her feet leave the plate. The interval from the start of propulsion to takeoff lasts about 0.20 s. After takeoff the center of mass rises to a measured peak height of 0.45 m above its takeoff position before falling back. Treating the body as a point mass at the center of mass and neglecting air resistance, the researchers reconstruct the takeoff velocity, the mechanical energy of the jump, and the forces during landing.
On landing, the athlete returns to the plate moving downward, and the platform again registers a large force as she decelerates to rest over about 0.15 s. The researchers note that athletes who land with stiff legs stop in a shorter time and record much larger peak forces than athletes who flex their knees and ankles to cushion the impact. Throughout, the platform measures the contact force between athlete and plate; gravitational acceleration is taken as g = 10 m/s^2.

Keq = [products]/[reactants]; a large Keq means products dominate at equilibrium. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

items.stem: "If the bridge is not repaired, the town will be cut off during floods. The bridge was repaired. Therefore, the town will not be cut off during floods." This argument is:

choices.text: Valid, because it correctly negates both the condition and the consequence.
Valid, because bridges prevent all flooding.
Invalid — this is "denying the antecedent"; repairing the bridge removes one risk but other causes of being cut off (e.g. landslides, road closures) may remain.
Invalid, because the original conditional statement is false.

items.explanation: The original statement only tells us what happens if the bridge is NOT repaired; it says nothing about what guarantees safety once it is repaired. Other causes of being cut off could still exist. From "if A then B," you cannot validly conclude "if not-A then not-B." The conditional only tells you about the presence of A, not what happens in its absence — a very common invalid pattern in GAMSAT-style arguments. Memory tip: "Fixing one door doesn't lock the whole house": repairing the bridge closes one named route to disaster, but other doors (other causes) may still be open. Never assume removing one stated cause removes every cause. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

passage.title: The Caption (1981)
passage.body: In “The Caption” (1981), Fatima Al-Hassan writes from inside court translation. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: A 10 N force is applied to a door at a point 2 m from the hinge. The angle between the position vector from the hinge to that point and the force vector is 30 degrees. The magnitude of the torque about the hinge is:
items.explanation: Torque magnitude is τ = r F sin θ, where θ is the angle between r and F. Here r = 2 m, F = 10 N, and θ = 30°, so sin 30° = 1/2 and τ = (2)(10)(1/2) = 10 N·m. Only the component of force perpendicular to the lever arm produces torque; that component is F sin 30° = 5 N, and 5 N times 2 m is again 10 N·m. Using sin 90° treats the force as fully perpendicular and doubles the torque.

distractorRationales.B: This is r F with sin θ omitted, as if the force were perpendicular to the door. The 30° angle cuts the perpendicular component in half.
distractorRationales.C: This uses sin 60° or cos 30° (about 0.87) in place of sin 30°. The problem defines θ as the angle between r and F, whose sine is 1/2.
distractorRationales.D: This is (1/2) F or r sin 30° without multiplying by the remaining factor, giving half of the already-halved result.

items.stem: In a psychophysics demonstration, a participant can just notice when 2 g are added to a 100 g weight. According to Weber's law, which added mass would the participant be most likely to just notice when lifting a 300 g weight?
items.explanation: Weber's law states that the just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus intensity. If 2 g is just noticeable for 100 g, the Weber fraction is 2/100 = 0.02. For 300 g, 0.02 × 300 g = 6 g. Common miss: Assuming that the smallest detectable change is the same absolute amount at every stimulus intensity. This is correct. The just-noticeable difference scales proportionally with stimulus intensity. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.B: This treats the difference threshold as constant rather than proportional to the starting weight.

items.stem: During a high NADH/NAD+ ratio, flux through the citric acid cycle slows. Besides pyruvate dehydrogenase, which pair of cycle enzymes is most directly inhibited by elevated NADH?

choices.text: Aconitase and fumarase, which are NAD+-dependent dehydrogenases
Succinyl-CoA synthetase and citrate synthase, which use NADH as a substrate
Succinate dehydrogenase and malate dehydrogenase, both of which are activated by NADH

items.explanation: The NAD+-dependent oxidative decarboxylations of isocitrate and of α-ketoglutarate are major irreversible control points of the cycle. Both dehydrogenases are inhibited by NADH (and α-KGDH also by succinyl-CoA), so a high NADH/NAD+ ratio throttles flux in addition to PDH inhibition. Aconitase and fumarase are not NAD+-dependent dehydrogenases. Neither succinyl-CoA synthetase nor citrate synthase uses NADH as a substrate; mammalian citrate synthase is not primarily NADH-gated the way bacterial citrate synthase can be. NADH does not activate SDH or malate dehydrogenase; a high NADH/NAD+ ratio instead opposes malate oxidation at the near-equilibrium MDH step.

distractorRationales.B: Aconitase and fumarase catalyze hydration/dehydration reactions and do not use NAD+. They are not the NADH-sensitive control points of the cycle.
distractorRationales.C: Succinyl-CoA synthetase uses the thioester energy of succinyl-CoA to make GTP; citrate synthase uses acetyl-CoA and OAA. Neither consumes NADH as a substrate.
distractorRationales.D: NADH does not activate these enzymes. High NADH actually disfavors NAD+-dependent malate oxidation, and SDH uses FAD rather than NAD+.

A buffer is made from ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.76) and sodium ethanoate. Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log10([A−]/[HA]). Three mixtures, all at 25 °C:

Mixture | [HA] (M) | [A−] (M)
P | 0.10 | 0.10
Q | 0.10 | 0.20
R | 0.20 | 0.10

log10(2) = 0.30. What are the three pH values?

choices.text: P 0.00; Q 0.30; R −0.30, reporting only the log term

items.explanation: When [A−]=[HA], log10(1)=0 and pH=pKa=4.76. Mixture Q has [A−]/[HA]=2, so pH=4.76+0.30=5.06. Mixture R has ratio 0.50, log10(0.50)=−0.30, pH=4.46. Inverting the ratio swaps Q and R. Constancy of pKa does not freeze pH when the buffer ratio changes—that is the point of Henderson–Hasselbalch. The log term alone is not a pH.

distractorRationales.A: pKa is the centre, but pH still follows the log ratio, as Q and R show.
distractorRationales.B: Those figures omit pKa; pH values near 0 or negative are not ethanoic buffers.
distractorRationales.D: Q is the acetate-rich buffer and must sit above pKa; R is acid-rich and sits below.

items.stem: Myelination of a peripheral axon increases conduction speed primarily because myelin:

choices.text: decreases membrane resistance and increases membrane capacitance, so local-circuit current leaks more readily through internodes
increases membrane resistance and decreases membrane capacitance, forcing depolarizing current to jump between nodes of Ranvier
replaces voltage-gated Na+ channels uniformly along the internodal membrane, producing a continuous (non-saltatory) wave of depolarization
converts the axon into a gap-junction electrical synapse that no longer requires ion channels to propagate an impulse

items.explanation: Myelin is a high-resistance, low-capacitance wrapping. Higher internodal membrane resistance reduces transverse leak, so axial current travels farther; lower capacitance means less charge is needed to depolarize the internodal membrane. Voltage-gated Na+ channels concentrate at the unmyelinated nodes of Ranvier, and the action potential is regenerated there—saltatory conduction. The internodes are not paved with Na+ channels, and the axon remains an excitable membrane, not a gap-junction synapse. The opposite cable changes (low Rm, high C) would slow conduction.

distractorRationales.A: Those cable changes are what myelin prevents. Decreasing Rm and increasing C would increase leak and the charge needed per unit length, slowing—not speeding—propagation.
distractorRationales.C: Internodal membrane is poor in voltage-gated Na+ channels; the channels cluster at nodes. Conduction is saltatory, not a continuous internodal Hodgkin cycle.
distractorRationales.D: Myelin does not turn the axon into an electrical synapse. Propagation still depends on local-circuit current and nodal Na+ influx.

items.stem: Use PV = nRT with R = 0.080 L atm mol−1 K−1. A cylinder contains 2.0 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K in 24 L. What is the pressure? After a leak at constant T and V the pressure falls to 1.0 atm, how many moles remain?

Initial P = 2.0 atm; 1.0 mol remains after the leak

items.explanation: P = nRT/V = 2.0 × 0.080 × 300 / 24 = 48 / 24 = 2.0 atm. At the same T and V, P is proportional to n, so halving P to 1.0 atm halves n to 1.0 mol. Inverting n and V would give 0.50 atm. Fixed T and V do not freeze n when gas leaks; P would then stay 2.0 atm. Using V in place of nRT/V gives 24 atm, which is the volume number, not the pressure.

distractorRationales.A: A leak at falling P must remove moles; T and V being fixed is why n tracks P.
distractorRationales.B: 24 is the volume in litres, not P, and 0.080 is R, not the remaining n.
distractorRationales.D: 0.50 atm is V/(nRT) or a swapped n and V; the leak cannot increase the mole count to 4.0.

items.stem: When the proton-motive force is high and ADP is scarce, electrons dwell on Complex I and III cofactors and can reduce O2 univalently to superoxide. Which statement about this oxidative-stress path is correct?

choices.text: Superoxide is harmless because it is more reduced than water and cannot damage Fe–S proteins.
Catalase is the first enzyme that converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide in the mitochondrial matrix.
Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and O2; glutathione peroxidase (and catalase in some compartments) then removes H2O2.
Uncoupling proteins always increase superoxide production by slowing electron transport.

items.explanation: Electron leak from reduced flavin or Q-cycle intermediates onto O2 produces superoxide (O2−). Mitochondrial MnSOD (and Cu/ZnSOD in the intermembrane space/cytosol) dismutates two superoxide molecules to hydrogen peroxide and O2. H2O2 is then reduced to water by glutathione peroxidase (important in mitochondria) or disproportionated by catalase (especially peroxisomes). Superoxide can oxidize and inactivate Fe–S clusters, so it is not harmless. Uncoupling generally lowers ROS by accelerating electron flow and oxidizing the leaky centers, rather than always increasing superoxide. The SOD → peroxidase/catalase sequence is the standard detoxification path tested on the MCAT.

distractorRationales.A: Superoxide is a reactive oxygen species that can oxidize Fe–S clusters and lead to further radicals; it is not harmless simply because it is a reduced form of oxygen.
distractorRationales.B: Superoxide dismutase, not catalase, is the enzyme that acts on superoxide. Catalase acts on H2O2 after SOD (or other H2O2 sources) produces it.
distractorRationales.D: Mild uncoupling typically decreases mitochondrial ROS by relieving highly reduced, high-Δp states that favor electron leak, so ‘always increase’ is the opposite of the usual effect.

items.stem: For competitive inhibition, K_m,app = K_m (1 + [I]/K_i). Using Table 1 and [Q] = 2.0 μM, the K_i of Compound Q is
items.explanation: Compound Q raises apparent K_m from 0.50 mM to 1.50 mM at constant V_max, which is the competitive signature. Substituting into K_m,app = K_m (1 + [I]/K_i) gives 1.50 = 0.50 (1 + 2.0 μM / K_i). Dividing through by 0.50 yields 3 = 1 + 2.0/K_i, so 2.0/K_i = 2 and K_i = 1.0 μM. The numerical answer is fixed by the tabulated K_m pair and the stated 2.0 μM dose; a different row of Table 1 would give a different constant. Treating Q as noncompetitive and using the V_max ratio is invalid because Q does not change V_max.

distractorRationales.B: 0.67 μM is [I] × K_m / K_m,app = 2.0 × 0.50/1.50, which omits the correct rearrangement of the competitive factor (1 + [I]/K_i).
distractorRationales.C: 2.0 μM is the inhibitor concentration itself, or the noncompetitive K_i one would extract from Compound P’s halved V_max; it is not Q’s competitive K_i.
distractorRationales.D: 3.0 μM is the dimensionless ratio K_m,app/K_m misread as a micromolar dissociation constant.

passage.title: Reversible inhibitors of a cytosolic dehydrogenase
passage.body:
Investigators purified a cytosolic NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase that oxidizes a small-molecule metabolite S. Initial velocities were measured at 25 °C by following NADH formation in 1.00 mL assays. Nonlinear fits of v versus [S] produced the apparent Michaelis constants and maximal velocities in Table 1. When an inhibitor was present, its concentration was 2.0 μM in the assay mix. Dialysis that removed unbound compound restored full catalytic activity after incubation with P, Q, or R, indicating reversible binding rather than covalent inactivation. Active-site titration with a tight-binding stoichiometric inactivator found 4.0 nmol of catalytic sites per milligram of protein.

Table 1. Apparent kinetic parameters from initial-rate fits

| Condition | Apparent K_m (mM) | Apparent V_max (nmol s^{-1} mg^{-1}) |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------------------------|
| No inhibitor | 0.50 | 80 |
| Compound P (2.0 μM) | 0.50 | 40 |
| Compound Q (2.0 μM) | 1.50 | 80 |
| Compound R (2.0 μM) | 0.25 | 40 |

In a separate progress-curve experiment, 25 μg of the same enzyme protein was mixed with 0.50 mM S and no inhibitor in a 1.00 mL reaction. Product concentration was recorded as a function of time (Table 2).

Table 2. Product appearance at [S]_0 = 0.50 mM without inhibitor

| Time (s) | [Product] (μM) |
|----------|----------------|
| 0 | 0.0 |
| 10 | 9.9 |
| 20 | 19.6 |
| 30 | 29.1 |
| 60 | 56.2 |
| 120 | 102.4 |

items.stem:
Cardiac output (CO) = heart rate × stroke volume. Three measurements on one subject:

State | HR (min−1) | SV (mL)
Rest | 70 | 80
Exercise | 140 | 100
Haemorrhage | 120 | 40

Which comparison of CO is correct?

choices.text: Rest 5.6 L min−1; exercise 7.0 L min−1 (using resting SV); haemorrhage 9.6 L min−1
All three states have the same CO because the product HR × SV is conserved by homeostasis
Rest 5.6 L min−1; exercise 14.0 L min−1; haemorrhage 4.8 L min−1
Rest 150 mL min−1; exercise 240; haemorrhage 160, summing HR and SV

items.explanation: Rest: 70 × 80 = 5600 mL min−1 = 5.6 L min−1. Exercise: 140 × 100 = 14 000 mL min−1 = 14.0 L min−1. Haemorrhage: 120 × 40 = 4800 mL min−1 = 4.8 L min−1. Adding HR to SV is not a cardiac output. Using resting SV in exercise underestimates CO, and using 120 × 80 would invent a 9.6 L haemorrhage output the table does not contain. The three products are different, so CO is not conserved across these states.

distractorRationales.A: Exercise SV is 100 mL not 80, and haemorrhage SV is 40 mL not 80.
distractorRationales.B: The three products 5.6, 14.0 and 4.8 L min−1 are unequal, so CO is not invariant.
distractorRationales.D: Cardiac output is a product of rate and volume ejected per beat, not a sum, and the units would not be mL min−1 in that sense.

The next sentence grants they are not wrong about the market and immediately denies that the market is a theory of meaning. That pairing is an explicit retrieval, not an inference from tone. passage.title: The courtesy of untranslatability
passage.body:
Historians of language like to treat translation as a pipe: meaning enters one end, equivalent wording exits the other, and any turbulence is a defect in the plumber. The figure is flattering to publishers, who can then sell fluency as fidelity, and it is flattering to readers, who can then consume a foreign argument as if it had always been written in their kitchen. The figure is also false. A translation is not a transfer of a stable cargo. It is a series of decisions about which silences will remain audible and which will be paved over so that a page turns without snagging.

Consider the ordinary boast that a novel has been rendered into "perfectly natural" English. Natural for whom? The boast treats the target language as a climate rather than as a historically specific set of habits, class markers, and tolerated opacities. When a rural insult is recast as a metropolitan joke, or a liturgical cadence is recast as a magazine paragraph, the text has not been rescued from awkwardness. It has been enrolled in a local etiquette. The reader who thanks the translator for making the book "not feel translated" is thanking the translator for hiding the fact that hospitality occurred. Hospitality, if it is more than a smile, leaves a trace of the guest.

This is not an argument for wooden calques or for the museum of untranslated words left standing like exhibits. Those tactics can become their own piety, a performance of difficulty that congratulates the reader for enduring it. The more serious failure is the opposite one: the belief that a text which does not delay us has therefore been understood. Delay is sometimes the only honest report of a conceptual mismatch. A legal term that organizes a whole civic world cannot be swapped for a near-synonym without smuggling in the civic world of the synonym. To refuse the delay is to pretend that the two worlds already agreed.

Publishers will object that readers abandon books that snag. They are not wrong about the market. They are wrong to treat the market as a theory of meaning. A culture that will only receive what has already been made to sound like itself is not receiving; it is recruiting. The translated page then becomes a mirror with a foreign name on the title page, and the prestige of the foreign name is used to ratify what the reader already believed. That is why "accessible" can function as a political adjective. It names not a reading level but a refusal of conceptual immigration.

None of this requires contempt for the reader. It requires a different courtesy: the courtesy of letting a sentence remain slightly foreign so that the reader can notice the foreignness as information rather than as a stain. The translator's invisibility, long praised as professionalism, is in this light a kind of disappearance of evidence. We might instead want translators to be visibly responsible for their choices, not as celebrities, but as people who can be asked why a silence was kept or filled.

The practical consequence is modest and severe. Reviewers should stop treating smoothness as a synonym for accuracy. Teachers should stop treating a bilingual dictionary as a moral instrument. And readers who want to be hosts rather than consumers should learn to tolerate, even to prize, the small resistances that prove a text has not been entirely naturalized. What cannot be made to sound like us is often the part that most needed to travel.

passage.title: The Caption (1975)
passage.body: In “The Caption” (1975), Kwame Boateng writes from inside municipal archives. The argument is that expertise without a named audience is just private language. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.
