passage.title: psg-cars-5
passage.body:
Beauty and sublimity are often treated as synonyms in everyday speech, but the aesthetic tradition has long maintained a crucial distinction between them. Beauty, on the classical account, is associated with harmony, proportion, and pleasure: the beautiful object is one whose parts cohere in a way that the observer finds immediately gratifying. Sublimity, by contrast, involves an experience of excess — of forms or magnitudes that exceed the observer's capacity to take them in all at once. The encounter with the sublime is therefore double-edged: it produces both awe and a kind of distress, a sense of being overwhelmed that coexists with exhilaration.
Eighteenth-century theorists were among the first to treat the sublime as a distinct aesthetic category. One influential account located the cause of sublimity in attributes such as vast extent, darkness, and the suggestion of danger or power. A stormy ocean, a jagged mountain range, the interior of a vast cathedral — these provoke a response that differs qualitatively from our response to a well-proportioned garden or a graceful melody. The difference lies not in mere intensity but in the character of the response: the sublime suspends our habitual sense of comfort and security.
A subsequent philosophical tradition shifted the locus of the sublime from the external object to the observer's mental activity. On this view, what is truly sublime is not the mountain itself but the mind's discovery of its own capacity to conceive of what it cannot perceive — to think totality even when the senses are overwhelmed by the magnitude before them. The initial feeling of inadequacy thus gives way to a recognition of the mind's superiority: the faculty that can frame the idea of infinity is, in this sense, greater than any finite spectacle.
These two accounts — one locating sublimity in the object's properties, the other in the observer's cognitive response — are not necessarily incompatible. Objects with certain properties may reliably trigger the cognitive response that constitutes the full experience of the sublime. What both accounts agree on, however, is that the sublime cannot be reduced to beauty: the sublime disrupts the comfortable relationship between the observer and the world, while beauty affirms and soothes it.
The distinction carries an ethical resonance that later writers were quick to draw out. Because the sublime confronts the observer with magnitudes that dwarf the human frame, it has often been tied to humility — to a chastening awareness of finitude that beauty, with its reassurances of order and fit, does not compel. Standing before a storm or an abyss, the spectator is reminded that the world is not arranged for human convenience. And yet, on the observer-centered account, the very same encounter can enlarge the self, for the mind that registers its own smallness is also the mind capacious enough to entertain the immensity that occasions the feeling. This union of abasement and elevation is what makes the sublime so stubbornly resistant to the vocabulary of ordinary pleasure.
Contemporary critics have extended the concept of the sublime to non-natural contexts. The technological sublime finds its occasion in artifacts of overwhelming scale or power: a vast suspension bridge, a particle accelerator, a data center housing more information than any mind could process. Whether such objects genuinely provoke the traditional experience of mingled awe and inadequacy, or whether they produce only spectacle and wonder, remains a live debate in aesthetic theory.

passage.title: psg-cars-14
passage.body:
Social contract theory attempts to ground the legitimacy of political authority in the hypothetical or actual consent of those who are governed. If the state can be understood as an agreement among free and equal individuals to submit to common rules in exchange for mutual protection and the benefits of social cooperation, then political obligations are not arbitrary impositions but self-incurred commitments. The theory has its roots in early modern political philosophy and was given its most rigorous contemporary formulation through the thought experiment of choosing principles of justice from behind a veil of ignorance about one's place in society.
The veil of ignorance is designed to neutralize the effects of morally arbitrary advantages. Behind this veil, contractors do not know their natural talents, social class, or the particular conception of the good that they happen to hold. Because they must choose principles without knowing whether they will turn out to be among the advantaged or the disadvantaged, the argument holds that they will prefer principles that make the situation of the worst-off members of society as good as possible -- the so-called difference principle. Rational self-interest, operating behind the veil, converges on an egalitarian outcome not through altruism but through prudent risk-avoidance. The reasoning is a form of maximin: facing a choice under radical uncertainty, one does best to make the worst available position as tolerable as it can be made, since for all one knows that worst position will turn out to be one's own. It is worth being precise about what the argument does and does not claim. It does not assert that inequality is inherently wrong, nor that talent may never be rewarded; it permits inequalities precisely insofar as they improve the prospects of those at the bottom. What it refuses to countenance is an arrangement that leaves the least advantaged worse off merely so that the already fortunate may gain still more. Equality functions here as a baseline from which any departure must earn its keep.
Libertarian critics have challenged this argument on two fronts. First, they deny that the veil of ignorance is a neutral device: by requiring contractors to ignore their distinctive identities and life plans, it smuggles in a particular egalitarian assumption about what matters morally. Second, they argue that the difference principle violates individuals' entitlements by requiring redistribution from those who have acquired their holdings through legitimate means. On this view, just distributions are determined by the history of how holdings were acquired and transferred, not by any end-state principle about the pattern of distribution. Taxing the talented to benefit the worst-off, on this account, is no different in principle from forced labor.
Communitarian critics raise a different objection: the veil of ignorance presupposes a conception of persons as atomistic, self-sufficient choosers whose identities and commitments are separable from their social contexts. This picture, they argue, is a philosophical fiction. Actual persons are constituted by their particular communities, traditions, and relationships; the self that chooses behind a veil of ignorance is an abstraction too thin to generate substantive principles of justice. A more adequate theory would begin not with hypothetical individuals stripped of their particulars but with the historically situated communities that persons actually inhabit.
The social contract tradition, despite these challenges, remains influential because it takes seriously two commitments that are difficult to honor simultaneously: the idea that political authority must be justifiable to each individual governed, and the idea that just social arrangements must be insensitive to morally arbitrary differences in natural talent and social fortune.

passage.body:
A biomechanics laboratory studies vertical jumping with a force platform, a rigid plate that records the force a person exerts on it as a function of time. A 60 kg athlete stands motionless on the platform and then performs a maximal jump: she dips down, drives upward, and leaves the plate. High-speed video tracks a marker on her hip to follow the vertical motion of her center of mass.
While the athlete stands still, the platform reads a steady value equal to her weight. During the propulsion phase the reading rises well above this baseline, climbs to a peak, and then drops abruptly to zero at the instant her feet leave the plate. The interval from the start of propulsion to takeoff lasts about 0.20 s. After takeoff the center of mass rises to a measured peak height of 0.45 m above its takeoff position before falling back. Treating the body as a point mass at the center of mass and neglecting air resistance, the researchers reconstruct the takeoff velocity, the mechanical energy of the jump, and the forces during landing.
On landing, the athlete returns to the plate moving downward, and the platform again registers a large force as she decelerates to rest over about 0.15 s. The researchers note that athletes who land with stiff legs stop in a shorter time and record much larger peak forces than athletes who flex their knees and ankles to cushion the impact. Throughout, the platform measures the contact force between athlete and plate; gravitational acceleration is taken as g = 10 m/s^2.

passage.title: psg-cars-14
passage.body:
Social contract theory attempts to ground the legitimacy of political authority in the hypothetical or actual consent of those who are governed. If the state can be understood as an agreement among free and equal individuals to submit to common rules in exchange for mutual protection and the benefits of social cooperation, then political obligations are not arbitrary impositions but self-incurred commitments. The theory has its roots in early modern political philosophy and was given its most rigorous contemporary formulation through the thought experiment of choosing principles of justice from behind a veil of ignorance about one's place in society.
The veil of ignorance is designed to neutralize the effects of morally arbitrary advantages. Behind this veil, contractors do not know their natural talents, social class, or the particular conception of the good that they happen to hold. Because they must choose principles without knowing whether they will turn out to be among the advantaged or the disadvantaged, the argument holds that they will prefer principles that make the situation of the worst-off members of society as good as possible -- the so-called difference principle. Rational self-interest, operating behind the veil, converges on an egalitarian outcome not through altruism but through prudent risk-avoidance. The reasoning is a form of maximin: facing a choice under radical uncertainty, one does best to make the worst available position as tolerable as it can be made, since for all one knows that worst position will turn out to be one's own. It is worth being precise about what the argument does and does not claim. It does not assert that inequality is inherently wrong, nor that talent may never be rewarded; it permits inequalities precisely insofar as they improve the prospects of those at the bottom. What it refuses to countenance is an arrangement that leaves the least advantaged worse off merely so that the already fortunate may gain still more. Equality functions here as a baseline from which any departure must earn its keep.
Libertarian critics have challenged this argument on two fronts. First, they deny that the veil of ignorance is a neutral device: by requiring contractors to ignore their distinctive identities and life plans, it smuggles in a particular egalitarian assumption about what matters morally. Second, they argue that the difference principle violates individuals' entitlements by requiring redistribution from those who have acquired their holdings through legitimate means. On this view, just distributions are determined by the history of how holdings were acquired and transferred, not by any end-state principle about the pattern of distribution. Taxing the talented to benefit the worst-off, on this account, is no different in principle from forced labor.
Communitarian critics raise a different objection: the veil of ignorance presupposes a conception of persons as atomistic, self-sufficient choosers whose identities and commitments are separable from their social contexts. This picture, they argue, is a philosophical fiction. Actual persons are constituted by their particular communities, traditions, and relationships; the self that chooses behind a veil of ignorance is an abstraction too thin to generate substantive principles of justice. A more adequate theory would begin not with hypothetical individuals stripped of their particulars but with the historically situated communities that persons actually inhabit.
The social contract tradition, despite these challenges, remains influential because it takes seriously two commitments that are difficult to honor simultaneously: the idea that political authority must be justifiable to each individual governed, and the idea that just social arrangements must be insensitive to morally arbitrary differences in natural talent and social fortune.

items.explanation: Observational learning = learning by watching/imitating a model (Bandura's social cognitive theory). Takeaway: Observational learning = learn by watching/imitating a model. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Observational learning (modeling) is acquiring behavior by watching others — the basis of Bandura's social cognitive theory. items.stem: The trichromatic (Young–Helmholtz) theory explains color vision by proposing that:

choices.text: There are four cone types arranged in opposing pairs
There are three cone types (roughly red, green, and blue), and their combined activation yields all perceived colors
Each distinct color has its own dedicated photoreceptor

items.explanation: Trichromatic theory: three cone types (red/green/blue) whose combined firing produces all colors. It operates at the receptor (cone) level. Takeaway: Trichromatic = 3 cone types (R/G/B); their combined firing makes all colors. Receptor-level. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Three cone types tuned to long (red), medium (green), and short (blue) wavelengths combine to produce every perceived color. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.A: Opposing pairs describe opponent-process theory; trichromatic theory posits three cone types.
distractorRationales.C: Cones — not rods — detect color; rods handle dim-light vision.
distractorRationales.D: Colors arise from combinations of just three cone types, not one receptor per color.

Task B — 30 minutes. Leo is writing to these comments:

“A border is a sentence that some people have to live inside.”
“We ration; we merely prefer not to say the word.”
“Progress is the replacement of one nuisance with another.”

Which approach is most likely to score?

choices.text: Inventory every comment in order so the marker sees completeness.
Specific scenes instead of platitude. Do that with particular examples; do not inventory the comments.
Write a generic paragraph that could fit any prompt this century.
Spend the first twenty minutes outlining and the last two typing.

items.explanation: GAMSAT S2 is production under a clock. What scores is: Specific scenes instead of platitude. Use a clear position or a precise personal scene; comments are pressure, not a checklist. Inventory, generic filler, and outline-without-prose are the three ways this hour fails to raise a mark. Leo's comments only change the prompt pairing.

distractorRationales.A: Comment inventory is the named failure mode for S2.
distractorRationales.C: Generic voice is the opposite of particular/theme precision.
distractorRationales.D: Under time, an unused outline does not score.

items.stem: If the actuator gas warms from 298 K to 313 K at constant pressure, approximately how much expansion work is done by the gas against 1.00 atm?
items.explanation: At constant pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature. DeltaV = 2.00 mL x (313 - 298)/298 = about 0.101 mL = 1.01 x 10^-7 m3. Work is PDeltaV = (1.01 x 10^5 Pa)(1.01 x 10^-7 m3) = about 0.010 J. Common miss: Using the final gas volume rather than the volume change in the work calculation. This correctly combines Charles's law with pressure-volume work. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.B: This is too small by about a factor of 10.
distractorRationales.C: This is too large by about a factor of 10.
distractorRationales.D: This is far too large for a 0.101 mL expansion at 1 atm.

passage.title: Conductivity Assay for Ester Hydrolysis
passage.body:
A fictional ester Q hydrolyzes in aqueous buffer to form carboxylic acid R and alcohol S: Q + H2O -> R + S. Compound R has pKa = 4.8. When R is deprotonated, the resulting carboxylate increases the solution conductivity. Conductivity is monitored between two electrodes using a 5.0 V source. A gas-filled actuator in the device initially contains 2.00 mL of ideal gas at 298 K and 1.00 atm; it expands at constant pressure when warmed. The droplet image is monitored with a converging lens of focal length 10 cm.

Assay results after 20 min at different pH values.
pH | Resistance between electrodes (kohm) | Fraction of R deprotonated | R recovered by ion-exchange (%)
3.8 | 12.0 | 0.09 | 18
4.8 | 5.0 | 0.50 | 54
5.8 | 2.5 | 0.91 | 83
7.4 | 1.8 | 0.998 | 86

Optical focusing during the conductivity assay. — When the droplet is 20 cm from the 10 cm focal length lens, a sharp real image forms 20 cm from the lens. If the droplet moves closer to the lens, the camera must be repositioned to maintain focus.

items.stem: Glucose entry into erythrocytes is saturable, strongly prefers D-glucose over L-glucose, and continues after cellular ATP is depleted. This process is:

choices.text: simple diffusion through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer
primary active transport by a glucose ATPase
facilitated diffusion through a carrier protein

items.explanation: Saturability and stereospecificity indicate a finite number of protein binding sites, which rules out dissolving through the lipid core. Independence from ATP rules out primary active transport. GLUT-mediated facilitated diffusion matches all three observations: passive net flux down a concentration gradient, carrier kinetics, and no direct energy coupling. Endocytosis is neither the physiologic route for erythrocyte glucose nor typically stereospecific in this way.

distractorRationales.A: Simple diffusion through lipid is not saturable and does not distinguish D- from L-glucose at this level. Glucose is too polar for rapid uncatalyzed permeation.
distractorRationales.B: Primary active transport would slow or stop when ATP is depleted. The stem says uptake continues.
distractorRationales.C: Endocytosis is not how RBCs take up glucose and would not explain classic carrier saturation plus ATP independence in this assay.

items.stem: "Some argue that remote work harms company culture. But teams that meet in person quarterly report just as strong a sense of belonging as fully office-based teams." What is the function of the second sentence?

choices.text: It restates the counterargument without addressing it.
It introduces an unrelated new topic.
It presents evidence that rebuts the counterargument mentioned in the first sentence.
It is an ad hominem against remote workers.

items.explanation: The passage first raises an opposing view (remote work harms culture), then immediately offers evidence against it — a rebuttal structure common in persuasive writing. Strong persuasive writing often raises the other side's best point (concession) before countering it (rebuttal). Recognising this structure helps you separate what the author actually believes from the objection they're temporarily voicing. Memory tip: Listen for "yes... but": strong persuasive writing often concedes the other side's best point first ("yes, I hear that...") before pivoting to the rebuttal ("...but here's why"). The "but" is your cue. Source: gamsat-trainer original practice (not ACER). Unverified.

items.stem: Why does the tertiary substrate react by SN1 while the primary substrate reacts by SN2?

choices.text: The primary carbon forms a more stable carbocation than the tertiary carbon.
Hydroxide is intrinsically a better nucleophile toward tertiary carbons.

The tertiary carbocation is stabilized by its three attached alkyl groups (favoring SN1), while the primary carbon forms an unstable carbocation but is sterically open to concerted backside attack (favoring SN2).
Tertiary substrates present less steric hindrance to backside attack.

items.explanation: Carbocation stability increases 3 > 2 > 1 (alkyl groups donate electron density and provide hyperconjugation), so tertiary substrates readily ionize (SN1); a primary carbocation is too unstable, but the uncrowded primary carbon is open to direct backside attack (SN2). Choice 1 inverts the stability order; choice 2 is false; choice 3 has the steric argument backwards (tertiary is MORE hindered). Source: ReadyMCAT (CC BY-SA 4.0), grounded in OpenStax/LibreTexts. Unverified.

passage.title: psg-cp-9
passage.body:
Nucleophilic substitution is central to organic and biochemical reactivity, from laboratory synthesis to the alkylation of DNA. A class studies how two bromoalkanes react with hydroxide ion, which acts as the nucleophile, in a hydroxylic solvent.
The first substrate is 1-bromobutane, a primary alkyl halide in which the carbon bearing bromine is attached to only one other carbon. With a good nucleophile it reacts by a one-step, concerted mechanism (SN2): hydroxide attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving bromide, and as bromide departs the other three groups invert like an umbrella in the wind. The measured rate depends on the concentrations of both the substrate and the hydroxide.
The second substrate is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide), a tertiary halide whose brominated carbon is attached to three other carbons. It reacts by a two-step mechanism (SN1): the carbon-bromine bond breaks first to give a carbocation, which the nucleophile then captures. The measured rate depends only on the concentration of the substrate, and because the carbocation is trigonal planar, a nucleophile can approach from either face.
The class also revisits structure. They note that a carbon bonded to four different groups is a stereocenter and examine 2-bromobutane as an example. They track how the functional group changes when hydroxide replaces bromide, and they rank the stability of primary, secondary, and tertiary carbocations to explain why substrate structure dictates the mechanism. The instructor stresses that the same electronic and steric principles govern reactions of biological molecules such as the phosphate esters of nucleotides.

passage.title: psg-cp-1
passage.body:
A biomechanics laboratory studies vertical jumping with a force platform, a rigid plate that records the force a person exerts on it as a function of time. A 60 kg athlete stands motionless on the platform and then performs a maximal jump: she dips down, drives upward, and leaves the plate. High-speed video tracks a marker on her hip to follow the vertical motion of her center of mass.
While the athlete stands still, the platform reads a steady value equal to her weight. During the propulsion phase the reading rises well above this baseline, climbs to a peak, and then drops abruptly to zero at the instant her feet leave the plate. The interval from the start of propulsion to takeoff lasts about 0.20 s. After takeoff the center of mass rises to a measured peak height of 0.45 m above its takeoff position before falling back. Treating the body as a point mass at the center of mass and neglecting air resistance, the researchers reconstruct the takeoff velocity, the mechanical energy of the jump, and the forces during landing.
On landing, the athlete returns to the plate moving downward, and the platform again registers a large force as she decelerates to rest over about 0.15 s. The researchers note that athletes who land with stiff legs stop in a shorter time and record much larger peak forces than athletes who flex their knees and ankles to cushion the impact. Throughout, the platform measures the contact force between athlete and plate; gravitational acceleration is taken as g = 10 m/s^2.

items.stem: Which new case is most analogous to the test in Soren Adeyemi’s “The Hiring Rubric” (1983), vol. 200015, no. 2?

choices.text: A proof in Euclidean geometry that names every axiom
A recipe that lists oven temperature
Soren Adeyemi winning a literary prize
A hospital checklist that cannot be described without the word “quality,” yet quality is never defined

items.explanation: Apply-to-new-context: the analog is a practice that depends on an undefined official word. Geometry and recipes are explicit; a prize is off-axis. Changing names does not change the analog. Neighbouring options fail because they name a different relation, drop a required conversion, or contradict a number given in the stem (GAMSAT.S1.compare.t2#800013). Those traps are not a second live key.

distractorRationales.A: Named axioms are the opposite of hidden adjectives.
distractorRationales.B: A temperature is an operational instruction, not an official perfume.
distractorRationales.C: A prize is biographical, not analogical.

passage.title: The Hiring Rubric (1983)
passage.body: Soren Adeyemi's 1983 essay “The Hiring Rubric,” on broadcast newsrooms, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. The piece admits that some gatekeeping keeps fraud out. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Based on the TLC results, which fraction most likely contains purified compound A after the bicarbonate extraction sequence?

choices.text: The original organic layer before extraction
The organic layer after bicarbonate extraction, showing Rf 0.62 and 0.35
The acidified bicarbonate extract re-extracted into ethyl acetate, showing Rf 0.12
The strong-base extract after prolonged heating, showing Rf 0.12 and 0.18

items.explanation: The passage states that compound A becomes a water-soluble carboxylate in bicarbonate. After acidification, it becomes neutral and can be extracted into ethyl acetate. The fraction with a single Rf 0.12 spot after acidified bicarbonate workup is therefore the best purified A fraction. Common miss: Equating the organic layer after the first extraction with the desired recovered acid fraction. This is the expected recovered carboxylic acid fraction and shows a single TLC spot. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.A: The original organic layer contains the mixture, not purified A.
distractorRationales.B: This fraction contains compounds that did not move into bicarbonate, consistent with P and N.
distractorRationales.D: This fraction contains an additional new spot, consistent with side reaction or hydrolysis products.

passage.title: Extraction of Substituted Benzoic Acids
passage.body:
A student separates a fictional mixture containing compound A, a substituted benzoic acid; compound P, a substituted phenol; and compound N, a neutral aromatic ester. The mixture is dissolved in ethyl acetate and extracted with aqueous base. Charged species partition strongly into the aqueous layer, whereas neutral species remain mostly in the organic layer. Sodium bicarbonate solution has pH 8.3, and sodium hydroxide solution has pH 12.0. After aqueous extracts are acidified, neutral acidic compounds can be recovered by extraction into fresh ethyl acetate. Prolonged heating of esters in strong aqueous base may hydrolyze ester bonds.

Properties of compounds in the mixture.
Compound | Main functional group | Relevant pKa | Dominant form at pH 8.3 | Expected layer at pH 8.3
A | carboxylic acid | 4.2 | deprotonated carboxylate | aqueous
P | phenol | 10.0 | mostly neutral phenol | organic
N | ester | none in this range | neutral ester | organic

TLC results on silica gel after workup.
Fraction analyzed | Observed spots by Rf
Organic layer after bicarbonate extraction | 0.62 and 0.35
Acidified bicarbonate extract re-extracted into ethyl acetate | 0.12
Strong-base extract after prolonged heating and acidification | 0.12 and a new spot at 0.18

Acid-base extraction workflow. — The original organic solution is first shaken with aqueous sodium bicarbonate. The aqueous bicarbonate layer is separated, acidified to pH 2, and extracted with fresh ethyl acetate. The remaining organic layer contains compounds that were not appreciably deprotonated by bicarbonate.

passage.title: Who Counts (1979)
passage.body: Owen Blake published “Who Counts” in 1979 after a season in court translation. The argument is that expertise without a named audience is just private language. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Two 4.0 μF capacitors are available, plus a 12 V battery. Combination S is the pair in series; combination P is the pair in parallel. C_series−1 = C1−1 + C2−1; C_parallel = C1 + C2. passage.title: On keeping a promise to a stranger
passage.body:
When the magistrate asked why he had returned the purse, the clerk did not say honesty. He said habit. He had been taught, in a household that measured virtue by small repetitions, that a found object remains someone else's until the world has been given a fair chance to reclaim it. The purse contained little money and a letter, unsealed, beginning: I will not be there when you arrive. He did not finish it. To finish it, he thought, would convert a duty into a story, and stories have a way of making the finder important.

Philosophers like to treat this as a puzzle about property and knowledge. If he does not know the owner, is the duty weaker? If the letter would have saved a marriage, does withholding it become a harm? The clerk would have found the questions indecent. He was not refusing knowledge so much as refusing a role. The city had clerks for lost property; it did not have clerks for other people's farewells.

A later commentator, writing after the clerk was dead, praised him as a Kantian saint: he acted from a maxim he could will as universal. The praise is too clean. The clerk's maxim was local and slightly ashamed. He did not want to be the man who had read the letter. Shame, not universality, kept his eyes off the page. That is not a lesser ethics. It is an ethics that knows how quickly curiosity dresses itself as concern.

The owner collected the purse the next morning and did not thank him. In the commentary this becomes a test of whether virtue needs recognition. The clerk, if asked, would have said only that the counter was busy.

passage.title: psg-ps-5
passage.body:
Researchers ran three studies of behavior in groups. In Study 1, a participant judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line, answering aloud after several confederates. On critical trials the confederates unanimously gave an obviously wrong answer. Participants conformed to the wrong answer on about 35% of critical trials, and three-quarters conformed at least once; conformity fell sharply when a single confederate broke from the majority. Most conformers later said they knew the group was wrong but did not want to stand out.
In Study 2, participants completed either a simple, well-practiced task or a complex, unfamiliar task, alone or in front of an audience. An audience improved performance on the simple task but worsened it on the complex task.
In Study 3, participants heard what sounded like a fellow participant having a medical emergency in another room. When participants believed they were the only witness, 85% sought help within a minute; when they believed four others were also present, only 31% did, and those who helped took longer. Interviews suggested that the presence of others reduced each individual's felt responsibility.
The authors distinguished going along with a group to fit in from the effect of an audience on task performance, and linked Study 3 to a well-documented reduction in helping as the number of bystanders rises. They emphasized that these effects reflect the social situation rather than stable personality differences among the participants.

items.stem:
A CRISPR–Cas9 experiment targets exon 2 of gene F. Readouts in a clonal cell line:

Assay | result
Sanger of exon 2 | 1 bp deletion, frameshift
mRNA (RT–qPCR, exons 4–5) | 70% of wild-type level
Western blot, antibody to C-terminus | no band
Rescue: cDNA of F lacking the guide site | Western band restored; phenotype reversed

Which interpretation is most cautious and complete?

choices.text: The remaining 70% mRNA means the protein must still be present at 70%, so the Western is wrong
The phenotype is an off-target effect that the rescue cannot address
A 1 bp deletion is too small to affect a gene, so F is unchanged
A frameshift knockout of F protein is likely causal, because protein is lost, a little mRNA remains, and a guide-resistant cDNA restores protein and phenotype

items.explanation: A single-base deletion in an exon shifts the reading frame and typically triggers loss of the C-terminal epitope, matching a blank Western. Residual mRNA at 70% is compatible with incomplete nonsense-mediated decay; mRNA is not a stoichiometric report of protein. Re-expressing a cDNA that cannot be recut by the guide restores the Western band and reverses the phenotype, the standard cis-rescue that argues the phenotype runs through F rather than an off-target. A 1 bp coding deletion is among the most disruptive small lesions, not a null-effect.

distractorRationales.A: Frameshifts and NMD uncouple mRNA level from full-length protein; the C-terminal antibody is the relevant protein assay.
distractorRationales.B: A guide-resistant cDNA rescue that restores both protein and phenotype is exactly the experiment used to argue against off-target causation.
distractorRationales.C: Frameshifts of one base are not silent; they scramble every codon after the lesion and usually introduce a premature stop.

items.stem: Transfer of a hydrophobic side chain from water into the protein core is favorable near room temperature even though the side chain loses conformational freedom. Which statement best identifies the dominant thermodynamic contribution?

choices.text: Exposed hydrophobics form stronger hydrogen bonds to water than they do in the core, so burial is enthalpy-driven by those H-bonds
The protein backbone gains a large amount of conformational entropy upon folding, which outweighs all other terms
Ordered water in the solvation layer is released into bulk solvent, increasing solvent entropy enough to outweigh the solute’s entropy loss
Van der Waals contacts with water are stronger than packing interactions in the core, so burial is never entropy-driven

items.explanation: Hydrophobic side chains in water induce a more ordered hydrogen-bond network (the solvation or clathrate layer). Burial of those side chains releases that water into bulk solvent, producing a large positive ΔS for the solvent. That solvent-entropy gain is the classical hydrophobic effect and typically dominates ΔG of transferring nonpolar groups out of water near room temperature. The chain itself loses entropy on folding, which opposes folding. Hydrophobic groups do not hydrogen-bond strongly to water, and core packing van der Waals contacts are at least as favorable as those with solvent.

distractorRationales.A: Aliphatic side chains do not donate or accept strong hydrogen bonds. Any H-bond advantage belongs to polar groups, not to the hydrophobic effect.
distractorRationales.B: Folding restricts backbone and side-chain rotamers, decreasing the protein’s conformational entropy. That term opposes, rather than drives, folding.
distractorRationales.D: Close packing in the core provides favorable van der Waals contacts. The distinctive driving force of hydrophobicity is solvent entropy, not weaker core packing.

items.explanation: A sugar is reducing if it has a free anomeric carbon that can open to an aldehyde (or, for a ketose after tautomerization, an enediol). Maltose (Glc α1→4 Glc) and lactose (Gal β1→4 Glc) each leave one anomeric carbon free. Sucrose is Glc α1↔2β Fru, so both anomeric carbons are locked in the glycosidic bond until acid or sucrase hydrolyzes it, after which glucose and fructose both react with Benedict’s reagent. Fructose can reduce Cu(II) after isomerization, so ‘ketoses never reduce’ is false. Benedict’s test is for reducing sugars, not peptide bonds, and maltose is an unbranched α-1,4 disaccharide, not cellulose.

distractorRationales.B: Acid hydrolysis of sucrose releases fructose, which is reducing via tautomerization to an aldose; the intact disaccharide is nonreducing because both anomers are tied up, not because ketoses are intrinsically nonreducing.
distractorRationales.C: These molecules are carbohydrates, not peptides; Benedict’s reagent reports a free anomeric carbon, not nitrogen content.
distractorRationales.D: Maltose is Glc α1→4 Glc without cellulose-like β-1,4 chains or glycogen-like branching; reducing character comes from the free anomeric carbon.

items.stem: In a menstrual cycle, a midcycle estradiol peak normally triggers an LH surge and ovulation. If pituitary GnRH receptors are pharmacologically blocked, the estradiol peak still occurs but LH does not surge. Estradiol's ovulatory action is therefore:

choices.text: Positive feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis that requires GnRH-driven gonadotroph LH release
Direct luteinization of the oocyte in the absence of LH
Inhibition of all ovarian steroidogenesis as the only feedback mode throughout the cycle
Secretion of LH from the posterior pituitary, which does not use GnRH receptors

items.explanation: For most of the follicular phase estradiol exerts negative feedback, but at high, sustained levels it switches to positive feedback, increasing GnRH pulse patterns and pituitary sensitivity so that gonadotrophs fire the LH surge. The surge then causes ovulation and luteinization. Blocking GnRH receptors prevents that pituitary LH release even if the ovary still makes estradiol, proving estradiol does not ovulate the follicle by a fully ovary-autonomous route. LH is an anterior-pituitary glycoprotein, not a posterior-pituitary peptide. Negative feedback is not the only estradiol mode at midcycle.

distractorRationales.B: Ovulation requires the LH surge; estradiol does not replace LH at the oocyte.
distractorRationales.C: Midcycle estradiol is stimulatory to LH release, not purely inhibitory.
distractorRationales.D: LH is anterior pituitary; posterior hormones are ADH and oxytocin.

distractorRationales.A: Neither neuron is destroyed; the connection is strengthened.
distractorRationales.B: Myelin isn't stripped; the synapse is potentiated.
distractorRationales.D: Silencing a synapse is the opposite of potentiation.

items.stem: A reconstituted vesicle contains bacteriorhodopsin (a light-driven proton pump) and mitochondrial ATP synthase, but no electron-transport proteins. Illumination in the presence of ADP + Pi produces ATP. Which conclusion does this classic experiment support?

choices.text: A respiratory complex is still required as a covalent high-energy intermediate between the pump and ATP synthase.
A proton electrochemical gradient is a sufficient coupling intermediate between proton pumping and ATP synthesis.
Light directly phosphorylates ADP on the F1 domain without proton movement.
Uncouplers would increase ATP yield by accelerating proton leak into the vesicle.

items.explanation: The Racker–Stoeckenius reconstitution showed that a proton pump unrelated to the respiratory chain, plus ATP synthase, is enough for photophosphorylation of ADP when a proton gradient is generated. That result supports the chemiosmotic hypothesis: the delocalized proton electrochemical potential, not a mandatory electron-transport-bound high-energy chemical intermediate, couples pumping to ATP synthesis. Light acts through bacteriorhodopsin’s proton transport, not by directly phosphorylating ADP on F1. An uncoupler would collapse the gradient and decrease, not increase, ATP. The vesicles contained no Complexes I–IV, so those complexes cannot be required as the coupling intermediate in this system.

distractorRationales.A: The vesicles lacked respiratory complexes yet still made ATP, which is evidence against an obligatory ETC-bound covalent intermediate in this experiment.
distractorRationales.C: Bacteriorhodopsin uses light to pump protons; ATP synthase then uses the resulting Δp. Light does not directly phosphorylate ADP on F1.
distractorRationales.D: Uncouplers dissipate the proton-motive force and would lower ATP synthesis, not raise it.

passage.title: Extraction of Substituted Benzoic Acids
passage.body:
A student separates a fictional mixture containing compound A, a substituted benzoic acid; compound P, a substituted phenol; and compound N, a neutral aromatic ester. The mixture is dissolved in ethyl acetate and extracted with aqueous base. Charged species partition strongly into the aqueous layer, whereas neutral species remain mostly in the organic layer. Sodium bicarbonate solution has pH 8.3, and sodium hydroxide solution has pH 12.0. After aqueous extracts are acidified, neutral acidic compounds can be recovered by extraction into fresh ethyl acetate. Prolonged heating of esters in strong aqueous base may hydrolyze ester bonds.

Properties of compounds in the mixture.
Compound | Main functional group | Relevant pKa | Dominant form at pH 8.3 | Expected layer at pH 8.3
A | carboxylic acid | 4.2 | deprotonated carboxylate | aqueous
P | phenol | 10.0 | mostly neutral phenol | organic
N | ester | none in this range | neutral ester | organic

TLC results on silica gel after workup.
Fraction analyzed | Observed spots by Rf
Organic layer after bicarbonate extraction | 0.62 and 0.35
Acidified bicarbonate extract re-extracted into ethyl acetate | 0.12
Strong-base extract after prolonged heating and acidification | 0.12 and a new spot at 0.18

Acid-base extraction workflow. — The original organic solution is first shaken with aqueous sodium bicarbonate. The aqueous bicarbonate layer is separated, acidified to pH 2, and extracted with fresh ethyl acetate. The remaining organic layer contains compounds that were not appreciably deprotonated by bicarbonate.

passage.title: Construction Site (1979)
passage.body: Hanae Morioka published “Construction Site” in 1979 after a season in heritage listing. The argument is that fairness talk often arrives after the decision has already been made. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem:
A particle’s velocity–time graph is described as follows:

Interval | v(t)
0 to 5.0 s | v = +6.0 m s−1 (horizontal line)
5.0 to 8.0 s | v changes linearly from +6.0 m s−1 to −6.0 m s−1
8.0 to 12.0 s | v = −6.0 m s−1 (horizontal line)

Velocity is zero at the axis crossing during 5.0–8.0 s. What is the net displacement from t = 0 to t = 12.0 s?
items.explanation: Displacement is the signed area. From 0 to 5.0 s the area is 6.0 × 5.0 = +30 m. From 5.0 to 8.0 s the line is antisymmetric about v = 0, which occurs at the midpoint t = 6.5 s, so the +4.5 m triangle and the −4.5 m triangle cancel. From 8.0 to 12.0 s the area is (−6.0)×4.0 = −24 m. The net is 30 + 0 − 24 = +6.0 m. A total of zero would require the negative area to cancel the entire +30 m. +30 m ignores the motion after t = 5 s. −24 m is only the last segment. Direction reversal on a v–t graph does not by itself make the net displacement zero.

distractorRationales.A: The positive area (30 m) is larger than the negative area (24 m). Cancellation of the middle triangles does not cancel the whole motion.
distractorRationales.C: 30 m is the displacement during the first 5 s only. The later negative-velocity segment contributes −24 m.
distractorRationales.D: −24 m is the displacement from 8 s to 12 s only, omitting the earlier +30 m.

items.stem: A 2 kg laboratory cart is at rest on a level air track. A constant net force then gives it a uniform acceleration of 2 m/s^2 for 5 s. How far does the cart travel during those 5 s?
items.explanation: From rest, displacement under constant acceleration is x = (1/2) a t^2. Substituting a = 2 m/s^2 and t = 5 s gives x = (1/2)(2)(25) = 25 m. Equivalently, the final speed is v = a t = 10 m/s, so the average speed is 5 m/s and x = 5 m/s times 5 s = 25 m. Using the final speed in x = v t doubles the distance to 50 m, and dropping the factor of one-half or using t instead of t^2 undercounts the displacement.

distractorRationales.A: This is a t = 10 m, which omits the 1/2 in x = (1/2) a t^2, or it is the change in speed rather than the distance traveled.
distractorRationales.C: This is v_final t = 50 m. That would be correct only if the cart had traveled at 10 m/s for the entire interval; it started from rest, so the average speed is 5 m/s.
distractorRationales.D: This is (1/2) a t = 5 m, treating t as if it were t^2. Time must be squared in the rest-start displacement formula.

items.stem: Which statement about computer-based S2 typing is most accurate as craft advice?

choices.text: Spelling will be invisibly corrected, so muddy thinking will look precise.
You should spend the first ten minutes designing an elaborate outline with numbered subsections you will not have time to fill.
Assume little rescue from later proofreading: prefer one claim per sentence, read a paragraph back once for dropped words, and do not chase ornamental vocabulary you cannot spell under pulse.

items.explanation: The craft topic is clarity under timed typing, including sentence control without treating spellcheck as a substitute for thought. Whether a given sitting offers light correction or none, ornamental words you cannot securely type will cost you. One claim per sentence is a hedge against dropped subjects and lost verbs. A giant outline that is never filled is a common computer-exam failure. Eye-closed typing is a joke, not a method. The accurate advice is modest: readable units, one pass for missing words, vocabulary you can actually produce. C states that. It is retrieval of how the task works, not a request to write the essay here.

distractorRationales.A: Relying on invisible correction to launder unclear thought is exactly the false comfort this topic warns against.
distractorRationales.B: Over-outlining is a time thief; structure should be light enough to fill.
distractorRationales.D: Authenticity is not produced by not looking at the screen.

passage.title: psg-cp-11
passage.body: The following six questions are discrete and passage-independent: each stands alone and is not based on a shared passage, mirroring the freestanding question groups that appear between passages on the MCAT Chemical and Physical Foundations of Biological Systems section. Each question tests a single core physics principle - statics and torque, buoyancy, electrostatics, sound intensity, periodic atomic properties, or momentum conservation - and should be answered from fundamental principles rather than any preceding text. Constants are stated where needed; take g = 10 m/s^2.

items.stem: A person can just detect the difference between a 2.0 lb and a 2.2 lb weight. Assuming Weber's law holds, the smallest weight reliably distinguishable from a 5.0 lb weight is about:
items.explanation: Weber's law says the JND is a constant fraction of the baseline: k = ΔI/I = 0.2/2 = 0.1. At 5.0 lb, ΔI = kI = 0.1 × 5 = 0.5 lb → about 5.5 lb. Takeaway: JND is a constant proportion of the baseline (ΔI = kI), not a fixed amount. Heavier start → larger absolute change to notice. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. ΔI = 0.1 × 5 = 0.5 → 5.5 lb. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.A: 5.2 assumes a constant absolute JND (0.2 lb), exactly the misconception Weber's law corrects.
distractorRationales.C: 5.05 uses far too small a change; the JND grows with the baseline.
distractorRationales.D: 7.0 (a 2 lb change) is much larger than the proportional JND requires.

items.stem: Free aspartic acid (pKa ≈ 2.0, 3.9, and 9.9) is loaded onto a cation-exchange resin, which bears immobilized negative charges, in a pH 7.0 buffer. The amino acid flows through without binding. Which explanation is best?

choices.text: At pH 7 aspartate has a net negative charge and is electrostatically repelled by the resin
At pH 7 aspartate is a zwitterion of net charge zero and therefore has no ionic interaction with the resin
At pH 7 aspartate is net positive and binds so tightly that it cannot be loaded onto the column in the first place
Cation-exchange resins bind amino acids only through aromatic stacking, and aspartate lacks an aromatic ring

items.explanation: At pH 7 both carboxyl groups of aspartate (α-carboxyl pKa ~2 and side-chain pKa ~4) are deprotonated, while the α-amino group (pKa ~10) remains protonated, giving a net charge of −1. A cation exchanger presents negative charges intended to bind cations. A net-negative solute is repelled and appears in the flow-through. Aspartate’s isoelectric point is acidic (average of the two carboxyl pKa values, near 3), so pH 7 is well above the pI and the anion predominates. Cation-exchange chromatography is electrostatic, not aromatic stacking.

distractorRationales.B: The net-zero form of aspartate exists near pH 3, not at pH 7, where the net charge is −1.
distractorRationales.C: A net-positive aspartate would require pH below the pI; at pH 7 the residue is anionic, not tightly bound.
distractorRationales.D: Cation exchangers separate by charge. Aromatic stacking is not the binding mode of a sulfonate or carboxylate resin.

items.stem: A premature neonate produces insufficient pulmonary surfactant. Alveolar surface tension remains high. Which set of mechanical consequences is expected?

choices.text: High surface tension, alveolar collapse (atelectasis), and decreased lung compliance, raising the work of inflation
Increased compliance so that small alveoli overexpand while large ones empty
A higher FEV1/FVC ratio as the primary surfactant deficiency phenotype, identical to asthma
A right shift of the hemoglobin-O2 curve as surfactant’s main chemical role

items.explanation: Surfactant, largely dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine from type II pneumocytes, lowers alveolar surface tension gamma. Laplace's relation P = 2 gamma / r says that without that reduction, small alveoli generate large collapsing pressures, empty into larger ones, and the lung becomes stiff (low compliance). Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is the clinical picture: atelectasis and high work of breathing. Asthma is an obstructive FEV1/FVC fall, not a surfactant-deficient restrictive pattern. Surfactant is not a hemoglobin allosteric effector. Compliance falls, it does not rise.

distractorRationales.B: High tension decreases compliance and promotes collapse of small alveoli, the opposite of easy overexpansion.
distractorRationales.C: Surfactant deficiency is restrictive physiology, not an asthma-like obstructive ratio increase as the core lesion.
distractorRationales.D: The O2 dissociation curve is not controlled by alveolar surfactant lipids.

passage.title: Conditioning and Sound Sensitivity in a Virtual Environment
passage.body:
A behavioral science lab used a virtual environment to study how neutral sounds can acquire emotional significance. During acquisition, participants repeatedly heard Tone A immediately before an unpleasant but safe burst of white noise. Tone B was presented equally often but was never followed by the white noise. Skin conductance response was recorded as an index of autonomic arousal. In an extinction phase, both tones were presented without the white noise. In a final test, participants heard Tone C, which was acoustically similar to Tone A but slightly lower in pitch.

Mean skin conductance response in arbitrary units
Phase and stimulus | Mean response
Late acquisition: Tone A | 0.78
Late acquisition: Tone B | 0.22
Late extinction: Tone A | 0.31
Late extinction: Tone B | 0.20
Final test: Tone C | 0.49

Stimulus arrangement — Tone A and Tone C were similar in pitch, whereas Tone B was clearly distinct from both.

passage.title: Politeness as Gate (1975)
passage.body: In “Politeness as Gate” (1975), Ibrahim El-Sayed writes from inside heritage listing. The argument is that expertise without a named audience is just private language. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: In a Baddeley working-memory clinic task, repeating “the, the, the” aloud (articulatory suppression) abolishes the phonological-similarity effect for visually presented letter strings, while Corsi block span is unchanged. Which component was occupied, and which was spared?

The visuospatial sketchpad was occupied; the phonological loop was spared
Long-term episodic memory was occupied, which is why Corsi span survived
Sensory iconic memory was occupied, which is the only store Baddeley named

items.explanation: Baddeley’s multicomponent model assigns verbal rehearsal to the phonological loop. Articulatory suppression fills that rehearsal process, removing phonological confusions among letters. Corsi blocks load the visuospatial sketchpad and the central executive’s spatial control, so they should survive a purely verbal suppressor. Long-term episodic memory is not the working-memory buffer under test. Iconic memory is a brief sensory register in the older modal model, not the named Baddeley loop.

distractorRationales.B: The suppressor is verbal; it loads the loop, not the sketchpad.
distractorRationales.C: Corsi span is a working-memory spatial index, not proof that long-term memory was the occupied store.
distractorRationales.D: Baddeley’s model is loop, sketchpad, central executive (and later episodic buffer), not iconic memory alone.

items.stem:
Halogen data:

Element | covalent radius (pm) | IE1 (kJ mol−1) | electron affinity (kJ mol−1, exothermic as negative)
F | 64 | 1680 | −328
Cl | 99 | 1255 | −349
Br | 114 | 1140 | −325

Electron affinity here is the enthalpy of X(g) + e− → X−(g). Which reading is supported?

choices.text: F has the most exothermic EA because it has the highest IE1
Br is the smallest halogen, which is why its IE1 is lowest
EA becomes steadily more exothermic from F to Br as radius increases
Radius and ease of removing an electron both increase down the group, but Cl has the most exothermic EA because F’s compact 2p shell raises electron–electron repulsion in F−

items.explanation: Covalent radius increases 64 → 99 → 114 pm and IE1 falls 1680 → 1255 → 1140, the standard down-group weakening of attraction to valence electrons. Electron affinity, however, is most negative for Cl (−349), not F (−328): adding an electron to tiny F crowding a 2p subshell is less favourable than adding to Cl. EA is therefore not a monotone function of IE1 or of radius. Br is the largest listed atom, not the smallest, which is why its IE1 is the lowest of the three.

distractorRationales.A: F’s EA is −328, less exothermic than Cl’s −349, so the highest IE1 does not produce the most exothermic EA.
distractorRationales.B: Br’s radius 114 pm is the largest in the table.
distractorRationales.C: EA goes −328, −349, −325, a peak at Cl, not a steady trend toward Br.

passage.title: Gluconeogenic flux in hepatocyte-like cells
passage.body:
Researchers used fictional hepatocyte-like HGL cells to study glucose production from lactate and alanine. Pyruvate generated in the cytosol must enter mitochondria through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC). In the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate carboxylase (PC) uses ATP, bicarbonate, and a biotin cofactor to convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate. Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) then uses GTP to convert oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate. The pathway requires substantial energy input and is sensitive to cellular ATP availability.

Metabolic effects of perturbing gluconeogenesis from lactate and alanine.
Condition | Glucose output (%) | Cytosolic pyruvate (%) | Mitochondrial OAA/malate pool (%) | O2 consumption (%) | ATP/ADP ratio
Control | 100 | 100 | 100 | 100 | 5.0
MPC inhibitor B | 20 | 190 | 35 | 90 | 4.8
PC inhibitor C | 12 | 220 | 28 | 82 | 3.9
PEPCK knockdown | 18 | 120 | 210 | 85 | 4.2
Low-dose ETC inhibitor | 44 | 115 | 82 | 34 | 1.5
Acetyl-CoA analog | 135 | 70 | 155 | 112 | 4.6

Simplified route from lactate and alanine to glucose. — Lactate and alanine are converted to cytosolic pyruvate. Pyruvate enters mitochondria through MPC and is carboxylated by PC to oxaloacetate. Oxaloacetate-derived carbon returns to the cytosol and proceeds through gluconeogenic reactions to form glucose.

passage.title: psg-bb-5
passage.body:
To probe how mitochondria couple fuel oxidation to ATP synthesis, researchers suspended isolated mitochondria in a buffered chamber fitted with an oxygen electrode, so that the rate of oxygen consumption could be followed continuously. Because the electron transport chain uses O2 as its final electron acceptor, oxygen consumption serves as a readout of electron flow.
The team added an oxidizable substrate (to feed electrons into the chain) plus ADP and inorganic phosphate (the raw materials for ATP synthesis). Oxygen consumption rose to a brisk, steady rate, and ATP accumulated in the chamber. They then added oligomycin, a compound that blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase. Oxygen consumption fell almost to zero, and ATP synthesis stopped. Finally, they added 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), a small molecule that ferries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Oxygen consumption surged back to a high rate, yet no ATP was produced; the released energy instead appeared as heat.
The investigators explained the pattern in terms of the proton-motive force. Electron transport pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building an electrochemical gradient; ATP synthase normally lets those protons flow back into the matrix, harnessing the gradient to make ATP. Blocking ATP synthase lets the gradient build until it opposes further pumping, so electron flow (and O2 use) slows. A protonophore like DNP short-circuits the gradient, so electron transport races ahead while its energy is dissipated as heat rather than captured as ATP.

items.stem: A premed still endorses the cultural goal of a physician’s income and prestige but, facing a bottleneck of seats, begins selling stolen exam banks. In Merton’s strain (anomie) typology, this adaptation is which cell?

items.explanation: Merton’s strain theory says anomie arises when culturally approved goals (here, professional success) are not matched by equally available legitimate means. Conformity, the fifth cell, would keep both goals and legal means. Durkheim’s broader anomie idea is the parent of this typology, but the named cells are Merton’s.

items.stem: A labeled mRNA is transcribed in a cultured eukaryotic cell, then nuclear-pore export of that mRNA is blocked. The most likely observation is that:

choices.text: translation of that mRNA increases in the cytosol
the mRNA remains nuclear and protein produced from that mRNA falls

items.explanation: Eukaryotic mRNA must exit through nuclear pores to meet cytosolic ribosomes. Blocking export traps the transcript in the nucleus, so cytosolic translation of that message falls. Mitochondria do not import random nuclear mRNAs for translation, and cytosolic ribosomes do not routinely enter the nucleoplasm to translate chromatin-associated mRNA. A 900-nucleotide coding sequence (300 amino acids, no introns) is mutated. Experimental readouts:

Mutant | DNA change | mRNA length | protein
W | TGG at codon 80 → TGA | 900 nt | 79 amino acids
X | TGG at codon 80 → TGC | 900 nt | 300 amino acids, one residue different
Y | +1 bp insertion in codon 10 | 901 nt | 18 amino acids
Z | promoter −10 box ATATAA → GGATCC | none detected | none

TGG = Trp, TGA = stop, TGC = Cys. Which assignment is correct?

choices.text: W deletion of the gene; X silent; Y inversion; Z RNA editing
W nonsense; X missense; Y frameshift to a premature stop; Z promoter loss of transcription
W missense; X nonsense; Y silent; Z frameshift
W splice defect; X conservative substitution only if Cys equals Trp; Y promoter mutation; Z missense

TGG → TGC is Trp → Cys with a 300-residue protein: missense. A +1 insertion near codon 10 scrambles the reading frame and typically hits a stop soon after (here at residue 18) with an mRNA one nucleotide longer: frameshift. passage.title: Two ways of hearing a census
passage.body:
Poem (untitled, 2019)

We counted rooms as if rooms were people.
The spare one kept its coat on.
In the column for language we wrote the kettle.
Nobody asked the stairs their age.

Commentary by L. Okonkwo, catalogue essay for an exhibition of household inventories:
The poem is easy to misread as anti-data. It is not. It notices that a census already poetizes: it decides what may stand for a life (rooms, language, age) and what must remain downstairs, unasked. The coat on the spare room is not a joke about furniture. It is a figure for surplus — the part of a household that official forms cannot rent. When the poem puts a kettle in the language column, it is not claiming kettles speak. It is showing how quickly a form will accept a proxy if the proxy is small and warm.

A table printed beside the poem in the gallery listed visitors by hour and by whether they photographed the stairs:
Hour 10: 14 visitors, 2 photographed stairs
Hour 11: 31 visitors, 18 photographed stairs
Hour 12: 9 visitors, 0 photographed stairs (docent talk in progress)
The curator captioned the table: Attention is not the same as attendance.

A radio host later called the exhibition “political because it made a kettle into a citizen.” Okonkwo's essay had already refused that flattening. The political cut, for her, is not enfranchising objects. It is noticing which human details a state is willing to miss.

items.stem:
Clearance C = U V / P, with U urine concentration, V urine flow, P plasma concentration. Simultaneous measurements:

Marker | P | U | V
Inulin | 4.0 mg L−1 | 200 mg L−1 | 2.0 mL min−1
PAH | 2.0 mg L−1 | 1000 mg L−1 | 2.0 mL min−1

Inulin clearance estimates GFR. PAH clearance estimates effective renal plasma flow. What are GFR, RPF, and filtration fraction GFR/RPF?

choices.text: GFR 50 mL min−1; RPF 500 mL min−1; FF 0.10
GFR 100 mL min−1; RPF 200 mL min−1; FF 0.50
GFR 100 mL min−1; RPF 1000 mL min−1; FF 0.10
GFR 1000 mL min−1; RPF 100 mL min−1; FF 10

items.explanation: Convert V to 0.0020 L min−1. Inulin: C = 200 × 0.0020 / 4.0 = 0.40 / 4.0 = 0.10 L min−1 = 100 mL min−1. PAH: C = 1000 × 0.0020 / 2.0 = 2.0 / 2.0 = 1.0 L min−1 = 1000 mL min−1. Filtration fraction = 100/1000 = 0.10. Swapping the two clearances inverts FF to an impossible 10. Halving both would require using V = 1.0 mL min−1. Using U/P without V for PAH gives 500, not 1000 mL min−1, and 200 mL min−1 would be a typical RBF mis-scale.

distractorRationales.A: Those values would follow if V were taken as 1.0 mL min−1 instead of 2.0.
distractorRationales.B: RPF 200 mL min−1 underuses the PAH U/P ratio of 500 together with the 2 mL min−1 flow.
distractorRationales.D: That pair swaps inulin and PAH clearances and makes FF = 10, which cannot be a fraction of plasma filtered.

items.stem:
The slope of a velocity–time graph is acceleration. A cart’s v–t record is:

Interval | v(t)
0.0 to 3.0 s | v decreases linearly from 12.0 m s−1 to 0
3.0 to 5.0 s | v = 0 (at rest)
5.0 to 8.0 s | v increases linearly from 0 to 6.0 m s−1

What is the acceleration in the interval 0.0–3.0 s?
items.explanation: Acceleration is Δv/Δt. From 12.0 m s−1 to 0 in 3.0 s, a = (0 − 12.0)/3.0 = −4.0 m s−2. The negative sign means the velocity is decreasing (the cart is slowing while still moving in the original positive direction). Zero acceleration applies to the 3–5 s rest interval, not to 0–3 s. The later +2.0 m s−2 is (6.0 − 0)/3.0 for 5–8 s. Dropping the sign and quoting +4.0 m s−2 reports the magnitude of the first interval’s acceleration but not the signed kinematic value asked for.

distractorRationales.B: Zero slope occurs only while the cart is at rest (3–5 s). The 0–3 s segment has a clear negative slope.
distractorRationales.C: +2.0 m s−2 is the slope of the 5–8 s segment, not of 0–3 s.
distractorRationales.D: +4.0 m s−2 is the magnitude of the first interval’s acceleration with the sign omitted. Velocity is decreasing, so a is negative.

items.stem: A conducting rod of length ℓ = 0.20 m slides at 4.0 m s−1 on rails in B = 0.50 T, B perpendicular to the area. Motional emf ε = B ℓ v. The circuit resistance is 2.0 Ω. Induced current I = ε/R. The magnetic drag is F = B I ℓ. What are ε, I, and F?

choices.text: ε = 0.40 V; I = 0.20 A; F = 0.020 N opposing the motion (Lenz)
ε = 0.40 V; I = 0.20 A; F = 0, because magnetic fields do no work
ε = 0.40 V; I = 2.0 A (R omitted as 0.20 Ω); F = 0.20 N

items.explanation: ε = 0.50 × 0.20 × 4.0 = 0.40 V. I = 0.40/2.0 = 0.20 A. F = 0.50 × 0.20 × 0.20 = 0.020 N. Lenz’s law requires that force to oppose the change in flux, i.e. to drag against the imposed velocity, so a pulling agent must do mechanical work that becomes I²R heat. ‘Magnetic fields do no work’ refers to F·v on individual charges in the B field, not to the external agent. Dropping a factor of 10 in Bℓv gives 4.0 V. Using R = 0.20 Ω instead of 2.0 Ω inflates I tenfold.

distractorRationales.B: The 0.40 V and 0.20 A are right, but the current-carrying rod in B feels 0.020 N opposing the motion; the hand pulling the rod does the work.
distractorRationales.C: ε = Bℓv = 0.40 V, not 4.0 V; the later I and F scale from that error.
distractorRationales.D: R is 2.0 Ω, so I = 0.20 A not 2.0 A; F then is 0.020 N.

items.stem: Oxidation numbers in Cr2O7 2− + 3 SO2 + 2 H+ → 2 Cr3+ + 3 SO4 2− + H2O are assigned with O as −2 and H as +1. items.stem: A protease isolated from a mammalian pancreas hydrolyzes peptides composed of L-amino acids with a measured kcat/Km of 2×10^5 M−1 s−1. passage.title: psg-ps-9
passage.body:
Sociologists analyzed how a chronic illness is understood and managed in a mid-sized city. Using surveys and interviews, they documented three patterns. First, physicians and hospitals coordinated with schools and workplaces so that ill members could be temporarily excused from normal duties while being expected to seek treatment and cooperate with doctors. Second, patients with more education and income obtained diagnoses and specialist care far faster than poorer patients, who often relied on crowded clinics; the researchers traced this to differences in insurance, flexible work hours, and familiarity with medical institutions. Third, behaviors once seen as ordinary or as moral failings - such as persistent sadness or restlessness - were increasingly defined and treated as medical conditions.
The team framed each pattern with a different theoretical lens. The coordinated excusing of the sick was described as an institution maintaining social stability by managing how illness disrupts roles. The unequal access was described in terms of groups with different amounts of resources and power competing for a scarce good. The redefinition of ordinary behaviors as illnesses was described as a process by which the meaning of 'sickness' is negotiated and expanded within a society. In interviews, patients described how a formal diagnosis changed how others treated them, sometimes granting sympathy and sometimes attaching stigma. The authors noted that the fastest-growing diagnoses clustered among specific age groups, and that the city's aging population was projected to raise overall demand for chronic-disease care over the coming decades.

Chronic stress (via sustained cortisol) suppresses immune function — studies show slower wound healing and greater susceptibility to infection. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. passage.title: The courtesy of untranslatability
passage.body:
Historians of language like to treat translation as a pipe: meaning enters one end, equivalent wording exits the other, and any turbulence is a defect in the plumber. The figure is flattering to publishers, who can then sell fluency as fidelity, and it is flattering to readers, who can then consume a foreign argument as if it had always been written in their kitchen. The figure is also false. A translation is not a transfer of a stable cargo. It is a series of decisions about which silences will remain audible and which will be paved over so that a page turns without snagging.

Consider the ordinary boast that a novel has been rendered into "perfectly natural" English. Natural for whom? The boast treats the target language as a climate rather than as a historically specific set of habits, class markers, and tolerated opacities. When a rural insult is recast as a metropolitan joke, or a liturgical cadence is recast as a magazine paragraph, the text has not been rescued from awkwardness. It has been enrolled in a local etiquette. The reader who thanks the translator for making the book "not feel translated" is thanking the translator for hiding the fact that hospitality occurred. Hospitality, if it is more than a smile, leaves a trace of the guest.

This is not an argument for wooden calques or for the museum of untranslated words left standing like exhibits. Those tactics can become their own piety, a performance of difficulty that congratulates the reader for enduring it. The more serious failure is the opposite one: the belief that a text which does not delay us has therefore been understood. Delay is sometimes the only honest report of a conceptual mismatch. A legal term that organizes a whole civic world cannot be swapped for a near-synonym without smuggling in the civic world of the synonym. To refuse the delay is to pretend that the two worlds already agreed.

Publishers will object that readers abandon books that snag. They are not wrong about the market. They are wrong to treat the market as a theory of meaning. A culture that will only receive what has already been made to sound like itself is not receiving; it is recruiting. The translated page then becomes a mirror with a foreign name on the title page, and the prestige of the foreign name is used to ratify what the reader already believed. That is why "accessible" can function as a political adjective. It names not a reading level but a refusal of conceptual immigration.

None of this requires contempt for the reader. It requires a different courtesy: the courtesy of letting a sentence remain slightly foreign so that the reader can notice the foreignness as information rather than as a stain. The translator's invisibility, long praised as professionalism, is in this light a kind of disappearance of evidence. We might instead want translators to be visibly responsible for their choices, not as celebrities, but as people who can be asked why a silence was kept or filled.

The practical consequence is modest and severe. Reviewers should stop treating smoothness as a synonym for accuracy. Teachers should stop treating a bilingual dictionary as a moral instrument. And readers who want to be hosts rather than consumers should learn to tolerate, even to prize, the small resistances that prove a text has not been entirely naturalized. What cannot be made to sound like us is often the part that most needed to travel.

items.stem: A winch pulls a crate horizontally at a constant 2 m/s. The tension in the cable is a constant 10 N. The instantaneous mechanical power delivered by the tension is:

choices.text: 0 W, because kinetic energy is not changing

items.explanation: Instantaneous power delivered by a force is P = F · v = F v when force and velocity are parallel. Here P = (10 N)(2 m/s) = 20 W. Constant speed means the net force on the crate is zero, so friction (or another opposing force) cancels the 10 N and net work is zero, but the tension still does positive work at rate F v. The opposing force does an equal negative work, which is why KE stays constant. Over any 1 s interval the tension does 20 J of work, which is 20 W of power from that one force.

distractorRationales.A: Zero net work (and unchanging KE) does not mean every force delivers zero power. Tension does +20 W; the opposing force does −20 W.
distractorRationales.B: This is F/v = 10/2. Power is the product F v, not the quotient; N/(m/s) is not a watt.
distractorRationales.D: This is 2 F v, perhaps inserting a leftover 2 from (1/2) m v^2. That factor does not belong in P = F v.

passage.title: The Archive Test (1977)
passage.body: Ingrid Nilsen's 1977 essay “The Archive Test,” on broadcast newsrooms, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that expertise without a named audience is just private language. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: psg-bb-1
passage.body:
Researchers characterized a bacterial hydrolase, EnzA, that cleaves a colorless substrate into a yellow product, allowing the initial reaction velocity to be measured by absorbance. Working at constant enzyme concentration, saturating buffer, and 37 deg C, they varied the substrate concentration [S] and recorded the initial velocity (v0). As [S] increased, v0 rose steeply at first and then leveled off, tracing the hyperbolic curve expected for a single-active-site enzyme. From these data the team estimated a maximum velocity (Vmax) of 100 micromol/min and a Michaelis constant (Km) of 2.0 mM, where Km is the [S] at which v0 equals half of Vmax.
The team then repeated the assay in the presence of two candidate drugs. With a fixed concentration of Inhibitor A, the measured Vmax remained 100 micromol/min, but the apparent Km rose to 6.0 mM; adding excess substrate fully restored the maximal rate. With a fixed concentration of Inhibitor B, the apparent Km stayed at 2.0 mM, but Vmax fell to 50 micromol/min, and no amount of added substrate recovered the original maximal rate.
A double-reciprocal (Lineweaver-Burk) plot summarized the results: the control line and the Inhibitor A line shared the same y-intercept but differed in slope, whereas the control line and the Inhibitor B line shared the same x-intercept but differed in y-intercept. The researchers concluded that the two inhibitors act by distinct mechanisms, a distinction that matters clinically because it determines whether raising the physiological substrate concentration can overcome the drug's effect.

passage.title: Electrodialysis Removal of Lactate
passage.body:
A fictional electrodialysis device removes lactate from a small waste stream. Lactic acid has pKa = 3.9, and lactate carries a -1 charge. The feed chamber initially contains 100 mL of 0.100 mM total lactate species. An anion-exchange membrane separates the feed chamber from a collection chamber near the positive anode. Each run lasts 300 s. Current can be carried by lactate and by other ions in the buffer. Joule heating may broaden concentration gradients and reduce separation efficiency.

Electrodialysis conditions and lactate removal.
Run | Feed pH | Voltage (V) | Current (mA) | Temperature rise (C) | Salt condition | Total lactate removed from feed (%)
1 | 3.0 | 20 | 2.0 | 0.2 | low salt | 8
2 | 7.0 | 20 | 10.0 | 1.0 | low salt | 45
3 | 7.0 | 40 | 20.0 | 4.5 | low salt | 70
4 | 7.0 | 40 | 20.0 | 1.0 with cooling | low salt | 78
5 | 7.0 | 20 | 25.0 | 5.0 | high salt | 30

Electrodialysis chamber arrangement. — Negatively charged lactate migrates through an anion-exchange membrane toward the positive anode. Neutral lactic acid is much less efficiently transported by the electric field.
