passage.title: Cartoon: Clinic time
passage.body:
A single-panel cartoon, unsigned, published on a letters page.

Foreground: a waiting-room bench. Four people sit. Above each head a small clock; the hands are at 1:10, 2:40, 4:15, and 9:50. None of the clocks match the large wall clock, which has no hands.

On the wall, a framed motto: WE VALUE YOUR TIME. The frame is gold. The glass is cracked.

To the right, a receptionist window. The receptionist smiles with many teeth and holds a clipboard titled TRIAGE (PRIVATE). On the clipboard the only visible line is: “Can they still sit up?” A potted plant on the sill is fake; its price tag remains.

Under the bench, a fifth clock, face-down.

Caption, in small type: “The system is coping.”

A letter printed beneath, from “Concerned, Upper Shore”: “Cartoons like this undermine dedicated staff. If people arrived on time and did not bring relatives, clocks would match.”

items.stem:
Haemoglobin–oxygen saturation on two dissociation curves at the same PO2 values:

PO2 (mmHg) | sat % at P50 = 26 mmHg | sat % at P50 = 32 mmHg (low pH / high 2,3-BPG)
100 | 97 | 95
40 | 75 | 60
26 | 50 | 38

Venous muscle PO2 is 40 mmHg; arterial PO2 is 100 mmHg. Which statement about oxygen unloading is supported?

choices.text: The right shift prevents unloading because saturation at 40 mmHg is lower
Arterial saturation falling from 97% to 95% is the main physiological effect of a P50 increase
P50 is the PO2 at 100% saturation, so 26 mmHg already represents full loading
The right-shifted curve unloads more O2 in tissue (35 percentage points versus 22) with little change in arterial loading

items.explanation: Unloading is arterial minus venous saturation. For P50 = 26 mmHg: 97 − 75 = 22 points. For P50 = 32 mmHg: 95 − 60 = 35 points. The Bohr/2,3-BPG right shift therefore delivers more oxygen at a venous PO2 of 40 mmHg, while arterial loading at 100 mmHg barely changes (97 vs 95). Lower venous saturation means more, not less, unloading. P50 is the PO2 at 50% saturation by definition, not at 100%.

distractorRationales.A: A lower saturation at 40 mmHg is exactly greater unloading if arterial saturation remains near 95–97%.
distractorRationales.B: The 2-point arterial change is trivial beside the 15-point extra venous desaturation.
distractorRationales.C: The table itself shows 50% saturation at 26 mmHg on the first curve; that is the definition of P50.

passage.title: Politeness as Gate (1973)
passage.body: Marta Górska published “Politeness as Gate” in 1973 after a season in museum captions. The argument is that local knowledge is treated as anecdote until a model needs it. The author grants that standards exist for a reason and that amateurs can be wrong. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Developing mouse paws treated with a pan-caspase inhibitor retain interdigital webbing that normally regresses before birth. DNA from the untreated interdigital mesenchyme shows internucleosomal ladders. The morphogenetic process that was blocked is:

choices.text: Mitotic expansion of ectoderm that physically pushes digits apart
Ossification of the radius, which secondarily erases webbing
Programmed cell death (apoptosis) of interdigital mesenchymal cells
Fertilization of residual polar bodies in the limb bud

items.explanation: Digit separation in mice depends on apoptosis of the interdigital mesenchyme. Caspases execute that program; inhibiting them leaves a bat-like web. Internucleosomal DNA cleavage (ladders) is a biochemical hallmark of apoptosis, distinct from random necrotic smears. The process is spatially patterned death, not a requirement that ectoderm outgrow the web or that the radius ossify to cut the tissue. Polar-body fertilization is unrelated to limb morphogenesis. Comparative anatomy (webbed duck feet have less interdigital apoptosis) is the same mechanism in another species.

distractorRationales.A: Digits are sculpted by death of cells between them, not by mitotic wedging alone.
distractorRationales.B: Radius ossification does not explain caspase-sensitive webbing or DNA ladders in the mesenchyme.
distractorRationales.D: Polar bodies are meiotic products in the ovary/zygote, not limb-bud cells.

passage.title: Gas Collection During Electrolysis of a Buffer
passage.body:
A fictional laboratory exercise uses water electrolysis to calibrate a gas-volume sensor. At the cathode, hydrogen gas forms according to: 2H2O + 2e- -> H2 + 2OH-. At the anode, oxygen gas forms separately and is not collected in the cathode tube. The cathode gas is collected over water. At 298 K, the vapor pressure of water is 0.031 atm. The gas collection tube is adjusted so that the total pressure of the collected gas equals 1.031 atm. The Faraday constant is 96500 C/mol e-. A 6.0 V source supplies the cell through external circuit elements.

Electrolysis trials and collected cathode gas.
Trial | Current (A) | Time (s) | Total gas pressure (atm) | Temperature (K) | Collected cathode gas volume (mL)
1 | 0.100 | 1930 | 1.031 | 298 | 24.0
2 | 0.100 | 3860 | 1.031 | 298 | 48.0
3 | 0.200 | 1930 | 1.031 | 298 | 46.5
4 | 0.100 | 1930 | 1.031 | 310 | 25.0

Cathode gas collection apparatus. — Hydrogen produced at the cathode bubbles into an inverted graduated tube filled with water. The gas volume is read after equalizing the water levels inside and outside the tube.

passage.title: Aesthetics — why originals matter
passage.body:
Suppose a forger produces a copy of a painting so exact that no expert, however equipped, could tell it from the original. Most of us would still prefer to own the original, and would pay vastly more for it. This preference is easy to mock as mere snobbery — a fetish for provenance that adds nothing to what the eye receives. If two canvases are visually identical, the skeptic asks, how can one be aesthetically superior to the other? Whatever we are paying for, it cannot be the look of the thing.

The skeptic assumes that the value of a painting must reside entirely in its present visual surface. But this assumption is far from obvious. When I stand before a canvas that Rembrandt himself touched, I am in physical, causal contact with the very object his hand shaped. The forgery, however exquisite, offers no such contact; it is the terminus of a different causal chain, one that runs back not to Rembrandt but to a clever imitator in a rented studio. To value the original is to value that lineage, and there is nothing irrational about caring where a thing comes from.

An analogy makes the point. A letter in a beloved's handwriting is treasured over a flawless photocopy, though the copy conveys every word. We do not think the person who keeps the original has made a perceptual error, as though they had failed to notice that the words are the same. They are responding to something the photocopy lacks: a direct trace of the writer's presence. Paintings, on this view, are less like texts, whose value is exhausted by their content, and more like relics, whose value depends on their history.

Yet the analogy should not be pressed too far. Relics are valued almost wholly for contact and hardly at all for how they look; the point of a saint's bone is not its appearance. Great paintings are not like this. Their history matters, but so, undeniably, does what they show — the very composition and color the forger has reproduced. A defender of originals need not deny that appearance carries much of a painting's worth. The claim is only that appearance does not carry all of it, and that the remainder, however hard to name, is not nothing.

This more modest thesis is also the more defensible one. It grants the skeptic everything plausible in the skeptical position — that the visible work is most of what we prize — while denying the further, unargued step from "most" to "all." The forger's triumph, if it is one, is to have captured the larger share of a painting's value. It is not to have shown that the smaller share was an illusion all along.

passage.title: Working Memory, Sleep Restriction, and Retrieval Cues
passage.body:
A fictional laboratory study examined how one night of sleep restriction affects memory performance. Participants were randomly assigned to either a normal-sleep group or a restricted-sleep group. The next morning, all participants studied 30 neutral word pairs. After a 20-minute filler task, they completed two tests. In the free-recall test, participants wrote down as many target words as possible. In the cued-recall test, participants were shown the first word of each pair and attempted to retrieve the associated target word. Participants also completed a 2-back task as a measure of working memory updating.

Memory and working-memory performance
Group | Free recall: mean words recalled | Cued recall: mean words recalled | 2-back accuracy (%)
Normal sleep | 18.4 | 24.1 | 87
Restricted sleep | 13.2 | 20.2 | 73

Self-reported fatigue and motivation
Group | Fatigue rating, 1 to 7 | Motivation rating, 1 to 7
Normal sleep | 2.3 | 5.8
Restricted sleep | 5.9 | 5.6

Retrieval benefit — Both groups recalled more words on cued recall than on free recall, but the restricted-sleep group performed worse than the normal-sleep group on both tests.

Four nuclides are listed as (Z, A):
P: (17, 35); Q: (17, 37); R: (18, 37); S: (16, 32).
Isotopes are nuclides with the same proton number Z and different mass number A. Neutron number is A − Z.
Which pair are isotopes of the same element?

choices.text: Q and R, because both have A = 37
P and R, because neutron numbers are 18 and 19, nearly equal
P and Q, because both have Z = 17

items.explanation: Z is the proton count and defines the element. P and Q both have Z = 17, with A = 35 and 37, so they are isotopes (17 protons; neutrons 18 and 20). Q and R share A = 37 but differ in Z (17 vs 18); those are isobars, not isotopes. Nearly equal neutron numbers do not make P and R the same element (Z = 17 vs 18). An accidental equality of two differences for R and S is not the isotope definition.

distractorRationales.A: Same A and different Z are isobars (here 37Cl and 37Ar), not isotopes.
distractorRationales.B: P has 18 neutrons and R has 19, but Z differs (17 vs 18), so they are different elements.
distractorRationales.D: Subtracting Z and A between two nuclides is not a test for isotopes; R and S have different Z and A.

items.stem: A 400-Da fluorescent tracer is added to the apical bath of a polarized MDCK monolayer. In wild-type cultures the tracer remains apical for hours. Monolayers lacking claudin-1 allow the tracer to appear in the basolateral compartment within minutes without any drop in transcellular transporter activity. The missing epithelial structure is the:

Tight junction (zonula occludens), whose claudin strands form the paracellular seal
Focal adhesion, which occludes the lateral intercellular space at the apical pole

items.explanation: Polarized epithelia separate apical and basolateral compartments with tight junctions. Claudins polymerize into anastomosing strands that limit paracellular flux of small solutes; losing claudin-1 opens that shunt so an apical tracer reaches the basolateral bath. Gap junctions (connexins) couple the interiors of adjacent cells and do not form the apical seal. Isometric tetanic tension of a skeletal fibre versus sarcomere length (relative tension, 100 = plateau):

Length (µm) | tension (%)
1.5 | 55
2.0 | 100
2.2 | 100
2.6 | 80
3.6 | 0

Thick filaments are 1.6 µm; thin filaments from each Z-line are 1.0 µm; the H-zone has no thin-filament overlap. Which mechanical interpretation fits?

choices.text: The plateau at 2.0–2.2 µm means no cross-bridges attach in that range
Tension at 1.5 µm is low because thin filaments have detached from Z-lines
3.6 µm is zero overlap so zero force; 2.0–2.2 µm is optimal overlap; 1.5 µm is excessive overlap that impairs force
Force is maximum at 3.6 µm because cross-bridges have the most room to swing

items.explanation: At 3.6 µm a 1.6 µm thick filament plus two 1.0 µm thin filaments end-to-end span 3.6 µm, so overlap—and force—is zero, matching the table. The 2.0–2.2 µm plateau is the region of constant maximal overlap of cross-bridge zones. At 1.5 µm opposite thin filaments crash into each other and thick filaments hit Z-lines, reducing force to 55%, not because Z-line attachments are lost. Maximum force is therefore at intermediate, not extreme stretched, length. The plateau is maximal attachment, not zero attachment.

distractorRationales.A: 100% tension on the plateau is the maximum number of active bridges, not zero.
distractorRationales.B: Thin filaments remain anchored at Z-lines; force falls at short length because of double overlap and compression, as the 1.5 µm row shows residual 55% tension.
distractorRationales.D: The 3.6 µm row is 0% tension; there is no overlap for cross-bridges to swing on.

items.stem: In guinea pigs, black (B) is dominant to brown (b) and rough coat (R) is dominant to smooth (r). The loci assort independently. A dihybrid BbRr is crossed to another BbRr. Among 160 offspring, how many are expected to be black and smooth (B_ rr), and what fraction of all offspring are brown and rough (bb R_)?
items.explanation: Independent assortment gives 9:3:3:1 among the four phenotypic classes of a double heterozygote self-cross. Black-smooth is B_ rr = (3/4)×(1/4) = 3/16, and 3/16 × 160 = 30. Brown-rough is bb R_ = (1/4)×(3/4) = 3/16, not 1/16 (that is bb rr) and not 1/4 (that is a single recessive class). Ten would be 1/16 of 160. Forty would be 1/4 of 160, the combined recessive-at-one-locus count if the other locus were ignored incorrectly.

distractorRationales.A: 10 is 1/16 × 160, the double-recessive class, not B_ rr.
distractorRationales.B: 40 is 1/4 × 160, which would be all smooth coats regardless of colour, not the black-smooth subset.
distractorRationales.C: The headcount 30 is right, but brown-rough is 3/16, not the 1/16 double recessive.

items.stem: Glycogen and cellulose are both homopolymers of D-glucose. Glycogen is readily mobilized by glycogen phosphorylase in animals; cellulose is not digested by human enzymes and forms rigid fibrils. Which chemical difference is most responsible?

choices.text: Cellulose uses α-1,6 branches every 8–12 residues; glycogen is an unbranched β-1,4 polymer.
Cellulose is composed of galactose, the C4 epimer of glucose; glycogen uses glucose, so only glycogen matches phosphorylase specificity.

Glycogen has α-1,4 chains with α-1,6 branches, producing a helical, hydrated polymer with many nonreducing ends; cellulose has β-1,4 linkages that form straight, hydrogen-bonded sheets resistant to human amylases and phosphorylase.
The two polymers are chemically identical; only the organism of origin determines whether human enzymes can hydrolyze them.

items.explanation: Glycosidic stereochemistry dictates polymer conformation and enzyme specificity. α-1,4 linkages in glycogen curve the chain into a hydrated helix, and α-1,6 branches create many nonreducing ends for phosphorylase. β-1,4 linkages in cellulose produce extended chains that hydrogen-bond into fibrils; human amylases and glycogen phosphorylase do not hydrolyze β-1,4 glucans. Both polymers are poly-D-glucose, not galactose. Branching is a glycogen feature, not a cellulose feature, and digestibility is a chemical-recognition issue rather than a mere label of plant versus animal origin.

distractorRationales.A: This swaps the architectures: glycogen is the branched α polymer; cellulose is unbranched β-1,4.
distractorRationales.B: Cellulose is a glucose homopolymer; galactose is not the repeating unit, and C4 epimerization is not the glycogen/cellulose distinction.
distractorRationales.D: The polymers differ in anomeric configuration and branching; those chemical differences, not the source organism alone, explain enzyme resistance.

passage.title: On keeping a promise to a stranger
passage.body:
When the magistrate asked why he had returned the purse, the clerk did not say honesty. He said habit. He had been taught, in a household that measured virtue by small repetitions, that a found object remains someone else's until the world has been given a fair chance to reclaim it. The purse contained little money and a letter, unsealed, beginning: I will not be there when you arrive. He did not finish it. To finish it, he thought, would convert a duty into a story, and stories have a way of making the finder important.

Philosophers like to treat this as a puzzle about property and knowledge. If he does not know the owner, is the duty weaker? If the letter would have saved a marriage, does withholding it become a harm? The clerk would have found the questions indecent. He was not refusing knowledge so much as refusing a role. The city had clerks for lost property; it did not have clerks for other people's farewells.

A later commentator, writing after the clerk was dead, praised him as a Kantian saint: he acted from a maxim he could will as universal. The praise is too clean. The clerk's maxim was local and slightly ashamed. He did not want to be the man who had read the letter. Shame, not universality, kept his eyes off the page. That is not a lesser ethics. It is an ethics that knows how quickly curiosity dresses itself as concern.

The owner collected the purse the next morning and did not thank him. In the commentary this becomes a test of whether virtue needs recognition. The clerk, if asked, would have said only that the counter was busy.

passage.title: psg-cars-3
passage.body:
Few debates in literary theory have proved more durable than the question of authorial intent: does the meaning of a text reside primarily in what its author meant to communicate, or does meaning emerge through the activity of reading itself? At one extreme, the intentionalist holds that misreading is always possible — that interpretations diverging from the author's design are simply mistaken, however ingenious or culturally resonant they may be. At the other extreme, the anti-intentionalist insists that once a text is released into the world, the author's psychological states become strictly irrelevant: what the words mean is fixed not by biography but by the conventions of the language and genre in which they are embedded.
The anti-intentionalist position gained influential expression in mid-twentieth-century criticism, when theorists argued that treating the author's intention as the criterion of correct interpretation commits a category error. Evidence about what a poet hoped to achieve, they maintained, cannot settle what a poem achieves, because a poem is a verbal artifact that may realize meanings its creator did not foresee — meanings that become available only through the community of readers over time. The celebrated example of an ironic text serves as illustration: a writer may compose a scathing satire of nationalistic rhetoric while sincerely believing the rhetoric they are parodying; the satiric meaning is there in the text whether the author intended it or not.
Intentionalists counter that language is an intentional practice: utterances mean what speakers mean by them, and written language does not somehow escape this fundamental feature of linguistic communication. To read a text in complete disregard of what its author was trying to do, they argue, is to treat it as a natural object rather than a human creation — to decode it the way one might decode an accidental inkblot rather than a deliberate message. Moreover, intentionalists point out that appeals to 'the language and genre' still presuppose communicative conventions that are themselves constituted by the intentions of the linguistic community.
A mediating view distinguishes between actual authorial intention (the historical individual's specific psychological states) and what might be called the implied author: the authorial persona that a competent reader constructs from the textual evidence alone. On this account, interpretation aims neither at private biography nor at free-floating textual play but at the coherent communicative project that the text itself invites. The implied author is, in effect, the best hypothesis about what an ideally communicative author of this text would have intended — a construct that disciplines interpretation without requiring access to historical documents.
What unites all parties to this dispute is the recognition that texts are not transparent windows onto authors' minds or onto a language-independent reality. They are artifacts whose significance is never simply given but must always be construed — a fact that makes hermeneutics, the theory of interpretation, as much a practical as a philosophical discipline.

passage.title: psg-bb-2
passage.body:
A biochemistry lab studied how a small globular enzyme, RibN, loses activity when it unfolds. In its native state, RibN is stabilized by a hydrophobic core, numerous hydrogen bonds within its alpha-helices and beta-sheets, and a single disulfide bond linking two cysteine residues. The team monitored folding both by measuring enzyme activity and by tracking buried tryptophan residues, which fluoresce differently when the protein unfolds. Slowly heating the wild-type enzyme, they found that activity was retained up to about 55 deg C and then fell sharply, with a melting temperature (Tm, the temperature at which half the protein is unfolded) of 65 deg C.
They compared three samples. A cysteine-to-alanine mutant that cannot form the disulfide bond behaved like wild type at low temperature but had a Tm of only 52 deg C. Adding 6 M urea, a chemical denaturant, to wild-type enzyme lowered its Tm dramatically and abolished activity even at room temperature; on dialysis to remove the urea, activity slowly returned. Boiling followed by cooling left the protein inactive and aggregated, yet sequencing showed that the polypeptide's amino acid sequence was fully intact.
The investigators emphasized that all of these treatments disrupted the folded shape without breaking the peptide bonds of the backbone, and that the enzyme's function depended on maintaining its three-dimensional conformation, not merely on possessing the correct sequence.

passage.title: psg-cp-8
passage.body:
Purifying the product of a reaction is a routine but crucial task. A student runs a reaction that yields a mixture of a carboxylic acid (benzoic acid) and a neutral, nonpolar hydrocarbon, both dissolved in an organic solvent, and sets out to separate and identify them.
She first checks the mixture by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) on a silica gel plate, a polar stationary phase, developed in a relatively nonpolar solvent. After development, one spot has traveled 3.0 cm from the origin while the solvent front has advanced 5.0 cm. She records the retention factor (Rf) for the spot and notes that, on polar silica, more polar compounds cling to the plate and move less, whereas less polar compounds travel farther.
To separate the two components in bulk, she performs a liquid-liquid extraction, shaking the organic solution with aqueous sodium hydroxide in a separatory funnel. The carboxylic acid reacts with the base and is converted to its sodium carboxylate salt; the neutral hydrocarbon does not react. After the layers settle, she drains them apart and then treats the aqueous layer with hydrochloric acid to reverse the reaction and recover the purified acid.
Finally, she considers how to separate two miscible liquids that differ in boiling point and reviews simple distillation, in which the mixture is heated, the vapor is drawn off and condensed, and the collected liquid is enriched in one component. Throughout, she relies on differences in polarity, acid-base behavior, and volatility - the physical and chemical handles that separations exploit.

passage.title: Fidelity of a threonyl-tRNA synthetase
passage.body:
A fictional threonyl-tRNA synthetase, ThrRS-F, attaches threonine to tRNAThr during translation. The first active site activates threonine by forming threonyl-AMP from threonine and ATP; the amino acid is then transferred to the 3' end of tRNAThr. Because valine is structurally similar to threonine, ThrRS-F also contains an editing domain that hydrolyzes mischarged Val-tRNAThr. A reporter protein loses activity when valine is inserted at positions normally encoded by threonine codons.

Aminoacylation and editing properties of ThrRS-F.
Condition | Thr-tRNAThr charging rate (%) | Val-tRNAThr accumulation (%) | ATP-to-AMP conversion rate (%) | Active reporter protein (%)
Wild-type ThrRS-F + wild-type tRNAThr | 100 | 1 | 100 | 98
Editing-site D201A + wild-type tRNAThr | 95 | 28 | 125 | 62
Activation-site K55A + wild-type tRNAThr | 8 | 1 | 10 | 12
Wild-type ThrRS-F + acceptor-stem mutant tRNAThr | 18 | 1 | 22 | 20
Editing-site D201A + excess free valine | 90 | 45 | 140 | 45
Wild-type ThrRS-F + noncognate tRNAAla | 3 | 0.5 | 5 | 8

Two-site model of ThrRS-F specificity. — The activation site forms aminoacyl-AMP intermediates using ATP. Correct threonylated tRNA is released for translation. Incorrect Val-tRNAThr can enter an editing domain, where the aminoacyl ester bond is hydrolyzed before the tRNA reaches the ribosome.

items.stem: What is the most likely explanation for blood lactate rising sharply above a certain exercise intensity?

choices.text: Above that intensity, the muscles' demand for energy outpaces the oxygen supply, so a growing share of energy production shifts to anaerobic respiration, which produces lactate as a byproduct.

items.explanation: As intensity rises, oxygen delivery eventually cannot keep pace with muscle energy demand, forcing a shift toward anaerobic respiration, which produces lactate as a byproduct — explaining why lactate rises sharply only above a threshold intensity, not at low intensity. The body defaults to efficient aerobic respiration when oxygen supply can meet demand. Once demand outpaces supply, cells increasingly rely on faster but less efficient anaerobic respiration, which is why lactate (its byproduct) only accumulates sharply past a certain effort level. Memory tip: "Oxygen can't keep up, so the body switches lanes": below threshold, oxygen supply matches demand (aerobic lane); above it, demand outruns supply and the body merges into the anaerobic lane, producing lactate as the toll. passage.title: Return-of-service bond: two letters
passage.body:
Two letters appeared in the same metropolitan daily after the health minister proposed a "return-of-service" bond: new doctors whose training was publicly subsidised would owe three years in designated underserved clinics before they could take an unrestricted urban post.

Letter A
A public scholarship is not a gift ribbon. It is a wager the public makes on a scarce skill. If the graduate then sells that skill immediately to the densest private market, the wager has been privatised without a receipt. Three years is not indenture; it is the time in which a clinic learns a name and a name learns a clinic. Those who call the bond a "mobility tax" speak as if mobility were a natural right unpolluted by the taxes that built the teaching hospitals. Rights that forget their invoices are just appetites with better stationery. Underserved towns are not a lifestyle choice the profession may decline, like a sport. They are the other half of the ledger.

Letter B
The minister has misdiagnosed a staffing failure as a character failure in the young. Clinics are empty of doctors for the same reasons they are empty of radiographers and nurses: housing costs, school deserts, professional isolation, and locum markets that pay more for a weekend than a bonded year pays for a winter. A bond does not staff a town; it parks a resentful beginner there and calls the parking "justice." Meanwhile the budget that should have made the posting liveable is spared the embarrassment of being seen. Coercion is cheaper than housing. If the public wants doctors in those rooms, it should furnish the rooms, not hostage the people it trained. A ledger that counts only the graduate's debt, and never the state's, is not a ledger. It is a sermon.

Editor's note: Letter A was signed by a retired regional physician; Letter B by a recent graduate now in a metropolitan hospital.

items.stem: A T-even bacteriophage is grown so that its DNA is labeled with 32P and its capsid protein with 35S. After adsorption to bacteria and shear that strips empty coats, 32P is recovered in the bacterial pellet while 35S remains in the supernatant. The structural implication is that:

The phage envelope fuses with the bacterial plasma membrane, mixing 35S into the cytoplasm

That partition shows the capsid is a delivery device, not the hereditary substance. Typical T-even phages are non-enveloped and are not taken up whole by bacterial phagocytosis. Protein staying outside is the opposite of protein-as-gene.

passage.body: Hanae Morioka published “A Form of Fairness” in 1976 after a season in a coastal fishery. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the standard is being used to hide a choice about who counts as a speaker. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

items.stem: Two positive point charges have electric potential energy U when separated by distance r. If their separation is increased to 2r, what is the new electric potential energy?
items.explanation: Electric potential energy for two point charges is U = kq1q2/r. Doubling the separation halves the potential energy, so the new value is U/2. Common miss: Confusing the 1/r potential energy dependence with the 1/r^2 force dependence. This correctly uses the inverse-distance relationship for electrostatic potential energy. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.A: This incorrectly applies an inverse-square relationship, which applies to force magnitude, not potential energy.
distractorRationales.B: This reverses the effect of increasing separation.
distractorRationales.C: This incorrectly makes energy increase with the square of distance.

items.stem: A rapidly dividing cell has abundant NADPH but needs more ribose 5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis. Which metabolic strategy best matches this need?

choices.text: Convert ribose 5-phosphate directly into lactate to regenerate NAD+.
Run the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway repeatedly to maximize CO2 release from glucose carbon 1.
Block all transketolase reactions so that ribose 5-phosphate cannot equilibrate with glycolytic intermediates.
Use nonoxidative pentose phosphate pathway reactions to convert glycolytic intermediates into ribose 5-phosphate.

items.explanation: When a cell needs ribose 5-phosphate more than NADPH, the reversible nonoxidative reactions of the pentose phosphate pathway can convert fructose 6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate into ribose 5-phosphate without requiring additional oxidative NADPH production. Common miss: Assuming ribose 5-phosphate production must always be coupled to new NADPH production. This directly supplies ribose 5-phosphate from glycolytic intermediates while avoiding excess NADPH production. Source: OpenMCAT (AGPL-3.0). Unverified AI practice; not AAMC.

distractorRationales.A: Ribose 5-phosphate is used for nucleotide synthesis, not direct lactate fermentation.
distractorRationales.B: The oxidative phase is useful for NADPH generation and CO2 release, which is not the stated need.
distractorRationales.C: Blocking transketolase would impair interconversion between pentose phosphates and glycolytic intermediates.

items.stem: A chemist measures the specific rotation of enantiopure (R)-2-butanol as −13.9°. A second sample of 2-butanol is prepared as a 1:1 mixture of the R and S enantiomers. What optical rotation is expected for the second sample under the same conditions?
items.explanation: Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light by equal magnitudes in opposite directions. In a racemate the two enantiomers are present in equal concentration, so the rotations cancel and the observed rotation is zero. The mixture is not optically active even though each molecule is chiral. The −13.9° value is the rotation of the pure R enantiomer; the S enantiomer would read +13.9°; doubling to −27.8° has no physical basis. Optical purity (ee) of zero is the defining optical property of a racemic mixture.

distractorRationales.A: That is the rotation of enantiopure (R)-2-butanol, not of a racemate.
distractorRationales.B: That would be the rotation of enantiopure (S)-2-butanol, not of an equal mixture.
distractorRationales.D: Rotations of enantiomers cancel rather than add; a racemate does not double the magnitude.

passage.title: psg-ps-7
passage.body:
Researchers studied how people view themselves and explain behavior. In Study 1, community volunteers completed a scale measuring their belief that they could organize and execute the actions needed to reach specific goals. Independently, they rated how much they felt their life outcomes were controlled by their own actions versus by luck or powerful others. Volunteers high on the first measure attempted harder tasks, persisted longer after setbacks, and reported less anxiety. Those who attributed outcomes mostly to outside forces set fewer goals and gave up sooner.
In Study 2, participants read vignettes about a student who failed an exam. When explaining the student's failure, observers most often cited the student's laziness or low ability, rarely mentioning the situation (an unfair test, a family emergency). Yet when participants recalled a time they themselves had failed, they overwhelmingly cited situational causes. In a variation, participants watched a peer perform poorly under obvious time pressure; even so, most still rated the peer as low in ability.
The authors linked Study 1 to two related constructs: a person's belief in their capability to succeed at specific tasks, and a general expectancy about whether outcomes are internally or externally controlled. They interpreted Study 2 as showing a systematic bias in how observers explain others' behavior, together with a divergence between how people explain their own versus others' outcomes. They stressed that these attribution tendencies operate even when situational information is clearly available.

items.stem: The fovea gives the sharpest vision partly because light there reaches the photoreceptors directly rather than passing through overlying neural layers. This is because the fovea is:

choices.text: A pit (dimple) where the overlying cells and axons are displaced, so light hits the cones directly
Covered by an extra-thick layer of axons
Packed with rods rather than cones
The point where the optic nerve exits

items.explanation: The fovea is a pit where overlying cells/axons are pushed aside, so light hits the cone-packed floor directly → sharpest vision. (At the periphery, light passes through axon layers first.) Takeaway: Fovea = a dimple where light hits cones directly (no overlying axons) → highest acuity. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The fovea is a depression where inner retinal layers are pushed aside, so light strikes the densely packed cones with minimal scattering — maximal acuity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractorRationales.B: The opposite — overlying layers are displaced at the fovea, not thickened.
distractorRationales.C: The fovea is cone-packed, not rod-packed.
distractorRationales.D: That describes the optic disc (blind spot), not the fovea.

items.stem: An ethereal solution contains equimolar benzoic acid (pKa ≈ 4.2), 4-methylphenol (pKa ≈ 10.3), and naphthalene. The solution is shaken with saturated aqueous NaHCO3 and the layers are separated. Which species is found predominantly in the aqueous layer?

choices.text: Sodium benzoate, because bicarbonate is basic enough to deprotonate the carboxylic acid but not the phenol
Sodium 4-methylphenolate, because phenols are stronger acids than carboxylic acids
Naphthalene, because it is the least polar and therefore prefers water
All three solutes, because NaHCO3 is a general organic-soluble detergent

items.explanation: Aqueous bicarbonate is a weak base whose conjugate acid (carbonic acid) has pKa near 6.4. Proton transfer HA + HCO3− ⇌ A− + H2CO3 is favorable only when pKa(HA) is below that value. Benzoic acid meets that criterion and is extracted as water-soluble benzoate. 4-Methylphenol (pKa ≈ 10) is not deprotonated by bicarbonate and remains in ether, as does non-ionizable naphthalene. The complementary extraction of the phenol requires a stronger base such as NaOH. Carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenols, not the reverse.

distractorRationales.B: Phenols are weaker acids than carboxylic acids (pKa ~10 vs ~4–5). Bicarbonate does not generate phenolate in useful amounts.
distractorRationales.C: Naphthalene is a nonpolar hydrocarbon and partitions into ether, not into aqueous bicarbonate.
distractorRationales.D: Bicarbonate is not a detergent that solubilizes all organics; it ionizes only sufficiently acidic solutes.

passage.title: Unacknowledged Method (1983)
passage.body: Kwame Boateng's 1983 essay “Unacknowledged Method,” on municipal archives, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that a metric can become the mission that it was supposed to measure. A paragraph concedes that not every complaint is evidence of capture. The turn is that fraud-control language is being stretched to cover disagreement. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. items.stem: Ksp(PbCl2) = 1.6 × 10−5 = [Pb2+][Cl−]2. Equal volumes of 0.20 M Pb(NO3)2 and 0.20 M HCl are mixed, so immediately after mixing, before any precipitation, [Pb2+] = 0.10 M and [Cl−] = 0.10 M. The reaction quotient Q = [Pb2+][Cl−]2. Does PbCl2 precipitate?

choices.text: No; Q = 0 because solids have activity 1
No; Q = 1.0 × 10−3, which is less than Ksp
Yes; Q = 0.10, set equal to [Pb2+] alone

items.explanation: After equal-volume mixing both ions are 0.10 M, so Q = (0.10)(0.10)2 = 0.10 × 0.010 = 1.0 × 10−3. Ksp is 1.6 × 10−5, and 1.0 × 10−3 > 1.6 × 10−5, so the solution is supersaturated and PbCl2 precipitates. Q is not smaller than Ksp. Omitting the square on chloride gives 0.010, still > Ksp, but the listed distractor 0.10 ignores chloride entirely. Q for the dissolved ions is not zero; the solid’s activity is 1 only once the solid is present at equilibrium, which is the state the comparison is testing for.

distractorRationales.A: Q is computed from the ion concentrations before precipitation; it is 1.0 × 10−3, not 0.
distractorRationales.C: 1.0 × 10−3 is larger than 1.6 × 10−5, so the inequality predicts precipitation.
distractorRationales.D: Q must include [Cl−]2; using [Pb2+] alone is not the Ksp expression.

passage.title: psg-cp-10
passage.body:
A research team studies both how fast a reaction goes and whether it goes at all - kinetics and thermodynamics, two independent questions. They first examine the decomposition of a reactant, X, measuring its initial rate as they vary the starting concentration at fixed temperature. In three trials the initial concentration of X is 0.10, 0.20, and 0.30 M, and the corresponding initial rates are 2.0x10^-3, 8.0x10^-3, and 1.8x10^-2 M/s. From these data they extract the reaction order in X and the rate constant.
They then vary temperature and find, as expected, that the rate rises steeply as the sample is warmed. They interpret this with the Arrhenius picture: only molecules with at least the activation energy can react, and warming increases that fraction. Adding a catalyst speeds the reaction further, and the team is careful to note what a catalyst does and does not change.
Separately, they assess the reaction's thermodynamics. Calorimetry gives a standard enthalpy change delta_H = +50 kJ/mol, and the standard entropy change is delta_S = +100 J/(mol.K). Using the Gibbs relation delta_G = delta_H - T*delta_S, they compute the free-energy change at 298 K to judge spontaneity, and they determine the temperature above which the reaction becomes spontaneous. They stress that kinetics (how fast) and thermodynamics (how favorable) are separate: a reaction can be thermodynamically favorable yet immeasurably slow, or fast yet unfavorable. They treat delta_H and delta_S as approximately constant over the range considered.

items.stem: A lineage tracer injected into a single cell of embryonic ectoderm after gastrulation later labels spinal-cord neurons and epidermal keratinocytes but never cardiomyocytes, skeletal muscle, or hepatocytes. The labeled clone was restricted to:

choices.text: Mesoderm, which produces epidermis and the neural tube
Endoderm, which produces the entire central nervous system
Ectoderm, which generates both surface epidermis and neuroectoderm
Trophectoderm only, which forms the embryo proper rather than extraembryonic tissues

items.explanation: After gastrulation the three germ layers are allocated. Ectoderm produces the epidermis and, after neural induction, the neural plate/tube (CNS neurons). Mesoderm produces heart, skeletal muscle, and many internal supporting tissues; endoderm produces hepatocytes and gut epithelium. A clone that marks epidermis plus spinal neurons and excludes heart and liver is therefore ectodermal. Trophectoderm is extraembryonic (placenta) and is not the source of the embryo proper's neurons. Mixing up which organs come from which layer is the usual error.

distractorRationales.A: Mesoderm makes muscle and heart, not epidermis and CNS neurons.
distractorRationales.B: Endoderm makes gut-derived viscera such as liver, not the neural tube.
distractorRationales.D: Trophectoderm is extraembryonic; it does not produce spinal neurons or epidermis of the embryo proper.

items.stem: 2,4-Dinitrophenol is added to mitochondria that had been synthesizing ATP from ADP + Pi while oxidizing succinate. Which set of immediate effects is expected?

choices.text: The proton gradient increases, ATP synthesis rises, and oxygen consumption falls.
ATP synthesis rises because protons enter more rapidly through ATP synthase.
Oxygen consumption falls to zero because Complex IV is inhibited by DNP.
The proton-motive force collapses, ATP synthesis falls, and oxygen consumption increases as electron transport is uncoupled from phosphorylation.

items.explanation: 2,4-Dinitrophenol is a protonophore: it shuttles protons across the inner membrane, dissipating ΔpH and Δψ. ATP synthase requires that proton-motive force, so ATP synthesis falls even though ADP and Pi are present. With the back-pressure of the gradient gone, electron transport accelerates and oxygen consumption rises; energy is released as heat rather than captured as ATP. DNP does not inhibit cytochrome oxidase, and it does not route extra protons through F0 in a way that increases ATP. The same pattern is seen with UCP1 in brown adipose tissue, a physiologic uncoupler.

distractorRationales.A: Uncouplers decrease, not increase, the proton gradient. ATP synthesis therefore falls while respiration typically speeds up, opposite this choice.
distractorRationales.B: Protons re-enter through the uncoupler, not productively through ATP synthase, so phosphorylation decreases rather than rises.
distractorRationales.C: DNP does not block Complex IV. Oxygen consumption increases because electron flow is no longer limited by the proton gradient.

passage.title: Fit and Hiring (1979)
passage.body: Marta Górska published “Fit and Hiring” in 1979 after a season in vaccine campaigns. The argument is that institutions remember procedures better than people. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that slowness was never evenly distributed; some people were always rushed. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: psg-cp-7
passage.body:
The physical properties of a substance are set largely by the forces between its molecules. Consider a data set the students assemble. Among the hydrides of Group 16, hydrogen sulfide (H2S) boils at -60 C, yet water (H2O), a lighter molecule, boils at +100 C - a striking exception to the usual trend that heavier molecules boil higher. The students also compare two compounds with the identical formula C2H6O: ethanol, which boils at 78 C, and dimethyl ether, which boils at -24 C. Finally, they tabulate the boiling points of the noble gases and find a steady rise from helium through xenon.
To interpret the data they review molecular structure. Oxygen is far more electronegative than hydrogen, so each O-H bond is polar; in water the two O-H bonds and two lone pairs on oxygen arrange the electron domains tetrahedrally, giving the molecule a bent shape with an H-O-H angle near 104.5 degrees and a net dipole moment. They classify the intermolecular forces available to each substance: London dispersion forces (present in all molecules, stronger in larger and more polarizable electron clouds), dipole-dipole forces (between permanent dipoles), and hydrogen bonding (the especially strong attraction when H bonded to N, O, or F is drawn to a lone pair on another such atom).
Their goal is to connect each measured boiling point to the strongest intermolecular force a molecule can form, and to explain the anomalies - water's high boiling point, ethanol versus its isomer, and the noble-gas trend - in terms of hydrogen bonding, polarity, geometry, and polarizability.

items.stem: Standard reduction potentials: NAD+ / NADH, E°′ = −0.32 V; a typical enzyme-bound FAD / FADH2, E°′ = 0.00 V; ½ O2 / H2O, E°′ = +0.82 V. Using ΔG°′ = −nFΔE°′ with n = 2, which statement follows for oxidation of the two carriers by O2?

choices.text: FADH2 oxidation is more exergonic because its E°′ is closer to that of oxygen
The two oxidations have identical ΔG°′ because both ultimately reduce O2
NADH cannot reduce oxygen because its potential is negative
NADH oxidation has the larger ΔE°′ (1.14 V vs 0.82 V) and therefore the more negative ΔG°′, consistent with NADH electrons entering the chain at a higher-energy (more reducing) level than FADH2

items.explanation: Electrons flow from the more negative to the more positive couple. For NADH to O2, ΔE°′ = 0.82 − (−0.32) = 1.14 V. For FADH2 to O2, ΔE°′ = 0.82 − 0.00 = 0.82 V. Because ΔG°′ = −nFΔE°′, the larger ΔE°′ makes NADH oxidation more exergonic. That extra free energy is why NADH feeds Complex I and supports more proton pumping than FADH2, which enters at Complex II. A negative E°′ for NAD+/NADH means NADH is a strong reductant, not that it is forbidden from reducing oxygen through the chain. Sharing O2 as the terminal acceptor does not equalize ΔE°′.

distractorRationales.A: A smaller gap to oxygen means a smaller ΔE°′ and a less negative ΔG°′. FADH2 is the lower-energy reductant.
distractorRationales.B: The donor potentials differ, so ΔE°′ and ΔG°′ differ even though both paths end at O2.
distractorRationales.C: A negative E°′ identifies a good reductant. NADH reduces the chain, and ultimately oxygen, with a large positive ΔE°′.

items.stem: Using the uninhibited V_max in Table 1 and the active-site titration result, k_cat of the dehydrogenase is closest to
items.explanation: Turnover number is V_max expressed per mole of catalytic sites. Table 1 lists uninhibited V_max as 80 nmol of product per second per milligram of protein. The passage states that active-site titration found 4.0 nmol of catalytic sites per milligram, so k_cat = 80 nmol s^{-1} mg^{-1} divided by 4.0 nmol mg^{-1} = 20 s^{-1}. The milligram units cancel, and the result does not use the inhibitor rows. Treating the V_max number as already a first-order rate constant, multiplying by the site titer, or inverting the ratio all ignore one of the two experimental numbers the passage supplies.

distractorRationales.A: 80 s^{-1} copies the V_max magnitude while dropping the site-titer division; V_max in nmol s^{-1} mg^{-1} is not k_cat until it is normalized per site.
distractorRationales.C: 320 s^{-1} multiplies V_max by the 4.0 nmol mg^{-1} titer instead of dividing, which has the wrong dimensions for a first-order rate constant.
distractorRationales.D: 0.050 s^{-1} is the inverted ratio 4.0/80; that construction does not convert a specific activity into a turnover number.

passage.title: Reversible inhibitors of a cytosolic dehydrogenase
passage.body:
Investigators purified a cytosolic NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase that oxidizes a small-molecule metabolite S. Initial velocities were measured at 25 °C by following NADH formation in 1.00 mL assays. Nonlinear fits of v versus [S] produced the apparent Michaelis constants and maximal velocities in Table 1. When an inhibitor was present, its concentration was 2.0 μM in the assay mix. Dialysis that removed unbound compound restored full catalytic activity after incubation with P, Q, or R, indicating reversible binding rather than covalent inactivation. Active-site titration with a tight-binding stoichiometric inactivator found 4.0 nmol of catalytic sites per milligram of protein.

Table 1. Apparent kinetic parameters from initial-rate fits

| Condition | Apparent K_m (mM) | Apparent V_max (nmol s^{-1} mg^{-1}) |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------------------------|
| No inhibitor | 0.50 | 80 |
| Compound P (2.0 μM) | 0.50 | 40 |
| Compound Q (2.0 μM) | 1.50 | 80 |
| Compound R (2.0 μM) | 0.25 | 40 |

In a separate progress-curve experiment, 25 μg of the same enzyme protein was mixed with 0.50 mM S and no inhibitor in a 1.00 mL reaction. Product concentration was recorded as a function of time (Table 2).

Table 2. Product appearance at [S]_0 = 0.50 mM without inhibitor

| Time (s) | [Product] (μM) |
|----------|----------------|
| 0 | 0.0 |
| 10 | 9.9 |
| 20 | 19.6 |
| 30 | 29.1 |
| 60 | 56.2 |
| 120 | 102.4 |

passage.title: psg-ps-1
passage.body:
Researchers investigated how listeners detect faint tones and how expectations shape perception. In Experiment 1, 40 young adults sat in a soundproof booth and reported whether a brief 1000-Hz tone was present on each of 400 trials. The tone was actually presented on only half of the trials; on the rest, participants heard only background noise. Investigators varied the tone's intensity to estimate each listener's absolute threshold, defined as the intensity detected on 50% of trials. They also recorded four response categories - hits, misses, false alarms, and correct rejections - and computed a sensitivity index (d') separately from each listener's response criterion.
In Experiment 2, the same listeners were told before each block whether tones would be 'rare' or 'common.' When told tones were common, listeners reported hearing a tone more often, producing more hits but also more false alarms, even though the physical stimuli were identical across blocks. Sensitivity (d') did not change between the 'rare' and 'common' blocks; only the criterion shifted.
In Experiment 3, listeners judged whether two successive weights differed. The smallest detectable difference grew in proportion to the starting weight: distinguishing 102 g from 100 g was as hard as distinguishing 204 g from 200 g. Finally, when a steady tone played continuously, listeners' reported loudness declined over several minutes, though an abrupt change in intensity was noticed at once. The authors concluded that detection reflects both sensory capacity and decision processes, and that the sensory system is tuned to change rather than to constant stimulation.

items.stem: What effect makes carboxylic acids much more acidic than alcohols (by stabilizing the conjugate base)? Name it.

choices.text: The carboxyl group (a carboxylic acid), which combines a carbonyl (C=O) and a hydroxyl (O–H) on the same carbon.
Resonance stabilization of the carboxylate anion: the negative charge is delocalized over two equivalent oxygens, making the conjugate base (and therefore the acid) much more stable.

items.stem: The paragraph that begins “The rhetorical trick is hygiene” primarily functions to

passage.title: Who may be loud
passage.body:
Noise ordinances are written as if they were thermometers. A number of decibels is named; a clock hour is named; a fine is attached. The language of public health does real work here: sleep is not a luxury, and a child whose window faces a compressor is not being precious. But the thermometer conceals a second instrument, which is a social sorting device. Cities do not merely suppress loudness. They decide which kinds of loudness will be classified as vitality and which as nuisance, and the decision tracks, with embarrassing regularity, the prestige of the people making the sound.

Walk a mixed street after dark and the taxonomy is audible. A licensed terrace with heaters and a playlist is "activation of the night-time economy." A storefront church whose singing lasts past the same hour is a complaint waiting to be logged. A terrace is a business; a congregation is a disturbance that happens to own a building. Street vendors packing ice and calling prices are "chaos"; a restaurant's Friday overflow onto the pavement is "vibrancy," provided the overflow has paid for a permit. The ear that writes the ordinance has already been trained to hear money as atmosphere and unpaid sound as aggression.

Defenders of the ordinances will say that the issue is volume, not culture. Sometimes it is. A speaker stack aimed at a bedroom is a harm whether the music is sacred or commercial. The author's claim is narrower and more awkward: when two sounds of similar intensity are sorted differently, the sorting is not acoustics. It is a theory of who belongs in the air. "Quiet" is then sold as a natural baseline, like clean water, when it is often an aesthetic associated with certain housing and certain hours of salaried rest. Night-shift workers returning at dawn, whose rest is real, rarely get to define the city's sonic morals. People who sleep when the ordinance writers sleep do.

None of this is a brief for unlimited noise, or for the romance of the unregulated street. A city that cannot protect sleep will punish the poorest first, because they cannot buy distance from compressors. The decent aim is not a louder city but a less hypocritical one: a city that admits that permission to be loud is a scarce good, distributed by licensing, policing, and taste, and that "quality of life" is never only a medical phrase. It is also a claim about whose life is the measure.

The rhetorical trick is hygiene. Once noise is framed as dirt, opposition to a particular sound can wear the costume of sanitation rather than of preference. Dirt, unlike preference, does not have to justify itself at a public meeting. It only has to be pointed at. That is why a campaign against a night market can speak the idiom of rats and refuse even when the photographs show swept stones, and why a campaign for a waterfront festival can speak the idiom of civic joy even when the sound spill is identical. The same wave-form, two moral uniforms.

If the argument holds, then reform is not a new app for logging complaints. It is a requirement that like sounds be given like reasons, and that exemptions be named as political choices rather than as nature. A hospital generator may deserve its exemption. So, perhaps, does a funeral that spills into a street. What cannot be defended is the pretense that the ordinance is only a meter reading. Meters do not know the difference between a hymn and a brand. Officials do, and they should have to say so.

passage.title: psg-cp-6
passage.body:
Water's ability to dissolve ions and to resist changes in acidity underlies much of physiology. Blood plasma is held near pH 7.4 largely by the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer: dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which dissociates into a hydrogen ion and bicarbonate, H2CO3 H+ + HCO3-. The effective pKa for this equilibrium in plasma is about 6.1. Normally the concentration of bicarbonate is roughly twenty times that of dissolved carbonic acid, and the lungs and kidneys adjust the two components to hold that ratio steady. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation links the pH to the ratio of conjugate base to weak acid.
To study buffering directly, students titrate a weak acid at 25 C. They place 0.10 M acetic acid (pKa 4.74) in a flask and add sodium hydroxide from a burette while a pH meter records the curve. Early on the pH rises slowly through a buffering plateau; near the end it climbs steeply through the equivalence point, where exactly enough base has been added to neutralize all the acid. A separate reference solution at 25 C is measured to have a pH of 3.0.
The students note that at 25 C the ion product of water fixes pH + pOH = 14, and that a solution's acidity reflects the balance between hydrogen and hydroxide ions produced when water and solutes interact. They also test the buffer's resilience by adding a few drops of strong acid to the bicarbonate system and to plain water, comparing how far the pH of each moves.

Fick’s law is written V̇gas = (A / T) × D × ΔP. Three lung conditions are compared at the same ΔP and D:
Healthy: A = 70 m², T = 0.5 µm, relative rate = 100.
Emphysema: A = 35 m², T = 0.5 µm.

What are the relative diffusion rates for emphysema and fibrosis?

choices.text: Both remain 100, because ΔP is unchanged
Emphysema 200; fibrosis 50, because thinning always accompanies emphysema
Emphysema 50; fibrosis 200, because thicker barriers conduct faster

items.explanation: Rate scales with A/T. Healthy A/T = 70 / 0.5 = 140 (in m² µm−1). Emphysema halves area at the same thickness, so A/T = 70, half the healthy value (relative 50). Fibrosis doubles thickness at the same area, A/T = 70, again half (relative 50). The stem holds T fixed in emphysema and A fixed in fibrosis, so one should not invent extra thinning or argue that thicker tissue conducts faster. Unchanged ΔP does not cancel a change in A/T.

distractorRationales.A: Fick’s law still contains A/T; holding ΔP constant isolates that geometric factor, which did change.
distractorRationales.C: The emphysema row keeps T = 0.5 µm; doubling rate would require doubling A/T, which does not occur.
distractorRationales.D: T is in the denominator, so doubling thickness halves, rather than doubles, rate.

collapse of every mitochondrion in the sheet
increased paracellular flux of solutes between lumen and basolateral space

items.explanation: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) seal the paracellular route and help maintain apical-basolateral polarity of the barrier. When they open, solutes and water can leak between cells rather than being forced through transcellular transporters. Microvilli, mitochondria, and cholesterol content are not the junction's direct structural products, so they are not the immediate readout of a tight-junction toxin.

distractorRationales.A: Microvilli are actin-supported apical specializations. Tight-junction loss does not transdifferentiate them into axonemal cilia.
distractorRationales.B: Mitochondria are intracellular organelles; a junctional toxin does not globally collapse them as its primary action.
distractorRationales.C: Cholesterol is a bilayer lipid. Junction disruption is a protein-complex event, not a bulk delipidation.

items.stem: A reversible inhibitor is added to a Michaelis–Menten enzyme. Double-reciprocal plots with and without inhibitor intersect on the ordinate; the apparent Km increases while Vmax is unchanged. Which mechanistic description fits these data?

choices.text: Uncompetitive inhibition in which inhibitor binds only the ES complex
Pure noncompetitive inhibition in which inhibitor binds E and ES with equal affinity
Irreversible active-site titration that permanently lowers the concentration of functional enzyme
Competitive inhibition in which inhibitor and substrate compete for free enzyme

items.explanation: Competitive inhibitors bind free enzyme in a manner that overlaps substrate binding, so they can be overcome by high [S]: Vmax is unchanged and apparent Km rises. On a Lineweaver–Burk plot that pattern is a shared y-intercept (1/Vmax) and a larger x-intercept magnitude. Uncompetitive inhibition lowers both Km and Vmax and gives parallel lines. Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax without changing Km (shared x-intercept). Irreversible inactivation lowers Vmax because active enzyme concentration falls and is not reversed by substrate in the same way. The ordinate intersection with higher Km is the competitive signature.

distractorRationales.A: Uncompetitive lines are parallel; both apparent Km and Vmax decrease, unlike these plots.
distractorRationales.B: Noncompetitive inhibition decreases Vmax; the y-intercept would increase, not stay fixed.
distractorRationales.C: Irreversible loss of enzyme molecules reduces Vmax; substrate cannot restore the original maximum velocity.

passage.title: Table: Verbs in the morning
passage.body:
A media researcher counts finite verbs in the first paragraphs of four papers on the same Monday, all covering the same ministry announcement.

Paper | “said” | “claimed” | “admitted” | “revealed” | “insisted” | Other verbs of speaking
North Evening | 12 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 2
Civic Daily | 3 | 8 | 1 | 0 | 4 | 1
Harbour Post | 7 | 1 | 6 | 0 | 0 | 3
The Signal | 2 | 2 | 0 | 9 | 1 | 2

Caption under the table, written by the researcher: “Speaking is never only speaking. The ministry released one statement. The city woke in four grammars.”

A talkback host that night: “This is just synonyms. Nobody is doing politics with a verb chart. Grow up.”

items.stem: A blastomere from the prospective neural plate of an early gastrula is transplanted into ventral epidermis of a same-stage host and differentiates as epidermis. The equivalent cell taken from a late neurula and transplanted ventrally still forms neural tissue. These results show that:

choices.text: Determination has occurred by the later stage, so fate is no longer redirected by the new environment
Totipotency increases as development proceeds, which is why the older transplant ignores host cues
Induction never occurs, because the early transplant could change fate
The late transplant undergoes apoptosis and the host then makes a ghost neural tube

items.explanation: Specification and determination are operationally defined by transplantation. An undetermined cell is competent to follow inductive cues in a new location (here, ventral epidermis). Once determined, the cell's developmental commitment is stable and it differentiates according to its original identity (neural) even in a foreign environment. That is a restriction of potency over time, not an increase in totipotency. The early result actually demonstrates that induction/environment can still assign fate. The assay scores differentiated neural tissue from the graft, not host apoptosis artifacts.

distractorRationales.B: Potency generally decreases; totipotency does not rise after gastrulation.
distractorRationales.C: The early cell's change of fate is evidence that inductive environment still acts.
distractorRationales.D: The experiment's point is autonomous neural differentiation of the late graft, not cell death.

items.stem: A peptide (amide) C–N bond does not rotate freely at room temperature, so the six atoms of the amide unit lie in a plane. Which hybridization statement best explains that restricted rotation?

choices.text: The carbonyl carbon is sp3 and the nitrogen is sp3, producing a purely sigma C–N bond that happens to be short.
Only hydrogen bonding between N–H and C=O, not orbital hybridization, can prevent C–N rotation.
The carbonyl carbon is sp and the nitrogen is unhybridized, producing a linear C–N–H array.
Resonance donation from nitrogen into the carbonyl makes both the carbonyl carbon and the amide nitrogen sp2, giving the C–N linkage partial double-bond character.

items.explanation: The amide resonance contributor that places a lone pair from nitrogen into the C=O π* orbital gives a C=N double-bond picture with charge-separated O− and N+. Both the carbonyl carbon and the nitrogen therefore have three electron domains and are treated as sp2, and the C–N bond order is between 1 and 2. Partial double-bond character creates a substantial rotational barrier, which is why the peptide unit is planar. Hydrogen bonding can stabilize secondary structure, but it is not required to explain the amide rotational barrier in a simple peptide bond.

distractorRationales.A: An sp3–sp3 single bond would rotate freely and would not force planarity of the six amide atoms.
distractorRationales.B: Hydrogen bonding is important in proteins but is not the origin of the amide C–N rotational barrier; isolated amides are still planar.
distractorRationales.C: An sp carbonyl carbon would be linear (as in ketene or CO2), which does not match the trigonal planar amide carbon.

items.stem: Observers read a briefly flashed, degraded clinic note in which several letters are ink-smudged. They still report the intended words when the sentence is medically plausible, but they misread the same marks in a scrambled letter string. Richard Gregory’s constructivist account treats this as which kind of processing?

choices.text: Pure bottom-up feature detection, because Hubel and Wiesel cells finish the job before knowledge acts
Top-down processing, in which stored knowledge and context generate perceptual hypotheses that disambiguate incomplete sensory data
Gibsonian direct pickup of optic-array invariants, which needs no hypothesis testing
Weber scaling of ink density, which uniquely determines each letter

items.explanation: Gregory argued that perception is hypothesis-testing: incomplete retinal data are interpreted using memory and context (top-down, constructivist). Sentence meaning helping smudged letters is that influence. Strict bottom-up feature detection would not improve once the same marks sit in a meaningful sentence. Gibson’s ecological theory emphasizes direct invariants and downplays such inference. Weber’s law scales intensity differences; it does not read words.

distractorRationales.A: Context changing the percept of identical marks is the signature that bottom-up feature maps are not sufficient.
distractorRationales.C: Gibsonian direct perception denies the need for knowledge-driven hypotheses that the stem demonstrates.
distractorRationales.D: Weber fractions do not explain lexical restoration of smudged letters.

items.stem: A 2 kg point mass sits at x = 0 and a 6 kg point mass sits at x = 4 m, both on the x-axis and otherwise isolated. The x-coordinate of the system's center of mass is:
items.explanation: The center of mass of two point masses is the mass-weighted average x_cm = (m1 x1 + m2 x2) / (m1 + m2). Substituting gives (2 kg)(0) + (6 kg)(4 m) all over 8 kg, which is 24/8 = 3 m. The center of mass therefore lies closer to the heavier 6 kg mass than to the 2 kg mass, as expected, but it is not at the 6 kg mass itself. Equal-mass averaging would put it at the geometric midpoint 2 m, which does not apply here.

distractorRationales.A: This inverts the mass weighting or uses (2/8)*4 m. The heavier mass should pull x_cm toward 4 m, not toward 0.
distractorRationales.B: This is the geometric midpoint, correct only if the two masses were equal. The 6 kg mass outweighs the 2 kg mass three to one.
distractorRationales.D: The center of mass coincides with a mass only if the other mass is zero or is located at the same point. The 2 kg mass still shifts x_cm left of 4 m.

passage.title: Official Adjectives (1977)
passage.body: Elena Rossi's 1977 essay “Official Adjectives,” on a coastal fishery, opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. The piece admits that some gatekeeping keeps fraud out. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not.

passage.title: psg-cars-15
passage.body:
The concept of the unreliable narrator invites readers to question the testimony of a fictional voice that presents itself as authoritative. An unreliable narrator is one whose account of events, characters, or motives the reader has grounds to distrust -- not necessarily because the narrator lies deliberately, but because their perception is limited, their self-understanding deficient, or their emotional investment in a particular version of events distorts what they report. The detection of narrative unreliability is, accordingly, one of the more sophisticated interpretive skills literary fiction demands of its readers, requiring attention to gaps, contradictions, and moments when the narrator's self-presentation strains against the evidence the text itself provides. The concept therefore depends on a tacit collaboration between author and reader carried on over the narrator's head. Behind the speaking voice stands an implied author who arranges the evidence so that a discerning reader can measure the narrator's claims against it, catching what the narrator misses or conceals. This is why unreliability is a matter of degree and of inference rather than a property simply switched on or off: the same first-person account may strike a careless reader as candid and a careful one as riddled with evasions. Recognizing it depends less on any single tell-tale sentence than on the accumulating weight of discrepancies between what is said and what, on reflection, the text as a whole gives the reader reason to believe.
Narrative theorists have identified several sources of unreliability. The most philosophically interesting is self-deception: the narrator who sincerely believes their own account while systematically misrepresenting it, particularly with respect to their own motives and moral quality. Such narrators often generate irony at their own expense -- the gap between what they report and what the text implies about them becomes the site of the reader's critical engagement. A narrator who insists on their generosity in every paragraph while every described action suggests self-interest produces a portrait more damning than any external indictment could achieve.
A second source is cognitive limitation: the narrator who simply lacks the knowledge or experience to interpret correctly what they observe. A child narrator reporting on adult conflicts without understanding their significance, or an outsider narrator describing an unfamiliar culture through inappropriate categories, produces unreliability through innocence rather than self-interest. In such cases, the reader must supply interpretive frameworks that the narrator cannot, and the gap between the narrator's report and the reader's inference becomes the text's most productive space.
A third source, less often discussed, is structural: some narratives are built on multiple competing narrators whose accounts cannot all be true, or on a narrator who explicitly announces their own limitations and invites the reader to read against them. In the former case, unreliability is dispersed across the text; in the latter, it is ironized through self-consciousness. Both strategies challenge the assumption that narrative access to events is, even in fiction, transparent and unmediated.
The broader significance of narrative unreliability extends beyond literary technique. It models a stance of critical reading that has application outside the text: the recognition that all reported experience is shaped by the particular perspective, interests, and cognitive limitations of the reporter -- a recognition that is as relevant to journalism, autobiography, and legal testimony as it is to fiction. Learning to read unreliable narrators teaches a transferable epistemic skill: suspending credulity and attending to the conditions under which any account is produced.

passage.title: psg-cars-8
passage.body:
Ritual occupies a paradoxical place in modern social thought. On one hand, it has been systematically studied as a fundamental mechanism of social solidarity: shared symbolic performances bind participants together, express and reinforce collective values, and mark the transitions — birth, initiation, marriage, death — that punctuate the human life course. On the other hand, modern societies tend to regard ritual with a degree of unease, as if elaborate ceremony were a relic of pre-rational ages unsuited to a world governed by science and voluntary choice.
Early sociological and anthropological accounts emphasized the integrative functions of ritual. Ceremonies, on this view, do not merely reflect an already-existing social order; they actively produce and sustain it. When a community gathers to mark a harvest, a coronation, or a national founding, participants do not simply observe an event — they enact membership in a collectivity that transcends any individual. The shared emotional experience generated by such occasions — what early theorists called collective effervescence — temporarily dissolves the boundaries between self and group, creating a felt sense of unity that persists in social memory long after the ceremony has concluded.
Later anthropologists complicated this functionalist picture by attending to the internal diversity and contestation that characterize real rituals. Ceremonies are rarely performed identically across time or across the different status groups within a community. The ruling class and the subjugated, men and women, elders and youth — each may experience the same ceremony quite differently, and the ritual may serve to reinforce not solidarity across the board but specific hierarchies of power. From this perspective, treating ritual purely as a mechanism of integration ignores its role in legitimating and reproducing asymmetric social arrangements.
A third approach draws attention to ritual's cognitive and communicative dimensions. Rituals encode information in a form — embodied action, sensory symbol, repeated performance — that is particularly durable and memorable. Unlike propositional statements that can be contested or forgotten, knowledge embedded in ritual is resistant to revision precisely because it is experienced rather than merely asserted. This explains why ritual tends to be invoked when other communicative resources fail: in the face of death, catastrophic loss, or radical uncertainty, shared performance provides a structure of meaning that discursive language alone cannot furnish. Grief rituals in particular demonstrate how embodied collective action can sustain communities through episodes of radical disruption that would otherwise threaten social fabric. The contrast with ordinary instruction is telling. A fact conveyed in a lecture can be doubted the moment the lecture ends; a truth rehearsed year after year in fasting, procession, or song is renewed in the body and rarely submitted to cross-examination at all. This is why communities so often entrust their most load-bearing commitments — who belongs, what is owed to the dead, which obligations the future imposes — not to argument but to observance. The very features that make ritual knowledge conservative, and sometimes an obstacle to reform, are also what allow it to hold a group together when argument alone would divide it, carrying shared meaning across generations that never meet.
Each of these accounts captures something genuine. Ritual is simultaneously a mechanism of solidarity, an arena of power and contestation, and a form of embodied knowledge. Understanding any particular ceremony requires attending to all three dimensions and to the historical context that shapes their relative salience.

Standard enthalpies of formation (kJ mol−1): CH4(g) −75; CO2(g) −394; H2O(l) −286; O2(g) 0. For CH4 + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O(l), ΔH = Σ ΔHf(products) − Σ ΔHf(reactants).

choices.text: −966 kJ mol−1 (forgetting to subtract ΔHf of CH4)
−75 kJ mol−1, the formation enthalpy of methane

items.explanation: Products: −394 + 2(−286) = −394 − 572 = −966 kJ. Reactants: −75 + 2(0) = −75 kJ. ΔH = −966 − (−75) = −891 kJ mol−1. Methane combustion is strongly exothermic, matching the negative sign. Dropping the methane term leaves −966, which is only the product sum. The formation enthalpy −75 kJ is the methane building reaction from C and H2, not this combustion.

distractorRationales.B: Σ ΔHf(products) is −966 kJ; Hess’s law still subtracts ΔHf of CH4 (−75).
